Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the bamboo-slat case the assembly's responses all fail to accord, after which a monk asks for instruction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然「音律不差」，而「下語用字，全不可讀」，也沒有文學價值
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Allowlisted modern scholarly body prose contrasts acceptable musical regulation with unreadable wording and characters. It is retained as a provenance/control outlier, not promoted to a separate Chan sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: not blind to cause and effect
AlternateTargets: not ignorant of cause and effect
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'not blind to cause and effect' or 'not obscuring cause and effect.' The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong's commentary explicitly contrasts the two phrases: 'not falling into cause and effect is rejecting it through the view of annihilation; not being blind to cause and effect is obtaining the marvelous while following the flow' (不落因果是撥無斷見。不昧因果。是隨流得妙). The same commentary records an objection: 'as for not being blind to cause and effect, he still has not shed the fox body' (只如不昧因果。也未脫得野狐身). Dahui repeatedly answers questions about why the former Baizhang fell into a fox body after saying 'not falling' and why the latter Baizhang's 'not being blind' led to shedding it only by saying, 'just raise it this way to people' (逢人但恁麼舉). Later records continue asking whether 'not falling' and 'not being blind' are the same or different.
Senses.Note: The primary sense is the shared phrase in the historical Baizhang public case, not a Baizhang-specific meaning. The fox-body sequence is translated because the record literally states it; no broader account is inferred from it. Wansong's contrast is reported as Wansong's explicit wording, while the two monks' objection and later same-or-different questions show that the record does not reduce the pair to one uncontested gloss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老人曰。大修行人還落因果也無。師曰。不昧因果。老人於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, explicit Baizhang Huaihai section. The old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect; Baizhang answers 'not blind to cause and effect.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不落因果是撥無斷見。不昧因果。是隨流得妙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong's commentary on case eight, 'Baizhang's fox.' This is the corpus's clearest explicit contrast between the two phrases and is attributed to the commentator, not to Baizhang's original exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一僧曰。只如不昧因果。也未脫得野狐身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Within Wansong's commentary, an unnamed monk says that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect,' the fox body has still not been shed. The quoted speaker is unnamed, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 前百丈云。不落因果。為甚麼墮野狐身。師云。逢人但恁麼舉。進云。只如後百丈道不昧因果。為甚麼脫野狐身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own assembly record. A monk contrasts the former Baizhang's 'not falling' and the later Baizhang's 'not being blind'; Dahui responds to the first question, 'just raise it this way to people.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問不落因果為甚麼墮野狐身。師曰。廬山五老峯。曰不昧因果為甚麼脫野狐身。師曰。南嶽三生藏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp. A question contrasts falling into and shedding the fox body; the local master answers with Mount Lu's Five Elders Peak and Nanyue's Three-Life Treasury. The rough lineage head does not safely expose the local master's roster identity, so MasterName is null.

AlternateTargets: not lodged in the written word
Senses.Explanation: (不立) = not setting up / not establishing; (文字) = written graphs, letters. It travels as one member of the four-phrase formula of the school — "a separate transmission outside the teachings; not setting up words; pointing directly at the human mind; seeing nature, becoming Buddha" (教外別傳，不立文字，直指人心，見性成佛) — and is bound in the record to Bodhidharma's coming from the West: (達磨西來不立文字) verbatim 16 times in 14 allowlist files, and (不立文字) within ten characters of (直指人心) in 140 places across 87 files. The corpus states what the phrase covers in its own words. (懶菴), quoted in (禪林寶訓): "that the great master Bodhidharma sailed here and did not set up letters made plain the purport of the markless; it is not that Bodhidharma produced a new idea of his own and set up a separate gate" (達磨大師航海而來不立文字者。蓋明無相之旨。非達磨自出新意別立門戶). On the two graphs themselves, the Platform Sutra records Huineng: "those who cling to emptiness slander the scriptures, saying flatly 'use no letters'; but having said 'use no letters,' one ought not speak either — this very speech is the mark of letters" (執空之人有謗經，直言不用文字。既云不用文字，人亦不合語言。只此語言，便是文字之相), then (又云)：『(直道不立文字)。』"even the two graphs (不立) are themselves letters" (即此不立兩字，亦是文字; parallel wording in the Dunhuang-lineage 壇經, T/T48/T48n2007.xml); and (覺浪道盛) asks "is being unversed in letters to be taken as not setting up letters?" (將以不通文字，為不立文字乎哉). Attested deployment: recited as the four-phrase set; spoken under the Bodhidharma ascription in (上堂)/(小參) discourse; and posed as a question — a novice asks (如何是不立文字的佛法) ('what is the Buddha's teaching of not setting up letters?'), and Fazhou Daoji (法舟道濟) calls the novice, who responds, then says "what letters are involved?" (涉甚麼文字 — 天寧法舟濟禪師剩語, J/J40/J40nB491.xml). Attested expansions: (不立文字語句) ('not setting up words or phrases'; 30 hits / 14 files), (不立文字語言) ('not setting up words or speech'; 12 hits / 11 files).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The phrase is pan-Chan; individual masters invoke it rather than own it, so occurrences are attributed to the master using it in his own discourse. Very well attested: 435 raw hits across 188 allowlist files (tag-stripped grep, 2026-07-11). Collocation counts: (不立文字) followed within ten characters by (教外別傳) in 53 places / 47 files, the reverse order in 39 / 32.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又云：『直道不立文字。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (六祖大師法寶壇經), head (付囑第十) — Huineng's parting instruction. The continuation (即此不立兩字)，(亦是文字) ('even the two graphs "not-set-up" are themselves letters') falls on the next source line, so the Kwic is trimmed to this single source line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來不立文字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), head (小參五). The slogan bound to Bodhidharma; continues (直指人心見性成佛) ('directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha') on the next line (the four-phrase formula), so Kwic trimmed to one line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不立文字，教外別傳，直指人心，見性成佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), head (觀音殿燈節夜茶筵垂示) — Juelang Daosheng's (垂示) ('instruction shown to the assembly'). The full four-phrase formula in one verbatim line; Juelang (覺浪道盛) is in master-dates.json.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蓋達磨不立文字直指人心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天目中峰廣錄), head (山房夜話上) — Zhongfeng Mingben's own night-talk essay. Independent (Yuan-dynasty) witness pairing (不立文字) with (直指人心) under Bodhidharma.

Senses.PreferredTarget: not be a companion to the myriad things
AlternateTargets: the one who is not a companion to the myriad things
Senses.Explanation: Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers, including 'Guanyin,' 'Where have all the many people in Hongzhou gone?' and 'passing through a hundred flowers without one leaf sticking to the body.' Yuanwu's instruction explicitly says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' A preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever he raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 446 matches in 153 files. The person-question form has 139 matches in 73 files, while the longer nominal form ending in 'the one who' has 269 matches in 117. Three passages in three files directly ask, 'What is not being a companion to the myriad things?' One text explicitly calls it the public case of not being companion to the myriad things, and one instruction uses the naming formula 'the ancients called him the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' The distribution supports one corpus-wide fixed expression rather than a meaning restricted to Layman Pang, Shitou, or Mazu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 唐貞元初謁石頭。乃問。不與萬法為侶者是甚麼人。頭以手掩其口。豁然有省。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps records Layman Pang visiting Shitou and asking, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' Shitou covers Pang's mouth, and Pang suddenly understands.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後參馬祖。問曰。不與萬法為侶者是甚麼人。祖曰。待汝一口吸盡西江水。即向汝道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same record says that Pang later visits Mazu and asks, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' Mazu answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問不與萬法為侶者是什麼人。師曰。觀世音菩薩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Huai Cheng, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The teacher answers, 'Guanyin.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：不與萬法為侶者是甚麼人？師曰：汝道洪州城裏如許多人甚麼處去？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Caoshan, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' Caoshan answers, 'Tell me: where have all the many people in the city of Hongzhou gone?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 每舉到不與萬法為侶公案。已是拕泥帶水。落第二義。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A preface to Yuanwu's record says, 'Whenever he raised the public case of not being a companion to the myriad things, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人謂之不與萬法為侶底人，亦號如來正徧知覺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's instruction says, 'The ancients called him the person who is not a companion to the myriad things, and also titled him the Thus-Come One of correct and universal knowing.'

Senses.PreferredTarget: does not fall into cause and effect
AlternateTargets: not falling into cause and effect
does not enter cause and effect
Senses.Explanation: The phrase literally says “does not fall into cause and effect.” Its central corpus setting is Baizhang's real wild-fox public case. An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes a monk's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The entry preserves the case's people, answers, stated five-hundred-life consequence, correction, and later comments without replacing those recorded details with an added theory of cause and effect. The paired abbreviated form “not falling, not obscuring” (不落不昧) occurs 86 times in 45 files; “not falling versus not obscuring” (不落與不昧) occurs 12 times in eight files. No “not dropping into cause and effect” (不墮因果) variant was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 於過去迦葉佛時。曾住此山。因學人問。大修行底人還落因果。也無。某甲對云。不落因果。五百生墮野狐身。今請和尚。代一轉語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's case text records the old man's confession: in Kāśyapa Buddha's time he lived on the mountain; when a student asked whether a person of great conduct still falls into cause and effect, he answered “does not fall into cause and effect,” and for five hundred lives fell into a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang for a substitute turning phrase. As a raised public case with multiple speakers, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無門曰。不落因果。為甚墮野狐。不昧因果。為甚脫野狐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's own comment asks: “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 有學人問。大修行底人還落因果也無對他道不落因果墮野狐身五百生今請和尚代一轉語丈云。不昧因果老人於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong's case text repeats the exchange: a student asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect; the old teacher answers “does not fall into cause and effect,” the record says he falls into a wild-fox body for five hundred lives, Baizhang answers “does not obscure cause and effect,” and the old man awakens at the words. The occurrence is narrated case text.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又一日，以百丈野狐話詰之曰：且道不落因果便墮野狐身，不昧因果便脫野狐身，利害在什麼處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A tower inscription narrates a teacher testing a student with Baizhang's wild-fox case: “Say: with ‘does not fall into cause and effect’ he fell into a wild-fox body; with ‘does not obscure cause and effect’ he left the wild-fox body. Where is the critical difference?” The teacher then shouts before the student answers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是解修行底人。師曰。汝是什麼人。曰恁麼即不落因果也。師曰。莫作野干鳴。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a broad-record dialogue, a monk asks about a person who understands conduct. The teacher asks what person he is. The monk says, “then he does not fall into cause and effect”; the teacher replies, “do not make a wild-jackal cry.” The nearest heading does not identify the master securely.

Senses.Explanation: A formulaic imperative: “now say!” or “tell me then.” The first graph supplies “for now/just” and the second demands speech. In a live exchange Puhua turns Linji's question back on him—“you tell me: am I ordinary or holy?”—but the formula is especially dense in teaching-seat addresses and case commentary, where it pivots from narration or quotation to a public demand on the listeners. Its continuation shows what response is being demanded. It asks for identification (“whose conduct is this?”), cause (“why is building temples and ordaining monks wholly without merit?”), comparison (“is this the same as or different from what Bodhidharma said?”), existence (“are host and guest still present?”), fault (“where is the error?”), outcome (“ultimately, how?”), a proposed reply (“how would you respond?”), resemblance (“does this portrait resemble me?”), or a forced alternative (“use the hook, or use the awl?”). In a ceremonial address it asks how to voice “Baoxun's phrase,” and the speaker supplies a line blessing the emperor. A pause, action, capping line, or further challenge may follow; the marker itself does not promise a verbal answer. Zen bends this ordinary command into a recurrent public-interview gate: commentary does not merely explain a case but turns and asks the assembly to answer now.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 18,624 occurrences in 400 texts. Frequent continuation families include “how?” (如何), “what is it?” (是甚麼 / 是什麼), “how?” (作麼生), “is there still…?” (還有), “ultimately” (畢竟), “with the ancient…” (與古), “where is the fault?” (過在), and “is it the same or different?” (是同是別). Item-8 review found one imperative across direct dialogue, hall address, ceremonial capping, and commentary; these are deployment positions, not different things. Eleven witnesses cover the principal continuation grammars and both direct-interlocutor and commentator voices. Speaker fields remain null where the formula belongs to compiled commentary or a multi-speaker line rather than an independently verified roster utterance.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “the one honored by the world,” this title names Śākyamuni as a figure invoked throughout the Chan record. The entry defines that figure through the record's public cases rather than an outside sacred biography. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, “the World-Honored One held up a flower; Kāśyapa smiled” (世尊拈花，迦葉微笑), and the account continues with entrusting “the treasury of the true teaching eye” to Mahākāśyapa. In the teaching-seat case, he mounts the seat; Mañjuśrī strikes the sounding block and says, “carefully observe the teaching king's teaching; the teaching king's teaching is thus” (諦觀法王法，法王法如是), whereupon the World-Honored One leaves the seat. Asked by an outsider not about words and not about no words, he remains silent for a while. The corpus also raises his birth gesture and declaration; Yunmen follows that recital with his own attributed statement that he would have struck him dead and fed him to a dog, “valuing peace throughout the world” (貴圖天下太平). Other cases have the World-Honored One direct Mañjuśrī and name Wangming Bodhisattva in the woman-in-composure exchange, point to the ground for a temple before Indra plants a blade of grass, and display a color-changing jewel while questioning the five heavenly kings. Later masters restage and compare these acts: Zhenjing Kewen raises his staff after reciting the flower case, and Zhanran Yuancheng compares the World-Honored One's mounting and silence with the same acts by the people before him. The Chan deviation is concrete and public: the title chiefly names the invoked figure who holds up the flower, mounts and leaves the teaching seat, pauses in an interview, and acts within repeatedly raised cases. Each later appraisal remains attributed to its speaker; none is made the World-Honored One's intention.
Senses.Note: The 8,093 exact matches occur in 406 allowlisted files. This is one title/person sense across the flower, teaching-seat, silence, birth, woman-in-composure, grass-temple, and jewel cases; different episodes do not create different referents. “Śākyamuni” (釋迦) is the name-form, and “old man Śākyamuni” (釋迦老子) is a separate familiar Chan form. Compare buddha (佛), Kāśyapa (迦葉), Ānanda (阿難), holding up the flower (拈花), mounting the seat (陞座), leaving the seat (下座), and remaining silent for a while (良久).

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔日靈山會上世尊拈花，迦葉微笑，世尊道：吾有正法眼藏分付摩訶大迦葉流傳，母令斷絕，至于今日。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Essentials of the Old Worthies; a raised historical account: at the assembly on Vulture Peak the World-Honored One holds up a flower, Kāśyapa smiles, and the World-Honored One says that he entrusts the treasury of the true teaching eye to Mahākāśyapa for transmission.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊陞座，文殊拍椎云：『諦觀法王法，法王法如是。』世尊便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Chan Master Minshu; the complete raised case: the World-Honored One mounts the seat, Mañjuśrī strikes the block and announces, “Carefully observe the teaching king’s teaching; the teaching king’s teaching is thus,” and the World-Honored One immediately leaves the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊因外道問：不問有言，不問無言。世尊良久，外道歎曰：世尊大慈大悲，開我迷雲，令我得入。遂作禮而去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Ancient Cases of the Chan School; the outsider asks neither about speech nor no speech, the World-Honored One remains silent for a while, and the outsider praises him and departs.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：世尊拈花，迦葉微笑。乃拈起拄杖曰：洞山拈起拄杖子，你諸人合作麼生？遂擊香卓。

Occurrences.Kwic: 且如世尊陞座，你諸人也陞座；世尊默然，你諸人也默然。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng; he says, “The World-Honored One mounted the seat; you people also mount the seat. The World-Honored One was silent; you people also are silent.” This anchors later direct redeployment of the two public acts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊初生時，一手指天，一手指地，周行七步，目顧四方，云：『天上天下，惟我獨尊。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Chan record raises the birth case: the World-Honored One points one hand to heaven and one to earth, walks seven steps, looks to the four directions, and says, “above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored” (天上天下，惟我獨尊).

Occurrences.Kwic: 不見世尊生下周行七步目顧四方。一手指天一手指地云。天上天下唯吾獨尊。雲門云。我當初若見一棒打殺與狗子喫却。何以如此。貴圖天下太平。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After reciting the World-Honored One's birth gesture and declaration, the record attributes to Yunmen: “if I had seen him at the time, I would have struck him dead with one blow and fed him to a dog,” followed by “valuing peace throughout the world” (貴圖天下太平). This preserves Yunmen's stated appraisal without assigning it to the World-Honored One.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊命文殊出，文殊卻出女子定不得。世尊曰：『下方有罔明菩薩出得。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the woman-in-composure case, the World-Honored One commands Mañjuśrī to bring her out of composure. When Mañjuśrī cannot, he says, “below there is Wangming Bodhisattva, who can bring her out” (下方有罔明菩薩出得).

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊與眾行次，以手指地上云：『此處宜建梵剎。』天帝釋持一莖草插於地上云：『建梵剎已竟。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Walking with the assembly, the World-Honored One points to the ground and says, “a temple should be built here” (此處宜建梵剎). Indra plants a blade of grass and says, “the temple has already been built” (建梵剎已竟).

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日示隨色摩尼珠。問五方天王。此珠而作何色。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The World-Honored One displays a color-changing jewel to the five heavenly kings and asks, “what color does this jewel make?” (此珠而作何色). This anchors another display-and-question case.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘the boy of the bing and ding fire stems.’ The phrase occurs 128 times in 70 allowlisted texts. Its central case begins when a monk asks Qingfeng, ‘what is the student's own self?’ and receives ‘the fire-stem boy comes seeking fire.’ The monk explains that bing and ding belong to fire, so this is fire seeking fire, or oneself seeking oneself; Fayan rejects that explanation, has him ask the same question again, repeats the same words forcefully, and the record says the monk awakened. Later records preserve the phrase as the name of this public case, raise it at the opening of the furnace, and address the ‘fire-stem boy’ while throwing down a funeral torch. Thus the corpus keeps the fire wordplay visible while also making the phrase a repeatable case and fire-ceremony address; it does not authorize the rejected explanation as the entry's definition.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is a calendrical fire figure turned into the exact answer and title of the Qingfeng–Fayan case, then re-used in furnace and torch settings. These deployments retain the same fire figure rather than establishing different referents. The alternate target keeps the stem names searchable, while the preferred target translates their function.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk explains that bing and ding belong to fire; Fayan rejects his explanation.

AlternateTargets: Danxia's burning of the wooden buddha
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘Danxia burns a buddha’; in the narrated case the referent is explicitly a wooden buddha-image. The compact headword occurs 14 times in eight allowlisted texts. The repeated account says that, finding it cold at Huilin monastery, Danxia Tianran took a wooden buddha and burned it for a fire. When the temple officer rebuked him for burning ‘my wooden buddha,’ Danxia stirred the ashes with his staff and said he was looking for relics. The officer answered that a wooden buddha has no relics; Danxia then requested two more images to burn. The record adds that afterward the officer's eyebrows and beard fell out. Later masters preserve this as a numbered public case, ask whether Danxia's own eyebrows remain, warn against denying cause and effect, and group it in one roster with Manjusri holding the sword, Guizong cutting the snake, and Muzhou shutting the door. One later verse explicitly calls the deed ‘not light,’ mentions the officer's facial hair, and says that what one does one receives. These are the corpus's narrated actions and comments; this entry does not acquit or condemn Danxia.
Senses.Note: The graph for ‘buddha’ (佛) here refers to a physical wooden image, not the awakened person/teaching-seat figure covered by the standalone ‘buddha’ (佛) entry. This is therefore a required family cross-check, but not a second sense of the fixed case title: every occurrence names the same burning case. The guide identifies this among possible precept-violation cases; the harvested passages supply rebuke, ‘the deed is not light,’ and cause-and-effect warnings, but none explicitly names a particular precept. The entry therefore reports those attestations without asserting an unattested precept charge.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十五則丹霞燒佛第二十五則丹霞燒佛示眾云：熱則趂凉，非為分外；寒時向火，亦是尋常。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Empty Valley Collection labels this ‘case twenty-five: Danxia burns the buddha’ and opens its instruction: ‘when hot seek cool; when cold face the fire—also ordinary.’

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse says: ‘Danxia's burning the buddha was no light deed; the officer's eyebrows and beard grow in the fire. What one does, one has always received; who says cause and effect are unclear?’

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A temple-rebuilding notice pairs ‘Danxia burns the buddha’ with ‘Deshan tears down the hall,’ calling both rare in past and present.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘guest within host,’ one of the four positional names built from guest and host. In the Linji-house definition preserved by The Eye of Humans and Gods, the teacher having a ‘nose-hole’ is host-within-host, the student having one is host-within-guest, the teacher lacking one is guest-within-host, and the student lacking one is guest-within-guest; the compilation immediately warns that this differs from Caodong guest-and-host. That explicit definition makes ‘guest within host’ (主中賓) here the position in which ‘the teacher lacks a nose-hole; this is named guest within host’ (師家無鼻孔，名主中賓), rather than a free synonym for the whole guest-host pair. The same compilation records the term as a question answered by Fengxue (‘the returning simurgh, the two luminaries renewed’), as a verse heading, and in several masters' complete four-position catechisms. Later records continue asking ‘what is guest within host?’ and answer with fresh lines such as ‘green mountains cover white clouds’ and ‘empty-handed, mingling with the dusty world.’ The changing answers remain answers to one named public-interview position; this entry reports them without choosing a hidden interpretation.
Senses.Note: 344 hits in the wave plan. The source compilation explicitly distinguishes Linji and Caodong formulations, so this corpus-wide sense does not silently transfer Caodong bent/upright or interchange language into it. The gloss order follows the graphs: guest within host (主中賓); compare host within guest (賓中主). One sense, because poems and catechism answers keep the same positional label.

Senses.Explanation: Host, master of a house, or the one in charge (主人), plus a personifying honorific such as 'sir' or 'master' (公), forms the personified 'master-in-charge' (主人公). The locus classicus is Ruiyan Shiyan (瑞巖師彥), who every day sat on his rock and called out to himself — 'each day he calls "Master!" and himself answers "Yes"' (每日喚主人公復應諾) — then warned himself 'stay wide awake… don't let anyone deceive you' (惺惺著…莫受人謾); this is case 12 of the Wumenguan (無門關, 'Gateless Checkpoint'). The record groups it with Linji's 'true person of no rank' (無位真人) and 'mind itself is buddha' (即心是佛): 'many take Ruiyan's master-in-charge and Linji's true person of no rank…' (多將箇瑞巖主人公臨濟無位真人). Asked 'what is Zhaozhou's master-in-charge?' (如何是趙州主人公), Zhaozhou barks (咄): 'this bucket-hooping fellow!' (這箍桶漢, a menial-cooper insult). The record sets it against the 'bright, numinous' identity-consciousness (昭昭靈靈的識神), faulting the one who guards that and imagines he has realized the master: 'guarding the bright-numinous identity-consciousness and taking that to be realizing the master-in-charge' (守住個昭昭靈靈的識神便是悟得主人公也). Zhaozhou identifies it in the first person in his own record: 'before there was a world, this nature already was; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish. Since once seeing this old monk — it is no one else, just this master-in-charge' (未有世界早有此性世界壞時此性不壞從一見老僧後更不是別人只是箇主人公), continuing 'why hunt outside for this one?' (者箇更向外覔作麼) (the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhaozhou Shen 趙州諗禪師語錄, inside the Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Ancients 古尊宿語錄, C077n1710; the saying is raised again as a case in Yuanwu's Recorded Sayings 圓悟語錄, T47n1997). Deployed as a standing examination question, 'where is the master-in-charge?' appears as (主人公在甚麼處) 70 times in 44 allowlist texts and in the graph variant (主人公在什麼處) 26 times in 18 texts. It is typically framed 'no dream, no thought, no seeing, no hearing — where then is the master-in-charge?' (無夢無想無見無聞主人公在甚麼處, so B27n0152; punctuated with 'just when asleep' 正睡著時 in J25nB171); the record tells how Xueyan Qin (雪巖欽) put it to Gaofeng (高峰): 'Gaofeng strove bitterly five years; the pillow slid to the floor, and he greatly awakened' (峰苦志五年，推枕子墮地，大悟, J26nB177, also J26nB178). Another exchange answers 'where is the master-in-charge right now?' (主人公即今在什麼處) with 'no autumn wind fanning, yet the cassia scent drifts' (秋風不扇，桂蕊飄香) in three lamp records (X81n1568, X82n1571; X80n1566 writes the variant graphs 桂蕋 and 甚麼處). The Chan House Tortoise-Mirror (禪家龜鑑) lists it among the things called out: 'under the ancestral masters' gate there are also those who call "Amitābha" and those who call "Master!"' (祖師門下亦有或喚阿彌陀佛者，或喚主人公者, X63n1255). Tianru Weize gives a second explicit equivalence in his own record: 'what is called mind? Mind, on each person's own share, is called oneself and is also called the master-in-charge' (何者謂之心？心在諸人分上喚作自己，又喚作主人公). This Tianru Weize witness is independent of the Ruiyan self-calling and Zhaozhou exchanges.
Senses.Note: The central corpus use is contrastive: the recurring warning is against taking the identity-consciousness (識神), the 'bright and numinous' (昭昭靈靈), for the master-in-charge (esp. B27n0152). Origin: Ruiyan's self-calling (Wumenguan case 12). Compare 'true person of no rank' (無位真人) — the record itself lists Ruiyan's master-in-charge and Linji's true person of no rank side by side as equivalents. Current allowlist counts: master-in-charge (主人公) 738 hits in 198 texts; the graph variant 'master-in-charge' (主人翁), with 'old man' as the honorific (翁), 242 hits in 98 texts; and the calling formula 'calling the master-in-charge' (喚主人公), 54 hits in 35 texts. A second witness to the identity-consciousness contrast: 'wrongly construing the flickering shimmer-and-shadow of the bright-numinous before one's eyes, taking it for the master-in-charge' (妄自和會箇目前昭昭靈靈底浮光幻影。認為主人公, B25n0145 0796a06).

Senses.Explanation: (乾) dry + (屎) shit + (橛) a short stub/stake: "a dry shit-stick" — the (廁籌), the wood or bamboo stick used to wipe in a latrine before paper (or a stick of dried dung). Attested uses in the corpus: Linji, having presented "the true person of no rank" (無位真人), strikes the questioner and says (無位真人是甚麼乾屎橛), then returns to his quarters; Yunmen answers "What is Buddha?" (如何是佛) with (乾屎橛) (Wumenguan 21), and answers "What is Śākyamuni's body?" (如何是釋迦身) the same way in his own Extended Record; Deshan Xuanjian (德山宣鑒) says (釋迦老子是乾屎橛)。(文殊普賢是擔屎漢); and it occurs as the idiom "what dry shit-stick are you hunting for here?" (覓什麼乾屎橛). The texts assign the word no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One term, one meaning, deployed in two distinct cases by different masters — do not cross-attribute them: (1) Linji's dismissal of (無位真人) with (乾屎橛) (五燈會元, 古尊宿語錄, and raised-case retellings); (2) Yunmen's answer to (如何是佛) (五燈會元, 禪宗頌古聯珠通集, and Yunmen's own 廣錄, the 釋迦身 variant). The paired sayings ‘Yunmen’s dry shit-stick’ (雲門乾屎橛) and ‘Dongshan’s three catties of hemp’ (洞山麻三斤) recurs across the record (e.g. B25n0145, J37nB396). Cross-ref (無位真人).

The line is Linji's (濟拓開曰 無位真人是甚麼乾屎橛); Yantou (巖頭) sticks out his tongue and Xuefeng (雪峯) comments. A raised/retold case, not Linji's own record — so MasterName null per the raised-case rule, though the case is Linji's. X-canon lb ed=X 0227a10 (co-located ed=R138 0399b13 not used).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雲門匡真禪師廣錄); the dismissive idiom — "what dry shit-stick are you hunting here to chew on?" (覓什麼乾屎橛咬). Yunmen's own record.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (禪宗頌古聯珠通集) (file head 禪宗頌古聮珠通集卷; a by-master compilation); the question (雲門因僧問如何) opens on the prior lb 0808c23, followed here by verse-commentary (頌曰). Independent witness of the same Yunmen case.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the Five Ranks (of the upright 正 and the crooked 偏)
AlternateTargets: the five ranks of ruler and minister (君臣五位)
Senses.Explanation: The technical name of the Caodong house's signature scheme, created by Dongshan Liangjie and systematized by Caoshan Benji. 'Five' configurations arrange two terms — the upright or straight (正) and the crooked or bent (偏) — as: crooked within the upright (正中偏), upright within the crooked (偏中正), coming from within the upright (正中來), arriving from both together (兼中至 / 偏中至), attained in both together (兼中到). The same five are recast as ruler and minister (君臣, the 君臣五位); Dongshan also taught parallel fivefold sets — the five ranks of merit/achievement (功勳五位) and the five ranks of princes (王子五位) — and Caoshan's 'five ranks facing the guest' (五位對賓) works them into interview form ('I come from the crooked position, please receive me into the upright'). Across the corpus the term functions as the emblem of the Caodong house, almost always named in one breath with its Linji-house counterpart, the three mysteries (and three essentials) (臨濟三玄（三要）) — 'Dongshan's five ranks / Linji's three mysteries' (洞山五位／臨濟三玄), 'not Linji's three mysteries, not Caodong's five ranks' (不是臨濟三玄不是曹洞五位) — so that 'the Five Ranks' effectively names the Caodong house the way 'three mysteries' names the Linji house. The scheme is defined inside the house's own records. Dongshan's record has him compose the verses: 'The master composed the verses on the five ranks of ruler and minister: Crooked within the upright — the third watch, early in the night, before the moon shines; no wonder that meeting they do not recognize each other, dimly still harboring the old days' estrangement' (師。作五位君臣頌云。正中偏。三更初夜月明前。莫怪相逢不相識。隱隱猶懷舊日嫌, T47n1986B). Caoshan, asked for the essential formula of ruler and minister (君臣旨訣), lays the terms out: 'the upright position is the realm of emptiness — originally not a thing; the crooked position is the realm of form — having the shapes of the myriad images; crooked-within-upright: turning from principle toward affairs; upright-within-crooked: leaving affairs and entering principle; both-together: darkly answering the many conditions without falling into any existent' (正位即空界。本來無物。偏位即色界。有萬象形。正中偏者背理就事。偏中正者舍事入理。兼帶者冥應眾緣。不墮諸有) and 'ruler = the upright position, minister = the crooked position; minister facing ruler is upright-within-crooked, ruler regarding minister is crooked-within-upright, ruler and minister's ways joined is the both-together saying' (君為正位。臣為偏位。臣向君是偏中正。君視臣是正中偏。君臣道合是兼帶語) (T47n1987A, the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Caoshan Yuanzheng of Fuzhou (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄); the 'ruler = the upright position' (君為正位) mapping recurs 11 times, incl. T47n1987B and the Eye of Humans and Gods 人天眼目 T48n2006). The Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) also glosses each fivefold set: 'the five ranks of merit clarify the stages of effort in study, up to the stage beyond effort; the five ranks of ruler and minister clarify the conditioned and the unconditioned; the five ranks of princes clarify that inward succession is originally complete of itself, while outward succession has an end and a beginning; roughly, the Caodong house style is nothing beyond substance/function, upright/crooked, host/guest, to clarify the road going beyond' (功勳五位者。明參學功位至於非功位也。君臣五位者。明有為無為也。王子五位者。明內紹本自圓成。外紹有終有始也。大約曹洞家風。不過體用偏正賓主。以明向上一路) — and the ranks in substance/function terms: 'crooked-within-upright: substance giving rise to function; upright-within-crooked: function returning to substance; arriving-from-both: substance and function arriving together; attained-in-both: substance and function both extinguished' (正中偏者。體起用也。偏中正者。用歸體也。兼中至。體用並至也。兼中到。體用俱泯也) (T48n2006). Like other stock house vocabulary, it is asked as an interview question: asked 'What are the five ranks of the Dong[shan] school?' (如何是洞上五位), a master answers 'old door-gods on New Year's Eve' (除夜舊門神) (問：「如何是洞上五位？」荅：「除夜舊門神。」, J27nB189).
Senses.Note: Attribution (not disputed, but a division of labour): the upright-crooked (正偏) Five Ranks are Dongshan Liangjie's; the ruler-minister (君臣) formulation and the 'facing the guest' (五位對賓) catechism are especially Caoshan Benji's. Witness J10nA158 is a LINJI master reciting the four fivefold schemata (ruler-minister 君臣, upright-crooked 偏正, princes 王子, merit 功勳) precisely to contrast them with Linji's own 'true person of no rank' (無位真人) — an outside witness that still fixes the term's meaning. SenseKey is null because the scheme becomes shared Caodong-house vocabulary; Dongshan's historical origin does not make the later meaning private to him. Zen-allowlist grep counts: the Five Ranks (五位), 1,155 hits in 212 of 462 texts. Rank names: crooked within the upright (正中偏) 315, upright within the crooked (偏中正) 296, attained in both (兼中到) 270, coming from within the upright (正中來) 269; for the fourth rank both 'arriving from both' (兼中至, 192) and 'arriving from the crooked' (偏中至, 86) are attested. Emblems and set names: ruler-and-minister (五位君臣 188 / 君臣五位 46), Dongshan's five ranks (洞山五位) 111, Caodong five ranks (曹洞五位) 30, the Dong-school five ranks (洞上五位) 13, princes (五位王子 41 / 王子五位 11), merit (功勳五位 20 / 五位功勳 17), facing the guest (五位對賓) 16 (variant graph 對賔 1).

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary Chinese reading — 'five positions/ranks/stages' — used non-technically even inside Zen texts: as a plain ordinal ('who is the fifth-ranked sage?'), or as the path-positions of the scholastic literature ('lodged in the five causal positions' 寄因五位, the provisional positions up to the fruit-position; also embedded in 五十五位, the fifty-five bodhisattva stages). Distinguished from the Caodong technical sense purely by context: no pairing with upright/crooked (正/偏) or ruler/minister (君臣), no link to Dongshan/Caoshan, and no coupling with Linji's three mysteries (臨濟三玄). Recorded only so the 'Five Ranks' reading is not projected onto every place these two graphs occur.
Senses.Note: Peripheral and heterogeneous (an ordinal in one witness, scholastic path-stages in the other); the two share only 'NOT the Caodong term.' Kept minimal, for disambiguation. Provisional because it is not a single unified Zen sense so much as the residue of the plain Chinese word. Other generic uses inside the allowlist, with grep counts: the fifty-five bodhisattva stages (五十五位) 9, the hundred things in five groups (五位百法) 3, the five stages in the womb (在胎五位) 1 (Records of the Source-Mirror 宗鏡錄, T48n2016).

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘five houses,’ this is a corpus label for a five-part grouping of Chan lines and their recorded styles of address. The allowlisted corpus has 376 hits in 128 texts, including ‘five-house lineages’ (五家宗派, 54 hits in 41 texts), ‘purports of the five houses’ (五家宗旨, 115 hits in 58 texts), and ‘records of the five houses’ (五家語錄, 12 hits in 4 texts). One preface supplies an exact enumeration: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. The same preface says that differing encounter language came to form five houses without deliberate division. Zhongfeng gives two direct definitions: ‘What are called the five houses are five in their people, not five in their way,’ and ‘What are now called the five houses arise from Nanyue and Qingyuan; below those two branches the stream reached these five people.’ A recension preface likewise begins with the Nanyue and Qingyuan branches and says that five lineages later divided from them. The corpus also has four occurrences in four texts of the expanded label ‘five houses and seven lineages’ (五家七宗), including Yuanwu’s critical comment that people divided them and established separate gateways. Accordingly, this entry reports each text’s label or enumeration and does not impose one later sectarian table on every occurrence.
Senses.Note: The formula search found three occurrences of ‘the five houses are’ (五家者) in two texts; Zhongfeng’s two distinct definitions are both included. The selected evidence also covers an exact five-name enumeration, the two-branch genealogy, the five-versus-one relation drawn within the corpus, and the five-houses/seven-lineages extension. ‘House’ is used as the corpus’s organizational label without importing an external classification.

Senses.Explanation: The five binding precepts. The expression occurs 334 times in 117 allowlisted texts. One Chan text enumerates them among the rule classes for laypeople, novices, monks, and bodhisattvas and calls the five precepts the root of the larger code. A lamp record has a mountain deity request rules and receive the five precepts from a master. Encounter records also turn the formula 'not keeping the five precepts' (五戒不持) into a recurring rebuke. In one sequence a master says it to a monk from Jingshan and immediately explains, 'Here I do not accept novices'; elsewhere he says it to a lecturer on the Diamond Scripture before questioning him with his staff. A verse commentary links a written character for 'buddha' with having formerly kept the five precepts. The Zen deviation is this full deployment range: the fixed rule-list is enumerated and conferred by masters, but it is also spoken as an accusation in public encounters.
Senses.Note: The evidence establishes a hard rule-list and a stock encounter rebuke. It does not establish one uniform reason for every occurrence of the rebuke.

Senses.PreferredTarget: take away neither the person nor the surroundings
AlternateTargets: neither person nor surroundings taken away
Senses.Explanation: The fourth member of Linji's four statements later called the Four Selections: ‘at times, take away neither the person nor the surroundings.’ In Linji's own record it appears as one member of the complete four and immediately becomes a public question. Asked ‘what is taking away neither person nor surroundings?’ Linji answers, ‘the king ascends the jeweled hall; the rustic elder sings.’ The record does not explain the formula beyond that exchange. Later collections preserve Linji's wording, attach Kefu's verse—beginning ‘thought does not incline to either side; guest and host differ little; question and answer are both complete’—and invite many later masters to answer the same named question with new lines, including Fengxue's ‘the emperor remembers: in the third month south of the river, amid the partridge's cry the hundred flowers are fragrant.’ The formula circulates as a case heading, verse heading, and recurring public-interview question.
Senses.Note: 350 hits in the wave plan; preflight count retained by root. This formula must be read beside the other three members and the Four Selections (四料揀). Person (人) and surroundings (境) are translated literally here. It is corpus-wide in later use: later answers and verses address the same named formula rather than different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有時奪人不奪境、有時奪境不奪人、有時人境俱奪、有時人境俱不奪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji states all four members together in his late-evening address.

Senses.PreferredTarget: take away both person and scene
AlternateTargets: both person and surroundings taken away
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘person and scene both taken away.’ The phrase occurs 168 times in 99 allowlisted texts. Linji lists it as the third of four alternatives: sometimes take away the person but not the scene; sometimes the scene but not the person; sometimes both; sometimes neither. The records preserve Kefu's answer to ‘what is taking away both person and scene?’ as ‘news from Bing and Fen is cut off; alone in one quarter.’ Later masters repeatedly submit the roster-member to fresh public questions: one answers ‘gather in,’ paired with ‘let out’ for taking away neither; another declines the inherited four choices and asks for a sentence in which person and scene are not taken away. The entry reports the roster and its recorded answers without assigning a hidden condition to ‘person’ or ‘scene.’
Senses.Note: Zen bends ordinary removal language into one named member of Linji's fourfold roster. It is a roster term and public-interview prompt, not a report that two physical objects disappeared. Cross-checking the other three members supports one sense, not four readings of this member.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later interview pairs ‘gather in’ with ‘let out.’

Senses.Explanation: Literally "hand over, entrust" (付) the "teaching" (法): "entrust the teaching," attested 608 times in 143 allowlisted texts. Lamp records use it for a named predecessor handing the teaching to a successor: "after the buddha's extinction, the teaching was entrusted to Kasyapa and mind was transmitted by mind" (佛滅後付法於迦葉，以心傳心). Narrative closure frequently says "after the patriarch had entrusted the teaching" (祖付法已), followed by his departure or death. The compound "verse on entrusting the teaching" (付法偈) names verses spoken or recorded at that handover.
Senses.Note: The verses themselves often question the wording of transmission. One early verse says, "originally a teaching was entrusted; after entrusting it, [one] says there is no teaching; each must awaken for oneself; once awakened, there is no no-teaching" (本來付有法，付了言無法，各各須自悟，悟了無無法). A later preface asks why transmission verses are recorded for earlier buddhas and patriarchs but not below Mazu: was there no entrustment, or was it kept from disclosure? Another instruction ranks a thousand who have opened up below one person entrusted with the teaching, and a thousand entrusted below one who goes out into the world. These are text-stated comparisons within the same verb sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又佛滅後付法於迦葉，以心傳心
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An Ancestral Hall question states that after the buddha's extinction, the teaching was entrusted to Kasyapa and mind transmitted by mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 從上佛祖皆見有付法偈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A preface reports the claim that buddhas and patriarchs from earlier times all have verses on entrusting the teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本來付有法付了言無法各各須自悟悟了無無法阿難付法眼藏竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Early transmission verse: originally a teaching was entrusted; after entrusting it, one says there is no teaching; each must awaken for oneself. The narrative then says Ananda finished entrusting the eye-treasury of the teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖付法已。即現神變而入涅槃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Lamp narrative closure: after the patriarch entrusted the teaching, he manifested transformations and entered extinction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 千個省發者不如一付法者，千個付法者不如一出世者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A letter ranks a thousand who have opened up below one entrusted with the teaching, and a thousand entrusted below one who goes out into the world.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, words in another's place. Chan records use the term for supplying a response where the person questioned has no answer, where an assembly's answers do not accord, or where a case is reopened and another answer is offered. A layman reports a monk's remark and asks the master to supply a response; the master answers, “a household without a thousand days' goods does not have a steward.” In another exchange a monk is speechless, the master orders the assembly to supply responses, rejects their submitted words, and then supplies his own: “I did not beat the grass for its own sake; I only wanted to startle the snake.” Other records explicitly distinguish the failed substitute response of a monk from the master's own supplied response, and show an assembly first giving responses before requesting the master to supply one. The term belongs to public Chan testing: the unanswered or contested question does not end in silence but is handed to the community or master, whose alternative wording is recorded alongside the original exchange.
Senses.Note: The graph “speech” (語) is translated here as the actual response, not left as an unexplained “word.” The recurring sequence “had no response” (無對) → “ordered the assembly to respond in his place” (命眾代語) → “submitted responses did not accord” (下語不契) → “the master supplied one” (師代) establishes the institutional sense directly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧無對。士舉似師，求代語。師代云：「家無千日貨，不是掌財人。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a monk has no response, a layman reports the exchange and asks the master for a substitute response, which is quoted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師命眾代語，眾下語不契，師代云：「不圖打草，只要蛇驚。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master orders the assembly to respond, rejects their submitted responses, and supplies his own.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師令僧代語不契師自代云某甲罪犯彌天便出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk's requested substitute response does not accord, so the master supplies his own response and leaves.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾下語畢，請師代語。師云：「歸隱林泉榮祖業，那管長安車馬喧。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the assembly has submitted responses, it asks the master to supply a response; his exact reply follows.

Senses.Explanation: By means of (以) mind (心), transmit (傳) mind (心): transmitting mind by mind. In the Platform Sutra, when the Fifth Patriarch hands Huineng the robe, he says, 'the teaching is transmitted mind by mind; all are made to awaken and understand for themselves' (法則以心傳心，皆令自悟自解). The phrase names the mode of patriarchal transmission. The Jingde-era lamp record says that after the Buddha's nirvana the teaching was entrusted to Kasyapa and transmitted mind by mind (佛滅後付法於迦葉，以心傳心). Dahui says that each transmitted mind by mind in unbroken succession (各各以心傳心，相續不斷). The phrase repeatedly stands beside 'not setting up words and letters' (不立文字), as in the statement that Bodhidharma came from the west, transmitted mind by mind, and did not set up words and letters (達磨西來，以心傳心，不立文字). Dahui contrasts it with transmission by language: the sages from of old had no transmission by words and spoke only of transmitting mind by mind (從上諸聖，無言語傳授，只說以心傳心而已). The record also preserves criticism of the phrase itself. One address says, 'Driving out a wedge with a wedge turns into a beaten track; transmitting mind by mind, the disease turns deeper still' (以榍出榍，翻成途轍；以心傳心，其病轉深). The allowlist contains 110 occurrences in 56 texts. The Chan Gate Treasury Record explicitly presents a historical attribution as that text's claim: 'as for transmitting mind by mind, these are Great Master Bodhidharma's words' (以心傳心者，是達磨大師之言也). It then records Master Ke asking what written teaching-canons there are for study, and Bodhidharma answering, 'my teaching transmits mind by mind and does not set up written words' (我法以心傳心，不立文字).
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide lineage phrase, commonly paired with 'not setting up words and letters' (不立文字) and contrasted with transmission by language (以語言傳授). The record deploys the same phrase affirmatively and under criticism; the critical use is not a separate lexical meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 代代相承；法則以心傳心，

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來，以心傳心，不立文字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要). The standing collocation joins 'transmitting mind by mind' (以心傳心) to 'not setting up words and letters' (不立文字) and attributes the arrival from the west to Bodhidharma.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無言語傳授。只說以心傳心而已。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄), instruction to Layman Zhitong. Dahui says the sages from of old had no transmission by words, only transmitting mind by mind, and contrasts it with contemporary learned interpretation passed through language (從上諸聖，無言語傳授，只說以心傳心而已；今時多是師承學解).

Occurrences.Kwic: 以心傳心，其病轉深。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), in an address to the assembly. The phrase is criticized: transmitting mind by mind makes the disease turn deeper (以心傳心，其病轉深), paired with driving out a wedge by means of a wedge.

Occurrences.Kwic: 以心傳心者，是達磨大師之言也。因可和尚次問：此法有何文字教典習學？大師答云：我法以心傳心，不立文字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Chan Gate Treasury Record (禪門寶藏錄) makes the attribution as a text claim: 'as for transmitting mind by mind, these are Great Master Bodhidharma's words.' It records Master Ke asking what written teaching-canons there are for study, followed by the answer, 'my teaching transmits mind by mind and does not set up written words.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, entrust to movement or let the course proceed. The compound occurs 1,101 times in 250 allowlisted texts. As a predicate it describes conduct or functioning that proceeds without forced direction. A Keqin letter gives an explicit comparison: 'what is called proceeding of itself is like a dull-witted person whose household has a capable person caring for him.' Other records pair it with following circumstances in both word orders, with freedom, and with the doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself.' Concrete lines place it after drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry, or say that at all times and places one proceeds of oneself freely and responds without a fixed direction.
Senses.Note: The doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself' occurs 140 times in 94 texts. 'Proceed of itself and follow circumstances' and its reverse each occur 27 times; 'proceed of itself freely' occurs five times in five texts. This predicate is distinct from the exact title of the seventh oxherding section recorded below.
