Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Keqin letter provides the only direct 'what is called' comparison for the term.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山川草木總屬尋常，老幼賢愚一味平等，同彼同此，無是無非，渴飲饑餐隨緣任運，更說甚佛法玄妙、菩提涅槃？直饒臨濟當前也開臭口不得。政
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse places following circumstances and proceeding of itself immediately after drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一花開天下春。衲僧變態。須是恁麼始得。便乃一切時一切處。任運自在。應用無方。諸人還委悉麼。風行草偃。水到渠成。上堂云。好
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Hongzhi discourse pairs proceeding of itself with freedom and response without a fixed direction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 憐鵝護雪，只是應時應節不失其宜，大盡三十日、小盡二十九，饑餐渴飲，任運騰騰，佛界不收、魔界不攝，直得皇風蕩蕩、帝道平平，野老謳謌、
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A release-period discourse joins eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty to the doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 旨如何。師曰。水內覓魚踪。師進心珠歌曰。心如意。心如意。任運隨緣不相離。但知莫向外邊求。外邊求。終不是。枉用工夫隱真理。識心珠
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record song says that proceeding of itself and following circumstances do not separate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但能隨緣消舊業任運著衣裳要行即行要坐即坐無一念心希求佛果
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Linji saying joins following circumstances to naturally putting on clothes, walking, and sitting, without a thought seeking buddhahood.

Senses.Explanation: As an exact title in Puming's oxherding sequence, (任運) names the seventh section. Its verse places the herdboy by the spring river and says that hunger is met by food and thirst by drink as time passes. The title is a named textual unit, not merely another translation of the predicate 'proceed of itself.'
Senses.Note: Two independently allowlisted J23 records preserve the exact seventh-section heading. Their wording is closely related, but each anchors the title as a title.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無拘。山童穩坐青松下，一曲昇平樂有餘。任運任運普明禪師頌任運第七柳岸春波夕照中，淡煙芳草綠茸茸。饑餐渴飲隨時過，石上山童
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Puming's oxherding sequence labels the seventh verse “Spontaneous Accord” (任運) and immediately describes hunger, thirst, and passing with the time.

Occurrences.Kwic: 納允菴居士任運任運第七圖任運第七圖任運第七頌任運第七頌柳岸春波夕照中，淡煙芳草綠茸茸，饑餐渴飲隨時過，石上山童睡正濃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second oxherding collection repeatedly labels the seventh picture and verse “Spontaneous Accord” (任運) before preserving the same thematic verse.

Senses.Explanation: A doubled imperative: "rest" or "stop" (休去) and "cease" or "settle" (歇去): "rest; cease," attested 123 times in 68 allowlisted texts. Shishuang's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and a later speaker refuses both lists. Dahui reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: a teacher says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease?" (何不休去歇去). The entry records the command, its stock sequence, its contrary, and the corpus's criticisms; it does not turn the words into a prescribed system.
Senses.Note: Counted companions: "one thought for ten thousand years" (一念萬年去), 115; "cold and still" (冷湫湫地去), 48; "old-shrine incense burner" (古廟香爐去), 72; "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), 5. Orthography varies between "cold autumn-like" and "cold and still" in witnesses. The sole late naming formula is excluded because its surrounding sentence applies the words to a different labeled expression, whereas the older imperatives and their recorded criticisms bear the headword directly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石霜云休去歇去一念萬年去寒灰枯木去古廟香爐去一條白練去冷秋秋地去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yulin's record raises Shishuang's sequence: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still." Raised quotation, so unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一向嘴盧都地打坐。謂之休去歇去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's instruction to Lü Shunyuan critically reports people who "sit slack-jawed in one direction and call it resting and ceasing."

Occurrences.Kwic: 以至莫妄想放下著古廟香爐休去歇去等語為證。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, then criticizes that citation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門曰：「自今以往，休去歇去。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A memorial narrative quotes the teacher: "from now on, rest; cease." Historical quoted speech remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：何不休去歇去？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Dafang Yin's section: "the master said, why not rest and cease?" No validated roster value is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂休去歇去，唇上醭生去，如古廟香爐去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate instruction calls it resting and ceasing, letting mold grow on the lips, and becoming like an incense burner in an old shrine.

Senses.Explanation: The two graphs overlap in stopping and resting: 'rest,' 'cease,' or 'come to rest.' The allowlisted record has 698 occurrences in 194 texts. The word functions as a verb in imperatives such as 'go rest' (休歇去), as a predicate in questions such as 'have you yet found rest?' (還得個休歇也未), and as an attributive noun in 'a resting place' (休歇處) and 'ground of rest' (休歇地). Linji says, 'better to be without concerns and go rest; hungry, eat; tired, close your eyes' (不如無事休歇去，飢來喫飯，困來合眼). Qingyuan Weixin's address says that after first seeing mountains as mountains, then not as mountains, he had now 'found a resting place' and again saw mountains simply as mountains and waters as waters (而今得箇休歇處，依然見山秖是山，見水秖是水). Another lamp-record address asks what the resting place is and answers, 'when cold, sit around the stove; when at leisure, sleep as one pleases' (寒則圍爐座，閑時任性眠). The record also challenges the expression: one master answers 'what did you get that you do not rest?' (汝得箇什麼即不休歇去), and Zhenxie Qingliao rejects making a resting place out of dwelling in empty stillness and guarding the lifelessness before a dead tree, saying that this 'has no connection' (沒交涉). Thus the corpus records rest, questions about rest, named resting places, and an explicit rejection of one claimed resting place.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 698 hits in 194 texts. Attested formations include 'go rest' (休歇去), 101/54; 'resting place' (休歇處), 65/49; 'great rest' (大休歇), 67/40; doubled 'stop and rest' (休去歇去), 123/68; 'have [you] rested yet?' (休歇也未), 6/6; and 'ground of rest' (休歇地), 10/8. The single 'is called a resting place' (喚作休歇處) occurrence is Zhenxie Qingliao's rejection of that label, not his endorsement of it. The single 'one who seeks rest' (休歇者) hit asks why the ancestral teachers sought people's rest; it is a question, not a self-definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心住空寂、坐空劫中，守枯木岩前孤危死底，喚作休歇處，且喜沒交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhenxie Qingliao's own record, in the section 'do not chase conditions; do not dwell in empty endurance' (莫逐有緣勿住空忍). He describes dwelling in empty stillness, sitting in an empty aeon, and guarding a solitary lifelessness before a dead tree, then says calling that 'a resting place' has no connection. This is a text-drawn exclusion, not the entry's inference.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不如無事休歇去。飢來喫飯，困來合眼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head in the Linked Lamps Compendium (聯燈會要) is Linji Yixuan. He says, 'better to be without concerns and go rest; hungry, eat; tired, close your eyes.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師西來道箇休歇。敢問諸人。作麼生是休歇處。還會麼。寒則圍爐座。閑時任性眠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Continued Record of the Lamp (續傳燈錄), under the heirs of Huilin Yuanzhao Zongben, the speaker says, 'the ancestral teacher came from the west and spoke of rest; what is the resting place?' He answers, 'when cold, sit around the stove; when at leisure, sleep as one pleases.' The rough head pointer does not securely expose the immediate speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而今得箇休歇處。依然見山秖是山。見水秖是水。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Continued Record of the Lamp identifies the address as Qingyuan Weixin's. He says, 'now I have found a resting place; again I see mountains simply as mountains and waters simply as waters.' Qingyuan Weixin has no exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問古人得箇什麼即便休歇去。師曰。汝得箇什麼即不休歇去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Lamp Record (景德傳燈錄), under an heir of Luohan Guichen, a monk asks, 'what did the ancients get that they then went to rest?' The master replies, 'what did you get that you do not go rest?' The local pointer does not securely expose a roster-linked master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨曰。與汝安心竟。二祖當時便休歇去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui Zonggao retells the encounter in which Bodhidharma says, 'I have finished settling your mind for you,' and the second ancestor 'then and there went to rest.' It is Dahui's raised retrospective of an earlier exchange, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還得個休歇也未？若得個休歇
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Miyun Yuanwu's own record, during his second residence at Guanghui Monastery on Mount Jinsu. He asks the assembly, 'have you yet found rest? If you have found rest...' The retained span records the interrogative deployment without extending into later claims.

Senses.Explanation: The graph names a buddha and, with the article, the Buddha. It occurs 116,053 times in 459 allowlisted texts, but the Chan record gives this extremely broad title a sharply observable deployment of its own. The Buddha in the lineage-opening scenes is a participant in public actions: the World-Honored One mounts the seat, Kashyapa announces that the Buddha has finished speaking, and the Buddha leaves the seat; at Vulture Peak he holds up a flower before the silent assembly and Kashyapa smiles. The same bare word is made the object of the stock public question "What is Buddha?" (如何是佛), to which the records preserve mutually different answers rather than a common descriptive biography: Yunmen says "a dry shit-stick" (乾屎橛), Dongshan says "three catties of hemp" (麻三斤), and Huangbo says "this very mind is buddha; no-mind is the Way" (即心是佛，無心是道). Linji supplies an explicit formula in answer to "What are the true buddha, true teaching, and true Way?": "buddha is the mind's purity; the teaching is the mind's brightness; the Way is unobstructed pure light everywhere" (佛者，心清淨是；法者，心光明是；道者，處處無礙淨光是), then calls all three empty names without real existence (三即一，皆是空名，而無寔有). The corpus also turns against the title itself. Zhaozhou's recorded saying is "the one word 'buddha'—I do not like to hear it" (佛之一字，吾不喜聞). A lamp record attributes to Deshan a longer roster beginning "here there is no buddha and no patriarch" (這裏佛也無，祖也無) and ending "buddha is an old barbarian's shit-stick" (佛是老胡屎橛). Linji places buddha first in a five-part roster of whatever one meets inside or outside: "meet a buddha, kill the buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" (逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷). Later comments keep the lineage-opening scene open to appraisal: Dongshan Shouchu says people know only the flower and smile but do not know the World-Honored One, while Yulin calls the flower and smile the single transmission of the treasury of the true teaching eye and says it has made clear-eyed people laugh ever since. This is where Chan bends the word: its Buddha is recorded through the flower and teaching-seat actions, answers and self-formulas in public exchanges, refusal and abuse of the title, later appraisal of the lineage-opening scene, and the title's place in a killing roster—not through an outside religious life story.
Senses.Note: This sense covers the figure/title and the word as deployed in Chan, not the physical image separated below. Longer compounds keep their own articles and should not be silently substituted for it: 'buddha-nature' (佛性); the question 'What is Buddha?' (如何是佛); 'this very mind is buddha' (即心是佛); 'meet a buddha, kill the buddha' (逢佛殺佛); and 'denounce buddhas and revile patriarchs' (呵佛罵祖). The graph 'buddha' (佛) in 'the Buddha's teaching' (佛法) is also a compound constituent and does not by itself justify leaving the entire compound untranslated. The curated evidence spans an early lamp compilation, Linji's own record, and Huangbo's record; later compilations and commentaries repeatedly preserve and comment on the same scenes and formulas.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日陞座，大眾集定，迦葉白槌云：世尊說法竟。世尊便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Joint Lamp Record presents the Chan Buddha as an actor in a public teaching-seat scene: he mounts the seat, Kashyapa says that he has finished speaking, and he leaves the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊在靈山會上，拈花示眾，眾皆默然，唯迦葉破顏微笑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The next founding scene records the World-Honored One holding up a flower before the assembly, the assembly's silence, and Kashyapa's smile.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師垂語云：佛之一字，吾不喜聞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's recorded saying refuses not a proposition about buddha but the single spoken word itself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又僧問雲門：如何是佛？門云：乾屎橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk's plain question 'What is Buddha?' receives Yunmen's recorded answer 'a dry shit-stick.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是佛？師云：麻三斤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same public question receives Dongshan Shouchu's different recorded answer, 'three catties of hemp.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是佛。師云。即心是佛。無心是道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo answers the same question, 'this very mind is buddha; no-mind is the Way.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是真佛？真法？真道？乞垂開示。」師云：「佛者，心清淨是；法者，心光明是；道者，處處無礙淨光是。三即一，皆是空名，而無寔有
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own record supplies an explicit three-part formula and immediately calls the three one and empty names without real existence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但莫受人惑，向裏向外逢著便殺——逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷——始得解脫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji places buddha first in the complete five-object killing roster in his address to followers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山老漢見處即不然，這裏佛也無，祖也無，達磨是老臊胡，十地菩薩是擔屎漢，等妙二覺是破戒凡夫，菩提涅槃是繫驢橛，十二分教是鬼神簿、拭瘡疣紙，四果三賢、初心十地是守古塚鬼，自救得也無？佛是老胡屎橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp record attributes this roster to Deshan: here there is no buddha and no patriarch; Bodhidharma is a stinking old barbarian; tenth-stage bodhisattvas are dung-carriers; the two grades of equal and wondrous awakening are ordinary precept-breakers; awakening and extinction are donkey-tethering stakes; the twelvefold teaching is a ghost register and sore-wiping paper; the fruits, worthies, and stages are old-grave ghosts unable to save themselves; buddha is an old barbarian's shit-stick.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。世尊拈華。迦葉微笑時。人祇知拈華微笑。要且不識世尊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a later hall address, Dongshan Shouchu says that when the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kashyapa smiled, people knew only the flower and smile and did not know the World-Honored One.

Occurrences.Kwic: 至於拈華微笑謂之單傳正法眼藏也引他明眼人至今好笑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yulin's later record calls the flower-holding smile the single transmission of the treasury of the true teaching eye and says it has caused clear-eyed people to laugh up to the present.

Senses.Explanation: The same bare graph can name a physical buddha image rather than a person or title. The Record of the Chan Gate's Forged Reflections lists the twenty-fifth case as “Danxia burns a buddha” (丹霞燒佛). An independent allowlisted record names the same Danxia burning case with the material object explicit: “Danxia burns a wooden buddha” (丹霞燒木佛). The shortened and expanded case names therefore identify the burned buddha as a wooden image. This is a different object from the buddha addressed, questioned, rejected, or invoked in the primary sense, so the image receives its own sense rather than being folded into a reading of the title.
Senses.Note: The exact shortened form is anchored beside an independent expanded case name that makes the wooden-image referent explicit. Cross-checking the wooden-buddha family confirms the material referent: records say Danxia burned a wooden buddha for warmth, ask how a wooden buddha could contain relics, and contrast gold, wood, clay, and the 'true buddha.' The longer compound 'wooden buddha' (木佛) remains a related entry rather than replacing this bare-word sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二十五、丹霞燒佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The case list reads 'Twenty-five: Danxia burns a buddha.' The independent expanded case name 'Danxia burns a wooden buddha' identifies the burned referent as an image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 丹霞燒木佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second allowlisted record names the material object explicitly: 'Danxia burns a wooden buddha.'

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “buddha” (佛), and the second means “nature” (性): 'buddha-nature.' The term reaches the Chan record as a sutra line the masters quote and put in play — (一切眾生皆有佛性) ('all sentient beings have buddha-nature'): Yanguan Qi'an preaches the line straight to his assembly, and it stands inside the stock phrase (見性成佛) ('see the nature, become buddha'). The corpus also records the term against social rank: told a 'Lingnan barbarian has no Buddha-nature,' Huineng answers (人則有南北)，(佛性無南北) ('people may be north or south, but Buddha-nature is neither north nor south'). The record's most-repeated instruction bearing the term is given as a scripture quotation in Baizhang's mouth at Guishan's awakening over the stirred ember (五燈會元, 溈山靈祐 chapter): (經云)。(欲識佛性義)。(當觀時節因緣)。(時節既至)。(如迷忽悟) ('the sutra says: if you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, observe times and conditions; when the time arrives, it is like waking suddenly from delusion') — the clause (欲識佛性義) recurs 178x in 103 allowlist texts. The word is also put as a test-question, (如何是佛性) ('what is buddha-nature?', 43x/32): (普明大師) (Great Master Puming) answers a monk (汝無佛性) ('you have no buddha-nature') and, pressed with (蠢動含靈皆有佛性學人為何却無) ('wriggling and sentient creatures all have buddha-nature — why do I alone lack it?'), grounds it (為汝向外求) ('because you seek outward', 傳燈玉英集); one master answers (誰無)？ ('who lacks it?') where another answers (誰有)？ ('who has it?', 象田即念禪師語錄); an emperor's asking is answered (不離陛下所問) ('not apart from what Your Majesty is asking') — (帝乃問如何是佛性師曰不離陛下所問帝默契) ('the emperor asked: what is buddha-nature? the master said: not apart from what Your Majesty is asking; the emperor silently accorded', 禪宗頌古聯珠通集). A recurring test poses the earthworm cut in two — (蚯蚓斬為兩段)，(兩頭俱動)，(未審佛性在阿那頭) ('an earthworm is cut in two and both ends move: in which end is the buddha-nature?'): (延慶法端) (Yanqing Faduan) spreads both hands (師展兩手, 景德傳燈錄), while (長沙景岑) (Changsha Jingcen) answers (莫妄想) ('no fantasizing') and, pressed (爭柰動何) ('but what about the moving?'), says (會即風火未散) ('understand: the wind and fire have not yet dispersed', 聯燈會要). (仰山問中邑)：「(如何是佛性義)？」 ('Yangshan asked Zhongyi: what is the meaning of buddha-nature?') draws the simile (如室有六窗)，(中安一獼猴) ('like a room with six windows and a monkey placed inside'; raised in 宏智覺禪師語錄 and repeatedly after). The question frame (還有佛性也無) ('does it have buddha-nature or not?') recurs 334x/123 (counting 有佛性也無). The same corpus-wide headword is also deployed in Zhaozhou's dog case. A monk quotes the statement 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature' (一切眾生皆有佛性) and asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature. Zhaozhou answers, 'no' (無). Pressed—'from the buddhas down to ants everything has it; why not a dog?'—he says, 'because it has action-consciousness nature' (為伊有業識性在). Elsewhere he answers 'yes' (有) for a cypress tree, and once answers, 'every gate opens onto the road to Chang'an' (家家門前通長安). Zhaozhou also groups buddha-nature, awakening, extinction, and true thusness (佛性、菩提、涅槃、真如) as 'clothes worn against the skin—also called vexations' (貼體衣服，亦名煩惱). Guishan makes a related inversion for a whole assembly: 'no sentient being has buddha-nature' (一切眾生皆無佛性). The word 'no' is what a later record tells its addressee to look at: Dahui says to look at the saying (看箇話頭)—a monk asked Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature, and Zhaozhou said no—and to keep raising it at all times (時時提掇). The case is case 1 of the Wumenguan. It circulates as 'the dog's buddha-nature' (狗子佛性, 217 hits in 77 allowlisted texts) and 'the dog has no buddha-nature' (狗子無佛性, 427 in 119); 'does a dog have buddha-nature?' (狗子還有佛性) recurs 277 times in 110 texts. The bare answer is called 'the word no' (無字, 801 raw string matches across 173 texts) and 'Zhaozhou's word no' (趙州無字, 77 in 35).
Senses.Note: This sense records the sutra line as the record quotes and deploys it — reported as the texts' quotation, not as this entry's claim about what beings have. Zhaozhou's dog-case deployment belongs to this same corpus-wide sense. Zen-scoped counts: (佛性) 4,137x in 363 allowlist texts; (一切眾生皆有佛性) 64x/46; (欲識佛性義) 178x/103 (its continuation 當觀時節因緣 'observe times and conditions' 229x/124); (如何是佛性) ('what is buddha-nature?') 43x/32; the earthworm test (蚯蚓斬)… 16x/13 (佛性在阿那頭 'in which end is the buddha-nature' 18x/9). Anchors for quotes in the Explanation: Baizhang/Guishan X80n1565 ed="X" lb 0185a22; (普明大師) B14n0082 (傳燈玉英集) lb 0254b12; (法端) T51n2076 lb 0284c06; emperor exchange C078n1720 lb 0684a22; (仰山)/(中邑) J32nB272 lb 0195b07. He answers (有) ('yes') for a cypress and lumps (佛性) with (菩提)、(涅槃)、(真如) (awakening, nirvana, true thusness) as (貼體衣服)，(亦名煩惱) ('clothing worn against the skin — also called vexations'). The assembly-wide inversion (一切眾生皆無佛性) ('no sentient being has buddha-nature') recurs 13x in 6 allowlist texts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 溈山示眾云：「一切眾生皆無佛性。」鹽官示眾云：「一切眾生皆有佛性。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yanguan states the sutra line verbatim (一切眾生皆有佛性, 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature'); in the same passage Guishan states the inversion (一切眾生皆無佛性) ('no sentient being has buddha-nature'; the same sense also includes the dog-case deployment).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「汝嶺南人，無佛性也。」行者云：「人則有南北，佛性無南北。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng (the 行者, lay postulant) before Hongren; (佛性無南北) ('buddha-nature has no south or north') turned against social rank.

Occurrences.Kwic: 竺尚書問：蚯蚓斬為兩段，兩頭俱動，未審佛性在阿那頭？師云：莫妄想。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (聯燈會要) (X-canon; FromLb is the ed="X" number), section (湖南長沙景岑禪師) (cb:mulu): Secretary Zhu's earthworm-cut-in-two question and Changsha's (莫妄想) ('no fantasizing'); the exchange continues (竺云)：(爭柰動何)？(師云)：(會即風火未散)。 ('Zhu: but what about the moving? The master: understand — the wind and fire have not yet dispersed.') The term deployed as a test-question about where the buddha-nature is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「狗子還有佛性也無？」師云：「無。」學云：「上至諸佛下至螘子皆有佛性，狗子為什麼無？」師云：「為伊有業識性在。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The canonical answer, in Zhaozhou's own record (趙州錄).

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩提、涅槃、真如、佛性，盡是貼體衣服，亦名煩惱。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou groups (佛性) with (菩提)、(涅槃)、(真如) (awakening, nirvana, true thusness) as (貼體衣服)，(亦名煩惱) ('clothing worn against the skin — also called vexations').

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「柏樹子還有佛性也無？」師云：「有。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: He answers (有) ('yes') for a cypress.

Occurrences.Kwic: 溈山示眾云：「一切眾生皆無佛性。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Second master stating the same inversion (皆無佛性, 'all without buddha-nature').

Occurrences.Kwic: 只教就未拔處。看箇話頭。僧問趙州。狗子還有佛性也無。州云無。行住坐臥但時時提掇
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui sets the student to look at the phrase (看箇話頭) — Zhaozhou's (無) ('no') — and to keep holding it up at all times (時時提掇).

AlternateTargets: how is my hand like the Buddha's hand?
Senses.Explanation: The stock 'Buddha-hand' term names one of Huanglong Huinan's three public-interview barriers. Huanglong asks where the monk's native connection is, stretches out his hand and asks, 'how is my hand like the Buddha's hand?', then lowers his foot and asks how it resembles a donkey's foot. Records say he posed the three for over thirty years and that communities called them Huanglong's Three Barriers. Later masters answer, verse, criticize, and re-ask the Buddha-hand question. Zen thus bends an ordinary possessive phrase into a short case-name for a recurring public-interview checkpoint.
Senses.Note: The question, Buddha-hand/donkey-foot/native-connection set, and Huanglong's Three Barriers converge on this named lexical object. Fingered citron and Buddha-hand Rock are separate compounds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師室中常問僧曰：人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處？正當問答交鋒，却復伸手曰：我手何似佛手？又問諸方參請宗師所得，却復垂脚曰：我脚何似驢脚？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing account places the Buddha-hand question in a chamber interview.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中舉手問僧：我手何似佛手？垂足曰：我脚何似驢脚？人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處？學者莫有契其旨，叢林目之為黃龍三關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp record says communities called the set Huanglong's Three Barriers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又問。我手何似佛手。閑云。月下弄琵琶。又問。我脚何似驢脚。閑云。鷺鷥立雪非同色。黃龍每以此三轉語。垂問學者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Longqing answers, and the text identifies the recurring questions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。我手何似佛手。師曰。金鍮難辯。曰。我脚何似驢脚。師曰。黃龍路險。曰。人人有箇生緣。如何是和尚生緣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingxiang answers the stock sequence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂德山呵佛罵祖承其言者多見德山者少黃龍佛手驢脚見黃龍者眾善其機者稀驀拈拄杖云欲得見德山麼遂左邊卓云看要知佛手驢脚麼復右邊卓云看
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master names and performs the case family from the teaching seat.

Senses.Explanation: Elsewhere the graphs literally denote a buddha's hand. In the jewel exchange the heavenly kings say, 'there is no jewel in the buddha's hand'; a verse says 'the buddha's hand cannot cover it.' This body-part referent is different from Huanglong's case-name.
Senses.Note: Literal body part versus conventional interview-barrier name. The two body-part texts assign the hand no further gloss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊復藏珠入袖。却擡手曰。此珠作何色。天王曰。佛手中無珠。何處有色。世尊嘆曰。汝何迷倒之甚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase locates the absence of a jewel in the buddha's hand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問衣下事師荅火燒山佛手遮不得人心似等閒嵗晚年來正苦寒千林木葉盡凋殘
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says the buddha's hand cannot cover the burning mountain.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'one who does or makes': a doer of a craft. Across the Chan corpus the word overwhelmingly marks tested competence—an adept, a real hand, or someone accomplished in the role named beside it. It modifies an adept master (作家宗師), an adept battle-general (作家戰將), and an adept Chan guest (作家禪客); an adepts' meeting (作家相見) names a meeting of people credited with that competence, while the doubled exclamation 'a real hand! a real hand!' (作家作家) praises it. The public interview can ask directly, 'What is an adept?' (如何是作家), and a master can dismiss a monk with the negative verdict, 'Not an adept—out!' (不是作家出去). One transmitted exchange applies the same adjective to 'an accomplished poet' (作家詩客). Poet and Chan master are different roles, but the headword contributes the same expert status in each; the corpus does not establish a separate modern 'author' or 'writer' sense.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide expert/adept sense is retained after the item-8 family test. The poet phrase occurs in seven allowlisted files, but all seven transmit the same Dayu Zhi encounter; no productive reversed or related poet family was found. Expert poet (作家詩客), adept master (作家宗師), adept battle-general (作家戰將), and adept Chan guest (作家禪客) are applications of one accomplished-person meaning, not different things. Allowlist count: 2,744 hits in 331 texts. Productive families include adepts' meeting (作家相見), 117; an adept's means (作家手段), 34; doubled praise (作家作家), 22; adept fellow (作家漢), 14; adept eye (作家眼), 10; and adept forge (作家爐韛), 4. The modern default 'author/writer' is unsupported.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這僧不妨是箇作家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's prose commentary (評唱) on the Yunmen case, (碧巖錄) case 15. 'This monk is quite the adept.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 大凡作家宗師。要與人解粘去縛。抽釘拔楔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's commentary: 'Generally an adept master unsticks and unbinds people, pulls out nails and draws out wedges.' Defines the role-word (作家宗師).

Occurrences.Kwic: 爾若要作家相見。便與爾作家相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu on Changsha/Yangshan: 'If you want an adepts' meeting, I'll give you an adepts' meeting.' The collocation (作家相見).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師乃掩耳而已。居士云。作家作家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), (石林和尚) section: Layman Pang (龐居士 = Pang Yun) exclaims '(作家作家)!' ('a real hand! a real hand!') in praise of Shilin. Speaker is Pang, verified from the (石林和尚) head + running (居士云).

Occurrences.Kwic: 若是作家戰將。便請單刀直入。更莫如何若何。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Quoted (示眾) of (興化和尚) (Xinghua Cunjiang) inside the (廬州澄心院旻德和尚) section: 'If you are an adept battle-general, come straight in single-blade — no more of your what-ifs.' (作家戰將) = an adept of real skill.

Occurrences.Kwic: 鉗鎚佛祖，必須作家。如何是作家？」師云：「殺人不眨眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct interview asks, ‘To hammer buddhas and patriarchs requires an adept. What is an adept?’ The master answers, ‘One who kills without blinking.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 時有僧出礼拜師云不是作家出去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk comes forward and bows; the master gives the public verdict, ‘Not an adept—out!’

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。路逢劍客須呈劍。不是詩人不獻詩。曰作家詩客。師曰。一條紅線兩人牽。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the visitor says that one presents a sword to a swordsman and a poem only to a poet, Dayu replies, ‘An accomplished poet.’ The phrase applies the same expert adjective outside the Chan-master role.

Senses.Explanation: A colloquial interrogative: “how?”, “in what way?”, or “what about it?” It occurs 25,720 times in the allowlisted corpus. Chan dialogue uses it to demand the next word or act: Baizhang asks how one speaks with throat and lips shut; Shitou asks Yaoshan, after ruling out thus and not-thus, “you—how?” Productive forms press again (又作麼生), ask how someone understands (作麼生會), ask how it should be (合作麼生), or insist “ultimately, how?” (畢竟作麼生). The phrase also asks about another master’s meaning or response. Early and later records preserve three graphic forms meaning “how?” (作勿生, 作摩生, 怎麼生). These are graphic forms of the same interrogative. Its distinctive Chan deployment is the accountable public-interview demand for a response; the entry reports that dialogue role without assigning an intent.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide interrogative sense. The questioned object and answer type vary, but the word does not acquire a different referent. The narrower family phrase “how do you say it?” (作麼生道) remains separate because its final graph means “say” (道).

Occurrences.Kwic: 是爾如今與麼聽法底人作麼生擬修他、證他、莊嚴他？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's Record (臨濟慧照禪師語錄): 'this you, right now, the one listening to the teaching just so (與麼)—how (作麼生) would you refine it, verify it, or adorn it?' Here 'how' (作麼生) means 'in what way' and is paired with 'just so' (與麼).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問溈山。併却咽喉唇吻。作麼生道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (百丈懷海) chapter (師 = 百丈懷海; 溈山．五峯．雲巖侍立次). KWIC trimmed to Baizhang's own question (single speaker) — 'shut off throat and lips — how will you speak (作麼生道)?' — the demand-to-utter collocation; Guishan's reply (却請和尚道) follows in the source but is dropped to keep a clean one-speaker attribution.

Occurrences.Kwic: 恁麼不恁麼總不得。子作麼生。師罔措。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (藥山惟儼) chapter. After the thus/not-thus double bind, Shitou (頭=石頭) throws the challenge at the person: (子作麼生) 'you — what will you do?'; Yaoshan (師) is left at a loss (罔措).

Occurrences.Kwic: 後溈山問仰山：「此二尊宿意作麼生？」仰山云：「和尚作麼生？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (臨濟語錄), (勘辨) (testing) section. Guishan Lingyou probes Yangshan Huiji on an exchange: (此二尊宿意作麼生) 'what was these two elders' meaning?'; Yangshan flips it back (和尚作麼生) 'how about you, master?'. (意作麼生) as a probe of a case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。翹足又作麼生。僧無對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master presses again and the monk has no response.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：你作麼生會？僧便喝，師曰：未在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master asks how the monk understands it, then appraises the shout.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今朝啟建聖節，合作麼生舉唱？擊拂子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address uses the normative form “how should it be raised and proclaimed?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：畢竟作麼生？覺以拂子驀口打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question “ultimately, how?” receives a blow with the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：作勿生是？答：亦不作勿生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Shenhui record preserves an early graphic form meaning “how?” (作勿生).

Occurrences.Kwic: 向上人分上合作摩生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Zutang ji preserves a graphic form meaning “how?” (作摩生) in a normative construction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧曰。未審怎麼生下手。師曰。適來幾合喪身失命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk uses a variant meaning “how?” (怎麼生) to ask how to begin; the master answers with a retrospective verdict.

AlternateTargets: what do you make of it?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “how understand?” In the Chan record it is a recurrent public-interview question put to one monk or to the whole assembly after a saying, action, quotation, or case has been raised. Linji asks how a monk understands the four stated uses of a shout and answers the monk's hesitation with a shout. Wufeng asks “how do you understand it?” (你作麼生會) after an exchange; the monk shouts, and Wufeng says “not yet” (未在) before asking what comes after one shout or two. In a whisk case, a senior asks how the respondent understands Guishan's intention in raising the whisk; the offered account is rejected with “you had better return to Guishan” (且歸溈山去好). Later case commentary likewise says that National Teacher Huizhong and his attendant both still lacked understanding and asks, “how do you understand it now?” (如今作麼生會). The phrase therefore records a demand for an answer that can itself be answered, rejected, or tested in public; the texts do not define it as silent inward comprehension.
Senses.Note: The unstated object is supplied by the immediately preceding saying, action, or case. The graph for “understand” (會) supplies the verb.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曾有僧問溈山。如何是西來意。溈山舉起拂子。上座作麼生會溈山意。曰。借事明心。附物顯理。甘曰。且歸溈山去好。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The raised-whisk case is followed by an explicit demand for the respondent's understanding and rejection of his answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：你作麼生會？僧便喝，師曰：未在。僧又喝，師曰：一喝兩喝後作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An individual public-interview demand; two shouted replies remain subject to the master's verdict and follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 翠巖芝云：國師與侍者總欠會在，如今作麼生會？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Later case commentary reopens the National Teacher's three calls to his attendant and asks the audience how it understands the case now.

Occurrences.Kwic: 盡十方世界是一顆明珠。汝作麼生會。曰。盡十方世界是一顆明珠。用會作麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prior reply is put back to its speaker as the answer to the master's demand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人作麼生會？向這裏辨得，羅紋十字，一任橫行。苟或未然，切忌亂走。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat address asks the whole assembly and immediately distinguishes discerning it from not yet doing so.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日，龍問：風幡話子作麼生會？師曰：逈無入處，乞師方便。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question tests a monk on the wind-and-banner saying; the monk openly reports having no entry.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "how (作麼生) say (道)?" The phrase occurs 3,336 times in 309 allowlisted texts. It is a direct demand for words in the Chan public interview. Baizhang asks Guishan, "with throat and lips shut, how do you say it?" (併却咽喉唇吻，作麼生道); Baizhang then puts the same demand to Wufeng and Yunyan. Records also use it to demand "a phrase not involving the teaching framework" (不涉化門一句), "a phrase not falling into words" (不落言詮), or an answer from the speaker's own breast. In retrospective questions, it asks how another teacher spoke: "how did Jingshan say it to you?" (徑山向汝作麼生道). The grammatical subject changes, but the demand or report remains speech in an accountable encounter.
Senses.Note: This is not private self-inquiry. Even when a formal address supplies its own answer after a pause, the recorded form openly demands that a phrase be said.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問溈山。併却咽喉唇吻。作麼生道。山曰。却請和尚道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang asks Guishan, "with throat and lips shut, how do you say it?" Guishan asks the teacher to say it instead.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百丈問溈山。併却咽喉唇吻。作麼生道溈山云。却請和尚道丈云。我不辭向汝道。恐已後喪我兒孫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record re-presents the Baizhang–Guishan public case and its reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不涉化門一句。作麼生道。陣雲橫海上。拔劍攪龍門。下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu demands, "how do you say a phrase not involving the teaching framework?" then supplies a verse and steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 朝參暮請，盖是尋常，不落言詮，作麼生道？拈拄杖，云：三世諸佛總在這裏看看
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address asks, "not falling into verbal explanation, how do you say it?" and then takes up the staff and speaks.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。徑山向汝作麼生道。曰。他道一切總無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A retrospective interview question: "how did Jingshan say it to you?" The layman reports Jingshan's answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云我問你苐二句作麼生道進云不會師云灼然灼然
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The teacher asks, "I ask you: how do you say the second phrase?" The interlocutor says, "I do not understand."

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘following what came before.’ The expression occurs 758 times in 196 allowlisted texts and marks that a condition, action, or result remains unchanged. In encounter records a monk asks again ‘as before’ after receiving no answer, and a messenger answers Xuefeng ‘entirely in the same words as before.’ It also closes appraisals: ‘recognize it and it still is not it,’ ‘the blind remain blind and the mute remain mute,’ and ‘open your mouth and miss it; calculate and fail; still be embarrassed.’ A widely repeated three-stage statement says that after first seeing mountains as mountains, then not as mountains, one finally ‘still sees mountains only as mountains and water only as water.’ Verse and discourse also apply the phrase to recurring moonlight, spring, meals, and unchanged objects. The corpus supplies no specialized second referent: Zen bends this ordinary adverb chiefly by using it as the recurrent verdict that a new answer, recognition, or maneuver has left matters unchanged.
Senses.Note: Family check: compared standalone “as before” (依前) with “ask as before” (依前問), “the words as before” (依前語), “recognize it and it still is not it” (認著依前還不是), and “still sees mountains” (依前見山). These are deployment shapes of the same adverb, not different things; no sense split is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 却回舉似師。師曰。汝更去問。待他有答。汝便噓兩聲。峯又去。依前問。石頭乃噓兩聲。峯又無語。回舉似師。師曰。向汝道石頭路滑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An encounter uses the expression for repeating the same question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其僧到雪峯。一依前語祇對。峯曰。也須是趙州始得。問。如何是出家。師曰。不履高名。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A messenger gives Xuefeng the response wholly in the same words as before.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。古人道。認著依前還不是。實難會。土宿頷下髭鬚多。波斯眼深鼻孔大。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse quotes the verdict ‘recognize it and it still is not it.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。以木為船筏。曰。恁麼即得度也。師曰。盲者依前盲。瘂者依前瘂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The paired construction says the blind remain blind and the mute remain mute.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眨眼滲漏，開口蹉過，計較不成，依前懡㦬。拘那含牟尼佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compact appraisal places remaining embarrassed after blinking, speaking, and calculating.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後來親見知識，有箇入處，見山不是山，見水不是水。而今得箇休歇處，依前見山只是山，見水只是水。大眾，這三般見解，是同是別？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The three-stage statement returns to seeing mountains and water as before.

Senses.PreferredTarget: draw a gourd following the model
AlternateTargets: copy the gourd from its pattern
Senses.Explanation: Literally, follow (依) a model (樣) and draw (畫) a gourd (葫蘆). One master makes the wording concrete: after saying 'draw a gourd following the model,' he traces a circle with his hand and says, 'this is the model for the gourd.' Chan records most often use the idiom to appraise copied words or conduct in public exchanges. When a student repeats the form of an earlier answer, a master calls it drawing a gourd from the model and rebukes him. Another record explicitly denies that its handling of an old case is following another's heels or drawing a gourd from the model. A later address applies the phrase across famous lineage gestures: the Buddha holding up the flower, Bodhidharma facing the wall, Linji's shout, and Deshan's staff are followed by descendants who 'each draw a gourd following the model.' The Zen deviation is this ordinary craft-copying idiom used to audit repeated case answers, gestures, verses, and recorded lineages. Since masters also use it self-referentially, the phrase is not condemnation by definition.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 32 hits in 26 texts. One copying-action sense. Family checked against following another's heels (隨人腳跟轉), stamped from a printing block (印板上打來), released from a mold (模子裏脫出), and copying a model (依樣).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Concrete demonstration: the master draws a circle and calls it the gourd's model.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有來依樣畫葫蘆，也道：某甲有口有耳有眼，和尚作麼生接？山僧向他道：咬人屎橛，不是好狗。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public-questioning use: a copied answer is identified and rebuked.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Text-drawn contrast: neither following another's heels nor drawing a gourd from the model.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊拈花，徒標形影；達磨面壁，早涉程途。引得兒孫不唧溜，人人依樣畫葫蘆。臨濟喝、德山棒，總是一場乾打鬨；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Lineage-wide deployment covering the flower, wall-facing, shout, and staff.

Senses.PreferredTarget: cling to grass and attach to trees
AlternateTargets: depend on grass and cling to wood
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “depend on grass and attach to trees.” Across 128 occurrences in 71 allowlisted texts, Chan masters use the phrase chiefly in the fixed labels “spirits that cling to grass and trees” (依草附木精靈) and “people who cling to grass and trees” (依草附木漢). Its targets are explicit and varied: making a livelihood on circumstances and objects or seeking clever explanations in principle and nature (機境上作活計，理性中求妙解), understanding under a “dead phrase” (死句), and even the stock teaching-seat actions of striking the bench, raising the whisk, blinking, and raising the eyebrows. The phrase therefore shifts from literal plant-dependence to a recurring Chan rebuke for speech, gestures, or understanding that depends on something named in the passage. The record itself supplies “spirit,” “person,” and the criticized dependencies; this entry adds no supernatural account.
Senses.Note: The construction modifies both “spirit” (精靈) and “person” (漢). Those are different bearers of the same predicate, not different senses of the headword. No plain botanical referent was established in the sampled Zen deployments.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敲床竪拂，瞬目揚眉，指東劃西，皷脣搖舌，亦未免依草附木。
大盡三十日，小盡二十九，此依草附木，不知不覺一向迷將去。
機境上作活計，理性中求妙解，皆為依草附木之妖訛。
說得說失得麼。若有恁麼。盡是依草附木精靈。
若於死句下明得，依草附木，埋沒宗風，自救不可。

AlternateTargets: then stepped down from the seat
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "then descended from the seat" (便下座). In Chan records this is a formal scene-closing action tied to the high teaching seat, not merely someone sitting down or leaving ordinary furniture. The Buddha cases make the institutional structure explicit: the Buddha mounts the seat (陞座), the assembly settles, Manjusri or Kasyapa strikes the sounding block and announces the king of teachings' teaching or that the talk is finished, and the Buddha then descends. The phrase can close a spoken address after a final question, as when Linji tells the assembly to ask the two hall leaders about host and guest and descends. It also closes action without a final speech: after Magu exits during the exchange of seats, Linji descends. In the Mazu-Baizhang encounter, Baizhang rolls up the mat as soon as Mazu mounts the hall, and Mazu descends and continues the exchange in his quarters. The distinctive Chan deployment is the visible termination of the formal teaching-seat event; sometimes the descent itself is the entire recorded close.
Senses.Note: The phrase has 2,853 hits in 295 allowlisted texts. It regularly follows a final statement, verse, gesture, unanswered question, sounding-block announcement, or disruption of the seat event. The Buddha and Kasyapa/Manjusri cases are central #0g evidence for the Zen deployment of the Buddha as mounting and leaving the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日陞座。大眾集定。文殊白椎曰。諦觀法王法。法王法如是。世尊便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps record has the Buddha mount the seat, Manjusri strike the block and announce the teaching, and the Buddha descend.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日陞座。大眾集定。迦葉白椎曰。世尊說法竟。世尊便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A parallel Buddha case has Kasyapa announce that the talk is finished before the Buddha descends.

Occurrences.Kwic: 麻谷便出去，師便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji descends after Magu exits during their exchange of the high seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「大眾要會臨濟賓主句，問取堂中二首座。」便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji closes a host-and-guest notice by directing the assembly to the two hall leaders and descending.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明日馬祖昇堂纔坐師出來卷却簟馬祖便下座師隨至方丈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Mazu-Baizhang encounter, Baizhang rolls up the mat immediately after Mazu mounts the hall; Mazu descends and Baizhang follows him to the quarters.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “then” or “thereupon,” and the second means “shout”: “thereupon shouted.” This narrative action phrase occurs 4,723 times across 345 allowlisted texts. Either party may perform it: “the master thereupon shouted” and “the monk thereupon shouted” alternate within exchanges. In one, the monk shouts and the master says, “This old monk has taken your one shout.” Hesitation is a recurrent trigger: after being told “return my mirror,” the monk hesitates and the master thereupon shouts. The phrase also runs beside “thereupon struck”: the master strikes, the monk shouts, and the master covers his ears. It may follow a newcomer's arrival or a monk's bow. The expression records the timing and vocal act without adding an interpretation.
Senses.Note: This is a corpus-wide narrative action phrase. The curated occurrences describe actions by a generic master or monk in exchanges, so their speaker fields remain null. Compare “thereupon struck,” “shout,” “a single shout,” and “hesitation.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 三度被打僧擬議師便喝隨後打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: the master shouts when the monk hesitates and then follows with a strike, inside a raised Huangbo and Linji exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便喝。師曰。老僧被你一喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium: the monk shouts and the master says that he has taken the monk's one shout.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師便打，僧便喝，師掩耳，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Rain Mountain: the master strikes, the monk shouts, and the master covers his ears.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其僧禮拜，師便喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Strict Unification of the Five Lamps: the master shouts in response to the monk's bow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有僧從外來。師便喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium: the master shouts when a monk arrives from outside.

Occurrences.Kwic: 還我鏡來。僧擬議，師便喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps: the master shouts when the monk hesitates.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟陞堂有僧出師便喝僧亦喝便禮拜師便打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a raised Linji encounter, the master shouts, the monk shouts in return and bows, and the master strikes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師見僧來豎拂子其僧便喝師曰喝即不無且道老僧過在什麼處
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master raises the whisk when a monk arrives; the monk thereupon shouts, and the master asks what his own fault was.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “then or thereupon” (便), and the second means “strike or hit” (打): “thereupon struck.” It is a stock action formula of encounter dialogue. The framed form “the master thereupon struck” (師便打) occurs more than four thousand times, while the bare form occurs 7,585 times across 360 allowlisted texts. The action is not the master's alone: a monk strikes back in an investigation exchange, another monk explicitly slaps the master with one palm, and an old monk narrates receiving a punch, immediately striking, and striking again when the other hesitates. The formula also appears with an explicit object, as a palm slap, and before the recipient is driven out of the monastery. It stands beside the parallel formulas “thereupon shouted” (便喝) and “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), and records pair Deshan's staff with Linji's shout. The corpus attaches striking to named masters as a habit—Deshan is said to have loved chasing and beating monks who came to consult—and preserves direct remarks about a blow, including Mazu's “if I did not strike you, all quarters would laugh at me” (我若不打汝諸方笑我也). The action frequently follows a bow or a shout. The Chan deviation is its extraordinary density as public-interview punctuation and response, performed reciprocally by masters and monks. The texts narrate each act and consequence; this entry does not assign the blow an unstated pedagogical meaning.
Senses.Note: A stock action-formula performed by many masters and monks across the corpus (師便打 4254× in 271 texts). Occurrences are left unattributed (MasterName null) unless a single master's formal address (示眾) frames one — none of the curated occurrences is such a frame; each is dialogue or a raised/narrated case, so MasterName is null throughout even where the acting (師) is identifiable (Linji, Deshan, Mazu). Cross-ref (便喝) · (便棒) · (棒) · (喝) · (禮拜) · (無位真人).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師便打。僧擬提坐具。師又打云。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (鎮州臨濟慧照禪師語錄) (Linji's own record), a (勘辨) exchange: the master strikes (師便打), the monk moves to take up his sitting-cloth (僧擬提坐具), the master strikes again (師又打). The acting (師) is Linji; MasterName null per the stock-formula rule (dialogue, not 示眾).

Occurrences.Kwic: 也是。僧便打。師云。老僧過在什麼處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Same record; here the MONK strikes (僧便打) and the master asks "where is this old monk's fault?" (老僧過在什麼處). Demonstrates that (便打) is reciprocal, not master-only. The same exchange recurs in (古尊宿語錄) (C077n1710, lb 0756a07, 勘辯 section) and D48n8939 (lb 0875b08). MasterName null (the monk acts).

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟見僧來舉起拂子僧禮拜師便打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (王隨's abridged lamp record), (諸方雜舉徵拈代別語) (miscellaneous raised cases) section; third-person account of Linji — a monk comes, the master raises his whisk, the monk bows (僧禮拜), the master strikes (師便打); the account continues "another monk came" (別僧來) and, on the next line (lb 0302a11), "the master also struck" (師亦打). Links the bow (禮拜) to the blow. The same whisk episode appears in (祖堂集), (臨濟) section (師豎起拂子，僧便禮拜，師便打之, B25n0144 lb 0661a10). Raised/narrated case → MasterName null (the case is Linji's).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是無位真人師便打云無位真人是什麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集), (鎮州義玄禪師) section; the (無位真人) case — asked "what is the true person of no rank?" (如何是無位真人) the master strikes and says (無位真人是什麼)…; the next physical line completes it (乾屎橛) (lb 0223b07). Linji's case, narrated in a lamp digest → MasterName null. Cross-ref (無位真人) / (乾屎橛).

Occurrences.Kwic: 落浦遂喝，師便打之。因德山見僧參愛趁打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集), (臨濟) section; Linji questions Luopu (師問落浦：從上有一人行棒，有一人行喝…), Luopu shouts (落浦遂喝), and the master strikes him with the object-variant (師便打之). The clause "because Deshan, on seeing monks come to consult, loved to chase and beat" (因德山見僧參愛趁打) opens the following anecdote, in which Linji sends his attendant to test Deshan. Links (喝) to (打), shows the (之)-object variant, and characterizes the blow as a named master's habit. Dialogue → MasterName null (the acting 師 is Linji).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問如何是西來意師便打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集), (江西道一禪師) (Mazu) section; a monk asks "what is the meaning of the coming from the west?" (如何是西來意) and the master strikes (師便打), then remarks "he then said: if I did not strike you, all quarters would laugh at me," (乃云我若不打汝諸方笑我也 lb 0182a12) — an in-corpus comment on the act, which recurs in (古尊宿語錄) (C077n1710 lb 0616c21, 馬祖大寂禪師語錄). Narrated in a lamp digest, two-speaker → MasterName null (the acting 師 is Mazu).

Occurrences.Kwic: 淵與老僧一拳，老僧便打，淵擬議，老僧又打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a first-person account, Yuan gives “this old monk” a punch; “this old monk thereupon struck” (老僧便打), and when Yuan hesitates, the old monk strikes again. This anchors reciprocal and repeated action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 座曰：是。師便打趁出院。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the lecturer answers “yes” (是), the master “thereupon struck and drove him out of the monastery” (便打趁出院). The consequence is explicit but does not change the action sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便打一掌，師拓開云：山僧招得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk “thereupon dealt one palm slap” (便打一掌) to the master. The master pushes him away and says, “this mountain-monk brought it on” (山僧招得). This reverses the usual agent and recipient.

Senses.Explanation: In questions about what follows recognition or arrival, “guard and maintain” (保任) asks how something is to be kept in charge over time. The compound occurs 517 times in 180 allowlisted texts, while the question wording “how to guard and maintain?” (如何保任) occurs 158 times in 89. The records preserve sharply different replies. Asked how to guard and maintain from beginning to end, Baizhang Huaihai says, “Like a cattle-herder holding a staff and watching it, not letting it trespass on other people’s seedlings” (如牧牛人執杖視之，不令犯人苗稼). Guizong Zhichang answers, “One film is in the eye; empty flowers fall in confusion” (一翳在眼，空華亂墜). Another record answers the question “How is this matter guarded and maintained?” with “Take care!” (切忌), Deshan Zhixian answers “Guarding and maintaining is itself wrong” (保任即錯), and Qingyuan Weiyin answers Dahui, “Eat when hungry; sleep when tired” (饑來喫飯，困來打眠). A later direct definition by Yongjue Yuanxian says that what he calls guarding and maintaining is “not a fabricated conditioned act” but “nothing more than constantly being alert and not being mixed with ordinary mind” (非假造作有為之法，不過嘗惺惺地，不為凡心所雜而已). The entry reports these attested formulations without making one answer cancel the others.
Senses.Note: This is the primary Chan deployment. “From beginning to end, how to guard and maintain?” (始終如何保任) occurs 12 times in 11 texts, and “throughout the day, how to guard and maintain?” (時中如何保任) occurs 9 times in 9. The lone exact string “guarding and maintaining is itself wrong” (保任即錯) is retained because it is a text-drawn correction to the headword itself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。未審始終如何保任。百丈曰。如牧牛人執杖視之不令犯人苗稼。師自茲領旨更不馳求。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Changqing Da'an biography explicitly identifies Baizhang as the speaker of the cattle-herder reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 宗曰。即汝便是。師曰。如何保任。宗曰。一翳在眼空華亂墜
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Guizong lineage section records Guizong’s reply to the master later known as Furong Lingxun.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問此事如何保任師曰。切忌。問如何是最初一句。師便喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The exchange stands under a lineage subsection headed as a Sansheng Huairan descendant; the nearby heading does not safely supply a roster-linked speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 然所謂保任者，非假造作有為之法，不過嘗惺惺地，不為凡心所雜而已。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: This is Yongjue Yuanxian’s explicit definition in the general-discourse section of his extended record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：時中如何保任？師云：保任即錯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing section names Dingzhou Deshan Zhixian; no exact roster link exists for this Deshan, who must not be confused with Deshan Xuanjian.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慧曰：如何保任？師曰：饑來喫飯，困來打眠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui asks Qingyuan Weiyin how to guard and maintain; Weiyin answers, 'Eat when hungry; sleep when tired.'

Senses.Explanation: With a person as beneficiary and a proposition as object, the same compound means “vouch for” or “guarantee.” Damei Fachang tells a monk, “I now vouch for this matter for you; it will never be false” (我今為汝保任此事，終不虛也). This denotes an act of assurance rather than continued custody or maintenance, so no single precise English action covers both referents.
Senses.Note: The exact opening “I vouch for [it] for you” (我為汝保任) occurs twice in two texts, apparently as two witnesses to the same recorded exchange. It is therefore kept separate but not promoted to an independent multi-source validation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：我今為汝保任此事，終不虗也。僧作禮。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Damei Fachang section identifies Damei as the speaker.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘Juzhi's one finger.’ The phrase occurs 87 times in 47 allowlisted texts and names Juzhi's recorded response of raising one finger. The Lamp Record supplies the narrative behind the label: Tianlong showed Juzhi one raised finger; thereafter Juzhi raised one finger to visiting monks; when a boy copied him, Juzhi cut off the boy's finger, called him back, and raised his own finger. Later records place ‘Juzhi's one finger’ beside Xuefeng's rolling ball, Yunmen's looking-and-‘look!,’ Muzhou's ‘ready-made,’ Deshan's staff, and Linji's shout as a named response associated with a master. Verses call it ‘one-finger Chan,’ say it was used throughout Juzhi's life, and repeatedly ask or comment on where he was accurate. The entry reports the gesture, its narrative, and its later case-label use; the texts do not supply a further gloss for what the finger denotes.
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary finger into the stable name of Juzhi's public response and case. The headword is the case/device label, not a separate body-part sense. Cross-check with ‘one-finger Chan’ (一指頭禪): that compound names the same recorded device, so no second sense is created here. The underlying Lamp Record narrative is attested in T51n2076 even though its wording does not use the compact headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪峯輥毬雲門顧鑑。睦州見成俱胝一指。如生鐵鑄就。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's record lists ‘Juzhi's one finger’ among named masters' established responses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 俱胝一指頭上用此時節。鳥窠吹布毛處見此時節。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate Yuanwu passage says Juzhi used this occasion upon one fingertip and pairs it with Niaoke blowing a cloth hair.

Occurrences.Kwic: 俱胝一指頭，一毛拔九牛。華嶽連天碧，黃河徹底流。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse opens with the case label: ‘Juzhi's one fingertip; one hair pulls nine oxen.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 報言達磨西來意只在俱胝一指頭
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A collected verse says: ‘report that the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the west lies only on Juzhi's one fingertip.’ This is quoted as the verse's wording, not adopted as a definition.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘Qiannu’s soul leaves.’ In the Chan corpus this is the title and shorthand of a public case built around Wuzu Fayan’s question, ‘Qiannu’s soul departed—which one is the real one?’ The records preserve the question as an entering-interview topic, a case heading, a verse topic, and a question masters put directly to monks and laypeople. Wumen repeats Wuzu’s wording and follows it with a comment about knowing the real one, entering and leaving a shell as though lodging at an inn, and a warning not to run about wildly. Other records keep the case open through its own alternatives: ‘is it one or two?’, ‘is she karmic consciousness or mind-born?’, and ‘which one is real?’ One master answers the one-or-two question with ‘there is no need to display form and shadow’; another responds to the real-one question by striking twice and warning, ‘take great care against eloping.’ The case was also used for sustained examination: one lamp record says Yuanwu repeatedly pressed Xian Fuyan with it, and another records Fuyan warning a layman not to fasten onto Qiannu. Zen usage thus turns the tale-name into a compact, repeatedly interviewed case formula; the entry reports the alternatives the texts themselves ask and does not choose one for them.
Senses.Note: One thing: the named Qiannu departed-soul case. Its many answers and commentarial readings are not separate senses. Qiannu is a literary figure invoked inside Zen records, so #0g requires definition by this recorded deployment rather than by an outside hagiography or tale summary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 倩女離魂倩女離魂五祖問僧云。倩女離魂。那箇是真底。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's case heading and Wuzu's governing question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無門曰。若向者裏悟得真底。便知出殼入殼。如宿旅舍。其或未然。切莫亂走。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's attached comment supplies the shell-and-lodging language and warning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 鑑舉倩女離魂話，反覆窮之，大豁疑礙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The case is repeatedly used to examine Xian Fuyan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 嘗謁福嚴雅禪師，與論倩女離魂，話未終，雅曰：隨他去也。公曰：師意如何？雅曰：切忌向倩女處著到。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fuyan discusses the case with a layman and warns him not to fasten onto Qiannu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：倩女離魂事若何？師曰：月淡花移影。曰：未審他是業識？是意生？師曰：風搖水作波。曰：畢竟是一個？是兩個？師曰：形影不須彰，便脫狐窠臼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange explicitly asks whether the two are one or two and preserves the master's replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：倩女離魂，那箇是真底？師便打，僧無語，師曰：會麼？僧擬議，師又打，曰：切忌私奔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The stock real-one question receives two blows and the recorded warning against eloping.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一居士問：「倩女離魂，那個是真？」師曰：「河裏失錢河裏摝。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A layperson asks the fixed question and receives a different recorded reply.

Senses.Explanation: The components mean “biased or tilted” (偏), “within” (中), and “upright or straight” (正): "the upright within the biased." It is the second of the (五位) (Five Ranks) of (洞山良价) (Dongshan Liangjie), whose (五位君臣頌) gives it: (偏中正)，(失曉老婆逢古鏡)。(分明覿面別無真)，(休更迷頭猶認影). (曹山本寂) (Caoshan Benji), asked the (五位君臣旨訣), supplies the corpus's own definition: (正位即空界)，(本來無物)。(偏位即色界)，(有萬象形)。(正中偏者)，(背理就事)。(偏中正者)，(舍事入理) — i.e. "(偏中正): setting aside affairs and entering into principle" (偏中正者，舍事入理), the exact inverse of (正中偏者)，(背理就事). In his ruler-minister scheme (君為正位，臣為偏位) he assigns it: "the minister facing the ruler is (偏中正)" (臣向君是偏中正). It is deployed as a stock test-question — (如何是偏中正)？ — answered with a turning phrase (宏智正覺: 師曰：白髮老婆羞看鏡). A later sermon maps the ranks onto Linji-school terms (以濟宗論之): (正中偏奪人也)，(偏中正奪境也). Beyond the graphs and these attested self-definitions the texts add no further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The verse is (洞山良价)'s (五位君臣頌); the (舍事入理) / (空界)·(色界) / (君臣) definitions are (曹山本寂)'s, given in answer to (五位君臣旨訣) — do not cross-attribute the verse and the gloss. Both are witnessed across ≥2 independent lamp records (禪宗正脉 X85n1593, 五燈全書 X81n1571) AND in the masters' own recorded sayings: the verse in (瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄) (T47n1986B), the (旨訣) answer in (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄) (T47n1987A). Pairs with and inverts (正中偏) (舍事入理 vs 背理就事; 臣向君 vs 君視臣). Member of the Five Ranks (五位) with (正中偏) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到).

Senses.Explanation: Chan records deploy Layman Fu through a small set of repeated cases, verses, and writings. Their own identification says he lived at Yunhuang Mountain, planted two trees called the Twin Grove, and called himself the Future Layman Shanhui. His central public case has Liang Emperor Wu invite him to lecture on the Diamond Scripture: Fu strikes the desk once and leaves the seat; when the emperor says he does not understand, Zhigong says, 'the layman has finished lecturing.' Masters repeatedly quote and criticize his sayings. One address cites 'if you wish to know where buddha goes, it is only this voice,' then says Fu did not distinguish good from bad. Another says Fu only knew how to wash while clinging to a bridge pillar and release a boat, adding that this was stamped from a printing block and released from a mold. A biography records a monk awakening at words from Fu's Heart-King Inscription: 'the taste of salt in water, blue pigment in color—decidedly present, its form unseen.' A portrait inscription calls him neither Confucian, Daoist, nor Chan and criticizes his made-up conduct. His verse 'empty-handed I hold a hoe; walking, I ride an ox; a person crosses over the bridge; the bridge flows, the water does not' also circulates widely. The Zen deviation is this figure's life in the record as lecturer who strikes and leaves, quoted author, verse speaker, portrait subject, and target of masters' criticism—not a general biography of Fu.
Senses.Note: Exact count: 551 hits in 173 allowlisted texts. Layman-Fu-lectures (傅大士講) has 34 hits in 29 texts; Heart-King Inscription by Layman Fu (傅大士心王銘) 27 in 17; empty-handed holding a hoe (空手把鉏頭) 35 in 22; striking the desk once (揮案一下) 32 in 25. One person sense. Layman Fu is an invoked pre-lineage figure, not a Chan lineage master roster entry.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, transmit the lamp. The expression uses one lamp lighting the next for continuation from teacher to successor. Records pair it with continuing the flame, say that lamp follows lamp and ancestor transmits to ancestor, and ask what is being continued. The preface to the Jingde Record explicitly calls it 'the comparison of transmitting the lamp.' A later preface gives its own intensified definition: 'transmitting the lamp is transmitting this hot flame.' That hot-flame equation belongs to that preface's five-lamps discussion and is not imposed on every occurrence.
Senses.Note: Across both senses the headword occurs 982 times in 210 allowlisted texts. The succession formula 'lamp after lamp continues' occurs 71 times in 58 texts; 'continue the flame and transmit the lamp' occurs twice in two texts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'transmit the robe.' The compound occurs 430 times in 162 allowed texts. In lineage histories it names a physical handover associated with succession. The fullest direct account is Hongren's answer after giving Huineng the inherited robe. He says, 'When Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet trust; therefore the robe was transmitted to make clear that the teaching had been obtained. Now confidence is mature, the robe has become a source of contention; it stops with you and will not be transmitted again' (昔達磨初至，人未知信，故傳衣以明得法。今信心已熟，衣乃爭端，止於汝身，不復傳也). This account both states the robe's recorded evidentiary function and the reason given for ending its transmission. Other histories narrate that the time to transmit the robe arrived, that Hongren gave Huineng the robe and told him to guard what was entrusted, and that the transfer occurred secretly at night. Later records use the event as chronology, lineage claim, question, and criticism: one asks what is entrusted after Caoxi because 'from this point the robe and bowl were not transmitted' (自此不傳衣鉢), while Fuyan Baozong's address lists 'Huineng transmitting the robe through six generations, seeking that small advantage' (盧公六代傳衣，圖他小利). The collocation 'transmit the robe and entrust the teaching' (傳衣付法) occurs 26 times in 22 texts, 'transmit robe and bowl' (傳衣鉢) 31 times in 26, and 'not transmit the robe' (不傳衣) 16 times in 15.
Senses.Note: The primary sense is the lineage robe handover recorded across lamp histories, discourse records, and later comments. The entry does not treat possession of the robe as proof beyond Hongren's own quoted explanation, and it preserves the corpus's criticism and discontinuation language. Repetitions of the Hongren-Huineng event are parallel witnesses to one reported event, not separate events.

Senses.Explanation: The recurring narrative formula “a monk asked” (僧問). It identifies the questioner and opens or advances the public interview; the answer may be speech, a shout, a blow, another question, or an action. The monk can be wholly anonymous, introduced as “a monk,” marked as already present by “the monk,” or narrowed by a modifier, as when a monk who lectures on the Flower Garland scripture asks about the arising of true nature. The formula combines with event frames: “on account of a monk asking” introduces the dog-and-buddha-nature case; “after taking up residence, a monk asked” moves a biography into a master's recorded exchanges; “at the time a monk asked” introduces a challenge inside later comment; and “again raising [the case]: a monk asked Baizhang” quotes an older exchange in a later teaching-seat address. It also occurs with a master standing in the street and with questions about a temple's scene, Buddha, the ancestral teacher's coming from the west, the great purport, and the gate of not-two. These subjects do not create senses of the formula. The Zen deviation lies in the formula's structural work: it is the hinge by which lamp records, recorded sayings, and case collections preserve the questioner's public approach and the recorded response. It remains ordinary subject-plus-verb grammar, not the title of a fictional genre and not a noun meaning “public interview.”
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 27,950 occurrences in 406 texts. Translate with English article choice from context: normally ‘a monk asked’ on first mention and ‘the monk asked’ when already identified. Item-8 review found one grammatical event formula, not separate event and heading senses: “on account of a monk asking” (因僧問), “a monk asked” (有僧問), “at the time a monk asked” (時有僧問), “after taking up residence, a monk asked” (住後僧問), and “again raising [the case]: a monk asked” (復舉僧問) all retain the proposition that a monk asked, even when a compiler uses it to open a case. Eleven witnesses cover early and later lamp records, Linji's own record, case compilation, a raised old case, modified and anonymous questioners, speech and action answers, and biographical transition.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the 'monks' hall.' The term occurs 1,743 times in 275 allowed texts and denotes a physical communal building with an inside, front, door, bell, places, beds, and stored robe-and-bowl sets. 'In front of the monks' hall' (僧堂前) occurs 488 times in 155 texts; 'enter the monks' hall' (入僧堂) occurs 200 times in 101 texts; and 'inside the monks' hall' (僧堂內) occurs 94 times in 51 texts. The monastic regulations direct that the bell before the hall be struck three times before the assembly disperses (鳴僧堂前鐘三下。大眾問訊而散), and prescribe a donor's place inside the hall for a meal (僧堂內設施主位). In an encounter record, a monk puts down his axe and returns to the hall; the teacher later enters and finds him sitting beneath his robe and bowls. Dongsi Ruhui's students become so numerous that the hall's beds collapse, giving him the name 'Broken-bed Hui' (僧堂牀榻為之陷折。時稱折牀會也). In Zhaozhou's section, the assembly reaches the front of the hall and Zhaozhou shuts the hall door. Xuansha lists stream, buddha hall, and monks' hall as visible named places, then says, 'the stream is the stream, the buddha hall is the buddha hall, and the monks' hall is the monks' hall' (溪水是溪水，佛殿是佛殿，僧堂是僧堂). These predicates establish a building and its communal uses; the article adds no figurative reading.
Senses.Note: Required self-definition searches found no ordinary definition of the noun. One direct 'what is the monks' hall?' exchange in Xuansha's record answers 'not the monks' hall'; the broader preceding statement is included because it preserves the text's explicit three-place naming. Spatial collocations, regulations, beds, bell, door, and movement were harvested across independent genres.
