Occurrences.Kwic: 學徒既眾。僧堂牀榻為之陷折。時稱折牀會也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongsi Ruhui's biography says the hall beds collapsed under the numerous students and records his resulting nickname. The biographical narration remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大眾一時到僧堂前，師乃關却僧堂門，大眾無對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Zhaozhou section. During a narrated group encounter at Nanquan, the assembly reaches the hall and the door is shut; the case remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸上座！溪水是溪水，佛殿是佛殿，僧堂是僧堂，且作麼生會？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha's own record lists and repeats the stream, buddha hall, and monks' hall before asking the senior monks how they understand.

Senses.PreferredTarget: at the gate of light and shadow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "at the gate or threshold of light and shadow." The phrase occurs 28 times in 22 allowlisted texts. The corpus supplies its architectural contrast directly: people have not recognized "the coarse, shallow business under the gate of light and shadow" and mistake it for "the matter inside the house" (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere students are said to "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己), and an address warns, "do not bury yourself at the gate of light and shadow" (切忌向光影門頭自埋沒). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-deployment: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.
Senses.Note: One spatially loaded idiom covers the sampled uses. Warnings, criticisms, and Hongzhi's qualified acceptance are different appraisals of the same light-and-shadow threshold, not different things. The corpus's own gate/inside-house and formed-image/not-yet-formed-image contrasts establish the definition without requiring an added reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今人未認得光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事又爭得？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage explicitly calls it the coarse, shallow business under the gate of light and shadow and contrasts it with the matter inside the house.

Occurrences.Kwic: 惟認光影門頭當作自己。汾陽禪師亦云：『五位參尋切要知，纖毫纔動即差違。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The criticism says students recognize only the light-and-shadow gate as themselves, then quotes Fenyang on investigating the five positions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光影門頭休駐足，色聲叢裡好撐睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says not to halt at the light-and-shadow gate and to open the eyes amid the thicket of forms and sounds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然如是。光影門頭了事底漢即得。祇如賓主未分。影像未具時。如何履踐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi allows a person who settles the matter at the light-and-shadow gate, then asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed.

Senses.Explanation: Literally to enter settledness. Chan records narrate someone sitting and entering settledness, speak of later coming out of settledness, ask what it is for a monk to enter settledness, and repeatedly examine whether settledness can properly have entry and exit. In the Ancestor Hall Collection, a teacher asks Zhihuang whether he enters with mind or without mind; when Zhihuang says that while entering he sees neither a mind that is present nor one that is absent, the teacher replies that this would be constant settledness and should have no further entry or exit. In the Sanghanandi case, Sanghanandi says body and mind are both settled and that entry and exit do not lose the settled condition; Rahula asks what, then, enters and exits. Baizhang says not to take settledness and enter settledness, not to take Chan and think of Chan, and not to take buddha and seek buddha. Mazu classifies choosing good, rejecting bad, looking into what is empty, and entering settledness as contrivance. These literal predicates and recorded challenges define the entry without substituting another category for the Chinese wording.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted Chinese Chan corpus has 542 matches in 177 files. Eight matches in five files use the nominal formula 'as for entering settledness'; one passage asks what an entering-settledness monk is and answers that the four seas are originally clear. The Mirror Record quotes an outside treatise defining entry in terms of seeing a speck's nature as empty and the true principle of the ten directions; because the passage explicitly identifies that source and supplies a framework not established by the Chan encounters, it is inventoried but not adopted as this entry's definition. Narrative formulas also place entering and leaving settledness side by side: 'enter settledness, leave settledness' has six matches in six files, and its reversed order has five in five.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：「入定者為有心入定耶，為無心入定耶？若有心入定者，即一切有情悉皆有心，亦合得定；若無心入者，一切無情亦合得定。」智皇曰：「吾正入定之時，不見有無之心。」師曰：「若不見有無之心，即是常定，不應更有出入也。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Ancestor Hall Collection records a teacher asking Zhihuang, 'When entering settledness, do you enter with mind or without mind? If with mind, all living beings have mind and should also obtain settledness; if without mind, all nonliving things should also obtain settledness.' Zhihuang says that while entering settledness he sees neither a mind that is present nor one that is absent. The teacher replies, 'Then it is constant settledness and should not have further entry and exit.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 取善捨惡，觀空入定，即屬造作。更若向外馳求，轉疎轉遠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mazu says, 'Choosing good and rejecting bad, looking into what is empty and entering settledness, belong to contrivance. If you run outward seeking, you become increasingly distant.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 亦是三昧定，不用將定入定，不用將禪想禪，不用將佛覓佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang says, 'This too is complete command in settledness. Do not take settledness to enter settledness; do not take Chan to think about Chan; do not take buddha to seek buddha.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 至彼見僧伽難提安坐入定。尊者與眾伺之。經三七日方從定起。尊者問曰。汝身定耶。心定耶。曰身心俱定。尊者曰。身心俱定何有出入。曰雖有出入不失定相。如金在井金體常寂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Lamp Record narrates Sanghanandi sitting and entering settledness, then coming out after twenty-one days. Asked by Rahula whether body or mind is settled, he answers that both are. Rahula asks, 'If body and mind are both settled, how can there be entry and exit?' Sanghanandi replies that entry and exit do not lose the settled condition, like gold in a well whose substance remains still.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧曰：如何是入定僧？師云：四海本澄澄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Xiangji Zi, 'What is a monk who enters settledness?' Xiangji answers, 'The four seas are originally clear and clear.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 只謂離念入定。厭境求真。不知塵塵是文殊。念念即普賢故。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record criticizes 'merely leaving thought and entering settledness, rejecting objects and seeking the true,' saying this fails to know that each speck is Manjusri and each thought is Samantabhadra.

Senses.PreferredTarget: enter the chamber for an interview
Senses.Explanation: Literally "enter the room" (入室); in the primary Chan institutional deployment, enter a master's chamber for a private question, examination, or report: "enter the chamber for an interview." The headword occurs 2,365 times in 313 allowlisted texts across both senses. Productive interview forms include "entered the chamber and asked" (入室問, 31), "entered the chamber and presented his understanding" (入室陳解, 3), "chamber-entering disciples" (入室弟子, 44), and "during a chamber interview" (入室次, 204). Huqiu Shaolong enters and is questioned by Yuanwu. Another biography records a student entering to present his understanding, followed by the teacher asking how he understands. Tianyi Yihuai is tested during a chamber interview. A lineage notice counts 139 "chamber-entering disciples" and says each became a lineage master in one region. A later case describes Ciming placing a sword, sandals, and a basin in the chamber and saying "look, look" whenever someone entered; those who hesitated by the sword were shouted out. The term names the institutional setting, access, and status; it does not by itself guarantee approval, succession, or a particular result.
Senses.Note: The institutional noun "chamber-entering disciple" is an attested status label, but a single interview occurrence does not make a person a lineage heir. Speaker attribution must still follow each exchange's turns rather than the interview heading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日入室，悟問：見見之時，見非是見
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huqiu Shaolong's biography: "one day he entered the chamber; Yuanwu asked..." The narrative includes student and teacher, so unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師忽有省。入室陳解。遠云。子作麼生會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biography: "the master suddenly had an insight, entered the chamber and presented his understanding. Yuan asked, how do you understand?" Multi-speaker narration remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 入室次，覺曰：恁麼也不得，不恁麼也不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyi Yihuai's biography: "during a chamber interview, Xuedou said, thus will not do; not thus will not do." The quoted teacher is Xuedou; the interviewee is Yihuai, so unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 依白蓮僊法師。入室問具變之道，僊指行燈曰：如此燈者，離性絕非，本自空寂，理則具矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The biography says the student relied on Master Bailian Xian, entered the chamber to ask about the Way of complete change, and received an answer pointing to a moving lamp.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師入室弟子一百三十九人各為一方宗主轉化無窮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage notice counts 139 chamber-entering disciples and says each became a lineage master in one region.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慈眀室中插劒一口以草鞋一緉水一盆置劒邊每見入室即曰看看有至劒邊擬議者師曰嶮喪身失命了也便喝出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later case says Ciming placed a sword, sandals, and a basin in the chamber; whenever someone entered he said, 'look, look,' and shouted out anyone who hesitated by the sword.

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary motion sense is simply "enter a room." Biographical narration uses it outside the interview formula. One biography says, "he then entered the room, sat upright, and died at the age of seventy-four" (即入室，安坐而逝，壽七十有四). Another account says someone "entered the room to fetch the Complete Meaning Sutra and verify it" (入室取《楞嚴經》證之), then opened the book to a quoted passage. These are spatial movements into a room, not chamber interviews.
Senses.Note: Two independent allowlisted witnesses establish ordinary room entry through distinct following actions: sitting upright and dying, and fetching a named book. This remains separate so death-room and retrieval movements are not misread as interviews.

Occurrences.Kwic: 即入室。安坐而逝。壽七十有四。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongren's biography: "he then entered the room, sat upright, and died at the age of seventy-four." Ordinary spatial narration.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上下虛明如大圓鏡相似，入室取《楞嚴經》證之。開卷見「汝身汝心，外及山河、虛空大地咸是妙明真心中物。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography says the subject entered the room to fetch the Complete Meaning Sutra for verification and then opened it to a quoted passage.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to enter (入) mud (泥) and enter water (水). In Chan records it is a stock description of a master becoming involved in words, teaching, or an encounter for others. One passage expressly calls the interlocked condition 'gain within no-gain and no-gain within gain' entering mud and water, then pairs it with 'ride the thief's horse and pursue the thief's band.' Before an assembly a master says that he does not avoid others' scrutiny and enters mud and water 'for you people'; another record places the phrase as an answer in a numbered question-and-answer sequence. A historical contrast says that at Magadha the edge was already exposed and before Shaoshi Peak Bodhidharma 'entered mud and water.' The Zen deviation is this repeated use of ordinary muddy immersion for the teaching-seat act of entering entangling speech and encounters for an audience; the texts also criticize particular instances, so the phrase is not praise by definition.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 193 hits in 99 texts. No different referent requiring a split was found. Family checked against enter water and enter mud (入水入泥), drag through mud and trail water (拖泥帶水), mix mud and blend water (和泥合水), receive and guide (接引), and creeping vines or verbal entanglement (葛藤).

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇是無得失中有得失。有得失中無得失。喚作入泥入水。騎賊馬趕賊隊。借婆帔子拜婆年。難奈何。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Explicit naming formula and text-drawn companion images.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧不避諸方檢責，入泥入水，為儞諸人莫有會底麼？出來通箇消息看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master describes entering mud and water for the assembly and calls for a response.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰，如何是七同得失？師曰，入泥入水。曰，如何是八同生殺？師曰，自救不了。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct answer in a numbered public interview.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以摩竭陀國已露鋒鋩，少室峯前入泥入水，到這裏須是箇人始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Historical deployment linking Magadha and Bodhidharma at Shaoshi Peak.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'raise or present in full.' The expression occurs 1,834 times in 308 allowlisted texts. Chan records contrast it with a half-presentation: one discourse says that seeing no single form is only 'half presented' (半提) and that one must still know a time of full presentation. It regularly modifies a saying or command. Records ask how to speak 'one saying fully presented' (一句全提), pair it with 'the ancestral master's true command' (祖師正令), and call the flower at Vulture Peak and the snow at Shaoshi the separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented. Thus the Chan deployment is not merely completeness in the abstract: it is an utterance, command, or teaching-seat presentation brought forward without remainder. The texts also use the fixed compounds 'the true command fully presented' (全提正令) and 'a single saying fully presented' (一句全提).
Senses.Note: No second referent or word-class emerged. Uses with command, saying, and presentation are deployment shapes of the same act, not separate things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不見一色，始是半提
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse supplies the explicit contrast: even seeing no single form is only half-presentation; the following sentence requires knowing a time of full presentation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師正令，今古全提
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse pairs full presentation across past and present with the ancestral master's true command.

Occurrences.Kwic: 格外全提一句作麼生道
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks how to speak a single beyond-rank saying in full.

Occurrences.Kwic: 靈山花發，親示別傳；少室雪寒，全提正令
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat discourse joins the Vulture Peak flower, Shaoshi snow, separate transmission, and the true command fully presented.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一句全提，千差併會
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A recorded discourse says that when one saying is fully presented, the thousand differences gather together.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘whole or complete’ (全) + ‘trigger, pivot, or dynamic’ (機): the whole dynamic or full pivotal function. The compound has 843 occurrences in 224 allowlisted texts. It is especially visible in ‘the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用), with 115 occurrences in 60 texts. Yuanwu says this ‘whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches’ (全機大用觸處見成); elsewhere his record says ‘as the grass bends and the wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed’ (草偃風行全機獨露), then asks what one says without relying on any thing or phrase. ‘The whole dynamic alone exposed’ (全機獨露) occurs 21 times in 19 texts; ‘the whole dynamic thoroughly freed’ (全機透脫) occurs 5 times in 5; and ‘the whole dynamic alone functioning’ (全機獨用) occurs twice in 2. The Blue Cliff Record uses it both in the rubric ‘the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere’ (全機隨處齊彰) and in its comment that several actions are all ‘places of the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用處). A lamp-record master also uses the compound predicatively: ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search?’ (我若全機，汝向甚麼處摸索). These attested combinations supply the article's wording; the corpus gives no formula equating the compound with a further noun.
Senses.Note: The one hit for ‘whole dynamic + one who’ (全機者) occurs in ‘one who broadly displayed the whole dynamic’ (廓顯全機者); the final graph nominalizes the person and does not define the term. The one question ‘what is the whole dynamic?’ (如何是全機) receives the recorded answer ‘in the dead of night, the sun is bright’ (半夜日頭明); the record supplies no explanatory gloss, and this entry adds none. The same corpus-wide wording spans direct discourse, case rubrics, verse, and prose comment, so no master-specific key or second sense is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 全機大用觸處見成。溢目清光貫通今古。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's own record, first formal address: ‘the whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches; clear light filling the eyes passes through past and present.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 草偃風行全機獨露。正當恁麼時不依倚一物一句作麼生道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's own record, fourth formal address: ‘as grass bends and wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed; just then, without relying on one thing or one phrase, what do you say?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 直下更無纖翳。全機隨處齊彰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record, case-pointer rubric: ‘directly there is not the slightest screen; the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere.’ Editorial rubric rather than an encounter speaker, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。我若全機。汝向甚麼處摸索。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wudeng huiyuan, Fuzhou Baoguo Zhao section: in a formal address the master says, ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search?’ The section master is not linked through the roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然總是全機大用處。俱不如禾山解打鼓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record prose comment: ‘although all are places of the whole dynamic and great function, none equals Heshan's “knows how to beat the drum.”’ Editorial comment comparing recorded actions, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the entire body. The term occurs 1,418 times in 299 allowlisted texts and ranges grammatically from a noun ('fall short of the whole') to an extent expression ('entirely is the pearl'); these describe the same thing as a complete whole rather than different referents. Its characteristic Chan collocations make that whole 'appear' (378 hits in 174 texts) or be 'exposed' (153 in 95). Xuansha's pearl exchange says, 'the whole body is the pearl—who else would you have recognize it?' Teaching-seat verses pair a raised whisk, staff, dust mote, or opened sleeve with the whole body's appearing.
Senses.Note: The different grammatical placements do not warrant a split: noun, modifier, and extent readings all designate completeness of the same referent. The deviation lies in the recurring public formulas 'the whole body appears' (全體現) and 'the whole body is exposed' (全體露), not in an imported claim about a metaphysical 'total reality.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 既是一顆明珠，學人為甚不識？沙曰：全體是珠，更教誰識？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha's recorded pearl exchange predicates the whole body as the pearl.

Occurrences.Kwic: 極目青天無片雲，萬象森羅全體露。若也擬議更商量，特地翻成箇露布。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat verse uses the recurrent 'whole body exposed' formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉拂子云。盧舍本身全體現。當機直下沒纖毫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The whole body's appearance is spoken while the master raises the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 驀拈拄杖云：「龍袖拂開全體現，象王行處絕狐蹤。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master raises the staff and quotes the recurring whole-body-appears line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當機微笑，窺見一斑；依位無言，猶虧全體。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interview question contrasts seeing one patch with falling short of the whole.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the two halls fight over the cat
AlternateTargets: the two halls dispute the cat
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “the two halls fight over the cat.” The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 29 allowlisted texts; expanded forms specify “the east and west halls.” In the Chan record it is the opening formula and a short name for Nanquan's cat case. The monks of the two halls dispute a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” no one answers, and he cuts it. When Zhaozhou returns, Nanquan recounts the event; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head and leaves, and Nanquan says that had Zhaozhou been present, he would have saved the cat. Later records quote the formula before asking what should have been said, composing verses on the case, or giving prose comments. The exact headword names the dispute that occasions the case; it is not a separate event from “Nanquan cuts the cat.” Elsewhere the corpus explicitly asks why Nanquan cut the cat if killing living beings is a major precept, but no occurrence of this exact formula states Nanquan's reason.
Senses.Note: The explicit precept question belongs to the linked cat-cutting family and is anchored under “cut the cat” (斬猫) and “Nanquan cuts the cat” (南泉斬猫), whose headwords it contains. It is not duplicated here as a headword-free occurrence. The corpus alternates the two graphs for “cat” (貓 and 猫) and often adds “east and west” (東西).

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉東西兩堂爭貓兒，泉來堂內，提起貓兒云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻。」大眾下語皆不契泉意，當時即斬卻貓兒子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's record preserves the east-and-west-halls opening and Nanquan's demand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因兩堂爭貓，乃提起云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉便斬之。趙州自外至，泉舉前話，州脫草履安頭上而出，泉云：「子若在，即救得貓兒也。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later recorded-sayings collection gives the full dispute, cutting, and Zhaozhou sequel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日兩堂爭貓，泉提起貓云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉斬貓為兩段。南泉舉問趙州，州脫鞋戴出，泉云：「子在，救得貓兒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's verse-commentary collection restates the entire case before its verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日兩堂爭貓，泉提起貓，云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉斬貓為兩段。南泉舉問趙州，州脫草鞋戴出，泉云：「子在救得貓兒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Boshan Wuyi's collected comments quote the event as a public case before commenting on it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉禪師因東西兩堂爭貓兒，遂提起貓兒示眾，云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻也。」眾無對，泉便斬卻。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guxue Zhe's record introduces a verse with the east-and-west-halls narration.

Senses.Explanation: Literally (公) (public / government office) + (案) (case-file, legal record). In Chan it names a recorded encounter or saying of the old masters that is taken up and set before a student. Attested uses in the corpus make the legal-office figure explicit. Zhongfeng Mingben, asked what the 'public cases' spoken of everywhere are, answers that (公案) is a figure for the case-documents of a government office (公府之案牘): (公) is the shared principle the sages all travel by, (案) is the (正文) (the authoritative text) recording how they governed; and just as a litigant who cannot settle a matter brings it to the office to be decided by the case-files, a student who has some understanding he cannot settle brings it to his teacher, who 'raises a public case to decide it' (舉公案以决之). The (碧巖錄序) (三教老人) says flatly that the two graphs are (世間法中吏牘語) — clerkly-document language of worldly law — and that reading a case is like an old clerk judging a crime in court (老吏據獄讞罪); the patriarchs 'established them as public cases and left them to instruct the monasteries' (立為公案，留示叢林). Wumen Huikai in his own preface describes taking the ancient men's public cases as a knock-on-the-door tile (敲門瓦子) to guide students according to their capacity. The (碧巖錄) preface further dates and names the genre — (甞謂祖教之書)。(謂之公案者)。(倡於唐而盛於宋) ('the books of the patriarchs' teaching, called public cases, arose in the Tang and flourished in the Song') — and enumerates (其用有三) ('their uses are three'), each by a legal simile: (如老吏據獄讞罪)。(底裏悉見)。(情欵不遺) ('like an old clerk taking up the case-file and adjudging the crime — the bottom of it fully seen, no deposition left out'); (如廷尉執法平反)。(出人於死) ('like the commandant of justice applying the law to overturn a verdict and bring a man out from death'); (如官府頒示條令)。(令人讀律知法) ('like the office promulgating statutes so that people read the code and know the law'); summing up: (具方冊)。(作案底)。(陳機境)。(為格令) ('set down in volumes, made into case-files, presenting the encounter-situations, serving as regulations'). Inside the same book, the commentary to case 98 states how the things so named arose: (未有問答)。(未有公案已前)。(還有禪道麼)。(古人事不獲已)。(對機垂示)。(後人喚作公案) ('before there were questions and answers, before there were public cases — was there a Chan way? The men of old, having no other recourse, gave pointers according to the occasion; later people called these public cases'). A Qing-era record keeps the clerk figure: (言言見諦)、(著著歸宗)，(如老吏斷獄)，(引經合律)，(一毫頭也出入不得)，(所以喚作公案) ('…like an old clerk deciding a case, citing the canon and matching the statutes, with not a hair's breadth of leeway — that is why they are called public cases', 雲溪俍亭挺禪師語錄). The word is also spoken at the sight of an arriving monk — Muzhou's (現成公案放汝三十棒) ('a ready-made case: I spare you thirty blows'), raised by Dahui (舉睦州纔見僧云。現成公案放汝三十棒, 'he raised: Muzhou, as soon as he saw a monk, said, a ready-made case — I spare you thirty blows') and in the stock litany (德山見僧入門便棒)，(臨濟見僧入門便喝)，(雪峰見僧入門便道是甚麼)，(睦州見僧便道現成公案放你三十棒) ('Deshan, seeing a monk enter the gate, struck; Linji, seeing a monk enter the gate, shouted; Xuefeng, seeing a monk enter the gate, said, what is it?; Muzhou, seeing a monk, said, a ready-made case — I spare you thirty blows'); biographies later show that line itself given to students as a saying (話) to take up (源舉現成公案放汝三十棒話，不契 — '[the monk] Yuan raised the saying 'a ready-made case — I spare you thirty blows' and did not accord'), and Zhongfeng extends the collocation: (無邊眾生各各脚跟下有一則現成公案) ('boundless beings each have one ready-made case under their own heels'). The etymology is even posed as a test-question: (座下無席帽)，(案邊無胥吏)，(階下無荊條竹根)，(為甚麼祖師語言喚作公案)？ ('no magistrate's cap on the seat, no clerks by the desk, no switches below the steps — why are the patriarchs' words called public cases?', 聚雲吹萬真禪師語錄). The texts gloss the two graphs by the legal-record figure and add nothing beyond it, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Consistent across three independent Zen witnesses spanning Song to Yuan (碧巖錄序; 無門關 self-preface; 天目中峰廣錄), all foregrounding the legal-record sense. No master bends the term to a private meaning, so a single corpus-wide sense. Zen-scoped counts: (公案) 3,800x in 363 allowlist texts. Attested collocations: (現成公案) ('a ready-made case') 382x/154 texts; (古人公案) ('the old men's public cases') 138x/73; (一則公案) ('one case', counted with the measure word 則) 84x/57; the corpus's own tally of the case-literature, (千七百則公案) ('the seventeen hundred cases') 64x/45 (e.g. 凡一千七百則公案 'in all one thousand seven hundred cases', 天目中峰廣錄 0731a13); (舉公案) ('raising a public case') 22x/20; (看公案) ('looking at public cases') 16x/9 (諸方愛教人看公案 'everywhere they love to set people looking at public cases', 古尊宿語錄 C077n1710 0847a18); (公案未圓) ('the case not yet rounded off') 17x/15.

Occurrences.Kwic: 公案乃喻乎公府之案牘也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Answer (答) in (天目中峰廣錄); the speaker '(幻)' is (幻住), Zhongfeng Mingben's studio name. The locus classicus for the legal-record etymology.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二字乃世間法中吏牘語

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師所以立為公案。留示叢林者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (碧巖錄序) (三教老人). 'The reason the patriarchs established them as public cases and left them to instruct the monasteries.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂將古人公案。作敲門瓦子。隨機引導學者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen Huikai's own preface to (無門關) (慧開 names himself just before): he took the ancient men's public cases as a 'knock-on-the-door tile' to guide students.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未有問答。未有公案已前。還有禪道麼。古人事不獲已。對機垂示。後人喚作公案。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (碧巖錄), the commentary (評唱) to case 98 (cb:mulu '98', the 天平兩錯 'Tianping's two errors' case) — the book's commenting voice, (圜悟克勤): 'before there were questions and answers, before there were public cases — was there a Chan way? The men of old, having no other recourse, gave pointers according to the occasion; later people called these public cases.'

Senses.PreferredTarget: at the gates of the six faculties
AlternateTargets: at the gateways of the six faculties
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "at the gate-heads" or "gateways" (門頭) of the "six faculties" (六根): eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The phrase occurs 116 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says, "there is a phrase at the staff-head, beneath the straw sandals, three thousand miles away, and at the gates of the six faculties; if recognized at the gates of the six faculties, there is no need to seek separately three thousand miles away" (有一句子在六根門頭，向六根門頭薦得). Yuanwu describes the six faculty-gates as "clean-naked and bare" and then says the audience will not "turn the light around and look back" (六根門頭淨裸裸赤灑灑，只是不肯回光返照). Huangbo's record speaks of scraping and clearing at the gates of the six faculties until not a hair of greed or craving remains untreated (於六根門頭刮削併當，貪愛有纖毫治不去). Later addresses say a "natural ancient buddha" constantly "shines light and shakes the earth at the gates of the six faculties" (六根門頭放光動地), while Ying'an describes them simply as "bare" throughout the twelve double-hours. These are observable predicates and locations assigned by the texts; the entry does not substitute a general theory of sensation.
Senses.Note: Counted collocations: "shine light and shake the earth at the gates of the six faculties" (六根門頭放光動地), 14; "clean-naked at the gates" (六根門頭淨裸裸), 1; "scrape clean at the gates" (六根門頭刮削), 4; "recognize at the gates of the six faculties" (向六根門頭薦得), 1. No direct dictionary-style self-definition was found; the stable locative construction and its predicates define the deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有一句子在六根門頭。向六根門頭薦得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's instruction to Xiyou: "there is a phrase at the gates of the six faculties; if it is recognized at the gates of the six faculties..."

Occurrences.Kwic: 六根門頭淨裸裸赤灑灑。只是不肯回光返照。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's informal address: "the gates of the six faculties are clean-naked and bare; you only refuse to turn the light around and look back."

Occurrences.Kwic: 於六根門頭刮削併當貪愛有纖毫治不去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Huangbo's record: "at the gates of the six faculties, scrape and clear; if a hair of greed or craving remains untreated..."

Occurrences.Kwic: 常在六根門頭放光動地。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later formal address says it "constantly shines light and shakes the earth at the gates of the six faculties." The speaker has no validated roster link used here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二六時中卓卓地，六根門頭裸裸地
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ying'an's instruction to Wei: "throughout the twelve double-hours, standing distinct; at the gates of the six faculties, bare." No exact roster value is used.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to possess the eye — to have genuine discernment
Senses.Explanation: To possess or be equipped with (具) the eye (眼): to have the eye, meaning to possess genuine discernment. The eye is what distinguishes true from false in the recorded case comments. Recurrent closing invitations include 'let one who possesses the eye discern' (具眼者辨看), 'let one who possesses the eye look and take it up' (具眼者看取), and 'let one who possesses the eye distinguish it' (具眼者辯取); the form 'one who possesses the eye' (具眼者) occurs 363 times in 162 texts. A person may be called 'a patch-robed monk who possesses the eye' (具眼衲僧, 77 occurrences in 54 texts) or 'an adept who possesses the eye' (具眼作家, 4). Related forms are 'possess one eye' (具一隻眼, 381), 'possess the true eye' (具正眼, 52), and 'one who possesses the eye' (具眼底, 70). The headword occurs 1,346 times in 280 allowlist texts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Its recurrent closing formula invites one who possesses the eye to judge a raised case (具眼者辨看 / 看取 / 辯取); named possessors include a patch-robed monk (具眼衲僧) and an adept (具眼作家).

Occurrences.Kwic: 為復是神通妙用？具眼者辨看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Empty Valley Collection (空谷集), old cases and verses by Touzi Qing with comments by old Linquan (林泉老人評唱投子青和尚頌古), case four. The closing invitation 'let one who possesses the eye discern' (具眼者辨看) asks the reader to judge the raised case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 可中若個具眼衲僧出來道
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhusheng of Qingcheng (青城竹浪生禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). It calls for a patch-robed monk who possesses the eye (具眼衲僧) to come forward and speak.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若是具眼作家，句句之中須有超脫之機
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu (百愚禪師語錄), Longhua Temple record (龍華寺語錄). The phrase 'an adept who possesses the eye' (具眼作家) is followed by the demand that every phrase contain a working of release.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久，曰：具眼者看取。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Sengyin (僧印禪師). After a long pause, the master says, 'Let one who possesses the eye look and take it up' (具眼者看取).

Occurrences.Kwic: 瑯瑘門下還有具眼衲僧、真正道流麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), section on Chan Master Langya Huijue (瑯瑘慧覺禪師). The question asks whether Langya's followers include a patch-robed monk who possesses the eye and a genuine person of the Way (具眼衲僧、真正道流).

Senses.PreferredTarget: to be complete or fully endowed
Senses.Explanation: To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. The headword occurs 2,264 times in 303 allowlisted texts. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents.
Senses.Note: The former predicate/adjective targets were grammatical uses of the same completeness word and are merged. The Chan deployment includes both lack-nothing formulas and the corpus's criticism of resting on such formulas. The full-precepts compound remains under the precepts gate and should receive longest-match priority when indexed separately. Compare fully endowed from the beginning (本來具足), completely formed (圓成), lack (欠少), full precepts (具足戒), receiving precepts (受戒), and precept (戒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人具足，人人成現。問：如何是諸佛興慈運悲？師云：猫兒狗子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha says, "each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest," before the next public question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不論僧俗、男女、賢愚、貴賤，悉皆具足，曾無欠少。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The address explicitly ranges across social classes and says all are "fully endowed, without the least lacking."

Occurrences.Kwic: 無量劫中。本來具足。圓陀陀地。曾無一毫頭許欠少。曾無一毫頭許盈餘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's record says "fully endowed from the beginning" and directly glosses the range as neither a hair's breadth lacking nor a hair's breadth in excess.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人具足，物物圓成。拈一機則千機萬機頓赴，說一句則千句萬句流通。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address pairs "each person is fully endowed" with "each thing is completely formed."

Occurrences.Kwic: 最初被箇本來具足不假外求之說一印印定。次以聰明之資直下領過。自以為易不復究明。不覺置之無事甲裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's record criticizes being stamped and fixed by the saying "fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside," then taking it as easy and ceasing investigation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 徒知具足之虛談。終莫能得止飢之實效。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same passage calls merely knowing "fully endowed" empty talk that cannot actually stop hunger.

Occurrences.Kwic: 往鐘陵開元寺道玄律師受具足戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha's biography says he went to Vinaya master Daoxuan at Kaiyuan monastery and received the full precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 詣嵩嶽受具足戒。初習相部舊章。究毗尼篇聚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanquan's biography says he went to Mount Song, received the full precepts, studied the old rules, and investigated the Vinaya sections.

Occurrences.Kwic: 即為剃度。授具足戒。仍告之曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage biography records shaving the novice's head and then giving the full precepts.

Senses.Explanation: (兼) both / holding-together / combining + (中) within, amid + (到) arrive, reach: "arrival within both." It is the last of the Five Ranks (五位) that Dongshan Liangjie composed as the (五位君臣頌) in his own record — (正中偏) · (偏中正) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到) — his verse-line being (兼中到)。(不落有無誰敢和)。(人人盡欲出常流)。(折合還歸炭裏坐) (T47n1986B); the closing image "...fold back and return to sit in the charcoal" (折合還歸炭裏坐) is quoted 24 times across 20 texts. In the corpus it is deployed as a fixed catechism-question — (如何是兼中到) occurs 104 times in 57 texts, each master capping it (師曰。撥開雲外路。脫去月明前; 崑崙夜裏行; 十道不通耗; and so on) — and as a lemma the commentators define. Their self-definitions: "substance and function, thus-and-thus, is arrival within both," (體用如如為兼中到 X73n1457); "...the utmost of reaching the Way, principle and phenomena both extinguished," (此即兼中到也。造道之極，理事俱泯 X72n1437); and it is placed opposite the 4th rank by a (功)／(位) (merit/position) contrast — "(兼中至) is set where merit and position are both manifest, (兼中到) where both are extinguished," (兼中至，約功位雙彰時立，兼中到，約功位雙泯時立 X72n1441); the phrase (功位俱隱), which X72n1437 ties to this rank (兼中到，就功位俱隱時立), recurs 27 times across the corpus — though most of those (19 of 27) sit in the distinct (功勳) four-question catechism (轉功就位／功位齊彰／轉位就功／功位俱隱) that carries no explicit (兼中到) label. As with (正中來), one (五燈全書) (上堂) maps a single shout onto the ranks — (我此一喝)，(聖凡情盡)，(能所兩忘)，(妙盡有無)，(是兼中到也) — and in its Linji-school restatement says (兼中到)，(即元要妙旨也) (X82n1571). The graphs read alike across witnesses; the term carries no gloss here beyond its literal reading and its terminal place in Dongshan's set.
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide sense (SenseKey null): 276 occurrences in 84 allowlist texts. (Counts are whole-file, tag-stripped with <note>/<rdg>/<orig> apparatus excluded; gate-2 recount, confirmed by two independent recounts.) The source verse is Dongshan Liangjie's own (T47n1986B, 師。作五位君臣頌云…) — attributed to him; the remaining curated items are the fixed (如何是兼中到) catechism and later Caodong analytical prose, narrated/raised, MasterName null. VARIANT (the 至/到 question): (兼中到) (到 = arrive/reach) is the FIFTH and terminal rank and is stable across the corpus; it is distinguished from the 4th rank (兼中至) (至 = arrive) not by graph-sense — (到) and (至) are near-synonyms — but by the (功位雙泯) (both extinguished) vs (功位雙彰) (both manifest) contrast the texts draw (X72n1441). The real cross-text instability is at the 4th-rank NAME, not the 5th: (兼中至) (207×) is emended to (偏中至) (85×) by (寂音) (Juefan Huihong) (以對正中來), which X72n1437 records and rejects as (大悞後學). So (兼中到) as 5th rank should not be confused with the 4th-rank pair (兼中至)／(偏中至).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: X72n1437 (永覺元賢禪師廣錄, compiled by 道霈; 無異元來's own 廣錄 is the separate text X72n1435), (曹洞五位) commentary: (此即兼中到也)。(造道之極)，(理事俱泯)… A commentator's (永覺元賢, 無異元來's lineage-heir) self-definition. Analytical prose, MasterName null. lb ed=X 0541b19 (ed=R125 0715a08 not used).

Occurrences.Kwic: 兼中至，約功位雙彰時立，兼中到，約
Occurrences.AttributionNote: X72n1441 (五位宗旨 section): (兼中至)，(約功位雙彰時立)，(兼中到)，(約功位雙泯時立)，(大意如此)，(且止葛藤)。 The merit/position contrast distinguishing 4th (雙彰, both manifest) from 5th (雙泯, both extinguished). Senses.PreferredTarget: arriving within togetherness (the fourth of Dongshan's Five Ranks)
AlternateTargets: variant of the fourth-rank name (偏中至)
Senses.Explanation: (兼) both-together / combined + (中) amid, within + (至) arrive, reach: the fourth of the Five Ranks (五位) of the Caodong house. In (洞山良价)'s own (五位君臣頌) the cycle runs (正中偏) → (偏中正) → (正中來) → (兼中至) → (兼中到), the (兼中至) stanza reading "two blades cross points, no need to dodge; a good hand is like a lotus in fire" (兼中至。兩刃交鋒不須避。好手猶如火裏蓮。宛然自有冲天志). The corpus preserves TWO names for this fourth rank. (a) (兼中至) (Zen-scoped 207 hits / 64 texts) is used in Dongshan's (頌) and by later masters — (汾陽善昭) (問如何是兼中至師云意氣不從天地得英雄豈藉四時推), (密雲圓悟) (his own 頌: 兼中至，一棒當頭沒迴避), and the stock (如何是兼中至) catechism (88 hits / 46 texts). (b) (偏中至) (85 hits / 33 texts) is the name in (曹山本寂)'s (五位旨訣), which defines it by the (中孚) hexagram: (偏中至者中孚也)。(隨物不礙)。(木舟中虛虛通自在) (so the 本寂 edition; the 元證 edition punctuates 木舟中虛。虛通自在). The corpus itself records the two names as contested: (覺浪道盛), in his (洞宗標正), writes "'(正來)' and '(偏至)' have been litigated to this day" (正來偏至，聚訟至今) and (乃知偏中至不可以兼中至而重犯兼中到也). The variance runs inside a single master's record: at the identical prose slot (曹山本寂)'s (本寂) edition (T47n1987B) reads (塵中未帶名)。(是曰兼中至) while the (元證) edition (T47n1987A) reads (塵中未帶名)。(是曰偏中至). Both names denote the SAME fourth rank and are distinct from the fifth rank (兼中到) (276 hits / 84 texts; stanza 兼中到。不落有無誰敢和); the form (偏中到) does not occur in the corpus. (覺浪道盛) further glosses "the minister acting as regent" (偏中至者，即臣攝政也). The texts assign the rank no meaning beyond these stated formulations, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense — a rank name. Origin: (洞山良价)'s (五位君臣頌) (瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄, T47n1986B), which uses (兼中至). (曹山本寂)'s (五位旨訣) (撫州曹山本寂/元證禪師語錄) names the same fourth rank (偏中至) and its self-definition (偏中至者中孚也)… is a X(者)…(也) gloss. (汾陽善昭) (in the 汾陽昭禪師語錄 section of 古尊宿語錄, verified at the cb:mulu) and later masters use (兼中至); (覺浪道盛) (天界覺浪盛禪師語錄, 洞宗標正) uses (偏中至) and documents the (兼)/(偏) dispute. The (元證) (T47n1987A) and (本寂) (T47n1987B) editions of Caoshan's record disagree at the same prose slot — both cited above. Watch the three forms: (兼中至) = (偏中至) (the 4th rank, two names) != (兼中到) (the 5th rank). Counts measured over the 462-text allowlist, main body text (notes/apparatus excluded). Multi-source: Dongshan, Caoshan, Fenyang, Miyun, Juelang; T, C, J canons.

Occurrences.Kwic: 兼中至。兩刃交鋒不須避。好手猶如火裏蓮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄); (洞山良价)'s own (五位君臣頌) (師。作五位君臣頌云…). The origin, using the name (兼中至) for the fourth rank; the stanza continues (宛然自有冲天志) (0525c06). Primary source.

Senses.PreferredTarget: knowing hot and cold for oneself
AlternateTargets: one knows the water's temperature for oneself
Senses.Explanation: Literally, one knows (自知) cold and warmth (冷暖) for oneself, usually in the comparison “like a person drinking water, knowing hot and cold for himself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Huiming uses it after Huineng's instruction to report that he now has an entry; Huangbo joins it to conduct in each movement, dwelling, and instant; and other teachers pair it with looking for oneself rather than seeking from another. The phrase also becomes an object of interrogation: Longmen Foyan grants that hot and cold can be known, then asks what the one who knows for himself is. Daodu pairs “knowing hot and cold for oneself” with “handling slow and urgent matters for oneself” and says the matter cannot be spoken out even when both parties exert themselves. The Chan bend is this sensory commonplace's use as a first-person report, an answer about the Way, and a question about the knower; the texts preserve the water comparison and these recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 68 exact occurrences in 54 allowlisted files. The full water comparison occurs widely; variants reverse the order or substitute a fish drinking water. Distinct deployments include Huiming's report, Huangbo's instruction, a self-versus-other contrast, Daodu's paired formula, and Foyan's corrective question.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huiming reports to Huineng that he now has an entry, like a person drinking water and knowing hot and cold for himself.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo joins the water comparison to each movement, dwelling, and instant without difference.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Foyan hears the water formula, accepts knowing hot and cold, then deeply doubts and asks what the one that knows for itself is.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp record contrasts looking for oneself with seeking from another and gives the water comparison alongside each person exerting himself while climbing a mountain.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daodu says both parties cannot speak the matter out and pairs knowing hot and cold oneself with handling slow and urgent matters oneself.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a bean pops in cold ashes
AlternateTargets: a bean bursts in cold ash
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “a bean pops in cold ashes.” The image occurs 47 times in 37 allowlisted texts, chiefly in seventeenth-century Chan records. Its recorded neighbors make the image concrete: “the cold furnace has no smoke; a bean pops in cold ashes” (寒爐煙絕，冷灰豆爆); a public question asks, “leaving aside a withered tree flowering, what about when a bean pops in cold ashes?” and receives “a thunderclap on level ground” (平地一聲雷). Other addresses follow the phrase with impossible growth—stone bamboo shoots sprout, flame comes from an icy river, an iron tree flowers, and a wooden man claps—or simply with “suddenly, one sound” (驀地一聲). The corpus also speaks of “a person in whom a bean has popped in cold ashes” (冷灰豆爆底人), making the image an appraisal in an interview. Zen bends a domestic image of an unlikely pop from spent ash into a stock address and interview phrase, repeatedly paired with sound and impossible renewal. Those pairings are the texts’ own; this entry assigns no hidden event to the image.
Senses.Note: Event phrase, attributive person-label, and poetic heading all retain the same cold-ash image. They do not name different things. The family comparison with “dead ashes” (死灰), “cold ashes” (寒灰), and “a withered tree flowers” (枯木開花) supports the contrast visible in the passages but not an imported psychological explanation.

師問眾：「枯木開花即不問，冷灰豆爆時如何？」定侍者云：「平地一聲雷。」

AlternateTargets: ordinary feelings and a sage's views
Senses.Explanation: A paired expression: ordinary feelings (凡情) and holy views (聖見). Caoshan's recorded statement supplies its defining deployment: ordinary feelings and holy views are the golden lock on the dark road and must turn back and forth (凡情聖見是金鎖玄路，直須回互). Later records preserve that statement, ask how the required interchange is accomplished without falling into one of Caoshan's three fallings (三種墮, 'three fallings'), say that the activity produced by ordinary feelings and holy views both ceases (凡情聖見所作俱息), or say that the two mutually interchange (凡情聖見共相回互). Another recorded address says there is no need to pick them away before naming cold as cold everywhere and heat as heat everywhere. These uses describe what the texts do with the pair without recasting it as a generic abstraction.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 20 exact occurrences in 15 texts. The Caoshan witnesses vary between golden lock (金鎖) and golden pin (金銷), and between dark road (玄路) and dark pass (玄關). The exact four-graph headword remains stable. SenseKey is null because Caoshan's statement became a stock formula quoted and examined across the corpus; its historical attribution does not make the later meaning private to Caoshan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 。從來離名狀。天真忘性相。是曰兼中到。三種墮三種墮師曰。凡情聖見是金銷玄路。直須回互。夫取正命食者。須具三種墮。水牯牛。

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingning Jing (攖寧靜禪師語錄), in a response concerning Dongshan. It says ordinary feelings and holy views mutually interchange (凡情聖見共相回互), directly preserving the verb in Caoshan's formulation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the place where one comes out.' The compound occurs 620 times in 162 allowed texts. It appears in questions about a student's place to emerge and the buddhas' place to emerge, and as a predicate of words and answers: Yuanwu says that a line 'has a place to emerge' (句裏有出身處) and that saying either 'it is destroyed' or 'it is not destroyed' has such a place. One lamp encounter gives the shortest direct answer. Asked whether there is a place to emerge when the spirit platform is not established, Huaguang Fan says there is; asked, 'What is the place to emerge?' he answers, 'Emerge' (如何是出身處。出). Another record contrasts having one with lacking one: 'There must be a place to emerge; if there is no place to emerge, it is also like a black ox lying in dead water' (須有出身處始得。若無出身處，也似黑牛臥死水). The stock question 'What is the buddhas' place to emerge?' receives many recorded answers, including Yunmen's 'East Mountain walks on water' (東山水上行). A question about the student's place to emerge receives 'Xuefeng was originally a man from Lingnan' (雪峰元是嶺南人), using the graphs' ordinary sense of geographic origin inside the same question form. The corpus also has 66 occurrences of 'the one route of emergence' (出身一路), 61 of 'have a place to emerge' (有出身處), and 13 of 'have no place to emerge' (無出身處).
Senses.Note: The entry keeps the observable range—question, answer, predicate, contrast, and geographic wordplay—without assigning an unstated significance to any answer. The numerous repetitions of Yunmen's East Mountain case are later records and comments on the same public case, not independent definitions.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies, Yunmen section. Yunmen answers the stock question about the buddhas' place to emerge.

Occurrences.Kwic: 句裏有出身處。劫火光中立問端。衲僧猶滯兩重關。這僧問處。先懷壞與不壞。是兩重關。若是得底人。道壞也有出身處。道不壞也有出身處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu's prose on case twenty-nine. He predicates a place of emergence of a line and of both answers to the destruction question.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Strict Continuation of the Five Lamps. An assembly address directly contrasts having and lacking a place to emerge, then asks for an emerging line.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a lid fitting the box, heaven and earth
AlternateTargets: box and lid, heaven and earth
lid matching box — heaven and earth
Senses.Explanation: The components mean “box or case” (函), “lid or cover” (蓋), and “heaven and earth,” literally qian and kun, the first two trigrams of the Book of Changes (乾坤): "a lid fitting the box, heaven and earth." The corpus attests (函蓋) as a box and its lid that correspond — the collocation (函蓋相稱) / (函蓋相應) recurs (e.g. B25n0144 著函，函蓋相稱故, "[the lid] on the box, because box and lid correspond"), and (乾坤) is the standard pairing for the whole cosmos. The phrase is the FIRST of the (雲門三句) (Yunmen's three phrases), paired with (截斷眾流) and (隨波逐浪). Its attested history in the corpus: Yunmen (雲門文偃) delivers it in his own (廣錄) as a (示眾) — (函蓋乾坤目機銖兩)。(不涉春緣) (T47n1988; this edition reads 不涉春緣, where other editions read 不涉萬緣); his heir (德山緣密) (德山圓明密) (遂離其語為三句) — "then separated his words into three phrases": (函蓋乾坤句)、(截斷眾流句)、(隨波逐浪句) (人天眼目 T48n2006; also J29nB244). (圜悟克勤) (recorded in 人天眼目 as 圓悟曰) glosses the first phrase with a (則)X(也) formula: (本真本空)。(一色一味)。(非無妙體)。(不在躊躇)。(洞然明白)。(則函蓋乾坤也) (T48n2006). In the record it is widely put as a test-question (如何是函蓋乾坤句) (54 occurrences in 33 allowlist texts) and answered variously (日出東方夜落西 T51n2077/X78n1556; 遍界黑漫漫 J25nB175; 吞吐虛空 J25nB171), and carried by verse-commentary (函蓋乾坤體自然，箇中原不著毫端; 函蓋乾坤事莫窮，頭頭物物露真風). The texts assign the phrase no gloss beyond the literal image and the (則)X(也) lines quoted above, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The three-phrase set (雲門三句) = (函蓋乾坤) · (截斷眾流) · (隨波逐浪). Structural facts (describe-only): (1) the phrase originates in Yunmen's own (示眾) as one line of the triad (函蓋乾坤)、(目機銖兩)、(不涉萬緣) (春緣 in T47n1988); the numbered (三句) framing and the phrase-name (函蓋乾坤句) are the systematization of his heir (德山緣密), recorded in (人天眼目) and the lamp/(語錄) texts. (2) ORTHOGRAPHIC VARIANT: the water-radical form (涵蓋乾坤) occurs once in the allowlist (J40nB472), there in a different phrase (有時芥子藏身，有時涵蓋乾坤), not the (雲門三句) context. Do not cross-attribute the retold cases: Yunmen's own (示眾) (T47n1988) vs. the compiler-systematized exposition (人天眼目) vs. later (上堂) that merely raise the three (五燈會元 昔日雲門有三句).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雲門匡真禪師廣錄) (Yunmen's own Extended Record); a (示眾云) (示眾云…作麼生承當。代云。一鏃破三關). Yunmen's own record, single-speaker instruction — the primary source of the phrase. Occurrences.AttributionNote: (嘉興藏) text (J29nB244); (頌) (verse-commentary) on (函蓋乾坤句), following the same page's systematization (後德山圓明密禪師遂離其語為三句)：(函蓋乾坤句)、(截斷眾流句)、(隨波逐浪句) (德山圓明密 = 德山緣密). Verse-commentary → MasterName null; shows the (頌古) deployment of the phrase.
