Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元); a (上堂) raising the three (昔日雲門有三句。謂函蓋乾坤句。截斷眾流句…). Raised → MasterName null. X-canon lb ed=X 0373a24 (co-located ed=R138 0693a09 not used).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是函蓋乾坤句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (信州西禪欽禪師) section; the stock test-question deployment (如何是函蓋乾坤句) (answer 師曰。天…). Two-speaker (僧問) → MasterName null. X-canon lb ed=X (co-located ed=R138 0575… not used).

Senses.Explanation: To divide (分) and to distinguish or separate (別): 'to distinguish' or 'tell apart,' and as a noun, distinguishing. The Chan corpus most often places it in negative constructions: 'do not arouse distinguishing' (不起分別), 'do not distinguish' (莫分別), and 'apart from distinguishing' (離分別). It is paired with 'thinking' (思量)—'thinking and distinguishing' (思量分別, 165 occurrences)—and with 'deluded thought' (妄想), as 'deluded-thought distinguishing' (妄想分別). Dahui says, 'this matter is not what thinking and distinguishing can grasp; now say—when you neither distinguish nor think, what is it?' (是法非思量分別之所能解。且道不分別不思量時是箇甚麼). One passage says, 'because of second-thought distinguishing there are marks; apart from distinguishing there really are no marks' (以第二念分別故有相；若離分別，實無有相). Another says, 'when the distinguishing mind arises, one sees objects existing—this is called ignorance' (分別心起，見有境界，名為無明). A positive use also occurs: the Platform Record preserves the line, 'well able to distinguish the marks of all things, yet unmoved from the first principle' (能善分別諸法相，於第一義而不動). Attested collocations include 'the distinguishing mind' (分別心, 88 occurrences), 'without distinguishing' (無分別, 436), 'arouse or not arouse distinguishing' (起／不起分別), 'thinking and distinguishing' (思量分別), and 'deluded-thought distinguishing' (妄想分別). The entry records these uses without replacing 'distinguish' with an abstract theory.
Senses.Note: The Chan-record deployment is predominantly "the distinguishing to be dropped" (不起／莫／離分別, "do not arouse / do not / apart from distinguishing," paired with "thinking" (思量) and "deluded thought" (妄想)), while the Platform Sutra preserves a positive "well able to distinguish the marks of all things" (善分別諸法相). The Records of the Source-Mirror (宗鏡錄) witness by Yongming Yanshou (永明延壽) comes from expository prose and supplies the explicit equation that the arising of the distinguishing mind (分別心) is called ignorance (無明). Compare "thinking" (思量), "deluded thought" (妄想), and "the distinguishing mind" (分別心).

Occurrences.Kwic: 能善分別諸法相，於第一義而不動。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Ancestor's Teaching Treasure (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Ancestor's Teaching Treasure (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Ancestor's Teaching Treasure (六祖大師法寶壇經))); a Vimalakīrti-sūtra line quoted approvingly (故經云…, "therefore the sutra says…") — the preserved positive sense: skillful distinguishing that does not disturb the first principle. Raised sutra quote, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是法非思量分別之所能解。且道不分別不思量時是箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄), by Dahui Zonggao, his upper-hall address (上堂) — he abruptly takes the staff and strikes it down once (驀拈拄杖卓一下), then says this; distinguishing (分別) paired with thinking (思量) as what cannot reach "this matter" (是法).

Occurrences.Kwic: 以第二念分別故有相；若離分別
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Teaching Altar of Chan Master Shiyu (石雨禪師法檀), the record of Shiyu Mingfang (石雨明方), in an address to the assembly (示眾). The passage says that marks arise with second-thought distinguishing and are absent apart from it (分別). Shiyu Mingfang is absent from the roster, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 分別心起。見有境界。名為無明。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Records of the Source-Mirror (宗鏡錄), by Yongming Yanshou (永明延壽). The passage equates the arising of the distinguishing mind (分別心) with seeing objects as existing (見有境界), and names that ignorance (無明). It is cited only for this explicit equation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, unable to separate and set out an account. The phrase occurs 100 times in 63 allowlisted texts. It appears both as self-report and as an interview verdict: a monk says he cannot account for a distinction between expounding teachings and responding to the occasion; a master tells a questioner, 'look at you, unable to account for it'; and masters themselves say they cannot account for a fan-name test, a north-or-south salutation, or which recorded saying is deep or shallow. Zhaozhou's 'the highest way is not difficult' exchange supplies a famous duration formula: he says someone once asked him and he was unable to account for it for five years. A later address turns the verb back on the listener: if unable to account for it, one must carefully account for it.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation lies in public interview: ordinary inability to explain becomes both the participant's admission and the examiner's verdict, while masters also use it of their own inability. 'Explain,' 'distinguish,' and 'sort out' are contextual English renderings of the same act of furnishing an account, not different things; the corpus does not warrant multiple senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。是時人窠臼否？師曰：曾有人問我，老僧直得五年分疏不下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's exchange supplies the fixed five-year formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：王爺還是演教？還是酬機？王云：先演教，後酬機。云：衲子分疏不下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk explicitly reports inability to account for the distinction made in a public exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 萬指叢中，請師端的。」師云：「看你分疏不下。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master uses the phrase as an interview verdict on the questioner.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「和尚不妨著眼。」師云：「老僧分疏不下。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master applies the phrase to himself in a fan-naming test.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧到者裏直是分疏不下，正不知那一句是深、那一句是淺？那一則是難、那一則是易？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse spells out the distinctions the speaker says he cannot account for.

Occurrences.Kwic: 居士向者裏還分疏得下麼？分疏看。若分疏不下，直須仔細分疏
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address contrasts being able and unable to account, then issues the command to account carefully.

Senses.PreferredTarget: strictly avoid / take care not to
Senses.Explanation: An emphatic warning governing an action or error: literally 'urgently avoid,' hence 'strictly avoid,' 'take care not to,' or 'beware of.' The object supplied by the record must be translated rather than replaced by a general spiritual warning. Daowu says, 'where knowledge does not reach, strictly avoid speaking of it' (智不到處，切忌道著); Daoqian answers a question about words that display the Way with 'strictly avoid choosing' (切忌揀擇); Tianyin tells the assembly 'strictly avoid conjecturing' (切忌卜度). Other high-seat warnings preserve concrete allusions: 'the sword has long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat' (劍去久矣，切忌刻舟), and 'if you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, beware being branded on the forehead' (不是龍門客，切忌遭點額). Its Chan deployment is a direct warning embedded in interviews and public addresses, not a commentator's private aside.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 2,532 hits in 319 texts. Frequent governed families include speaking, choosing, conjecturing, mistakenly citing, and missing or mishandling something. Cross-check with 'strictly do not' (切莫) and 'do not' (莫): the adverb 'urgently/strictly' (切) supplies urgency, while the following verb phrase supplies the prohibited act. No distinct noun or title use found, and no master-specific sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 泉曰。智不到處。作麼生宗。師曰。切忌道著。泉曰。灼然。道著即頭角生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Encounter warning: where knowledge does not reach, 'strictly avoid speaking of it'; Nanquan immediately agrees and continues the wording.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：至道無言，借言顯道。如何是顯道之言？師曰：切忌揀擇。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct interview answer: to a question about language that displays the Way, the master says 'strictly avoid choosing.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還覺毛寒骨豎麼？切忌卜度。」便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: High-seat warning against conjecturing, immediately followed by stepping down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拍膝，云：劍去久矣，切忌刻舟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Concrete warning using the lost-sword/marked-boat allusion: the sword is long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不是龍門客，切忌遭點額；邢箇是龍門客，一齊點下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dragon Gate warning: one who is not its successful guest must beware the forehead brand; the speaker then brands all together.

AlternateTargets: before and after are cut off
Senses.Explanation: Literally, the limits (際) before and after are cut off (斷). The records repeatedly place the phrase in the formula 'when not one thought arises, the before-and-after limits are cut off' (一念不生，前後際斷), and biographies use it for a recorded event occurring at words or while raising a question. Chan usage does not make that condition a final verdict: Dahui quotes people who obtain bodily and mental extinction, the before-and-after limits cut off, resting and ceasing, and take it as ultimate, then says that this 'fine condition' obstructs them. Another lamp record says of the same event that the person had 'died and could not come alive'; a public interview answers 'what about when the before-and-after limits are cut off?' with 'raise thirty blows,' followed by an actual strike. The Zen deviation is therefore the phrase's use as both a named event and something masters publicly test and criticize; this entry does not turn it into the roadmap's unattested 'timeless gap.'
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 211 hits in 95 texts. One corpus-wide sense: the different appraisals concern the same condition and do not warrant interpretive sense menus.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故心要牋云。若一念不生。則前後際斷。照體獨立。物我皆如。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recurring formula: no thought arises and the before-and-after limits are cut off.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今人多是得箇身心寂滅前後際斷。休去歇去一念萬年去。似古廟裏香爐去。冷湫湫地去。便為究竟。殊不知。却被此勝妙境界障蔽。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Explicit criticism of treating the condition as ultimate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師於言下，忽然前後際斷，雖然動相不生，却坐在淨躶躶處。悟謂曰：也不易，你得到這田地，可惜死了不能得活，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical event followed by the teacher's criticism that the person has died and cannot come alive.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：未生事如何？師云：劫風吹不起。曰：已生後如何？師云：逆水泛輕舠。曰：前後際斷又如何？師云：提起三十棒。曰：即今在甚麼處？師便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public-interview deployment: the phrase is questioned and answered with thirty blows and a strike.

Senses.Explanation: A noun for a very short interval. The corpus measures events within “one instant,” compares three years to “the interval of an instant,” and states directly that an instant is swift as a finger-snap. In expository passages it is the unit in the sequence “the previous instant ceases; the next instant arises,” while other records contrast awakening “in an instant” with wandering for myriad ages. Chan deployment repeatedly makes this inherited time-word the smallest stated interval for a change, contrast, or event. The texts do not make it a title or person, and the differing events assigned to the interval are readings of the same time-unit rather than separate senses.
Senses.Note: No master-specific or title/person sense was found. The entry describes the unit and its attested comparisons; it adds no claim beyond those comparisons.

Occurrences.Kwic: 匪用剎那之力。頓獲玄珠
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Source-Mirror says it does not require even an instant's effort before the next clause, “suddenly obtain the dark pearl.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 此流水。剎那生滅。前剎那滅。後剎那生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An explicit temporal sequence compares flowing water with arising and ceasing instant by instant: the former instant ceases and the latter arises.

Occurrences.Kwic: 倐忽三載，若剎那際
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Three years are retrospectively compared to the interval of an instant.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無一剎那而不受生。無一剎那而不變滅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng states that there is no instant without undergoing birth and no instant without change and cessation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 悟即剎那成佛，迷而萬劫輪流
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse contrasts becoming a buddha in an instant upon awakening with cycling for myriad ages while confused.

Occurrences.Kwic: 剎那疾如彈指
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct comparison says, “an instant is swift as a finger-snap.”

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the cutting edge of a sword. Chan records repeatedly place speech and encounter “on the sword-edge.” The Blue Cliff Record preserves the explicit contrast: “if you go on the sword-edge, it is quick; if you look from discriminating consciousness, it is slow.” A collected address pairs the sword-edge with thin ice and asks who can tread there, immediately before saying that the lineage's wondrous phrase is hard to state by the road of words. Another master calls “the phrase that meets the occasion” a sword-edge matter and records that asking “how?” or “what?” already leaks. The expression also appraises a recorded response: after Yangshan pushes out a pillow, Guishan says that Huiji used a sword-edge matter; a later master quotes that verdict and disputes whether it qualifies. Elsewhere masters speak of walking, turning the body, eating, dressing, or meeting on the edge. The deviation is the corpus's own recurrent deployment: a literal weapon-edge becomes the named ground on which Chan answers, phrases, actions, and appraisals are recorded as taking place; this entry does not assign the image a further mystical meaning.
Senses.Note: Translate the object, not as an unexplained metaphor. The evidence links it especially to “the phrase that meets the occasion” (當機一句), quick response, and later appraisal of an encounter. It remains distinct from “sword” (劍), the whole weapon, and from the broader public-interview terms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人道。若向劍刃上走則快。若向情識上見則遲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record quotes an explicit contrast between going on the sword-edge quickly and looking from discriminating consciousness slowly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 劍刃輕氷，誰當履踐？宗乘妙句，語路難陳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address pairs sword-edge and thin ice, asks who will tread them, and follows with the lineage's phrase being hard to state by the road of words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當機一句是劍刃上事，不得如何若何，纔動著已成滲漏了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master directly calls the phrase that meets the occasion a sword-edge matter and rejects delayed “how/what” speech as leakage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 仰推出枕子。溈山曰：『寂子用劍刃上事。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guishan appraises Yangshan's act of pushing out a pillow as using a sword-edge matter.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "outside the eon." The Chan corpus uses it as a productive modifier and location in sayings and verse: "spring light beyond the eon" (劫外春光), "the spring beyond the eon returns and the ten thousand things wither" (劫外春回萬物枯), and "the true lineage beyond the eon" (劫外真宗). It is paired explicitly with the time before buddhas and patriarchs were born: "before buddhas and patriarchs were born, outside the empty eon" (佛祖未生空劫外). It also enters public address as a demand to "take responsibility beyond the eon" (於劫外承當), contrasted in the same question with meeting now (而今相見, "meeting at present"). The corpus thus bends chronological language into a recurrent Chan register for the sayings, activity, spring, and lineage it places outside or before measured epochs.
Senses.Note: Count: 740 occurrences in 221 allowlisted texts. Title uses such as "Record Beyond the Eon" (劫外錄) are proper-title compounds but do not make "beyond the eon" (劫外) itself a different thing. Related "empty eon" (空劫) should be cross-checked as a distinct headword, not silently equated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 儻肯於劫外承當，更何必而今相見？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case commentary contrasts taking responsibility beyond the eon with meeting now.

Occurrences.Kwic: 壺中消息。劫外春光。還他一氣連枝。須是同身共命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's upper-hall record uses the recurrent spring-light compound.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛祖未生空劫外，正偏不落有無機。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later upper-hall verse explicitly connects the phrase with before buddhas and patriarchs were born.

Occurrences.Kwic: 劫外春回萬物枯，山河大地一塵無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange answers with the verse line 'spring beyond the eon returns; all things wither.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 克揚劫外真宗，維暢今時懿矩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission-oriented prose passage calls it the true lineage beyond the eon and pairs it with present-day standards.

Senses.PreferredTarget: stir a thought and at once deviate
AlternateTargets: move a thought and immediately go astray
raise a thought and at once miss
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” (擬心即差), but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” (當體便是，動念即乖), then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes (不離目前). Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” (不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計). Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” (不擬不動，土木無殊，行脚人須得轉身一句). In direct questions, Tianyin answers “What is the body of things?” (如何是法身) with the phrase, while Linye Qi answers “How, finally, should one head toward it?” (畢竟如何趨向) with it and answers the follow-up “what about when thought does not move?” with “the eyebrows are above the eyes” (眉毛在眼上). The record thus bends an ordinary warning about a wayward thought into a portable Chan verdict while its own corrections exclude “do not think” as a complete gloss.
Senses.Note: The common parallel begins with either “form an intention” (擬心) or “raise the mind” (舉心), followed by “at once err” (即差). The entry does not infer why moving thought deviates; it records the phrase's question-answer and verdict deployments and the texts' explicit dead-water, wood-and-earth, and eyebrow replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當體便是。動念即乖。猶如虛空無有邊際不可測度。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo's Essentials of Transmitting Mind, recorded by Pei Xiu; the phrase occurs as a direct compact verdict after “it is just this.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬心即差動念即乖有人觧者不離目前
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings, explicitly under Linji's section; the paired formula is followed by “one who understands is not apart from what is before the eyes.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬心即差，動念即乖。不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Compendium, Shimen Cizhao section; the master's own explicit dead-water correction. The roster has no securely matched canonical spelling for this section, so MasterName remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬心即差，動念即乖；不擬不動，土木無殊。行脚人須得轉身一句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Compendium, explicitly under Huanglong Huinan; a separate correction comparing mere non-movement to wood and earth.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「畢竟如何趨向？」師云：「動念即乖。」進云：「不動念時如何？」師云：「眉毛在眼上。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linye Qi's Recorded Sayings, question-and-answer encounters; the headword answers how to head toward it, and the follow-up about unmoving thought receives the concrete eyebrow reply.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “investigate, interrogate, or put to the test” (勘); the second means “break open or expose” (破). (勘破) is what a master does in a live encounter: he tests someone and sees through them. The stock capping declaration (勘破了也) ('[I have] seen him through') marks the testing as complete. The paradigm case is Zhaozhou, who hears of an old woman on the road to Mt. Wutai who answers every pilgrim's question with '(just) go straight on'; he goes up to test her (待我去勘過), comes back, and tells the monk (臺山婆子為汝勘破了也) ('I have seen the Mt. Wutai crone through for you'). Commentators then keep the word working by asking (什麼處是勘破處) ('and just where is the point where she got seen through?'). The verb is also turned reflexively: Dahui says to a monk (老僧被爾勘破) ('this old monk has been seen through by you') and, when the monk hesitates, hits him. In the (無門關) (the Gateless Barrier) the word both titles and closes cases: its case-table lists (趙州勘婆) ('Zhaozhou tests the crone'), the case itself ends (州歸謂眾曰)。(臺山婆子我與爾勘破了也), Wumen's comment turns the word into the probe (且道那裏是趙州勘破婆子處) ('say then: just where is the place Zhaozhou saw the crone through?'), and on the two-hermits case (州勘庵主) he writes (爭奈趙州却被二庵主勘破) ('but alas, Zhaozhou was himself seen through by the two hermits') — the tester can be out-tested. The probe form recurs in raised-case commentary: (老宿拈云)。(什麼處是勘破處) ('an old worthy took it up: where is the seeing-through point?'). The preliminary step has its own verb (勘過) ('go and test'): Zhaozhou announces (待我去勘過) ('wait till I go test her'), and Xuansha counters Xuefeng's praise of a student's verse (此子徹去也, 'this one has broken through') with (未可)。(此是意識著述)。(更須勘過始得) ('not yet — this is composition by the conceptual mind; he must still be tested').
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense; no master bends the word idiosyncratically. (勘破) is also used of 'seeing through' a case (公案) or checkpoint, but the defining Zen use is person-to-person testing. The Mt. Wutai crone case recurs verbatim across lamp records (燈錄), case-commentary, and recorded sayings (語錄), which is what makes the reading multi-source. Counts (462-text allowlist grep): (勘破) 1503 hits in 253 texts; the verdict formula (勘破了也) 241 in 118; the passive (被我勘破) 23 in 18; the commentators' probe (勘破處) 51 in 38 (什麼處是勘破處 7 hits in 7 texts, e.g. 老宿拈云。什麼處是勘破處 T47n1997 0804b28; 甚麼處是勘破處 2); the preliminary verb (勘過) 296 in 129 (待我去勘過 X80n1565 0092b11; 更須勘過始得 X80n1565 0152c22); the sibling term (勘辨) 171 in 77. (無門關) material: case-table (趙州勘婆) T48n2005 0292c06; (臺山婆子我與爾勘破了也) 0297a13; (且道那裏是趙州勘破婆子處) 0297a17; (爭奈趙州却被二庵主勘破) 0294b14.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師歸院謂僧曰。臺山婆子為汝勘破了也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Section head is (趙州觀音院從諗禪師); (師) = Zhaozhou, returning to tell the monk he has seen the Mt. Wutai woman through. (Wudeng Huiyuan, a lamp record 燈錄.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇著語云。勘破了也。一似鐵橛相似。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuedou's capping phrase (著語) on the Deshan-visits-Guishan case; Yuanwu's commentary then asks (什麼處是勘破處) / (且道勘破德山勘破溈山). (Blue Cliff Record.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 萬松道。勘破了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong's own capping ('萬松道。勘破了也') on the same Mt. Wutai woman case, adding the reflexive twist (亦乃累及萬松) ('it even implicates Wansong'). (Book of Serenity.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。老僧被爾勘破。僧擬議。師便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (師) = Dahui in his own recorded encounter; the inverted use — the master says HE has been seen through, then strikes. (Dahui's recorded sayings 語錄.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 州歸院云。婆子被我勘破了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The line (婆子被我勘破了也) is Zhaozhou's (州), here raised and commented on ('趙州不施韜略...又却失利') in Xutang Zhiyu's yulu — an independent witness to the stock phrase.

Senses.Explanation: As a verb, "to examine and discriminate" (勘辨) joins "to examine or interrogate" (勘) with "to discriminate or distinguish" (辨). Chan records use it for testing interlocutors and claims in the public record. One master says that after examination and discrimination are clear and the matter is firmly grasped, activity in the dusty net is unobstructed; another record rebukes a man who claimed he could examine masters everywhere; Xutang says, "I too cannot examine and discriminate you," and contrasts an amicable one-question, one-answer meeting with having "so much examination and discrimination." The Chan deviation lies in its institutional object: this legal-investigative wording names how masters question, check, and distinguish people and their answers.
Senses.Note: 170 occurrences in 78 allowlisted texts across verbal use and section/genre headings. Split under depth-gate item 8 because the corpus also uses the same graphs as the name of a record section.

Occurrences.Kwic: 勘辨既明，把捉既定，却不妨向塵勞世網中大抹高揮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text says, "once examination and discrimination are clear, once grasping is settled..."

Occurrences.Kwic: 真點胸自謂百了千當，勘辨諸方
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record says Zhen Dianxiong claimed complete competence and examined masters in every quarter; the following exchange tests that claim.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我也不能勘辨得爾。只要諸人知道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xutang says, "I too cannot examine and discriminate you; I only want all of you to know."

Occurrences.Kwic: 當時勘辨諸方底手眼向甚處去？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address asks where the capacity formerly used to examine masters in every quarter has gone.

Senses.Explanation: As a record heading, "examinations and discriminations" names a collected section of encounter dialogues. The Old Records of the Venerable Ones places the heading immediately before Huangbo's kitchen exchange with the rice steward. Later recorded-sayings tables of contents coordinate it with "posed questions, question-and-answer, and occasions of encounter" and divide the material across volumes. Here the graphs denote a textual category containing public exchanges, rather than the finite verb "to examine someone."
Senses.Note: This noun/genre use is anchored separately because it denotes a section of a record, not merely another interpretation of the verbal act.

Occurrences.Kwic: 勘辨勘辨黃檗因入厨次問飯頭作什麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The duplicated section heading "examinations and discriminations" immediately precedes Huangbo's question to the rice steward.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第十六卷垂問勘辨問答機緣上第十七卷勘辨問答機緣下
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The table of contents labels volumes 16–17 "posed questions, examinations and discriminations, question-and-answer, and occasions of encounter."

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and the pictures made from them. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, a teacher interrupts a monk asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?" (牛在甚麼處). The deviation from an ordinary count of cattle is documentary: "the Ten Oxen" (十牛) functions as the proper name of a Chan verse-and-picture series, circulated, recited, questioned, and criticized inside the record.
Senses.Note: Attested 33 times in 18 allowlisted texts. The title/series is primary and all curated occurrences concern that same work. Ordinary mentions of ten literal cattle, if encountered, would be a different thing, but the harvested allowlisted evidence did not establish such a second sense for this entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collection title: Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baichi places Liangshan's Ten-Ox verses within the Chan school's ox-herding discourse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梁山老漢做箇十牛頌子，可謂慈悲之故，落草之談
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baichi criticizes Liangshan's Ten-Ox verses as compassionate talk descending into the weeds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後來人錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baichi says later people made a wrong move and painted the Ten-Ox forms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聞汝和梁山十牛頌，試舉看。師擬對，德遽掩其口曰：牛在甚麼處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher asks for the verses, stops the attempted reply, and asks where the ox is.

Senses.Explanation: The “thousand hands and eyes,” attested 242 times in 108 allowlisted texts, is the invoked form of Great Compassion, or Guanyin. Chushi Fanqi’s image record identifies it directly: “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes are Guanyin’s responsive transformation-body” (大悲千手眼者，觀音大士應化之身也). In the Chan record the figure is repeatedly placed inside public interviews asking which is the “true eye.” Daowu asks, “Among Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes, which is the true eye?” and receives “like a person at night reaching behind for a pillow” (如人夜間背手摸枕子); the Magu–Linji encounter turns the same question into grabbing, demanding an immediate answer, and changing seats. A later teacher raises the whisk and says, “This is Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes” (此是大悲千手眼).
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the invoked figure's deployment as a recurring public-interview question and as a designation applied to a raised teaching-seat implement. “The thousand hands and eyes” (千手眼), “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes” (大悲千手眼), and “the hundred-thousand hands and eyes” (百千手眼) retain one figure/image across noun phrase, question, verse, and demonstration, so no split is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悲千手眼者，觀音大士應化之身也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct image-record definition identifies the thousand hands and eyes as Guanyin's responsive transformation-body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悲千手眼。那箇是正眼。師曰。如人夜間背手摸枕子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daowu asks which is the true eye; the reply describes reaching behind for a pillow in the dark.

Occurrences.Kwic: 麻谷問。大悲千手眼。那箇是正眼。師搊住曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Magu's question to Linji begins an acted public exchange involving grabbing and the teaching seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃驀豎拂子，曰：此是大悲千手眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher raises the whisk and identifies it as Great Compassion's thousand hands and eyes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百千手眼一毫頭，個個須開頂上眸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse places the hundred-thousand hands and eyes on a single hair-tip and calls for each crown-eye to open.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to strike the staff on the floor
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to strike or plant (卓) the staff (拄杖): "to strike the staff on the floor." The phrase occurs 5,243 times in 287 allowlisted texts. In the Chan record it is a teaching-seat action, not merely a description of walking with a stick. A master strikes once and says, "all at once, smashed to pieces" (卓拄杖一下，云：一時粉碎), or strikes and supplies the demanded phrase. The action can punctuate a public exchange, accompany a shout, or close a formal address immediately before "stepped down" (下座). The corpus counts the blows explicitly: "once" occurs 777 times and "three times" 32 times. These observable placements are the Chan deviation; the entry assigns no unstated meaning to the blow.
Senses.Note: The phrase is a stock stage direction in recorded public addresses. It describes contact of the staff with the floor or platform; it is distinct from raising, pointing with, or throwing the staff.

Occurrences.Kwic: 卓拄杖一下，云：一時粉碎。又卓拄杖一下，云：話在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the record of Xuzhou Pudu: "he struck the staff once and said, 'all at once, smashed to pieces'; he struck it once again and said, 'the words remain.'"

Occurrences.Kwic: 師卓拄杖一下。僧曰：答即便答，又卓個甚麼？師曰：百雜碎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange: the master strikes once; the monk asks why he struck instead of answering; the master says, "smashed into a hundred pieces."

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道晝行夜臥一句作麼生道？良久，以拄杖卓一下，云：德山證明。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After demanding, "how do you say the phrase 'walking by day and lying down at night'?" the speaker pauses, strikes once with the staff, and says, "Deshan bears witness."

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久曰。水流千派月。山鎖一磎雲。卓拄杖下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A pause and verse are followed by striking the staff and stepping down, anchoring the closing-stage-direction use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 卓拄杖，喝一喝，便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record sequences three formal actions: strike the staff, give a shout, and immediately step down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 卓拄杖三下，云：「從來古路如弦直，著腳何非化國民？」下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker strikes the staff three times, gives a verse, and steps down; this anchors explicit counting beyond the common single strike.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道如何是此事？聽山僧拄杖子與你們註解。」卓拄杖兩下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After asking what the matter is, the master tells the assembly to listen to his staff explain it and strikes twice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是蕩蕩無為之句？卓拄杖云：含弘光大，品物咸亨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The staff strike directly introduces the supplied phrase in response to a formal question.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “Nanquan cuts the cat.” This graph form occurs 128 times in 46 allowlisted texts and names the same public case as “Nanquan cuts the cat” (南泉斬貓). The case text records the east and west halls fighting over a cat, Nanquan holding it up and demanding a word, the assembly's failure to answer, the cat cut in two, and Zhaozhou's later sandal-on-the-head response. The wording functions as a case heading, an object of questions, and the subject of later verses and comments. In one direct public exchange a questioner asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; the master tells him to repent. That passage attests the precept relation without explaining Nanquan's intention. Jueyin's recorded answer to “What is the import of Nanquan cutting the cat?” is exactly, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui separately rejects the students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules” for this case and Guizong's snake-cutting.
Senses.Note: The two graphs for “cat” (猫 and 貓) are orthographic variants here, not evidence of two senses. The case, the later questions, and the rejected explanations concern one recorded event.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日。東西兩堂爭猫兒南泉見遂提起云。道得即不斬眾無對泉斬却猫兒為兩段泉復舉前話問趙州州便脫草鞋。於頭上戴出泉云。子若在。恰救得猫兒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Book of Serenity preserves the complete case under this exact variant heading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：殺生是大戒，為什麼南泉斬猫，歸宗斬蛇？師曰：汝寔恁麼問那？曰：是。師曰：汝當懺悔去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An explicit killing-precept question under Miyun Yuanwu; the reply is addressed to the questioner.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初參覺印問曰。南泉斬猫兒意旨如何。印曰。須是南泉始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Continuation of the Lamp gives Jueyin's exact verdict in Weishang's biography.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歸宗斬蛇。南泉斬猫兒。學語之流。多謂之當機妙用。亦謂之大用現前不存軌則。殊不知。總不是這般道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui explicitly rejects two reported readings of the paired cases.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉南泉斬猫兒話，乃曰：南泉提起下刀誅，六臂修羅救得無？設使兩堂俱道得，也應流血滿街衢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse introduced by the exact case name.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “Nanquan cuts the cat.” This form occurs 217 times in 108 allowlisted texts and names the same public case as “Nanquan cuts the cat” (南泉斬猫). The case records the east and west halls fighting over a cat, Nanquan raising it and demanding a word, the assembly's failure to answer, the cat cut in two, and Zhaozhou's later sandal-on-the-head response. The wording functions as a case name, the object of public questions, and the subject of later verses and comments. One question states that killing living beings is a major precept and asks why Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake; the master tells the questioner to repent. A sermon quoting the animal-rescue rule asks how the cat and snake could have been saved. Jueyin's recorded answer to “What is the import of Nanquan cutting the cat?” is “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui rejects two labels students apply to the paired cutting cases. The entry preserves these attested challenges and refusals and does not provide an unrecorded intention for Nanquan.
Senses.Note: Nanquan is a lineage master and remains on the master roster; this dictionary article is for the portable lexical case-name. The cat-graph variants are separate searchable articles, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉一日兩堂爭貓，泉提起貓云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉斬貓為兩段。南泉舉問趙州，州脫鞋戴出，泉云：「子在，救得貓兒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case collection preserves the entire event behind the case-name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「殺生是大戒，為甚麼南泉斬貓、歸宗斬蛇？」師云：「汝實恁麼問麼？」云：「是。」師云：「汝當懺悔去。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The explicit precept challenge names the headword and receives a command to repent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊道：若見世人殺畜生時，應方便救護，解其苦難。祇如南泉斬貓、歸宗斬蛇，當恁麼時，作何方便可以救得？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon places the named case directly after an animal-rescue rule.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初參覺印，問曰：南泉斬貓兒，意旨如何？印曰：須是南泉始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question about the case receives Jueyin's terse answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大慧云：『歸宗斬蛇，南泉斬貓。學語之流多，謂之當機妙用，亦謂之大用現前，不存軌則。殊不知總不是這般道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui reports and rejects the two labels rather than endorsing either.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘divine or forecast’ (卜) + ‘measure or estimate’ (度): to calculate and guess, or speculative reckoning. The compound has 702 occurrences in 206 allowlisted texts. Its recurrent coordinations identify its deployment without supplying a separate theory: ‘thinking and conjectural calculation’ (思量卜度) occurs 25 times in 18 texts; ‘reckoning by affective cognition’ (情識卜度) 10 times in 6; ‘reckoning under the root of thought’ (意根下卜度) 47 times in 33; and ‘weighing and conjectural calculation’ (摶量卜度) 7 times in 3. Dahui's record says, in a list, ‘do not reckon under the root of thought; do not give a phrase; do not remain silent for a long time’ (不得向意根下卜度，不得下語，不得良久). His memorial inscription says, ‘Chan, Chan: do not use thinking and conjectural calculation; it does not concern written words and speech’ (禪禪不用思量卜度，非干文字語言). The Blue Cliff Record asks whether the cited matter can be reckoned by affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼), while a Wudeng huiyuan master says not to conjecture inside cognition, adding that this becomes inverted imagining (莫向意識裏卜度，却成妄想顛倒). Another master answers an appraisal with ‘if you conjecture, you lose body and life’ (卜度則喪身失命). Across these uses the word names the act of reaching a guess by mental estimation; the quoted records themselves state their objections to it.
Senses.Note: All required definition-form searches were negative for a true self-definition. Nine hits for ‘one who conjectures’ (卜度者) use the final graph as a person marker, not as the definition formula ‘as for conjectural calculation.’ The term appears in questions, prohibitions, appraisals, verse, and later addresses. Its literal act and these observed constructions remain stable, so a single corpus-wide sense is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不得向意根下卜度。不得下語。不得良久。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own record: ‘do not reckon under the root of thought; do not give a phrase; do not remain silent for a long time.’ Direct instruction in a formal address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪禪不用思量卜度。非干文字語言。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's memorial inscription: ‘Chan, Chan: do not use thinking and conjectural calculation; it does not concern written words and speech.’ Inscriptional voice rather than Dahui's directly governed speech, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。畢竟作麼生辨的。直饒鐵眼銅睛。也摸索不著。到這裏。以情識卜度得麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record prose: ‘say, then: ultimately how is it distinguished? Even with iron eyes and bronze pupils, one cannot feel it out. Here, can it be reckoned by affective cognition?’ Editorial comment, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫向意識裏卜度。却成妄想顛倒。無有出期。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wudeng huiyuan, Fuzhou Baoguo Zhao section: ‘do not conjecture inside cognition; that becomes inverted imagining, with no time of emergence.’ The section master is not linked through the roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。卜度則喪身失命。問。如何是學人自己。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wudeng huiyuan, Xijing Shaoshan Yunmen Daoxin section: the master says, ‘if you conjecture, you lose body and life’; the next question asks, ‘what is the student's own self?’ The section master is not linked through the roster.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Bian He, presenter of the uncut jade
Senses.Explanation: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name occurs 78 times in 47 allowlisted texts. The Book of Serenity retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by saying, “I bring the uncut jade to the master and ask the master to carve and polish it”; when the master refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Another verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.
Senses.Note: Finder, presenter, amputated man, and student-adopted role all refer to the same allusion figure. Differences in whether a passage stresses jade, recognition, repeated presentation, or punishment are deployments, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 卞和於荊山崐岡谷得璞。獻楚厲王。王曰。石也遣刖一足。
白玉無瑕卞和刖足。
抱璞投師。請師雕琢。師曰。不為棟梁材。曰。恁麼則卞和無出身處也。
堪笑卞和三獻玉。縱榮刖却一雙足。
荊山美玉何須辨，赤水玄珠不用拈。罔象無心黃帝重，卞和有智楚王嫌。

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "seal" (印) and "approve or permit" (可): "approve and certify," attested 761 times in 173 allowlisted texts. Lamp and lineage records use the verb for recorded acts of approval. After a student opens to understanding at Tianyi's assembly, Tianyi "approves him, saying: this is my house's thousand-mile colt" (印可曰，此吾家千里駒也). Another account says a teacher approved six people individually and told them, "you six people together verify my body; each accords with one part" (汝等六人，同證吾身，各契其一). Narrative forms include "all received approval" (皆蒙印可), "deeply received approval" (深蒙印可), and "received the teacher's approval" (承師印可). These passages record approval, the teacher's words at approval, and who received it; they do not make every occurrence a single theory of what was certified.
Senses.Note: Approval is not always the end of examination. In the Zhang Shangying case, after Donglin has approved the commissioner, Doushuai asks whether he still has any doubt about the words and teachings of buddhas and ancestral teachers. Historical notices also distinguish a person's approving teacher from the lineage teacher ultimately named in succession: one person can receive approval from more than one teacher while a later record names a particular succession relation. The headword records the approval event; lineage assignment remains a separate structural claim.

Occurrences.Kwic: 衣印可曰：此吾家千里駒也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyi gives approval and calls the student his house's thousand-mile colt.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師各印可曰：汝等六人，同證吾身，各契其一。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised lineage account: the teacher approves six disciples individually and says each accords with one part.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謁汾陽、葉縣，皆蒙印可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical narrative: the student visits Fenyang and Yexian and receives approval from both.

Occurrences.Kwic: 東林既印可運使，運使于佛祖言教有少疑否？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Doushuai asks: since Donglin approved the commissioner, does the commissioner still have any doubt about the words and teachings of buddhas and patriarchs?

Occurrences.Kwic: 謁金鑾善、葉縣省，皆蒙印可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second multi-teacher narrative: visits to Jinluan Shan and Yexian Sheng both result in approval.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records load the ordinary printing block into a criticism of sayings and conduct reproduced from fixed models. One record asks, 'what is block-stamped?' and answers: people who grope along walls, have no genuine understanding of their own, and rely entirely on ancient sayings as a staff. Another defines 'printing-block Chan' as reading the records of Yuanwu, Dahui, and Zhongfeng and turning out something resembling them. The widespread paired formula says that teachers or learned sayings are 'stamped from a printing block and released from a mold,' then contrasts this with responding as circumstances arise. The Zen deviation is this printing-shop language for publicly criticized, model-bound Chan speech; the term does not merely mean generic sameness.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. Family checked against mold (模子), printing-block Chan (印板禪), stamped from a printing block (印板上打來), and released from a mold (模子裏脫出).

Occurrences.Kwic: 印板禪印板禪何謂印板？有等靠墻摸壁，自無真正見解，全藉古人言句做拄杖子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct definition formula: reliance on ancient sayings without one's own genuine understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 印板禪者，熟讀圓悟、大慧、中峰諸尊宿語錄，依稀脫出者是也；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Definition within a three-part taxonomy: producing a resemblance after reading masters' records.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而今天下老和尚多是師承學解，露布葛藤，印板上打來，模子裏脫出。當人若是明去，何不一切臨時？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The recurring printing-block/mold formula contrasted by the text with acting as circumstances arise.

Senses.Explanation: The physical engraved block used to print a text. One colophon records carving a set of printing blocks for the Continued Transmission of the Lamp, comprising three cases. An imperial instruction orders Zhongfeng's writings printed and entered into the canon wherever canon printing blocks are held. This book-production object is a different thing from speech criticized as block-stamped, so it has its own sense.
Senses.Note: Literal object sense, independently attested in a printing colophon and an imperial book-production record. No specifically Chan bend belongs to this physical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 彫造續燈錄印板一部，計三函。時崇寧二年十月日謹題。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Colophon recording an engraved printing-block set for the Continued Transmission of the Lamp.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但有藏經印板處。教刊板入藏經。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Imperial instruction to carve and print the text wherever canon printing blocks exist.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛): the first 'this very' (即) identifies mind, and the second identifies buddha. The phrase is recorded as a saying, a question, a quoted case, and the first member of a recurring contrast with 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). In the record of Huineng and Fahai, Fahai asks for an explanation of 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛願垂指喻); Huineng answers by pairing 'the preceding thought not arising is this mind' (前念不生即心) with 'the following thought not ceasing is this buddha' (後念不滅即佛), then 'forming every characteristic is this mind' (成一切相即心) with 'leaving every characteristic is this buddha' (離一切相即佛). In Mazu's recorded exchange, when asked why he says it, he answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼); when asked what happens after the crying stops, he says, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Damei Fachang is later quoted saying that Mazu told him 'this mind is this buddha' and that, whatever Mazu now says about 'not mind, not buddha,' he retains the former words. Later masters also ask 'How is it when this mind is this buddha?' (即心即佛時如何) and place the phrase beside 'not mind, not buddha' and 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' (不是心不是佛不是物).
Senses.Note: The exact four-character form occurs 955 times in 241 allowlisted texts. Definition-form searches found three occurrences of 'as for this mind being this buddha' (即心即佛者), one of 'the so-called this mind is this buddha' (所謂即心即佛), three of 'it is called this mind is this buddha' (謂之即心即佛), and one of 'call it this mind is this buddha' (喚作即心即佛); these mostly label or repeat the saying rather than independently define its words. The Huineng-Fahai passage is the fullest literal explanation found. Do not collapse the phrase into its paired reversal: the corpus preserves the sequence and later comments on both forms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 信入。三藏後不知所終。韶州法海禪師韶州法海禪師者曲江人也。初見六祖問曰。即心即佛願垂指喻。祖曰。前念不生即心。後念不滅即佛。成一切相即心。離一切相即佛。吾若具說

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings (古尊宿語錄), a transmitted Mazu exchange: asked why he says 'this mind is this buddha,' Mazu answers, 'to stop a small child crying'; the passage is transmitted narrative, so no direct master link is assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大梅一人直下承當，何況後代？你看僧問大梅：因何便住此山？梅云：我當時見馬大師向我道：即心即佛。便向此住。僧云：于今大師又道：非心非佛。梅云：者老漢惑亂人未有了日在，任你非心非佛

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：三點如流水，曲似刈禾鎌。師後居伏牛山，上堂曰：即心即佛是無病求藥句，非心非佛是藥病對治句。僧問：如何是脫灑底句？師曰：伏牛山下古今傳。示滅於隨州開元寺。京兆興善

Occurrences.Kwic: ，詔師居之。上堂曰：五五二十五，案山雷，主山雨。明眼衲僧，莫教錯舉。上堂：若向這裏說即心即佛，大似頭上安頭。若說非心非佛，何異迷頭認影？賞箇名，安箇字，定箇是，立箇非，向甚麼處

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'this very mind is Buddha.' The variant 'this very mind is itself Buddha' (即心即佛) is used interchangeably. The stock public frame is Damei asking Mazu, 'what is Buddha?' and Mazu answering, 'this very mind is Buddha' (如何是佛；即心是佛). Sikong Benjing pairs it with another formula: 'if you seek to become Buddha, this very mind is Buddha; if you wish to ask after the Way, no-mind is the Way' (若求作佛，即心是佛；若欲問道，無心是道). A monk tells Nanyang Huizhong that 'venerable teachers everywhere also say this very mind is Buddha' (諸方尊宿亦言即心是佛), documenting that the phrase is corpus-wide rather than one master's property. Huangbo places it beside 'seeking Buddha outward' (向外求佛). The record also preserves explicit responses to the phrase. Asked why he says it, Mazu answers, 'to stop a small child's crying' (為止小兒啼); asked what follows once the crying stops, he says, 'not mind, not Buddha' (非心非佛). Damei replies, 'let him say not mind, not Buddha; I only say this very mind is Buddha' (任他非心非佛，我只即心即佛). Nanquan quotes Mazu and says instead, 'not mind, not Buddha, not a thing' (不是心，不是佛，不是物). Another recurrent line calls saying the phrase 'temporarily mistaking the servant for the master' (權且認奴作郎). These are recorded explanations, refusals, extensions, and warnings surrounding one lexical statement. They do not create additional dictionary senses for the statement itself.
Senses.Note: Zen-scoped variant counts: 'this very mind is itself Buddha' (即心即佛), 955 hits in 241 texts; 'this very mind is Buddha' (即心是佛), 388 in 120; 'mind itself is Buddha' (心即是佛), 73 in 44; 'one's own mind is Buddha' (自心是佛), 86 in 46. Counterpart phrases include 'not mind, not Buddha' (非心非佛), 727 in 213, and 'no-mind is the Way' (無心是道), 94 in 34. The earlier master-specific second sense was removed: Mazu's withdrawal, Damei's refusal, Nanquan's extension, and the stock warning are stances toward the same phrase, not different referents.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The Accord of Difference and Sameness
AlternateTargets: Shitou's Accord of Difference and Sameness
Senses.Explanation: The title combines joining or taking part (參), sameness (同), and accord or tally (契): The Accord of Difference and Sameness. In the Chan corpus it names Shitou Xiqian's poem. Lamp records say Shitou wrote one piece called by this title, describe its wording as deep, and report that explanations circulated widely. The transmitted text begins, 'The heart of the great Indian immortal is intimately entrusted east and west' (竺土大仙心，東西密相付), then sets bright source against dark-flowing branches, asks how each field both interrelates and remains in its place, and closes, 'On hearing words you must meet the source; do not establish rules of your own ... I respectfully tell investigators of the mystery: do not waste the daylight' (承言須會宗，勿自立規矩……謹白參玄人，光陰莫虛度). A later lamp record links its composition to Shitou's reading, 'the sage has no self; there is nothing that is not himself' (聖人無己，靡所不己). The Zen deviation is bibliographic and lineage-specific: in these records the title is the proper name of Shitou's Chan verse, printed in full and repeatedly quoted inside later cases and comments.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 88 exact occurrences in 50 allowlisted files. It repeatedly attributes the poem to Shitou, prints the whole verse under the title, quotes individual lines in case commentary, and groups it with named Chan compositions such as the Trust-in-Mind Inscription and Song of Realizing the Way. The primary target translates the title in this attested Chan bibliographic use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師著參同契一篇。辭旨幽𤀹頗有注解大行於世。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Transmission of the Lamp biography says Shitou wrote one Accord of Difference and Sameness, whose wording was deep and for which explanations circulated widely.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南嶽石頭和尚參同契南嶽石頭和尚參同契竺土大仙心。東西密相付。

Occurrences.Kwic: 石頭初看肇論，至會萬物為己者，其惟聖人乎，則曰：聖人無己，靡所不己。乃作參同契

Occurrences.Kwic: 承言須會宗，勿自立規矩。觸目不會道，運足焉知路。進步非近遠，迷隔山河固。謹白參玄人，光陰莫虗度。

Senses.Explanation: To join, attend, or report to the communal hall. Biographical records use the expression for formal admission: people seeking to join the hall might wait for months, while a favored visitor is admitted that same day; Wuzu orders Yuanwu to join the hall immediately, after which Yuanwu enters the attendants' quarters. In encounter records the imperative 'go to the hall' regularly closes or dismisses an exchange. Wuju says it after striking two visitors, and Wenshu Siye shouts it to a former butcher, who then goes down to the hall. In commentary on the rhinoceros-fan case, a monk tells the entire assembly to go to the hall, and Yuanwu explicitly says that the monk has seized the authority of the host. The institutional and imperative uses share the same hall-directed action.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 529 matches in 137 files. The imperative 'go to the hall' accounts for 349 matches in 99 files, including seven matches in six files that address the whole assembly. The nominal form 'those who seek or attend the hall' occurs four times in four files; 'ordered him immediately to join the hall' occurs ten times in ten files, and 'then went down to the hall' occurs nineteen times in sixteen. These forms distinguish this institutional use of 'join' from other senses of the first graph elsewhere in Chan vocabulary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。汝既不會。後面箇師僧祇對看。紹擬近前。師便打。曰。信知同坑無異土。參堂去。

Occurrences.Kwic: 時四方來學雲趨水赴，求參堂者或累旬月而不得。間有得者，如登龍門。師徑懷香詣方丈相看。佛鑑顧師敦厖，識為法器。即日歸堂，眾皆驚訝。

Occurrences.Kwic: 時有一禪客出云。大眾參堂去。這僧奪得主家權柄。道得也殺道。只道得八成。

Occurrences.Kwic: 殊曰：你正殺猪時，見箇甚麼便乃剃頭行脚？師遂作鼓刀勢。殊喝曰：者屠兒參堂去！師便下參堂。

Senses.Explanation: (參) = to investigate, consult, look into (as one 參 a teacher or 參究 a matter); (禪) = Chan. (參禪) is the recorded activity of investigating Chan, which the corpus binds to the one great matter of life and death. Gaofeng Yuanmiao states its temper: (參禪須是鐵漢) — to investigate Chan one must be an iron man — (著手心頭便判) (the moment you set to it the mind is decided). He binds it to the one great matter: (只遮生死一大事)，(乃是參禪學道之喉襟) (this single great matter of life-and-death is the very throat-and-collar of investigating Chan and studying the Way), and states the comparison plainly: (資生貴圖求富)，(參禪貴圖求悟) (as making a living prizes seeking wealth, investigating Chan prizes seeking awakening). Zhongfeng Mingben describes people who say they investigate Chan while doing so only with their mouths: (人心浮淺口說參禪) — shallow-minded people 'investigate Chan' only with their mouths, wanting to understand the recorded exchanges as material for conversation, (初無一念要决了生死大事之心) (without a single thought of resolving the great matter). Later records pair the expression with looking at sayings (看話). Render it as ‘investigate Chan,’ following the literal ‘consult / look into’ sense; note the fixed collocation (參禪學道) ('investigate Chan and study the Way'). The records also define the word by its concrete referent: Shitian Faxun (石田法薰) writes (參方衲子)，(出一藂林)，(入一藂林)，(撥草瞻風)，(不憚寒暑)，(喚作參禪) (wandering monks leaving one grove and entering another, parting the grass to gaze at the wind, undeterred by cold and heat — this is 'called 參禪'), then immediately presses (畢竟禪作麼生參) (but after all, how is Chan investigated?) (X70n1386). Shiwu Qinggong opens an evening address: (現前一眾久在叢林)，(謂之參禪)、(謂之辦道)，(殊不知一念未生已前更無別物)，(纔擬心時錯了也) (this assembly has long been in the groves — it is called investigating Chan, called working at the Way — quite unaware that before one thought arises there is no other thing; the instant the mind deliberates, it has already gone wrong) (X70n1399; raised again in 列祖提綱錄 X64n1260). Baichi (百癡) turns the word on itself at a (小參) (informal address): (無禪可參是名參禪)，(無道可悟是名悟道) (no Chan that can be investigated — that is named investigating Chan; no Way that can be awakened to — that is named awakening to the Way) (J28nB202). Two stock formulas recur: (參禪無秘訣)，(只要生死切) (investigating Chan has no secret formula — only that life and death be urgent; 13 hits in 10 allowlist texts, also written 秪要生死切), and the full iron-man quatrain (參禪須是鐵漢)，(著手心頭便判)，(直趣無上菩提)，(一切是非莫管) (25 hits in 20 texts), which the record credits to the layman Li Duwei (李都尉) — (李都尉云)：「(參禪須是鐵漢)，(著手心頭便判)，(直趍無上菩提)，(一切是非莫管)。」 (J26nB183; J26nB182 narrates his awakening verse, 李忽契悟，亦呈偈云).
Senses.Note: Two independently-attributed masters (Gaofeng Yuanmiao 高峰原妙, his 語錄 recorded sayings; Zhongfeng Mingben 中峰明本, his 廣錄 extensive record) use (參禪) (investigate Chan) for the same activity — one framing its temper and aim, one policing genuine vs. mouth-only inquiry. Dahui Zonggao is the acknowledged systematizer of (看話參禪) (‘investigating Chan by looking at sayings’) and is named in the explanation, but no Dahui occurrence is curated here: the strongest Dahui (參禪) passage (T47n1998A, 0864c) sits in a section expounding Linji's (四照用) (his 'four illuminings-and-functions') and invoking Yunmen, where speaker attribution was not cleanly separable, so it was left out per the verify-attribution rule. Zen-scoped grep counts (tag-stripped, 2026-07-11): (參禪) 2950 hits in 336 of the 462 allowlist texts; (參禪學道) 213/111; (參禪人) 135/71; (參禪者) 83/46; (參禪辦道) 4/4. The mouth-only polemic is itself multi-witness: besides Zhongfeng's (口說參禪)。(但欲明悟機緣以資談柄) ('investigate Chan with the mouth only, merely wanting the encounter-stories as talk-fodder'; B25n0145), the (浮石禪師語錄) (Fushi's recorded sayings) has (人心不古)，(口說參禪)，(但欲讀熟幾則機緣以資談柄) ('hearts are not what they were: they investigate Chan with the mouth, only wanting to read up a few encounter-cases as talk-fodder'; J26nB185), and a (五燈全書) (Complete Book of the Five Lamps) verse has (口說參禪心不了) ('the mouth says investigate Chan while the mind is not settled'; X82n1571). The iron-man quatrain Gaofeng deploys is circulating stock credited within the record to the layman Li Duwei (李都尉), not a Gaofeng coinage (J26nB182, J26nB183).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to investigate the head of the talk: the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in the record. The compound occurs 187 times in 76 allowlisted texts. The texts specify the raised wording itself: one record identifies an unresolved scripture or public case as the personally investigated word, while Mingben names Zhaozhou's question 'why did Zhaozhou say the word no?' and instructs the listener to investigate that wording and raise great doubt. Other records say to place one's own investigated saying before one, to investigate it earnestly, or criticize merely hunting it in books and other people's mouths. A contrary witness asks what difference there is between those who do and do not perform the associated work. Thus the Zen bend is the selection of actual words from recorded exchanges for sustained investigation; the corpus also records criticism of reifying that activity.
Senses.Note: Translate the term according to its local object—word, saying, question, or conversational thread—and keep every attested imperative as a literal action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或是經教有所未明、公案有所未透，即此不明不透處便是本參話頭，頓在面前微著眼覷
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record explicitly identifies the personally investigated wording with what remains unresolved in a scripture or public case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 予勸兄弟，各將自己本參話頭著實參去，定有下落。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct instruction says to investigate one's own selected saying in earnest.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text criticizes seekers who hunt the wording in books and at other people's mouths.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若謂別有念佛參話頭工夫以為超越者，究竟到頭與未念佛未參話頭者有何差別？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record explicitly questions the difference between performing and not performing the associated work.

Senses.Explanation: A verb or verbal noun for visiting or attending (參) and making inquiry or requesting instruction (請): "visit and inquire." It occurs 243 times in 121 allowlisted texts. Chinese Chan records show both its institutional and encounter uses. A monk may leave one teacher, travel to another place, and "join the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請); another biography says that at Shishuang he merely followed the assembly and "no longer visited and inquired" (更不參請). The monastic regulations place "traveling from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請) under a heading that literally lists departure from one's teacher, seeking a respected elder, requesting lodging, first reporting to the guest office, and next registering at the hall office. The term can also describe the encounter itself: a visitor "bent his knees to visit and inquire" (屈膝參請), after which the teacher addressed his understanding; members of an assembly visited and inquired morning and evening while the teacher answered them without weariness (晨夕參請，師與唱酬無倦). The recorded actions are visits, institutional participation, questions, and responses in Chinese Chan texts.
Senses.Note: Productive constructions mark the same range: "join the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請, 23 occurrences), "enter the room to visit and inquire" (入室參請, 2), "travel from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請, 6), and headings for "circumstances of visiting and inquiry" (參請因緣, 2). Fayan can ask what scripture someone reads "apart from visiting and inquiry" (於參請外), placing it among the ordinary activities of a visitor's life. The Blue Cliff Record contrasts a superintendent's not having "visited and inquired or entered the room" (不曾參請入室) with Fayan subsequently asking why he does not come enter the room. The overlap between travel, residence in an assembly, and direct exchange is native to the term, so these are kept as deployments of one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師聞此語。禮辭至韶陽。隨眾參請。不言來處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After hearing the instruction, the monk bows farewell, reaches Shaoyang, and joins the assembly to visit and inquire without saying where he came from.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後到石霜。但隨眾而已。更不參請。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At Shishuang, the visitor merely follows the assembly and no longer visits and inquires. The negative construction defines the expected institutional action by its absence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眼問曰。子於參請外。看甚麼經。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fayan asks what scripture the visitor reads apart from visiting and inquiry, marking the term as an ordinary category of his activity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遊方參請遊方參請稟辭師長。慕有道尊宿處。依棲求掛搭古規首到客司相看。次往堂司掛搭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Institutional heading and procedure: leave one's teacher; seek a respected elder; request lodging; first report to the guest office; next register at the hall office.

Occurrences.Kwic: 企靈隱泰道眼精明，乃屈膝參請焉。泰甞謂師曰：我舉拂子，你便向拂子上會；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A visitor esteems Lingyin Tai's discerning eye, bends his knees to visit and inquire, and is then directly addressed by Tai.

Occurrences.Kwic: 晨夕參請，師與唱酬無倦，一時達者稱為大慧再來。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Morning and evening the assembly visits and inquires, and the teacher responds without weariness.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The superintendent had never visited and inquired or entered the room; Fayan then asks why he does not come enter the room.

Senses.Explanation: To receive binding precepts from a precept-giver, commonly as a dated event in a master’s biography: a lamp record says Huike served Bodhidharma for nine years and later received the precepts at Jizhou. It is also a public act. The Platform Record places Huineng on the high seat to confer formless precepts and tells the whole assembly, ‘each must receive the formless precepts in your own person’ (總須自體與受無相戒). The corpus does not leave the compound as ceremony alone. Yongjue’s precept-bestowal address asks, ‘What is a precept? How is a precept received?’ (云何為戒？戒云何受？), and later rebukes those who ‘have the name of receiving precepts but entirely lack the reality of receiving precepts’ (但取受戒之名，全無受戒之實). Juelang Sheng states that recipients and non-recipients are far apart and that receiving without keeping is an offense. Thus Chan records retain formal biographical and public reception while applying an explicit name-versus-reality test and linking reception to subsequent keeping.
Senses.Note: The entry describes a formal event and the record’s explicit test of name against reality. Exact count: 658 hits in 157 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 信於言下大悟服勞九載。後於吉州受戒侍奉尤謹。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography records receiving precepts as a subsequent dated life event.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖曰受戒，但取受戒之名，全無受戒之實。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue contrasts the name of receiving precepts with its reality.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以受戒人與不受戒，相去甚遠。受戒不能持，固是罪也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang distinguishes recipients from non-recipients and says receiving without keeping is an offense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 兼授無相戒弘法弟子法海集記第一折惠能大師於大梵寺講堂中，昇高座，說摩訶般若波羅蜜法，授無相戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record frames reception through Huineng's public high-seat conferral of formless precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善知識！總須自體與受無相戒。一時，逐惠能口道，令善知識見自三身佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng tells the assembled recipients that each must receive the formless precepts in their own person.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "just as for" (只如). Across Chan discourse and case commentary it is a grammatical pivot: a speaker provisionally leaves the preceding statement in place, selects a concrete case or condition, and reopens questioning. Yuanwu moves from a claim about a world that is entirely a diamond eye to "just as for... how do you observe it?" (只如……且作麼生觀), and elsewhere from passing beyond form and sound to "just as for... how is a message conveyed?" (只如……如何通信). Lamp commentary uses it to press whether Vajra-Equality saw the obstructing demon king, to turn from a general claim to Mazu's exact words, and even to compare the issue with having eaten and walking down the east or west corridor. The imperial birthday addresses likewise move from ceremonial description to "just as for the people of the Way in the forest... how is the line raised?" (只如林下道人……一句如何舉唱). There is no special lexical departure from the ordinary connective; its Chan value is the repeatedly attested dialogue structure of concession or setup followed by a pointed case-question.
Senses.Note: The phrase has 4,021 hits in 321 allowlisted texts. It is overwhelmingly connective rather than a technical headword. Common continuations include 'how?' (如何), 'what about it?' (作麼生), 'what do you say?' (且道), and a named earlier saying or case. The curated occurrences come from discourse, lamp commentary, and a formal high-seat address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如盡華藏世界海。窮虛空邊際。都盧是箇金剛眼。且作麼生觀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu uses the pivot to turn a claim about the whole world as a diamond eye into the question of how to observe it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如透出形聲。且道。如何通信。還委悉麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate Yuanwu discourse pivots from passing beyond form and sound to asking how a message is conveyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如金剛齊，還見障蔽魔王麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Joint Lamp commentary turns to the named Vajra-Equality case and asks whether he saw the obstructing demon king.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如儞喫了飯，東廊上，西廊下，不可總問人得與不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Joint Lamp encounter uses the pivot for the concrete comparison of eating and then walking down either corridor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如林下道人共樂昇平，同歸化育一句如何舉唱？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An imperial birthday address pivots from ceremonial praise to asking how the line for forest-dwelling people of the Way is raised.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a phrase whose head fits or joins. The expression occurs 126 times in 85 allowlisted texts. Its defining proverb says, 'one conforming phrase ties up a donkey for ten thousand ages.' Masters use the label as an immediate verdict on an answer and warn 'take care against conforming phrases.' Yunwai Ze lists stock replies—including 'when the sky is clear the sun comes out' and 'when it rains the ground is wet'—as dead sayings delivered as conforming phrases; elsewhere he describes people using such phrases to answer when questioned. Yuanwu says his own teaching seat does not make conforming phrases or look-alike phrases. Later commentary can dispute the verdict: Yushan says that treating Yunmen's 'the body exposed in the golden wind' as a conforming phrase fails to recognize it.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the public-interview use of an ordinary idea of fitting: 'fitting' becomes a critical classification of an answer that matches a ready verbal pattern. The term names one thing across noun modifiers and verdicts; noun and attributive deployments do not require separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人道一句合頭語萬刼繫馿橛作麼生明得免此過
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record quotes the defining proverb and immediately asks how to escape its fault.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云。兵隨印轉去也。師云。一句合頭語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu applies the label as a verdict on a monk's answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云。虎頭帶角出荒草。師云。切忌合頭語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu explicitly warns against this answer class.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunwai Ze supplies a list of stock examples and contrasts living use with dead sayings.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu enumerates conforming and merely similar phrases among what he says he does not make.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今人擬以合頭語論之，可謂不遇中郎鑑，還同野舍薪也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later discourse rejects classifying Yunmen's answer as a conforming phrase.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to put out the tongue. The Chan record repeatedly makes this visible gesture part of public encounters, but does not give it one invariant emotional gloss. Huangbo involuntarily sticks out his tongue (不覺吐舌, “without realizing it, stuck out his tongue”) on hearing that Baizhang was deaf for three days after Mazu's shout. Elsewhere a visitor sticks out his tongue and says, “truly a dragon-elephant”; a monk leaves with his tongue out after a rebuke; and a later monk says that the teacher's gesture shows he has been caught out. Masters also deliberately use the action as an answer: Nanyuan sticks out his tongue when asked for “one word,” and Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what his appearance as abbot is for. Thus the ordinary bodily gesture is bent into an answer or demonstrative act in the teaching hall as well as remaining a recorded reaction; the texts themselves decide its local force, and this entry does not assign one motive to every occurrence.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 548 matches in 194 texts. The retained evidence covers involuntary reaction, spoken appraisal, answer to a one-word question, answer concerning an abbot's public function, and an adversarial interview. Formula searches yielded no corpus-wide verbal definition. Family revalidation against “tongue; capacity to speak” (舌頭) and the “broad, long tongue-mark” (廣長舌相) supports one action sense: reaction and deliberate answer are different deployments of the same bodily act, not different things under depth-gate item 8.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧昔被馬大師一喝。直得三日耳聾。黃檗聞舉。不覺吐舌。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang says, ‘This old monk was once shouted at by Master Ma and was deaf for three days.’ Hearing it, Huangbo ‘without realizing it, stuck out his tongue.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。一言作麼生。師乃吐舌云。待我有廣長舌相。即向汝道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘What is one word like?’ Nanyuan sticks out his tongue and says, ‘Wait until I have the broad, long tongue-mark; then I will tell you.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 年復喝。師以手劃一劃。年吐舌曰。真是龍象。師曰。是何言歟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After another shout and the teacher's hand gesture, the visitor sticks out his tongue and says, ‘Truly a dragon-elephant’; the teacher challenges that statement.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked what his appearance as abbot is for, Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue to show it; the monk asks, ‘Only this—anything else?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是末後句？」師覤上覷下。進云：「為甚解舉不解荅？」師吐舌，僧禮拜云：「今日被學人捉敗。
