Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “toward” and “above”: “upward.” In the Chan records this is a recurrent lexical register, especially in compounds translated as “the upward matter,” “the one road upward,” “the upward vehicle of the house,” “the upward barrier” or “upward barrier-latch,” “an upward move,” “the upward aperture,” “the upward pivot,” “an upward person,” “the upward handle,” and “the upward pincers and hammer.” It is explicitly contrasted with “downward.” Records quote, “The one road upward, the thousand sages do not transmit,” and ask what the untransmitted upward matter is. Another recurrent question asks whether there is still an upward matter; in one recorded case the answer is “no.” Records also ask directly, “What is the upward vehicle of the house?” The expression identifies this upward or further-up register but is not given a single explanatory gloss by the records.
Senses.Note: This is the primary corpus-wide sense and is distinct from ordinary spatial direction. It appears in a family of compounds and questions and is explicitly paired with “downward.” The stock quotations and dialogues have multiple speakers, so curated speaker fields remain null. Compare “the one road upward,” “downward,” “the upward matter,” and “the upward vehicle of the house.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問向上一路千聖不傳如何是向上不傳底事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Highlights of the Lamp: a monk quotes “the one road upward, the thousand sages do not transmit” and asks what the untransmitted upward matter is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正當一色時還有向上事也無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Patriarchs' Hall Collection: the Bian senior-monk case asks whether an upward matter remains when there is a single undivided color; the answer is “no.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便問如何是向上宗乘
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: after other acts are said not to amount to the upward vehicle of the house, a monk asks what that vehicle is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 向上關捩子有此眼目方辨得邪正宗黨
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: “the upward barrier-latch” is placed beside having the eye by which true and false lineages can be distinguished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 處處盡歌皇化，何須演妙譚元。向上一竅又且如何？驀拈拄杖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of the Five Lamps asks directly how the further-up aperture is, then records the master's lifting and striking down his staff.

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary locational sense is “up” or “upward,” distinct from the recurrent register in the first sense. It appears in phrases such as “look upward,” “eyebrows raised upward,” “head upward,” and “above is.” One passage says, “Raise the eyebrows and look up: above, no sky is seen; look down: below, no ground is seen.” The attachment to looking, the eyebrows, or the head and the direct pairing with downward movement identify the spatial sense.
Senses.Note: This secondary corpus-wide sense prevents every occurrence from being forced into the recurrent upward register. It is independently attested across multiple files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眉毛向上看，上不見天。向下看，下不見地。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A recorded saying uses the plain spatial sense in the paired directions “look upward” and “look downward,” followed by “above, no sky is seen; below, no ground is seen.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 向上看佗師口恰似失妳孩兒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Highlights of the Lamp uses “looking up at him” in a simile. This is an independent witness of the ordinary directional sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 剔起眉毛向上看，丈夫自有沖天憤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse instructs the listener to raise the eyebrows and look upward, an unambiguously spatial use.

Senses.Explanation: The single 'road upward.' Its locus classicus is Panshan Baoji's sermon: after weighing (即心即佛) ('this mind is Buddha') as still too green and (非心非佛) ('not mind, not Buddha') as merely 'the far limit of pointing,' he says (向上一路)，(千聖不傳)，(學者勞形)，(如猿捉影) ('the road upward — the thousand sages do not transmit it; the student wears himself out, like an ape grabbing at reflections'). (千聖不傳) ('the thousand sages hand it down to no one') is its standing collocation. Later masters keep the phrase in use by riffing on it: Ciming answers (向上一路)，(千聖不然) ('...the thousand sages do not make it so'), Xiangfu (向上一路)，(掘地覓天) ('...digging the ground to look for heaven'), and elsewhere (盤山道向上一路滑) ('the road upward is slippery'). Asked flat out (如何是向上一路) ('what is the road upward?'), masters point rather than define — one raises his robe-collar (師舉衣領示之), one says (汝且向下會取) ('understand it going downward'), others answer with nonsense-tallies (七六八 / 一口針三尺線 / 九九八十一). The record also lines up three masters' one-line characterizations as a set: (盤山道)：『(向上一路滑)。』(南院道)：『(壁立萬仞險)。』(臨濟道)：『(石火電光鈍)。』 ('Panshan says: the road upward is slippery; Nanyuan says: a sheer wall of ten thousand fathoms — perilous; Linji says: flint-spark and lightning-flash — dull', J27nB189; raised as 瑯琊覺's 上堂 in J39nB454, and condensed into an 示眾 of its own in J37nB383: 向上一路滑，壁立千仞險，石火電光遲，諸人各具眼). Masters also throw it at the assembly as a challenge: (還有知得向上一路者麼) ('is there anyone who knows the road upward?', J36nB362; likewise 還有知向上一路者麼, J38nB414).
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide stock phrase, not one master's property. Panshan Baoji is the locus classicus (attested independently in 景德傳燈錄 and 五燈會元); the (千聖不傳) tag and the pointing-not-defining answers recur across the record. RelatedTerm (向上) is a genuine constituent (the 'upward' direction); (千聖不傳) is its standing collocation. Attestation (allowlist grep): (向上一路) 955 hits in 213 texts, joined directly to its tag as (向上一路)(，)(千聖不傳) in 338 hits across 149 texts (千聖不傳 alone: 529 in 192); the test-question (如何是向上一路) 99 hits in 48 texts; the Panshan riff (向上一路滑) 24 in 20. The question is also posed in the waived form (向上一路即不問)，(千聖不傳事若何)？ (J26nB180; similarly J33nB281). Neighboring (向上)-compounds for scale: (向上一著) 279 in 113, (向上事) 1363 in 222.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若言非心非佛。猶是指蹤極則。向上一路。千聖不傳。學者勞形。如猿捉影。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), in the (幽州盤山寶積禪師) section — the locus classicus.

Occurrences.Kwic: 猶是指蹤之極則。向上一路千聖不傳。學者勞形如猿捉影。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Independent witness of the same sermon in (景德傳燈錄), (幽州盤山寶積禪師) section — establishes multi-source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉盤山道：向上一路，千聖不傳。慈明道：向上一路，千聖不然。師曰：不傳不然，海口難宣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui Zonggao's (上堂) quoting Panshan and Ciming (Shishuang Chuyuan) back to back — shows the phrase as shared, riffed property. Governing section head in X82n1571 (五燈全書) is (臨安府徑山宗杲大慧普覺禪師); the same sermon appears in Dahui's own (大慧語錄) T47n1998A (…向上一路千聖不然。師云。不傳不然海口難宣). MasterName stays null because the headword (向上一路) occurs only inside the quoted Panshan/Ciming lines (two-speaker/raised-case rule), not in Dahui's own (師曰) frame.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是向上一路。師舉衣領示之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the (越州洞巖可休禪師) section. Asked to define the road upward, the master points instead of answering — raises his robe-collar. (Dongyan Kexiu is a minor master, not in the canonical roster.)

Senses.Explanation: Toward or facing (向), above or further up (上), and matter or affair (事): the upward matter. It runs in a recurrent dialogue. A monk asks whether there is still an upward matter (向上還有事也無／還有向上事也無); the master says yes; the monk asks, 'What is the upward matter?' (如何是向上事); and the master gives an answer such as 'break the mirror and come; I will meet you' (打破鏡來，與汝相見), 'a person from Silla does not wrap his head' (新羅人不褁頭), or 'downward the text runs long' (向下文長). It also appears in 'knows that there is an upward matter' (知有向上事, 69 occurrences) and its negation. One line says that Xuefeng had words only after he knew there was an upward matter (雪峯知有向上事始有語話分). The expression can be dismissed with 'What upward matter are you talking about?' (說甚麼向上事). The corpus also attaches 'upward' to named limits: 'the matter upward from buddha' (佛向上事, 149 occurrences) and 'upward from Vairocana' (毘盧向上). It is paired with 'the last word' (末後句) in the statement that one must also know the upward matter and the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得). Related forms include 'the upward road' (向上一路, 957), 'the upward move' (向上一著, 279), 'the upward aperture' (向上一竅, 270), 'the upward pivot' (向上關捩子, 101), 'the upward person' (向上人, 229), and 'the upward vehicle of the lineage' (向上宗乘, 462).
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide term, with 1,363 hits in 222 allowlist texts. The full dialogue—whether there is an upward matter, yes, then what it is—recurs across houses. The word 'upward' (向上) is relative to whatever the text has just named, as shown by 'the matter beyond Buddha' (佛向上事) and 'beyond Vairocana' (毘盧向上).

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。如何是向上事。師曰。打破鏡來。與汝相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), section on Chan Master Lingyun Zhiqin in Fuzhou (福州靈雲志勤禪師). The stock question 'What is the upward matter?' (如何是向上事) receives the answer, 'Break the mirror and come; I will meet you' (打破鏡來，與汝相見). Lingyun Zhiqin is absent from the roster.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此人還知有向上事也無。師曰。不知。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), section on Zhaozhou Congshen. Asked whether such a person knows that there is an upward matter (知有向上事), Zhaozhou answers, 'does not know' (不知).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄), Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Foyan (佛眼禪師語錄). The instruction pairs knowing that there is an upward matter with the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云向上還有事也無師云有僧云如何是向上事師云新羅人不褁頭
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄), section on Shoushan Xingnian. The complete dialogue asks whether there is still an upward matter, receives 'yes,' asks what it is, and receives 'a person from Silla does not wrap his head' (新羅人不褁頭).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是向上事師云向下文長
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄), Muzhou section. The stock question 'What is the upward matter?' (如何是向上事) receives the answer, 'downward the text runs long' (向下文長).

AlternateTargets: lord and minister in the Five Ranks
Senses.Explanation: The Caodong technical configuration of lord and minister. The term occurs 960 times in 217 allowlisted texts. Caoshan maps the lord to the upright position and the minister to the crooked, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister-in-accord (君為正位。臣為偏位). Another record equates the final relation with arriving within both, while a direct answer identifies the Caodong house by “lord and minister in accord” (君臣道合). A house comparison sets this five-position configuration beside Linji’s three mysteries and three essentials. A later text disputes whether Caoshan originally arranged the answers as a separate fivefold set; that is an attested historical disagreement about classification, not a reason to remove the technical configuration.
Senses.Note: Primary Caodong sense. Cross-check the broader Five Ranks entry (五位); prince, upright-crooked, and merit rank systems remain related families rather than extra senses here. The Zen deviation is the conversion of political hierarchy into named rank relations and a house-identifying answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 君為正位。臣為偏位。臣向君是偏中正。君視臣是正中偏。君臣道合是兼帶語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄) (Caoshan Benji's recorded sayings); the master's answer (師曰, 'the master said') to a monk's question about the essential formula of the five positions of lord and minister (僧問五位君臣旨訣) — the canonical mapping of (君)/(臣) onto (正)/(偏) and the three relational ranks.

Occurrences.Kwic: 君為正位，臣乃偏位，臣向君是偏中正，君視臣是正中偏，君臣道合
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Independent witness quoting Caoshan (frame 豈不見曹山道：…, 'have you not seen Caoshan say: …') inside another master's discourse; same definition, so MasterName=null (quotation).

Occurrences.Kwic: 兼中到者，即君臣道合也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天界覺浪盛禪師語錄) (Juelang Daosheng's yulu); the passage sits under the governing heads (洞宗標正) ('setting upright the Dong lineage') → (洞曹君臣正偏及功勳父子主賓五位參同宗旨) ('the concordant purport of the Dongshan-Caoshan lord-minister, upright-crooked, merit, father-son, and host-guest five positions') — the named master's own teaching words (法語) essay expounding the five-position (五位) cross-mapping (正中偏=君視臣, 偏中正=臣向君, 兼中到=君臣道合). Juelang Daosheng (覺浪道盛) is in master-dates.json, so per the governing-section-head rule MasterName=Juelang Daosheng.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是曹洞宗？」師云：「君臣道合。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (君臣道合) ('lord and minister in accord') given as the one-line emblem of the Caodong house in a catechism on the essential principles of the five houses (五家宗旨); two-speaker Q&A (the follow-on questioner 進云 'he went on to ask' asks, the master 師 answers), so MasterName=null per the two-speaker rule. The answering master is determinate — the text is (天隱和尚語錄) (Tianyin Yuanxiu; attribution line 明 圓修說, 'spoken by Yuanxiu, Ming dynasty'; in master-dates.json).

Occurrences.Kwic: 曹山就話荅話，當面具陳，初未嘗與五位為配。後人不辯，以此為君臣五位語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The intra-corpus dispute: the author argues (君臣) was answered ad hoc by Caoshan and only later mislabelled a separate (君臣五位) scheme. Meaning of (君)=(正)/(臣)=(偏) is not contested.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謂具三玄三要者，覿體全真；謂分五位君臣者，宛轉回互。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A house-device comparison sets the three mysteries and essentials beside the five lord-minister positions, which are described as winding through mutual interchange.

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary political and ethical roles of lord and minister. Two allowlisted discourses place their duty beside affection between father and son, distinctions between spouses, age order, and trust among friends (君臣有義). These are social roles, not the Caodong rank configuration.
Senses.Note: Ordinary corpus-wide sense. Kept separate because actual political/ethical persons and a technical rank schema are different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 父子有親，君臣有義，夫婦有別，長幼有序，朋友有信。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse lists affection between father and son, duty between lord and minister, distinction between spouses, age order, and trust between friends.

Occurrences.Kwic: 父子有親，君臣有義，長幼有序，朋友有信
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second text places duty between lord and minister in an ordinary social list with family, age, and friendship relations.

Senses.PreferredTarget: revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs
AlternateTargets: scold the buddhas and abuse the patriarchs
Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “scold or shout down” (呵, also written 訶), “buddhas” (佛), “curse or revile” (罵), and “patriarchs” (祖): "revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs." Zen-scoped the string (呵佛罵祖) occurs 232 times across 118 texts; the graphic variants (訶佛罵祖) (33 hits / 24 texts), (呵佛叱祖) (4 hits, all the 楊岐 line below) and the inverted (罵祖呵佛) (2) also occur. Attested deployment: (1) as an epithet for a master's conduct — most often (德山)'s: (上堂德山呵佛罵祖承其言者多見德山者少) (a 上堂 of 真淨克文 in 古尊宿語錄), and paired with (臨濟)'s shout in another of the same master's (上堂) — (德山呵佛罵祖臨濟喝) (the same passage carried in both the C- and D-canon editions of 古尊宿語錄); (2) spoken in a master's own record of himself — (楊岐一語)。(呵佛叱祖)。(明眼人前)。(不得錯舉) (楊岐方會's record); (3) as an answer to a question — to "what is the shortcut teaching gate?" (如何是徑截法門) a master answers (訶佛罵祖去), and to "what is host-within-host?" (如何是主中主) another answers (訶佛罵祖); (4) as a conduct-label for a master — (和尚終日訶佛罵祖) (spoken by an attendant to the dying 真點胸), and (據猊床)，(而訶佛罵祖) (of a master on the lion-seat); (5) in a letter of (玉林通琇) — "that we could not, in the days when venerables stood thick as forests, go off to a solitary peak, tie together a grass hut, and revile the buddhas and curse the patriarchs — but instead prop up the tottering great house with chicken-rib strength, sorting demons and rebutting the different — is truly a great misfortune" (我輩不能于尊宿林林之日向孤峰絕頂蟠結草庵呵佛罵祖去迺以鷄肋之力撑持大廈之危辯魔斥異誠大不幸). The corpus also records a reply that glosses it: to "who is one who reviles buddhas and curses patriarchs?" (訶佛罵祖是甚麼人) a master answers "an icchantika" (闡提漢). The texts set the phrase beside "sort demons and screen the different" (辨魔揀異): (辨魔揀異)，(須是頂門具眼)；(訶佛罵祖)，(還他腦後見腮) (2 texts). The texts assign the phrase no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense; the four graphs are stable, and the variants (訶/呵, 叱/罵, inverted 罵祖呵佛 2, 罵佛呵祖 1) are grep-verified; (訶佛叱祖) and (呵佛喝祖) do not occur. Attribution: (楊岐方會) speaks the (呵佛叱祖) line in his own record (袁州楊岐山普通禪院會和尚語錄, T47n1994A). The two (德山)-epithet passages are (上堂) of (真淨克文) (雲庵真淨禪師語錄, inside the 古尊宿語錄 compilation; 德山宣鑒 is the SUBJECT, not the speaker). The B27n0152 letter passage is (玉林通琇)'s own reply (its duplicate at 0656a20 opens 師復書云); the correspondent's incoming letter is the inline (附原書) note. The J-canon answers (徑截法門, 主中主, 闡提漢) are from Ming/Qing (語錄) whose masters — (大溈五峰學) (Wufeng Ruxue), (蓮月), (三山燈來) — are not on the roster, so MasterName null; do NOT read the Tang roster master (五峰) into (大溈五峰學). Multi-source: T, C, B, D and J canons, multiple independent texts and masters.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。楊岐一語。呵佛叱祖。明眼人前。不得錯舉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (袁州楊岐山普通禪院會和尚語錄) (楊岐方會's own record; document title 楊岐方會和尚語錄); a (上堂) in which he characterizes his own word — (楊岐一語)。(呵佛叱祖). The (叱) variant of the phrase (all 4 Zen-scoped 呵佛叱祖 hits are this line: T47n1994A, C077n1710, D48n8939, X78n1556). Primary-source, master speaking of himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂德山呵佛罵祖承其言者多見德山者少
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄) (C-canon edition), (卷)43, cb:mulu (雲庵真淨禪師語錄一) — the (上堂) speaker is (真淨克文) (雲庵真淨); (德山宣鑒) is the SUBJECT (those who take his words are many, those who see him few). The same master's (卷)44 record pairs the epithet with Linji's shout — (德山呵佛罵祖臨濟喝) (0939a05); both passages are carried again in the D-canon edition of (古尊宿語錄) (D48n8939).

Occurrences.Kwic: 向孤峰絕頂蟠結草庵呵佛罵祖去迺以鷄肋之力撑持大廈之危辯魔斥異
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄), section (復寶華朝和尚) (reply to Baohua Chao): the correspondent's incoming letter is the inline (附原書) note, and this main-text passage (我輩不能于尊宿林林之日向孤峰絕頂…) is (玉林通琇)'s own reply — confirmed by the duplicate at 0656a20, which opens (師復書云). The phrase stands beside (辯魔斥異). Roster spelling (玉林通琇).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是徑截法門？」師云：「訶佛罵祖去。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大溈五峰學禪師語錄); answer to (總持道人)'s question "the shortcut teaching gate" (如何是徑截法門). Speaker (大溈五峰學) (Wufeng Ruxue, Ming/Qing) is not the Tang roster (五峰), so MasterName null. (訶) variant.

Occurrences.Kwic: 訶佛罵祖是甚麼人？」師云：「闡提漢！」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (三山來禪師語錄), (問答) section; the in-corpus gloss-by-reply — asked (訶佛罵祖是甚麼人) the master answers (闡提漢) (an icchantika). Speaker (三山燈來) (Ming/Qing) not on roster, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是主中主？」師云：「訶佛罵祖。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (蓮月禪師語錄); answer to (如何是主中主) (host-within-host) — (訶佛罵祖). Speaker (蓮月) (Ming/Qing) not on roster, MasterName null. Cf. the same record's contrast (辨魔揀異)，(須是頂門具眼)；(訶佛罵祖)，(還他腦後見腮) (0399c02; the pairing recurs in X85n1590).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'laugh loudly, ha-ha.' The phrase occurs 1,508 times in 278 allowlisted texts and is written into public encounters as an audible action, sometimes followed by speech and sometimes serving as the whole recorded response. The records preserve its range without assigning one fixed interpretation to it. Baizhang laughs after a colleague asks why he had just cried, and answers only, 'Just now I cried; now I laugh.' Zhaozhou laughs during an exchange and then repeats the other speaker's cry, 'Heaven! Heaven!' Jinniu dances with the rice tub, laughs loudly, and calls the assembly to eat. Another monk reports returning to eat after hearing the meal drum, whereupon the master laughs. A discourse can even laugh and then ask, 'Laugh at what?' The deviation lies in its textual role: laughter is preserved as a speaker-turn and public-interview action, not reduced to an editorial note about emotion.
Senses.Note: Different occasions do not establish different things. The phrase consistently denotes the audible act of laughing; the texts do not authorize a menu of motives.

Occurrences.Kwic: 適來哭，如今為甚却笑？師云：適來哭，如今笑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked why he now laughs after crying, Baizhang answers only that earlier he cried and now he laughs.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舁飯桶到堂前作舞。呵呵大笑曰。菩薩子。喫飯來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jinniu dances with the rice tub, laughs loudly, and calls the assembly to eat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 州呵呵大笑。山曰：作什麼？州曰：蒼天！蒼天
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's loud laugh is itself queried in the encounter, after which he repeats 'Heaven! Heaven!'

Occurrences.Kwic: 某甲早辰未喫粥聞鼓聲歸喫飯師呵呵大笑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk says he heard the drum and returned to eat because he had not eaten gruel; the master laughs loudly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久，呵呵大笑曰：笑箇甚麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a pause, the master laughs loudly and explicitly asks what is being laughed at.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a root of life: in Chan records, the hold described as being cut, broken, or gathered up. The phrase occurs 829 times in 226 allowlisted texts. Luyuan spreads his hand and says that the life-roots of all the old masters and senior monks are “all here” (all the old masters and senior monks' life-roots are all here). Hui'an Miguang supplies the corpus's clearest physical comparison: cutting a tree once at the root severs its life-root, whereas chopping its branches does not (one cut at the root severs the life-root; if you chop at the branches, can you sever the life-root?). Ying'an's record says that when a blind was rolled up, “the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot” (the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot). A public exchange asks whether one who has let go at a cliff has yet severed the life-root; the answer postpones speech until the questioner's own life-root is severed. The recurring collocations thus make cutting or breaking the life-root a Chan-loaded use, distinct from the enumerated vital faculty in the second sense; the entry makes no claim about an inward meaning beyond those recorded predicates.
Senses.Note: Common forms include 'the life-root is not severed' and 'sever the life-root.' Gao-feng's question, 'a person who has completely broken through is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?' (a completely broken-through person is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?), became a repeatedly cited saying.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天下老和尚．諸上座命根。總在這裏。有僧出曰。還收得也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under Luyuan Heshang: he spreads his hand and says, 'the life-roots of all the old masters and senior monks are all here.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如人斫樹，根下一刀，則命根斷矣。汝向枝上斫，其能斷命根乎？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Hui'an Miguang's biography: 'one cut at the root severs the life-root; if you chop at the branches, can you sever it?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日見卷簾，豁然漆桶破，命根嚗地斷，便說箇頌子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ying'an's record reports: on seeing a blind rolled up, 'the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：懸崖撒手底人命根還斷也未？師云：待闍黎命根斷即道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public question and answer in Wuyi Yuanlai's record: asked whether the life-root is severed, the master says he will speak when the questioner's is severed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大徹底人本脫生死，因什命根不斷？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sanfeng Cang quotes Gao-feng's enduring question: 'a completely broken-through person is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪別無奇特，祇要當人命根斷，疑情脫，千眼頓開
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address says that investigating Chan requires the person's life-root to be severed and the mass of doubt to fall away.

Senses.Explanation: In enumerative prose, the same graphs name the vital faculty as one faculty among others. The Record of the Source-Mirror says, 'among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost' (among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost). This is a different referent from the Chan idiom that masters locate, seize, and sever, so it is retained separately rather than blurred into that usage.
Senses.Note: This sense is included because it is attested within the allowlisted record, not because a Buddhist glossary controls the Chan sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如諸根中。命根為最。佛正法正行中。此心為最。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Source-Mirror uses the term in an explicit comparison: 'among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost.'

Senses.Explanation: An abrupt exclamation, conventionally rendered “Bah!” In the Chan record it is a spoken action: a master inserts it before a rebuke, uses it alone as an answer, or directs it at a named interlocutor. The Stove-Breaker strikes the stove and says “Bah! This stove is only made of mud and tiles” (咄。此竈只是泥瓦合成); Danyuan says “Bah! Foolish fellow! Who is in the well?” (咄。癡漢。誰在井中); and one record answers “What is the Way?” (如何是道) simply with the exclamation before ordering the monk away. Its Chan deviation is this regular placement inside encounter dialogue as an answer or verbal blow, rather than merely narrative punctuation. The corpus gives the sound no further lexical gloss.
Senses.Note: The exact graph occurs 3,892 times in 343 allowlisted texts. It appears independently as rebuke, address, answer, and commentary interjection; no definition formula or morphological variant supplies a second lexical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊咄曰。文殊。吾四十九年住世。未曾說一字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium retells Buddha addressing Manjusri: “Bah, Manjusri. In my forty-nine years in the world, I never said one word.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 以杖敲竈三下曰。咄。此竈只是泥瓦合成。聖從何來。靈從何起。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Stove-Breaker section: after striking the stove three times, he says, “Bah! This stove is only made of mud and tiles. Where does holiness come from? Where does efficacy arise?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是道。師便咄。僧曰。學人未領旨。師曰。去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An encounter preserved in the Five Lamps Compendium: asked “What is the Way?” the teacher immediately says “Bah!” and later “Go!”

Occurrences.Kwic: 耽源曰。咄。癡漢。誰在井中。仰山不契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record raises Danyuan's reply: “Bah! Foolish fellow! Who is in the well?” The occurrence is in a retold case.

Senses.Explanation: The normal Chan use is a title for the person who teaches and presides over a monastic community. It follows a personal name in lineage headings, as in “Master Bodhidharma” (菩提達摩和尚), and opens biographies such as “Master Puhua of Zhenzhou, who ...” (鎮州普化和尚者). A student can state that he comes from Master An of Songshan, while lamp records quote an authority with “Master Wuzu Fayan said” (五祖演和尚曰). The title also marks institutional and public relations. The “master at the head of the hall” (堂頭和尚) is asked to address the assembled community; another monk asks the master to “speak the teaching for the assembly” (請和尚為眾說法). Direct address changes English capitalization and syntax but not the referent. Huike says, “I only beg you, Master, to show compassion” (惟願和尚慈悲); a monk asks the Cloth-Bag Monk, “Master, what are you doing here?” (和尚在這裏作甚麼); and a cloister director asks after the master's health before the reply “Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha.” A collective public saying can gather “all the old masters under heaven” (天下老和尚) in one place. Across these forms, the Chan deviation is institutional and documentary: the word identifies the named person questioned in encounters, invited to teach from the seat, cited in lineage, and quoted as the head of a community.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 52,209 occurrences in 441 texts. Render direct address as capitalized “Master”; in narrative prose use “the master,” a named form such as “Master Bodhidharma,” or “abbot” only where the office is explicit. Direct address is grammatical variation, not a separate sense. The embedded form “monk-fellows” (和尚子) is a separate compound. The ordination-preceptor role is separately attested below and must not be merged into this teaching relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十八祖菩提達摩和尚三三〇第二十九祖師慧可禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Patriarchs' Hall Collection table of contents places the title after Bodhidharma's name: "the twenty-eighth patriarch, Master Bodhidharma."

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖憫而問曰。汝久立雪中。當求何事。光悲淚曰。惟願和尚慈悲。開甘露門。廣度羣品。

Occurrences.Kwic: 師在街衢立，有僧問：和尚在這裏作甚麼？師曰：等箇人。曰：來也，來也。師曰：汝不是這箇人。

Occurrences.Kwic: 五祖演和尚曰。今時叢林學道之士。聲名不揚。匪為人之所信者。蓋為梵行不清白。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Admonitions of the Chan Grove introduces a quotation with the authorial title, "Master Wuzu Fayan said."

Occurrences.Kwic: 今五祖堂頭和尚，此日幸對人天廣眾，請不悋慈悲，重為顯揚，使先宗有據，吾道益明
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Ancestral Essentials calls Wuzu the “master at the head of the hall” and asks him to address the broad assembly, anchoring the title's presiding institutional use.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The cloister director asks after the master's health; the master replies, “Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 鎮州普化和尚者不知何許人也。師事盤山密受真訣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography opens with Master Puhua of Zhenzhou and identifies his teacher relation to Panshan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天下老和尚緫在這裏我若放一線道從汝七縱八橫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address gathers all the old masters under heaven “here,” a collective use of titled teaching figures.

Senses.Explanation: In ordination accounts the same title names the person from whom someone receives the precepts, a different office from the teaching master. Biographical sequences distinguish the roles explicitly: one nun "first shaved her head at Wanyuan Cloister, investigated under Guixi Zhuang, then received the precepts from Preceptor Baochi, and finally heard the teaching from Old Man Yi'an" (初披剃於萬緣寺，參學於桂谿莊，繼受戒於寶池和尚，終聞法於易菴老人). Another record separates "listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye" from "receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin" (聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚). The office is also named directly: a woman asks "Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze to serve as the preceptor from whom she received the precepts" (乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師), while incense verses honor a "preceptor from whom the precepts were received" (得戒和尚) alongside the distinct tonsure teachers. This is a precept-family deployment of the title: it identifies the human conferrer in an ordination relation, not merely a respectful reading of the teaching-master sense.
Senses.Note: Do not infer this sense from every occurrence of “precept/Master Jie” (戒和尚). In early lamp records that sequence often means “Master Jie,” where Jie is a personal name, especially Wuzu Jie. The verified line “arrived at Master Wuzu Jie” (到五祖戒和尚處) is a teacher-name use, not ordination. Assign the preceptor sense only when receiving or conferring precepts, the explicit title “preceptor from whom the precepts were received” (得戒和尚), or an equivalent role statement supplies the relation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初披剃於萬緣寺，參學於桂谿莊，更歷寒暑，道念愈堅。繼受戒於寶池和尚，終聞法於易菴老人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The biography separates tonsure, investigation, receiving precepts from Preceptor Baochi, and finally hearing the teaching from Yi'an, making the ordination role explicit.

Occurrences.Kwic: 余挂錫半載，辭水月方丈，北遊燕山，聽教於不夜天師、受戒於玉林和尚。後住崇寧禪院
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker distinguishes "listening to the teaching under Teacher Buye" from "receiving the precepts from Preceptor Yulin."

Occurrences.Kwic: 復乞漏澤箬菴和尚為得戒師，是時余居三師之列。違今年已六十矣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record says that Preceptor Ruo'an of Louze was asked to serve explicitly as the "preceptor from whom the precepts were received."

Occurrences.Kwic: 此瓣香，分弗為兩，析不成三，爇向爐中，奉上高峰得戒和尚、薙髮二位尊師，伏願三聚嚴明
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An incense verse offers incense to the Gaofeng "preceptor from whom the precepts were received" and to two separate tonsure teachers.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, mixing (和) mud (泥) and blending (合) water (水): "mixing mud and blending water." The phrase occurs 343 times in 113 allowlisted texts. Chan records make the ordinary mixing image an appraisal of sayings, explanations, and speakers. In a recasting of three phrases, "understanding from the first phrase" is called "mixing mud and blending water," followed by "binding oneself without a rope" and "landing with all four edges on the ground" (第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地). Another record groups it with "speaking a dream without a dream" and "not knowing good from bad" (無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡). Yet the phrase also stands as a direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?" (如何是大道真源), and one discourse pairs "where wind cannot enter" with "mixing mud and blending water" in both directions. Another contrasts failing to mark the moment, when black and white remain undistinguished, with marking it too late, called "mixing mud and blending water." These are different recorded placements of one image. The texts do not supply the uniform gloss “descending to the student's level,” so neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The phrase's evaluative direction varies with its sentence. Favorable and unfavorable modern readings are not separate lexical objects and are not split into senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A three-part appraisal assigns mixing mud and water to understanding from the first phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與麼說話，可謂無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is grouped with speaking a dream without a dream and not knowing good from bad.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是大道真源？師云：和泥合水。僧云：便恁麼去時如何？師云：截斷草鞋跟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: It is the direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 風吹不入處，和泥合水；和泥合水處，風吹不入。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse pairs where wind cannot enter and mixing mud and water in a reciprocal formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 點時不到。皂白未分。到時不點。和泥合水。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is contrasted with failing to mark the moment while black and white remain undistinguished.

Senses.Explanation: An exclamatory sound, occurring 1,147 times in 223 allowlisted texts. Chan records preserve it inside teaching-seat speeches and public exchanges as a standalone vocal turn or a marked break before the next words. A discourse cries 'Yi!' before reversing 'red-bearded foreigner' into 'foreigner with a red beard'; another says 'Yi! Look at Elder Xue's conduct'; and another pauses, cries 'Yi!', and asks, 'What connection is there?' In direct exchange, a participant can offer only 'Yi!', to which the master answers. The corpus also lists 'Yunmen's look and yi' (雲門顧鑑咦) as a recognizable expression. English cannot fix one emotion for all these uses, so the preferred target transliterates the sound while the explanation records its observable placement. Its Chan deviation is that the records retain the exclamation as part of the master's or questioner's actual interview turn.
Senses.Note: Surprise, challenge, interruption, and emphasis would be readings of the same vocal act, not different things; the corpus does not warrant separate senses for inferred motives.

Occurrences.Kwic: 咦！不分析，將謂赤鬚鬍，更有鬍鬚赤
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The exclamation marks the turn before a reversed pair of phrases.

Occurrences.Kwic: 咦！且看雪上座行履
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat speech cries 'Yi!' and directs the assembly to look at Elder Xue's conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久，云：「咦！有什麼交涉？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a pause, the speaker cries 'Yi!' and asks what connection there is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「咦。」師云：「禹力不到處，水聲流向西。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interlocutor gives only the exclamation; the master responds with a full line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山末後句，雲門顧鑑咦
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse lists Yunmen's look-and-yi beside Deshan's final saying as a recognizable deployment.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “to bite and chew” (咬嚼), the term is attested 209 times in 109 allowlisted texts. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: one teacher tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Other comments use the resistance of food as an explicit comparison: a saying can be “unable to be chewed through” (咬嚼不破), while Donglin offers only “wooden-slat soup and iron-nail rice—chew as you will” (木札羹、鉄釘飯，任汝咬嚼). The record also issues the opposite verdict, “strictly avoid chewing” (切忌咬嚼), after the answer “a thousand-year peach pit.”
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is ordinary mastication used as a verb for sustained handling of a sentence, saying, or public case, with edible and inedible images kept visible. The corpus's affirmative instruction and prohibition are different appraisals of the same act, not separate senses. No independent high-value literal meal occurrence was found that would justify splitting actual eating from this lexicalized use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且去咬嚼他一個顛撲不破的現成句子。咬嚼來、咬嚼去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct instruction tells beginners to chew over a ready-made sentence and repeats the action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只這秦時𨍏轢鑽，咬嚼不破。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A saying is described as impossible to chew through.

Occurrences.Kwic: 托缽公案，無盡一生咬嚼不破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The bowl-carrying public case is what Wujin could not chew through in his lifetime.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老宿曰：千年桃核。林泉道：切忌咬嚼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After “a thousand-year peach pit,” Linquan comments: strictly avoid chewing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇有木札羹、鉄釘飯，任汝咬嚼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Donglin offers wooden-slat soup and iron-nail rice for the listener to chew as desired.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "question and answer" (問答). In Chan records it names the spoken exchange itself, a recurring division of masters' records, and a component of the compound "question-and-answer encounters" (問答機緣). Zhaozhou is asked how he responds when every question-and-answer falls in the thinking faculty; he answers, "Ask" (問), so the record places the term inside an enacted exchange. Zhongfeng describes question and answer "racing across one another" (問答交馳), with the question in the answer and the answer in the question. Other records preserve headings for question-and-answer, pair it with requests for instruction, entry into the room, and examination, or state "question-and-answer was not recorded" (問答不錄) before retaining the subsequent address.
Senses.Note: The corpus does not treat the label as sufficient by itself. One record objects that "recently many take question-and-answer to be Chan" (近世多以問答為禪) and says the houses' styles thereby become unclear. Another master raises the whisk and says, "set question-and-answer encounters aside" (機緣問答且置), then asks whether the assembly understands the whisk. These are attested restrictions on equating a recorded format with Chan; they do not remove public questioning from the records. Family check: "a monk asked" (僧問) is the speaker-turn formula; "request instruction" (請益) names a request for instruction; "enter the room" (入室) identifies admission or entry; "supply a phrase" (下語) names supplying a phrase or judgment. "Question-and-answer" (問答) names the reciprocal exchange and does not replace those narrower terms. The headword has 1,242 occurrences in 244 allowlisted texts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「凡有問答，落在意根；不落意根，師如何對？」師云：「問。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A question about all question-and-answer falling in the thinking faculty receives the answer: Ask.

Occurrences.Kwic: 便見問在答處答在問處。問答交馳無儞入處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The address places question in answer and answer in question and calls them racing across one another.

Occurrences.Kwic: 近世多以問答為禪家家風不明古人事一向逐末不反可怪可怪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct criticism of taking question-and-answer itself to be Chan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大凡學人請益，問處真實，方見答處的當。若問答相違，則聾瞽不相入矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A general address relates a genuine place of asking to an apt place of answering and calls mismatched question and answer mutually inaccessible.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃驀豎拂子云：「機緣問答且置，會得這箇麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master raises the whisk, sets question-and-answer encounters aside, and asks whether the assembly understands this.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂斂衣就坐。問答不錄。乃云。大道無為。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Editorial formula marking that question-and-answer occurred but was not recorded before the address.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “ask words”: to put a question in an encounter, and by extension the questioning or the person who does it. The public role is grammatical and institutional in the records: a master calls, “is there anyone with a question? Quickly bring the question forward” (更有問話者麼，速致問來), or “let anyone who knows how to question come forward” (有解問話者出來). Monks compete to step out and question during an ascending-the-hall address, and another record calls a participant “the monk who asked the question” (問話僧). The corpus also examines the quality of questioning. An essay titled “Warning on Questioning” says recent questioning attracts criticism because people do not know the purpose of “putting forward a question, presenting a doubt, and requesting instruction” (伸問、致疑、咨請), and instead use congratulatory and seasonal phrases. Deshan's recorded “tonight I will not answer; anyone who questions gets thirty blows” still produces a monk who steps forward, and later records repeatedly raise and comment on that encounter. The term thus names an exposed speaking turn open to answer, refusal, rebuke, or later appraisal; it does not guarantee a successful or approved question.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 871 hits in 210 texts. Productive forms include “questioner / anyone who questions” (問話者, 274 hits / 124 texts), “questioning monk” (問話僧, 52 / 36), and “a monk came out to question” (僧出問話, attested across multiple records). The Zen bend is the term's public-interview role and the tradition's explicit scrutiny of how a question is put, not merely the ordinary verb “ask.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 誡問話近代問話多招譏謗蓋緣不知伸問致疑咨請之意後生相承多用祝賛順時語並非宗乗中建立
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings, “Warning on Questioning”: defines the relevant purpose by the sequence “put forward a question, present a doubt, request instruction,” contrasting it with congratulatory seasonal language.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山示眾道今夜不荅話問話者三十棒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later discussion quotes Deshan's address: “tonight I will not answer; anyone who questions gets thirty blows.” The record treats the questioner's exposed role as part of a named encounter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 更有問話者麼速致問來你纔開口早勿交涉也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings: during the teaching assembly the master asks whether anyone has a question and calls for it to be brought promptly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂云有觧問話者出來時有僧出禮拜師云是者老漢罪過便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings: ascending the hall, the master calls for anyone able to question; a monk comes forward and bows, and the master descends from the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。有數僧爭出問話。師曰。但一齊出來問。待老僧一齊與汝答。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium: several monks compete to come out and question during an ascending-the-hall address; the master tells them to ask together and promises to answer together.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the chick pecks and the hen taps at the same instant
AlternateTargets: pecking and tapping at the same instant
Senses.Explanation: Literally, the chick pecks from inside the shell while the hen taps from outside at the same instant. The phrase occurs 221 times in 71 allowlisted texts. A later record defines the image graph by graph: the chick pecks, the mother taps, and neither precedes the other. In the Chan record it names a matched teacher-student exchange and is extended into an 'eye,' a 'function,' and a 'responsive mechanism.' Nanyuan's repeatedly quoted public interview distinguishes possessing the eye from possessing the function, then says that when adepts meet they do not peck and tap: doing so at the same instant misses it. Yuanwu applies the phrase to Fayan's answer 'you are Huichao' and to teachers who respond to circumstances. This deployment as a technical description of timing in public exchange is the corpus-specific bend of the hatching image.
Senses.Note: The sources themselves preserve a tension: one defines simultaneity through the chick-and-hen image, while the Nanyuan case says adepts who enact the named peck-and-tap miss it. This entry reports both formulations without resolving their intent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「師資緣契，啐啄同時，子啐母啄，啄與啐不先不後，是為同時。南院上堂示眾云：『諸方只具啐啄同時眼，不具啐啄同時用
Occurrences.AttributionNote: This discourse explicitly defines the hatching image and then introduces Nanyuan's eye/function distinction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝州南院慧顒禪師上堂諸方只具啐啄同時眼不具啐啄同時用時有僧便問如何是啐啄同時用師曰作家相見不啐啄啐啄同時失
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case collection preserves Nanyuan's public interview about the phrase's eye and function.

Occurrences.Kwic: 法眼禪師。有啐啄同時底機。具啐啄同時底用。方能如此答話。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu applies its mechanism and function to Fayan's answer in a public case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大凡行脚人。須具啐啄同時眼。有啐啄同時用。方稱衲僧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A commentary makes the eye and function qualifications of an itinerant monk.

Senses.Explanation: Literally a “good knowing acquaintance,” this corpus-wide person label names a good teacher, guide, or good friend. The term occurs 2,832 times in 311 allowlisted texts. Dahui directly says, “those called good teachers guide all beings and cause them to see nature” (夫稱善知識者，引導一切眾生，令見佛性), then describes observing people's capacities and giving teaching as medicine matches illness. He calls such reception and guidance “the proper work a good teacher ought to do” (善知識本分合做底事), and elsewhere mentions “a good teacher's eye for distinguishing people” (善知識辨人眼). The Five Lamps Compendium describes travelling people “visiting good teachers” (參善知識). Another narrative has a student say, “a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages; now that I have met one, why begrudge body or life?” (大善知識歷劫難逢，今既得遇，豈惜身命). Asked “what is a good teacher?” (如何是善知識), Fohai replies that lanterns, pillars, cats, and dogs are all called good teachers. The same label supplies the vocative “Good friends!” when speakers address assemblies. Direct address changes who is being hailed, not the lexical kind of label.
Senses.Note: Dahui's role definition and Fohai's materially different answer are both retained, preventing an exclusively institutional or human-office definition. The former role/vocative targets applied the same label to people in referential and direct-address grammar and are merged. Compare accomplished person (作家), lineage teacher (宗師), visiting a good teacher (參善知識), general address (普說), and ascending the hall (上堂).

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫稱善知識者。引導一切眾生。令見佛性。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own record. He directly defines those called good teachers as guiding beings and causing them to see nature.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇是善知識本分合做底事。豈是彊為。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui calls receiving and maturing those who travelled to the gathering 'the proper work a good teacher ought to do,' not something forced.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是善知識。臣云。燈籠露柱猫兒狗子。皆稱善知識何必更問。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp narrates Fohai's report to the emperor of his exchange with Zeng Kai. Asked what a good teacher is, Fohai names lanterns, pillars, cats, and dogs. As a reported two-person exchange, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 凡行脚人參善知識。到一叢林。放下瓶鉢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Baozi Xingyan section. The master speaks of travelling people visiting good teachers and arriving at a community; no exact roster link is available.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非但失却善知識辨人眼。亦乃賺他百劫千生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record names 'a good teacher's eye for distinguishing people' while criticizing acceptance of a person's presentation for irrelevant reasons.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善知識！一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Platform Record, Huineng addresses the assembly as “Good friends!” before defining complete command of the single conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善知識！一言半句實有起死回生之力、翻窠倒臼之施
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address hails the assembly as “Good friends!” before speaking of a word or half a phrase. No exact roster link was assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大善知識歷劫難逢。今既得遇，豈惜身命！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student says that a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages and, having now met one, asks why he should begrudge body or life.

Senses.Explanation: A sharp vocal cry: a shout. In Chan records it is a public-interview action available to both sides, not a sound reserved to masters. A master may shout at an arriving monk, a monk may shout and be struck, and the two head monks of Linji's halls shout simultaneously; Linji says host and guest are distinctly present in that encounter. Linji's record gives four explicit comparisons: a shout like the Diamond-King Treasure Sword, like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground, like a probing pole and shadowing grass, and a shout not used as a shout. When the monk hesitates over them, Linji shouts. The Eye of Humans and Gods later states that a shout distinguishing host and guest has host and guest within it and that a shout carrying illumination and function has both within it. The public interview also judges rather than automatically ratifies a shout: after answering a question on the great purport with a shout, Linji asks whether it was a good shout, and the exchange continues through fault and repeated offense. Another instruction expressly tells the assembly not to shout blindly or shout at random. A recorded shout can have an immediate bodily effect—after Mazu's shout, Baizhang is said to have been deaf for three days—but the corpus does not assign that effect or any one result to every shout. The act also closes teaching-seat speech in the stage direction “shouted once and left the seat,” and lists of house devices pair Linji's shout with Deshan's staff. The ordinary baseline remains audible in the Puhua episode, where an officer cries out to clear the road and Puhua also cries out while making a wrestling gesture. These are all the same vocal act in different institutions and sentence positions. The longer compounds “cheer” (喝采), “shout abuse” (喝罵), and “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) must be translated as compounds; no allowlisted drinking use was established.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count at the depth audit: 35,032 hits in 411 texts. High-frequency families include “one shout” (一喝), “shout once” (喝一喝), “the master then shouted” (師便喝), “the monk then shouted” (僧便喝), “four shouts” (四喝), “a shout not used as a shout” (一喝不作一喝用), and “staff and shout” (棒喝). The former entry's two senses—‘a shout’ and ‘to shout/cry out’—were merged because they paraphrased the same vocal event; noun and verb syntax alone did not establish different things. Targeted tests found no allowlisted drinking sense in “drink tea” (喝茶), “drink wine” (喝酒), or “drink water” (喝水). “Cheer” (喝采) and “shout abuse” (喝罵) are separately lexicalized compounds, while “clear the road by shouting” (喝道) supplies the ordinary calling-out baseline. Twelve witnesses preserve definition, master and monk use, simultaneous use, later systematization, explicit appraisal, warning against blind/random shouting, bodily effect, teaching-seat closure, house-device pairing, and ordinary road-clearing use without padding duplicate shouts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問僧：「有時一喝如金剛王寶劍、有時一喝如踞地金毛師子、有時一喝如探竿影草、有時一喝不作一喝用，汝作麼生會？」僧擬議，師便喝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own Four Shouts passage gives four comparisons and then records Linji shouting when the monk hesitates.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是日，兩堂首座相見，同時下喝。僧問師：「還有賓主也無？」師云：「賓主歷然。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The two hall heads shout simultaneously; Linji answers that host and guest are distinctly present. The multi-speaker occurrence remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一喝分賓主者。一喝中。自有賓有主也。照用一時行者。一喝中。自有照有用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compiled in-corpus gloss: a shout that distinguishes host and guest contains both; one carrying illumination and function contains both.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟喝。德山棒。天皇餅。趙州茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later device list places Linji's shout beside Deshan's staff, Tianhuang's cake, and Zhaozhou's tea.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖振威一喝。師直得三日耳聾。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The narrative says Mazu gave a forceful shout and Baizhang was deaf for three days; the line has two figures and remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有僧從外來。師便喝。僧曰。好箇來由。師曰。猶要棒在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An arriving monk is met by the master's shout, answers it verbally, and is told that the staff is still needed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便喝。師便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk shouts and the master strikes, proving that the interview shout is not restricted to the teaching-seat speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝一喝，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Stage direction: the speaker shouts once and leaves the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或行棒，或行喝，或詞辨縱橫，或寂寥無說
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An enumeration places wielding the shout beside wielding the staff, verbal eloquence, and silence as recorded modes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 普化見馬步使出喝道師亦喝道作相撲勢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ordinary baseline: an officer comes out crying for the road to be cleared, and Puhua also cries out while making a wrestling gesture.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又有僧問：「如何是佛法大意？」師便喝，僧禮拜，師云：「爾道好喝也無？」僧云：「草賊大敗。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji answers the great-purport question with a shout, then explicitly asks whether it was a good shout; the monk's verdict keeps the exchange open.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸上座不得盲喝亂喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction explicitly warns the assembly not to shout blindly or at random, proving that the corpus evaluates rather than automatically validates the act.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “shout one shout,” this is the records' stock narrative formula for a master's or monk's performed shout. In a public interview it can answer another shout: Muzhou says, “today this old monk was shouted at once by you” (老僧今日被汝喝一喝), asks what comes after three or four shouts, and strikes the monk when he has no words. Feiyin shouts amid a high-seat address and then says, “if I had not stopped it with a shout, this entangling talk would nearly have gone on without end” (若不喝住，幾乎打葛藤無有了時也). One record performs four shouts in sequence and follows them respectively with “the lion roars,” “the elephant king stretches,” “a mad dog chases a clod,” and “a shrimp cannot leap out of the dipper”; these are the record's four stated comparisons, not four dictionary senses. Elsewhere a monk shouts and exits, a speaker shouts before ascending the formal seat and offering incense, and another shouts before returning to the abbot's quarters. The same formula can close an address before leaving the seat, combine with planting the staff, or precede questions to the assembly. The Chan deviation is grammatical and institutional: a shout is preserved as a performed move within the public interview or teaching-seat event. This entry reports its position and any stated classification without assigning it an unstated force.
Senses.Note: The formula occurs 7,091 times in 320 allowlisted texts. Family comparison: “shout” (喝) can be a noun or verb, “one shout” (一喝) counts it, and “gave a shout” (喝一喝) is the finite narrative action. Speaker, addressee, and sequence position are different deployments of the same action, not different things. Compare leaving the seat (下座), ascending the seat (陞座), planting the staff (卓拄杖), and the abbot's quarters (方丈).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問僧近離什麼處僧喝師云老僧今日被你喝一喝僧又喝師云三喝四喝後作麼生僧無語師便打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public interview: the monk shouts; Muzhou says he has been shouted at once, asks what follows three or four shouts, then strikes when the monk has no words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝一喝，云：「若不喝住，幾乎打葛藤無有了時也。且忽憶忽悟一句作麼生道？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker explicitly describes his performed shout as stopping an otherwise endless stretch of entangling talk, then asks how to state a line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂拈袈裟角，云：大眾！人人有分，須是頂門眼開始得。喝一喝，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: High-seat closure: a shout immediately followed by stepping down from the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久，云：向下文長，付在來日。喝一喝。良久，云：無為無事人，猶是金鎖難。喝一喝，卓拄杖，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two performed shouts punctuate the address; the second combines with planting the staff and stepping down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師顧視大眾喝一喝曰。諸禪德莫是賓主歷然麼。莫是先照後用麼。莫是照用同時麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master looks over the assembly, shouts, and immediately publicly questions three proposed Linji-house classifications.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝一喝曰。師子哮吼。又喝一喝曰。象王嚬伸。又喝一喝曰。狂狗逐塊。又喝一喝曰。鰕跳不出斗。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Four performed shouts are followed respectively by “the lion roars” (師子哮吼), “the elephant king stretches” (象王嚬伸), “a mad dog chases a clod” (狂狗逐塊), and “a shrimp cannot leap out of the dipper” (鰕跳不出斗). Counted as one occurrence object, this preserves the record's explicit classifications without converting them into lexical senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧喝一喝便出，師休去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk “gave a shout and thereupon went out” (喝一喝便出); the master says, “stop” (休去). This anchors an interlocutor, rather than the master, performing the action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝一喝便陞。拈香云：
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker gives a shout, immediately ascends the formal seat, and begins the incense offering. This places the action at the opening of teaching-seat ritual.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喝一喝，便歸方丈。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker gives a shout and “thereupon returns to the abbot's quarters” (便歸方丈), closing the event by returning rather than leaving the seat.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, lose the body (lose body) and lose life (lose life): 'lose body and life.' The phrase occurs 645 times in 217 allowlisted texts. The record deploys it as the stated cost at points where answering, hesitating, advancing, or merely constructing an understanding is dangerous. Xiangyan's tree case says that answering the question loses body and life, while silence fails the questioner. Zihu's posted notice says his dog takes head, heart, and feet, and that deliberation immediately loses body and life. In Xuefeng's turtle-nosed-snake case, Changqing says many in the hall will lose body and life. Baofu says of the matter that whether one catches it or does not, one cannot avoid losing body and life. Linji says, 'one who acts for the teaching does not avoid losing body and life' before recounting his three beatings under Huangbo. These are distinct public cases and deployment shapes of one idiom, not different referents; the texts state the danger but the entry does not decide what the losses signify.
Senses.Note: The reversible form 'lose life and body' also occurs. Frequent triggers include deliberation, coming near a sword or fire, and answering a public question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若開口答即喪身失命。若不答又違他所問。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiangyan's tree case states the double bind: answering loses body and life; not answering violates the question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子湖有一隻狗。上取人頭。中取人心。下取人足。擬議即喪身失命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zihu's public notice describes his dog and says deliberation immediately loses body and life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南山有一條鼈鼻蛇。汝等諸人切須好看。長慶出曰。今日堂中大有人喪身失命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Xuefeng's snake case, Changqing says many people in the hall will lose body and life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此事如擊石火閃電光。搆得搆不得。未免喪身失命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baofu's saying, quoted in Mingjue's chamber cases: whether one catches it or does not, one cannot avoid losing body and life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫為法者不避喪身失命我二十年在黃蘗先師處三度問佛法的的大意三度蒙佗賜杖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji says, 'one who acts for the teaching does not avoid losing body and life,' then recounts three beatings from Huangbo.

Occurrences.Kwic: 每見入室，即云：看！看！有至劒邊擬議者，師云：嶮喪身失命了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ciming's entering-room interview places a sword in the chamber; deliberation near it draws the verdict, 'danger—you have lost body and life.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to eat gruel. The phrase occurs 748 times in 182 allowlisted texts. The records retain the concrete monastic meal: one early encounter describes five or six hundred people gathered to eat gruel and rice, and a later discourse lists spreading out the bowl, eating gruel, sleeping afterward, drinking tea, meeting guests, and eating rice at the midday meal. Zen deployment also puts this ordinary action into public answers. Asked what the non-teaching is, a master answers, ‘eat gruel and eat rice’; asked to indicate an entrance, another gives the same answer. A monk says that he saw a master ‘at the place of eating gruel and rice,’ after which the questioner points to the fire tongs and asks about that. Another record enumerates investigating Chan, eating gruel and rice, defecating and urinating, walking, sitting, and sleeping as ‘your own fundamental matter.’ The gruel is still food; the corpus-specific bend is that masters repeatedly make eating it an answer, an instruction, and an item in such enumerations rather than reserving it for meal notices.
Senses.Note: The corpus supplies no different referent or word class requiring a second sense: literal meal reports and interview answers both name the same act of eating gruel. Do not duplicate the fixed Zhaozhou question here; ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ has its own entry and is linked below. Family cross-check: this definition remains compatible with gruel, gruel and rice, the bowl, wash the bowl, and Zhaozhou’s fixed question; robe-and-bowl as a succession token is a different family deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 好五六百人聚頭，喫粥喫飯，為復見處一般，見處別？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Anthology of the Patriarchal Hall records a community of five or six hundred gathered to eat gruel and rice, then asks whether their places of seeing are alike or different.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問法尚應捨何況非法如何是非法師云喫粥喫飯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public exchange, the answer to ‘what is the non-teaching?’ is ‘eat gruel and eat rice.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問乞師指箇入路師云喫粥喫飯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A request to indicate an entrance receives ‘eat gruel and eat rice’ as the complete answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 堂內展鉢喫粥，粥後打睡，睡起喫茶，見客相喚，齋時喫飯，日日相似，有甚麼過？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse places eating gruel in the concrete daily sequence of opening the bowl, sleeping, drinking tea, meeting guests, and eating the midday meal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遇曰。什麼處見。對曰。喫粥喫飯處見。遇插火筯於爐中云。者箇又作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk says he saw the master ‘at the place of eating gruel and rice’; the interviewer then points to the fire tongs and asks about them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪學道是汝本分事、喫粥喫飯是汝本分事、屙屎撒尿是汝本分事、行坐打眠是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse explicitly enumerates investigating Chan, eating gruel and rice, defecating and urinating, and walking, sitting, and sleeping as ‘your own fundamental matter.’

AlternateTargets: have you had your gruel yet?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘have you eaten your gruel yet?’ The exact question occurs 101 times in 67 allowlisted texts. It is the fixed opening reply in Zhaozhou’s wash-your-bowl case: a newly arrived monk asks for instruction; Zhaozhou asks whether he has eaten his gruel; when the monk says that he has, Zhaozhou says, ‘go wash your bowl.’ The record says that the monk awakened at the words. Later masters preserve the speaker turns and publicly examine them. Yunmen asks whether there was an instruction and, if not, why the monk awakened. Dahui repeats the case and reports that many places had raised it and added comments; elsewhere a verse begins with the question, names Zhaozhou, and continues with the command to wash the bowl. The question also recurs outside the copied case: asked ‘what is the student’s own self?’, a master replies with it and follows the student’s answer with ‘go wash your bowl.’ One later discourse reverses the received praise, calling ‘gruel eaten’ adding a head atop a head and ‘go wash the bowl’ drawing legs on a snake. Zen usage therefore bends an ordinary breakfast question into a recognizable public-case line whose recorded answer and later examinations travel with it.
Senses.Note: This is one fixed question and one corpus-wide case formula, not a master-specific sense: Zhaozhou supplies the named case, while later masters quote, verse, reuse, and criticize it. The direct question and its reuse still ask about the same completed meal, so item 8 does not license multiple senses. Distinguish the lexicalized question from the general phrase ‘eat gruel’ (喫粥); the two entries cross-reference rather than repeat definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問趙州。學人乍入叢林。乞師指示。州云。爾喫粥了也未。僧云。喫粥了。州云。洗鉢盂去。僧忽然大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui’s record preserves the complete case sequence: the newcomer requests instruction, Zhaozhou asks the fixed question, the monk answers, Zhaozhou tells him to wash the bowl, and the record says the monk suddenly awakened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是學人自己師云喫粥了也未云喫粥也師云洗鉢盂去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question is redeployed as the answer to ‘what is the student’s own self?’ and retains the bowl-washing follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云且道有指示無指示若道有指示向他道什麼若道無指示者僧何得悟去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Immediately after raising Zhaozhou’s case, the section’s master asks whether there was an instruction and, if not, why the monk awakened; the local speaker identity was not independently established, so it is left null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。諸方拈掇甚多。下注脚亦不少。未曾有一人分明說破。妙喜今日為諸人分明說破。喫粥了便洗鉢盂。且道。還曾指示無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says many places have raised the case and added comments, restates ‘when the gruel is eaten, wash the bowl,’ and asks whether any instruction was given.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫粥了也未。趙州無忌諱。更令洗鉢盂。太殺沒巴鼻。悟去由來不丈夫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse opens with the fixed question, explicitly names Zhaozhou, and continues with the command to wash the bowl and an appraisal of the awakening.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：喫粥了也，頭上安頭。洗鉢盂去，為虵畫足。更問如何日納敗闕？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later hall discourse gives an adverse appraisal: ‘gruel eaten’ is adding a head atop a head, and ‘go wash the bowl’ is drawing legs on a snake.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “drink,” “tea,” and “go”: “go drink tea.” In Zhaozhou Congshen's recorded sayings, he asks one of two newly arrived monks whether he has been there before. The monk says no, and Zhaozhou tells him to go drink tea. The other says yes and receives the same words. When the temple steward asks why both received the same instruction, Zhaozhou calls “Steward!”; after the steward answers, Zhaozhou again says, “Go drink tea.” Five Lamps Compendium preserves the same exchange but reverses the order of the two monks. Elsewhere a master answers a question about “three-by-three in front and three-by-three behind” by asking the monk's name and then saying, “Go drink tea.” The saying also becomes the named allusion “Zhaozhou's tea,” often paired with “Yunmen's flatbread.” The headword occurs 781 times across 170 allowlisted texts; the spelling variant using the alternate graph for “drink” occurs 14 times across 7 texts. The records give no gloss beyond the literal wording.
Senses.Note: The originating exchange has multiple speakers, so its occurrence attribution remains null even though the case is Zhaozhou's. The witnesses differ in whether the monk who had or had not visited appears first. The steward's question preserves the point that both answers receive the same words. A later retelling uses the alternate graph for “drink.” Compare “Zhaozhou's tea,” “wash your bowl,” and “the ordinary mind.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問二新到上座曾到此間否云不曾到師云喫茶去又問那一人曾到此間否云曾到師云喫茶去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters, Zhaozhou's recorded sayings: the originating exchange and the steward's follow-up. It has multiple speakers, so the speaker field is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問新到。曾到此間麼。曰。曾到。師曰。喫茶去。又問僧。僧曰。不曾到。師曰。喫茶去。後院主問曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Zhaozhou's section: an independent witness of the originating exchange, with the two monks in the reverse order. It has multiple speakers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔趙州住院，有僧參次，州云：『上座曾到這裡麼？』僧云：『不曾到。』州云：『吃茶去。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A retelling of Zhaozhou's exchange using the alternate graph for “drink”; the steward asks why both the visitor and nonvisitor are sent for tea.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問古人道前三三後三三意如何。師曰。汝名什麼。曰某甲。師曰。喫茶去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, section on Zifu Zhensui of Jizhou: another master answers an unrelated question with “go drink tea.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一切法無差，雲門胡餅趙州茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An upper-hall verse pairs the established allusion “Zhaozhou's tea” with “Yunmen's flatbread.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 州曰：喫茶去。院主問：和尚為甚曾到也喫茶去，不曾到也喫茶去？州喚院主，主應諾。州曰：喫茶去。保福展云：趙州慣得其便。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Zhaozhou exchange is raised for later comments by Baofu Congzhan and Jingqing. The combination of case and commentary has multiple speakers.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "single, sole" (單) and "transmit" (傳): "transmit singly," attested 692 times in 211 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says Bodhidharma's coming west is "called single transmission and direct pointing" and "at first had no twists and turns" (謂之單傳直指，初無委曲). In another address he gives a direct local definition: "the four holy and six ordinary [classes] are each originally complete; this is called single transmission," then asks, "what is transmitted?" (各各本來具足謂單傳，傳箇甚麼). Frequent compounds are "single transmission and direct pointing" (單傳直指), "single transmission of the mind-seal" (單傳心印), and "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳).
Senses.Note: The records place the term in lineage slogans, questions, and verse. One lamp record pairs, "Bodhidharma came from the west, singly transmitting the mind-seal; the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi did not know one written character" (達磨西來，單傳心印，曹溪六祖，不識一字). A later lineage statement says the flower-holding smile was entrusted as "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳). The four direct-question occurrences and twelve "termed single transmission" formulas belong to this shared lineage wording, not master-specific senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以達磨西來謂之單傳直指。初無委曲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng calls Bodhidharma's arrival single transmission and direct pointing, adding that it initially had no twists and turns.

Occurrences.Kwic: 四聖六凡各各本來具足謂單傳。傳箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's explicit local definition and immediate question: each is originally complete—called single transmission; what is transmitted?

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來，單傳心印。曹溪六祖，不識一字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record saying pairs Bodhidharma's singly transmitting the mind-seal with the Sixth Patriarch not knowing one written character.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故末後拈花微笑嫡付教外單傳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage statement says the final flower-holding smile was directly entrusted as single transmission outside the teachings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單傳直指意，覿體露堂堂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says: the meaning of single transmission and direct pointing; facing the body, exposed openly.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise or take up singly. Chan records use the verb with an expressed object: a single word 'no,' the first phrase, the upward move, the command, this matter, or a hair-blowing sharp sword. They also oppose 'raising alone and handling alone' to 'dragging through water and mud,' and place 'raise directly and singly' beside the transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words. The public-interview shape remains visible when a monk asks how the master treats people while 'today singly raising the command' and receives a blow. The Chan-specific bend is this productive teaching-seat verb: what is singled out may be a word, phrase, matter, sword, move, or command. Because those nouns are different objects of the same transitive act, they do not require separate senses.
Senses.Note: Wave-plan frequency: 401. Searches covered paired contrast, direct/single formula, word-'no' instruction, sword formula, phrase/move compounds, and public interview. Family check with raise (提起), raise singly (單單提起), the first phrase (第一句), the upward move (向上一著), no (無), and the command (正令) supports one productive verb rather than a fixed category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 垂示云。單提獨弄帶水拕泥敲唱俱行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's pointer contrasts raising and handling alone with dragging through water and mud, followed by paired knocking and singing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 教外別傳，不立文字，單提直截，究本明宗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon places direct single raising beside transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單單提一箇無字，如靠一座須彌山。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The expressed object is one word, 'no,' raised singly like leaning against Mount Sumeru.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單提一把吹毛利劒。逢佛殺佛逢祖殺祖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's address uses the verb with a hair-blowing sharp sword before the inherited kill-buddha/kill-patriarch line.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, succeed or inherit, and the transmission or lineage. In the Chan corpus the compound marks recognized succession from one teacher to another. It occurs 1,455 times in 241 allowlisted texts. As a verb it takes a teacher after 'from' or 'under': biographies say that a person visited a named master and then inherited the lineage, or inherited it from a named teacher. As an attributive expression it identifies the disciples or followers who inherited a compiler's teacher's lineage. As a counted class, records say that a master had many lineage successors or give their number. A letter can also distinguish holding an abbacy from inheriting the founding master's lineage, showing that institutional office and lineage succession are not interchangeable.
Senses.Note: The graph meaning 'transmission, model, lineage' is translated by the compound's attested Chan function, not automatically as a pan-religious proper noun. The most frequent construction is 'lineage-inheriting follower' (834 hits in 133 texts); 'lineage-inheriting disciple' has 102 hits in 45 texts. The verbal forms 'inherit the lineage from' and 'inherited the lineage' are also independently attested.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十卷佛事塔銘蔓堂集附百愚斯禪師語錄卷第一住國山善權寺嗣法門人智操住青龍隆福寺嗣法門人智湛編次住蘇州嘉定昭慶寺語錄住蘇州嘉
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The volume heading identifies two lineage-inheriting followers as compilers; this is documentary metadata rather than a master's speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 卷首，其他備乎林涵齋居士行業曲記云。時歲在丁酉仲冬下浣，嗣法弟子道霈焚香稽首題。No.1437-G鼓山晚錄序No.1437-
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A signed preface identifies its writer as a lineage-inheriting disciple.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後三處閱藏共九年，微恙而逝。敏樹相禪師敏樹相禪師隣水人。參萬峰明和尚，嗣法焉。住墊江百丈山。月旦，上堂：昨夜一聲獅子㖃，窟中抖擻金毛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biographical notice says the named master consulted Master Ming of Wanfeng and inherited the lineage there.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A memorial inscription says that Wufeng inherited the lineage from Tiantong Miyun and places him in a numbered succession.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明珠。一言勘破維摩詰。覺聞拊几稱善。後七坐道場。化行海內嗣法者甚眾。住後僧問。如何是佛。師曰。布髮掩泥橫身臥地。曰意旨如何
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography says that the master had very many lineage successors.

Senses.Explanation: A later label for four statements recorded in Linji's own late-evening address: at times he takes away the person but not the surroundings; at times the surroundings but not the person; at times both person and surroundings; and at times neither person nor surroundings. In Linji's record each member is followed by a monk's question and Linji's answer. For example, the first is answered with the warm sun spreading brocade over the ground, while the fourth is answered with a king ascending the jeweled hall and a rustic elder singing. The label itself does not occur in Linji's own record. The Eye of Humans and Gods later lists it beside the Three Mysteries, Three Essentials, Four Host-and-Guest Positions, and Diamond-King Treasure Sword. That compilation also grades the four: for a person of middle-lower capacity it gives taking away the surroundings but not the teaching; for middle-upper capacity, taking away surroundings and teaching but not the person, with a variant reading that takes away the teaching but not the surroundings; for one below the highest capacity, taking away both person and surroundings; and for a person beyond rank, taking away neither. This later wording uses person, teaching, and surroundings where Linji's recorded set uses person and surroundings. Nanyuan later tests Fengxue by asking, 'The Four Selections—what teaching do they select?' Fengxue answers, 'Ordinary words do not stick in ordinary feelings; they have already fallen into holy understanding.' Later records also use each member as a test question, borrow the label for the National Teacher Shao's separate set, and explicitly call a requested public case 'the Four Selections.'
Senses.Note: Current Zen-scoped counts are 121 matches in 75 files for the principal spelling and 35 in 21 files for the variant spelling. The four statements are Linji's; the collective label and student-capacity grading are later. The late-evening address and informal-convocation witnesses belong to Linji's record, while the Eye of Humans and Gods catalogue and the Nanyuan–Fengxue examination are compiled or raised material. Do not read the compilation's person/teaching/surroundings wording back into Linji's person/surroundings set, and do not attribute the National Teacher Shao's separate fourfold set to Linji.
