Senses.PreferredTarget: the Four Modes of Illumination and Function
AlternateTargets: Linji's four modes of illumination and function
Senses.Explanation: A four-member set recorded in Linji's sayings: first illuminate, then function; first function, then illuminate; illuminate and function simultaneously; and illuminate and function at different times. Linji states that he sometimes uses each mode. His following gloss says that in first-illuminate-then-function a person is present; in first-function-then-illuminate a teaching is present; simultaneous illumination and function drive away the plowman's ox, take the hungry person's food, strike the bone for marrow, and painfully apply needle and awl; illumination and function at different times have question and answer. The Eye of Humans and Gods preserves the labeled set and later comments. Shoushan turns its members into direct questions. Fenyang says that every phrase must contain the Three Mysteries and have illumination and function, whether illumination comes first, function comes first, both are simultaneous, or they occur at different times. Langye compares the first with showing a lion's claws and teeth, the second with releasing an elephant king's power, the simultaneous mode with a dragon obtaining water and making rain and clouds, and the different-time mode with guiding an infant and caring for a child. A compact compendium repeats Linji's person, teaching, driving-away-and-taking-food, and question-and-answer glosses. A later master maps the four onto four staff actions: holding the staff crosswise, raising it upright, turning it upside down, and striking it down once. Later lists place the set beside the Three Mysteries and Essentials, Four Selections, Four Host-and-Guest Positions, and Four Shouts. The corpus has 31 label matches in 22 files; the four member phrases circulate much more widely.
Senses.Note: Linji's full fourfold statement is valid main text in the Collection of Ancient Worthies, in his address to the assembly. In the Taisho edition of Linji's record, the same passage survives only in an apparatus note from another edition and is therefore excluded as main-text evidence; the running text has only the statement that illumination and function are simultaneous and originally have no before or after. The Eye of Humans and Gods and Compendium of the Five Lamps are compiled presentations. Shoushan, Fenyang, Langye, and Fojian Huiqin supply later questions, comparisons, and staff deployments; none of those later words is attributed to Linji. Current counts: Four Modes of Illumination and Function 31/22 files; first illuminate then function 191/75; first function then illuminate 185/74; simultaneous illumination and function 320/116; illumination and function at different times 188/74.

Senses.Explanation: The components mean “four” (四), “guest” (賓), and “host” (主): "the four guest-host [configurations]." In the corpus it names the four ways a teacher (主/host, 善知識) and a student (賓/guest, 學人) meet, one of the numbered device-sets of the Linji (臨濟) house. STRUCTURAL FACT: the compound (四賓主) does NOT occur in the primary (臨濟錄) (T47n1985, 0 occurrences of the compound, main text and apparatus alike); there Linji names the four in prose within his long (示眾), on teacher and student meeting (如主客相見便有言論往來) — (喚作客看主) (called guest-sees-host), (此是主看客) (this is host-sees-guest), (此喚作主看主) (this is called host-sees-host), (呼為客看客) (termed guest-sees-guest). So reads the Taisho main text, with (客) for the guest; the Ming-edition variant carried in the Taisho apparatus gives the passage with (賓) (喚作賓看主…主看賓…賓看賓), the graph used by the later tradition. The numbered label and the phrase-name (四賓主) are a later systematization, set out in (人天眼目) (T48n2006), under the head (臨濟門庭), with an explicit (四賓主者)…(也) definition keyed to "nostrils" (鼻孔): (師家有鼻孔)。(名主中主)。(學人有鼻孔)。(名賓中主)。(師家無鼻孔)。(名主中賓)。(學人無鼻孔)。(名賓中賓)。(與曹洞賓主不同). The corpus carries two enumeration schemes for the four — the (看)-scheme (客看主・主看客・主看主・客看客 in the Taisho 臨濟錄 main text; 賓看主・主看賓・主看主・賓看賓 in its Ming-edition variant and in later texts, e.g. X73n1457 有時賓看主，有時主看主，有時賓看賓) and the (中)-scheme (主中主)・(賓中主)・(主中賓)・(賓中賓) (人天眼目). The set is grouped with Linji's other numbered devices (三玄三要、四料揀、四照用、四喝): (昔臨濟大師建立四料揀)、(四賓主)、(四照用)、(三玄)、(三要). CONTRAST the texts themselves draw: Linji's (四賓主) vs. Caodong's — (人天眼目) states (與曹洞賓主不同) and, of the Caodong set, (四賓主)。(不同臨濟)。(主中賓)。(體中用也). The texts enumerate and name the four and distinguish Linji's from Caodong's; beyond the attested (有鼻孔)/(無鼻孔) glosses they add no further reading, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Describe-only structural facts: (1) the compound (四賓主) is a lamp/eye-of-humans-and-gods systematization of the guest-host prose in Linji's own record — the primary (臨濟錄) (T47n1985) names the four configurations but not the numbered set. (2) There are TWO distinct (四賓主) systems in the corpus — Linji's and Caodong's (曹洞) — the texts explicitly flag them as (不同) (與曹洞賓主不同 / 不同臨濟); do not conflate them. (3) Two co-existing enumerations of Linji's four: the (看)-scheme (X看Y; with 客 in the Taisho 臨濟錄 main text, 賓 in its Ming-edition variant and later texts) and the (中)-scheme (X中Y). Nested/related: (賓主) (t_6da91f8ce284) is the shorter constituent (a genuine constituent relation). Attribution: the (人天眼目) exposition and the enumerations are compiler/discourse material without a single-speaker head → MasterName null; only the primary (臨濟錄) (示眾) is attributed to (臨濟義玄).

Senses.Explanation: To turn or return (回) in reciprocal relation (互): mutual interchange. The corpus provides a compact self-gloss in the lines 'the objects at every gate interchange and do not interchange; turning, they further enter into one another; otherwise each remains in its position' (門門一切境，回互不回互，回而更相涉，不爾依位住). This wording permits both relation and distinct position rather than reducing the term to simple fusion. Caoshan says ordinary feelings and holy views must interchange (直須回互). In Caodong usage upright and crooked (正偏), light and dark (明暗), or guest and host (賓主) can mutually interchange; one later address expands the guest-host deployment as each containing the other and the two exchanging positions without a fixed rank.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 1,249 occurrences in 253 texts. The exact contrast 'interchange and do not interchange' (回互不回互) occurs 91 times in 54 texts; its gloss 'turning, they further enter into one another' (回而更相涉) occurs 40 times in 33 texts. The old gloss 'guests and hosts changing places freely' described only one deployment and was too narrow for the headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明之與暗，總妄明之顯晦，學者不可依之以自惑也。門門一切境，回互不回互，回而更相涉，不爾依位住。門，根也。境，塵也。諸根境有回互不回互二義。言回互者，謂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄), commentary on the Agreement of Difference and Unity (參同契註). It quotes and begins to explain the defining contrast: things interchange and do not interchange; turning, they further enter one another, or else remain in position.

Occurrences.Kwic: 唾。較量將來，有甚底止？豈不聞：石頭大師云：『執事元是迷，契理亦非悟。門門一切境，回互不回互。回而更相涉，不爾依位住。』諸昆仲！此是我洞上法幢所由立也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingning Jing (攖寧靜禪師語錄). The speaker quotes Shitou's lines and names them as a basis of the Dongshan house, demonstrating the phrase's later technical deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 。從來離名狀。天真忘性相。是曰兼中到。三種墮三種墮師曰。凡情聖見是金銷玄路。直須回互。夫取正命食者。須具三種墮。水牯牛。

Occurrences.Kwic: 下喝，賓主分明，賓則始終賓，主則始終主。雖然如是，未免賓主相待，彼此回互。直須賓不是賓、賓中有主，主不是主、主中有賓，賓主交參、互換無位

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "when tiredness comes, then sleep" (困來即眠). Its stable partner is "when hungry, eat" (饑來喫飯), and a recorded exchange supplies the decisive Chan distinction. Asked whether he exerts effort in following the Way, the master says yes and names eating when hungry and sleeping when tired. When the questioner objects that everyone does the same, the master says they differ: while eating, others do not consent simply to eat but make a hundred demands; while sleeping, they do not consent simply to sleep but make a thousand calculations (睡時不肯睡，千般計校). An independent song places the pair after refusing delight in heaven or merit-making and before saying fools laugh while the wise understand. A later Chan mirror names the shortened pair "when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep" (飢來即食、困來即眠) among the predicates of an at-ease person of the Way (閒道人). The words remain ordinary bodily actions; the Chan bend lies in the direct question-and-answer contrast between the master's stated exertion and the same-looking conduct burdened by demands and calculation.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 12 hits in 10 allowlisted texts. Several files transmit the same master-lawyer exchange; the separate song and later Chan mirror supply independent deployment shapes. Variant first halves are 'when hungry, eat a meal' (饑來喫飯) and 'when hungry, eat' (飢來即食).

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰何故不同。師曰。他喫飯時不肯喫飯。百種須索。睡時不肯睡。千般計校。所以不同也。

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：飢來喫飯，困來即眠。曰：一切人總如是，同師用功否？師曰：不同。

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂閒道人也。於戲！其為人也，本來無緣、本來無事，飢來即食、困來即眠，綠水青山任意逍遙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Chan Mirror uses the shortened hunger variant and lists the pair among predicates of an at-ease person of the Way.

Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated image built on "round" (圓): "round and rolling." It occurs 132 times in 81 allowlisted texts. The corpus repeatedly supplies concrete controls for the rendering. One line says it is "round and rolling, without edges or corners" (圓陀陀地無稜角). Another compares its movement to "a pearl running on a tray and a tray running around a pearl" and follows with "round and rolling, lively and active; emerging and disappearing, opening and folding, with nothing permitted or not permitted" (如盤走珠，如珠走盤，圓陀陀、活潑潑，出沒舒卷，無可不可). In a direct three-part exchange, "what is buddha?" receives "round and rolling" (圓陀陀), "what is the teaching?" receives "lively and active" (活潑潑), and "what is the monk?" receives "freely at ease" (任騰騰).
Senses.Note: Other predicates retain the same round, uncornered, mobile image. One verse pairs "round and rolling" with "shining and flashing" (圓陀陀，光爍爍), then says "large within large, narrow within narrow" (大中大，窄中窄). Another statement says, "round and rolling: never the least bit lacking, never the least bit in excess" (圓陀陀地，曾無一毫頭許欠少，曾無一毫頭許盈餘). The description is also criticized when made into a fixed stopping point: a later address says people take "the round-and-rolling, shining-and-flashing one" as the ultimate rule, while not knowing that it has no fixed body and that heading toward it goes astray (認著個圓陀陀、光爍爍的以為極則……無體性，趣向則乖). Productive forms include the adverbial "roundly and rolling" (圓陀陀地, 15 occurrences in 11 texts) and the exact light pairing "round and rolling, shining and flashing" (圓陀陀光爍爍, three in three).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'sit across and cut off.' The compound occurs 3,034 times in 339 allowed texts and takes concrete grammatical objects. Yuanwu answers a monk with 'sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (坐斷天下人舌頭), says that 'emerging and submerging are all sat across and cut off' (頭出頭沒悉皆坐斷), and records a monk's conclusion, 'then one sits across and cuts off the ten directions' (坐斷十方). Blue Cliff commentary says a master's half-phrase 'naturally sits across and cuts off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (自然坐斷天下人舌頭). The Ancestral Guidelines Collection says 'sit across and bar the critical crossing; do not let ordinary or holy pass' (坐斷要津，不通凡聖), and elsewhere, 'sit across and cut off the crown of Vairocana; do not receive Śākyamuni's text' (坐斷毗盧頂，不稟釋迦文). Other frequent objects include past and present, a thousand distinctions, the road's intersection, and the heads of buddhas. The verb is therefore transitive and spatially forceful in the corpus; it is not a term for seated quiet.
Senses.Note: Required formula searches yielded a handful of grammatical instances but no stable self-definition. The repeated objects establish the translation: tongues, ten directions, the critical crossing, a crown, and past/present are what the texts say are barred or cut off.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, sit and Chan. The compound occurs 1,121 times in 244 allowlisted Chinese Chan texts. It can name literal seated activity in the hall: a monastic rule says the assembly sits facing inward as in ordinary sitting Chan and turns outward when the drum sounds. The Platform Record asks, 'What is sitting Chan?' and gives its own graph-by-graph definition: toward all good and bad circumstances outside, thoughts not arising is called 'sitting'; inwardly seeing one's own nature unmoved is called 'Chan.' The wider record also preserves direct critiques. In the Nanyue tile case, Huairang asks what Daoyi seeks by sitting Chan and says, 'If polishing a tile cannot make a mirror, how could sitting Chan make a buddha?' A verse addressed to those attached to sitting Chan asks why prolonged sitting is needed. A raised Linji exchange says that the monks in his hall neither read texts nor sit Chan. These records do not present one uniform predicate beyond the literal compound.
Senses.Note: No exact mind-king/seat equation exists in the allowlist: 'mind-king seat,' 'seat of the mind-king,' 'sitting is the mind-king,' and 'the mind-king sits securely' all have zero hits. The closest explicit witness says that the mind-king is free and easy and then asks, 'Why restrain thoughts and sit Chan?'—a critique, not a seat definition. The contiguous string 'sit Chan seat' occurs 15 times in 14 texts, but in passages such as 'although seated on the Chan seat' it parses as the verb 'sit' plus the noun 'Chan seat'; this boundary does not redefine sitting Chan as furniture.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to let a question descend or to bestow a question. In Chan records it marks a master putting a question to monks and requiring an answer. The heading “questions put in the room” places it in the entering-interview setting; one such question asks how the patriarchal mind-seal is inscribed and how deep the buddhas' source is. A monk later recalls a question bestowed the previous day—“since it is not mind, not buddha, and not a thing, what is it after all?”—and returns to request instruction. Records also show questions put before a group: on a snowy day the master asks why the solitary peak is not white when snow covers the thousand mountains, and elsewhere monks give several replies to “when there is no buddha in the hall, what then?”, none of which the master accepts. The term therefore names an observable part of Chan's interview machinery: the master publicly or privately puts the question, monks answer or fail to answer, and the record preserves the ensuing acceptance, rejection, substitute response, shout, or blow.
Senses.Note: The literal downward/bestowing graph is retained in the alternate target, but ordinary English “put a question” best fits the repeated record headings and speaker turns. It is related to asking (問), public question-and-answer (問答), answers supplied for others (代語), and entering the room (入室), but is not interchangeable with them.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A room-interview heading introduces two questions put by the master: how the patriarchal mind-seal is written and how deep the buddhas' source is.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: After entering the hall, the master puts a question; the following monks answer and the master accepts none of their responses.

Senses.Explanation: A lexicalized textual object: the case-preface rubric or a catalogued indication in a recorded-sayings collection. The compound occurs 640 times in 178 allowlisted texts. The fixed rubric “the indication says” (垂示云) occurs 109 times in 21 texts, including 81 in the Blue Cliff Record, where it introduces prefatory pointer prose before the case. One begins, “a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations” (定乾坤句，萬世共遵). Yunmen's Extended Record separately counts “185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers” (室中語要一百八十五則，垂示代語二百九十則). Independent records also carry the section rubric “chamber indication” (室中垂示) before the master's words. A fixed editorial rubric and hundreds of counted textual items establish a textual referent distinguishable from the public act requested of a master.
Senses.Note: This sense is limited to the lexicalized textual rubric/object, not every nominal instance of “indication.” No equation-style self-definition was found, but the fixed rubric and counted collection division independently establish the object. “Indications and substitute answers” (垂示代語) occurs across several texts.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record pointer rubric: ‘the indication says: a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations; a dynamic that captures tigers and rhinoceroses, not distinguished by one thousand sages.’ Editorial case preface, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's Extended Record collection heading: ‘185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers.’ A textual division rather than a spoken turn, so MasterName is null.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to offer an indication in public exchange
Senses.Explanation: To offer an indication to an addressee in a public exchange. The request “please, master, offer an indication” (請師垂示) occurs 107 times in 56 texts, and “I beg the master to offer an indication” (乞師垂示) occurs 57 times in 26. In one exchange, “within the expedient gate, please, master, offer an indication” is followed by Jiufeng's answer, “buddha does not deprive living beings of their wishes.” In another, Touzi asks Cuiwei and Cuiwei replies, “do you want a second ladle of foul water?” A third request immediately receives “beneath the staff, a shooting star bursts forth” (棒下迸流星). These are requested speaking events, not the separately catalogued case-preface rubric.
Senses.Note: This is not split merely because it is verbal. The public request names an interpersonal speaking event, while the other target explicitly names a fixed editorial rubric or catalogued textual unit; the targets distinguish those referents on their own. Compare question-and-answer (問答), substitute answer (代語), picking up an old case (拈古), verses on old cases (頌古), and raising a case (舉).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, dust and toil. The compound occurs 1,353 times in 275 allowlisted texts and names the wear, bustle, and entanglement of ordinary affairs and responsive thought. Texts speak of worldly toil being unbroken, worldly affairs becoming empty, turning one's head within worldly toil, and having no worldly toil to avoid. One letter answers a complaint about the toil and commotion of the world by asking, 'Who is the worldly toil, and who is the one rejecting it?' A later address explicitly calls a quiet, easeful condition only a temporary rest from worldly toil and warns against recognizing it as final. Another discourse pairs being in dust and leaving dust, then says to leave the world in the midst of worldly toil.
Senses.Note: The frequent longer string 'worldly toil and vexation' occurs 36 times in 24 texts, but the entry preserves the headword's own concrete dust-and-labor wording. Formula searches found no stable bare self-definition; the apparent 'worldly toil is ...' strings mostly introduce a person located amid it.

AlternateTargets: mote after mote, land after land
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “every mote and every land”: the repeated nouns make the phrase distributive. Across 205 occurrences in 116 allowlisted texts, Chan masters pair it with “each thing and each particular” (物物頭頭), say that every mote and land “fully displays” (全彰), and place it in public addresses as the range of an action or disclosure. One address says, “every mote and every land once manifested awe-inspiring light; each thing and each particular fully displayed the true eye” (塵塵剎剎，曾現威光。物物頭頭，全彰正眼). Another gives the compact parallel, “each thing and each particular—the whole body; every mote and every land—the great function” (物物頭頭全身，塵塵剎剎大用). The phrase is also made a test: “if you understand, every mote and every land; if you do not, a kick to the head” (若也會得，塵塵剎剎；若也不會，當頭一蹋). The corpus thus bends a cosmological distributive into recurring teaching-seat language for an all-pervading range; this entry makes no claim beyond those deployments.
Senses.Note: No second referent was found. Reversal as “land after land, mote after mote” (剎剎塵塵) changes order, not the thing denoted.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a wall stands upright for a thousand fathoms. The corpus uses the whole clause as a predicate or appraisal of a statement, a person, a house style, or a position in an encounter. Nanyuan opens an address with “on the red flesh-lump, a thousand-fathom wall stands” (赤肉團上壁立千仞); a monk repeats the line back, overturns the Chan seat after Nanyuan confirms it, and is struck when he hesitates. A Dongshan record places “sometimes mingling with mud and mixing with water” beside “sometimes standing like a thousand-fathom wall” (有時和泥合水，有時壁立千仞), then says Dongshan is found in neither location. Yuanwu likewise sets “standing like a thousand-fathom wall” against “dragging through mud and water, ash-covered head and dirt-covered face,” and elsewhere writes that in the ash-covered, dirt-covered place one stands like a thousand-fathom wall, while in the thousand-fathom-wall place one is dirt-covered and ash-covered. A commentary classifies three turning phrases as respectively “standing like a thousand-fathom wall,” “sailing a boat on dry land,” and “host and guest interchanging” (一句壁立千仞，一句陸地行船，一句賓主交參). Langya appraises Nanyuan's line with the single word “dangerous” (險). The exact four-character phrase occurs 434 times in 113 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The scale varies without changing the image: “standing like a ten-thousand-fathom wall” (壁立萬仞) occurs 470 times in 166 files, and “standing like a thousand-xun wall” (壁立千尋) occurs 14 times in 11 files. No occurrence of a “ten-thousand-zhang wall” variant was found. The entry retains the contrasts and Langya's one-word appraisal because the texts themselves draw them; it adds no further force.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂云赤肉團上壁立千仞有僧問赤肉團上壁立千仞豈不是和尚語師云是僧便掀倒禪牀
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanyuan's own record: he addresses the assembly, “On the red flesh-lump, a thousand-fathom wall stands.” A monk asks whether this is Nanyuan's saying; when he says yes, the monk overturns the Chan seat. The continuation records Nanyuan's rebuke and blow.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a wall standing sheer for ten thousand fathoms. The expression occurs 470 times in 166 allowlisted texts. Chan records turn the sheer wall into public-interview language: a monk asks why a master is always a ten-thousand-fathom wall, and the master asks him to say a word at that place. Teaching-seat prose couples it with cutting off the ten directions, while another record applies it to everyone without the slightest alteration or deficiency. The corpus also supplies its own checks: Yuanwu says people wrongly identify silent blankness with the wall, and Dongshan's record says Dongshan is not to be found at the ten-thousand-fathom wall. Thus the wall is a stock Chan predicate and encounter-setting, but the records do not license equating it with mere silence or with a master.
Senses.Note: One figurative object across predicative and locative constructions. The different assessments are text-drawn deployments of the same sheer-wall image, not separate referents or interpretive senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 和尚為甚麼一向壁立萬仞？師曰：你試向壁立萬仞處道一句看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange questions the master's wall-like stance and demands a word at that place.

Occurrences.Kwic: 壁立萬仞坐斷十方。可以入大解脫門傳正法眼藏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's teaching-seat prose couples the wall with cutting off the ten directions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人分上，各各壁立萬仞，無一絲毫移易虧欠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later instructional record predicates the wall of each person without alteration or deficiency.

Occurrences.Kwic: 時流錯認，遂向泯默，以為無縫罅、無摸索，壁立萬仞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu explicitly reports the mistaken equation of silent blankness with the wall.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬欲向壁立萬仞處見洞山，洞山且不在壁立萬仞處；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan's record denies that Dongshan is found at the ten-thousand-fathom wall.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “great rest and great cessation.” The phrase occurs 93 times in 57 allowlisted texts. Chan records repeatedly call it a “secure field” or “field of great ease” (安穩之場; 大安樂田地), something one “reaches” or “personally arrives at” rather than an ordinary pause from activity. Yuanwu places it after “a great dead man has already lost his breath” and says, “upon reaching one’s own ground, great rest and great cessation” (到本分地上大休大歇). Xueyan immediately refuses to make that field an endpoint: “if you wish to head directly for the field of great rest, great cessation, and great ease, there is a great living road ahead” (前頭大有活路在). A later master criticizes descendants who bite onto Linji’s four shouts and take that for the field of great rest and cessation, calling the identification “a sheep’s substance in a tiger’s hide” (羊質虎皮). The Chan deviation is therefore an explicitly named field of arrival that remains subject to public correction; the entry reports those predicates without defining an inner state.
Senses.Note: The corpus’s place nouns are metaphors for the same named condition, not distinct referents. A late record itself names it “the sea of great extinction,” “the ground of actuality,” and “the idle person of no learning and no contrivance” (大寂滅海; 實際理地; 絕學無為閑道人); these are that text’s names, not this entry’s imported definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 透到大休大歇安穩之場，豈有二致哉？
似大死人已絕氣息。到本分地上大休大歇。
若欲直趣大休大歇大安樂田地，前頭大有活路在。
致令後代兒孫咬住矢橛，以為大休大歇的田地。正眼看來，大似羊質虎皮。
大休大歇，乃佛祖力行親到之處，謂之大寂滅海，謂之實際理地，謂之絕學無為閑道人

AlternateTargets: a person of great thorough awakening
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "greatly penetrate and greatly awaken": great thorough awakening. The phrase occurs 48 times in 30 allowlisted texts. It names an event or resulting qualification in biographies, appraisals, and questions. One record says that people of great thorough awakening have finished the matter of inquiry and afterward stayed by water and woods until pushed forward to address others (古人大徹大悟，參學事畢，且於水邊林下). A public exchange tests the qualification directly: one master says there is nobody of great thorough awakening in the hall; another asks, "which one is not of great thorough awakening?" and the first counters, "which one is?" (那箇不是大徹大悟的；那箇是大徹大悟的). A Dahui record places it beside "the mind-ground opens and passes through" (大徹大悟，心地開通) and calls Zhaozhou's dog public case a key that opens that mind-ground. A later address jokes that its third phrase could make people greatly and thoroughly awaken, then refuses to utter it because nobody would remain to watch the Chan hall. These records attest the phrase as event, qualification, question, and comic hall claim; this entry adds no meaning beyond those recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: Eventive and attributive grammar concern the same awakening, not different referents: “to awaken thoroughly” and “a thoroughly awakened person” remain one sense. The phrase is related to, but lexically stronger than, “great awakening” (大悟); this entry does not infer a graded awakening system absent an explicit passage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人大徹大悟，參學事畢，且於水邊林下長養聖胎，不惜口頭生醭，龍天推出，方乃為人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage says ancient people of great thorough awakening had finished inquiry and stayed by water and woods until pushed forward to address others.

Occurrences.Kwic: 柱云：「好一堂師僧，沒箇大徹大悟的。」師云：「瞎漢！那箇不是大徹大悟的？」柱云：「瞎漢！那箇是大徹大悟的？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two masters publicly counter-question whether anyone—or everyone—in the hall qualifies as greatly and thoroughly awakened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 也要得透脫生死，除非大徹大悟，心地開通。僧問趙州：狗子還有佛性也無？州云：無。此箇公案，正是開大徹大悟心地底鑰匙子也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage pairs great thorough awakening with the mind-ground opening and calls Zhaozhou's dog public case a key opening that ground.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第三句能令人大徹大悟，不敢舉，恐汝等皆大徹大悟，打筋斗去了，叫那箇守這禪堂？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address says the third phrase could cause great thorough awakening, then jokingly withholds it lest everyone somersault away and leave the hall unattended.

Senses.Explanation: (大) great / thorough + (悟) to wake up, to realize. The decisive, complete breakthrough, set against (小悟) (small, partial awakenings). Overwhelmingly a verb of the breakthrough moment: (於言下大悟) 'was greatly awakened at [these] words' — the classic form being Linji under Dayu (師於言下大悟…元來黃檗佛法無多子, 'was greatly awakened and said: so there isn't much to Huangbo's Buddha's teaching after all'). The fixed noun phrase (大悟底人) 'a greatly-awakened person' names one who has had it. It is waking up thoroughly. The case (大悟底人為甚麼卻迷) ('the greatly-awakened person, why do they fall back into delusion?') pairs (大悟) with (迷) (delusion), answered (破鏡不重照)，(落花難上枝) ('a broken mirror does not shine again; fallen blossoms do not climb back onto the branch'). Allowlist grep counts fix the breakthrough-verb profile: 2,711 hits in 308 of 462 texts; (言下大悟) 446 (師於言下大悟 151), (豁然大悟) 353, (忽然大悟) 205, (大徹大悟) 41, (遂大悟) 37, against (小悟) 58. The (迷) case's oldest lamp witness is the Zutang-ji, with archaic (什摩): (問)：「(大悟底人為什摩卻迷)？」(師云)：「(破鏡不重照)，(落花難上枝)。」 (B25n0144), and the (大悟底人) family (16 hits in 14 texts) extends to other test-questions: (僧問)：「(大悟底人還有憎愛也無)？」(師云)：「(能愛人)，(能惡人)。」 ('does the greatly-awakened person still have hatred and love? — He can love people, and can hate people', J10nA158). The record also carries the word in Yongjia's (證道歌) maxim (大象不遊於兔徑)。(大悟不拘於小節) ('the great elephant does not travel the rabbit's path; great awakening is not bound by small details', T48n2014; 大悟不拘於小節 13 hits, quoted e.g. as 故永嘉亦云。大悟不拘於小節, B25n0145), and as the stock question (如何是大悟無道) (大悟無道 22 hits), in several records asked in series with (如何是大富無糧) and answered divergently: (貧恨一身多) (J28nB220), (莫妄想) (X82n1571), (賊) (X68n1319). Dahui's record ties (悟) to doubt: (今時學道者多不自疑)。(却疑他人)。(所以道)。(大疑之下必有大悟) ('students today mostly do not doubt themselves — they doubt others; hence the saying: under great doubt there is necessarily great awakening', T47n1998A; 大疑大悟 33 hits in 28 texts).
Senses.Note: The famous self-report (大悟十八遍)，(小悟不計數) ('eighteen great awakenings, countless small ones'), popularly credited to Dahui Zonggao, is explicitly flagged in the Zen record (J10nA158) as (本是宋儒言)，(非大慧所說) — 'actually a Song-Confucian's phrase, NOT spoken by Dahui.' Do NOT credit the eighteen-awakenings line to Dahui as authentic. The base word (大悟) is itself rock-solid multi-source; only this quantified self-report's Dahui-attribution is disputed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師於言下大悟云。元來黃檗佛法無多子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), (臨濟義玄) section: (師) = Linji, awakened at Dayu's words after Huangbo's blows. The verbal-breakthrough use (於言下大悟).

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悟底人為甚麼却迷。師曰。破鏡不重照。落花難上枝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元): (師) = (華嚴休靜) (Huayan Xiujing), disciple of Dongshan; the preceding narrative has (後唐莊宗) summoning him to the capital. The (大悟底人卻迷) dialectic.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問華嚴：「大悟底人為甚麼卻迷？」嚴云：「破鏡不重照，落花難上枝。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Independent (頌古) witness citing the case (舉): a monk asks, (華嚴) (嚴云) answers. MasterName null because this KWIC is a two-speaker quoted case citation, not a single-speaker saying; it corroborates the X80 Huayan attribution of the case (names 華嚴/嚴 as the answering master).

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悟十八遍，小悟不計數，本是宋儒言，非大慧所說。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse-annotation flagging the '18 great awakenings' line as a misattribution to Dahui (非大慧所說). Cited for the attribution caveat, NOT as Dahui's words.

AlternateTargets: the great trigger and the great use
Senses.Explanation: The components mean “great” (大), “pivot, trigger, loom-mechanism, or latent capacity” (機), “great” again (大), and “function, activity, or use” (用): 'great capacity, great function.' The corpus itself splits the compound into (大機) and (大用) and assigns each to a master: in (仰山慧寂)'s (語錄), (溈山) asks about (百丈)'s second visit to (馬祖) (raising the whisk) and (仰山) answers '(此是顯大機大用)'; to '(幾人得大機)？(幾人得大用)？' he answers '(百丈得大機)，(黃檗得大用)，(餘者盡是唱導之師)' — the same dialogue recurs in (古尊宿語錄) and elsewhere. It is split further into (大機之用) (72× in 43 files) and (大用之機) (13× in 10): '(如何是大機大用)？(如何是大機之用)？(如何是大用之機)？' (posed in 天隱圓修's record). It names what (黃檗) said he saw in (馬祖): '(見馬祖大機大用然且不識馬祖)'. In expanded couplet form it runs '(大機圓應大用縱橫)' (圜悟克勤) and '(大機圓應大用直截)' (1×, 禪宗頌古聯珠通集 C078n1720) (大機圓應 16× in 12 files; 全機大用 115×; 大用現前 447×). It is also a term masters warn against misusing: '(以麄放狂亂為大機大用)' (玉林通琇, 客問) and '(觸著則任意揮張)，(便道大機大用)…(可見大機大用不在蒲團禪板上)' (天隱圓修). (大機大用) occurs 276× in 124 allowlist files. The texts deploy it as praise of a master's activity, as a test-question split into (機) and (用), and as a target of caution, without assigning it a gloss beyond the literal, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The compound's own structure is set by the corpus, not by the annotator: (大機) (988× in 245 files) and (大用) (2094× in 330) are the two halves, and the stock (溈山)–(仰山) dialogue distributes them — (百丈得大機)、(黃檗得大用) — the line (百丈得大機) recurring in 23 allowlist files, incl. (仰山慧寂語錄) (T47n1990), (古尊宿語錄) (C077n1710), (五燈會元) (X80n1565), (續傳燈錄) (T51n2077), (從容庵錄) (T48n2004), and (禪宗頌古聯珠通集) (C078n1720). Do NOT read the split as this entry's interpretation; it is the texts'. Three attested deployments: (1) praise / description of a master's activity (黃檗 seeing 馬祖's 大機大用; the 圓應…縱橫 / 直截 couplet); (2) a test-question further split into (大機之用) / (大用之機); (3) an error masters name and warn against (以麄放狂亂為大機大用; 大機大用不在蒲團禪板上). Roster witnesses across houses: (仰山慧寂), (圜悟克勤) (Linji line), (天隱圓修), (玉林通琇). The (溈山)–(仰山) exchange is a two-speaker dialogue and the (黃檗)/(馬祖) line is (黃檗)'s reported speech inside (百丈)'s section, so those are left unattributed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百丈得大機，黃檗得大用，餘者盡是唱導之師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (袁州仰山慧寂禪師語錄) (T47n1990). The line is (仰山慧寂)'s own answer ('師云') to (溈山)'s '(幾人得大機)？(幾人得大用)？', inside (仰山)'s (語錄) — but it is a two-speaker (溈山問仰山) dialogue, so MasterName null per the raised/dialogue rule. This is the defining locus that splits (大機大用) into (大機) (百丈) and (大用) (黃檗).

Occurrences.Kwic: 百丈得大機黃檗得大用餘者盡是唱道之師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄), (百丈懷海禪師語錄) section; the same (溈山問仰山) dialogue ('此是顯大機大用…幾人得大機幾人得大用…百丈得大機黃檗得大用'), an independent witness. Raised dialogue → null. C-canon unpunctuated (verbatim); note (唱道) here vs (唱導) in T47n1990.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是大機大用？如何是大機之用？如何是大用之機？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天隱和尚語錄) (天隱圓修). The assembly's (問) ('古人道：一人得大機，一人得大用') driving toward (師答) — a two-speaker test-question, so MasterName null. Attests the further split into (大機之用) and (大用之機).

Occurrences.Kwic: 見馬祖大機大用然且不識馬祖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄), (百丈懷海禪師語錄) section; the stock case where (黃檗) (檗曰) tells (百丈) he 'saw (馬祖)'s (大機大用) yet did not know (馬祖)'. Reported speech of (黃檗) inside (百丈)'s record, two-speaker → null. Attests the term as praise/description of a master's activity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 可見大機大用不在蒲團禪板上。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天隱和尚語錄) (天隱圓修), own critique of false teachers: '(觸著則任意揮張)，(便道大機大用)…(學人問著蒲團)，(即將蒲團打)…(若將不得)，(可見大機大用不在蒲團禪板上)'. Own words. The term as a named error.

Occurrences.Kwic: 以麄放狂亂為大機大用
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄) (玉林通琇), (客問) (cb:mulu: 客問評註) — in the master's reply to the (客), under (第三須悟處諦當), a list of mistakes: '(以鹵莾承當為有力量)…(以麄放狂亂為大機大用以顢頇為透脫無餘)'. The answering voice is (玉林)'s own; second independent witness of the term deployed as a warning. B-canon unpunctuated (verbatim).

Occurrences.Kwic: 大機圓應大用縱橫。不墮千聖機關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (圓悟佛果禪師語錄) (= 圜悟克勤; roster spelling 圜悟克勤), '(師云)。(大機圓應大用縱橫)…(舉一機千機截斷)。(拈一事萬事齊彰)'. Own words; the expanded couplet form (大機圓應 / 大用縱橫).

Senses.Explanation: (大) great + (死) death / to die: 'the great death.' The corpus glosses the term in its own words. Yuanwu (圜悟) on the type: (大死底人)。(都無佛法道理玄妙得失是非長短) — the greatly-dead person has no Buddha's teaching, no stated principle, no mystery, no gain-and-loss, no right-and-wrong, no long-and-short; in the same Blue Cliff Record (碧巖錄) commentary he reports his teacher's wording — (五祖先師)。(謂之命根不斷)。(須是大死一番)。(却活始得) ('Wuzu, my late master, called it [having anything to lean on or any interpretation] the life-root not yet cut: one must die the great death once; only coming back to life will do'). Two idioms carry it. (1) (大死一番), 'die the great death once' (22 hits / 16 files): (直須絕名利)、(忘人我)，(大死一番方堪湊泊) ('you must cut off name-and-gain, forget self-and-other, and die the great death once — only then can you moor'; the recorded sayings of Chan Master Baiyu, 百愚禪師語錄), (秪管大死一番)，(不怕不活) ('just die the great death once — no fear you will not come back to life'; the recorded sayings of Chan Master Miyun, 密雲禪師語錄), and alongside it the stock verse (絕後再甦)。(欺君不得) ('revived after utter cutoff — he cannot be cheated'; 3 verbatim hits, 絕後再甦 alone 222 hits / 119 files, also written 絕後再蘇, 34 / 22). (2) (大死底人), 'the person who has died the great death' (99 hits / 58 files), which stands almost always inside the Zhaozhou–Touzi question — (大死底人) followed by (却)/(卻活時如何) ('when he comes back to life, what then?') in 74 of the 99 hits: (州問)。(大死底人)。(却活時如何) ('Zhou asked: the person who has died the great death — when he comes back to life, what then?') → Touzi answers (不許夜行)。(投明須到) ('no travelling by night; you must arrive by daylight'); the exact second clause (投明須到) recurs 192 times in 104 files. The compound (大死大活) ('greatly die, greatly live') is attested but rare (4 hits / 2 files). In Dahui's (大慧) letter (示東峯居士) ('shown to the layman Dongfeng') the phrase appears in a chain of appellations: (喚作默而常照)。(又喚作如大死底人)。(又喚作父母未生時事)。(又喚作空劫已前事) ('it is called "silent yet constantly shining"; also called "like a person who has died the great death"; also called "the matter before father and mother were born"; also called "the matter before the empty eon"'). One late imperial anthology's general preface gives a source-specific equivalence: 'this is called passing the heavy barrier; it is called one who greatly dies and greatly lives' (是則名為透重關，名為大死大活者). The explicit equation with 'passing the heavy barrier' (透重關) is a single late explanatory witness and remains provisional within the broader corpus-wide entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense; the (大死底人) ('person who has died the great death') case (Zhaozhou–Touzi) and the (大死一番) ('die the great death once') exhortation are two forms of the same term, and both are attested with revival wording alongside (却活時如何 'when he comes back to life, what then?' / 却活始得 'only coming back to life will do' / 不怕不活 'no fear you will not come back to life' / 絕後再甦 'revived after utter cutoff'). Multi-source across independent records (the 五燈會元 Compendium of the Five Lamps / the 碧巖錄 Blue Cliff Record / Dahui's recorded sayings 大慧語錄). Raw grep: (大死) 343 hits / 132 allowlist files (tag-stripped, 2026-07-11).

Occurrences.Kwic: 州問。大死底人。却活時如何。師曰。不許夜行。投明須到。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), mulu head (舒州投子山大同禪師) (Touzi's section). The KWIC is an explicit two-speaker exchange — (州問) (Zhaozhou asks) … (師曰) (Touzi answers) — so MasterName is null per the two-speaker rule. The defining answer (不許夜行投明須到) is Touzi Datong's (Touzi is retained in RelatedMasters); the corpus-wide sense's multi-source status holds independently via (大慧) / (圜悟) / (柏山楷).

Occurrences.Kwic: 大死底人。都無佛法道理玄妙得失是非長短。到這裏只恁麼休去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (碧巖錄) case 41 (圜悟 commentary on the Zhaozhou–Touzi case); (圜悟)'s in-commentary gloss of the term. Raised-case commentary → null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喚作默而常照。又喚作如大死底人。又喚作父母未生時事。又喚作空劫已前事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大慧普覺禪師語錄), (示東峯居士); Dahui's own letter — (如大死底人) stands in his chain of appellations (喚作…又喚作…).

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲學斯道，必須大死一番始得。古德曰：「死盡偷心，方堪入室。絕後再甦，欺君不得。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (柏山楷禪師語錄), (與太谷眾居士) (his own letter; master not in the roster). Shows (大死一番) alongside the stock (絕後再甦) verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是則名為透重關，名為大死大活者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The imperial general preface to the Selected Recorded Sayings (御選語錄) says, 'this is called passing the heavy barrier; it is called one who greatly dies and greatly lives' (是則名為透重關，名為大死大活者). This is a late preface's explicit equivalence, not the older Zhaozhou–Touzi case.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, great (大) function or use (用): "great function." The term occurs 2,094 times in 330 allowlisted texts. Its dominant formula is "great function manifests before you" (大用現前, 447 occurrences in 170 texts), frequently followed by "it does not preserve rules" (不存軌則). In one public interview a monk asks what it is like when great function manifests without preserving rules; the answer is, "if you can use it, then use it" (汝用得但用), after which the monk bares his shoulder and is struck. Another asks separately, "what is great capacity?" and "what is great function?" and receives a blow across the back for each. The corpus coordinates "great function" with "great capacity" (大機大用, 276 occurrences), and "great function" with "the whole capacity" (全機大用, 115). It also records the explicit contrast "you people have obtained only the great body, not great function" (汝等諸人只得大體不得大用). These are named formulas, questions, pairings, and contrasts in the record; the entry makes no claim about a metaphysical entity behind them.
Senses.Note: No distinct referent emerged from 'great function' (大用), 'great function manifests before you' (大用現前), 'great capacity and great function' (大機大用), 'the whole capacity and great function' (全機大用), and the 'great body/great function' (大體/大用) comparison. 'Use' and 'function' are alternate English readings of the same attested thing, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “great function appears before one”: “great” (大), “functioning or use” (用), and “appears before one or is manifest” (現前). The phrase occurs 447 times in 170 allowlisted texts. It is frequently followed by “does not retain rules” (不存軌則); the unpunctuated five-character continuation occurs 21 times in 12 texts. The records deploy the headword as an assertion, a question, and a line in an address. In an early collected discourse, the statement “great function appearing is the unequalled body of the teaching” (大用現前即是無等等法身) directly equates it with another named expression. Asked, “When great function appears and does not retain rules, what then?”, Changqing Da'an says, “If you can use it, just use it” (汝用得但用). Yunmen states the stock line, receives the question “What is great function appearing?”, raises his staff, and calls out, “Old man Shakyamuni has come!” (釋迦老子來也). Fengxue Yanzhao tells the assembly that at the encounter they must have great function appear and not constrain themselves to small details. Yuanwu Keqin’s case commentary pairs the stock line with using a blade of grass as a sixteen-foot golden body and using a sixteen-foot golden body as a blade of grass. Dahui Zonggao supplies an explicit corrective witness: students of sayings call Guizong’s killing a snake and Nanquan’s killing a cat “timely wondrous function” and also “great function appears, not retaining rules,” but Dahui says that is not the account. The correction prevents those two cases from being made definitions of the headword.
Senses.Note: The question “What is great function appearing?” (如何是大用現前) occurs 22 times in 19 texts, and the exact collocation “at the encounter, great function appears” (臨機大用現前) occurs twice in two. The corpus supplies many different replies and actions; the entry reports representative deployment shapes and Dahui’s explicit rejection without assigning a single hidden force to them.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: This direct equivalence occurs in the collected ‘extended sayings from various regions’; the section head does not safely identify a roster-linked speaker.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘great doubt.’ The phrase occurs 196 times in 91 allowlisted texts. A direct definition says, ‘doubt has no large or small; only when the doubt is weighty is it called great doubt, and when light it is called small doubt’ (疑情無大小，但疑之重，是謂大疑；疑之輕，是謂小疑). The same record says that when one cannot refrain from raising it, ‘therefore it is named great doubt.’ Across other texts it appears in the fixed contrast ‘great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening,’ in questions about ‘a person of great doubt,’ and in biographies where a master ‘greatly doubted’ after an exchange or saying. Thus the corpus uses the phrase both as a named weight of doubt and verbally for becoming deeply doubtful; English ‘great doubt’ covers both without positing different referents.
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary degree phrase by making it a named category explicitly defined against small doubt and repeatedly paired with great awakening. The family comparison with ‘doubt-mass’ (疑情) and ‘ball of doubt’ (疑團) supports one sense, not a noun/verb split: both constructions name the same doubt.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但疑之重，是謂大疑；疑之輕，是謂小疑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The richest direct definition, including contrast with small doubt.

Senses.Explanation: The headword (契悟) literally means "to tally and realize." In Chan transmission biographies it is an event verb marking a person's reported realization after a word, question, case, accident, or exchange. Huike is told "I have finished settling your mind for you" and then greatly realizes (光即大契悟). Daoquan hears "smoke rises beneath your feet" and realizes on the spot, after which he travels no farther (師當下契悟，更不他遊). Other records place it after hearing the cypress-tree case during an entering interview, and after a rider falls when his donkey's foot breaks through a bridge. The narrative can immediately report the person's next speech: after realizing, Huike runs to Bodhidharma and says that he has put external conditions to rest. The Chan deviation is institutional and documentary: lamp and sayings records use "to tally and realize" (契悟) to mark the realization event within a teacher-student biography and often preserve its trigger and aftermath. The word itself does not say that the realization "matches the master's mind," and this entry does not add that claim.
Senses.Note: Count: 571 occurrences in 153 allowlisted texts. Cross-checked "realize the way" (悟道) and related realization vocabulary. The graph "to tally" (契) contributes the literal idea of tallying, but the corpus uses the compound as one realization event verb; no independent "contract" referent was found. Triggers vary without creating senses.

Senses.PreferredTarget: take away the person, not the surroundings
AlternateTargets: person taken away, surroundings not taken away
remove the person but not the scene
Senses.Explanation: The first member of Linji's four statements later called the Four Selections: ‘at times, take away the person but not the surroundings.’ Linji's own record gives the complete set and then records the monk's question ‘what is taking away the person but not the surroundings?’ Linji answers, ‘the warming sun brings forth brocade spread over the ground; an infant's hanging hair is white as silk.’ The formula subsequently circulates as a verse heading and repeatable public question. Kefu's verse begins ‘its conditions themselves carry entangling error; if you try to seek the mysterious purport, deliberation instead reproaches you.’ Fengxue answers the inherited question with ‘a newly emerged red-furnace golden pellet strikes through the monk's iron face-door,’ while another later master answers ‘the home country has a road that no one reaches.’ These answer-lines are recorded deployments of the formula.
Senses.Note: 339 hits in the wave plan. Cross-read against all four members and the Four Selections (四料揀). The English keeps person (人) and surroundings or scene (境) literal. It is corpus-wide in later use: later verses and masters take up the same named question.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later recorded master answers the same question: the home country has a road that no one reaches.

Senses.PreferredTarget: take away the situation, not the person
AlternateTargets: remove the surroundings, not the person
Senses.Explanation: The second member of Linji's “four selections” (四料揀): literally, “take away the situation, not the person.” Here “situation” (境) is the presented surroundings or objects, while “person” (人) is the person. Linji first enumerates four possibilities in an evening instruction: sometimes take away the person but not the situation; sometimes take away the situation but not the person; sometimes take away both; sometimes take away neither. In the recorded follow-up he answers this member with, “the king's command has already gone throughout the realm; the general beyond the frontier has ended smoke and dust” (王令已行天下遍，將軍塞外絕煙塵). Later masters retain the exact category but supply different answers: “secretly transmit the emperor's edict; double the journey by a hundred stages,” “build the altar and appoint the general,” “muddy head and earthy face,” or paired states such as “silent, silent; alert, alert.” The category is therefore a reusable public-interview question within Linji's fourfold roster, not a proposition whose intent this entry resolves. Its Zen deviation lies in the bureaucratic verb “take away” becoming one axis of a named appraisal scheme for person and presented situation.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 404 matches in 145 texts. The retained evidence includes Linji's four-member enumeration, Linji's own transmitted answer, and three independent later question-and-answer deployments. Family revalidation against the “four selections” (四料揀), “take away the person, not the situation” (奪人不奪境), “take away both person and situation” (人境俱奪), and “take away neither person nor situation” (人境俱不奪) confirms that this is one roster member rather than an independent statement. Different answers are readings/deployments of the same category and must not be split under item 8. SenseKey remains null: Linji supplies the historical source, but the same category and meaning recur across later masters and texts, so historical origin does not make the sense master-specific.

AlternateTargets: like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself” (冷暖自知 / 冷煖自知). Its Zen-specific deployment is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself” (如人飲水冷暖自知). Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it” (除非親證親悟，方可見得). The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?” (悟道明宗，如人飲水，冷暖自知，云何說其行相), and elsewhere pairs the comparison with “only verification knows; it is difficult to measure” (唯證乃知難可測). Poshan states the same deviation in domestic language: “only each person understands inside his own belly” (只是各人肚裏明白), followed by the water comparison. Thus the corpus retains the ordinary act of drinking but makes the drinker's private knowledge of cold or warmth its recurring Chan predicate.
Senses.Note: The complete stock form has the graphic variants “cold and warm” (冷暖) and “cold and warm” with the alternate graph for warm (冷煖). The short headword is frequently followed immediately by one of them. The Huiming occurrence is a retold early encounter, so it is not linked to a governing speaker.

Senses.Explanation: A stock question in recorded meetings: 'What is Buddha?' (如何是佛). The interrogative asks for the identity or meaning of Buddha, and the record preserves sharply different answers by different masters. Tianyi Yihuai answers, 'spreading the hair to cover mud, laying the body across the ground' (布髮掩泥，橫身臥地); Xuefeng answers, 'Blue sky! Blue sky!' (蒼天，蒼天); Mazu answers, 'this very mind is Buddha' (即心是佛). The translator should preserve the same plain question across these cases so the differing recorded answers remain visible. These are accounts of questions put to named people, not invented literary devices.
Senses.Note: The raw substring occurs 3,795 times in 319 allowlist texts, but that total includes longer expressions such as 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha's teaching?' (如何是佛法大意). Punctuation-specific counts for the standalone question are 446 occurrences of the period form (如何是佛。) in 30 texts and 1,676 occurrences of the question-mark form (如何是佛？) in 237 texts; duplicated recensions and heading material remain included. Use 'What is Buddha?' consistently within a text unless its established English style requires the article.

Senses.PreferredTarget: what is the central meaning of the buddhas' teaching?
AlternateTargets: what is the main point of the buddhas' teaching?
what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?
Senses.Explanation: A stock public-interview question: literally, 'what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?' In this compound, the law or teaching graph (法) names the teaching under question. The formula occurs 831 times in 125 allowlisted texts and receives no standardized answer. Daolin answers Bai Juyi with 'do no evils; carry out the many goods'; Qingyuan Xingsi asks the price of rice in Luling; Linji shouts, and in another exchange raises the whisk before the monk shouts and Linji strikes; another record answers 'pay your respects,' then cuts off the monk's attempted continuation. A Linji case also records him leaving the Chan seat, seizing Ding, slapping him, and pushing him away. The repeated question is therefore a public demand put to a master, while its recorded answers range across speech, counter-question, shout, implement, and bodily action. The records supply no single answer shared by all these exchanges.
Senses.Note: The phrase itself is one question, not several senses defined by its unlike answers. The ordinary Buddhist-looking wording is bent by the Chan record into an extensively repeated public-interview formula whose answer remains case-specific. Closely related variants such as 'what is the ancestral teacher's meaning in coming from the West?' remain separate questions.
