Senses.PreferredTarget: what is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?
AlternateTargets: why did the Patriarch come from the West?
what is the point of the Ancestral Teacher's coming from the West?
what is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?' (如何是祖師西來意: 如何是, 'what is'; 祖師, 'the Patriarch'; 西來, 'coming from the West'; 意, 'meaning or intent'). The Patriarch is Bodhidharma, and the west is India in relation to China. This is the most frequently repeated set question put to masters in the lamp records and recorded sayings: the full eight-graph form occurs 1,858 times in 231 allowlist texts, while the shorter phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意) occurs about 2,081 times. The records preserve different replies by named people. Zhaozhou answers 'the cypress tree in the garden' (庭前柏樹子); Linji, asked while washing his feet, answers 'just now this old monk is washing his feet' (恰值老僧洗脚); National Teacher Huian answers 'why not ask about your own meaning?' (何不問自己意); Mazu says 'lower your voice; come closer' (低聲，近前來) and then strikes the questioner; Jingshan Daoqin says 'your question is improper' (汝問不當); and Damei Fachang answers 'there was no meaning in the coming from the West' (西來無意). The corpus also lists this question and Zhaozhou's answer beside the question 'What is Buddha?' and Dongshan Shouchu's answer 'three catties of hemp' (如何是佛，麻三斤). The entry preserves the plain question so that the different historical answers remain distinct.
Senses.Note: A stock question spoken between two people, not one master's private idiom. MasterName is null on these narrated or raised exchanges; each AttributionNote identifies the questioner and answerer. Compare the shorter noun phrase 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West' (祖師西來意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 然則如何是祖師西來意。師云。庭前柏樹子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity (從容庵錄), case 47, 'Zhaozhou's Cypress' (趙州柏樹). A monk first objects, 'do not use an object to show a person' (不將境示人), then asks the question; Zhaozhou answers 'the cypress tree in the garden' (庭前柏樹子). As a raised case, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有僧坦然、懷讓問：如何是祖師西來意？師云：何不問自己意？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), section on National Teacher Huian of Mount Song (嵩山慧安國師). Tanran and the young Nanyue Huairang ask the question, and Huian answers, 'Why not ask about your own meaning?' (何不問自己意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州行脚時參師，遇師洗脚次，州便問：如何是祖師西來意？師云：恰值老僧洗脚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tiansheng Expanded Lamp Record (天聖廣燈錄), section on Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou (鎮州臨濟義玄). While traveling, Zhaozhou asks Linji as Linji washes his feet; Linji answers, 'Just now this old monk is washing his feet' (恰值老僧洗脚).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是祖師西來意？師云：西來無意。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), section on Damei Fachang of Mingzhou (明州大梅法常). Damei denies the question's premise with 'there was no meaning in the coming from the West' (西來無意).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是祖師西來意。師曰。汝問不當。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), section on Jingshan Daoqin of Hangzhou (杭州徑山道欽禪師). Daoqin rejects the question with 'your question is improper' (汝問不當).

Occurrences.Kwic: 洪州泐潭法會禪師問馬祖。如何是祖師西來意。祖曰。低聲。近前來。向汝道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元). Fahui of Letan in Hongzhou asks Mazu; Mazu says, 'Lower your voice; come closer; I will tell you' (低聲，近前來，向汝道) and then strikes him.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “what is the way?” Across the Chan record this is a stock public question put to a master. Nanquan answers Zhaozhou, “the ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道); when Zhaozhou asks whether one can head toward it, Nanquan says that intending to head toward it departs from it (擬向即乖). Other records preserve unlike answers without a single harmonizing gloss: “white clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies love the courtyard flowers” (白雲覆青嶂，蜂蝶戀庭華), “every household's gate opens onto Chang'an” (家家門口通長安), and “what is sweet is licorice” (甜底是甘草). One master merely rebuffs the question and sends the monk away. In a longer written questionnaire, the answer begins “unobstructed is the Way” (無礙是道). Zhaozhou's record also makes the ordinary road-word audible: the master first answers “the one outside the wall” (墻外底); when the monk says he means the great Way, the answer is “the great road runs through Chang'an” (大道透長安). The dictionary therefore retains the literal question and its observable public-interview role; the mutually different recorded answers are not converted into an interpretive menu.
Senses.Note: Capitalize “Way” when the exchange distinguishes it from an ordinary road, but translate the road wordplay explicitly where it occurs.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道。州云。還可趣向否。泉云。擬向即乖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Nanquan–Zhaozhou public case and its immediate follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師曰。白雲覆青嶂。蜂蝶戀庭華。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A terse verse-like answer in an encounter record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一問。如何是道。何以修之。為復必須修成。為復不假功用。答。無礙是道。覺妄是修。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A written ten-question sequence supplies a direct answer formula rather than a short encounter reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師便咄。僧曰。學人未領旨。師曰。去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question receives a rebuff; the monk's request for clarification is answered with “go.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師曰。墻外底。曰。不問這箇。師曰。你問那箇。曰。大道。師曰。大道透長安。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's exchange explicitly plays the Way against the road outside the wall and the great road through Chang'an.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是道？師云：家家門口通長安。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate lamp-record answer uses the road-to-Chang'an wording.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是道？師云：甜底是甘草。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compact answer: “what is sweet is licorice.”

Senses.Explanation: A proper name, literally "Mighty-Sound King" (威音王), occurring 487 times in 171 allowlisted texts. The extended form "Mighty-Sound King Buddha" (威音王佛) occurs 80 times. Chan records most often place the name in temporal and spatial formulas: "before Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已前, 181 occurrences), "after Mighty-Sound King" (威音王已後, 33), and "the far side of Mighty-Sound King" (威音王那畔, 17). In the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange, Huangbo says he followed the Way "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan answers, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang" (猶是王老師兒孫在), using Nanquan's surname Wang in the reply. In the Yongjia record, Xuanze says, "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders" (威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道). Xuedou records "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King" as "the second phrase" (是第二句). A late Sanfeng record supplies an explicit internal gloss: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing" (威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也). This entry reports the proper name and the corpus's formulas without adding another framework.
Senses.Note: Dahui also reports and rejects a contemporary equation: people "close the brows and shut the eyes" and call that "news from the far side of Mighty-Sound King, from before father and mother were born," also calling it "silent yet constantly illuminating" (閉眉合眼，謂之威音王那畔父母未生時消息，亦謂之默而常照). This is included as Dahui's critical report, not adopted as the headword's meaning. The Huangbo-Nanquan wording is a two-speaker case and is therefore not assigned to either speaker in the occurrence link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 檗曰。威音王已前。師曰。猶是王老師兒孫在。下去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Nanquan Puyuan's section of the Compendium of Five Lamps. Huangbo says, "before Mighty-Sound King"; Nanquan replies, "you are still a descendant of old Master Wang—get down." MasterName is null because the headword occurs in Huangbo's turn inside a two-speaker exchange governed by Nanquan's section.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云威音王已前南泉云猶是王老師孫在師便下去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Huangbo Wanling Record's independent witness of the Nanquan-Huangbo exchange: Huangbo says "before Mighty-Sound King" and Nanquan answers that he is still old Master Wang's descendant. The two-speaker occurrence remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王已前即得，威音王已後無師自悟，盡是天然外道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Yongjia Xuanjue section of the Linked Lamps, Xuanze speaks this line to Yongjia: "before Mighty-Sound King, it is acceptable; after Mighty-Sound King, awakening by oneself without a teacher is entirely the way of outsiders." The speaker is Xuanze, not the section master, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 閉眉合眼。謂之威音王那畔父母未生時消息。亦謂之默而常照。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Dahui Zonggao's reply to Zhang Anguo. Dahui critically lists people who "close the brows and shut the eyes" and call this "news from the far side of Mighty-Sound King, from before father and mother were born," also calling it "silent yet constantly illuminating."

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王已前無師自悟。是第二句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Xuedou Chongxian's own record: "awakening by oneself without a teacher before Mighty-Sound King is the second phrase."

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音王者，形聲之外，未有出載，無所考據，文字以前最上事也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct self-definition in the Sanfeng Zang record: "Mighty-Sound King is outside form and sound, not yet set out in records, without evidence to examine—the highest matter before writing." No roster-safe master value is used for this late record.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the old woman burns the hermitage
AlternateTargets: the old woman's burning of the hermitage
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘the old woman burns the hermitage.’ The phrase occurs 75 times in 34 allowlisted texts as the title of a public case. In its repeated narrative, an old woman supports a hermitage-dweller for twenty years and sends a young woman to attend him. The young woman embraces him and asks, ‘at just such a time, how is it?’ He answers, ‘a withered tree leans against a cold cliff; through the three winter months there is no warmth.’ On hearing the report, the old woman says that for twenty years she has supported only a common fellow, drives him out, and burns the hermitage. Later masters cite, verse, question, and re-appraise the case: one asks why various quarters support the monk; another proposes that the hermitage-dweller should have laughed when approached; another says that to uphold the school and establish the teaching requires such a person, speaking of the old woman. These opposed recorded appraisals belong to the case's reception; this entry does not decide between them.
Senses.Note: Zen bends a domestic act of arson into a named case continually reopened in public comment and questioning. The label names the whole encounter, not only the final fire. The usual graph for ‘hermitage’ (庵) and its witness variant (菴) spell the same word. Cross-checking ‘a withered tree leans against a cold cliff’ (枯木倚寒巖) and ‘through the three winter months there is no warmth’ (三冬無暖氣) confirms the quoted hermitage-dweller's response without turning that response into a second sense of the case title.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉婆子燒庵話，師曰：大凡扶宗立教，須是其人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master raises ‘the old woman burns the hermitage’ case and begins: ‘generally, to uphold the school and establish the teaching requires such a person.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 龍門問：「婆子燒庵話，謂諸方扶起這僧，是何眼目？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Longmen asks: ‘In the old-woman-burns-the-hermitage case, on what discernment do various quarters support this monk?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 婆子燒庵。拈云：「這婆子俗氣不除，宛擬大人之作，當時庵主早辯來機，未免呵呵大笑。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later comment says the old woman had not shed ordinary airs and proposes that the hermitage-dweller should have recognized the approach and laughed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 婆子燒庵撲面來時無一物，明眼衲僧莫輕忽。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse headed by the case says: ‘when it comes straight at the face there is not one thing; clear-eyed patched-robed monks, do not take it lightly.’ The verse is reported without adopting it as a definition.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'solitary brightness.' The term occurs 243 times in 112 allowed texts. Its most frequent expansion is 'solitary brightness, distinct and distinct' (孤明歷歷), with 42 occurrences in 35 texts; another recurring form is 'solitary brightness shining alone' (孤明獨照). Linji's record identifies 'the person right now before your eyes, listening in solitary brightness, distinct and distinct' (即今目前孤明歷歷地聽者此人). Dahui likewise speaks of sitting and standing plainly, 'solitary brightness, distinct and distinct,' while speaker and listener meet. Yet the collections refuse to let the phrase name a terminus. One says that being profoundly clear and lucid, with solitary brightness distinct and distinct, 'is not yet news of arriving home' (未是到家消息). In another address, the question 'Whose radiance is the distinct solitary brightness?' (歷歷孤明，是誰光彩) is followed by the warning that calling it 'true suchness and the actual limit' (真如實際) resembles cutting a sore into sound flesh. These corrections keep the recurring description from being treated as an attainment or procedure.
Senses.Note: The graph-literal translation is supported by both affirmative uses and express corrections. The records describe solitary brightness as distinct and shining alone, while also saying that it is not yet news of arriving home.

Occurrences.Kwic: 孤明獨照。廓徹妙存。自然心花發明。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi describes solitary brightness shining alone, thoroughly open and subtly present, followed by the heart-flower naturally becoming evident.

Occurrences.Kwic: 孤明獨照。默味至游。智到環中。事隔關外。箇是卓卓一段不生滅底。須是退步歸家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi describes gathering remaining conditions, oneself alone being clear, and solitary brightness shining alone, then says one must step back and return home.

Occurrences.Kwic: 湛湛澄澄，孤明歷歷，未是到家消息。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct qualification: profound clarity and distinct solitary brightness are not yet news of arriving home.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道流即今目前孤明歷歷地聽者此人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies, Linji section. Linji points to the person presently listening in solitary brightness, distinct and distinct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 現今坐立儼然。孤明歷歷地。說法聽法賓主交參。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui describes people presently sitting and standing plainly, with solitary brightness distinct and distinct, while speaker and listener meet.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歷歷孤明，是誰光彩？若道真如實際，大似好肉剜瘡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The address asks whose radiance the distinct solitary brightness is, then rejects naming it true suchness and the actual limit as resembling cutting a sore into sound flesh.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “a ghost that guards a corpse.” The epithet occurs 16 times in 15 allowlisted texts. Its central named case addresses the immortal Lü Dongbin: after he asks about hiding a world in a grain and cooking mountains and rivers in a small pot, Huanglong points and says, “this corpse-guarding ghost” (這守屍鬼). Lü invokes a drug of deathlessness; Huanglong replies, “even after eighty thousand ages, in the end you fall into empty extinction” (饒經八萬劫，終是落空亡). Other Chan records apply the same epithet to sitting inert on a cushion, a tenth-stage sage, and anyone who lives a hundred or thousand years but remains “a dead person whose ghost does not disperse” (鬼魂不散底死人). Yet Gaofeng also instructs someone to remain cool, level, pure, and constant “like a corpse-guarding ghost, guarding on and on,” followed in his sentence by the doubt-clump bursting with a sound. The Chan deviation is the use of this macabre epithet across case verdict, criticism, and even an attested simile in instruction. The differing appraisals are preserved rather than harmonized.
Senses.Note: The corpus applies one epithet to an immortal, inert sitter, sage, long-lived person, and instructed comparison. These are different targets of the same label, not different referents of the label itself. No occurrence in the researched set establishes an independently narrated ghost as a second lexical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 龍指曰：這守屍鬼。呂曰：爭柰囊有長生不死藥。曰：饒經八萬劫，終是落空亡。
况枯坐蒲團如守屍鬼。且禪豈可以坐而得邪。
一念萬年去，如箇守屍鬼子守來守去，疑團子欻然𪹼地一聲，管取驚天動地。
十地聖人是守屍鬼、二乘聲聞是擔屎漢
縱饒你活到一百壽、一千壽，總喚作守屍鬼魂、不散底死人。

Senses.Explanation: To set the mind at ease or to be at ease. The expression occurs 932 times in 245 allowlisted texts, and its central Chan deployment is the Bodhidharma-Huike public case. Huike says that his mind is not at peace and asks Bodhidharma to settle it; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind, Huike says he has searched for it and cannot find it, and Bodhidharma answers, 'I have finished setting your mind at ease.' Later records name the second patriarch's mind-settling matter, quote the closing words as an interview answer, versify searching for mind and not finding it, and openly criticize both request and response. Ordinary situational uses say that arrivals are at ease and that a master should rest easy while an attendant turns away a visitor. Those causative and intransitive constructions share the same mind-at-ease referent; grammar alone does not make separate senses.
Senses.Note: The Bodhidharma-Huike case is the decisive Zen deployment, reused across independent records, verses, interviews, and criticism. The entry reports disagreement over the case without deciding what it accomplishes. Ordinary reassurance remains in the same sense as a lexical control rather than being split merely because English changes valency.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光曰：我心未寧，乞師與安。曰：將心來，與汝安。光曰：覔心了不可得。曰：與汝安心竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The early lamp record preserves the complete question, command, response, and closing formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖曰我心未寧乞師安心磨曰將心來與汝安祖曰覔心了不可得曰與汝安心竟祖於此悟入。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The case collection repeats the exchange and records Huike's entry afterward.

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉二祖安心話，遂曰：覓心不得乃安心，悟了爭如未悟深？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fojian names the second patriarch's mind-settling story and gives the formula searching for mind and not finding it is mind-settling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「二祖安心事如何？」師打云：「安心竟。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later public interview asks about the second patriarch's mind-settling matter and answers with a blow and the inherited closing words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉二祖問達磨安心公案，頌曰：長安深夜雪漫漫，欲覓心安轉不安。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master raises the case and counters seeking peace of mind with becoming still less at peace.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後來二祖却似癡猿捉月，來問安心。這老漢也是憐兒不覺醜，向他道：將心來，與汝安。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later discourse criticizes both Huike's request and Bodhidharma's response.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到者安心，全忘諸念。善行者不移雙足，善入者不動雙扉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse describes those who arrive as at ease and forgetting all thoughts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 高峰聞得，忙然不知何者為機鋒。侍者曰：『和尚安心，待我退他。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The attendant tells the master to rest easy and promises to turn the visitor away.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a 'source-line teacher' or 'lineage master': the ancestral source-line (宗) joined to teacher (師). The term occurs 1,445 times in 257 allowed texts and names a teacher judged or presented in relation to the Chan lineage. A collected assembly address gives a direct role statement: 'As for a lineage master, he takes away the poor child's pearl sewn in his clothes and examines the accomplished person's viewpoint' (夫宗師者，奪貧子之衣珠，究達人之見處). Dahui says, 'In general a lineage master decides right and wrong and must open people's eyes; he cannot rely only on blind cangues and sightless blows' (大凡宗師決斷是非。要得開人眼目。不可一向盲枷瞎棒). Yuanwu calls Zhaozhou 'a great-handed lineage master' (大手宗師) and records that he does not discuss mystery, marvel, occasion, or object but meets people solely with the fundamental matter. Yuanwu also calls Dongshan Shouchu, Zhimen Guangzuo, Deshan Yuanmi, and Xianglin Chengyuan 'great lineage masters' (皆為大宗師). The label can be withheld or mocked: a case anthology says of an inadequate answer, 'calling oneself a lineage master like this and wanting to open the eyes of humans and gods—only in the donkey year' (如此自稱宗師，欲開人天眼目，驢年去). The records therefore use the noun as title, appraisal, role description, and rebuke of a failed claimant.
Senses.Note: All direct-definition formulas and common modifiers were searched. 'Great lineage master' (大宗師) occurs 113 times in 49 texts; 'lineage-master household' (宗師家) occurs 87 times in 47; 'lineage-master eye' (宗師眼) occurs 22 times in 20; and 'a generation's lineage master' (一代宗師) occurs nine times in eight. The role is corpus-wide and is not keyed to a single teacher.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫宗師者，奪貧子之衣珠，究達人之見處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An assembly address in the Ancestral Guidelines Collection directly states two actions of a lineage master. The section speaker was not assigned a roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大凡宗師決斷是非。要得開人眼目。不可一向盲枷瞎棒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own assembly address states that lineage masters decide right and wrong and open people's eyes, then rejects relying solely on blind blows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此是大手宗師。不與爾論玄論妙。論機論境。一向以本分事接人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff prose appraises Zhaozhou as a great-handed lineage master and lists what Zhaozhou does and does not discuss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後出四哲。乃洞山初。智門寬。德山密。香林遠皆為大宗師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu names four later teachers under Yunmen and calls all four great lineage masters.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此自稱宗師，欲開人天眼目，驢年去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Collected Ancient Cases of the Lineage uses the title in a rebuke of someone who claims it without an adequate answer. This is later commentary, not a direct master link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若是宗師湏以本分事接人始得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Ancient Worthies, Zhaozhou section. The narration says a lineage master must meet people with the fundamental matter; the surrounding case remains unkeyed.

Senses.Explanation: The governing or essential purport of a teaching, transmission, house, or master. The corpus records two overlapping deployments. First, the purport is transmitted or fixed. In the Bodhidharma narrative, the seal of the teaching is transmitted to tally with verified mind, while the robe is conferred outwardly to fix the purport. A later preface parallels Shakyamuni holding up the flower and transmitting the subtle mind to Kashyapa with Bodhidharma facing the wall and entrusting the purport to Shenguang, later named Huike. Other formulas speak of revealing the purport and receiving it personally. Second, the purport belongs to a named house or teacher. A biography says someone awakened to Huanglong's purport. Another exchange calls raising the teaching banner and establishing the purport the teacher's ordinary tea and rice. Dedicatory prose says a compiler gathered the material to completion and thereby fixed the purport. The noun takes verbs translated as fix, establish, clarify, receive, reveal, and bury; named forms include Bodhidharma's purport and the purport of the buddha teaching. The records give the governing object and verb each time rather than a separate universal definition.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense covering transmitted purport and the purport of a named house. Current count: 2,171 matches in 315 files; 'clarify the purport' 99/71; 'this purport' 10/4; 'Bodhidharma's purport' 2/2; 'the purport of the buddha teaching' 3/3. The selected occurrences are transmission narrative, preface, biography, stock question, and dedicatory prose, so their occurrence master keys remain null. The formula ending in 'as for the purport' refers to people who take something as their purport and does not define the noun.

Occurrences.Kwic: 外付袈裟。以定宗旨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (初祖菩提達磨大師) section (transmission narrative): (傳法印以契證心)。(外付袈裟)。(以定宗旨) — the robe conferred outwardly "to fix the purport" (以定宗旨). Narrative, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨面壁而宗旨付於神光。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈全書), (僉判劉經臣居士) section (a layman's essay-preface on transmission): (世尊拈花而妙心傳於迦葉)，(達磨面壁而宗旨付於神光) — the (宗旨) conferred on Huike (Shenguang). Preface statement, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 得悟黃龍宗旨
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈全書), (長沙石霜琳禪師) biographical entry: (未幾)，(得悟黃龍宗旨)，(機鋒頴脫) — (宗旨) as a particular house's purport (Huanglong). Third-person biography, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 建法幢、立宗旨者，是和尚尋常茶飯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈全書); a (僧問) exchange — "raise the teaching-banner, establish the purport" (建法幢、立宗旨) called "the master's ordinary tea and rice" (和尚尋常茶飯). Shows the collocation (立宗旨). MasterName null (stock 僧問 frame).

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃集大成、乃定宗旨
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄) (preface/dedicatory prose): (超而隨之)，(乃集大成)、(乃定宗旨) — the collocation "fix the purport" (定宗旨), an independent witness (Jiaxing canon). MasterName null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the 'source-gate' or 'lineage gate.' The term occurs 1,934 times in 285 allowed texts. Yuanwu supplies a direct graph relation: 'Buddha's words take mind as the source; when the source is penetrated, speech is also penetrated; since it is called the source-gate...' (佛語心為宗。宗通說亦通。既謂之宗門). Across encounter records, the compound names the Chan lineage as the field within which a matter, question, or saying is presented. 'Within the lineage gate' (宗門中) occurs 350 times in 108 texts, and 'under the lineage gate' (宗門下) occurs 175 times in 71 texts. A lecturer explicitly sets aside the three vehicles and twelve divisions of teaching and asks, 'What is the matter within the lineage gate?' (三乘十二分教即不問如何是宗門中事). Another monk asks the teacher to raise and proclaim 'the matter within the lineage gate' (宗門中事。請師舉唱). Fachang Yiyu draws a line with his staff, sets that aside, and asks how the lineage-gate matter goes (這箇即且止，宗門事作麼生). Wuyi Yuanlai contrasts what he calls the utmost reach of the teaching families with 'the strong point within the lineage gate' (宗門中長處), and elsewhere asks directly what that strong point is. The same word also heads titles of collected lineage records; those titles attest the institutional and textual range without creating a separate sense.
Senses.Note: Definition-formula searches found Yuanwu's explicit derivation and three occurrences of 'called the lineage gate.' Sixty-three occurrences in 31 texts ask 'what is the lineage gate' or a longer question beginning that way. The corpus-wide sense covers lineage, its recorded affairs, and collection titles; no master-specific meaning was established. The English target does not leave the graph meaning to a religious loanword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛語心為宗。宗通說亦通。既謂之宗門。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's instruction to Zongjue directly links the source graph to mind and then uses the compound lineage gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有座主問三乘十二分教即不問如何是宗門中事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Ancient Worthies, Muzhou section. A lecturer sets aside the classified teachings and asks about the matter within the lineage gate; the two-speaker exchange remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。宗門中事。請師舉唱。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Tianzhu Chonghui section. A monk asks the teacher to raise and proclaim the matter within the lineage gate, so the dialogue is not keyed to one speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 以拄杖畫一畫，曰：這箇即且止，宗門事作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Fachang Yiyu section. The master draws a line, sets it aside, and asks about the lineage-gate matter; the surrounding exchange is left unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此是教家極則，若以思惟心測度，如將螢火燒須彌山，終不能著。然雖如是，更須知有宗門中長處始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wuyi Yuanlai's record contrasts what it calls the teaching families' utmost reach with a strong point within the lineage gate. No roster link was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道：如何是宗門下長處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Later in Wuyi Yuanlai's record, an assembly address directly asks for the strong point under the lineage gate.

Senses.Explanation: The two graphs mean “lineage or house” and “wind”: “the wind of a house,” its characteristic manner or style. A preface names “the Caodong house wind” and describes it as the wondrous accord of upright and inclined. The expression takes verbs meaning expand, rouse, inherit, and revive: one may greatly expand a house wind, vigorously rouse it, inherit it later, or revive the Caodong house wind. Biographical language places inheriting the house wind beside fulfilling a Guiyang prediction, greatly rousing the ancestral working, and transmitting the true eye of the teaching. The house wind can itself become the object of a question: “What is the phrase by which the house wind does not fall?” Related expressions are “family wind,” “gate wind,” and “essential purport.” The records use the term for a lineage's manner without reducing it to one fixed list of traits.
Senses.Note: This is one corpus-wide sense. It may attach to a named house and combines with verbs of expansion, rousing, inheritance, and revival. The curated passages are prefaces, biographical narrative, and a multi-speaker question, so their speaker fields remain null. Compare “family wind,” “gate wind,” and “essential purport.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞上宗風，正偏妙協
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Juelang Sheng of the Celestial Realm, preface: the Caodong house wind is described through the accord of upright and inclined.

Occurrences.Kwic: 重興洞上宗風
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same preface region speaks of reviving the Caodong house wind in Jiangxi and eastern Yue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大闡宗風
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, biographical section on Deshan Xuanjian: after he is invited to reside in the prefecture, he greatly expands the house wind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後嗣宗風，應溈仰懸記，大振祖機，傳正法眼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Lamp Record from the Jianzhong Jingguo Era, biography of Fengxue Yanzhao: inheriting the house wind appears in a lineage-transmission sequence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是宗風不墜底句
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Yaoshan Weiyan section: a monk asks for the phrase by which the house wind does not fall.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'stability' (定) and 'discernment' (慧). The compound occurs 962 times in 196 allowed texts. Huineng devotes a named section to it and gives the richest direct relation: 'Stability and discernment are one body, not two. Stability is the substance of discernment; discernment is the function of stability' (定慧一體，不是二。定是慧體，慧是定用). He continues, 'At the time of discernment, stability is in discernment; at the time of stability, discernment is in stability' (即慧之時定在慧，即定之時慧在定), then names this 'equal learning in stability and discernment.' He explicitly rejects making them successive: 'Do not say first stability produces discernment or first discernment produces stability as separate' (莫言先定發慧、先慧發定各別), and compares their relation to lamp and light—two names whose substance is one. An independent lamp text gives a water-and-wave formulation: 'Stability is substance, discernment is function; from stability discernment arises, from discernment one returns to stability; like water and wave, one body with no before or after' (定是體慧是用從定起慧從慧歸定如水與波一體更無前後). Huangbo answers a question about their equal learning with 'throughout the twelve periods, do not rely on a single thing' (十二時中不依倚一物). A later letter supplies a corrective naming statement: 'Provisionally it is called stability and discernment; it is not an actual thing. As for this mind, it is originally self-stable and self-discerning' (方便喚作定慧，不是實法也。若論此心，本來自定自慧). Another record directly describes the graphs: inner and outer wholly clear is called stability, while responding to conditions and things with function without end is called discernment. The entry reports these corpus definitions without recasting the pair as a staged regimen.
Senses.Note: Direct definitions, substance/function equations, order contrasts, analogies, and corrective witnesses were all harvested. 'Equal stability and discernment' (定慧等) occurs 80 times in 44 texts; 'stability and discernment are one body' occurs in two independent texts; the substance/function formulas occur in four each. The pair remains one corpus-wide sense, led by Huineng's explicit rejection of separation and sequence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我此法門，以定慧為本。大眾！勿迷，言定慧別。定慧一體，不是二。定是慧體，慧是定用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Platform Record, section four. Huineng directly states the one-body and substance/function relation of stability and discernment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 即慧之時定在慧，即定之時慧在定。若識此義，即是定慧等學。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng continues the direct equation and names it equal learning in stability and discernment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸學道人，莫言先定發慧、先慧發定各別。作此見者，法有二相。口說善語，心中不善。空有定慧，定慧不等。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng explicitly rejects treating stability and discernment as separate sequential productions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問如何是定慧等學師曰定是體慧是用從定起慧從慧歸定如水與波一體更無前後名定慧等學
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Transmission of the Lamp's Finest Flowers preserves a direct question and a water-and-wave answer. The mixed collection heading does not provide a safe speaker link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師又別時問黃檗。定慧等學此理如何。黃檗云。十二時中不依倚一物。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of the Transmission of the Lamp narrates Nanquan asking Huangbo about equal learning in stability and discernment. As a two-speaker case, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 方便喚作定慧，不是實法也。若論此心，本來自定自慧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zongbao Daodu's letter to Layman Weng calls the pair a provisional name rather than an actual thing and says mind is originally self-stable and self-discerning. No roster link was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫戒定慧者，乃法中之妙用也。佛祖雖嘗有言，而未達者有所執。今略而言之，庶資開悟。然其心境兩忘，一念不動曰戒。覺性圓明，內外瑩徹曰定。隨緣應物，妙用無窮曰慧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Selected Recorded Sayings, Explanation of Precept-Stability-Discernment. The prose directly assigns separate predicates to stability and discernment; it is not linked to a roster master.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. The distinct Chan deployment appears in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded classification: “one's own mind is buddha; illuminating function belongs to bodhisattva; mind after mind is the ruler; illuminating function belongs to guest-dust” (自心是佛，照用屬菩薩；心心是主宰，照用屬客塵). Here “guest-dust” is not merely a name for dirt or an outside visitor; Baizhang places it on the “illuminating function” side of a ruler/guest classification and immediately compares it to speaking of water by way of waves (如波說水). The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings and the Expanded Lamp preserve this wording independently. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery but also bends it into Baizhang's explicit ruler/function classification.
Senses.Note: The corpus-wide sense remains one article because the Baizhang classification depends on the same guest-versus-ruler morphology as the broader compound. The explanation describes the recorded classification without adding an outside account of affliction or purity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自心是佛照用属菩薩心心是主宰照用属客塵如波說水照萬像以無功
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings preserves Baizhang Huaihai's ruler/guest-dust classification. Because the surrounding compilation head is not explicit in the toolkit result, the occurrence is not linked directly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自心是佛，照用屬菩薩。心心是主宰，照用屬客塵。如波說水，照萬像以無功。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Expanded Lamp, explicitly under the Baizhang Huaihai section; an independently preserved, punctuated witness of the ruler/guest-dust classification.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不知是客塵煩惱。十六行中嬰兒行為最。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Jingde Lamp Record; in a discourse on the infant comparison, learned explanations are called guest-dust troubles.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當淨意根下無始時來客塵煩惱之染。如虛空之寬曠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's Recorded Sayings, instruction to layman Li; guest-dust troubles occur with the explicit predicate “stain.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 身心客塵透漏無門。迷悟且說逆順休論。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Admonitions for the Monastic Gate, in Foyan Qingyuan's Inscription on Sitting Chan; a distinct “body-and-mind guest-dust” compound.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “inside the room” or “in the chamber.” In Chan records the recurrent institutional chamber is a place of direct examination: masters “question a monk in the chamber” (室中問僧), present an old saying there, or arrange an object and test each person who enters. One biography says a head monk was assigned to share the chamber seat and “grasp the bamboo switch to test students” (令分座室中，握竹篦以驗學者); another records the no-buddha-nature saying being presented repeatedly in the chamber, followed by a strike when the student began to speak. Recorded-sayings collections can therefore label a section “chamber encounters” (室中機緣). The word names the location and institutional setting, not the student's entrance: “enter the chamber for an interview” (入室) names the entrance, whereas “in the chamber” (室中) names the setting. Nor does the setting itself certify approval or succession.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count across both senses: 1,566 hits in 274 texts. Distinct technical deployments preserved here are a direct chamber question, delegated examination by a head monk, presentation of a named old saying, an arranged-object test for entrants, and the section label “chamber encounters.” The Zen bend is the chamber's repeated use as an interview and testing setting.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中問僧：無手人能行拳，無舌人解言語。忽然無手人打無舌人，無舌人道箇甚麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete: the formula says the master questioned a monk in the chamber, followed by the question itself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未幾，令分座室中，握竹篦以騐學者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Lamp Orthodox Lineage: a head monk is assigned to share the chamber seat and grasp the bamboo switch to test students.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中每示狗子無佛性話。一日，師擬開口，用以竹篦劈口便𭣟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Lamp Surviving Draft: the no-buddha-nature saying is repeatedly presented in the chamber; when the student begins to speak, the bamboo switch is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師室中插劒一口，以草鞋一對，水一盆，置在劒邊。每見入室，即曰：看！看！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Strict Lineage: the master arranges a sword, sandals, and water in the chamber and addresses each person entering.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中機緣師問僧。巖頭纔跨德山門便問。是凡是聖。德山便喝。巖頭禮拜。意作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's Recorded Sayings: a section headed “chamber encounters” opens with Dahui questioning a monk about the Yantou–Deshan exchange.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary spatial narration, the headword simply means “inside a room” (室中). A verse says, “idle inside the room, I cannot be bothered to burn incense” (室中無事懶燒香); another describes someone “lying ill in a single room” (臥病一室中). These rooms are living or sick rooms, not the master's institutional interview chamber. No special Chan deviation is attested in this sense.
Senses.Note: Split under #0f.8 because the physical room in these passages is a different referent from the institutional chamber-interview setting. The surface locative wording is shared, but “chamber interview” would be false for these witnesses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 寄友室中無事懶燒香，危坐多時倦即橫，一覺惺來人不見
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse to a friend: “idle inside the room, I cannot be bothered to burn incense”; an ordinary private room with no interview action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臥病一室中，機用恁唧溜。命徒問疾來，香飯曾借否？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse describes lying ill in a single room and disciples coming to ask after the illness; the room is a sickroom, not an interview chamber.

AlternateTargets: the manner of a house or lineage
Senses.Explanation: Literally 'the wind/manner of a house.' In the records it names the distinctive teaching-style and household-manner of a particular master or lineage — how THIS house does things. Its commonest form is the stock interview question 'What is the master's family style?' (如何是和尚家風), which the master answers with a concrete, homely image of his own place and way: 'white clouds come and close the door' (Tianzhu), 'harvest in autumn, store away in winter,' or 'my old ears are deaf — ask louder' (adding, 'you ask MY house-style, but I already know YOURS'). The word is used equally of a single teacher (和尚家風) and of a whole lineage or the tradition at large — (臨濟家風) (the Linji house's way), (佛祖家風) / (古佛家風) (the way of the buddhas and ancestors), (野老家風) (the plain 'old rustic's' style). The register is domestic and self-characterizing, often plain ('eating gruel, eating rice — also to be done carefully'): the recognizable style, temper and household-manner a teacher hands down, by which one house is told from another. Zen-scoped grep counts: (家風) 3743 hits across 335 of the 462 allowlist texts; the interview question (如何是)…(家風) accounts for 1173 hits in 141 texts, of which the exact (如何是和尚家風) makes 819 in 113. Scale collocations: (古佛家風) 209/113, (臨濟家風) 64/46, (佛祖家風) 54/42, (野老家風) 20/15, (衲僧家風) 5/4. The records also use it as a verdict of succession: (吾宗門下曹山可謂妙得其家風者) (within our school, Caoshan may be said to have marvelously gotten his family-wind; J40nB494), with the same formula (可謂妙得其家風者) said of another heir at J34nB299.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense: the term is a shared, house-neutral word applied to every master and lineage, not bent by any single master. Extremely broad attestation (3743 occurrences in 335 allowlist files, tag-stripped re-concordance 2026-07-11; an earlier count of ~613 was low), so multi-source is beyond doubt. No master-specific sense warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問如何是天柱家風師曰時有白雲來閉戶更無風月四山流
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianzhu-shan Chonghui (天柱崇慧禪師). The stock question (如何是)…(家風) answered with a concrete image of the mountain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是和尚家風？」師云：「老僧耳背，高聲問。」僧再問，師云：「你問我家風，我卻識你家風。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Reflexive use: the 'house-style' is turned back on the questioner (你問我家風，我卻識你家風).

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛祖家風，衲僧活計，百姓日用，無不在內，喫粥喫飯，也要仔細。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Everyday register: (佛祖家風) (the buddhas-and-ancestors' house-style) glossed as ordinary daily life, gruel and rice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「臨濟家風則且置，曹洞宗旨是如何？」師云：「牽連斷貫索。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: House-style used at the lineage scale, (臨濟家風) set beside (曹洞宗旨).

Occurrences.Kwic: 因僧問：「如何是古佛家風？」師曰：「銀蟾初出海，何處不分明？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古佛家風) (the ancient buddhas' house-style) — the same stock question at the tradition scale.

Senses.Explanation: Hanshan is the pre-Zen figure whom the records pair with Shide and Fenggan. The string occurs 1,453 times in 271 allowlisted texts, but that total mixes the person with ordinary and place-name uses. As a figure, Hanshan is quoted by name: "my mind is like the autumn moon; the clear blue pool is bright and pure; no thing can be compared with it—how can I speak?" (吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔，無物堪比倫，教我如何說). Masters then criticize the verse: one says "Hanshan has slipped in speech" (寒山子話墮了也); another says Hanshan "labored without result" (寒山子勞而無功). In encounter lore Hanshan and Shide are visited at Guoqing monastery, imitate fighting oxen, bare their teeth, and later ask about the encounter. Elsewhere "Hanshan visits Shide" is given as the answer to a question about Vimalakirti's silence. Zen therefore deploys Hanshan as quoted poet, paired comic figure, and an answer in public interview.
Senses.Note: Primary figure sense. The expanded name Hanshanzi (寒山子), the pair Hanshan and Shide (寒山拾得), and Hanshan's poems (寒山詩) belong to this family. They are separated from the ordinary landscape phrase below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔。乃喝曰：寒山子話墮了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master quotes Hanshan's autumn-moon line and immediately says Hanshan slipped in speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔。無物堪比倫，教我如何說？寒山子勞而無功。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse is quoted and Hanshan is judged to have labored without result.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師因到天台國清寺見寒山拾得師云久響寒山拾得到來只見兩頭水牯牛寒山拾得便作牛闘師云叱叱寒山拾得咬齒相看

Senses.Explanation: Separately, the same graphs can denote a cold mountain or the mountain-place called Cold Mountain. One verse says, "the blue ravine's spring water is clear; Cold Mountain's moonlight is white" (碧澗泉水清，寒山月華白). Another says, "leaves are gone and flowers open by themselves, right within a cold mountain; the mountain is cold and people are seldom seen" (葉盡花自發，正當寒山中，山寒人見少). A poem describing ascent says, "climbing the Cold Mountain way, the Cold Mountain road does not end" (登陟寒山道，寒山路不窮). These landscape and route occurrences refer to a place, not to Hanshan the person.
Senses.Note: Split under item 8 because a person and a mountain/place are different referents. The longer proper name 'Cold Mountain Monastery' was removed as evidence for this sense: its first two graphs do not by themselves prove a cold-mountain referent rather than the person after whom the monastery is known.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A poem describes climbing the Cold Mountain way and the unending Cold Mountain road, with long streams, piled stones, and thick grass.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "cold ashes" (寒灰). The term occurs 215 times in 112 allowlisted texts and can name actual ash that has gone cold: a sick-room verse places cold ash in a stove beside frost on a mat. Chan addresses use that same material image in several recorded formulas. It is commonly paired with "dead wood" (枯木). One discourse states, "one thought for ten thousand years, cold ashes and dead wood—these are all still, sunken dead water" (一念萬年，寒灰枯木，俱是靜沉死水). Earlier transmitted wording lists "go like cold ashes and dead wood" (寒灰枯木去) beside "rest and cease" and "one thought for ten thousand years." The records also say "cold ashes burst into flame" (寒灰發焰), and one seasonal discourse sets "yesterday, cold ashes covered the ground" against "today, spring news fills the whole sky" (昨日匝地寒灰，今朝普天春信). These are literal and image-bearing deployments of the same ash, not different lexical things. The entry reports the contrasts without deciding what the reversal signifies.
Senses.Note: Related forms include cold ashes and dead wood (寒灰枯木), cold ashes bursting into flame (寒灰發燄/發焰), beans bursting in cold ashes (豆爆寒灰), and cold ash in a stove (爐有寒灰). Item-8 readjudication merges the former stove-ash sense because both targets denoted the same material; concrete placement and figurative deployment do not by themselves establish polysemy. Proper names or sobriquets containing the graphs for "cold ashes" (寒灰) are excluded.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Complete Command of the Precious Mirror
Senses.Explanation: The four graphs literally name the precious mirror (寶鏡) and complete command (三昧). In the Chan record this is not a generic state: it is the title and transmitted Caodong text associated with Dongshan Liangjie. Dongshan tells Caoshan that he personally received the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror from his former teacher Yunyan, that its matter exhausts the essential point, and that he now entrusts it to Caoshan (吾在雲巖先師處親印寶鏡三昧，事窮的要，今付于汝). A later commentary consequently calls it a book transmitted privately by Dongshan to Caoshan (寶鏡三昧一書，洞山室中密授曹山者也). The text itself opens, “This such thing was secretly entrusted by buddhas and ancestors; you have now obtained it, so guard it well” (如是之法，佛祖密付；汝今得之，宜善保護), then gives the paired images “a silver bowl filled with snow; the bright moon hiding a heron” (銀盌盛雪，明月藏鷺) and says that although their kinds are not the same, mixed together their places are known (類之弗齊，混則知處). Across later Caodong records its title is joined to the Five Ranks, upright and crooked, ruler and minister, and the paired wording “he is not me; I am precisely he” (渠不是我，我正是渠). A direct question, “What is the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror?” receives, “Do not reflect idle light and shadows; return his old face” (不照閒光影，還他舊面皮). These are the transmitted title, contents, relations, and recorded answer; the corpus supplies no single prose substitution for the whole text.
Senses.Note: #0g deviation: the phrase is deployed as the proper name of a Caodong transmission text and house inheritance, not merely as the ordinary image of a valuable mirror or the standalone word for complete command. Attribution of authorship is not fully uniform: Dongshan's record says he received it from Yunyan and entrusted it to Caoshan; later records also call it Dongshan's text or report older attributions. The entry therefore reports the transmission claims without deciding authorship. Allowlisted count: 117 hits in 49 texts; the title form “Song of the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror” (寶鏡三昧歌) occurs 3 times in one text.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, not (不) one inch of thread (寸絲) hanging or attached (掛): "not a thread hanging." This graph form occurs 59 times in 43 allowlisted texts; the variant with the simplified hanging graph (寸絲不挂) occurs 97 times in 57 texts, and the reversal "not hanging one thread" (不掛寸絲) occurs 14 times in 14 texts. Chan records make the clothing image into a repeatedly tested claim. When Xuanji answers Xuefeng's weaving question, "not a thread hanging," Xuefeng calls after him that the corner of his robe is dragging; Xuanji turns his head and Xuefeng strikes him, saying, "a fine 'not a thread hanging'!" (大好寸絲不掛). Nanquan asks the official Lu Gen what he does throughout the twelve periods; Lu replies with the phrase, and Nanquan answers, "you are still a man below the steps" (猶是階下漢). Jifei asks Fayun where the robe on his body came from if not a thread is hanging; Fayun answers by questioning whether it can be called a robe. Another exchange answers the condition "all affairs extinguished, not a thread hanging" with "you should be ashamed," then answers formal dressing and bowing with "the bare body fully exposed" (赤體露條條). The phrase therefore bends literal nakedness and weaving into a stock Chan claim whose own records repeatedly check it against robes, dressing, and the speaker's response; the corpus does not treat the words as a sufficient verdict by themselves.
Senses.Note: The graph for "hanging" varies between the standard form (掛) and its graphic variant (挂) without a sense change. The literal use also survives: one biographical notice says a monk left home empty-handed and without a thread on him. The curated witnesses foreground the distinct Chan wordplay and corrective encounters.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, honored or venerable, and senior or long-established. The compound occurs 1,906 times in 291 allowlisted texts and serves as a title for an established Chan elder. Biographies say that someone traveled to consult venerable elders; records speak collectively of venerable elders in every region, elder predecessors, and old venerable elders. It also appears in the title 'Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Venerable Elders.' In Huangbo's reported exchange, a monk objects that venerable elders everywhere gather communities and teach people after Huangbo says there are no Chan teachers; Huangbo replies that he did not say there was no Chan, only that there were no teachers. A portrait verse can use 'one of this sort is called a venerable elder' satirically, showing that the title can be quoted rather than simply bestowed by the narrator.
Senses.Note: The corpus provides no stable graph-formula definition of the bare title. The four strings ending in 'venerable elder is ...' are relative-clause constructions, not definitions. Productive modifiers include 'in every region' (71 hits in 55 texts), 'old' (22 in 19), and 'elder predecessors' (10 in eight).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to face or match the occasion. In Chan records it names responsive encounter rather than a private state. One early lamp compilation makes “encounters responding to the occasion” a section heading for recorded cases. A later questioner says that during “questioning and discrimination in responding to the occasion” his responses are not free-flowing, and asks where the fault lies; the master's answer examines him rather than treating interview performance as optional. A recorded dialogue asks where the three vehicles and twelve divisions of teaching were obtained, and the master answers, “they were obtained in responding to the occasion.” Hongzhi speaks of “an eye for responding to the occasion in engaging the world,” followed by the claim that the many conditions cannot bury it. The same verb extends to audience-responsive speech: Gu Xue records that those of sharp capacity are told to investigate Chan and those of middling or lower capacity to invoke buddha, calling this “speaking in response to the occasion,” then asks what is right or wrong. The corpus also uses the term in titles such as collections of hundreds of encounters, in appraisals of a speaker's response, and in compounds with answering and reception. Thus the ordinary graph “occasion” or “capacity” (機) is bent toward the live occasion or capacity presented by another: “respond to the occasion” (對機) means meeting it in an answer, action, exchange, or address preserved by the record.
Senses.Note: “Occasion” keeps the range of the graph “occasion/capacity” (機) without importing a mystical faculty. The heading, question-and-discrimination phrase, direct answer, and “eye” collocation all require an interpersonal responsive sense. Compare “meet the occasion” (當機), “occasion of encounter” (機緣), “question-and-answer” (問答), and “responsive engagement” (應酬); none is simply synonymous.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “small or minor” (小); the second means “assemble for instruction” (參) (as in 上堂 the great convocation and 晚參 the evening gathering). (小參) is the informal, lesser convocation, set against (上堂) (ascending the hall — the great, formal convocation). The monastic code (敕修百丈清規) defines it plainly: "the small convocation has no fixed place" (小參初無定所), held wherever suits the size of the assembly — the sleeping hall (寢堂) or the teaching hall (法堂) — announced by hanging a (小參牌) and given at the evening bell (昏鐘); hence its stock form "that evening's small convocation" (當晚小參) and (晚小參). The rule adds that the abbot "just as at the five-day (上堂)," (登座) so (小參) is procedurally the same address, only informal in place and timing. In the yulu it is a genre heading paralleling (上堂) in the table of contents (卷第八　上堂八　小參一). The code's fuller definition names occasions and register: (如住持入院)。(或官員檀越入山)。(或受人特請)。(或謂亡者開示)。(或四節臘則移於昏鐘鳴)。(而謂之小參)。(可以敘世禮)。(曰家教者是也)。(然亦不鳴放參鐘)。(謂猶有參也) (when the abbot takes office, or officials and donors come up the mountain, or on a special request, or as instruction for the dead, or at the four season-nodes — moved to the sounding of the evening bell it is called 小參; worldly courtesies may be recounted; this is what is meant by the 'house teaching' 家教; yet the release-bell is still not rung, meaning there is still convocation; T48n2025 1119c07), and its procedure: (至日午後)。(侍者覆住持云令客頭行者報眾)。(掛小參牌)。(當晚不鳴放參鐘)。(昏鐘鳴時行者覆住持)。(鳴鼓一通)。(眾集兩序歸位)。(住持登座提綱) (T48n2025 1119c12). A yulu preserves a live exchange about the word itself, set against (大參): (我曾問副寺師)：『(如何是小參)？』(寺曰)：『(吃粥)。』『(如何是大參)？』(寺曰)：『(吃飯)。』 (what is the small convocation? — eating gruel; and the great convocation? — eating rice; J37nB390, which also narrates 已掛小參牌了也). Occasion-prefixed forms carry most of its deployment: (當晚小參) 127 hits/62 texts, (晚小參) 160/81, (除夜)·(歲夜小參) 95/45, (解制)·(結制小參) 29/21.
Senses.Note: A genre / format marker, not a thesis. Distinguished from (上堂) by informality: no fixed place, evening timing, smaller occasion; very often (當晚小參) / (晚小參). The abbot's procedure otherwise matches (上堂). Cf. (晚參). Zen-scoped grep (tag-stripped, 2026-07-11): (小參) 7023 hits in 337 allowlist texts (上堂: 54942 in 402) — both pervasive genre headings; (小參牌) 3 hits in 2 texts (T48n2025, J37nB390).

Senses.PreferredTarget: take the road and return home
AlternateTargets: return home by way of the road
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “take the road and return home.” The Zen bend is visible in the corpus's repeated reversals and pairings: the phrase is a stock Chan verdict for a person's handling of what is already under discussion, yet the records deny that its homeward journey is an ordinary change of location. One record says that even if someone speaks of “turning back with mastery and taking the road home,” it is “a thousand miles and ten thousand miles” away (回途得妙，就路還家，便是千里萬里). Another sets “take the road and return home” against “leave home and take the road” (離家就路), then says that leaving does not move an inch and returning has no bodily image. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly pairs it with “turn around and return to the father” (轉身歸父). Shiyu Mingfang applies the phrase three times to actual travel stages—leaving Jinze by boat, passing Jiaxing and Chongde, and reaching Fojih monastery—so the literal journey remains available inside the stock expression. Juelang Sheng calls “responding to the occasion and benefiting beings; taking the road and returning home” (因機利物，就路還家) the staff-bearer's ordinary occupation, alongside “meeting conditions and acting as host” (遇緣作主) as his own-house style. The corpus therefore bends a homeward-road idiom into a recurring Chan appraisal while also recording literal journeys and explicit counter-journeys.
Senses.Note: No single master-specific sense is warranted. The phrase occurs across many late records, often with “turn around and return to the father” or the reversed “leave home and take the road.” The article reports those textual relations without assigning a spiritual force to “home.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒說箇回途得妙，就路還家，便是千里萬里。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, Shiyu Mingfang section; the text itself denies that merely saying the homeward formula is arrival.

Occurrences.Kwic: 離金澤，跨船舷，也是就路還家；過嘉興，由崇德，也是就路還家；到塘棲，入佛日，登戒錄，要羯磨，也是就路還家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shiyu's record applies the phrase repeatedly to named legs of a literal journey. The roster does not supply a securely matched canonical link for this section, so MasterName remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此是故鄉景象，若肯就路還家，便得轉身歸父。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wuyi Yuanlai's Extended Record, sermon at Boshan Nengren monastery; an exact pairing with “turn around and return to the father.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一人就路還家，一人離家就路。離家就路，寸步不曾移；就路還家，通身無影像。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Snow Zhe's Recorded Sayings, Cuiyan monastery section; the text draws the full return/leave contrast and supplies the no-movement and no-image predicates.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因機利物，就路還家，此是杖人尋常活計；到處稱尊，遇緣作主，此是杖人本分宗風。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang Sheng's Recorded Sayings; the phrase is explicitly classified as the staff-bearer's ordinary occupation and paired with meeting conditions as host.

Senses.PreferredTarget: mountains, rivers, and the great earth
Senses.Explanation: Literally, mountains, rivers, great, and earth. The expression names the whole visible terrain. Across the allowlisted corpus it occurs 2,224 times in 305 texts. Masters answer with it when asked what lies between heaven and earth and what the appearance of mind is; elsewhere they ask whether it is the same as or different from oneself, say that calling something by this name meets the object while refusing the name turns away from it, and include it with the sun, moon, and stars in what does not go outside one's mind. One later record gives its own local formulation: a portion of unknowing is called mountains, rivers, and the great earth. That formulation is reported as this record's wording, not imposed on the other occurrences.
Senses.Note: The reverse-order variant 'the great earth, mountains, and rivers' is frequent (562 occurrences in 211 texts). The evidence preserves the expression's ordinary collective reference while recording several distinct ways masters deploy it in questions and answers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 塚上草離離。問：上是天，下是地，未審中間是甚麼物？師曰：山河大地。曰：恁麼則謝師答話。師曰：大地山河。曰：和尚何得瞞人？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An anonymous monk asks a named master what is between heaven and earth; the exchange also immediately reverses the expression's word order.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子閑。蘄州四祖山法演禪師蘄州四祖山法演禪師桂州人。僧問：如何是心相？師曰：山河大地。曰：如何是心體？師曰：汝喚甚麼作山河大
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage identifies the master in the text; the name is left unlinked because this occurrence was not assigned a verified roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一念昏沉便是無明，無明生起一分有知，謂之眾生；一分無知，謂之山河大地。明暗色空，山河影現，搖動知覺謂之塵，知覺吸攬前塵謂之念
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A small-talk section of this discourse record supplies an explicit local wording for the term.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且放下著。我喚作露柱則觸。不喚作露柱則背。爾又如何奪。我喚作山河大地則觸。不喚作山河大地則背。爾又如何奪。有箇舟峯長老云。某
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse speaker applies the paired 'call it' and 'do not call it' formula first to a pillar and then to the landscape expression.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：不知最親切。又同三人舉肇論，至天地與我同根處，藏曰：山河大地與上座自己是同是別？師曰：別。藏竪起兩指，師曰：同。藏又竪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A two-speaker exchange tests both 'different' and 'same'; null attribution avoids assigning the entire exchange to one speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可更頭上安頭觜上加觜但莫生異見山是山水是水僧是僧俗是俗山河大地日月星辰揔不出汝心三千世界都來是汝箇自己何處有多般心外無法滿目青
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing section is the Wanling record of Huangbo; the roster link is left null pending an exact canonical-name check.

Senses.Explanation: Budai, literally "the Cloth-Bag monk," is the non-lineage figure defined in Chan records by the bag he carries and uses in public exchanges. His title occurs 200 times in 105 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is the cloth bag?" (如何是布袋), he puts the bag down; asked "what is the matter beneath the cloth bag?" (如何是布袋下事), he shoulders it and leaves. Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the monk who claims to have arrived. Later records quote his verse, "Maitreya, true Maitreya, divides into hundreds of thousands of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him" (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), then comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street monk whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.
Senses.Note: One person/title sense. The bag itself (布袋) is a related concrete headword, not a second sense of the full title. The corpus identifies the figure through the bag and the Maitreya verse; this entry adds no outside life story.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師放下布袋。叉手而立。白鹿和尚問。如何是布袋。師便放下布袋。曰。如何是布袋下事。師負之而去。先保福和尚問。如何是佛法大意。師放下布袋。叉手。福曰。為秖如此。為更有向上事。師負之而去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The lamp record preserves the putting-down and shouldering exchanges.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師在街衢立，有僧問：和尚在這裏作甚麼？師曰：等箇人。曰：來也，來也。師云：汝不是這箇人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the street Budai says he waits for a person and rejects the monk's claim to have arrived.

Occurrences.Kwic: 開山第一世布袋和尚偈曰：『彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record explicitly attributes the Maitreya verse to Budai.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或於稠人中打開布袋中物，攃下云：『看！看！』天童悟老人云：『少賣弄。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later case says Budai opened the bag and scattered its contents before a crowd; Tiantong comments, 'show off less.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 放下布袋等箇人，手裏把柄破木杓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An image praise joins putting down the bag, waiting for a person, and holding a broken wooden ladle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明州布袋和尚常攜一布袋
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later case introduction explicitly defines the figure by habitually carrying one cloth bag.

Senses.Explanation: A lion. Chan records repeatedly deploy the animal in lineage and speech vocabulary: a capable successor is a 'lion cub' and forceful proclamation is a 'lion's roar.' The Blue Cliff Record pairs an outstanding, keen fellow with a lion cub; Zhaozhou is called a true lion cub, well able to roar. A recorded old adept says that a lion uses its complete strength for both rabbit and elephant, then names that strength the strength that does not deceive. Another inherited formula contrasts proclamation with attainment, calling teaching with something obtained a jackal's cry and teaching without something obtained a lion's roar. These are explicit corpus deployments; the entry assigns no hidden animal symbolism.
Senses.Note: The exact form occurs 3,850 times in 301 allowlisted texts, including personal names and inherited Buddhist imagery as well as the Chan collocations described here. Name-bearing hits were excluded from this animal sense. The principal variants are lion cub and lion's roar.

Occurrences.Kwic: 出群須是英靈漢。敵勝還他師子兒。選佛若無如是眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record says that defeating the opponent belongs to a lion cub.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子且還老僧草鞋錢。然後老僧還子廬陵米價。師曰。恁麼則不識和尚也。未委廬陵米作麼價。山曰。真師子兒。善能哮吼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the Luling-rice exchange, the teacher calls the interlocutor a true lion cub, well able to roar.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔有一老宿。因僧問。師子捉兔亦全其力。捉象亦全其力。未審全箇甚麼力。老宿曰。不欺之力。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks what complete strength the lion uses for both rabbit and elephant; the old adept replies, the strength that does not deceive.

Occurrences.Kwic: 東西及南北。各行於七步。分手指天地。作師子吼聲。上下及四維。無能尊我者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium's Buddha account calls his birth proclamation making the sound of a lion's roar.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以道，說法有所得，斯則野干鳴。說法無所得，是名師子吼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An inherited direct naming formula contrasts a jackal's cry with what it calls a lion's roar.

Senses.Explanation: As a personal name, Siṃha denotes the Twenty-fourth Indian Patriarch, not the animal lion. The Patriarchs' Hall Collection heads his record 'The Twenty-fourth Patriarch, Venerable Siṃha,' identifies him as a man of central India, and records his entrusting the eye of the true teaching onward. A transmission roster independently places Venerable Siṃha between the Twenty-third and Twenty-fifth Patriarchs. Qianyan's record later raises the inherited case in which the king of Kashmir cuts off Venerable Siṃha's head. A person numbered in the lineage and beheaded by a king is a different referent from the lion used in lion cub and lion's roar. The Chan corpus invokes this pre-Chinese figure through his lineage place and death case; that Zen deployment defines the person sense here.
Senses.Note: Animal word and named lineage patriarch are different things. SenseKey and MasterName remain null because no exact canonical roster spelling for Siṃha was found in the local roster-backed entries; this avoids inventing a link while preserving the named-person sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十四祖師子尊者，中印土人。姓婆羅門。爾時師子告婆舍斯多曰：「如來以正法眼付囑迦葉，如是展轉，乃至於我。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Patriarchs' Hall Collection numbers Venerable Siṃha as the Twenty-fourth Patriarch and records the entrustment reaching him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 罽賓國王斬師子尊者頭，王臂自落。雪竇云：『作家君王，天然有在。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Qianyan's record raises the inherited case of the king of Kashmir cutting off Venerable Siṃha's head and quotes Xuedou's comment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 第二十三祖鶴勒那第二十四祖師子尊者第二十五祖婆舍斯多第二十六祖不如密多
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent transmission roster places Venerable Siṃha as the Twenty-fourth Patriarch between Hacelena and Vasiasita.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘the lion's roar.’ In the Chan record it names forceful speech or teaching and is repeatedly opposed to the cry of a jackal. One record supplies an explicit definition: ‘teaching with something gained is the jackal's cry; teaching with nothing gained is called the lion's roar’ (說法有所得，斯則野干鳴；說法無所得，是名師子吼). The phrase is not merely an appraisal applied by compilers: masters order monks to ‘try making a lion's roar,’ monks claim it, and it becomes a public-interview challenge. Guishan says that Shishuang's speaking of Chan is ‘like a lion's roar, frightening the foxes, wolves, and jackals to death.’ In another exchange a monk asks what happens on meeting a lion's roar; the master answers ‘let the jackal cry as it likes,’ after which the monk shouts. Thus an animal sound is bent into a name, test, and verdict for speech in the teaching encounter; the texts themselves establish the lion/jackal contrast without requiring an imported symbolic reading.
Senses.Note: 558 raw hits in 146 allowlist texts in the b025 preflight. The phrase also occurs in Buddha-birth narratives, but the entry foregrounds its Chan deployment as an appraisal and demanded performance in public exchange. It remains one sense: literal animal imagery, comparison, label, and challenge all refer to the same roar rather than different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說法有所得。斯則野干鳴。說法無所得。是名師子吼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps United supplies the direct naming formula: teaching with gain is a jackal's cry; teaching without gain is called the lion's roar.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝試作師子吼看。曰。若作師子吼。即無和尚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master orders a newcomer to try making a lion's roar; the monk answers that if he did so there would be no master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 寂子說禪如師子吼，驚殺狐狼野犴之屬。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guishan appraises Shishuang's speaking of Chan as like a lion's roar that frightens foxes, wolves, and jackals.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽遇師子吼時如何師云一任野干鳴僧便喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks what happens on meeting a lion's roar; the reply permits the jackal's cry, and the monk shouts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the ordinary or constant mind (平常心). Mazu's address supplies the most detailed in-corpus definition. After saying that the Way does not need refining but must not be defiled, he says, “ordinary mind is the Way,” then answers “what is ordinary mind?” with “no contriving, no right-and-wrong, no grasping-or-rejecting, no annihilation-or-permanence, no ordinary-or-holy” (無造作、無是非、無取捨、無斷常、無凡聖). In the Nanquan and Zhaozhou dialogue, Nanquan again answers “what is the Way?” with “ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道); when Zhaozhou asks whether one can head toward it, Nanquan says that trying to head toward it is already off. Other masters answer the direct question “what is ordinary mind?” (如何是平常心) with named daily acts and things. Changsha says, “when you want to sleep, sleep; when you want to sit, sit,” then “hot, take the cool; cold, go to the fire.” Zhaozhou says, “foxes, wolves, and jackals are it.” Xianglin says, “at dawn, the morning greeting; in the evening, take care.” These answers differ, but the headword continues to denote ordinary mind. The larger sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” is a proposition about that headword, not a second lexical thing.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 309 hits in 120 texts. The sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道) occurs 181 times in 100 texts, and the question “what is ordinary mind?” (如何是平常心) occurs 30 times in 19. Later records also warn against taking the sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” as an ultimate rule; that criticism concerns the same ordinary mind and does not create another sense. Item-8 readjudication therefore merges the former sentence-target sense with the headword gloss. Related family entries for the Way (道), “mind itself is buddha” (即心是佛), and “without contriving” (無造作) remain compatible with this description.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道不用修，但莫污染。何為污染？但有生死心，造作趣向，皆是染污。若欲直會其道，平常心是道。何謂平常心？無造作、無是非、無取捨，無斷常、無凡聖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mazu's address says that ordinary mind is the Way and directly answers what ordinary mind is with a list beginning “without contriving.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州問南泉：如何是道？泉云：平常心是道。州云：還可趣向也無？泉云：擬趣即乖。州云：不擬爭知是道？泉云：道不屬知，不屬不知。知是妄覺，不知是無記。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanquan answers Zhaozhou that ordinary mind is the Way and says that trying to head toward it is already off.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州問南泉：「如何是道？」泉云：「平常心是道。」州云：「還可趨向不？」泉云：「擬即乖。」州云：「不擬怎知是道？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent recorded-sayings witness preserves the same Nanquan and Zhaozhou dialogue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是平常心？師曰：要眠即眠，要坐即坐。曰：學人不會，意旨如何？師曰：熱即取涼，寒即向火。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked what ordinary mind is, Changsha answers with sleeping, sitting, taking the cool, and going to the fire.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是平常心？」師云：「狐狼野干是。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Zhaozhou's record, the question “what is ordinary mind?” receives “foxes, wolves, and jackals are it.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是平常心。師曰。早朝不審。晚後珍重。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xianglin answers “what is ordinary mind?” with the morning greeting and the evening farewell.

AlternateTargets: the everyday mind is the Way
ordinary mind, this is the Way
the normal mind is the Way
Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “level or ordinary” (平), “constant or everyday” (常), “mind” (心), “is” (是), and “the Way” (道): "ordinary mind is the Way." The slogan has two attested loci in the corpus. (1) Mazu (馬祖道一): in his (示眾) recorded in (傳燈玉英集) (B14n0082, under the head 江西大寂道一禪師) — (道不用修但莫污染) and (若欲直會其道平常心是道) — with an in-text (謂)X gloss: (謂平常心無造作無是非無取捨無斷常無凡無聖), continuing (非凡夫行非賢聖行是菩薩行) and (只如今行住坐臥應機接物盡是道). (2) The Nanquan (南泉普願)–Zhaozhou (趙州從諗) dialogue: (趙州問南泉)。(如何是道)。(泉云)。(平常心是道) (so B25n0145; 無門關 case 19 平常是道 reads 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道; also 景德傳燈錄 趙州章; 古尊宿語錄), continued (州云)。(還可趣向否)。(泉云)。(擬向即乖) (無門關; the form 還可趣向也無 is also attested, 15 allowlist hits) — and (道不屬知)。(不屬不知) (無門關) / (知是妄覺不知是無記) (景德傳燈錄). (天目中峰明本) records "this saying circulated through the monasteries" (此話流布叢林) and (古今之下鮮有不墮於意識者)。(盡謂著衣喫飯動靜語默一一天真). (平常心是道) is the full slogan; the shorter (平常心) is a separate, nested entry. The texts give the phrase the (謂)…(無造作)、(無是非)、(無取捨)、(無斷常)、(無凡無聖) gloss and the (道不屬知)、(不屬不知) continuation, and no gloss beyond these; neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attribution (describe-only): the Nanquan–Zhaozhou occurrences are a two-speaker dialogue (趙州問 / 南泉/泉云) → MasterName null per the raised/dialogue rule; Mazu's (示眾) sits under his own section head (江西大寂道一禪師) as single-speaker instruction → (馬祖道一). The phrase is deployed as (a) Mazu's instruction with a five-negation self-gloss, (b) Nanquan's answer to Zhaozhou (無門關 case 19), and (c) a widely raised saying for comment (古尊宿語錄; 天目中峰廣錄 notes 此話流布叢林). Nested: (平常心) (t_4ccf8aed47d3) is the shorter constituent — a genuine constituent relation, added to RelatedTerms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若欲直會其道平常心是道謂平常心無造作
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (殘卷); the passage sits under head (江西大寂道一禪師) (Mazu Daoyi). Mazu's (示眾) (道一禪師示眾云道不用修但莫污染…) — single-speaker instruction. The line (平常心是道) is immediately followed by the in-text gloss (謂平常心無造作無是非無取捨無斷常無凡無聖) (continues on lb 0310b04). KWIC trimmed to the physical line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (無門關) case 19 (title 平常是道). The Nanquan–Zhaozhou dialogue; continues (州云)。(還可趣向否)。(泉云)。(擬向即乖) (next lb). Two-speaker → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉曰。平常心是道。師曰。還可趣向否。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), in the (趙州從諗) (師) biography; (師)(Zhaozhou)(問南泉) — the same dialogue, with the (擬向即乖) / (道不屬知) continuation following. Two-speaker → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉和尚如何是道泉云平常心是道
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄), inside (龍門佛眼禪師語錄) (Foyan Qingyuan's record; cb:mulu 龍門佛眼禪師語錄五 → 普說) — NOT Zhaozhou's own section. Within a (普說) the master raises the case: (所以趙州問南泉和尚如何是道泉云平常心是道州從此頓息馳求) (Zhaozhou thereupon ceased his seeking). Raised two-speaker dialogue → MasterName null.
