Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天目中峰廣錄) (中峰明本); (趙州問南泉)。(如何是道)。(泉云)。(平常心是道)。(此話流布叢林)。(古今之下鮮有不墮於意識者)。(盡謂著衣喫飯動靜語默一一天真). The embedded phrase is the two-speaker dialogue → MasterName null; the surrounding remark on the saying's currency is Zhongfeng's.

Senses.Explanation: In the institutional compound 'the two ranks' or 'the two divisions' (兩序), rank or division (序) names one of the two sides of a Chan community's offices. The Baizhang Regulations labels its sixth chapter 'the chapter on the two divisions' (兩序章), then identifies 'head monks of the western division' (西序頭首) and 'officers of the eastern division' (東序知事). Recorded sayings use 'the two divisions' for the office-holders who request an ascent to the hall, receive thanks, or support the community. Baiyu's record says that the two divisions served mutually as arms and elbows and acted reciprocally as host and guest (兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓).
Senses.Note: This is the Chan-institutional use found especially in the fixed compound 'the two divisions' (兩序). The corpus itself supplies the western-division/eastern-division subdivision; the entry does not infer duties beyond the stated labels and recorded deployments.

Occurrences.Kwic: 兩序章第六西序頭首東序知事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Baizhang Regulations (勅修百丈清規) table of contents names chapter six as 'the chapter on the two divisions' (兩序章) and immediately lists the 'head monks of the western division' (西序頭首) and 'officers of the eastern division' (東序知事).

Occurrences.Kwic: 於中多賴兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baiyu's Recorded Sayings (百愚禪師語錄) says, 'within this, much depended on the two divisions serving mutually as arms and elbows and acting reciprocally as host and guest' (於中多賴兩序交為肘臂、互作主賓).

Senses.Explanation: In a title or section heading, a preface (序) is introductory prose placed before a recorded-sayings collection, anthology, or edition. The graph commonly follows the work title, as in 'Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Monk Foyan' (佛眼和尚語錄序), 'Preface to the Extensive Record of the Monk Yongjue' (永覺和尚廣錄序), and 'Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Monk Sanfeng Cang' (三峰藏和尚語錄序).
Senses.Note: The title or heading determines this bibliographic sense. Translate the heading rather than treating the graph as part of a master's name or the work's main title.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舒州龍門佛眼和尚語錄序佛眼禪師語錄序豫章徐俯撰佛眼禪師之語侍者道昕所錄
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄). The heading is the 'Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Monk Foyan of Longmen in Shuzhou' (舒州龍門佛眼和尚語錄序).

Occurrences.Kwic: 百年來僅此人，是聖是凡休浪說。No.1437-C永覺和尚廣錄序No.1437-C永覺和尚廣錄序鼓山大和尚永覺賢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄). The repeated editorial heading identifies the 'Preface to the Extensive Record of the Monk Yongjue' (永覺和尚廣錄序).

Occurrences.Kwic: 序熊開元序三峰藏和尚語錄序武林衛軍嘉魚學人熊開元撰
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Recorded Sayings of the Monk Sanfeng Cang (三峰藏和尚語錄). The heading names the preface and its author, Xiong Kaiyuan (熊開元).

Senses.Explanation: In running prose, sequence or order (序) names an ordered progression. The Jingde-era lamp record says that beginning students did not know the sequence (初心後學未知次序). Konggu Daocheng's record says that matters for someone newly entering have an order (初進工夫，一一皆有次序) and names taking refuge and requesting instruction first (皈依請益為先). These witnesses state order directly; they do not turn the graph into a technical Chan category.
Senses.Note: This sense is represented through the transparent compound 'sequence/order' (次序). It is kept separate from the bibliographic preface and the institutional rank/division senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其有初心後學未知次序。山僧所以不惜口業。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp (景德傳燈錄) says, 'there are beginning students who do not know the sequence; therefore this mountain monk does not begrudge the fault of speech' (其有初心後學未知次序。山僧所以不惜口業).

Occurrences.Kwic: 若問初進工夫，一一皆有次序，皈依請益為先
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Konggu Daocheng's Recorded Sayings (空谷道澄禪師語錄), in an instruction, says, 'if one asks about the work of first entering, each matter has its sequence; taking refuge and requesting instruction come first' (若問初進工夫，一一皆有次序，皈依請益為先).

Occurrences.Kwic: 觀其超然生死，實踐可知。因次序其行實，乃為之銘曰：
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biographical notice says that the writer therefore put the subject's deeds in order before composing the inscription.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the cypress tree in the garden
AlternateTargets: the cypress tree in front of the courtyard
Senses.Explanation: Zhaozhou's answer to the stock question "what is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?" (如何是祖師西來意): (庭前柏樹子) — the cypress tree in front of the hall. The word (柏) is the cypress/arborvitae of Chinese temple yards, an evergreen. In his own record the exchange continues: the monk says "Master, don't show people by way of an object" (和尚莫將境示人), Zhaozhou answers "I do not show people by way of an object" (我不將境示人), and to the question asked again gives the identical answer (庭前柏樹子). Zhaozhou speaks of the same tree elsewhere: asked (柏樹子還有佛性也無) (does the cypress have buddha-nature) he says (有); asked (幾時成佛) he says "when empty space falls to the ground" (待虛空落地); asked (虛空幾時落地) he says "when the cypress becomes a buddha" (待柏樹子成佛). The exchange hardened into a named case — (無門關) case 37 (headed 庭前柏樹) and (從容錄) case 47 (趙州柏樹; the case-name occurs 49 times / 34 files, plus the 趙州栢樹 graph 46 / 23) — raised constantly across the record: the answer stands within eight characters of (西來意) in 256 places across 111 files, and raw grep gives (庭前柏樹子) 401 hits / 151 files plus the variant graph (庭前栢樹子) 167 / 55 (bare 柏樹子 650 / 185; 栢樹子 313 / 65). Attested handlings of the raised case: (無門) comments (若向趙州答處)。(見得親切)。(前無釋迦)。(後無彌勒); (五祖法演) tells his assembly (恁麼會則不是了也) … (恁麼會方始是) (understood this way it is wrong; understood that way it is right); (圜悟) gives the bare phrase to the monk Anmin — (悟曰)。(庭前柏樹子)。(師即洞明). The record also carries a denial of the case: (法眼) asks (慧覺) (覺鐵嘴, Zhaozhou's heir) (承聞趙州有柏樹子話是否), (覺曰)。(無), and to the objection "everyone coming and going says so" (往來皆謂) answers "my late master really had no such saying — do not slander him" (先師實無此語。和尚莫謗先師好; 先師實無此語 19 hits / 17 files, 先師無此語 42 / 31, told in 從容錄 directly after case 47 and in 五燈會元's 光孝慧覺 section); the denial is itself then put to later masters — in (五燈會元) a monk presses (大溈慕喆) with (先師無此語)。(又作麼生).
Senses.Note: The famous older English rendering "the oak tree in the garden" is a mistranslation: (柏) is cypress (Platycladus / Chinese arborvitae), not oak. Attribution rule applied: the case is Zhaozhou's own (his record, J24nB137, carries his name); every later citation — (無門關) case 37, (從容錄) case 47, (五祖法演)'s (拈古), (圜悟)'s use with Anmin, the (覺鐵嘴) denial exchange — is a raising of Zhaozhou's case and is left MasterName=null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 時有僧問：「如何是祖師西來意？」師云：「庭前柏樹子。」學云：「和尚莫將境示人。」師云：「我不將境示人。」云：「如何是祖師西來意？」師云：「庭前柏樹子。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (趙州祖師語錄) (Zhaozhou's own record); (師) = Zhaozhou. The locus classicus, including the (我不將境示人) rider.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「柏樹子還有佛性也無？」師云：「有。」云：「幾時成佛？」師云：「待虛空落地。」云：「虛空幾時落地？」師云：「待柏樹子成佛。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's second play on the cypress (its buddha-nature). The head term (庭前柏樹子) is abbreviated to (柏樹子) here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便問。如何是祖師西來意。州云。庭前柏樹子。僧云。和尚莫將境示人。師云。不將境示人。僧云。然則如何是祖師西來意。師云。庭前柏樹子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (從容錄) case 47 ("趙州柏樹"): Zhaozhou's case set up for verse-commentary. Raised case → null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 五祖示眾：如何是祖師西來意？庭前柏樹子。恁麼會則不是了也。如何是祖師西來意？庭前柏樹子。恁麼會方始是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (宗門拈古彙集); (五祖法演) (Wuzu Fayan) raises Zhaozhou's case in his (示眾) (this way wrong / that way right). Raised case → null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 悟曰。你問我。師舉前話。悟曰。庭前柏樹子。師即洞明。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (密印安民) section; (悟) (圜悟克勤 / Yuanwu Keqin) hands Zhaozhou's phrase to Anmin, who at once penetrates. Raised case → null.

Senses.Explanation: Guang'e is the butcher figure Chan records invoke through one compact public case. The case says he slaughtered a thousand sheep each day, went to the Buddha, threw down his butcher's knife, and said, 'I am numbered among the thousand buddhas'; the Buddha answered, 'so it is, so it is.' Chan commentary then records and rejects two common accounts: that Guang'e was formerly a buddha appearing provisionally as a butcher, and that he was simply a killer who threw down the knife and became buddha on the spot. The figure also enters public interview: asked for the master's house style, one master answers 'Guang'e Candala'; another exhortation cites the fierce butcher Guang'e throwing down his knife. The Zen deviation is this butcher's deployment as a case figure, house-style answer, and object of explicit correction. This entry reports the case and the corrections without selecting a replacement explanation for what his act secretly means.
Senses.Note: Exact unsplit count: 194 hits in 92 allowlisted texts. Guang'e-the-butcher (廣額屠兒) has 116 hits in 79 texts; the butcher Guang'e (屠兒廣額) 4 in 4; fierce butcher Guang'e (廣額兇屠) 5 in 5; graphic variant Guang'e (廣頟) 7 in 4. Proper-name sense is distinct from anatomical broad forehead below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔廣額屠兒日殺千羊，一日至佛所，颺下屠刀，云：我是千佛一數。世尊云：如是，如是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Core case as raised in a hall address: daily slaughter, thrown-down knife, claim, and Buddha's reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又曰：廣額正是箇殺人不眨眼底漢，颺下屠刀，立地成佛。且喜沒交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same commentary explicitly rejects the on-the-spot-buddhahood account as unrelated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云如何是和尚家風師云廣額旃陀羅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public interview: Guang'e Candala is given as the answer for the master's house style.

Occurrences.Kwic: 要似他廣額兇屠，拋下操刀，便證阿羅漢果。直須恁麼始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Exhortatory deployment of the fierce butcher Guang'e dropping his knife.

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary anatomical phrase: broad (廣) forehead (額). Two independent biographies include it in physical descriptions. One describes sparse brows, handsome eyes, a broad forehead, and full cheeks; another describes a tall person with silkworm brows, river-shaped eyes, a broad forehead, full cheeks, and a curled beard. This physical feature is a different thing from the proper name Guang'e and therefore has its own sense. No specifically Chan bend appears in this anatomical use.
Senses.Note: The fixed physical-description phrase broad forehead and full cheeks (廣額豐頤) has 2 hits in 2 allowlisted texts. Both are anchored; neither passage concerns the butcher.

Occurrences.Kwic: 疎眉秀目，廣額豐頤。從季父沙門智隆於宛陵光孝，十八得度受具。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical physical description: sparse brows, handsome eyes, broad forehead, and full cheeks.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其人脩長，蠶眉河目，廣額豐頤，鬚如螺結。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Independent physical description: tall, silkworm brows, river-shaped eyes, broad forehead, full cheeks, curled beard.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the teaching establishment's gate and court
AlternateTargets: the gate and court set up for teaching
Senses.Explanation: Literally, the "gate and court" established for teaching or transformation. Chan records use it for the organized framework of explanations and responsive teaching, then explicitly place it below what questioners call the matter beyond or above it. One monk says, "one question and one answer still fall within the teaching establishment's gate and court" (一問一答猶落建化門庭) and asks how to raise the first principle. A sermon supplies a direct apposition: even a shout said to contain all these features "is still the teaching establishment's gate and court—responsive expedients—called a small resting place, not yet the treasure-site" (猶是建化門庭隨機方便，謂之小歇場，未至寶所). Another says that even holding the seal, raising the banner, and moving freely still falls within it and "is not yet the monk's essential road" (未為衲僧徑要一路). The Chan-specific use is evaluative and institutional: masters name their own question-and-answer and explanatory apparatus as a constructed teaching precinct, commonly in a contrast the texts themselves draw with what is "beyond or above" (向上) or the monk's essential road.
Senses.Note: Attested 43 times in 30 allowlisted texts. "Gate and court" (門庭) is architectural language bent into an institutional teaching precinct; "the teaching establishment's gate and court" (建化門庭) is not merely a physical gate. Answer, sermon, and contrast uses share that referent and do not warrant separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問一問一答猶落建化門庭。未審第一義中如何舉唱。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk calls one-question/one-answer part of the teaching establishment and asks how the first principle is raised.

Occurrences.Kwic: 猶是建化門庭隨機方便。謂之小歇場。未至寶所。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text apposes the phrase with responsive expedients and calls it a small resting place, not the treasure-site.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒到此猶落建化門庭。未為衲僧徑要一路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Even the preceding accomplishments are said still to fall within this framework and not yet be the monk's essential road.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若在衲僧門下，猶屬建化門庭，更須拈向一邊，直提向上。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record contrasts the teaching precinct with directly raising what is beyond it.

AlternateTargets: make a show with the vital spirit
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to play with the vital spirit. The term occurs 215 times in 108 allowlisted texts as a stock Chan rebuke. A later master applies it in sequence to talking of the lineage and teachings, of Chan and the Way, and of mind and nature. Yuanwu applies it to people who misread Bodhidharma's 'vast, no holy' and to Xianglin's offering words that displayed his understanding; another collection calls such people 'fellows who play with the vital spirit.' A record also applies the phrase to people sitting woodenly and guarding a dead corpse. The targets vary—speech, presented understanding, or fixed conduct—but the phrase remains the same disparaging action. The sampled records leave the literal 'vital spirit' unglossed.
Senses.Note: One idiomatic verbal sense. The object 'vital spirit' is retained literally because the sampled records define the rebuke by its targets. The agent noun 'a fellow who plays with the vital spirit' is a morphological deployment, not a separate person or title.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說宗說教，也是弄精魂；說禪說道，也是弄精魂；說心說性，也是弄精魂；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching statement enumerates several kinds of talk under the same rebuke.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今人多少錯會。却去弄精魂。瞠眼睛云。廓然無聖。且喜沒交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu uses the phrase while criticizing a repeated reading of Bodhidharma's words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 香林當時。也下語呈見解弄精魂。終不相契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu joins offering words and displaying understanding to the rebuked action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天童覺，舉：誌公語畢，云：弄精魂漢有什麼限？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A collected comment attests the agent noun 'fellows who play with the vital spirit.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 祗為他一輩弄精魂漢，終日呆樁樁地守個死屍，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record applies the agent noun to woodenly guarding a dead corpse.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the placeholder names “Zhang Three and Li Four.” Across 80 occurrences in 41 allowlisted texts, they denote unspecified, readily named people rather than two biographical figures. A master says that someone passing behind the buddha hall is seen to be Zhang Three or Li Four, then publicly asks why someone passing before it is not seen. Asked “what is the student’s own self?” another answers “Zhang Three and Li Four” (如何是學人自己；張三李四); asked “what is buddha?” another gives the same answer. The Ancestral Hall Collection places their names among distinctions that arise with seeing and hearing: “there are Zhang Three and Li Four, Hu comes and Han goes, the four surnames dwell mixed together” (便有張三李四，胡來漢去，四姓雜居). A later address puts them in the marketplace: “Zhang Three and Li Four sell noisy emptiness; Shide and Hanshan dispute cheap and dear” (張三李四賣囂虛，拾得寒山爭賤貴). Zen bends ordinary placeholder names into recurring answers, visible passersby, and market figures in public addresses; the entry does not decide what any single answer intends.
Senses.Note: The pair denotes generic named people throughout the researched corpus. Answering different questions with the same pair does not create different senses, and no occurrence establishes historical persons named Zhang Three and Li Four.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有人從佛殿後過見是張三李四。從佛殿前過為什麼不見。
僧問。如何是學人自己。師曰。張三李四。
問如何是佛。師曰。張三李四。
瞥爾暫起見聞，便有張三李四，胡來漢去，四姓雜居
張三李四賣囂虛。拾得寒山爭賤貴。

Senses.PreferredTarget: Mr. Zhang drinks the wine, but Mr. Li gets drunk
AlternateTargets: Zhang drinks, but Li is drunk
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “Mr. Zhang drinks the wine; Mr. Li gets drunk.” The stock line occurs 125 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Masters speak it as an answer to unrelated public questions: why the monastery superintendent lost his eyebrows after Danxia burned the wooden buddha; “what is the master’s meaning?”; and why there is no buddha teaching at the start of a good year. The corpus also expands the line into a comic exchange: “Mr. Li sobers up and questions Mr. Zhang, just making Mr. Zhang lose his good temper” (李公醉醒問張公，恰使張公無好氣). In a teaching-seat enumeration it stands beside “Zhong Kui can dance the eighteen beats, the golden cock sings dawn, and the stone woman roams in spring” (鍾馗解舞十八拍，金雞唱曉，石女游春). Later speakers turn the mismatch itself back into a question for the assembly: “since Mr. Zhang drank the wine, why is Mr. Li drunk?” (既是張公喫酒，因甚李公卻醉). Zen therefore bends a comic mismatch between actor and affected person into a highly reusable interview answer, verse line, teaching-seat enumeration, and new public question. The records do not supply a single gloss for what the mismatch means, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: All uses retain one stock sentence. Different questions answered by it and later questions about it are deployments, not separate senses. Zhang and Li are figures internal to the saying, not biographical persons.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽憶丹霞燒木佛，因何院主墮眉鬚？師曰：張公喫酒李公醉。
張公喫酒李公醉，子細思量不思議。李公醉醒問張公，恰使張公無好氣。
僧問秖如師意作麼生師云張公喫酒李公醉。
僧云：年年是好年，日日是好日，為什麼却無？教云：張公喫酒李公醉。
既是張公喫酒，因甚李公卻醉？
直得張公喫酒李公醉，鍾馗解舞十八拍，金雞唱曉，石女游春。

Senses.Explanation: Literally a rule, standard, or code. Across 3,110 occurrences in 360 allowlisted texts, it names ordained regulation, its specialists, regulated conduct, and the rules cited in public interview. The Platform Record’s ordination account distinguishes the Vinaya-master roles: Zhiguang bestows the precepts, Huijing conducts the formal act, Tongying instructs, and Jiduoluo recites the precepts. A master who declines an expected address says, ‘scriptures have scripture masters; rules have Vinaya masters’ (經有經師，律有律師), while another exchange begins, ‘the code says that hearing ornaments through a wall is called breaking the precepts’ (律中道。隔壁聞釵釧聲即名破戒) and then asks whether a crowded visual scene is or is not precept-breaking. The Baizhang account records a specifically Chan institutional bend: asked why he did not simply follow an existing greater-vehicle precept code, he says his tradition is neither confined to nor different from the greater and lesser vehicles, calls for standards fitted to circumstances, and establishes a separate Chan residence. The Record of the Source-Mirror says, ‘all one’s doings enter regulated conduct’ (所有施為，皆入律行). Yongjue also records and rebukes the dismissal, ‘holding and breaking are originally absent—what use are precepts and code?’ (本無持犯，何用戒律？). The headword therefore remains concrete code-language while Chan records assign it offices, cite it in interview, fit communal standards to circumstances, extend it to conduct, and preserve arguments over its cancellation.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: code-language is not excluded as generic Buddhism; the Baizhang record deploys it in the founding description of a separate Chan residence. Exact count: 3,110 hits in 360 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 西京智光律師為授戒師，蘇州慧靜律師為羯磨，荊州通應律師為教授，中天耆多羅律師為說戒，西國蜜多三藏為證戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record distinguishes the formal offices at Huineng’s ordination.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或曰。瑜伽論瓔珞經。是大乘戒律。胡不依隨哉。師曰。吾所宗非局大小乘。非異大小乘。當博約折中設於制範務其宜也。於是創意別立禪居。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked why he does not follow the greater-vehicle precept code, Baizhang says rules are fitted to circumstances and a separate Chan residence is established.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所有施為。皆入律行。自然成辦一切佛事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Source-Mirror says all doings enter regulated conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：經有經師，律有律師，爭怪得老僧？丹霞天然禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After declining an expected address, a master distinguishes scripture and rule specialists.

Occurrences.Kwic: 律中道。隔壁聞釵釧聲即名破戒。見覩金銀合雜朱紫駢闐。是破戒不是破戒。師曰。好箇入路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange cites the code's boundary and asks whether a second scene is precept-breaking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本無持犯，何用戒律？因果罪福，一切滅裂。至於貪名奪利，有如狂狗；恃氣起爭，不啻猛虎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue quotes and rebukes the claim that precepts and code are useless because holding and breaking are originally absent.

Senses.Explanation: In the compound (音律), (律) denotes regulated sound, meter, or tonal pattern rather than a monastic code. A Chan verse says that an old tune is not reducible to musical regulation before turning to the South Mountain turtle-nosed snake; two major lamp compilations preserve that deployment. Modern scholarly body prose in the allowlisted corpus likewise judges a song's musical regulation sound while rejecting its wording. The shared object is ordering of sound, not ordained conduct.
Senses.Note: This is a different referent from Vinaya or communal code. C077 and C078 preserve related recensions of one Chan verse; B25n0143 supplies an independent body-prose witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打皷弄琵琶相逢一會家雲門能合調長慶解隨邪古曲非音律南山鼈鼻蛇何人知妙訣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan verse moves from drum, lute, and matching the mode to the claim that the old tune is not musical regulation, then raises the turtle-nosed snake.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打鼓弄琵琶相逢一會家雲門能合調長慶觧隨邪古曲非音律南山鼈鼻蛇何人知妙訣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second lamp compilation preserves the same sound-and-mode verse, anchoring the headword “regulation” (律) inside “musical regulation” (音律).

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然「音律不差」，而「下語用字，全不可讀」，也沒有文學價值
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Allowlisted modern scholarly body prose distinguishes acceptable musical regulation from unreadable wording.

Senses.Explanation: A title for a specialist and teacher in the monastic rule code. The term occurs 407 times in 114 allowlisted texts. Chan biographies use it straightforwardly for ordination teachers, as when Huairang leaves home under Vinaya Master Hongjing. An early account places Vinaya Master Guangtong and the translator Bodhiruci in sustained dispute with Bodhidharma after they see him reject appearances and point to mind. Public cases also use the office as an interlocutor and a contrast. Vinaya Master Yuan asks Dazhu whether he uses effort in the way; after Dazhu answers with eating when hungry and sleeping when tired, Yuan falls silent. In Yaoshan's refusal to speak after the assembly gathers, Yaoshan says, 'Scriptures have scripture masters, treatises have treatise masters, and rules have Vinaya masters—how can you blame this old monk?' The Zen bend lies in those public deployments: the recognized rules specialist is brought into debate and interview, and the office may be named as the specialist role against which a Chan master declines an expected lecture. It is a foil only in those attested exchanges, not by definition everywhere.
Senses.Note: The title is translated by office. Biographical honorific uses remain ordinary; the explanation restricts the foil claim to quoted encounters.

Occurrences.Kwic: 依弘景律師出家通天二年受戒後習毘尼藏
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography names Vinaya Master Hongjing as the teacher under whom Huairang left home.

Occurrences.Kwic: 源律師問：和尚修道，還用功否？師曰：用功。曰：如何用功？師曰：飢來喫飯，困來即眠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Vinaya Master Yuan publicly questions Dazhu about using effort; the exchange supplies the office-holder's foil role.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：經有經師，律有律師，爭怪得老僧？丹霞天然禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yaoshan lists scripture, treatise, and Vinaya specialists after declining to deliver the expected address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光統律師流支三藏者乃僧中之鸞鳳也。覩師演道斥相指心。每與師論議是非鋒起。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An early transmission account says Vinaya Master Guangtong and Bodhiruci repeatedly argued right and wrong with Bodhidharma after hearing him reject appearances and point to mind.

Senses.Explanation: As a Chan exchange verb, "probe" (徵) means to probe, challenge, or press for an answer. Records use "the master probed" (師徵 / 師徵云), "the master probed the assembly" (師徵問大眾), and "repeatedly interrogated" (再四徵詰). In one public address, after citing Dongshan's answer about the place without cold or heat, the master probes the assembly with the apparent conflict between "no cold or heat" and "when cold, cold kills you; when hot, heat kills you." Another record classifies "probing the old cases" (徵古) as its own section: an old case is raised, earlier comments are quoted, and the present master adds a fresh challenge beginning "if there are words..." (若是有語). The ordinary graph is thereby bent into editorial and exchange machinery for reopening recorded cases as answerable questions.
Senses.Note: The probe sense is established by the recurrent compounds "probing question" (徵問), "interrogate" (徵詰), and "probe the old cases" (徵古), and by headings that enumerate probing, raising, answering-for, and distinguishing (徵拈代別). Family check: "examine and distinguish" (勘辨) is examination and discrimination; "question-and-answer" (問答) is the entire reciprocal exchange; "encounter" (機緣) is its occasion or recorded encounter. "Probe" (徵) here is the act of pressing a person, assembly, or inherited case with a further question. Summoning, exacting, requesting, verifying, and the musical pitch are different actions or objects and are split below. The headword has 1,578 occurrences in 283 allowlisted texts across all senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師徵問大眾曰既是無寒暑處為甚又寒時寒殺熱時熱殺既是寒時寒殺熱時熱殺如何道是無寒暑處
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After raising Dongshan's cold-and-heat case, the master probes the assembly through a sequence of questions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 徵古徵古舉：「臨濟兩堂首座齊下喝。僧問：『還有賓主也無？』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The section title Probing the Old introduces a raised Linji case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師徵云：「若是有語，又落在臨濟手裏。若是有喝，又落在天童手裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master probes the inherited comments by testing answers involving words or a shout.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧昔年到先師處，徵問到無結角下手處，不免盡力掀倒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Retrospective report of being probed by the former teacher until there was no corner on which to lay a hand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是徵問？」師云：「鈍置煞人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question asks what probing-question is; the master's recorded answer is literally that it greatly belabors a person.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中垂示勘辨學者徵拈代別皆有機語流布寰中久矣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Editorial description enumerates room instructions, examination of students, probing, raising, answering-for, and distinguishing as circulating encounter words.

Senses.Explanation: In biographies and lamp narratives, "summon" (徵) is the sovereign's act of summoning a teacher. One record says Emperor Xuanzong "summoned him to come" (玄宗徵赴), after which he had an audience. This is a political summons, not an interview probe.
Senses.Note: Split as a different action under #0f.8. One defining witness is curated here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 玄宗徵赴，駕幸詔應。得對天顏，言理允符
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The emperor summons the teacher to come, followed by an audience.

Senses.Explanation: In administrative prose, "exact" (徵) is to exact or collect a levy. A petition asks for release from "the burden of exacting grain" (徵糧之役). The object is a material assessment, distinct from pressing a respondent with a question.
Senses.Note: Split as a different action under #0f.8; it is retained because administrative documents occur inside the allowlisted Chan record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 收開墾之令、免徵糧之役，嚴令有司防範、僧徒守護。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A petition asks that the monastery be exempted from the burden of collecting a grain levy.

Senses.Explanation: In record-making prose, "request" (徵) can mean to request a contribution. When disciples prepare a deceased master's sayings for carving, they "request a preface from me" (徵序於予). The requested text is a preface, not an answer under examination.
Senses.Note: Split because soliciting a written contribution is a different action from probing or summoning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門人錄其語為帙，將鋟梓以傳，徵序於予。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Disciples prepare a sayings record for printing and request a preface from the writer.

Senses.Explanation: With "token" (信) or evidentiary language, "verify" (徵) is to verify or establish something as evidence. At an address for a donated robe, the master says, "today this old monk relies on the robe to verify the token" (老僧今日據衣徵信), then asks who knows the place of the token. Here a robe serves as evidence; no respondent is being probed by the headword itself.
Senses.Note: Split as an evidentiary action distinct from the primary public-interview verb.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師西來，傳衣表信；老僧今日據衣徵信。還有知信處底麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The robe marks a token, and the master says he relies on the robe to verify that token.

Senses.Explanation: "Zhi" (徵) also names zhi, one of the traditional musical pitches. A twelve-hours song says Fang Shuo mistakenly followed "gong and zhi" (宮徵). This is a musical noun and has no semantic relation to the exchange verb "probe."
Senses.Note: The romanization is supplied only to distinguish the named musical pitch; the English explanation identifies its object. Split by word-class and referent under #0f.8.

Occurrences.Kwic: 月圓日滿不曾虧方朔由來悞宮徵鷄鳴丑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse uses gong and zhi as musical-pitch names.

AlternateTargets: Deshan goes down with his bowl
Senses.Explanation: A case title, literally 'Deshan carries his bowl.' It occurs 115 times in 41 allowlisted texts. The case records Deshan going down with his bowl before bell or drum; Xuefeng asks where he is going, Deshan returns to his quarters, Xuefeng reports this to Yantou, and Yantou says Deshan has not understood the last phrase. Deshan summons Yantou, who privately states his meaning; the next day's ascent of the seat differs from usual, and Yantou says Deshan will live only three more years. The corpus turns this named encounter into a case heading, verse topic, question asked at the teaching seat, assigned object of inquiry, and point of later prose comment. Recorded replies to 'what is its meaning?' include 'no meaning' followed by 'if he wanted to go, he went; if he wanted to sit, he sat,' and, elsewhere, 'buying dear and selling cheap.'
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is institutional: an ordinary meal-bowl movement becomes the fixed public name of a multi-speaker case, repeatedly raised, questioned, versified, and assigned for inquiry. The corpus's divergent later comments are reported as comments, not combined into an interpretation of Deshan's intent. The title and descriptions name the same encounter and require one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山托鉢德山一日托鉢下堂。見雪峯問者。老漢鐘未鳴鼓未響。托鉢向甚處去。山便回方丈。峯舉似巖頭。頭云。大小德山未會末後句。山聞。令侍者喚巖頭來。問曰。汝不肯老僧那。巖頭密啟其意。山乃休去。明日陞座。果與尋常不同。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Wumen Guan preserves the case's action and speaker sequence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。德山托鉢意旨如何。師云。無意旨。進云。因什麼托鉢下僧堂。師云。要行便行。要坐便坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat exchange asks the case's meaning and records the answer 'no meaning.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。德山托鉢歸方丈。意旨如何。師云。貴買賤賣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Another public exchange names the return to the quarters and answers 'buying dear and selling cheap.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 悅因舉德山托鉢話令熟究之，公悵然不寐，至五鼓，忽垂脚飜溺器，猛省
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography records the case being assigned for sustained inquiry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山托鉢托鉢無言方丈去，諸方慢謂失便宜，不是巖頭傍著眼，從教後代逐狐疑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse treats the case under its fixed title and explicitly names Yantou's intervention and later doubt.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘Deshan's staff/blows,’ the compound that later Chan records pair with ‘Linji's shout’ (臨濟喝). Its contexts use the object-and-blow polysemy of ‘staff/blow’ (棒) rather than choosing only one side: device lists can name the implement as Deshan's staff, while ‘under Deshan's blows’ (德山棒下) records Xuefeng receiving the striking action. Later masters raise the pair as a public question—‘Linji's shout seldom meets one who knows its sound; Deshan's staff rarely meets an adept’—and ask what matter the two clarify. Other records call the paired devices a model left for Chan people, praise or criticize them, and compare Deshan's blows to falling rain. The compound therefore names Deshan's celebrated striking device as both implement and delivered blow; unlike bare ‘staff/blow’ (棒), these are two grammatically available faces of one named Deshan formula, not two independently functioning dictionary referents.
Senses.Note: 490 hits in 173 allowlist files in the b025 preflight. The entry cross-checks bare ‘staff/blow’ (棒) and its established object/blow split: staff-bearing catalogues license ‘Deshan's staff,’ while ‘under the blows’ (棒下) and rain-like striking license ‘Deshan's blows.’ Preferred English uses the act because the strongest case-level witness is Xuefeng under the blows, while the object rendering remains explicit. Do not attribute every later answer or appraisal to Deshan himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我當時在德山棒下。如桶底脫相似。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes Xuefeng's report: under Deshan's blows it was like the bottom falling out of a bucket. This anchors the act side of ‘staff/blow’ (棒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟喝，德山棒，留與禪人作模範。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master lists Linji's shout and Deshan's staff as models left for Chan people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：臨濟喝少遇知音，德山棒難逢作者。和尚今日作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk raises the paired formula in a public question, saying Deshan's staff rarely meets an adept.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山棒、臨濟喝，是三世諸佛慈悲喜捨之樂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later sermon appraises Deshan's staff and Linji's shout together as the joy of the buddhas' kindness, compassion, joy, and generosity; this is the text's appraisal, not the dictionary's.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問德山棒臨濟喝未審明得什麼邊事師云你試道看僧便喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks what side of the matter Deshan's staff and Linji's shout clarify; the master demands that he say, and the monk shouts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “awaken through-and-through.” The term appears 142 times in 71 allowlisted texts, both as a verb in encounter and biographical retrospectives and as a noun-like condition in instruction and contrast. Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss.
Senses.Note: Verbal and noun-like grammar denotes the same event/state and does not warrant a split. The related term “interpretive awakening” (解悟) is a text-drawn contrast, not an annotator’s ranking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一者從文字語言中得解悟，二者從己分上參究得徹悟。夫解悟者力弱，徹悟者力強。解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物。
如不徹悟决定不休。有此正因。不患大事之不我明也。
如世尊覩明星徹悟昔年張無盡雖然是俗人他一見便知其立地處
古今徹悟者如稻麻竹葦，錯會者如稻麻竹葦。
惟要諸人自徹自悟而後已。如徹悟也，剎剎塵塵無非固有之神通

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'mind' (心) and 'seal' or 'stamp' (印). The term occurs 1,374 times in 280 allowed texts and is repeatedly transmitted, received, secretly entrusted, applied, and tested in lineage records. One assembly address says, 'The ancestral mind-seal is neither long nor short, square nor round, inside nor outside, nor in between' (祖師心印，非長非短，非方非圓，非內非外，亦非中間). Another says it has 'no trace and no shape,' remains distinct through successive ages, and has never been interrupted (祖師心印，無痕無狀。歷劫分明，未嘗間斷). Fengxue's recorded formulation compares it to the mechanism of an iron ox: 'going, it seals and holds; staying, it seals and breaks' (去即印住。住即印破). A lamp address enumerates three applications: 'one seal seals empty space, one seals water, one seals mud' (一印印空。一印印水。一印印泥). An early record extends the stamp grammar in both directions: Bodhidharma 'secretly transmitted the mind-seal, sealing your own mind; mind seals the teaching, the teaching seals mind' (密傳心印印汝本心。以心印法，以法印心). Sengna draws a direct contrast: 'the ancestral mind-seal does not consist exclusively in harsh conduct' (祖師心印非專苦行). These are the corpus's own formal, material, and transmission predicates; the article does not turn the seal into an imported object.
Senses.Note: Required definition formulas found no single prose gloss of the bare compound, but several direct shape-negations and seal-mechanism explanations. 'Ancestral mind-seal' (祖師心印) occurs 336 times in 145 texts, while 'mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors' (佛祖心印) occurs 23 times in 17. Some hits are the bestowed title or name 'Mind-seal' borne by particular monks; those proper-name uses were excluded from the technical sense evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印，非長非短，非方非圓，非內非外，亦非中間。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Chuming Baoyin section. The master gives a sequence of direct shape and location negations for the ancestral mind-seal; no roster link was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印，無痕無狀。歷劫分明，未嘗間斷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Lamp from the Jianzhong-Jingguo Era. An assembly address denies trace and shape while stating continuity through successive ages.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印。狀似鐵牛之機。去即印住。住即印破。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium raises Fengxue's iron-ox mechanism formulation. As a transmitted case with a later section setting, it remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印。一印印空。一印印水。一印印泥。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp. The assembly address explicitly applies seals to empty space, water, and mud. The nearest lineage heading does not yield a safe roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 密傳心印印你本心以心印法以法印心心既如此法亦如此
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Ancient Worthies describes Bodhidharma's transmission to Huike and expands the seal grammar between mind and teaching. It is retrospective narration, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印非專苦行。但助道耳。若契本心發隨意真光之用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Sengna section. Sengna tells Huiman that the ancestral mind-seal is not exclusively harsh conduct and contrasts two uses of such conduct.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "mind" (心) and "ground" (地): "mind-ground," attested 1,568 times in 268 allowlisted texts. Huangbo's record calls it the "mind-ground gate" and says, "all things are established depending on this mind; meeting a scene, they exist; without a scene, they do not" (萬法皆依此心建立，遇境即有，無境即無). A transmission verse says, "mind-ground is originally unborn; the causal ground arises following conditions; conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another; flower and fruit are likewise" (心地本無生，因地從緣起，緣種不相妨，華果亦復爾). Another verse says it "contains all seeds" and that universal rain makes them sprout (心地含諸種，普雨悉皆萌). In a repeatedly raised exchange, Yunfeng answers "What is the mind-ground gate?" with "it is not obtained from another" (不從人得). The word also forms "mind-ground seal" (心地印, 132 occurrences) and "mind-ground gate" (心地法門, 157).
Senses.Note: The ground image is productive: seeds are contained, rain makes them sprout, and flower and fruit follow. Later records preserve conflicting enacted labels: one teacher raises a staff and says, "this is the mind-ground seal" (這箇是心地印), while another raises a staff and says it is not the seal. These are recorded deployments, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂心地法門。萬法皆依此心建立。遇境即有無境即無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo's record defines the mind-ground gate through things being established depending on this mind. The section is clear, but the occurrence remains unlinked for conservative attribution.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心地本無生因地從緣起緣種不相妨華果亦復爾
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission verse: mind-ground is originally unborn; the causal ground arises following conditions; conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another; flower and fruit are likewise.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雲峰因僧問：如何是心地法門？峰曰：不從人得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised Yunfeng exchange: asked what the mind-ground gate is, Yunfeng says it is not obtained from another.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈起拄杖，云：「這箇是心地印。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In instruction, the teacher raises a staff and says, "this is the mind-ground seal."

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以六祖云。心地含諸種。普雨悉皆萌。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi quotes the Sixth Patriarch: mind-ground contains all seeds; universal rain makes them sprout.

AlternateTargets: outside mind there is no separate thing
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "outside mind, no thing stands." The phrase occurs 199 times in 100 allowlisted texts. Here the graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is contextual: in the recurring pair "this thing is mind; outside mind no thing stands; this mind is the thing; outside it no mind stands" (此法即心，心外無法；此心即法，法外無心), it names what could be set up as a thing apart, not an untranslated religious loanword. Shao's frequently quoted verse places the phrase beside visible landscape: "the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes" (通玄峰頂，不是人間；心外無法，滿目青山). A later master quotes that verse and says it has been "broken into two pieces" (打成兩橛). Another hall address strikes the Chan seat and asks: "mind has not arisen—where could the things be established? Where did mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?" (心既不生，法從何立？山河大地，甚處得來). The corpus therefore records the line as a maxim, a verse, a question to the assembly, and an object of later criticism; this entry does not decide the criticism.
Senses.Note: The graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is resolved from the syntax of each quoted line. Its singular form is rendered "thing" or "what is established," while the plural compound "the myriad things" (萬法) is rendered according to its local syntax. The evidence does not warrant a separate sense merely because later speakers approve, question, quote, or criticize the same proposition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此法即心，心外無法。此心即法，法外無心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The paired formulation makes mind and the named thing reciprocal and denies either outside the other.

Occurrences.Kwic: 通玄峰頂，不是人間。心外無法，滿目青山。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shao's verse: “the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，拍禪床曰：心外無法，萬法唯心。心既不生，法從何立？山河大地，甚處得來？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address strikes the Chan seat, states the formula, and follows it with questions about establishment and the mountains, rivers, and earth.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉韶國師曰：通玄峰頂，不是人間。心外無法，滿目青山。師召大眾曰：韶國師好個頌子，只是打成兩橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later hall address quotes Shao's verse, calls it a fine verse, and says it is split into two pieces.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'mind-precept.' The phrase occurs 45 times in 27 allowlisted texts. Some hits are names, but direct Chan sermons make a technical deployment explicit. One says, 'mind is precept, precept is mind; mind and precept are not two.' Another contrasts mind-precept with form-precept, calls precept itself mind, and describes the form-precept through robes, bowl, and staff. A further sermon says its mind-precept is originally pure and has no contamination, explicitly contrasting a thought that seeks to receive some separate precept outside mind. Earlier lamp narratives say that laymen personally received a master's mind-precept; one adds that Bai Juyi repeatedly sat facing the master with no speech. The compound therefore also names something transmitted in a teacher-student relation. The Zen bend is attested in these equations, contrasts, and transmission notices: mind is made the locus and substance of precept, without making the precept optional.
Senses.Note: Name-like uses were excluded from the definition. The re-grounding is stated only from passages that directly equate or contrast mind and precept.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既於山僧處求受心地戒法，須知即心是戒、即戒是心，心戒無二，萬善從生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon gives the direct equation: mind is precept, precept is mind, and the two are not separate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 戒有兩般，心無二用。兩般者，心戒、相戒；二用者，體持、用持。戒者，心也；衣者，意也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon explicitly contrasts mind-precept and form-precept and says precept is mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉一念于心外求受別戒，早自埋沒己靈。蓋此心戒者，的體淨潔，了無纖染
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker rejects seeking a separate precept outside mind and describes this mind-precept as wholly clean and without contamination.

Occurrences.Kwic: 公親受南泉心戒。大夫問南泉：「弟子家中有一片石。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp narrative says Lu Gen personally received Nanquan's mind-precept before recording their stone-Buddha exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 白舍人親受心戒，又時對坐，並無言說。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate lamp narrative says Bai Juyi personally received the mind-precept and repeatedly sat facing the master without speech.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the place of mental activity is extinguished
AlternateTargets: the locus of mind's activity is gone
Senses.Explanation: Literally, the "place" (處) of the mind's "activity" or "movement" (心行) is "extinguished" (滅): "the place of mental activity is extinguished," attested 128 times in 65 allowlisted texts. The standard companion is "the road of language is cut off" (言語道斷, 171 occurrences). A transmission record explains the parallel syntax: "when principle is clear, the road of language is cut off—what words could discuss it? When the purport is met, the place of mental activity is extinguished—what contemplation could think it?" (理明則言語道斷，何言之能議；旨會則心行處滅，何觀之能思). Hongzhi asks, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?" (言語道斷心行處滅，又作麼生). A later address quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, the place of mental activity extinguished," then answers with a deliberate counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, mental activity is not extinguished" (心行不滅). Zhongfeng also reports an interpreter's equation: "cut off thought, then the place of mental activity is extinguished" (絕慮則心行處滅), before contesting that line of equation in the following passage. The entry therefore records the fixed pair, explicit parallel, question, and counter-witness rather than equating the phrase with blankness.
Senses.Note: The exact counter-form "mental activity is not extinguished" (心行不滅) occurs twice. "When the purport is met, the place of mental activity is extinguished" (旨會則心行處滅) occurs six times; Zhongfeng's "cut off thought" equation occurs once. The phrase is paired with language but also appears independently in later addresses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 理明則言語道斷。何言之能議。旨會則心行處滅。何觀之能思。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Transmission-lamp prose gives the explicit parallel: "when principle is clear, the road of language is cut off; when the purport is met, the place of mental activity is extinguished." The historical section remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可以智知，不可以識識，言語道斷，心行處滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address quotes: "it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished."

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可以智知，不可以識識，言語道斷，心行處滅。保寧道：亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same address joins the quoted line to Baoning's counter: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished." The longer exact span retains the headword as well as the unique counter-witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇如言語道斷心行處滅。又作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi asks: "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 絕言則言語道斷。絕慮則心行處滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng reports an interpreter's pairing: "cut off words, then the road of language is cut off; cut off thought, then the place of mental activity is extinguished." The following prose contests this equation, so it is not assigned as Zhongfeng's definition.

Senses.PreferredTarget: who is reciting the buddha’s name?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “who is reciting the buddha’s name?” The phrase occurs 63 times in 33 allowlisted texts, concentrated in later Chan biographies, instructions, headings, and public exchanges. Records call it a “saying” (話), say that a master “showed him the saying ‘who is reciting the buddha’s name?’” (示以念佛是誰話), or command a student to “investigate ‘who is reciting the buddha’s name?’” (參念佛是誰). One verse reverses it as “who is reciting the buddha’s name—who recites the buddha’s name?” (念佛是誰誰念佛), and another continues “who is the buddha?” (誰是佛). Wuyi Yuanlai says to “raise only one phrase” (單提一句), identifies “who” (誰) as the word in question, and compares it in that passage to a hair-cutting sword and a poison-coated drum. In a recorded interview, the student states the phrase; the master replies, “who is not reciting the buddha’s name?” (不念佛是誰) and raises a ceremonial scepter. Zen thus takes vocabulary associated with buddha-name recitation and makes the literal who-question a named saying, command, biographical turning point, and public exchange. The entry reports only those recorded actions.
Senses.Note: The independent question, quoted saying, heading, and command all concern the same wording. Reversals and replies remain transformations of that wording, not separate referents. This entry translates “reciting the buddha’s name” (念佛) by its literal verbal action in these passages and adds no outside Pure Land account.

Occurrences.Kwic: 法舟掩室於天寧，師往參叩，示以念佛是誰話。一日齋次，食器墜地，豁然有省。
命參念佛是誰，久之有省，呈偈曰：「念佛是誰誰念佛？一聲高了一聲低
念佛是誰誰是佛，非心非佛復何物。
教人單提一句：念佛是誰？即此誰字不明，吹毛劍、塗毒鼓，於斯可見。
曰：「念佛是誰？」師云：「不念佛是誰？」曰：「不會。」師舉如意示之

Senses.Explanation: The graphs join 'think' with 'measure or weigh': to ponder, reckon, deliberate, or think something over. The central recorded exchange is Yaoshan's. A monk asks, 'What are you pondering while sitting so fixedly?' Yaoshan answers, 'I ponder that which is not pondering.' The monk asks, 'How do you ponder that which is not pondering?' Yaoshan replies, 'Not pondering.' The Compendium of the Five Lamps and the Jingde Lamp Record independently preserve that exchange. Elsewhere the verb is regularly negated or marked as unable to reach: 'do not ponder,' 'not pondering,' and 'pondering cannot reach it.' It also follows verbs of intending or hesitating, as in 'about to ponder' and 'about to deliberate and ponder.' Dahui quotes, 'This matter is not what pondering and distinguishing can understand,' then asks, 'Now say: at the time of not distinguishing and not pondering, what is it?' These uses retain the ordinary act of mental reckoning and the records' own contrasts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Current counts: 2,410 matches in 322 files; not pondering 124/53; the distinct phrase 'not-pondering' 207/112; pondering and distinguishing 165/88; about to ponder 146/78; about to deliberate and ponder 135/86; pondering cannot reach it 20/16; ponder that which is not pondering 14/12. The two Yaoshan witnesses preserve the same case in independent lamp texts. Dahui's quoted line and the general negation formulas are separate deployments and are not attributed to Yaoshan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師坐次。僧問。兀兀地思量甚麼。師曰。思量箇不思量底。曰。不思量底如何思量。師曰。非思量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (澧州藥山惟儼禪師) section (head 澧州藥山惟儼禪師) — Yaoshan's own biographical record; the (思量箇不思量底)→(非思量) exchange. X-canon lb ed=X 0109c22.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師坐次有僧問。兀兀地思量什麼。師曰。思量箇不思量底。曰不思量底如何思量。師曰。非思量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), within Yaoshan's biography under (前石頭希遷法嗣) (Yaoshan is Shitou's heir); the master (師) is Yaoshan. Independent witness of the same case (五燈會元 above).

Occurrences.Kwic: 是法非思量分別之所能解。且道不分別不思量時是箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大慧普覺禪師語錄); Dahui's upper-hall — he raises the scriptural line (是法非思量分別之所能解) and turns it with (且道不分別不思量時是箇甚麼). Shows (思量) paired with (分別) as the faculty that cannot understand this matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 更莫思量。思量不及。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (金陵報恩匡逸禪師) section; the general negation/reach-failure formula (更莫思量)。(思量不及) (context 如太陽赫弈皎然地。更莫思量。思量不及。設爾思量得及。喚作分限智慧). Corpus-wide idiom — MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 更擬思量箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (節使李端愿居士) section; "about to ponder" (擬思量) deployed mid-dialogue as the discursive move — "what are you setting to ponder now?" (更擬思量箇甚麼). MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬議思量，千山萬水。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compact verdict says that deliberating and pondering produce a separation of a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters.

Occurrences.Kwic: 秪是窺覷不得、思量不得。何故？稍起思量，而墻千尺；纔涉窺覷，白雲萬里。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address says it cannot be pondered and that the slightest arising of pondering raises a thousand-foot wall.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。六祖云。善惡都莫思量。自然得入心體。洞山和尚云。學得佛邊事。猶是錯用心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A question quotes the Sixth Patriarch's instruction not to ponder good or bad, then places it beside Dongshan's warning.

Senses.Explanation: A colloquial demonstrative: “thus,” “like this,” or “in this way.” It occurs 28,391 times in the allowlisted corpus and points to a stated situation without naming a new object. The Sixth Patriarch asks Huairang, “what thing comes thus?” (什麼物恁麼來); records also pair coming thus with going thus and say that thus, not-thus, and both together will not do. In public interviews it marks a student’s inference (恁麼則), a proposed understanding (恁麼會), the exact moment at issue (正當恁麼時), and a condition (若恁麼). A later citation doubles both sides: “thus, thus” and “not thus, not thus.” The variant spelling “thus” (與麼) is the same word. Chan makes this ordinary pointer a pervasive hinge of question and answer, but its deictic referent remains one sense.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Different grammatical frames and positive or negative appraisals are readings of the same demonstrative, not different things. The “if so, then” compound (恁麼則) has its own entry; link it without collapsing it into the base.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖曰。什麼物恁麼來。曰說似一物即不中。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), (南嶽懷讓) chapter. MasterName left null: two-speaker line. The Sixth Patriarch (祖 = 六祖 Huineng) asks the newly-arrived Huairang (什麼物恁麼來) 'what thing comes thus?'; Huairang answers (說似一物即不中). The (恁麼) is Huineng's, not the chapter-master Huairang's. The founding (恁麼) exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頭曰。恁麼也不得。不恁麼也不得。恁麼不恁麼總不得。子作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (藥山惟儼) chapter. (頭) = (石頭) (Shitou Xiqian) puts the double bind to Yaoshan: thus won't do, not-thus won't do, both-together won't do — then (子作麼生) ('you — what will you do?'). (恁麼) as the bare deictic driven to a triple negation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又問。恁麼來不立。恁麼去不泯時如何。師曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (洛浦元安) chapter. MasterName left null: two-speaker line. The coming/going pair (恁麼來) ('come thus') / (恁麼去) ('go thus') is spoken by an anonymous monk (又問…); Luopu Yuanan (師) only answers. The demonstrative is the monk's, not Luopu's.

Occurrences.Kwic: 賓云總不與麼。師便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), (興化存獎) chapter. MasterName left null: two-speaker line. The (與麼) is spoken by the disciple Kebin (克賓, the precentor) — (賓云總不與麼) 'in no way thus' — and Xinghua strikes him (師便打, an action, not speech). The term is Kebin's, not Xinghua's. (Verbatim: 賓云總 ends lb 0295b10 and 不與麼 continues lb 0295b11, contiguous after tag-stripping.) Documents (與麼) as the graphic variant of (恁麼).

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。恁麼則順正歸元去也。師曰。歸元何順。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk introduces an inference with “if so, then,” and the master reverses it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 纔恁麼會。蹉過了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu appraises understanding it thus with the verdict that it has been missed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。正當恁麼時如何。蟬聲時到耳。雁影忽迎眸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address uses “right at such a moment” and demands a response.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若恁麼見得。便有自由分。不隨一切語言轉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu uses the demonstrative conditionally: “if seen thus.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 先德道恁麼恁麼又云不恁麼不恁麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A former worthy is cited doubling the positive form and then its negative counterpart.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：便恁麼會時如何？師曰：迢迢十萬不是遠。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk proposes understanding it thus and asks what follows; the master answers.

Senses.Explanation: A conversational connective: 'being so' followed by 'then,' hence 'if so, then.' It occurs 5,426 times in 317 allowlisted texts. Chan encounter records give it a conspicuous turn-taking role: a questioner repeats or draws an inference from a master's answer, and the master may confirm, reverse, test, or reject that inference. Recorded replies call the inference wild talk, reverse its premise, block it with an image, ask for the student's own part, or demand how the claimed conclusion is carried out. These outcomes are deployments of the same connective, not new senses. Its distinctive role is the recurrent public-interview hinge where a proposed understanding becomes answerable to the next line.
Senses.Note: The high count reflects ordinary connective use across encounter dialogue. The phrase normally introduces the student's inference, but speaker role and the next response must be read from each exchange. Its demonstrative base, meaning 'being so,' and its following connective, meaning 'then,' remain one fixed compound here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云恁麼則學人無著身處也。師曰。是爾著身處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The student's inference that he has nowhere to lodge his body is immediately reversed by the master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰恁麼則事同一家也。師曰。隔須彌在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The student's same-household inference receives the contrary answer that Mount Sumeru separates them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰恁麼則即相而無相也。師曰。也是狂言。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master calls the student's inference wild talk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云恁麼則音聲不入法界性也。師曰。離色求觀非正見。離聲求聽是邪聞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The student's inference about sound is followed by a corrective answer about seeking seeing or hearing apart from their objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。恁麼則順正歸元去也。師曰。歸元何順。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student's inference about returning to the source is answered by challenging the claimed direction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：恁麼則絕於言句去也。師曰：夢裏惺惺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The inference that the matter is cut off from words receives the reply 'awake within a dream.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧曰：恁麼則撒手那邊去也。師云：蝦跳不出斗。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk infers release on the far side; the master answers that a shrimp cannot jump out of the measure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「恁麼則均霑法利去也。」師云：「你本分事如何？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the student infers that all equally receive the benefit, the master asks about the student's own part.

Senses.Explanation: A verb phrase: “awaken” plus “the Way.” Chan records use it retrospectively in biographies and cases: Lingyun awakens on seeing peach blossoms, the Buddha on seeing the morning star, and other monks after an encounter or event; verses composed afterward are called “verses on awakening to the Way.” The stock pairing “awaken to the Way on hearing a sound; clarify mind on seeing a form” is itself raised and questioned in a hall address. The records also police the designation: one text calls memorizing two convenient sayings and naming that “awakening to the Way” one of the enumerated kinds of foolish Chan. Thus the term names an attested event and biographical verdict, while the corpus also records challenges to loose claims of it.
Senses.Note: The compound “verse on awakening to the Way” retains the same event sense and is not a separate referent for “awaken to the Way” itself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉古云聞聲悟道見色明心師云作麼生是聞聲悟道見色明心
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address raises the old saying “awaken to the Way on hearing sound; clarify mind on seeing form” and asks what that is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人見桃華悟道，子作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong asks about the old case of awakening to the Way on seeing peach blossoms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽然大悟乃有悟道頌云我有明珠一顆久被諸塵封褁
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A retrospective reports sudden great awakening and introduces a “verse on awakening to the Way.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 或有向古人方便語中記得兩句，謂之悟道，謂之通宗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanlai criticizes those who memorize two convenient sayings of the ancients and call it “awakening to the Way” and “penetrating the school.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 十二月八日明星現時，豁然悟道，大地有情，一時成佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address deploys the Buddha as a Chan figure by recounting his awakening to the Way when the morning star appeared.

Senses.Explanation: The compound functions as "as I knew," "sure enough," or "I knew it." It occurs 371 times in 147 allowlisted texts. Its frequent Chan setting is the public interview, where one turn marks the speaker's prior expectation or recognition of the other. One master says, "as I knew, you are at a loss" (情知汝罔措), and cuts off the monk as he is about to continue. Another hears that a visitor has come from Huangbo and says, "as I knew, you had been to see an adept" (情知你見作家來). Later case commentary uses the same construction to anticipate the reader: "as I knew, you misconstrue it here" (情知你向者裏錯會). The corpus also records the compact reply "I knew it" (情知), followed by the master's verdict, "a fierce tiger does not eat meat lying down" (猛虎不食伏肉). These grammatical forms attest recognition or expectation; they do not name a separate faculty of “feeling-knowledge.”
Senses.Note: Several early exchanges recur in multiple lamp compilations. Repeated recensions establish transmission, but the curated set does not count each recension as an independent event.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。情知汝罔措。僧欲進語。師曰。將謂老僧落伊古今。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master says, "as I knew, you are at a loss," then interrupts the monk's attempted continuation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。情知你見作家來。濟曰。特來禮拜和尚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: On hearing the visitor has come from Huangbo, the master says, "as I knew, you had been to see an adept."

Occurrences.Kwic: 且畢竟見何道理？莫在世尊良久處麼？情知你向者裏錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later case comment asks what was seen and says, "as I knew, you misconstrue it here."

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云：「情知。」師云：「猛虎不食伏肉。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk uses the term alone as "I knew it"; the master replies, "a fierce tiger does not eat meat lying down."

Occurrences.Kwic: 一僧曰：「也是一橛頭禪。」師曰：「情知你恁麼。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a monk offers a stock classification, the master says, "I knew you would be like that."

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘feeling/inclination-understanding.’ The phrase occurs 178 times in 88 allowlisted texts. In case commentary it is something readers ‘make’ from a saying (作情解), something words cause to arise (因言句轉生情解), and something commentators are repeatedly warned not to produce (切忌妄生情解). Yuanwu contrasts such explanations with seeing the old person’s intent, and writes that following another’s words generates this understanding. Other records speak of being stuck in it, forgetting it, or breaking its lair. These are the corpus’s recorded descriptions of the term.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is institutional and textual: ‘subjective understanding’ (情解) is a recurrent negative label in public-case commentary for understandings generated around quoted sayings. Cross-checking ‘intellectual understanding’ (知解), ‘discriminating feelings’ (識情), and ‘knowledge and views’ (知見) supports this narrower deployment. Apparent nominal and verbal surroundings do not make the headword itself different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若也不見。切忌妄生情解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu warns against arbitrarily generating subjective understanding when commenting on a case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方商量者多。作情解會者不少。不知古人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Case commentary contrasts making this understanding with knowing the ancient’s intent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今却因言句。轉生情解
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Explicitly identifies words and phrases as the occasion for its generation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 滯於情解、昧於識度
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate record pairs being stuck in subjective understanding with being darkened in discriminative measure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問答之頃，情解頓忘
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography says it was suddenly forgotten during question-and-answer.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph names feelings, sentiments, or affective responses; the second names recognizing or discerning cognition. Together they name cognition operating through feeling and recognition. Yuanwu repeatedly pairs it with estimating and reckoning: he asks whether a passage can be estimated through affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼) and calls explanations offered in public addresses affective-cognitive reckoning (情識計較). Xuedou says that even recognizing the lineage at the words still remains dim beyond affective cognition (言下知宗，尚昧情識之表). Another address excludes both affective cognition and distinguishing from a stated sentence (非情識分別). Liaoan describes people stuck to affective cognition as occupied with ornamental composition (彼膠於情識者，方以雕蟲篆刻為事). Across these passages the term is a noun, the base for the verbs estimate, reckon, and distinguish, and the object of the verbs stick to and exhaust. It occurs 475 times in 136 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The English head translates the two graphs and their attested verbal partners. It does not turn the term into a general religious theory. The frequent collocations include affective-cognitive estimating (10 hits in six files), distinguishing (eight in seven), reckoning (five in four), and exhausted cognition (10 in six).

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。畢竟作麼生辨的。直饒鐵眼銅睛。也摸索不著。到這裏。以情識卜度得麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's case commentary asks: “Say, how will it finally be distinguished? Even iron eyes and bronze pupils cannot feel it out. At this point, can it be estimated through affective cognition?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方陞堂入室。說箇什麼。盡是情識計較。若是情識計較。情盡方見得透。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu says: “Throughout the regions they ascend the hall and enter the room—what do they say? It is all affective-cognitive reckoning. If it is affective-cognitive reckoning, only when feeling is exhausted is it seen through.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以聲前悟旨。猶迷顧鑑之端。言下知宗。尚昧情識之表。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuedou's own record: “Thus, understanding the import before sound still misses the beginning of looking back; recognizing the lineage at the words still remains dim beyond affective cognition.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 我有一句子。不借諸聖口。不動自己舌。非聲氣呼吸。非情識分別。

Senses.Explanation: The graph means awake or alert (惺); reduplicated, it means alert or wide-awake (惺惺). The corpus records three deployments. First is the command 'stay awake' or 'stay alert' (惺惺著, 142 occurrences). Its best-known case has Ruiyan call to himself each day, 'Master!' and answer 'Yes!', then say, 'Stay awake; after this do not be fooled by anyone' (主人公……諾……惺惺著，以後莫被人瞞). The word also describes an alert fellow (惺惺底, 27; 惺惺漢, 6). Second is the fixed pair 'still and alert' (寂寂惺惺 / 惺惺寂寂, 47 / 35). Yongjia's Verse on Stopping (奢摩他頌) defines alert as not producing the signs of dull abiding or blank indeterminacy (惺惺謂不生昏住無記等相), and ranks alert-and-still as right, blank-and-still as wrong, still-and-alert as right, and scattered-and-alert as wrong (惺惺寂寂是，無記寂寂非，寂寂惺惺是，亂想惺惺非). Later texts explicitly attribute this wording to Yongjia. Third, the corpus records objections to these deployments. Ruiyan's self-calling is reported as dismissed by all quarters as 'playing with spirit-ghosts' (諸方謂其弄精魂); one master reverses the case by saying that the master called Ruiyan, rather than Ruiyan calling the master. Another record names still-and-alert among the fetters, paired with torpor and scattering (被寂寂惺惺、昏沉散亂縛). The headword occurs 1,135 times in 248 allowlist texts. The entry therefore keeps the attested gloss 'alert' while recording both the cited formula and the criticism preserved with it.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense, used of an alert condition and of an alert person. The still-and-alert pairing is attributed to Yongjia's Verse on Stopping (奢摩他頌), while the Chan record also preserves criticism of Ruiyan's command and names the pair itself as a fetter. The target remains the attested 'alert' or 'awake.' Yongjia and Ruiyan are named in the notes but are absent from the roster, so MasterName is null. Compare 'still' (寂寂), 'master-in-charge' (主人公), and 'playing with spirit-ghosts' (弄精魂).

AlternateTargets: what is the purport of that?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'what is the intent or purport?' It is a stock second-round question in recorded exchanges. A monk first asks, 'What is buddha?' The teacher answers, 'Spread the hair to cover the mud; lay the body crosswise on the ground.' The monk then asks, 'What is the purport?' and the teacher replies, 'Even Papiyan would furrow his brow.' The intensified form, 'I have not yet examined it—what is the purport?', likewise follows an answer: after a monk asks the intent of the ancestral teacher's coming from the west, the teacher gives a line about an old temple being difficult to read; the monk presses with the intensified question. The formula also follows a raised earlier saying. A monk quotes 'play a ball on swift water,' asks its purport, and receives 'thought after thought does not stop or remain.' In another exchange the first answer is 'the eyebrows divide into the figure eight'; the press receives 'both ears hang to the shoulders.' The phrase asks about the immediately preceding saying and does not supply that saying's answer itself.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide conversational formula, not a master's coinage. Current count: 3,178 matches in 292 files; the intensified 'I have not yet examined it—what is the purport?' has 194 matches in 45 files, and 'what is the teacher's purport?' has 13 in 12. It occurs after a first-round answer and after quotations of earlier cases. All selected witnesses are two-speaker or raised-case passages, so their occurrence master keys remain null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to meet or answer the occasion. The compound occurs 569 times in 200 allowlisted texts and repeatedly describes a master's apt response in public encounter: 'responding question-and-answer,' answering without error, and meeting people as occasion calls. One historical notice says Linji frequently used shouts when responding, then immediately records his warning to followers who merely copied his shouting. Another record says a master ordinarily responded with no fixed tracks; a lineage overview describes the five houses as each having a house style and responding in exchanges. The corpus also pairs the term with events and conditions: 'the teaching is originally without speech; it responds according to the affair,' and 'meet the occasion like lightning.' Thus the pivot (機) is the occasion or juncture presented, not automatically a student's graded capacity, and responding (應) is the recorded act rather than a generalized system.
Senses.Note: Answering, receiving people, and responding to circumstances are grammatical objects of one act, not separate things. The corpus-wide usage has no master-specific sense: Linji's frequent shout is explicitly a particular deployment that imitators cannot reproduce by copying the sound.

Senses.PreferredTarget: responding to things, showing a form
AlternateTargets: meet the object and manifest a form
show a form in response to things
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to respond to things (應物) and show a form (現形). The phrase occurs 209 times in 105 allowlisted texts. The records repeatedly pair it with the comparison "like the moon in water" (如水中月). They also make it a public-interview question: asked "what is responding to things, showing a form?" a master says, "bring the bed-seat over for me" (如何是應物現形；與我拈床子過來). In another exchange the monk asks which is the moon in the water comparison and the master raises the whisk. A later hall address says, "the body has no form; responding to things, it shows a form" (法身無象，應物現形), then raises the staff and measures the staff against the recorded heights of the World-Honored One and Maitreya. Thus the phrase is not left as an abstract proposition in the Chan corpus: masters put it into questions and answer it with the teaching-seat furniture and implements in front of the assembly.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense covers the grammatical uses found: the subject responds to an encountered thing by taking or displaying a form. The moon comparison, public-interview answers, and gesture deployments are different attestations of that same action, not different referents. The phrase is often embedded in older quoted wording; no quoted occurrence is reassigned to the later recorder.

Senses.Explanation: To answer when called, often with an acknowledging response. The word occurs 1,087 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Call-and-response is repeatedly the operative shape: the national teacher calls his attendant three times and receives three answers; the Buddha calls Ananda after Ananda asks about the former buddhas' procedure; Kasyapa calls Ananda in the robe-transmission case; Huangbo names Pei Xiu by calling him and declares the naming complete when Pei answers. Masters also call lecturers, monks, officials, or themselves, and the response becomes the next move in a public exchange. The same verb also records ordinary assent to an instruction, as when Ananda answers an order to enter the city with the bowl.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend lies in the records' repeated use of the simplest audible answer as the decisive next turn of a public interview or named case. The entry reports that structural deployment without asserting what the answer proves. Answering a call and assenting to an order remain the same response event, not different things.

Senses.PreferredTarget: let go at the cliff's edge
AlternateTargets: release one's grip at the precipice
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “to let go at the cliff's edge.” The phrase occurs 261 times in 120 allowlisted texts. The records use the cliff image in public questions, answers, sermons, verses, and death verses. It is repeatedly paired in the exact saying, “At the cliff's edge let go; accept and undertake it yourself. Revive after extinction; no one can deceive you” (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再蘇，欺君不得). Xingyang Xiyin is asked for “the line about letting go at the cliff's edge” and answers, “The bright moon illuminates the secluded valley” (明月照幽谷); asked next for the line about reviving after extinction, he answers, “White clouds arise in the great void” (白雲生太虗). Elsewhere “letting go from a ten-thousand-fathom cliff” answers “What is the affair of leaving home?”, while another question explicitly asks how to avoid losing one's life there. Yuanwu's letters compare the phrase with giving up one's life and with a dead person shortly reviving. The corpus thus bends a physical act into a stock verbal image linked by the texts themselves to loss of life and revival; the entry reports that recorded pairing without supplying an explanation of it.
Senses.Note: The expanded forms “ten-thousand-fathom cliff” and “ten-thousand-ren cliff” carry the same image. The paired wording “revive after extinction” (絕後再蘇) is a text-drawn relation, not an inferred interpretation.

Senses.Explanation: A precept is a binding rule. The word occurs 9,514 times across 412 allowlisted Chan texts, and the record preserves its full range as hard-rule language. A precept-giving ceremony begins to enumerate the received rules as ‘no killing, no stealing, no lying’ (不殺不盜不妄); biographies praise strict keeping, while Juelang warns against waiting for outward traces before calling conduct precept-breaking. The word also enters institutional regulation: a master asks a self-described precept-keeper why he does not observe the monastic code. The Platform Record publicly confers ‘formless precepts’ (無相戒), so the Chan bend does not erase the rule but places named precept forms and their reception inside the teaching record. Yongjue asks, ‘What is a precept? How is a precept received? Will you take the ordination platform as the precept, or purity as the precept?’ (云何為戒？戒云何受？將以壇場為戒耶？清淨為戒耶？). He also places two inherited sayings side by side: ‘the one word “precept” is what the buddhas take as teacher’ and ‘the one word “precept” is what the patriarchs avoid’ (戒之一字，諸佛所師 / 戒之一字，諸祖所忌). Huineng’s verse says, ‘the mind level, why labor at keeping precepts; conduct straight, what use is cultivating Chan?’ (心平何勞持戒，行直何用修禪). These attested rules, ceremonies, appraisals, violations, questions, and contrasts do not establish that the corpus uniformly upholds or discards precepts.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: Chan records retain precept as a real rule while also making its location, reception, and merely effortful keeping matters of direct address. No claim is made that the corpus uniformly upholds or discards rules. Exact allowlist count: 9,514 hits in 412 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人云：戒之一字，諸佛所師，甜瓜徹蒂甜。又云：戒之一字，諸祖所忌，苦瓜連根苦。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue Yuanxian juxtaposes two sayings: the precept as the buddhas’ teacher and as what the patriarchs avoid.
