Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Record of Chan Master Foyan of Longmen, the speaker recalls long service to his former teacher and says he often received the teacher's painstaking verbal prompting. The line is a memorial statement, so the former teacher is not assigned as its speaker.

Senses.Explanation: To raise, lift up, or bring something forward. The expression occurs 1,685 times in 307 allowlisted texts. In public encounters the object is often concrete and made visible: a whisk becomes the object of a question, a newcomer raises a sitting cloth and makes a circle, Nanquan raises the disputed cat and asks the assembly to speak, Yinfeng raises his rosary when asked his age, and a Chan visitor raises a tea cup when asked about “the other side.” Later instructional records use the same raising action with a saying or question as object: Mingben tells an assembly to bring forward a saying without flavor, the investigated saying, or the full question “the myriad things return to one; where does the one return?” Physical and discursive objects do not create different lexical actions. The Chan deviation is the density with which raising an object or matter becomes a visible or verbal move inside public exchange and instruction.
Senses.Note: The former concrete/abstract split was a literal-versus-extended reading of the same raising action and is merged. Compare whisk (拂子), sitting cloth (坐具), upright raising (豎起), raised saying (話頭), investigated saying (所參話), and lifting or citing (舉起). No fixed spiritual force is assigned to raising either kind of object.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光拈得拂子。趂至僧堂前。見師乃提起拂子曰。闍黎喚這箇作甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The whisk is physically lifted and immediately made the object of a question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日，六人新到相看，五人作禮，一人提起坐具，作一圓相。師云：我聞有一隻獵狗甚惡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A newcomer lifts the sitting cloth and makes a circle during an encounter with Huangbo.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師因兩堂爭猫兒，師遂提起猫兒云：大眾！道得即不斬，道不得即斬。眾無語，師遂斬之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanquan physically lifts the cat and addresses the assembly in the public case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 韓文公一日相訪。問師。春秋多少。師提起數珠。曰。會麼。公曰。不會。師曰。晝夜一百八。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinfeng lifts a rosary as his response to a question about his age.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單單提起箇無義味話頭，自最初一日立定脚頭，不得分毫移動，密密與之做向前去，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mingben's address commands bringing forward a saying without flavor. The object is discursive rather than physical, but the raising verb remains the same.

Occurrences.Kwic: 休息萬慮，單單提起箇所參話，向三根椽下盡其形命，一生了辨，不為分外。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate address names the object as the saying being investigated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十二時中單單提起箇萬法歸一、一歸何處話，行疑坐疑，猛利無間，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text supplies the complete question that is to be brought forward.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪客提起茶甌。泉曰：「此猶是這邊事，那邊事作麼生？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan visitor raises a tea cup in response to Nanquan's question; Nanquan says this is still the affair on this side and asks about the other side.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "swap out the eyes" (換卻眼睛). In ordinary wording this would name a bodily exchange; Chan records use it as an accusation that a saying, written formulation, sight, sound, or teacher has displaced a person's own seeing. A commentary says a monk asking Xuansha about his own self had his eyes swapped out by Xuansha's reply. Shiyu says altered wording and changed characters (改文易字) swap out people's eyes, and elsewhere says waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs do it. Sanyi warns against letting the writing brush exchange black beans for one's eyes (毛錐子將黑荳換卻眼睛), then identifies bird-script, dragon-writing, paper, ink, and written characters as fit for ordinary circulation rather than Chan discussion. A case comment even judges the words "Where is the eminent monk?" (高僧何在) themselves to have plainly swapped out the eyes. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore an adversarial verdict about seeing being commandeered; the texts apply it to both words and sensory displays, not to literal surgery.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 63 hits in 45 allowlisted texts, concentrated in later discourse records and case comments. Attested agents include a master's reply, rewritten words, landscape, sounds, written characters, and a case question. No in-corpus occurrence defines a physical operation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 玄沙因僧問：「如何是學人自己？」沙曰：「用自己作麼？」「者僧氣概天然，卻被玄沙換卻眼睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Miaoyun's old-case comment says Xuansha's answer to a question about the student's own self swapped out the student's eyes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只是改文易字，便被他換卻眼睛，至使參詢不歇。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shiyu names altered wording and changed characters as the agent that swaps out the eyes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 及乎到來，乃被水鳥樹林、鐘鈴鑼鼓換卻眼睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate Shiyu address lists waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs as swapping out the listeners' eyes.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫被者毛錐子將黑荳換卻眼睛，鳥篆龍章，紙墨文字，秪可作世諦流布，豈可作佛法商量？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sanyi warns that the writing brush exchanges black beans for eyes and immediately names ornate script, paper, ink, and writing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 斐相國道：高僧何在？分明換卻眼睛。黃檗更召相公，剛把鉢盂安柄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Collected Old Cases comment applies the verdict directly to Pei's question in the Huangbo encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘strike or clap the palms.’ The gesture occurs 746 times in 231 allowlisted texts, commonly as a visible turn in a public exchange. It may stand alone (‘clapped three times’), accompany departure, a shout, or a blow, or join laughter: ‘clapped his hands and laughed loudly’ occurs 98 times in 60 texts. The record does not assign one fixed attitude to it. One master claps and laughs before saying an answer is ‘not worth half a cent’; another monk claps once after shouting; Xiyuan claps three times when asked why he bathes without an attendant. Caoshan later explicitly calls the action ‘hand-clapping’ and distinguishes Xiyuan’s use from the same physical action elsewhere. In the Shuilao case, Shuilao rises after Mazu kicks him, claps and laughs, and speaks; later records repeatedly cite that sequence. Zen bends an ordinary gesture by making it an answer, rejoinder, appraisal, or recorded public-interview move, while the surrounding words—not the gesture alone—establish whether a given occurrence is laughter, challenge, celebration, or dismissal.
Senses.Note: Family check: “clap the hands” (撫掌), “hand-clapping” (拍手撫掌), “clap and laugh loudly” (撫掌大笑), “clap once” (撫掌一下), and “clap three times” (撫掌三下) all denote the same physical action. They differ in accompanying speech and count, not referent, so they remain one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃撫掌作舞，大笑云：「菩薩子喫飯來！」後有僧舉問長慶：「古人撫掌大笑，意作摩生？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The action accompanies dancing, laughter, and a call to eat; a later monk asks about it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：和尚不使沙彌童行，何得自燒？師撫掌三下。後僧舉似曹山，山云：一等是箇拍手撫掌，就中西園奇怪，俱胝一指頭禪，蓋謂承當處不諦當。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiyuan answers with three claps; Caoshan explicitly identifies the movement as hand-clapping.

Occurrences.Kwic: 主指曰：春雨霖霖。師撫掌大笑曰：不直半分錢。主便喝，師曰：者瞎漢向道不直半分錢，又惡發作什麼？主撫掌一下，師曰：且坐喫茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two speakers clap at different turns in a public exchange; one clap accompanies a stated appraisal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大師欄胷與一踏踏倒，當下大悟，起來撫掌大笑云：也大奇！也大奇！百千法門，無量妙義，只向一毫頭上識得根源去。便作禮。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Shuilao case preserves the sequence kick, rise, clap, laugh, speak, and bow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧以手面前一劃師云是何言欵僧便喝師云作甚麼僧撫掌一下便打師云瞎漢乱做作麼以坐具真打出法堂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk claps once and strikes during an exchange, showing the gesture outside laughter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂撫掌大笑良久曰大眾笑箇什麼山僧笑古往今來一切人有瞥地有不瞥地
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat occurrence begins with prolonged clapping and laughter and then explicitly asks what is being laughed at.

Senses.Explanation: A recorded teaching-seat action: to strike the Chan seat or bench, often with a staff or whisk. The phrase occurs 682 times in 137 allowlisted texts. It commonly closes an address immediately before the master leaves the seat, but the blow can also be made the audible member of an exchange. One record raises the whisk and asks 'do you see?', then strikes the Chan seat and asks 'do you hear?'; another explicitly says 'this is sound' when the seat is struck. The formula also appears with 'strike the Chan seat once,' and a cited verse follows a staff-blow on the seat with 'one strike, and what was known was forgotten.' Elsewhere a monk asks about buddha, the master strikes the seat once and says the monk has already forgotten it. The seat is furniture of the Chan teaching hall; the strike is recorded as part of the master's public address and question-and-answer conduct.
Senses.Note: The omitted instrument varies: texts explicitly supply 'with a staff' (以拄杖), 'with a whisk' (以拂子), or no instrument. These are grammatical specifications of one action, not separate things. The Chan graph (禪) names Chan here, so the object is the Chan seat. No corpus warrant was found for assigning the blow a single symbolic message.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是向下句。作麼生是不涉二途句。若識得頂門上出氣。若識不得土牛耕石田。擊禪床下座。金山瑞新禪師潤州金山瑞新禪師。僧問。吾有大患為吾有身。父母未生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The action directly precedes leaving the teaching seat, a frequent closing formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。華光寺主。便下座。上堂。藥多病甚。網細魚稠。便下座。示眾。以拄杖擊禪床一下云。大眾還會麼。不見道。一擊忘所知。更不假修持。諸方達道者。咸言
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A staff strikes the Chan seat once; the master asks whether the assembly understands and cites 'one strike, and what was known was forgotten.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 說不盡底、祖師提不起處，對眾八字打開去也。遂舉拂子，云：大眾還見麼？擊禪床，云：還見麼？見處透脫，聞處精明，一念返本還源，即具頂門三眼，萬里更
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, then strikes the seat and asks again; the following clause distinguishes seeing and hearing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 座問答罷，乃拈拂子召大眾曰：還見麼？手中拂子層層為諸人放百種寶光。復擊禪床曰：還聞麼？座下猊臺句句為諸人演一乘了義。諸人若向者裏悟得，則曠大劫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After public questions and answers, the whisk is raised with 'do you see?' and the Chan seat is struck with 'do you hear?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 在爐中從𦗟老僧葛藤時有僧問如何是佛師云還記得麼僧云若不請益爭知如是師擊禪床一下云早是忘却了僧云放和尚一線道師云一任𨁝跳問如何是洪州境荅云滕王閣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a direct exchange about buddha, the master strikes the seat once and says the monk has already forgotten it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 前。要且目前難覩。欲識大道真體。不離聲色言語。舉起拂子云。這箇是色。擊禪床云。這箇是聲。山僧只今口吧吧地。是言語那箇是大道真體。喝一喝云。即此
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text explicitly labels the raised whisk as visible form and the struck Chan seat as sound.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary usage, 'capture and release' (擒縱) is a commander's battlefield tactic — capturing the enemy and releasing him at will — and Chan bends it to the master's total control of an encounter, the taking-hold and letting-go that stay in his own hands: 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me' (擒縱非他。卷舒在我). That command register is the word's Zen bend. Literally, 'capture and release': 'capture' (擒) paired with 'let loose or release' (縱). The compound occurs 107 times in 73 allowed texts. Its most frequent fixed relations are 'capture and release, kill and bring to life' (擒縱殺活, 19 occurrences) and 'roll out and fold up, capture and release' (卷舒擒縱, 12). Yuanwu also records the reversed framing 'release and gather, capture and release' (放收擒縱) and says, 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me' (擒縱非他。卷舒在我). In an assembly address he writes that only afterward does one 'release and gather, capture and release, and obtain great freedom' (放收擒縱得大解脫). Another address says, 'within killing there is bringing to life, capturing and releasing humans and gods; within bringing to life there is killing, weighing buddhas and ancestors' (殺中有活擒縱人天。活中有殺權衡佛祖). His Essentials states: 'able to capture and release, skilled in killing and bringing to life—great teachers do not fail to use these' (能擒縱，善殺活，得大解脫，知識無不用之). Later commemorative prose similarly says 'capture and release, killing and bringing to life, are all complete' (擒縱殺活皆全). The corpus thus deploys the pair as the master's coordinated command of the encounter, commonly placed in four-part action strings.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend is the borrowed military register: the commander's capture-and-release of an enemy becomes the master's control of the encounter, held 'in me' (擒縱非他，卷舒在我). The required definition formulas produced only one grammatical headword-plus-nominalizer occurrence and no self-definition. The repeated coordinations supply the lexical structure directly: capture contrasts with release, just as gather contrasts with release and killing contrasts with bringing to life. No claim about a hidden spiritual force is added.

Occurrences.Kwic: 然後放收擒縱得大解脫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's own second volume of assembly addresses: 'afterward, release and gather, capture and release, and obtain great freedom.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 須知殺中有活擒縱人天。活中有殺權衡佛祖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's eighth volume of assembly addresses. The line makes capture/release govern 'humans and gods' and pairs it with killing/bringing to life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 能擒縱，善殺活，得大解脫，知識無不用之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Essentials, letter to Elder Chong of Fawang: 'able to capture and release, skilled in killing and bringing to life… great teachers do not fail to use these.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 擒縱非他。卷舒在我。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record pointer to case twenty-two: 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 權實照用俱備，擒縱殺活皆全。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancestral Guidelines Collection, memorial guideline prose: 'provisional and actual, illumination and function, are both prepared; capture and release, killing and bringing to life, are all complete.' The passage commemorates another master, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “carry,” “board,” and “fellow”: “a board-carrying fellow.” The records themselves repeatedly connect the name with seeing only one side. The stock line says, “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side,” and a later comment states directly, “Each sees one side: precisely a board-carrying fellow.” In the Muezhou case, Muezhou calls to a monk; when the monk turns his head, Muezhou calls him a board-carrying fellow. Xuedou and Huanglong then give opposing comments on why the monk should or should not receive the name, and a later speaker judges that each commentator sees one side. The label is not confined to that case. One address calls both contentment at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket instances of the same name. Another says that explaining five ranks, three mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients “only makes a board-carrying fellow,” then asks how the matter can be raised whole. A later direct naming formula says, “Learning without awakening is called overbearing pride; awakening without learning is called a board-carrying fellow.” The entry reports these recorded applications and the texts’ own one-sidedness wording.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 193 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the shorter “carry a board” form occurs 589 times in 186 texts. “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side” occurs 5 times in 5 texts. Three occurrences in two texts ask why the turned monk is or is not called a board-carrying fellow. The recurring Muezhou exchange and later comments must be kept distinct: Muezhou supplies the name in the case; Xuedou, Huanglong, and later speakers argue over its application.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各見一邊，正是擔板漢。今晚或云：『雲門與麼道，也是擔板漢。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu, an evening address commenting on Xuedou and Huanglong: “Each sees one side, precisely a board-carrying fellow. Tonight, if someone says, ‘Yunmen speaking this way is also a board-carrying fellow’...”

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方道。徐六擔板只見一邊。尚書不學牆面。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity commentary records two sayings: “Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side,” and “An officer who does not study faces a wall.” This unique short-form witness omits the final graph for “fellow” but supplies the corpus's recurrent one-side description of the full headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 睦州和尚一日喚僧云：『大德！』僧回首，州云：『擔板漢。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Muezhou case is raised: Muezhou calls “Worthy one!”; the monk turns his head, and Muezhou says, “Board-carrying fellow.” The exchange has multiple speakers, so the occurrence speaker remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Dongshan Meixi Du, presented to layman Li Zuiliang: “Learning without awakening is called overbearing pride; awakening without learning is called a board-carrying fellow.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐豐美筵席，唱太平曲子，無不爽心稱快，也是擔板漢。住荊棘叢林，入虎狼群隊，無不戰驚受懼，也是擔板漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhean Fan gives opposed applications: delight at a rich feast is called a board-carrying fellow, and fear amid thorns, tigers, and wolves is also called one.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只成擔板漢。此事如何舉得全？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same recorded sayings says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients “only makes a board-carrying fellow,” then asks, “How can this matter be raised whole?”

Senses.Explanation: Both graphs name bearing a load: to shoulder or carry it. One exact verse names physical firewood carried on one shoulder until the carrying pole breaks. Far more often the Chan corpus leaves the load unstated or names responsibility, succession, inheritance, or teaching. Productive forms include “shoulder it successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), and “shoulder it on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷). Yuanwu lists “accept successfully, shoulder successfully, head toward successfully, carry out successfully” (承當得，擔荷得，趣向得，行履得). Jiufeng Daoqian says, “knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession” (知向裏許承當擔荷，是為內紹), then says one must see “the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering” before reaching “one color” (須見無承當底人，無擔荷底人，始得同一色). The same load-bearing verb therefore spans physical cargo and the corpus's dominant responsibility and lineage deployments. Literal and figurative loads do not make the act of shouldering two lexical things.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 868 times in 243 allowlisted texts. The former physical/figurative targets name the same load-bearing action and are merged. Explicit firewood is rare; responsibility and lineage language dominate. Attested formations include “one who shoulders” (擔荷者), “shoulder successfully” (擔荷得), “shoulder with the whole body” (全身擔荷), “shoulder on one shoulder” (一肩擔荷), “accept and shoulder” (承當擔荷), and “unable to shoulder” (擔荷不起). The reversed form “carry a load” (荷擔) belongs to the family but does not create another referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 驀然有箇承當得。擔荷得。趣向得。行履得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's own discourse record, under 'addresses to the assembly, six.' He enumerates four parallel successful verbs: accepting, shouldering, heading toward, and carrying out.

Occurrences.Kwic: 少林演妙訣。唯許神光擔荷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's own discourse record, under 'minor addresses, three.' The sentence says, 'Shaolin expounded the subtle key; only Shenguang was allowed to shoulder it.' Shenguang is the name used here for the second ancestor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中有全身擔荷者出來與山僧相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Records of Ancient Worthies (古尊宿語錄), the speaker calls: 'if among the assembly there is one who shoulders it with the whole body, come out and meet this mountain monk.' The local head pointer is a generic collected-sayings heading and does not securely identify the speaker, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歷代祖師有擎山舉鼎之力，也擔荷不起
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the record of Sanyi Yu (三宜盂禪師), under his Yunmen Xiansheng Monastery addresses, the speaker says: 'the ancestral teachers of successive generations had the strength to lift mountains and raise tripods, yet could not shoulder it.' The master is named by the text but lacks an exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 知向裏許承當擔荷。是為內紹。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head in the Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元) is Jiufeng Daoqian. Asked about inner succession, he says, 'knowing to accept and shoulder it inwardly is inner succession.' This is the corpus's clearest explicit classification involving the headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須見無承當底人。無擔荷底人。始得同一色。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of Jiufeng Daoqian's same exchange: 'one must see the person with no accepting and the person with no shouldering; only then does one reach one color.' Kept separately because it supplies the text's direct contrast to the preceding definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有力量者進前來一肩擔荷得去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head in the Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書) is Xueqiao Yuanxin. He calls, 'those with strength, come forward and shoulder it on one shoulder.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 爭得盧公賽子雲，一肩擔荷柴衝折。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘How could Master Lu rival Ziyun? Carrying firewood on one shoulder, the carrying pole breaks.’ This is the sole researched exact-headword witness with explicit physical cargo.

Senses.PreferredTarget: carry snow to fill a well
AlternateTargets: fill a well by carrying snow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" (擔雪填井): the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" (談玄說妙，畫餅充饑), and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" (證龜成鱉). Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball (捏雪成團). Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing (吹網欲滿) and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 32 hits in 28 allowlisted texts. No formula self-definition was found; its predicates emerge from enumerations and explicit similes. Three distinct Baishan deployments are retained because they assign the image to different response shapes; independent Tian'an and Yinyuan passages establish broader use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若道拈來便用，何異擔雪填井。若道總不與麼，也是證龜成鱉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan compares picking up and immediately using the whisk to carrying snow to fill a well, and the contrary response to proving a turtle a soft-shelled turtle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈椎豎拂，望梅止渴，談玄說玅，畫餅充饑，一問一荅，擔雪填井，行棒行喝，無事生事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan's enumeration assigns carrying snow to fill a well to one-question-one-answer exchanges amid other paired appraisals.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若以寂默通，則擔雪填井；若以語言道，則證龜成鱉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan contrasts trying to pass through by silent stillness with trying to state it through words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐禪者，大似擔雪填井。吟詩者，何異捏雪成團？惟有說食者卻最親切。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tian'an compares sitting Chan to carrying snow to fill a well and composing poetry to kneading snow into a ball.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所作所為，擔雪填井，吹綱欲滿，縱經塵劫，無有是處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinyuan pairs the phrase with blowing into a net in hopes of filling it and extends the appraisal across ages.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to be on the point of answering. The term occurs 406 times in 96 allowlisted texts and functions as a compact turn-stage in Chan encounter narratives: a person makes to answer, and before the answer is recorded a master leaves, rebukes him, strikes him, or covers his mouth. One rebuke names the preceding delay directly: after the student looks from side to side and makes to answer, the teacher says that lingering thought has not passed through. Other transmission accounts place a blow or a covered mouth at this same turn and then report awakening. The word records the attempted reply; it does not name the interruption or its result.
Senses.Note: One verbal sense. Whether making to answer is met by departure, rebuke, blow, or covered mouth changes the encounter, not the referent of the headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良擬對，師拂袖便出，曰：見面不如聞名。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An attempted answer is cut off by the master's leaving and verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師左右視，擬對之。善叱曰：竚思停機，情識未透，何曾夢見？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher explicitly rebukes the hesitation preceding an attempted answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師擬對，悟劈口擊之，因墜一齒，即大悟，留天寧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission biography places a blow at the attempted reply and then reports awakening.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師擬對，鑑掩其口。師了然開悟，遂禮拜。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher covers the student's mouth when he makes to answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝記得話頭麼試舉看。師擬對。鑑掩其口。師了然開悟遂禮拜。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp record preserves the full public prompt, attempted response, interruption, and narrated result.

Senses.PreferredTarget: frame it in mind and already miss
AlternateTargets: form an intention and already go wrong
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "frame it in mind and already be off" (擬心即差). Chan records make this a compact warning and an answer: Huangbo places it after saying that mind is not to be sought with mind; another record answers "What is buddha?" with "frame it in mind and already miss; use mind and already go astray" (擬心即差，用心即乖). The fixed expansion "frame it in mind and already miss; stir a thought and already go astray" (擬心即差，動念即乖) is also tested rather than left as a slogan. Two Dong'an notices add that neither framing nor stirring leaves one "working for a livelihood in dead water" (正在死水裏作活計), while neither framing nor stirring makes one no different from wood and clay (土木無殊). Fayyi answers a student's quotation of the formula by asking why someone who is always framing does not miss, and then calls the student's next move "already a miss" (早成差也). Thus the Chan deviation is observable in the records' refusal to let either side—deliberation or inert non-deliberation—serve as the definition.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 74 hits in 40 allowlisted texts. It occurs as a warning, an answer, a quoted proposition challenged by a student, and a premise immediately corrected by masters. The common paired form with 'stir a thought and already go astray' is included; the two explicit corrections of non-framing are retained because they prevent a one-sided reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故修道人直下無心默契。擬心即差。以心傳心此為正見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp preserves Huangbo's warning after the three parallel statements that mind, buddha, and the teaching are not to be sought through themselves.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是佛師云擬心即差用心即乖云畢竟如何師云大盡三十日小盡二十九
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An encounter in the Record of Ancient Venerables uses the phrase as the answer to 'What is buddha?' and pairs it with 'use mind and already go astray.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾云：擬心即差，動念即乖。不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Joint Lamp notice quotes the paired formula and immediately describes neither framing nor stirring as working for a livelihood in dead water.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾，云：擬心即差，動念即乖；不擬不動，土木無殊。行脚人須得轉身一句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate Joint Lamp notice contrasts the paired warning with the statement that neither framing nor stirring is no different from wood and clay.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問擬心即差動念即乖。學人如何進道。師曰。有人常擬為什麼不差。曰即今事如何。師曰。早成差也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Lamp record of Fayyi preserves a question-answer correction: the master asks why someone always framing does not miss, then calls the follow-up already a miss.

Senses.Explanation: (擬) to be about to / intend + (議) to deliberate, discuss: "to hesitate and deliberate" — to hang back weighing a response rather than answering directly (4329 occ / 359 texts). The corpus pairs it with an immediate cut-off. As a verdict clause: "deliberate and you're already off," (擬議即乖 6), "…and you already miss," (擬議即差 7), set beside the parallel "open your mouth and it's already remote" (開口即邈) in (開口即邈)，(擬議即差). As the trigger of a blow or shout: "wait for him to deliberate, then hit," (待伊擬議便打 擬議便打 18), (僧擬議師便喝). As a barred delay: "permits no deliberating," (不容擬議 116), "cannot deliberate one's way to it," (擬議不來 97). And figured as a spatial gulf: (擬議之間)，(白雲萬里) / "in the space of deliberating, ten-thousand miles of white cloud / a long road," (長途萬里 擬議之間 91), "the moment you hesitate and deliberate, blood has already spattered the Brahma-heaven" (你纔擬議，早是血濺梵天了也). Collocation (擬議思量) (135). The texts state the cut-off and the gulf as facts of deployment and add no further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide term. Curated occurrences are stock formula-deployments (verdict clauses, blow/shout triggers, gulf images) by unnamed masters, so MasterName is null. Attested pairings: (開口即邈) (companion), (便打) / (便喝) (consequence), (白雲萬里) / (長途萬里) / (血濺梵天) (gulf images). Counts: (擬議) 4329/359; (擬議之間) 91; (不容擬議) 116; (擬議不來) 97; (擬議思量) 135.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直下便見，無第二人，擬議即乖，焉容鈍置？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雪關禪師語錄); the verdict clause (擬議即乖) (deliberate and you're off) against (直下便見) (see straight off). Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 開口即邈擬議即差。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄); the companion pair (開口即邈)，(擬議即差) (open the mouth → remote; deliberate → miss). Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如金剛王寶劍，你纔擬議，早是血濺梵天了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (宗門拈古彙集); the gulf image — the moment you deliberate (纔擬議), blood already spatters heaven. Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬議之間，白雲萬里。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天隱和尚語錄); the spatial-gulf figure (擬議之間)，(白雲萬里). Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擬議之間，長途萬里。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (嘉泰普燈錄); the same gulf figure with (長途萬里) (a long road of ten-thousand miles). Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 待伊擬議便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄); the blow trigger — (待伊擬議便打) (wait for him to deliberate, then hit); the surrounding text carries (云會麼). Stock formula, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三世諸佛不知有狸奴白牯卻知有僧擬議師便喝落堂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public exchange, the monk hesitates and deliberates; the master immediately shouts and ends the session.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喚作竹篦則觸，不喚作竹篦則背。速道，速道！擬議不來，劈脊便棒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At the bamboo-strip test, the master demands an immediate answer; when deliberation produces none, the passage records a blow across the back.

Senses.Explanation: A verb-object phrase: gather, collect, or draw in (攝) the mind (心), hence "gather the mind." It occurs 137 times in 71 allowlisted texts. Chinese Chan records preserve both literal instructions and direct objections to the wording. Asked to "show the way of gathering the mind" (示攝心之法), one teacher answers, "sit still for one stick of incense" (靜坐一爐香), but immediately calls this "a fine saying" and warns that it must not be misunderstood (好箇話頭，只是不得錯會). In a separate verse requested on the term, the answer says, "the myriad things are brightly clear—what thought and what consideration? If you intend to gather the mind, there is no basis to rely on. I now write these words for you; just this is the place of gathering the mind" (萬法朗然，何思何慮？擬欲攝心，無本可據……只此便是攝心處).
Senses.Note: A later address quotes "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒), then challenges it point by point: "what thing is mind that it can be gathered? What thing is gathering that it can gather mind? Water does not wash water" (心是何物而可攝？攝又是何物而可攝心？水不洗水). The Source-Mirror Record states that before reaching its stated gate, "saying right makes wrong; gathering the mind is still an error" (說是成非，攝心猶錯). Other occurrences retain the ordinary finite action: a community verse lists chanting and "gathering the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡). Counted forms include "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒, two occurrences in two texts), "gather the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡, two in two), "the way of gathering the mind" (攝心之法, one), "place of gathering the mind" (攝心處, one), and "gather the mind and illuminate within" (攝心內照, three in three). The entry records the action and the texts' own challenges without resolving those challenges into an external system.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「請和尚示攝心之法。」師云：「靜坐一爐香。」僧禮拜，師云：「好箇話頭，只是不得錯會。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked to show the way of gathering mind, the teacher answers sitting quietly for one stick of incense, then says it is a fine saying that must not be misunderstood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 萬法朗然，何思何慮？擬欲攝心，無本可據。我今為汝書此言，只此便是攝心處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse requested on gathering mind: the myriad things are clear; intending to gather mind has no basis to rely on; these words themselves are called the place of gathering mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又曰：攝心名戒。諸人將以攝心為戒耶？夫心是何物而可攝？攝又是何物而可攝心？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The address quotes gathering mind as the name of restraint, then asks what mind is that it can be gathered and what gathering is that it can gather mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若未到斯門。說是成非。攝心猶錯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Corrective statement: before reaching the stated gate, saying right makes wrong and gathering mind is still an error.

Occurrences.Kwic: 也要行道諷經。也要攝心除睡。藜羹黍飯塞飢瘡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Finite-action list in community verse: chant texts, gather the mind to drive off sleep, and use simple food to stop hunger.

RelatedTerms: place of gathering the mind (攝心處)
gather the mind to drive off sleep (攝心除睡)
gathering the mind is called restraint (攝心名戒)

Senses.Explanation: An imperative: 'put it down' or 'set it down,' with the final graph marking the command. The records use it for things held in the hands and for what a questioner says cannot be brought. When a monk raises his sitting cloth and asks for an answer, the teacher says, 'Put it down,' then says 'withdraw' when the monk starts to spread it. In the Yan Yang–Zhaozhou case, Yan Yang asks what to do when not one thing is brought; Zhaozhou says, 'Put it down.' When Yan Yang asks what there is to put down, Zhaozhou replies, 'If you cannot put it down, carry it away.' A second recorded exchange has Shakyamuni tell the Black-Clan Brahmin three times to put things down: first each flower, then, after both hands are empty, the six external objects, six internal faculties, and six intervening discriminations. Another exchange draws the text's own contrast: scattered thoughts are answered with 'put it down,' while not producing a single thought is answered with 'raise it up.' The phrase is an instruction within these specific exchanges; the entry preserves the imperative and its stated objects.
Senses.Note: The exact form has 340 matches in 126 files. The graph variant with the shorter form of the final character has nine matches in five files. The Yan Yang question 'when not one thing is brought' occurs eighty-four times in fifty-four files, and its follow-up 'since not one thing is brought' occurs fourteen times in fourteen. 'Put everything down at once' occurs five times in three files, while the direct opposite imperative 'raise it up' occurs once. None of the seven required definition formulas occurs, so the entry is built from complete exchanges, physical deployments, the text-drawn opposition, and later quotations of the case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 豈不聞昔有僧問趙州：一物不將來時如何？州曰：放下著。僧曰：一物不將來，放下箇甚麼？州曰：放不下，擔取去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address quotes the Yan Yang–Zhaozhou case: Yan Yang asks, 'What about when not one thing is brought?' Zhaozhou answers, 'Put it down.' Yan Yang asks, 'When not one thing is brought, what is there to put down?' Zhaozhou replies, 'If you cannot put it down, carry it away.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛曰。放下著。梵志遂放下左手一株華。佛又召仙人。放下著。梵志又放下右手一株華。佛又召仙人。放下著。梵志曰。世尊。我今兩手皆空。更教放下箇甚麼。佛曰。吾非教汝放捨其華。汝當放捨外六塵．內六根．中六識。一時捨却。無可捨處。是汝免生死處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps records Shakyamuni telling the Black-Clan Brahmin, 'Put it down.' The Brahmin puts down the flower in his left hand; at a second command he puts down the flower in his right. At the third command he says both hands are empty and asks what more to put down. Shakyamuni says he is not telling him to discard the flowers, but to discard at once the six external objects, six internal faculties, and six intervening discriminations, until there is no place of discarding; the record calls this his place of escaping birth and death.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又僧出眾，提起坐具，曰：請師答話。師曰：放下著。僧又作展勢，師曰：收。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk comes out of the assembly, raises his sitting cloth, and asks the teacher to answer. The teacher says, 'Put it down.' When the monk starts to spread it, the teacher says, 'Withdraw.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 恒鑒問云：「雜念紛飛時如何？」師云：「放下著。」進云：「一念不生時如何？」師云：「提起著。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hengjian asks, 'What about when miscellaneous thoughts fly about?' The teacher answers, 'Put it down.' Hengjian continues, 'What about when not one thought is produced?' The teacher answers, 'Raise it up.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 但請一時放下著。當人本體自周圓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says, 'I ask only that you put everything down at once; the person's own basic substance is complete of itself.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：向上還有事也無？師曰：放下著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks, 'Further above, is there still anything going on or not?' The teacher answers, 'Put it down.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'release' or 'let pass': to permit free movement rather than hold fast. The allowlisted record has 1,034 occurrences in 224 texts. Its recurrent formal counterpart is 'hold fast' (把定) or 'hold in place' (把住): one address says, 'holding fast: dripping water freezes and the rivers stop; releasing: the sun is warm, the wind mild, and the mountains and streams compete in beauty' (把定也，滴水滴凍，江河絕流；放行也，日暖風和，山川競秀), then asks which is good. Other records pair 'release' with 'draw back in' (收來) and use the compact binome 'drawing in and releasing' (收放). The term occurs as a finite verb, in the question 'what is a saying of release?' (如何是放行一句), in the phrase 'open a road of release' (放行一路), and in paired formulas such as 'holding fast and releasing' (把定放行). The texts give different recorded clauses under the two headings; this entry reports that deployment and does not assign a force beyond the words used.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 1,034 hits in 224 texts. Attested formations include 'release, then...' (放行則), 151 hits in 80 texts; 'drawing in and releasing' (收放), 310 in 143; 'holding fast and releasing' (把定放行), 15 in 13; 'a road of release' (放行一路), 7 in 6; 'what is release...?' (如何是放行), 11 in 11; and 'not release' (不放行), 40 in 36. No exact definitional formula of the forms 'X means release' or 'is called release' was found. The two hits for 'one who releases' (放行者) are predicative uses, not definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 把定也，滴水滴凍，江河絕流；放行也，日暖風和，山川競秀。且道把定好？放行好？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing head is the section for Tianzhang Yuanshan (越州天章元善禪師) in the Continuation of the Lamp from the Jianzhong Jingguo Era (建中靖國續燈錄). The address itself supplies the paired clauses and asks whether holding fast or releasing is good. The roster has no exact linkable spelling for this master, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如來正法眼藏委在今日。放行則瓦礫生光。把住則真金失色。權柄在手殺活臨時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Continued Record of the Lamp (續傳燈錄), under the heirs of Zhimen Zuo, the speaker says: 'the treasury of the true eye of the teaching is entrusted here today; on releasing, tiles and rubble shine; on holding in place, true gold loses its color; authority is in hand, killing and giving life follow the occasion.' The immediate master name is not exposed by the rough head pointer, so no roster attribution is asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今日打開布袋，放行一路，任汝諸人東跳西跳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinyuan Longqi's own record, in the Wanfu Chan Monastery at Mount Huangbo section. He says, 'today I open the cloth bag, open a road of release, and leave you all to jump east and west.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 把住即不問，如何是放行一句？」師云：「七通八達。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Northern Travel Collection of Tiantong Hongjue Min (天童弘覺忞禪師北遊集), the question sets holding in place aside and asks for 'a saying of release'; the master answers, 'open in seven directions and reaching in eight.' The roster has no exact linkable spelling for the named master, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。放行為人好。把住為人好。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's own discourse record. He asks, 'say: is releasing good for people, or is holding in place good for people?' The text records the question without selecting either member here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 把定放行各出一隻手。扶竪宗乘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen Huikai's comment under the public case headed 'Qianfeng's one road' (乾峯一路): 'holding fast and releasing each puts out one hand to raise the ancestral vehicle.' This is later case commentary, not speech attributed to either master in the encounter.

Senses.Explanation: On a battlefield, 'defeat' (敗) is a rout and 'breach' (闕) is a gap. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. The allowlisted corpus has 594 hits in 193 texts. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, 130 hits in 80 texts), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, 129 hits in 85 texts), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, 39 hits in 28 texts). In one direct exchange a monk asks, 'What failure do I have?' and receives the answer 'Wrong.' Elsewhere Dahui quotes Linji calling an old man's response 'a failure today,' then answers the question 'Where is his failure?' with 'The road is far and the night is long; stop carrying a torch, everyone, and blow it out while walking in the dark.' Yuan Cheng is asked how to have no failure and replies, 'Eat three meals.' A later comment can apply the verdict to both parties while also calling both adept: 'As failures, both are failures; as adepts, both are adepts.' These records leave the verdict attached to the cited exchange rather than supplying one universal defect that the word always names.
Senses.Note: The word carries a military register: 'rout' (敗) plus 'breach' (闕) becomes a verdict that an exchange has failed, as in 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕) and 'incur a failure' (納敗闕). All seven required definition formulas were searched; none produced a lexical definition. The entry therefore foregrounds the direct 'what failure?' exchange, the 'where is the failure?' retrospective, verdict uses, and the corpus's own two-party contrast. The rare 'no failure' construction (無敗闕) has one hit in one text. No occurrence is assigned to a master because each selected passage is a dialogue, a quoted case, or later commentary whose immediate speaker relation is carried in the attribution note.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日因僧入室師喚僧名僧應諾師云錯僧云某甲有什麼敗闕處師云錯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The ‘Examination and Discernment Sayings’ section records a monk asking what his failure is and the teacher answering ‘Wrong.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟云。這老漢今日敗闕。堂頭法叔禪師道。那裏是他敗闕處。妙喜道。路遠夜長休把火。大家吹殺暗中行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui comments on a raised Linji encounter after the presiding teacher asks where the failure lies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：如何得無敗闕？師曰：喫三頓飯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Questions and Answers section, Yuan Cheng answers the question how to have no failure with ‘Eat three meals.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 士便打，師一摑，云：不多好。師方拈棒，士把住，云：這賊今日一場敗闕。師笑云：是我拙？是公巧？士撫掌，云：平交，平交。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Qifeng encounter records a layman declaring a whole episode a failure, followed by the teacher’s question whether it was his clumsiness or the layman’s skill.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敗闕則二俱敗闕，作家則彼此作家
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later comment in the Cuiyan record applies both ‘failure’ and ‘adept’ to the two participants.

Occurrences.Kwic: 四十九年播土揚塵，三百餘會納盡敗闕。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A nirvana-day address says that forty-nine years and more than three hundred assemblies incurred failures throughout.

Occurrences.Kwic: 更問如何自納敗闕？良久，高聲召大眾，眾舉首，師曰：歸堂喫茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address asks how one incurs an exposed failure oneself, pauses, calls the assembly, and sends them back to drink tea.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a separate transmission outside the teachings
AlternateTargets: a special transmission apart from the scriptural teachings
Senses.Explanation: (教) = the scriptural or recorded teachings, (外) = outside/apart from, (別傳) = a separate transmission. The corpus glosses its own terms. Yunmen names (教) as the canon: (三乘十二分教豈是無言語)。(因什麼更道教外別傳) ('the three vehicles and the twelvefold teachings are hardly wordless -- why then go on to speak of a separate transmission outside the teachings?', T51n2076). (中峰廣錄) (Zhongfeng's extensive record) defines the phrase directly: (言說文字等乃教也)。(離言說文字等乃教外別傳也) ('speech and letters are the teachings; apart from speech and letters is the separate transmission outside the teachings') and (所云教外別傳者)。(即超出言象而妙契此心者也) ('what is called the separate transmission outside the teachings is precisely what goes beyond words and images and wondrously accords with this mind'); it names the referent -- (教外別傳者目之為禪)。(此禪即一心之異名) ('what is called the separate transmission outside the teachings is termed Chan; this Chan is another name for the one mind') -- and derives the label: (禪不依一切經法所詮)。(不依一切修證所得)。(不依一切見聞所解)。(不依一切門路所入)。(所以云教外別傳者也) ('Chan does not rest on what any scripture expounds, on what any refining and verifying obtains, on what any seeing-and-hearing understands, or on any gateway of entry -- therefore it is called the separate transmission outside the teachings'; all B25n0145; 教外別傳者 10 hits / 6 files). (古尊宿語錄) (the Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies) has (所謂教外別傳者蓋取其要妙也) ('what is called the separate transmission outside the teachings is so called for its essential subtlety', C077n1710). The charter scene is the Flower Sermon (世尊在靈山會上。拈華示眾。是時眾皆默然。唯迦葉尊者破顏微笑 -- 'the World-Honored One, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a flower and showed it to the assembly; the whole assembly was silent; only the venerable Kasyapa broke into a smile'), where the (正法眼藏) ('treasury of the true eye of the teaching') passes (不立文字)。(教外別傳)。(付囑摩訶迦葉) ('not setting up words -- a separate transmission outside the teachings -- entrusted to Mahakasyapa', X80n1565). Attested deployment: (a) the slogan -- adjacent to (不立文字) ('not setting up words') in 48 hits / 42 files (order reversed, 38 / 31), in the four-phrase frame with (直指人心) ('directly pointing at the human mind') / (見性成佛) ('seeing nature, becoming buddha'), the Blue Cliff Record variant carrying (單傳心印) ('the single transmission of the mind-seal'; 79 / 34); (b) a fixed test-question -- (如何是教外別傳) ('what is the separate transmission outside the teachings?'; 70 hits / 36 files), with the tails (一句) ('the one phrase of', 63 / 30), (底事) ('the matter of', 20 / 15), (底法) ('the teaching of', 7 / 6), (之旨) ('the purport of', 73 / 52) and the probe (別傳箇)/(個什麼) ('separately transmit WHAT?'; 13 files); recorded answers include Gushan's (喫茶去) ('go drink tea') and Shishuang's (非句) ('a non-phrase'); (c) Yunmen's question quoted above, asked of the phrase itself. B25n0145 also records an objection -- (豈教外果別有未盡之法為傳耶)。(儻別有所傳則名外道) ('is there really, outside the teachings, some further teaching left unexhausted to transmit? if something were separately transmitted, it would be called an outside way') -- and answers it in the same passage (茲復謂議者曰, 'then again he says to the objectors'), where the (言說文字) ('speech and letters') definition above appears together with (所云別傳者)。(非教外別有所謂禪也)。(非心外別有所謂法也) ('what is called separately transmitted is not that outside the teachings there is some separate thing called Chan, nor that outside the mind there is some separate thing called a teaching').
Senses.Note: 640 hits across 211 files of the 462-file allowlist (XML tags/notes/rdg stripped, whitespace collapsed, punctuation retained -- all counts in this entry use this convention). Two attested facets -- the four-phrase slogan and the test-question (如何是教外別傳) ('what is the separate transmission outside the teachings?') -- each appear across many independent masters and files. Curated occurrences span the founding legend in the (五燈會元) (Compendium of the Five Lamps), the (碧巖錄) (Blue Cliff Record), the (景德傳燈錄) (Jingde-era Lamp Record; Yunmen, Gushan), and the (古尊宿語錄) (Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies; Shishuang). ewk's 'outside the historical records' rendering is rejected against the Chinese, where the texts themselves gloss (教) as the scriptural teachings: (三乘十二分教) ('the three vehicles and the twelvefold teachings', T51n2076) and (言說文字等乃教也) ('speech and letters are the teachings', B25n0145).

Senses.Explanation: To appraise, sort out, or distinguish; noun constructions name the resulting appraisal or classificatory distinction. The term is attested 266 times in 126 allowlisted texts. A monk sets two episodes side by side and asks the teacher to “please appraise and distinguish” them (兩段不同，試請料揀); another record asks who can sort out a presented conjunction. The same appraisal vocabulary appears in Linji's “Four Selections” (四料揀). The Record of the Eyes of Humans and Gods asks, “the Four Selections—what do the selections select?” (四料揀，料揀何法), and another exposition begins with people of middle and lower capacity under that heading. A later record calls paired evaluative formulas “the old so-called selection sayings” (古所謂料揀語). The public act, resulting distinction, and named set remain one appraisal-and-selection family; noun and verb grammar alone do not create different lexical things.
Senses.Note: The former action/result targets were not independently distinguishable from their glosses. The standalone word remains compatible with the separate named Four Selections article and its four formulations. The Chan deviation is public appraisal of sayings, encounters, and speakers, plus its use in Linji classificatory vocabulary.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “cut the cat.” This graph form occurs 156 times in 53 allowlisted texts and is an orthographic variant of “cut the cat” (斬貓), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts it in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase is used as a case title, a monk's question, a subject for verse, and a later master's cited precedent. One later exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; the master tells that questioner to repent. The exchange attests that the corpus itself places the case beside the rule against killing, but it does not state why Nanquan acted. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports that students call Guizong's snake-cutting and Nanquan's cat-cutting “timely wondrous function” or “great function appears, not retaining rules,” and explicitly says neither label gives the account.
Senses.Note: The simplified-looking graph for “cat” (猫) is a historical orthographic form alongside the other “cat” graph (貓) in the corpus. The two forms are separate searchable articles but carry the same case sense. The entry reports the explicit precept question and Dahui's rejection; it does not supply an unrecorded rationale for the killing.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, cut (斬) kudzu-and-wisteria creepers (葛藤). The parent image names verbal entanglement in Chan records, but this exact compound is very thin and occurs only in late framing prose. One text praises a master for effacing forms and cutting vine-tangle; a preface says that Linji's staff and shout cut all vine-tangle; a biographical preface pairs cutting vine-tangle with destroying thorn thickets. The Zen deviation comes from the established Chan use of creepers for entangling words, here made the object of cutting. Unlike the much commoner longer forms 'cut off the vine-tangle' and 'sever the vine-tangle,' the exact phrase is not attested in this concordance as a live-exchange command, so this entry does not present it as one.
Senses.Note: Exact-form count: 3 hits in 3 allowlisted texts, all curated. One late paratextual sense, mechanically multi-source but narrowly stated. Family checked against vine-tangle (葛藤), cut off the vine-tangle (斬斷葛藤: 16 hits in 15 texts), and sever the vine-tangle (截斷葛藤: 100 hits in 70 texts). Evidence from those longer forms is not assigned to this exact headword.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'cut the snake.' In the Chan corpus the expression is chiefly a compact reference to Guizong Zhichang's public case: he cut a passing snake with a hoe, a lecture monk called him coarse, Guizong raised the hoe as 'coarse,' made a cutting gesture as 'fine,' and asked where the monk had seen him cut the snake. Later masters ask about 'the old man's snake-cutting,' pair it with Nanquan cutting the cat and Dasui burning the clearing, turn 'the snake-cutter' into a stock agent noun, and compare Guizong's act with raising the whisk. The case is also explicitly challenged from the precepts: records ask why Guizong cut the snake when killing living beings is a major precept or when a precept-keeper will not tread on living grass. One answer tells the questioner to repent; another asks, 'is it cutting, or is it killing?' A sermon quoting the rule to rescue animals from killing then asks what could have saved Guizong's snake. The corpus does not call this snake poisonous and does not say it threatened the community.
Senses.Note: The exact expression occurs 137 times in 65 allowlisted texts, across core case retellings, public questions, sermons, verse, and commentarial collections. Its plain verbal sense and case-label use name the same act, so item 8 does not require a split. The later record supplies incompatible appraisals rather than different referents: one verse calls the cutting compassion, Dahui rejects familiar functional explanations, and Tianran condemns imitating the case as license for unrestrained conduct. They remain reported evidence within one sense, not a menu of dictionary readings.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “cut the cat.” This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; the master tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”
Senses.Note: The two cat graphs (貓/猫) are orthographic variants and receive separate searchable articles with one shared case sense. The entry preserves the explicit precept challenges and refusals without deciding why Nanquan acted.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to sever an arm. In the Chan record it overwhelmingly names the founding episode in which Shenguang, later named Huike, stands in the snow before Bodhidharma, cuts off his left arm, and places it before him. The lamp account has Bodhidharma say, 'you have now cut off your arm before me; your seeking may be accepted,' and then rename him Huike. Later records compress the episode into paired formulas—'standing in the snow and cutting off the arm,' 'cutting off the arm and pacifying the mind,' or 'face the wall for nine years / cut off the arm and pacify the mind'—and repeatedly reopen it as a public question. One master asks, 'what did the cutting off of the arm accomplish?' and strikes the staff before leaving the seat. Another is asked why one cuts off an arm to seek the Way if this house style is inherent in everyone; he replies, 'there are many mistaken understandings.' Still another says, 'why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?' The Chan-specific bend is that Huike's bodily act becomes compact lineage and interview language, quoted, challenged, and criticized across later records. These later uses do not authorize this entry to declare the act a required sacrifice or explain its intention beyond what the accounts say.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 563 hits in 216 texts. Family check covered standing in the snow (立雪), Shenguang or Huike (神光／慧可), pacifying the mind (安心), seeking the Way or teaching (求道／求法), nine years facing the wall (面壁九年), and the Second Patriarch (二祖). All refer back to the same bodily act; narrative, epithet, and later question are not different things. Names remain contextual because Huike is a lineage patriarch and belongs on the master roster, not as a separate dictionary figure.
