Occurrences.AttributionNote: United Lamps Assembly (聯燈會要), under Yangzhou Guangxiao Huijue. In an exchange about age the master says, 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在), documenting the ordinary temporal construction.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the last word or final phrase
Senses.Explanation: Literally “the very last” (末後) plus “phrase or line” (句): the last word or final phrase. Its central case is the Deshan–Yantou story. Xuefeng reports Deshan's conduct to Yantou, who says, “for all his stature, Deshan has not yet grasped the last word” (大小德山未會末後句在). Asked for it, Yantou answers only, “want to know the last word? Just this” (要識末後句，只者是). The phrase becomes the stock question “what is the last word?” (如何是末後句), receiving many recorded answers. Other texts set it beside the first word and middle word, or say that “the last word only arrives at the locked barrier” (末後一句始到牢關). The same literal phrase is also used contextually for a master's actual final utterance or death-period words. Records ask for a late master's last word on a memorial day, say that dying seated or standing is “called the last word,” and narrate Sixin Wuxin answering a request for a last word with a verse before his death. These death and memorial uses are attested instances of the same last or final utterance, not a different lexical thing. The texts give many answers and situations but no single further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The phrase occurs more than one thousand times across more than two hundred allowlisted texts. The Deshan–Yantou case recurs across independent records, while the bare challenge and death or memorial uses have their own spread. The former “last word” and “master's last word at death” targets described a general phrase and a contextual subtype of that same phrase; they are merged. Compare the way up and beyond (向上一路), upward dynamic (向上機), last locked barrier (末後牢關), turning phrase (轉身句), late master's last word (先師末後句), memorial morning (忌晨), and dying seated or standing (坐脫立亡).

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪峰舉似巖頭。頭曰：「老漢未會末後句在。」山謂頭曰：「你不肯老僧那？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The central case: Yantou's verdict that Deshan has not yet grasped the last word.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧到巖頭舉似頭。頭云：「雪峰不會末後句。」僧請益巖頭。頭云：「雪峰與我同條生，不與我同條死。要識末後句，只者是。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yantou says only, “want to know the last word? Just this,” without supplying a dictionary definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 小德山未會末後句在。山聞。令侍者喚師去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent transmission-record witness of the Deshan verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是末後句。師曰。雙林樹下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase appears as the stock challenge “what is the last word?” and receives a recorded answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐脫立亡喚作末後句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text says, “dying seated or standing upright is called the last word,” an explicit death-context application.

Occurrences.Kwic: 偉哉大丈夫，不會末後句。」遂就寢，右脅而化。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master quotes the Deshan verdict, then lies down on his right side and dies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聲聲道：『願聞先師末後句！』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker repeatedly says, “I long to hear the late master's last word,” anchoring memorial usage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忌晨上堂先師當年末後句與人皮下挑出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A memorial-morning address raises the late master's last word of that year.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有乞末後句者。新與偈云。末後一句子。直須心路絕。六根門既空。萬法無生滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: During Sixin Wuxin's final illness, someone requests a last word and he answers with a verse; the biography then records his death.

Senses.Explanation: Literally the "final" or "last" (末後) "strong, locked" (牢) "barrier or checkpoint" (關): the "final locked barrier," attested 42 times in 22 allowlisted texts. The records speak of passing through or penetrating it, and use it as a severe last check. Yuan'an, after listing a series of named cases, calls "this whole tangle" (者一落索) the final locked barrier and criticizes estimating it through cognitive calculation. Juelang says even someone who has understood "this affair" but has "not passed through the final locked barrier" (未透末後牢關) can still mistake a shadow for a head. Yulin asks, "how many people have passed the final locked barrier?" (末後牢關幾人透得). Other formulations say it is "not measurable by humans or gods" (人天莫測) and "not understood by a thousand sages" (千聖不曉).
Senses.Note: The headword clusters with "pass through the final locked barrier" (透末後牢關, 7 occurrences), "break free through the final locked barrier" (透脫末後牢關), and the shorter "final checkpoint" (末後一關, 8). The related line "only with the final sentence does one first reach the locked barrier" (末後一句始到牢關, 54) explains the compound's final-position force without itself containing the exact four-graph headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 者一落索，謂之末後牢關
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a list of named cases, Yuan'an says, "this whole tangle is called the final locked barrier." The record's master name has no safe exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 即有已悟此事而未透末後牢關者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang says, "there are even those who have understood this affair but have not passed through the final locked barrier."

Occurrences.Kwic: 末後牢關幾人透得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yulin asks, "how many people have passed the final locked barrier?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 末後牢關，千聖不曉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang's line: "the final locked barrier—a thousand sages do not understand it."

Occurrences.Kwic: 末後牢關，人天莫測。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction in Baiyu's record says, "the final locked barrier cannot be measured by humans or gods." The speaker has no safe exact roster link.

AlternateTargets: originally there is not a single thing
from the first, not one thing
Senses.Explanation: (本來) from the root / origin, originally + (無) there is no + (一物) one thing: "from the origin, not one thing." The line is the third of (慧能)'s verse in the received (宗寶) (六祖大師法寶壇經): (菩提本無樹)，(明鏡亦非臺)；(本來無一物)，(何處惹塵埃) (the text writes his name 惠能). The corpus shows the line is a feature of the LATER Platform-Sutra text: the Dunhuang (壇經) (T48n2007) gives the same verse with the third line "the buddha-nature is ever pure" (佛性常清淨，何處有塵埃), without (本來無一物). Across the lamp records the couplet varies — (何處惹塵埃) (法寶壇經); (何處有塵埃) (祖堂集, which carries the verse twice, with first lines 菩提本無樹 and 身非菩提樹); and (本來無一物何假拂塵埃) with first line (菩提本非樹) (傳燈玉英集). Zen-scoped the phrase occurs 214 hits / 106 texts; the contracted (本無一物) 34 / 30. Attested deployment beyond the verse: (洞山良价) issues a verdict on the line — asked why (神秀)'s (時時勤拂拭) verse did not win the robe, (洞山答曰)：「(直道本來無一物)，(也未得衣缽在)。」 (祖堂集), and (師有時垂語曰直道本來無一物猶未消得佗鉢袋子) (傳燈玉英集): even to say "from the origin, not one thing" has not yet earned the robe-and-bowl. (黃檗希運) in the (宛陵錄) quotes (本來無一物何處有塵埃), and when a monk asks "from the origin not one thing — is 'no-thing' then it?" (本來無一物無物便是否) answers "even 'no-thing' is not it" (無亦不是). The line is also raised as a stock tag, e.g. (舉六祖云本來無一物長慶云萬象之中獨露身). The texts assign the phrase no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Primary attribution: (慧能)'s verse in the received (六祖大師法寶壇經) (T48n2008, 行由第一; the text spells the name 惠能, roster 慧能, editor 宗寶). The (傳燈玉英集) verse-variant (本非樹…何假拂塵埃) is the SAME Platform-Sutra episode transmitted in a Jingde-lamp digest, so attributed to (慧能) with the variant noted. (洞山良价) is the named speaker of the verdict (洞山答曰… / 師[=洞山]有時垂語…) in (祖堂集) and (傳燈玉英集) — two independent witnesses. (黃檗希運) in the (宛陵錄) (inside 古尊宿語錄, cb:mulu 黃檗斷際禪師宛陵錄); he quotes the couplet twice (0633b04, 0636c03). The B27n0152 raising (paired with 長慶's line) is a later stock raising, so MasterName null. The Dunhuang (佛性常清淨) reading is reported for contrast only and is NOT an occurrence of this headword — T48n2007 is therefore deliberately not listed in SourceTexts. Multi-source: (壇經), (祖堂集), (傳燈玉英集), (古尊宿語錄); masters (慧能), (洞山良价), (黃檗希運).

Occurrences.Kwic: 明鏡亦非臺；本來無一物，何處惹塵埃？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (六祖大師法寶壇經) (received 宗寶 edition), (行由第一); (慧能)'s verse (text: 惠能偈曰). The primary attestation — third line (本來無一物), couplet (何處惹塵埃).

Occurrences.Kwic: 本非樹心鏡亦非臺本來無一物何假拂塵埃
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (a Jingde-lamp digest), cb:mulu (三十二祖弘忍大師) (the robe-transmission episode falls in Hongren's chapter); the verse is written by (能) in the narrative (能自秉燭令童子於秀偈側寫一偈云菩提本非樹…大師後見此偈…). Records a variant wording: first line (菩提本非樹), couplet (何假拂塵埃). Attributed to (慧能) as the same episode, not a later raising.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山答曰：「直道本來無一物，也未得衣缽在。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集) (952), cb:mulu (洞山和尚); (洞山良价)'s verdict on the verse — asked why (神秀)'s (時時勤拂拭) did not win the robe, (洞山答曰)：(直道本來無一物)，(也未得衣缽在). Named speaker (洞山).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師有時垂語曰直道本來無一物猶未消得佗鉢袋子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集), cb:mulu (筠州洞山良价禪師) (師 = 洞山); the same verdict, worded (直道本來無一物猶未消得佗鉢袋子). Independent second witness of Dongshan's verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問本來無一物無物便是否師云無亦不是菩提無是處
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄), cb:mulu (黃檗斷際禪師宛陵錄) (黃檗希運); he quotes (本來無一物何處有塵埃) (0633b04), then when asked (本來無一物無物便是否) answers (無亦不是) (even 'no-thing' is not it). Master's own record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉六祖云本來無一物長慶云萬象之中獨露身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄), (小叅); a raised stock tag — (舉六祖云本來無一物長慶云萬象之中獨露身). A later raising pairing (慧能)'s line with (長慶)'s, so MasterName null per the raised-case rule.

AlternateTargets: the face you had before your parents were born
Senses.Explanation: Literally 'the face one originally has.' Its origin is the Dayu Ridge story: the monk Huiming, chasing Huineng for the robe, cannot lift it; Huineng says 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — right at such a moment, which is Elder Ming's original face?' (不思善，不思惡，正恁麼時，阿那箇是明上座本來面目), and Ming is awakened. From this it becomes one of the corpus's most common test-questions, above all in the form 'your original face before your father and mother were born' (父母未生前本來面目). In the record the answer is characteristically shown rather than defined: Fuchuan (覆船) sticks out his tongue; a Dongshan-line master answers 'not walking the bird's path' (不行鳥道) and 'seeing mountains as mountains, seeing waters as waters' (見山是山，見水是水). Asked head-on, 'what is … the original face?' (如何是…本來面目) is a standing test-question (274 hits in 116 allowlist texts); recorded exchanges include 'What is your original face?' — 'Eyebrows horizontal, nose straight' (「如何是你本來面目？」師云：「眉橫鼻直。」, J28nB210), and the monk who says 'it cannot be known by wisdom, cannot be cognized by consciousness' and is told 'I asked about your original face and you give me all these principles' (僧云：「不可以智知，不可以識識。」師云：「問汝本來面目，說許多道理」, J28nB202); in J28nB209 the monk's 'the wind cannot blow it away' (風刮不著) is met with 'Say more!' (師云：「更道看！」) — the monk is speechless, and the master strikes (僧無語，師便棒). The corpus's own lists of what students investigate name it among the standard sayings: 'some investigate the word no (無); some investigate the original face; some investigate who-is-reciting-the-buddha's-name — the cases differ, the doubt investigated is the same' (或有參無字者。或有參本來面目者。或有參究念佛者。公案雖異疑究是同, T48n2021; likewise J38nB429 'such as those investigating the original face before father and mother were born, or investigating who is the one reciting the buddha's name' 如參父母未生前本來面目者，或參念佛底是誰者, and J28nB208). On the origin story itself, one record cites 'which one is your original face, elder?' (阿那個是你上座本來面目) and asks: 'when did he ever say that the moment of not thinking good or evil IS your original face?' (亦何曾說不思善惡時，即是你本來面目乎？, J25nB174).
Senses.Note: Overwhelmingly attested (1320 hits across 264 allowlist texts) and uniform — no master bends the base meaning, so a single corpus-wide sense is honest. Some later masters (the line of Nanyue Jiqi 南嶽繼起 and Sanfeng Hanyue 三峰漢月, J34nB301) 'forbid even mentioning the original face' (不許人提著本來面目). Collocations (allowlist grep): the explicit question-form 'the original face before father and mother were born' (父母未生前本來面目) 92 hits in 57 texts (the framing 'before father and mother were born, which is your original face?' 父母未生已前，那箇是你本來面目 also attested, J28nB208); the pointing formula 'this is your original face' (是汝／你本來面目) 70 hits in 44 texts (plus the same phrase with the variant graph for 'your', 是爾本來面目, twice).

Occurrences.Kwic: 盧曰：不思善，不思惡，正恁麼時，阿那箇是明上座本來面目？師當下大悟，徧體汗流，泣禮數拜
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Dayu Ridge origin story (Huineng to Huiming), here in the Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書). The locus classicus of the phrase: 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — which is Elder Ming's original face?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問：「如何是父母未生前本來面目？」門云：「今日汝且隨我往頂山寺，回來與汝說。」門回，師跪而啟曰：「如今求老和尚為某甲說。」門驀豎起拳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The dominant question-form 'the original face before your parents were born' (父母未生前本來面目), put to the master as the saying under investigation; the master's answer is a suddenly raised fist (驀豎起拳). Independent witness in a Jiaxing-canon recorded-sayings collection (語錄).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「三峰老和尚不許人提著本來面目，和尚尋常不許人提著本來面目，因什今日又要這上座明取本來面目？」師曰：「哀哉！法門不幸。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Sanfeng / Nanyue Jiqi line forbids even mentioning the original face (不許人提著本來面目) — the monk presses the master on the inconsistency; the master answers 'Alas! Misfortune for the teaching gate' (哀哉！法門不幸).

AlternateTargets: the matter of one's own lot
Senses.Explanation: The graphs join 'one's own portion, allotment, or lot' (本分) to 'matter or affair' (事): the matter that belongs to one's own basic lot. The corpus sets it against 'outside one's lot' or 'extra' (分外) and records about 840 occurrences across 184 allowlisted texts. It is repeatedly asked as 'what is one's own fundamental matter?' (如何是本分事), 'what is the student's own fundamental matter?' (如何是學人本分事), and 'what is a monk's own fundamental matter?' (如何是衲僧本分事). In the early Patriarchs' Hall Collection (祖堂集), an official tells an old monk, 'one who has left home has an own-lot matter; what is your own-lot matter, monk?' (出家自有本分事。作摩生是和尚本分事？), and the monk has no reply (無對). A later record directly defines it: 'the own-lot matter is where the person's own root-destiny comes to rest' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). Asked 'what is Shanglan's own-lot matter?' (如何是上藍本分事), Shanglan answers, 'not borrowed from the thousand sages, not sought among the myriad devices' (不從千聖借豈向萬機求). Zhaozhou says a lineage master must 'receive people with the own-lot matter' (以本分事接人). Another master points at the questioner and says, 'it is your own matter' (是你本分事); another says, 'eating gruel and rice is your own matter' (喫粥喫飯是汝本分事). A recorded contrast says, 'the moment you speak of the own-lot matter, it has already become extra' (你纔說本分事早是分外了). The same 'own-lot' graph family includes 'own-lot fodder' (本分草料), 'own-lot tongs and hammer' (本分鉗鎚), and 'an own-lot master of the lineage' (本分宗師).
Senses.Note: This is the Chan technical use, not the ordinary role-duty sense recorded separately below. The corpus itself glosses it as "the own-lot matter is where the person's own root-destiny comes to rest" (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). Grep-verified counts (Zen allowlist): bare (本分) 2,482 hits in 321 texts; (本分事) as a contiguous string 773 in 181 (line-split hits raise the raw total toward the ~840 above).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰不從千聖借豈向萬機求
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (Wang Sui's abridgement of the Jingde-era transmission record); answer of (洪州上藍令超禪師) (Chan master Lingchao of Shanglan, Hongzhou) to the stock question on the prior line (如何是上藍本分事, 'what is Shanglan's own-lot matter?'). The answer states the own-lot matter is not borrowed from the sages nor sought among the myriad devices.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若是宗師，須以本分事接人始得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (趙州錄); Zhaozhou's principle that a genuine master receives people with the own-lot matter (以本分事接人), not with a stock teaching — his locus classicus, echoed across later texts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 指學人云：「是你本分事。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集); in a monk-master exchange (如何是本分事?) the master answers by pointing at the student — 'it's YOUR own matter.' Two-speaker exchange, section master not verified here, so MasterName left null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫粥喫飯是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hall-talk leveling the own-lot matter to the ordinary (part of a series: investigating Chan and studying the Way 參禪學道, eating gruel and rice 喫粥喫飯, shitting and pissing 屙屎撒尿, walking, sitting and sleeping 行坐打眠 are all 是汝本分事 'your own-lot matter'). Speaker not individually verified; MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你纔說本分事，早是分外了
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The (本分) / (分外) axis made explicit: to name the own-lot matter is already to make it 'extra' (分外). Speaker not individually verified; MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct in-corpus definition: the own-lot matter is where the person's own root-destiny comes to rest.

Occurrences.Kwic: 出家自有本分事。作摩生是和尚本分事？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An early public question insists that one who has left home has an own-lot matter and asks the monk what his is; the monk has no answer.

AlternateTargets: the business proper to one's role
Senses.Explanation: In ordinary institutional use, 'one's proper duty' (本分事) is the business that belongs to a person's role. A monastic admonition calls keeping the precepts a bhikshu's proper duty, then condemns neglect of rules and disorderly conduct. This is an assigned role-duty, not the fundamental matter asked about in Chan public exchanges.
Senses.Note: One allowlisted source presently anchors this distinct ordinary use; it is kept separate because the referent is an assigned monastic duty rather than the Chan fundamental matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既稱比丘持戒是本分事，忽略繩趨，放蕩規矩，取玷法門，自招罪過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monastic admonition identifies keeping precepts as a bhikshu's proper duty and rebukes neglect of regulated conduct.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the primary or original investigation. The possessives and verbal predicates in later Chinese Chan records make its local use concrete. A hall leader is told to know each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; another passage says that not knowing a person's primary investigation leaves the leader without a way to act. Speakers tell people to place the saying under their primary investigation before their eyes, raise their primary investigation, or warn that they have dropped one line of it behind their head. The compound can take 'public case' or 'word, saying, conversational thread' after it, and can itself be said to be broken through. One direct question asks, 'What is primary investigation?' The answer gives a particular example: if one trusts the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate who is recollecting buddha; this is what that speaker calls primary investigation. Another text says that the Chan house relies on primary investigation and that when primary investigation breaks through it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. These predicates describe the assigned subject and the act of investigating it without turning the term into a named system.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 232 matches in 100 files. The expanded phrase 'word or saying under primary investigation' has eighty-nine matches in fifty files; 'raise the primary investigation' has twenty matches in fifteen; 'public case of primary investigation' has four in four; and 'one line of primary investigation' has three in three. One text has the only direct 'what is primary investigation?' formula and its own example; two texts use 'the so-called primary investigation.' The phrase is strongly possessive: texts say 'each person's,' 'one's own,' 'the one assigned,' and 'not knowing his.' No evidence supports treating it as an untranslated foreign object or as a master-specific sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何謂本參？若於念佛法門信得及，但參是誰念佛，所謂本參也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A reply to a layman asks, 'What is primary investigation?' It answers, 'If you trust the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate only who is recollecting buddha; this is what is called primary investigation.' This is the speaker's particular example, not the only saying attached to the compound elsewhere.

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲至堂中，先須識禪眾之號與貌，與各各本參話頭，然後可以垂手鍛鍊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A text on managing the hall says, 'Before going into the hall, first know the names and appearances of the Chan assembly and each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; only then can you extend a hand and apply the forge.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 各將本參話頭頓在面前，如靠須彌山相似，直教心心無間，念念無虧，行住坐臥也如是
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher tells each person, 'Place the word or saying under your primary investigation before you, as if leaning against Mount Sumeru. Let mind after mind have no interval and thought after thought no gap; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are also like this.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 你平日疑情不切，將一句本參丟在腦後，如今豎起脊梁，把話頭放在面前
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'Ordinarily your condition of doubt is not urgent; you throw one line of your primary investigation behind your head. Now straighten your spine and put the word or saying before you.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 提起本參，晝夜切磋，琢磨千生業障，一刻冰消瓦解
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'Raise the primary investigation; cut and polish it day and night. Grind away the obstructions of a thousand lives, and in one instant ice melts and tiles dissolve.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 宗中之相，惟據本參。本參破如月印千江
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A text says, 'The Chan house's form relies only on primary investigation. When primary investigation breaks through, it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本參公案急要翻身，胸次疑團直須打破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'At the public case of primary investigation, urgently turn over; the mass of doubt in your breast must be broken open.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, native ground. The term occurs 529 times in 195 allowlisted texts. Its dominant Zen-loaded deployment is the fixed phrase 'native-ground scenery': records say to recognize one's original face and tread one's native-ground scenery, warn that wrong roads conceal each person's native-ground scenery, and ask that it be illuminated or fully seen through. A preface says the records return to the person's own native-ground scenery; teaching-seat records place it in bowing, turning, daily activity, or the lifting of a staff. The corpus treats this ground and its scenery as something belonging to each person and subject to public demand and display. It does not define it as a metaphysical substrate.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded referent. Split from the ordinary adjective 'local/native' because a person's figurative ground and local officials are different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝等諸人須信本來是佛，各須識取本來面目，蹋著本地風光。若識得本來面目，黃金世界白玉為身，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse directly pairs recognizing the original face with treading native-ground scenery.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是者兩般錯路，便掩蔽却人人本地風光，若不蹋著本地風光，終不能免此兩種錯路，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same record says two wrong roads conceal each person's native-ground scenery.

Occurrences.Kwic: 閱是語者，可盡五家差別之元，以明自己差別之智，總歸當人本地風光，全機大用出於文字之表，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Five Houses preface says the records return to the person's native-ground scenery.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已過關者，聞恁麼道，掉臂而去，二六時中折旋俯仰，無非本地風光；脫未諳悉，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat discourse applies native-ground scenery to bowing and turning throughout the day.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二要顯發判院朝奉本地風光，三要使其子子孫孫於無盡大光明藏中受用無盡。乃以拂子於空中點一點，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A memorial discourse explicitly proposes to display a named patron's native-ground scenery, then moves the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正當恁麼時，本地不動一句作麼生道？一切水月一月攝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address asks how to speak one phrase of the unmoving native ground, anchoring the bare headword outside the scenery compound.

Senses.Explanation: As an ordinary adjective, the same graphs mean local or native to a place. The monastic code's imperial proclamation lists 'local officials' among military officers, envoys, common people, and monks. This administrative referent is different from a person's native ground and therefore receives its own sense.
Senses.Note: One clear curated Zen-allowlist witness currently anchors the ordinary administrative sense; it is kept separate under the different-thing test.

Occurrences.Kwic: 城子裏達魯花赤官人每根底。往來使臣每根底。本地面官人每根底。百姓每根底。眾和尚每根底。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monastic code's proclamation uses the graphs adjectivally for local officials in an administrative list.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the native scenery of one's own ground
AlternateTargets: the scenery of one's home ground
Senses.Explanation: One's own ground or native place (本地), plus scenery or view (風光): Literally "the scenery of one's home ground." 382 occurrences across 161 allowlist files. The corpus pairs it with "original face" (本來面目): the two run together as "the native scenery of one's own ground, the original face" (本地風光本來面目; 4× in 2 files — Yuanwu's recorded sayings 圓悟語錄: 於動靜語默覺夢之間。無不皆是本地風光本來面目, "amid motion and stillness, speech and silence, waking and dream, there is nothing that is not the native scenery of one's own ground, the original face"; Dahui's recorded sayings 大慧語錄: 各人本地風光本來面目, "each person's own native scenery, original face") and stand in parallel clauses in Yuanwu Keqin's instructions: "step onto the native scenery of your own ground; clearly see the original face" (蹋著本地風光，明見本來面目) and "clearly attest the native scenery of your own ground; clearly see the original face" (明證本地風光，明見本來面目; both X69n1357). Attested verb collocations (allowlist, grep-verified): 'step onto the native scenery' (蹋著本地風光, 23× in 13 files), "clearly see," (明見本地風光 2×), "recognize for oneself," (自識本地風光 1× — Dahui: 故設方便誘引之。令其自識本地風光, "expedients are set up to lead one to recognize one's own native scenery"), "clearly attest," (明證本地風光 1×). Yuanwu's small-assembly talk sets it beside two negations: "treading on the native scenery of one's own ground — not following sound-and-form, not dwelling in profane or sacred" (踏著本地風光。不隨聲色不居凡聖). It is posed as a test question — "what is the native scenery of one's own ground?" (如何是本地風光; 8 allowlist files) — with recorded answers: "it has always been going in and out at your face-gate," (嘗在汝面門出入 Miyun's recorded sayings 密雲禪師語錄, J10nA158), "the heavens open, day after day new," (天開日日新 J27nB193), "the bright sun shines in mid-sky," (杲日麗中天 J37nB388), and raising the whisk with "do you see?" (見麼, J38nB424). One exchange draws a contrast with ordinary "scenery" (風光): asked "what is the native scenery of one's own ground?" (如何是本地風光), a layman answers "the crescent moon curves, shining on how many isles — how many people rejoice, how many grieve" (月子彎彎照幾洲，幾人歡樂幾人愁), and the questioner returns "I am not asking about that scenery," (不問者箇風光 X82n1571). The texts deploy the term through these pairings, verbs, and answers without assigning it a gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense recorded: the verb collocations and the pairing with "original face" (本來面目) recur across masters and centuries (counts in the explanation); no master-specific bending found. Extremely well attested (382 hits across 161 allowlist files). Keep the rendering on the graphs — "one's own ground," (本地) "scenery" (風光) — concrete; the texts do not state an abstraction ("the Absolute") in its place.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蹋著本地風光，明見本來面目
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Essentials of Mind of Chan Master Foguo Keqin (佛果克勤禪師心要 — Yuanwu Keqin's letters/instructions); governing head "shown to the monk Min" (示民上人) — his own "teaching words" (法語). The paired clauses "native scenery of one's own ground" (本地風光) / "original face" (本來面目), verb "step onto" (蹋著).

Occurrences.Kwic: 踏著本地風光。不隨聲色不居凡聖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), head "small assembly 4" (小參四) — Yuanwu's small-assembly talk. Sets "treading on the native scenery of one's own ground" (踏著本地風光) beside "not following sound-and-form, not dwelling in profane or sacred" (不隨聲色不居凡聖).

Occurrences.Kwic: 故設方便誘引之。令其自識本地風光
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄), head "shown to the layman Miaoming, Li Bohe of the Secretariat" (示妙明居士李知省伯和) — Dahui's "teaching words" (法語) to a layman. Expedients are set up (故設方便誘引之, "therefore expedients are devised to lead him on") to lead one to recognize one's own native scenery (本地風光).

Occurrences.Kwic: 比丘尼問：「如何是本地風光？」師云：「嘗在汝面門出入。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun (密雲禪師語錄). A nun asks and the master answers, so MasterName is null under the two-speaker rule. The answerer is Miyun Yuanwu: 'it has always been going in and out at your face-gate' (嘗在汝面門出入).

Senses.Explanation: Original or root mind. The word occurs 748 times in 157 allowlisted texts. The Mirror Record says mind has no form, color, root, lodging, arising, extinction, or observable contemplation; if something observable can be carried out, that text assigns it to reception, conception, activity, and discrimination rather than original mind. The Platform Record pairs recognizing one’s original mind with seeing one’s original nature (若識自本心，見自本性). Other records say it is neither joined nor separate, reject the claim that it first needs stillness, and place original nature and original mind together. These are differing corpus predicates of one textual term, not a menu of interpretations.
Senses.Note: Primary inherited Buddhist/Chan sense. Cross-check original nature (本性), true mind, and no-mind as neighboring entries with their own predicates. No single imported metaphysical definition is imposed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心無形色。無根無住。無生無滅。亦無覺觀可行。若有可觀行者。即是受想行識。非是本心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says, 'Mind has no form or color, no root and no lodging, no arising and no extinction, nor any noticing or contemplating that can be carried out. If something observable can be carried out, it is reception, conception, activity, and discrimination; it is not original mind.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲識汝本心非合亦非離
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says, 'If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不識本心，學法無益；若識自本心，見自本性
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'Not recognizing original mind, studying the teaching is of no benefit; if you recognize your own original mind, see your own original nature.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本心不寂要假寂靜。本來寂故何用寂靜。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record rejects the claim that original mind is not still and therefore requires stillness: 'Because it is originally still, what use is stillness?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖祖佛佛只說如人。本性本心別無道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record says, 'The patriarchs and buddhas only speak according to the person: original nature and original mind, with no other principle.'

Senses.Explanation: A person’s prior intention or purpose. In one event account the speaker says, “this day’s affair was not my original intention” (此日之事，故非本心) and immediately explains that he had not intended even to reside on a mountain. In a succession discussion another speaker says that nobody had accorded with his original intention except Mingyuan (無有契我本心者). These event and decision contexts refer to intention, not original mind.
Senses.Note: Ordinary intention sense. Copies of the same “this day’s affair” event in several compilations were treated as one transmitted witness. The phrase “depart from original mind/intention” was excluded because its referent is ambiguous.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大眾，此日之事，故非本心。實謂祇箇住山寧有意，向來成佛亦無心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says that the day’s event was not his original intention and immediately denies having intended even to reside on a mountain or become a buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我雖則繼席六載，無有契我本心者，惟明元隨我十餘年
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a succession discussion, the speaker says that during six years in the seat nobody accorded with his original intention except Mingyuan, who had followed him for more than ten years.

Senses.Explanation: One's nature as it is from the outset. Chan records repeatedly use 'see one's own original nature' beside 'recognize one's own original mind.' The Platform Record makes seeing it the distinction between remaining outside the gate and entering, and describes it as not arising or extinguishing. The Mirror Record says that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct. These are the texts' recorded descriptions; the English should preserve the plain noun phrase rather than substitute a later explanatory system. The omitted collocation "original nature empty" (本性空) occurs forty times in thirty texts, but it has more than one syntax. Twenty-seven occurrences in twenty-five texts belong to the fixed line, "understand body and mind, original nature empty; how would this person differ from buddha?" (了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別). A later Chan address raises that line and immediately comments, "the buddha-body is neither real nor empty; buddha-as-appearance is not appearance" (佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻). The Source-Mirror Record gives a separate explicit definition: "as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean" (本性空者，即是自性清淨心；本性即自性；空，即清淨義).
Senses.Note: The corpus has 667 matches in 152 files. The compound occurs in direct corrections, statements linking it with original mind, and descriptions of it as without difference. Six matches in six files explicitly pair original nature and original mind. The evidence supports one corpus-wide sense. The forty "original nature empty" matches are therefore not treated as forty copies of one bare equation. The fixed body-and-mind verse, the Source-Mirror definition, and the critical construction "rely on original-nature empty" (恃本性空, two occurrences in two texts) are distinct deployments. One Source-Mirror list criticizes people who follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty, alongside people who cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing (或隨結使而恃本性空，或執纏蓋而妄加除斷). Each predicate is reported as that text's wording rather than generalized beyond its occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝作此偈，未見本性，只到門外，未入門內。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'You composed this verse but have not seen original nature; you have only reached outside the gate and have not entered inside it.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 須得言下識自本心，見自本性不生不滅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'You must, at the words, recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, which does not arise and does not extinguish.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 若識自本心，見自本性，即名丈夫、天人師、佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'If you recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, you are then named a great person, a teacher of humans and gods, a buddha.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 始知本性無差。非因行得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says, 'Only then is it known that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本性本心別無道理。會取會取。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record says, 'Original nature and original mind: there is no other principle. Understand it; understand it.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋曰。本性空者。即是自性清淨心。本性即自性。空。即清淨義。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Source-Mirror Record explicitly says: as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或隨結使而恃本性空。或執纏蓋而妄加除斷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Critical list: some follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty; others cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：拘留孫佛云：見身無實是佛身，了心如幻是佛幻，了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別？師云：佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan address raises the fixed verse: see the body as unreal, understand mind as appearance, understand body and mind as original-nature empty; it then comments that the buddha-body is neither real nor empty and buddha-as-appearance is not appearance.

AlternateTargets: originally there is not a single thing
Senses.Explanation: Literally, fundamentally or originally (本) there is not (無) one thing (一物): "fundamentally, not one thing." It occurs 34 times in 30 allowlisted texts. The close form "originally, not one thing" (本來無一物) occurs 214 times in 106 and is fixed in Huineng's verse: "the bodhi tree fundamentally has no tree; the bright mirror also is no stand; originally, not one thing; where could dust be attracted?" (菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺，本來無一物，何處惹塵埃). The exact shorter headword is deployed as a predicate and repeatedly challenged. The Collection of the Patriarchal Hall says that turning the light back to one's own mind-source and finding "fundamentally, not one thing" is called becoming buddha there, contrasting it with gradual certification through myriad deeds. Yinyuan versifies, "the scenery beyond is not heard in the world; fundamentally, not one thing to present to you" (那畔風光世莫聞，本無一物可呈君). Another passage holds together "three heads, six arms, a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, yet fundamentally not one thing" with "the myriad forms run crosswise." Most decisively, a student asks, "fundamentally, not one thing—what does the student investigate?" and the master answers, "take yourself out" (自領出去). Chan thus bends a negative inventory statement into Huineng-linked verse language, an asserted predicate, and a proposition masters can test rather than an imported metaphysical definition.
Senses.Note: The headword and Huineng's longer form are grouped as close morphology but counted separately. The wording "fundamentally, not one teaching" (本無一法) occurs 22 times in 19 texts and remains a related phrase, not an interchangeable occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自己心原，本無一物，便是成佛。不從萬行漸漸而證
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Collection of the Patriarchal Hall directly predicates the phrase of one's own mind-source and contrasts it with gradual certification.

Occurrences.Kwic: 那畔風光世莫聞，本無一物可呈君。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinyuan Longqi's verse says there is fundamentally not one thing to present.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三頭六臂、千手千眼而本無一物，純真一如、無臭無聲而萬象縱橫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage juxtaposes elaborate bodily forms and myriad appearances with the exact headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「本無一物，學人參個甚麼？」師云：「自領出去。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student's inference from the phrase becomes a test question and receives a dismissal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩提本無樹。明鏡亦非臺。本來無一物。何處惹塵埃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps transmits Huineng's four-line verse containing the longer close form.

AlternateTargets: complete in itself from the origin
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "from the origin, of itself complete." The phrase occurs 77 times in 53 allowlisted texts. It appears in the Platform Record's list of Huineng's statements on the nature: "who expected the nature to be from the start pure … from the start complete … able to produce the myriad things?" (何期自性本自清淨；何期自性本自具足；何期自性能生萬法). The corpus also turns the wording into a direct question: "what is complete from the start?" The recorded answer is, "because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete" (因無一物可得，所以說具足). A prose criticism asks, "complete from the start—who picks it up or puts it down?" (本自具足，阿誰拈起放下). Other records set the phrase against outside acquisition: living beings are complete from the start and "do not depend on seeking outside" (不假外求). The Zen deployment therefore joins the phrase to the nature, direct questioning, the impossibility of picking it up or putting it down, and explicit refusal of outside acquisition; this entry reports those statements without converting them into a system of cultivation.
Senses.Note: The subjects vary—the nature, unconditioned knowing, living beings, and the matter under discussion—but the predicate remains the same: already complete rather than acquired. These are applications of one predicate, not different things denoted by the phrase itself. The related shorter form "complete" (具足) is broader and may carry ordinary quantitative uses outside this entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何期自性本自清淨何期自性本不生滅何期自性本自具足何期自性本無動搖何期自性能生萬法
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record list attributes to Huineng the statements that the nature is from the start pure, unborn and undying, complete, unmoving, and able to produce the myriad things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：如何是本自具足？王云：因無一物可得，所以說具足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question asks what “complete from the start” is; the answer says that because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本自具足，阿誰拈起放下？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prose criticism asks who could pick up or put down what is complete from the start.

Occurrences.Kwic: 況神通變化眾生本自具足不假外求如今人多是外求
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage says living beings are complete from the start and do not depend on outside seeking, then contrasts this with people who seek outside.

Senses.Explanation: The compound occurs 381 times in 145 allowed texts as a verdict on a person, answer, explanation, or speech, and as a verb for making such material up. A late direct naming statement criticizes assigning difficult cases to newcomers without matching the person and the case: after comparing it to fitting a square timber into a round hole and losing people's time, the text says, 'To call it fabricated—is that not fitting?' (謂之杜撰，不亦宜乎). A playful assembly exchange separates the graphs as a surname and personal name: the staff says, 'My surname is Du, given name Zhuan' (姓杜，名撰); asked why it is called 'fabricated,' it answers, 'If the elder did not fabricate, how could he spend all day talking about Zhang and Li?' (長老若不杜撰，如何終日與人說張說李). Dahui uses the word self-deprecatingly when he says, 'I have not read Guo Xiang's explanation or the various commentators' explanations; I only rely on my own fabrication to explain your silence' (我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解，只據我杜撰說破爾這默然). The stock rebuke 'fabricated elder' (杜撰長老) occurs 68 times in 40 texts, often in the fuller comparison 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet'—that is, extremely numerous (杜撰長老如麻似粟). 'Fabricated Chan fellow' (杜撰禪和) likewise appears as a verdict on a respondent, while 'fabricated conjectural talk' (杜撰臆說) names speech. These are grammatical deployments of one shared judgment; the texts do not establish a distinct sense from the proper name Du Mo, whose 18 hits refer to a person or to being silent.
Senses.Note: No corpus witness derives the headword from the person Du Mo. Those proper-name and silence occurrences were excluded rather than used to repeat an external etymology. The alternate 'bogus' is reserved for personal epithets such as 'bogus elder' or 'bogus Chan fellow'; 'fabricated' remains the broad target for speech, explanations, and claims.

Occurrences.Kwic: 最悞人者，有初進禪門，根本未悟，遂令參南泉斬猫，百丈野狐，丹霞燒佛，女子出定等話，此真方木逗圓孔，唐喪人光陰，而天地懸隔者矣。謂之杜撰，不亦宜乎？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sayings on Tempering the Chan Gate, section on selecting material. The author directly applies the name to mismatching a newcomer and the cases assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自云：「姓杜，名撰。」「你如何喚作杜撰？」自云：「被長老帶累。」「長老如何帶累你？」自云：「長老若不杜撰，如何終日與人說張說李？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Tian'an Sheng. A staged dialogue with the staff splits the two graphs as a name and then uses the compound as a verb.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解。只據我杜撰說破爾這默然。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Dahui's reply to a scholar. Dahui applies the word to his own explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰不涉程途一句作麼生道。師以坐具摵一摵曰。杜撰長老如麻似粟。拂袖而出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Ju's encounter with Langya. Ju uses the stock 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet' rebuke; the dialogue remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師嘗勘一新到曰：何方聖者？甚處靈祇？僧曰：臨朕碪。師曰：杜撰禪和，如麻似粟。參堂去！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Collection of the Five Lamps. A master tests a newcomer and gives the personal verdict 'fabricated Chan fellow'; the two-speaker exchange is unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫是智過佛祖耶？杜撰臆說耶？卓拄杖曰：好向暮天沙上望，西風驚起鴈行斜。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Collection of the Five Lamps. The phrase 'fabricated conjectural talk' applies the headword directly to speech.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “East Mountain walks on water.” The phrase occurs 290 times in 131 allowlisted texts. In Yunmen's record it is his answer when a monk asks, “What is the buddhas' place of emergence?” (如何是諸佛出身處). Later records quote it as “Yunmen's saying”, ask directly for its import, set it beside other answers to the same question, and compose verses on it. A lamp biography says the hermit Ru first clarified his own view while examining this saying. Yuanwu later repeats Yunmen's exchange and supplies his own different answer to the same question: “The fragrant wind comes from the south; the halls give rise to a slight coolness” (薰風自南來，殿閣生微涼). The corpus gives no lexical gloss explaining how the mountain walks; this entry therefore retains the sentence Yunmen spoke and reports its recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: This is a portable case-saying rather than an ordinary report about a mountain. East Mountain is translated rather than left as an unexplained place-name. The headword is linked to the broader “place of emergence” entry, but its wording is not treated as a definition of that separate term.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是諸佛出身處。師曰。東山水上行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's own record supplies the question and exact answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 台州天台如庵主久依法真。因看雲門東山水上行語。發明己見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography explicitly calls the phrase Yunmen's saying and records Ru examining it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問雲門：如何是諸佛出身處？門曰：東山水上行。若是天寧即不然，忽有人問：如何是諸佛出身處？只向他道：薰風自南來，殿閣生微涼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes Yunmen and visibly supplies a different answer to the identical question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：東山水上行，意旨如何？師曰：初三十一，不用擇日。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later public interview makes Yunmen's sentence itself the object of a question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雲門因僧問如何是諸佛出身處師曰東山水上行。頌曰。東山水上行出處甚分明好看塵沙佛波濤四面生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case-and-verse collection preserves the exchange and immediately begins a verse with its answer.

Senses.Explanation: The literal image of a withered or dry tree, deployed in several fixed phrases. In the crone-burning-the-hermitage case, the attendant embraces the hermit and asks what it is like. He answers, 'A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; through three winters there is no warm air.' The crone rejects his answer and burns the hermitage. 'Withered-tree hall' is a hall name and location, as in 'before the withered-tree hall, gibbons cry and tigers roar.' In the Xiangyan case, 'What is the Way?' receives 'a dragon hums inside a withered tree,' and 'Who is the person in the Way?' receives 'eyes inside a skull.' Hongzhi later comments, 'It may be called a withered-tree dragon hum—still carrying joy; eyes in a skull—still carrying consciousness.' Other recurring compounds are 'flowers on a withered tree,' 'withered tree and cold cliff,' and 'withered-tree Chan.' The image also forms an institutional epithet: Shishuang's biography says that students sat for long periods without lying down and stood rigid like stumps, so throughout the realm they were called the withered-tree assembly. These are separate attested phrases built from the same tree image.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide image with multiple fixed deployments. Current counts: withered tree 1,752/295 files; dragon hums inside a withered tree 108/39; withered-tree dragon hum 91/62; eyes inside a skull 97/37; flowers on a withered tree 106/67; withered-tree hall 63/42; withered tree leans against a cold cliff 47/43; withered tree and cold cliff 24/23. The crone-burning-the-hermitage and Xiangyan passages are raised cases and remain occurrence-key null. Hongzhi's appraisal is his own commentary. The withered-tree assembly is an institutional label distinct from the hall name and the dragon-hum phrase. The crone's rejection is recorded as part of that case, not made into a second lexical meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 枯木倚寒巖，三冬無煖氣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (永覺元賢禪師廣錄); the (婆子燒庵) case retold — (正恁麼時如何)？(主曰)：(枯木倚寒巖)，(三冬無煖氣)，after which the crone burns the hut. Raised/stock case, MasterName null. (Same phrase recurs at 0568c02 in this file, count=2.)

Occurrences.Kwic: 嚴曰。枯木裏龍吟。曰。如何是道中人。嚴曰。髑髏裏眼睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), within (撫州曹山本寂禪師) section, a raised case naming Xiangyan: (僧問香嚴)。(如何是道)。(嚴曰)。(枯木裏龍吟)…(髑髏裏眼睛) — (嚴) = (香嚴智閑). Raised case, MasterName null; the words are Xiangyan's. Pairs (枯木裏龍吟) with (髑髏裏眼睛).

Occurrences.Kwic: 可謂枯木龍吟。猶帶喜在。髑髏眼睛。猶帶識在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (宏智禪師廣錄), Hongzhi's own commentary: (可謂枯木龍吟)。(猶帶喜在)。(髑髏眼睛)。(猶帶識在)。(直是智不到處) — Hongzhi (Caodong) turning the (枯木龍吟)/(髑髏眼睛) pair. Master's own record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 枯木堂前，猨啼虎嘯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (建中靖國續燈錄), (潭州石霜崇勝院法永禪師) upper-hall: (霜華臺上)，(翠色回環)；(枯木堂前)，(猨啼虎嘯) — (枯木堂) as a locus in a parallel couplet. MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 學眾有長坐不臥。屹若株杌。天下謂之枯木眾也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元), in the biography of Shishuang Qingzhu's community: 'among the students were those who sat for long periods without lying down, standing rigid like stumps; throughout the realm they were called the withered-tree assembly' (學眾有長坐不臥。屹若株杌。天下謂之枯木眾也).

Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “standard or grading frame” and “outside”: “beyond the norms.” In this corpus it is applied to sayings, phrases, actions, workings, and people. Recurrent combinations include “upheld beyond the norms,” “workings beyond the norms,” “a saying beyond the norms,” “a phrase beyond the norms,” “a person beyond the norms,” and “the Chan purport beyond the norms.” The records draw explicit contrasts. What is upheld beyond the norms is said not to establish grades of capacity, unlike phrases directed to middle or lower capacities. A saying beyond the norms is contrasted with explaining meaning by relying on scripture. A comment applies the term to Zhaozhou's answer “the cypress tree in the front garden,” and catalogues characterize Yunmen's house as solitary and steep, upheld beyond the norms. Records also ask directly, “What is a phrase beyond the norms?” A later comment examines and rejects Yaoshan's claim to possess workings beyond the norms, judging that it reveals what it tries to hide. The headword occurs 1,113 times across 245 allowlisted texts. The entry reports these applications and contrasts without treating the label as automatically valid.
Senses.Note: This is a corpus-wide descriptor whose application may be asserted, queried, or rejected. The curated occurrences are hall addresses, case comments, and lineage catalogues, so their speaker fields remain null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘a phrase outside the standard.’ The corpus uses it as a named class of utterance in public questioning and case appraisal. Yuanwu’s pointer says that if one can distinguish such a phrase, ‘raise one and understand three’; later in the same collection he says one must know the phrase outside the standard so that, when public cases and words are raised, one knows their place. A monk can ask directly, ‘what is a phrase outside the standard?’ and receive the answer, ‘the staff-tip points out a thousand peaks; before the Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for fine news.’ Other speakers coordinate it with ‘the upward pivot,’ contrast it with ‘the basic-function mechanism,’ or attribute it to Yunmen while saying that Yunmen and the Buddha each displayed their own style but had not yet accorded with the basis. One later discourse dismisses ‘the phrase outside the standard’ as a worn-out straw sandal alongside ‘the upward pivot’ as rotten hemp rope. Zen usage therefore bends the ordinary ‘outside the norm’ modifier into a technical phrase-class that masters request, distinguish, perform, compare with other phrase and mechanism classes, and appraise in public interviews.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide technical phrase class. Individual answers and competing appraisals are not separate senses. The headword ‘outside the standard’ (格外) remains broader; ‘a phrase outside the standard’ (格外句) is its lexicalized phrase-class compound and is cross-referenced rather than collapsed into it.

AlternateTargets: the bottom drops out of the bucket
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the bucket-bottom comes off' or 'the bottom drops out of the bucket.' The phrase occurs 109 times in 75 allowed texts. Its comparison form 'like the bucket-bottom falls out' (如桶底脫) occurs 38 times, including 26 exact endings in 'resembling the bucket-bottom falling out' (桶底脫相似). Xuefeng reports that after Deshan struck him, 'at that time I was as if the bucket-bottom had fallen out' (我當時如桶底脫相似); Yantou immediately challenges what Xuefeng brought in through the gate. Yuanwu uses the same comparison after 'under one phrase' (一言之下) and elsewhere joins the literal image to 'the mechanisms are exhausted' (桶底脫機關盡). The phrase is also recorded as a direct answer: asked 'What is buddha?' (如何是佛), Shoushan Huaizhi says, 'the bucket-bottom falls out' (桶底脫). A separate kitchen encounter uses the words literally: while noodles are cooking, the bucket-bottom suddenly falls out, the assembly cries that it is a pity, and the master says, 'the bucket-bottom falling out should itself be cause for joy—why are you distressed?' (桶底脫自合歡喜), before agreeing that the lost bucket of noodles is regrettable. The physical event and its simile therefore share one graph-level sense while appearing in an answer, recollection, comment, and kitchen exchange.
Senses.Note: The corpus does not provide a required direct-definition formula. It does provide a literal control case involving a noodle bucket, which prevents the comparison from being replaced by an imported abstraction. Xuefeng's report is preserved together with Yantou's objection rather than being treated as a standalone verdict.

Senses.Explanation: A physical stick, cudgel, or staff. Its object grammar is explicit: a master picks it up and offers it to a monk, the monk tries to receive it, Zhaozhou grabs one and warns against striking people wrongly, and another teacher drives people out with one. A record calls Deshan's implement “the single white staff before his eyes.” Chan makes this portable object a teaching-seat and house device. Lists pair “Linji's shout” with “Deshan's staff,” Nanyuan picks up the staff before saying “under the staff, the forbearance of no-arising; meeting the occasion, one does not defer to the teacher,” and the fixed compound “staff and shout” joins it to the shout (喝). This object is not the same lexical thing as a held or planted walking staff (拄杖), and it is not the countable act of hitting recorded in the second sense.
Senses.Note: Object sense confirmed by pickup, transfer, attempted receipt, grasping, color, and instrumental “drive out” syntax (趁). Cross-check: “staff and shout” (棒喝) has its own entry and pairs the staff/blow family with the shout without erasing this split. No “bamboo strip” entry (竹篦) exists in the current termbase. Corpus inspection shows the bamboo strip (竹篦) as an object that can be raised, thrown down, and used to strike; one late line even says “give one blow with the bamboo strip” (打一竹篦). That family needs its own item-8 audit before any inference from the staff (棒) is copied to it. The present headword split is independently proved by its own grammar.

Senses.Explanation: A countable act of striking, not the wooden object. The grammar proves the split: the corpus assigns one blow to one welt, gives Manjusri and Samantabhadra twenty blows each, gives thirty blows whether a person can speak or cannot, speaks of eating or deserving a blow, qualifies Linji's three encounters as painful blows, and calls a requested beating “one bout of blows.” Xuefeng's report that under Deshan's blows it was like a bucket-bottom falling out preserves a named case deployment. None of these can mean one, twenty, or thirty physical staffs. Zen records use the stroke as answer, penalty, test, appraisal, and later case label; the entry reports those uses without claiming a single result for every blow.
Senses.Note: Allowlist counts recorded in the audit: the headword “staff/blow” (棒), 18,109 hits in 415 texts; “one blow” (一棒), 2,954; “thirty blows” (三十棒), 2,766; “twenty blows” (二十棒), 407; “one bout of blows” (一頓棒), 63; “receive a blow” (喫棒), 1,191; and “painful blows” (痛棒), 752. The object-versus-blow split is preserved and strengthened: six object witnesses and seven act witnesses, with every sense independently anchored. Attribution remains cautious because several formulas circulate in raised cases and later compilations, and witnesses differ over which Deshan bears the thirty-blows formula.

Senses.PreferredTarget: blows and shouts (the stick and the shout)
Senses.Explanation: A fixed compound pairing (棒), the stick/blow associated with Deshan Xuanjian (德山棒), and (喝), the shout associated with Linji Yixuan (臨濟喝) — (德山棒)、(臨濟喝). In the records: 'as soon as a monk enters the gate, Deshan hits, Linji shouts' (德山入門便棒／臨濟入門便喝); after Linji 'came forth, he taught only with stick and shout' (唯以棒喝示徒). The stock phrase is (棒喝交馳) ('blows and shouts flying back and forth'), glossed (令你捫摸不入)、(插足不得) ('leaving you no finger-hold and no foot-hold'). The records also turn the term against its own use: 'call it "stick-and-shout" and you drop into hell like an arrow' (喚作棒喝，入地獄如箭); warnings against 'blind stick and wild shout' and against 'coarse fellows who talk up Linji and do nothing but stick-and-shout' (專事棒喝). A late verse headed (勉謬行棒喝者) ('exhortation to those who wrongly go about with stick-and-shout') states each component's job in so many words — (棒須劈破有無見)，(喝要澄空迷悟情) ('the stick must split apart views of being and non-being; the shout must clear out the passions of delusion and awakening') — and ends by naming the practitioner: (棒頭喝下如親切)，(是則名為棒喝人) ('when at the stick's head and under the shout it is as if intimate, such a one is then named a stick-and-shout person', J39nB447). The corrective deployments continue: (為謬認棒喝者呵斥棒喝) ('for those who wrongly take stick-and-shout he rebukes stick-and-shout', J36nB359), and (至有纔著袈裟便行棒喝者)。(問之)，(則曰)：(臨濟宗也)。(臨濟宗固如是乎)？ ('there are now those who no sooner don the robe than they go about with stick-and-shout; ask them, and they say: the Linji school. Is the Linji school really like this?', X72n1435).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The two-graph compound is used jointly across the corpus; the master-specific attributions belong to its components (棒) (Deshan) and (喝) (Linji), not to the compound itself — hence a single corpus-wide sense here rather than split master senses. Broad attestation (232 allowlist files, 992 occurrences by tag-stripped grep; an earlier figure of ~487 was the 德山棒 count, corrected here). Attested collocations (allowlist grep): (棒喝交馳) 185 hits in 110 texts; (一棒一喝) 112 in 61; (棒頭喝下) 55 in 36; (棒喝齊施) 33 in 19; (棒喝交加) 9 in 8. The named components: (德山棒) 490 hits in 173 texts, (臨濟喝) 442 in 155.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “densely arrayed” and “the ten thousand forms”: “the myriad forms arrayed.” The four-graph collective occurs 685 times in 213 allowlisted texts. The reverse order, “the ten thousand forms arrayed,” is slightly more frequent, with 730 hits in 231 texts. In a direct exchange, Fayan answers “What is the second moon?” with the headword and “What is the first moon?” with the reverse order. Other discourses place the array beside rivers reaching their limit in the sea, place the moon within the array, call empty space illness and the array medicine, or repeat it in a chain where Vimalakirti, a master, a staff, the myriad forms, ordinary people, and holy people are each said to be ill. A scenery passage describes river-mountains and high halls and then gathers them under the headword. These are the subjects and predicates supplied by the records; the entry retains the literal collective instead of replacing it with a religious abstraction.
Senses.Note: No standard self-definition formula occurs. The six strings translated “within the myriad forms arrayed” occur in six independent texts. The headword and its reverse order frequently substitute for one another, most explicitly in Fayan’s paired first-moon and second-moon answers.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the occasion or pivot and its operation. The compound occurs 564 times in 189 allowlisted texts and names the responsive action displayed or exercised in encounters. Records say that Dahui exhausted or displayed all his responsive operation before Wuzu, that another master and his interlocutor's responsive operation 'matched closely,' and that a portrait praise had Linji's responsive operation without indiscriminately carrying out staff-blows and shouts. Appraisals call it cutting, like thunder and lightning, or say it runs like thunder; instructional prose pairs living responsive operation with changing circumstances and contrasts it with dead rules. The compound also expands as 'great responsive operation' and joins recurrent predicates such as display, exhaust, match, be lively, run crosswise and lengthwise, or be fully raised. These are corpus descriptions of observable encounter conduct; the pivot or occasion graph (機) does not by itself name a student's graded capacity, and the records assign no single hidden purpose to the actions.
Senses.Note: The graph pair behaves as one nominal compound across biographies, portrait praises, appraisals, and prose. Predicative differences do not create separate referents. Related 'great pivot and great operation' (大機大用) is an intensified family form, not a second referent within this headword.

Senses.Explanation: A compound of "occasion, trigger, or responsive capacity" (機) and "circumstance or connection" (緣). In Chan records it commonly names a teacher-student encounter and, by extension, its recorded words. It appears as a section heading introducing successive exchanges, in the stable compound "question-and-answer encounters" (問答機緣), and in catalogues alongside entering-the-room encounters (入室機緣). One compilation calls the 1,700 old cases "1,700 encounters" (一千七百則機緣); the same author asks about "buddhas' and patriarchs' encounters, commonly called public cases" (佛祖機緣世稱公案者). The institutional deviation is therefore visible in record structure: an ordinary occasion or connection becomes a countable, titled public exchange preserved and revisited by the lineage.
Senses.Note: This technical sense does not turn every raw match into a formal interview. It preserves the texts' cautions: Zhongfeng lists seeking in encounters beside seeking in language and the 1,700 entangling vines, and Fangrong raises the whisk while setting "encounter question-and-answer" aside. Family check: "question-and-answer" (問答) is the reciprocal verbal exchange; "a monk asked" (僧問) is one speaker-turn formula; "enter the room" (入室) identifies the room setting; "encounter" (機緣) is the wider encounter and its record. Fitting occasion or concord is separated below as a different referent. The headword has 1,568 occurrences in 303 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: Outside the countable encounter-record use, "encounter" (機緣) names circumstances coming together or an accord between people. Zhongfeng says "the occasion is touched by chance" (機緣偶觸). A record preface praises a teacher's transmission and says his "capacities and circumstances accorded" (機緣吻合) before quoting a succession charge. These denote a convergence or fit, not a titled question-and-answer record.
Senses.Note: This sense is split under #0f.8 because a circumstance or accord is a different thing from a countable public encounter and its transcript. The two English targets are not competing interpretations of one usage; they follow two independently anchored constructions within the broader non-record sense.

AlternateTargets: the cutting edge of a response
Senses.Explanation: A two-image compound: (機) is the trigger/spring of a crossbow — the pivoting mechanism that releases at a touch — and (鋒) is the point or cutting edge of a blade. The compound is applied to people and exchanges in the record. Its observed deployments include: (a) as a measure of a person's capacity — a master's (機鋒) is called (峭峻) / (高峻) ('steep and sharp'), (迅捷) / (敏捷) / (捷疾) ('quick and nimble'), (不可觸) ('cannot be touched'); and (b) as the actual thrust traded in dialogue — (互換機鋒), teacher and student 'trading pivotal points.' The similes are all speed-and-edge, with Zen-scoped grep counts: (睦州機鋒)。(如閃電相似) ('like a flash of lightning'; once, T48n2003), (霹靂機鋒) ('thunderbolt point'; once, T48n2006), (機鋒電掣) ('the point flashes like lightning'; 7 texts), and the descriptor collocations (機鋒峭峻)·(高峻) (7 hits/4 texts), (機鋒迅捷)·(迅利)·(敏捷) (75/49), (互換機鋒) (18/15), (機鋒不可觸) (19/15); (機鋒) totals 673 hits in 195 allowlist texts. The texts use (機鋒) as this descriptor of speed and edge — the released trigger and the blade's tip — and assign it no gloss beyond those two images. Deployment: (機鋒不可觸) serves as a reputation formula — (內翰蘇軾居士聞玉泉皓禪師機鋒不可觸)，(公擬抑之)，(即微服求見) (the scholar Su Shi, hearing that Yuquan Hao's 機鋒 could not be touched, planned to suppress him and visited incognito; J29nB239, also T51n2077) — and as a narrative verdict: (師於言下大悟)。(機鋒不可觸) (T51n2077). A record can sum up a master with it: (僧擬開口)，(師便打)。(其機鋒峭峻多此類) (a monk was about to open his mouth; the master struck — his 機鋒 was steep-and-sharp, and much was of this kind; X71n1419). The corpus also records the word itself asked about and left unglossed: a prince asks (相公能答機鋒者麼), the official (瞪目無言) and afterward asks the master (如何教作機鋒), who answers only (待汝悟後必知) (after you awaken you will surely know; J39nB471). Dahui records a corrective deployment of the same favorable-sounding vocabulary: after describing performance 'like a flash of lightning' where deliberation cannot arrive, the record says, 'this is called a swift pivotal edge that does not fall into the thinking root,' then immediately, 'little does one know that it is precisely identity-consciousness playing tricks with ghostly eyes' (謂之機鋒俊快不落意根。殊不知。正是業識弄鬼眼睛). Thus the corpus applies the label in praise-like reputation formulae and also explicitly criticizes what is called a swift pivotal edge; this entry does not decide what it accomplishes.
Senses.Note: Broadly attested as a descriptor across the songgu and denglu collections (碧巖錄, 人天眼目, 從容錄, 五燈會元 and the Jiaxing yulu). It is a shared critical vocabulary, not any one master's coinage, so a single corpus-wide sense is honest; no master bends the base meaning. Note the recurring pairing with (照用) (照用雷奔／機鋒電掣) and with (賓主) (賓中問主，互換機鋒); the word 'pivotal edge' (機鋒) occurs inside the recorded guest-and-host exchange.

Senses.PreferredTarget: when the crazed mind stops, that is awakening
AlternateTargets: once it stops, that is awakening
Senses.Explanation: The isolated four graphs say, 'stop (歇)—that is (即) awakening (菩提),' but the corpus's recurring full quotation supplies the omitted subject: 'the crazed mind does not stop; when it stops, that is awakening' (狂心不歇，歇即菩提). A historical compendium follows the phrase with its own explicit explanation, beginning 'as for “when it stops, that is awakening”' and describing what it calls awakening. Chan masters repeatedly take up the quoted line in hall discourse. One says that when dust-labor suddenly stops, 'when it stops, that is awakening,' then immediately asks the assembly, 'from where is it obtained?' Another says people run north, south, east, and west for years without a place to stop and asks, 'can you people stop?' The Zen deviation is the quotation's deployment as a public teaching-seat proposition and direct question. Restoring its attested subject avoids turning every kind of ceasing into the roadmap's broad 'ceasing itself is enlightenment.'
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 38 hits in 26 texts. One fixed-proposition sense. Family checked against stop/rest (歇), rest and cease (休歇), let it rest and cease (休去歇去), crazed mind (狂心), and awakening (菩提). The compendium's explanatory expansion is reported as that text's wording; this entry does not extend it beyond the quoted passage.

Senses.Explanation: (正) upright/correct + (中) within/amid + (來) come, coming: "coming from within the upright." Caoshan's own record pairs the graphs with the ruler-minister figure: "the lord is the upright position, the minister the inclined position..." (君為正位。臣為偏位。臣向君是偏中正。君視臣是正中偏, T47n1987A). It is the third of the Five Ranks (五位) that Dongshan Liangjie composed as the (五位君臣頌) in his own record, where (師)。(作五位君臣頌云) is followed by (正中偏) · (偏中正) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到); his verse-line for this rank runs (正中來)。(無中有路隔塵埃)。(但能不觸當今諱)。(也勝前朝斷舌才) (T47n1986B). In the corpus it is chiefly deployed two ways. (1) As a fixed catechism-question: (如何是正中來) occurs 102 times in 56 texts, each master supplying a capping phrase — (師曰)。(徧界絕纖埃) (五燈會元), (松瘁何曾老)。(花開滿未萌), (屎裏翻筋斗), (獼猴戴席帽), and so on. (2) As a lemma the commentators gloss: "...is the attaining of the body of the teaching, and is also the upright position" (正中來一位，即是得法身，亦即是正位, X72n1437); the same text calls it "...one who enters the upright position and turns the body" (入正位而轉身者也) and another "...the pivot of the Five Ranks," (正中來，乃五位之樞紐 the position the first two ranks enter and the last two issue from, X72n1441). One (五燈全書) (上堂) maps a single shout onto the ranks — (即此一喝)，(不帶名言)，(是正中來也) — and then restates them (以濟宗論之): "...both person and object snatched away" (正中偏奪人也，偏中正奪境也。正中來，人境俱奪也, X82n1571). The graphs are the same across witnesses; the term carries no gloss here beyond the literal reading and its place in Dongshan's set.
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide sense (SenseKey null): 288 occurrences in 85 allowlist texts. (Counts are whole-file, tag-stripped with <note>/<rdg>/<orig> apparatus excluded; gate-2 recount, confirmed by two independent recounts.) The source verse is Dongshan Liangjie's own (T47n1986B, 瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄, 師。作五位君臣頌云…) — so that occurrence is attributed to him; the rest are the fixed (如何是正中來) catechism answered by various masters within lamp compilations (五燈會元, 五燈全書, 續燈正統) and analytical prose by later Caodong commentators — narrated/raised, MasterName null. This is the THIRD rank in Dongshan's canonical order (正中偏) · (偏中正) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到); the ranks interrelate (see RelatedTerms). Note the neighbouring 4th-rank name is unstable across texts — (兼中至) (207×) vs (偏中至) (85×): X72n1437 records that (寂音) (Juefan Huihong) (改兼中至為偏中至)，(以對正中來) and calls the change (大悞後學); the 3rd rank (正中來) itself is stable.

Senses.Explanation: (正) upright / straight + (中) within + (偏) biased / tilted: "the biased within the upright." It is the first of the (五位) (Five Ranks) of (洞山良价) (Dongshan Liangjie), whose (五位君臣頌) opens with it: (正中偏)，(三更初夜月明前)。(莫怪相逢不相識)，(隱隱猶懷舊日嫌). (曹山本寂) (Caoshan Benji), asked the (五位君臣旨訣), supplies the corpus's own definition: (正位即空界)，(本來無物)。(偏位即色界)，(有萬象形)。(正中偏者)，(背理就事)。(偏中正者)，(舍事入理) — i.e. "(正中偏): turning the back on principle and going to affairs" (正中偏者，背理就事). In his ruler-minister scheme (君為正位，臣為偏位) he assigns it: "the ruler viewing the minister is (正中偏)" (君視臣是正中偏). It is deployed as a stock test-question — (如何是正中偏)？ — answered with a turning phrase (宏智正覺: 師曰：雲散長空後，虗堂夜月明). A later sermon maps the ranks onto Linji-school terms (以濟宗論之): (正中偏奪人也)，(偏中正奪境也). Beyond the graphs and these attested self-definitions the texts add no further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The verse is (洞山良价)'s (五位君臣頌); the (背理就事) / (空界)·(色界) / (君臣) definitions are (曹山本寂)'s, given in answer to (五位君臣旨訣) — do not cross-attribute the verse and the gloss. Both are witnessed across ≥2 independent lamp records (禪宗正脉 X85n1593, 五燈全書 X81n1571) AND in the masters' own recorded sayings: the verse in (瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄) (T47n1986B), the (旨訣) answer in (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄) (T47n1987A). Pairs with and inverts (偏中正) (背理就事 vs 舍事入理; 君視臣 vs 臣向君). Member of the Five Ranks (五位) with (偏中正) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the correct or proper command. The term occurs 1,503 times in 291 allowlisted texts. Chan records deploy it as the command that is issued, carried out, or fully brought forward by the person holding authority. Stock forms include 'the command is put into effect' (127 hits in 84 texts), 'fully bring forward the command' (170 in 103), and 'the command has already been carried out' (28 in 23). It appears in public questions about what the master will show when the command is in force, in appraisals of Yunmen's use of the staff, and beside military language of ruling within the realm and holding authority beyond the gate. One discourse also criticizes even 'raising the command's guiding principle' as making an artificial nest.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend is the transfer of governmental and military command language to the master's public seat, replies, staff, blows, and appraisals. The word names the command or order throughout; whether a passage praises or criticizes its deployment is not a second sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the true eye of the teaching
AlternateTargets: the eye of the true teaching
the correct eye of the teaching
Senses.Explanation: True or correct (正), teaching (法), and eye (眼): the true eye of the teaching. As a standalone term, distinct from 'treasury of the true eye of the teaching' (正法眼藏), the records say it is possessed, absent, brightened, or blinded. The forms 'possess the true eye of the teaching' (具正法眼, 15 occurrences) and 'better to possess the true eye of the teaching' (不如具正法眼好) name its possession. Its absence is described in the line 'one who does not possess the true eye of the teaching misses at every turn' (非具正法眼者，頭頭蹉過). Its presence verifies: 'if one possesses the true eye of the teaching, one will verify the nirvana-mind' (若具正法眼，必證涅槃心). The preface to Linji's record says that Linji illuminated the nirvana-mind by means of the true eye of the teaching (臨濟祖師以正法眼明涅槃心). It can also be blinded (瞎却正法眼). Most raw occurrences of the string belong to the longer compound 'treasury of the true eye of the teaching' (正法眼藏, 1,381 occurrences), so this entry is deliberately limited to the standalone eye. The standalone term also appears in direct test questions. In the repeated Ying'an–Mi'an case, Ying'an asks, 'what is the true eye of the teaching?' (如何是正法眼), and Mi'an immediately answers, 'a broken sand-pot' (破沙盆). This is distinct from questions about the longer 'treasury of the true eye of the teaching' (正法眼藏).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide standalone sense. Every curated occurrence uses 'true eye of the teaching' (正法眼) without the following graph 'treasury' (藏). The longer compound 'treasury of the true eye of the teaching' (正法眼藏) has its own entry and is related literally as the treasury of this eye.

Senses.PreferredTarget: lineage-transmission phrase: the treasury of the true eye of the teaching
AlternateTargets: the true eye of the teaching treasury
the store of the true eye of the teaching
the treasury of the eye of the right teaching
Senses.Explanation: Literally the storehouse / treasury (藏) of the eye (眼) of the right teaching (正法) — in the record, the thing the lineage hands down. Its founding story is the World-Honored One on Vulture Peak holding up a flower before the silent assembly; only Mahakasyapa breaks into a smile, and the Buddha says (吾有正法眼藏)，(涅槃妙心)…(付囑摩訶迦葉) ('I have the treasury of the true eye of the teaching, the wondrous mind of nirvana... I entrust it to Mahakasyapa'). Thereafter each patriarch transmits it — (付囑於汝)，(勿令斷絕) ('I entrust it to you; let it not be cut off'), and a master speaks of his OWN transmitted teaching the same way: Linji on his deathbed says (吾滅後不得滅却吾正法眼藏) ('after I am gone, do not let my treasury of the true eye of the teaching be destroyed'), and when Sansheng answers with a shout, (誰知吾正法眼藏向這瞎驢邊滅却) ('who would have known my treasury of the true eye of the teaching would be destroyed at this blind donkey's side'). The term is questioned from within the record: Wumen presses the flower story with (正法眼藏作麼生傳) ('how is the treasury of the true eye of the teaching transmitted?') and argues that if you say it WAS handed over, the 'yellow-faced old man' (the Buddha) is cheating the villagers, and if it was NOT, why was Mahakasyapa alone singled out. In the corpus the phrase names the lineage's transmitted eye of the teaching, and masters both hand it down and put it in question. Two in-corpus self-definitions gloss the term directly: an annotation in (三峰藏和尚語錄) states (正法眼藏者)，(師師相傳之法眼也) ('the treasury of the true eye of the teaching: the eye of the teaching transmitted from teacher to teacher'), and the (重刻正法眼藏序) in (湛然圓澄禪師語錄) glosses the graph (藏) by simile — (正法眼藏者)，(難言也)，(請以喻明)。(譬如眼之洞見森羅萬象)，(取之無窮)，(用之無盡)，(故名曰藏) ('…like the eye's thorough seeing of the myriad forms, drawn on inexhaustibly, used without end — hence it is called a treasury'). The term is also deployed as a stock challenge, (如何是正法眼藏) ('what is the treasury of the true eye of the teaching?', 48x in 36 allowlist texts); recorded answers include Mi'an's (破沙盆) ('a broken sand-pot') in the case (應菴問密菴)：『(如何是正法眼藏)？』(密云)：『(破沙盆)。』 ('Ying'an asked Mi'an: what is the treasury of the true eye of the teaching? Mi'an said: a broken sand-pot' — raised repeatedly across the record), the single word (瞎) ('blind!', 破山禪師語錄), and (福昌重善)'s (夜觀乾象) ('watching the heavens by night'). Linji's deathbed phrase is itself re-raised across the record: (滅却)/(滅卻正法眼藏) ('destroying the treasury of the true eye of the teaching') recurs 17x in 14 texts. The texts add no gloss beyond this, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: This primary sense is the lineage's transmitted eye of the teaching, running from the Buddha's flower through the patriarchs to a master's own teaching. The separate title sense below covers the recut case collection. Zen-scoped raw-string counts remain 1,381 occurrences in 279 allowlisted texts; the challenge 'What is the treasury of the true eye of the teaching?' (如何是正法眼藏) occurs 48 times in 36. The word/title split does not alter those undifferentiated counts.

Senses.PreferredTarget: book title: Treasury of the True Eye of the Teaching
Senses.Explanation: The exact graphs also name a book that can be gathered into fascicles, recut, and supplied with a preface. The heading 'Preface to the Recut Treasury of the True Eye of the Teaching' (重刻正法眼藏序) introduces a preface saying that Dahui selected material from the five houses, gathered more than one hundred masters into fascicles, and titled the resulting book Treasury of the True Eye of the Teaching (裒以成帙，目曰正法眼藏). The text then calls it 'this book' (是書也). A recut, prefaced book is a different referent from the treasury transmitted from teacher to teacher, although its title repeats the transmitted expression.
