Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：父母未生前，畢竟是什麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈全書) (X-canon; FromLb is the ed="X" number): a (上堂) (ascending the hall) of (袁州仰山雪巖祖欽禪師) (Xueyan Zuqin) — governing section head (袁州仰山雪巖祖欽禪師) verified, corroborated in-text by (莫道仰山今日無為人方便) ('do not say Yangshan today has no device for people'; 仰山 is his seat). 'Before your father and mother were born, ultimately what is it?' — the bare pointer form without (本來面目). The master's own hall discourse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慣教人參如何是我父母未生前本來面目。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: J25nB171, (荊溪磬山語錄): inside (磬山) (Tianyin Yuanxiu = 天隱圓修)'s own evening-assembly (晚參) address (大眾…汝等須是行也參、坐也參…, 'great assembly … you must investigate while walking, investigate while sitting') — '[my teacher] (禹門堂上幻有老人) ('the old man Huanyou in the hall at Yumen', i.e. 幻有正傳 Huanyou Zhengchuan) habitually made people investigate: what is my original face before my father and mother were born.' The master in his own voice, raising what his teacher habitually did — not narration; documents the phrase as a set question one is told to investigate (參).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a firm or fastened (牢) barrier or pass (關): "the tight barrier." The phrase occurs 594 times in 194 allowlisted texts. Luopu's recorded formulation says, "the last phrase first reaches the tight barrier; lock off the critical crossing; do not let ordinary or sage pass" (末後一句始到牢關，鎻斷要津，不通凡聖). Yuanwu and Dahui preserve the same wording with "hold fast" in place of "lock off" (把斷要津). The corpus also records the barrier as something to break (打破牢關, 30 occurrences), pass through (透過牢關, 7), get through (透得牢關, 10), hold fast (把定牢關, 26), and close (閉卻牢關, 1). One later question asks, "the final move first reaches the tight barrier; what is the tight barrier?" and receives, "break through and come meet me" (末後一著始到牢關，如何是牢關；打破來，與汝相見). These are the corpus's stated actions and formulas; this entry adds no further claim.
Senses.Note: The fixed wording "the last phrase first reaches the tight barrier" is transmitted in Luopu Yuanan's section and repeatedly quoted by later masters. A quotation of that line is not reassigned to the later speaker merely because it appears in that speaker's record. The compact form "final tight barrier" (末後牢關) occurs 42 times.

Occurrences.Kwic: 末後一句始到牢關。把斷要津不通凡聖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the third informal address section of Yuanwu Keqin's record. Yuanwu quotes an older formulation: "the last phrase first reaches the tight barrier; hold fast the critical crossing and do not let ordinary or sage pass." MasterName is null because the headword-bearing sentence is a quotation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古者道。末後一句始到牢關。把斷要津不通凡聖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Dahui Zonggao's record. The passage explicitly introduces the line as "an ancient said," then quotes: "the last phrase first reaches the tight barrier; hold fast the critical crossing and do not let ordinary or sage pass." The quoted speaker is not identified here, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打破牢關。天寬地寬。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Jiangshan Taiping Xingguo monastery discourse section of the Record of Master Mi'an: "break the tight barrier; heaven is broad and earth is broad." The section speaker has no validated roster link used here.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, tend or herd an ox. In Chan records this ordinary farm action becomes a recurrent vocabulary for restraining and directing the ox: when Mazu asks Shigong what he is doing, Shigong answers, 'herding the ox'; asked how, he says, 'whenever it enters the grass, I seize its nose and pull it back' (whenever it enters the grass, I seize its nose and pull it back). Mazu replies, 'you truly know how to herd the ox' (you truly know how to herd the ox). Baizhang's comparison describes an oxherd holding a staff, watching the animal, and not letting it trespass on others' crops. The preface to the Ten Ox Pictures explicitly traces the wording to the comparison, 'like herding an ox: hold a staff and watch it; do not let it run loose and trespass on people's seedlings' (like herding an ox: hold a staff and watch it; do not let it run loose and trespass on people's seedlings). Guting's preface then supplies an in-corpus definition for its illustrated usage: 'what is called herding the ox compares it to the wild restlessness of human nature' (what is called herding the ox compares it to the wild restlessness of human nature). These comparisons are stated by the cited texts; the entry attributes them to those texts and adds no further account.
Senses.Note: The corpus also tests and overturns its inherited imagery: Tianyou's verse says, 'two horns point to heaven, four feet tread the earth; the nose-rope snapped—what shit or fart is there to herd?' (two horns point to heaven, four feet tread the earth; the nose-rope snapped—what shit or fart is there to herd?). That is an attested criticism of the herding vocabulary, not a second referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖問：作甚麼？曰：牧牛。祖曰：作麼生牧？曰：一回入草去，驀鼻拽將回。祖曰：子真牧牛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shigong answers Mazu's public questioning by describing how he pulls the ox back by its nose.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如牧牛人執杖視之，不令犯他苗稼。安自此息意。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Wansong's comment on the Nanquan water-buffalo case, Baizhang's comparison says an oxherd watches with a staff and prevents crop trespass.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遺教經云：譬如牧牛，執杖視之，不令縱逸，犯人苗稼。則牧牛之說所自起也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Ten Ox Pictures preface explicitly identifies the earlier comparison from which its ox-herding language arose.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫謂牧牛者，譬人性之狂掉也。覺乃佛祖之真源，逸則輪迴之妄性。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guting's preface directly defines its illustrated ox-herding comparison as human nature's wild restlessness; the entry attributes rather than adopts the remaining claims.

Occurrences.Kwic: 兩角指天，四足踏地。拽斷鼻繩，牧甚屎屁。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyou's ox-herding verse breaks the nose-rope and asks bluntly what there remains to herd.

Senses.Explanation: As a title or section label, Oxherding names an illustrated or versified sequence rather than the act of tending an ox. The corpus preserves named sets such as Puming's Ten Oxherding Verses (Puming's ten oxherding verses), arranged through headings including 'not yet herded.' Other records title independent Oxherding Verses or a Ten Ox Pictures sequence. Because a textual work is a different thing from the activity it depicts, title-use is split and anchored separately.
Senses.Note: The title sense includes both picture-and-verse and verse-only sequences; these are title variants within the same kind of referent, not interpretive readings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 普明牧牛十頌普明牧牛十頌未牧未牧生獰頭角恣跑哮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A textual heading introduces 'Puming's Ten Oxherding Verses' and its first stage, 'not yet herded.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 牧牛頌牧牛頌曠劫娑婆日吼哮，翻來復去轉途遙，幾回要向南宸去，只謂時人不稼苗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent record uses 'Oxherding Verses' as a section heading and immediately begins the verse sequence.

Senses.Explanation: To violate or transgress a binding precept. The compound occurs 40 times in 31 allowlisted Chan texts. In a public case attributed to Jingshan, a person who has cultivated good all his life once violates the precept against taking what was not given; the passage then supplies an explicit naming formula: ‘the one who violates a precept is immediately named a thief’ (犯戒者即名為賊). Another recorded interview poses the opposed pair, ‘a precept-keeping monk does not ascend to heaven; a precept-violating monk does not fall into hell—what do you say?’ (持戒比丘不上天堂，犯戒比丘不落地獄，汝作麼生？). The Caoshan record quotes a former teacher saying, ‘to set the mind is to violate a precept; to acquire a taste is to break the fast’ (擬心是犯戒，得味是破齋), then repeats that taking pleasure in the ‘flavor of buddhas and ancestral teachers’ is violating a precept. Linquan quotes an ancient saying that neither honors people merely for keeping the fast and precepts nor slights them merely for breaking them, while still calling keeping them a monastic's own duty and breaking them the ground of an ordinary person. These are attested expansions and contrasts around the same violation category, not grounds for erasing the hard rule or for deciding why the records apply it as they do.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: an actual precept violation becomes the named status in public interview and is directly contrasted with keeping; the Caoshan passage also applies the category to setting the mind and acquiring a taste. ‘Violate a precept’ (犯戒) is narrower than ‘break the precepts’ (破戒): both denote violation in these records, but this entry preserves the corpus's explicit naming formula and does not claim a technical distinction not stated by the passages. The ordinary violation, public-interview comparison, Caoshan re-grounding, and quoted keep/break appraisal all concern what counts as violation rather than different referents, so the entry remains one corpus-wide sense. Exact count: 40 hits in 31 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善者一日偶犯不與取戒，惡者一念了悟自心。犯戒者即名為賊，了悟者即名為佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Jingshan case names the violated rule as the precept against taking what was not given and directly calls the violator a thief.

Occurrences.Kwic: 持戒比丘不上天堂，犯戒比丘不落地獄，汝作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question directly contrasts a precept-keeping monk with a precept-violating monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 先師曰。擬心是犯戒。若也得味是破齋。且喚什麼作味。只是佛味祖味。纔有忻心便是犯戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Caoshan record quotes a former teacher: setting the mind is violating a precept, acquiring a taste is breaking the fast, and taking pleasure in the flavor of buddhas and ancestral teachers is violating a precept. Because the immediate words belong to an unnamed former teacher, MasterName remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古德有語云：我見持齋守戒者亦不敬，我見破齋犯戒者亦不輕。何也？持齋守戒者，出家本分事也；破齋犯戒者，凡夫地面也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linquan quotes an ancient saying that neither honors a person merely for keeping the fast and precepts nor slights one merely for breaking them, while naming keeping them a monastic's own duty and breaking them the ground of an ordinary person. The quoted speaker is unnamed.

AlternateTargets: Zhaozhou's 'a dog has no buddha-nature' case
the dog has no buddha-nature saying
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a dog has no buddha-nature.' The corpus records 427 occurrences in 119 allowed texts; 228 add the noun 'saying' (話), and 91 explicitly prefix Zhaozhou's name. The phrase serves as a title or shorthand for the recorded exchange in which someone asks whether a dog has buddha-nature and Zhaozhou answers 'no.' Dahui's verse heading states 'Zhaozhou: a dog has no buddha-nature' (趙州狗子無佛性) and immediately restates the exchange as 'someone asked about a dog's buddha-nature; Zhaozhou answered, no' (有問狗佛性。趙州答曰無). Other records raise 'the saying that a dog has no buddha-nature' (狗子無佛性話), quote its word 'no' (無字), use it in questioning, and place it beside the separately attested wording 'a dog has buddha-nature' (狗子有佛性). The word 'no' is translated as English 'no.'
Senses.Note: No direct definition formula of the forms 'X is,' 'what is called X,' or 'what is X' was found, except one later question, 'What is “a dog has no buddha-nature”?' (如何是狗子無佛性), answered 'fishing' (釣). The term's stable corpus function is instead visible in headings, raised-case labels, verses, questions, and later reports about Zhaozhou's recorded case. The full earlier exchange and the later compound title are related evidence, not two meanings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州狗子無佛性。頌云。有問狗佛性。趙州答曰無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's Record, section 'verses on old cases' (頌古, 'verses on old cases'). It is a verse heading and restatement of Zhaozhou's earlier exchange, so the occurrence is left unkeyed rather than assigned to the person who compiled or recited it. It explicitly preserves 'no' as Zhaozhou's answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。舉狗子無佛性話。乃曰。二八佳人刺繡遲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium records an assembly address that raises 'the saying that a dog has no buddha-nature' and then gives a verse. Because it raises Zhaozhou's case inside another master's section, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 以狗子無佛性話。舉無字而提撕。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium, Jianfu Wuben biography. It reports taking up 'the saying that a dog has no buddha-nature' and raising its word 'no.' This is a biographical report, not a fresh reply by Zhaozhou, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慧舉狗子無佛性話問之。公擬答。慧以竹篦便打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Continued Transmission of the Lamp reports Dahui raising the saying to Wu Weiming; Wu starts to answer and Dahui strikes with a bamboo slip. It is a narrated two-person encounter, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是狗子無佛性？王云：釣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later rapid question-and-answer list asks, 'What is “a dog has no buddha-nature”?' and records the one-word answer 'fishing.' The governing speaker is called Wang in the exchange but is not safely linkable from the nearby index head, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: This is the graph variant of the traditional spelling of “cat” (貓兒). The dominant Zen deployment is Nanquan's cat case: the eastern and western halls fight over the cat, Nanquan says that speaking will save it and failure to speak will mean its cutting, the assembly gives no answer, and the record says he cuts it. Zhaozhou later places a straw sandal on his head, after which Nanquan says he would have saved the cat. Beyond that case, the corpus uses the same word for ordinary mouse-catching cats and records a teacher lifting a live cat before the assembly while explicitly recalling Nanquan.
Senses.Note: Later commentary preserves a factual and evaluative dispute. The Book of Serenity reports that one critic reproached Nanquan's group for "killing living beings and creating guilt" (殺生造罪), while a defender cited an old text in which Nanquan made only a simulated cutting gesture (以手作虛斫勢). The commentary then evaluates the two critics; this entry records the controversy without choosing between the transmitted narratives or assigning an unstated intention. The traditional spelling of “cat” (貓兒) is a separate searchable entry with the same sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師因東西兩堂爭猫兒。師遇之。白眾曰。道得即救取猫兒。道不得即斬却也。眾無對。師便斬之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Combined at the Source gives the halls' dispute, Nanquan's condition, the silence, and the cutting.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敢保救得猫兒。這一窟死老鼠。既無些子氣息。南泉已展不縮。盡令而行。遼朝上人𭣪作鏡心錄。訶南泉輩殺生造罪。文首座作無盡燈辨誤。救云。古本以手作虛斫勢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Book of Serenity records opposed later claims: killing guilt versus an old-text simulated-cutting variant.

Occurrences.Kwic: 五白猫兒爪距獰。養來堂上絕蟲行。分明上樹安身法。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse describes a piebald cat with fierce claws, kept in the hall to end the insects' movement and able to climb a tree.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中垂問曰：猫兒為甚麼愛捉老鼠？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interview question asks why a cat loves catching mice, preserving the ordinary animal referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔日南泉親斬却，今朝耶舍示玄徒。而今賣與諸禪客，文契分明要也無。良久，拋下猫兒，便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher lifts a live cat before the assembly, recalls Nanquan, offers it to the monks, then throws it down and leaves the seat.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “mysterious” or “dark purport”: “mysterious” (玄) modifies “purport” or “gist” (旨). The compound occurs 564 times in 162 allowlisted texts. It is repeatedly asked as “What is the mysterious purport?” (如何是玄旨), a formula found 39 times in 23 texts. Guizong Zhichang answers that no one can understand it, says that directing oneself toward it departs from it, and asks who is seeking it; Zhaozhou answers “money hanging on the wall” (壁上挂錢財); and Daoqin replies, “What purport does ‘mysterious’ have?” (玄有甚麼旨). Jiashan Shanhui gives an explicit reciprocal formulation: “Your mysterious purport is this old monk’s tongue; this old monk’s mysterious purport is your tongue” (闍梨玄旨是老僧舌頭，老僧玄旨是闍梨舌頭). The compound also occurs as the object of verbs of recognition: records say people “greatly awakened to the mysterious purport” (大悟玄旨) or “realized the mysterious purport” (領悟玄旨). The recorded answers are retained as distinct answers; the entry does not replace them with a single explanation of their force.
Senses.Note: The question formula occurs across many masters, and the answers differ. “Not recognizing the mysterious purport” (不識玄旨) occurs 48 times in 35 texts; “greatly awakened to the mysterious purport” (大悟玄旨) occurs 19 times in 14; and “realized the mysterious purport” (領悟玄旨) occurs 6 times in 6. These are grammatical deployments of the same compound, not separate master-specific meanings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是玄旨。師云。無人能會。僧云。向者如何。師云。有向即乖。僧云。不向者如何。師云。誰求玄旨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The surrounding Guizong Zhichang record supplies the monk’s question and Guizong’s successive replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是玄旨？師云：壁上挂錢財。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Zhaozhou Congshen section identifies Zhaozhou as the respondent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是玄旨？師曰：玄有甚麼旨？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing section is the record of Jinling Zhongshan Zhangyi Daoyin; the roster has no exact link value for this name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 闍梨玄旨是老僧舌頭，老僧玄旨是闍梨舌頭。坐却舌頭，別生見解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Jiashan Shanhui discourse section records Jiashan’s reciprocal formulation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 違順相爭。是為心病。不識玄旨。徒勞念靜。圓同太虗。無欠無餘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: This is the line containing the headword in the Inscription on Trusting Mind under Sengcan’s section.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師默而審之。大悟玄旨。尋晦迹鍾山。多歷年所。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Zhongshan Tancui biography records the phrase as a narrative event; the roster has no exact link value for Tancui.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs join “hidden” or “subtle” with a trigger, pivot, or working. Chan records use the compound for workings disclosed in sayings, gestures, and exchanges. One verse calls them “subtle workings and marvelous function” and immediately lists raising the whisk, lifting the eyebrows, and answering questions. Another stock line says that “subtle workings beyond the norms” seek one who knows; a verse warns that people who try to grasp what precedes the working violate it beneath the phrase. The corpus can also negate it: “the intent cuts off subtle workings” stands beside “the mind has no affairs” and “the myriad things do not arise.” The headword occurs 500 times across 187 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: The personal name Xuanji, borne by a nun in lamp biography, is a homonym and is excluded: lineage figures belong on the master roster, not in this lexical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 格外玄機為尋知己
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A stock hall-address line says that subtle workings beyond the norms seek one who knows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 玄機妙用縱多般，七縱八橫任抵對
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse couples subtle workings with marvelous function and the ability to answer in every direction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪者有玄機。機玄是復非。欲了機前旨。咸於句下違
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says Chan people have subtle workings and warns that seeking the purport before the working goes wrong beneath the phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心若無事。萬法不生。意絕玄機。纖塵何立
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address explicitly speaks of intent cutting off subtle workings.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the dark' or 'hidden road.' The term occurs 268 times in 116 allowed texts. It is especially prominent in Caodong records, where one text says Dongshan taught 'three roads' (三路): the hidden road, the bird road, and extending the hand (玄路、鳥道、展手). Asked, 'How does the hidden road receive people?' (如何是玄路接人), one master answers, 'Push father toward the inside' (推爺向裏頭). Another exchange asks, 'What is it that every line must travel the hidden road?' (如何是句句須行玄路); the answer is 'Follow the road straight to Hunan' (㳂路直到湖南). The named compound 'golden-lock hidden road' (金鎖玄路) has its own verse, whose lines say that brightness and darkness alternate, equal accomplishment makes turning difficult, and at the exhaustion of strength advance and retreat are forgotten. A later prose explanation calls the inability to turn when strength is exhausted 'the golden-lock hidden road' (若力窮而不能轉，是謂金鎖玄路). The term does not by itself mark completion: a later record says that even when host and guest are established and question and answer are voiced, raising the hidden road from the side is still only halfway. The corpus has ten occurrences each of 'open the hidden road' (開玄路) and the request 'please make the hidden road clear' (玄路請師明).
Senses.Note: The definition follows the graphs and the records' road imagery. The entry reports the named three-road grouping, questions, answers, verse, and explicit qualification without converting the road into an imported program or interpreting the recorded replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是玄路接人？師云：推爺向裏頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question asks how the hidden road receives people; the answer says to push father toward the inside. The exchange remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。何者三路。曰。玄路．鳥道．展手。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student reporting Dongshan's instruction directly names the three roads: hidden road, bird road, and extending the hand; the two-speaker exchange remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是句句須行玄路。師曰。㳂路直到湖南。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct exchange asks about every line traveling the hidden road; the answer says to follow the road straight to Hunan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 金鎻玄路偈曰。交互明中暗。功齊轉覺難。力窮忘進退。金鎻網鞔鞔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The collection preserves a verse explicitly titled 'Golden-Lock Hidden Road.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 若力窮而不能轉，則事理之迹未消，聖凡之情未盡，是謂金鎖玄路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later prose explanation directly calls exhaustion of strength without the ability to turn the golden-lock hidden road.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問答言陳，仍玄路旁提為唱。若能如是，猶在半途。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Strict Continuation of the Five Lamps. The record qualifies raising the hidden road from the side as still being halfway.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a dark, hidden, or subtle barrier/gate. The expression occurs 593 times in 212 allowlisted texts. One penetrates, passes, strikes, breaks, or kicks it down. Speakers ask about ‘the higher hidden barrier,’ call for one who has passed it, and ask publicly how it is passed. One discourse warns that ‘clinging to the hidden barrier’ loses the larger function; another says those not through it often construe Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing merely as facing a wall. Zen bends the gate into a public-interview checkpoint, but no corpus-wide sentence defines fixed content behind it.
Senses.Note: Family check: ancestral, higher, and double hidden barriers are qualified versions of one checkpoint image. Place-name compounds were excluded; no split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：未開口時先分付，擬思量處隔千山。莫言佛法無多子，未透玄關也大難。祇如玄關作麼生透？喝一喝，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse asks publicly how it is passed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云：四賓主諙蒙師指，向上玄關事若何？師曰：一陣兩陣清風生，吹散白雲千萬片。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks about the higher hidden barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 戀著玄關，全虧大用；灰身滅智，豈是良圖？裂破面門，救諸苦趣；為祥為瑞，今正是時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text warns against clinging to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未透玄關者往往只作面壁會却。上堂，舉：僧問首山：如何是祖師西來意？首山云：風吹日炙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: It is linked to a warning about construing wall-gazing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「結制安禪即不問，今朝解制事如何？」師云：「蹋倒玄關無障礙。」進云：「解制後又如何？」師云：「十方世界任逍遙。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interview answer says to kick it down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：孤村陋店，莫挂瓶盂。祖佛玄關，橫身直過。早是蘇秦觸塞，求路難回。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse names the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ hidden barrier.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, Wang, old master or teacher. In the Chan record this is Nanquan Puyuan's recurrent self-designation and the label later writers use when quoting or commenting on him. The compound occurs 760 times in 193 allowlisted texts. Nanquan's biography identifies him as Puyuan, a son of the Wang family of Zhengzhou, and immediately records him saying, 'Old Master Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?' Other self-references include the water-buffalo saying, 'Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since he was young,' asking Zhaozhou, 'Where is Old Master Wang at fault?' and saying that Old Master Wang, unlike Mazu, does not say 'mind is buddha' but 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing.' Later comments preserve the title while explicitly naming Nanquan.
Senses.Note: This is a person-title, not a generic entry for every teacher surnamed Wang. The explicit biography and repeated Nanquan section headings fix its principal referent. The full name 'Nanquan Old Master Wang' occurs 17 times in 12 texts; the selling-himself phrase occurs 41 times in 37.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二密古尊宿語錄卷第十三勿一南泉禪師語錄馬祖大寂禪師法嗣。南泉禪師諱普願鄭州王氏子也示眾云王老師賣身去也還有人買麼時有僧出眾云某甲買師云不
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Nanquan record identifies Puyuan as a son of the Wang family and immediately preserves his selling-himself saying.

Occurrences.Kwic: 泉進且無路，退亦無門。良久，云：別處容和尚不得。示眾云：王老師自小養一頭水牯牛，擬向溪東牧，不免食他國王水草；擬向溪西牧，不免食他國王
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Within Nanquan Puyuan's section, the master says that Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since youth.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與二十棒，趂出院去也。時趙州出眾曰：和尚棒教誰喫？泉曰：王老師過在什麼處？州便禮拜而出。雲門偃云：深領和尚慈悲，某甲歸衣鉢下，得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the two-halls cat case, Nanquan asks Zhaozhou where Old Master Wang is at fault; later commentary follows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 欄頻顧望，回首與誰同？南泉示眾云：江西馬大師說即心即佛，王老師不恁麼，不是心，不是佛，不是物。恁麼道還有過麼？鼓山珪頌云：剔
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A collected record explicitly identifies Nanquan before his contrast between Mazu's wording and Old Master Wang's wording.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉似南泉，泉曰：苦哉！浮盃被者老婆摧折一上。婆聞，笑曰：王老師猶少機關在。澄一禪客見婆，乃問：怎生是南泉猶少機關在？婆哭曰：可悲
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a reported exchange, an old woman hears Nanquan's response and says that Old Master Wang still lacks a turn of mechanism.

Occurrences.Kwic: 覺云：遇水喫水，遇草喫草，焉知畜生行？示眾云：諸和尚子！王老師十八上便解作活計，如今莫有解作活計底麼？出來共汝商量。良久，顧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanquan tells the assembly that Old Master Wang already knew how to manage the affair at eighteen.

Senses.Explanation: A formulaic “take care.” In recorded sayings a master ends a hall address, informal convocation, address to the assembly, or whisk talk with it and steps down. Recurrent formulas include “You have stood long, kind assembly; I humbly hope you take care; he stepped down,” and the shorter “Take care; he then stepped down.” It is also a parting word in dialogue: a departing monk says “take care” and leaves. A written final statement closes, “I humbly hope you take care” (伏惟珍重), before its author puts down the brush and asks whether to depart sitting or lying. This leave-taking formula is a separate speech act from the transitive verb “to treasure” an object.
Senses.Note: Primary corpus deployment: a formulaic close and parting word, not a specialized technical term. The curated passages show a whisk talk, a hall address, an address to the assembly, and a monk's farewell. The headword has 3,863 hits in 351 allowlisted texts; this high-frequency formula is distinct from the rarer transitive verb.

Occurrences.Kwic: 久立眾慈，伏惟珍重。下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs: the formula closes a whisk talk at the end of a retreat; the assembly is dismissed and the master steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 珍重便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: the word closes a hall address in the short formula “Take care; he then stepped down.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 與大眾舉一古人方便。珍重便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, section on the heirs of Guichen: after raising an old worthy's expedient, the speaker says “take care” and steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧珍重而去。代云。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fenyang Wude: in dialogue, a monk says “take care” and leaves; Fenyang then supplies an alternate reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今吾如是，豈不快哉！塵勞外緣，一時掃盡。荷諸山垂顧，咸願證明。伏惟珍重。置筆顧簡堂曰：某坐去好，臥去好？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A written final statement thanks the assembled mountain masters, closes 'I humbly hope you take care,' and is followed by the writer putting down the brush and asking whether to depart sitting or lying.

Senses.Explanation: A transitive verb meaning to treasure or value an object. Letters and prefaces record “treasure the teaching gate” (珍重法門), “treasure this record and circulate it widely” (珍重此錄，廣為流佈), and “if [you] wish to value that matter” (若欲珍重其事). Unlike the stock closing “take care,” these clauses name what is valued.
Senses.Note: The three independently sourced objects establish the distinct action of valuing something, not merely a grammatical variant or interpretation of the leave-taking formula. No special Chan deviation beyond the corpus objects is asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 屢承翰教，珍重法門，筆舌難盡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A letter says that its addressee treasures the teaching gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又能珍重此錄，廣為流佈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A preface praises treasuring this record and circulating it widely.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若欲珍重其事，且放過諸人一著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address uses the headword transitively of valuing that matter.

Senses.Explanation: Manifest or on hand (現) and completed or formed (成): ready-made, already there, or already complete. The record uses it adjectivally in such phrases as 'ready-made wherever one touches' (觸處現成), 'each one ready-made' (一一現成), 'everything ready-made' (一切現成, 73 occurrences), and 'ready-made and available for use' (現成受用, 78). Its chief compound is 'a ready-made public case' (現成公案), which occurs 382 times in 154 texts. The older graphic form 'a ready-made public case' (見成公案) occurs 119 times in 54 texts. Yuanwu, for example, says that his teacher Wuzu had a ready-made public case and raises it before the assembly (五祖老師有箇見成公案，對眾舉揚). A recurrent line says, 'one who comes in this way: a ready-made public case; one who does not come in this way: a target mound inviting arrows' (與麼來者，現成公案；不與麼來者，垛生招箭). The headword occurs 1,749 times in 292 allowlist texts; the older spelling occurs 337 times in 109 texts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The older graph form 'ready-made' (見成) has the same reading and deployment as 'ready-made' (現成). The dominant collocation is 'ready-made public case' (現成公案 / 見成公案).

Occurrences.Kwic: 全機大用，觸處現成，溢目清光
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), section on imperial guiding principles (受勅奉旨提綱). The adjectival phrase says, 'ready-made wherever one touches' (觸處現成).

Occurrences.Kwic: 與麼來者，現成公案。不與麼來者，垛生招箭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), guiding principles for the five-session day (五參提綱). The stock hall-address formula says that one who comes in this way is a ready-made public case (與麼來者，現成公案).

Occurrences.Kwic: 正緣五祖老師有箇見成公案。對眾舉揚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Yuanwu Foguo (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). Using the older graph, Yuanwu raises his teacher Wuzu Fayan's ready-made public case (五祖老師有箇見成公案).

Occurrences.Kwic: 當下七通八達，一一現成、一一圓妙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianru Weize (天如惟則禪師語錄), address to the assembly (示眾). The line says that each one is already there and each one fully effective (一一現成、一一圓妙).

Occurrences.Kwic: 更有不煩掃建處，一切現成
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Record of Chan Master Juelang Daosheng of Tianjie (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), in a preface (序). The phrase 'everything ready-made' (一切現成) describes what requires no further sweeping or construction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若論此事，本自現成，不假造作，只貴當人回光返照
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address says that this matter is originally ready-made and does not depend on fabrication.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自然穩坐家堂，現成受用，何須航海梯山，別求良導？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction describes sitting securely at home and using what is ready-made, without traveling elsewhere to seek a guide.

Senses.Explanation: A public case that is already complete, present, or ready to hand. The expression is fully attested in Chinese Chan records as a case-term and an utterance. One address says, 'One who comes this way is a ready-made public case.' Another teacher waits for the assembly to settle, says only that even a ready-made public case cannot be arranged, and steps down. A later record says that whenever a monk came, Muzhou said, 'Ready-made public case.' Teachers also ask directly what a ready-made public case is and answer with such lines as 'the eastern ravine's water flows into the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and the northern mountain.' Yuanwu says that before the ready-made public case is spoken its pattern is already manifest, and when its root is raised it leaks through layer after layer. The expression is also followed by 'there is no need to investigate' in fourteen matches across fourteen files. These Chinese uses supply both the literal compound and its deployment as an actual public-case expression.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 382 matches in 154 files. Six passages in six files ask, 'What is a ready-made public case?' One text uses 'this is called a ready-made public case,' another places it among a series of naming formulas, and the reversed order 'public case ready-made' occurs fifty-five times in forty-three files. Further fixed lines include 'ready-made public case, no need to investigate' (14/14), 'ready-made public case, already many-sided' (5/5), 'ready-made public case, without error or deception' (3/3), and 'ready-made public case, already overcomplicated' (7/7). All evidence here is from Chinese Chan sources.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與麼來者，現成公案。不與麼來者，垛生招箭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address says, 'One who comes this way is a ready-made public case. One who does not come this way piles up targets that invite arrows.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。大眾集定。乃曰。現成公案也是打堞不辦。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Lamp Continuation records a teacher ascending the hall. When the assembly has settled, he says, 'Even a ready-made public case cannot be arranged,' and steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敢問諸人，如何是現成公案？東澗水流西澗水，南山雲起北山雲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher asks the assembly, 'What is a ready-made public case?' and answers, 'The eastern ravine's water flows into the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and the northern mountain.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不見睦州凡遇僧來，便云：『現成公案。』如何是現成公案聻？雪到青山云不老，風來綠竹響笙簧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'Do you not see that whenever a monk came, Muzhou immediately said, Ready-made public case?' He then asks what a ready-made public case is and answers, 'Snow reaches the green mountain and says it does not age; wind comes to the green bamboo, which sounds like reed pipes.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 現成公案未言時。文彩已彰。洞徹根源才舉處。重重漏泄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu says, 'Before the ready-made public case is spoken, its pattern is already manifest. The moment its root, penetrated through, is raised, it leaks through layer after layer.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 現成公案不須參，也要諸人自委悉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'A ready-made public case does not need to be investigated, yet each of you must understand it for yourself.'

Senses.Explanation: A coordinate pair naming “principle” and “affairs, events, or matters.” Chan records ask how principle and affairs are unobstructed, say that both sides have been penetrated or are fully provided, and require them to be clearly distinguished. The Mirror Record gives one explicit account of their relation: “This principle is the principle that completes affairs; this affair is the affair that displays principle.” Ying’an says, “Penetrated on the side of principle and penetrated on the side of affairs: this is called principle and affairs fused through.” Other records speak of both being complete or ask directly, “What are principle and affairs?” The expression is translated as the coordinate pair stated by the texts rather than collapsed into one abstract category.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 850 matches in 198 files. Recurrent constructions include 'principle and affairs unobstructed' (117 matches in 63 files), 'principle and affairs perfectly fused' (24 in 21), 'principle and affairs both complete' (11 in 9), and 'principle and affairs distinct and clear' (9 in 6). Forty-six occurrences in thirty files ask, 'What are principle and affairs?' or use that wording within a fuller question. These distributions support one corpus-wide sense rather than a master-specific one.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或理事相即亦得。此理是成事之理。此事是顯理之事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says that principle and affairs may be mutually identical: this principle is the principle that completes affairs, and this affair is the affair that displays principle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是理事無礙法界？師曰：東西南北。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A question asks, 'What is the realm in which principle and affairs are unobstructed?' The teacher answers, 'East, west, south, north.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 理上也透，事上也透，所謂理事融徹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ying'an says, 'Penetrated on the side of principle and penetrated on the side of affairs: this is what is called principle and affairs fused through.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 宣揚默示，理事俱備
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record says, 'Whether proclaimed aloud or shown silently, principle and affairs are both complete.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 今宗鏡本意。要理事分明。方顯一心體用具足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says its basic intention requires principle and affairs to be distinct and clear; only then does it display the substance and function of one mind as fully present.

Senses.PreferredTarget: life and death is the great matter
AlternateTargets: the matter of life and death is great
life and death, the great matter
the great matter of life and death
Senses.Explanation: (生) birth + (死) death + (事) matter/affair + (大) great: "life and death is the great matter." In the corpus it is overwhelmingly a fixed four-graph line, and in 84 places across 56 allowlist texts it stands in the paired form "life and death is the great matter; impermanence is swift" (生死事大，無常迅速); (無常迅速) itself occurs 160 times, 76 of them outside the pair. One text names the pair for what it is — "...two ready-made phrases" (生死事大，無常迅速，兩句現話, J28nB208). The attested deployment range is observable and wide: (i) as the reason for leaving home or seeking a teacher — (念生死事大) (19×) and (為生死事大) (39×), as in (念生死事大)，(奮志尋師) and (念生死事大)，(乃薙染完具) (X82n1571); (ii) as a plea addressed to a master — "...I beg the master to save me" (問生死事大請師相救, 古尊宿語錄); (iii) as an inscription — the (續燈正統) biography of (雲棲蓮池袾宏大師) records "at seventeen... he kept writing the four graphs (生死事大) on his desk" (年十七，補邑庠，每書生死事大四字於案頭, X84n1583), and (弘覺忞禪師北遊集) records of the emperor's lodging that (堂門書)「(生死事大)」 ("the hall door bore ", J26nB180); (iv) as the opening of a (上堂) sermon — (上堂)：「(大眾)！(又是九月半也)，(生死事大)，(無常迅速) (J32nB273); (v) as a raised (示眾) with a directive — (天如和尚示眾云)：『(生死事大)。(諸禪德)！(須是將生死兩字貼在額頭上始得)。』 (" (生死事大)...you must paste the two graphs 'life and death' (生死) on your forehead", J25nB171). The most-cited setting is the Yongjia–Huineng exchange, narrated in many texts: (覺曰)：「(生死事大)，(無常迅速)。」(祖曰)：「(何不體取無生)，(了無速乎)？」 The graphs (大事因緣) / (一大事因緣) (the "one great matter," 699× / 415×) are a separate stock phrase. The texts assign (生死事大) no gloss beyond the literal reading of its graphs, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide sense (SenseKey null): 321 occurrences in 135 allowlist texts spanning the B, C, D, J, T and X canons and many independent masters and compilers — the multi-source gate is met many times over. (Counts are whole-file, tag-stripped with <note>/<rdg>/<orig> apparatus excluded; gate-2 recount, confirmed by two independent recounts.) Curated occurrences here are all narrated, raised, or biographical (a lamp record, a supplicant's plea, an inscription, a sermon opening, a raised 示眾), so MasterName is null; the Yongjia–Huineng exchange records the line as Yongjia Xuanjue's (永嘉玄覺) but is retold at third hand in every allowlist witness. The dominant collocate is (無常迅速); cross-ref (無常迅速) and (大事因緣).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (曹溪大休珠禪師六會語錄) (J27nB192); the Yongjia–Huineng exchange narrated within it. (覺) = (永嘉玄覺) (Yongjia Xuanjue) speaking to (祖) = (六祖) (Huineng). A retold historical exchange, so MasterName null per the raised/narrated-case rule.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問生死事大請師相救
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄) (C077n1710); a questioner's plea in a raised exchange — (問生死事大請師相救) (師云：三家村人失却火). Raised question, MasterName null. Shows the term deployed as a supplicant's opening to a master. The same eight-graph question also occurs earlier in the volume at lb 0808a20 with a different answer; this occurrence is the one at 0896c08.

Occurrences.Kwic: 每書生死事大四字於案頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (續燈正統) (X84n1583), a lamp compilation; the biographical notice of (雲棲蓮池袾宏大師): (年十七)，(補邑庠)，(每書生死事大四字於案頭)。(一日)，(失手碎茶甌)，(有省)。 MasterName null (biographical notice; the graphs are written, not spoken by a master). Occurrences.Kwic: 堂門書「生死事大」，壁書
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (弘覺忞禪師北遊集) (J26nB180); notice of the emperor's lodging — (上所居師蕘)，(堂門書)「(生死事大)」，(壁書)「(莫道老來方學道)，(孤墳盡是少年人)」(之句) — (上) (the emperor) then tells (忞) (木陳道忞): (每對此輒萬緣寢削). MasterName null (narrated notice; an inscription, not a master's utterance). Shows deployment as an inscription.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又是九月半也，生死事大，無常迅速，討甚
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (千巖禪師語錄) (J32nB273); the opening of an (上堂) (formal sermon) — (上堂)：「(大眾)！(又是九月半也)，(生死事大)，(無常迅速)… Raised in a compiled (語錄); MasterName null. Shows deployment as a sermon opener with the standard (無常迅速) pairing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (天隱和尚語錄) (J25nB171) raising (天如和尚) (the roster's 天如惟則): (舉)：「(天如和尚示眾云)：『(生死事大)。(諸禪德)！(須是將生死兩字貼在額頭上始得)。』 The raised exchange continues with a monk countering (只將不生不死四字貼在額頭上) and being driven out (遂拈拄杖趁出).
