Occurrences.AttributionNote: An imperial-command discourse pairs the whole-earth phrase with the predicate 'a true person.'

Senses.Explanation: Eye (目) plus in front or before (前): before the eyes, or what is right in front of someone. The headword occurs 3,984 times in 360 allowlist texts. Its best-known deployment is Jiashan Shanhui's formula: 'before your eyes there is no thing; the meaning is right before your eyes; it is not the thing before your eyes, not what eye and ear reach' (目前無法，意在目前；不是目前法，非耳目之所到). Lamp records place the statement in Jiashan's section, while later compilations raise it with the heading 'Jiashan addressed the assembly, saying' (夾山示眾云). Its clauses recur widely: 'before your eyes there is no thing' (目前無法), 262 occurrences in 120 texts; 'it is not the thing before your eyes' (不是目前法), 222 in 112; and 'not what eye and ear reach' (非耳目之所到), 181 in 95. Other forms point to this location: 'only right before you' (只在目前), 166; 'the Great Way is only right before you, yet what is before you is hard to see' (大道只在目前，要且目前難覩); and 'clearly right before you' (分明在目前), 115. The location can also be emptied in the line 'before your eyes there is no monk-you; here there is no old teacher' (目前無闍黎，此間無老僧), whose first clause occurs 78 times. The word remains a plain locative throughout these deployments; it does not name a state in which to dwell.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide locative sense: 'before the eyes' or 'in front of you.' Jiashan Shanhui (夾山善會) does not give the word a private meaning; he uses its ordinary locative force in the frequently cited formula 'before your eyes there is no thing' (目前無法). The formula receives Jiashan's MasterName only where the text's own heading places it in his record; raised versions remain null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 目前無法意在目前。不是目前法非耳目所到。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp (景德傳燈錄), in Jiashan Shanhui's own entry under the heirs of Chuanzi Decheng (船子德誠法嗣). Jiashan speaks the formula 'before your eyes there is no thing' (目前無法) to Daowu, who then smiles.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夾山示眾云目前無法意在目前不是目前法非耳目之所到。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Pearls Linking Verses on Old Cases in the Chan Lineage (禪宗頌古聯珠通集). The same formula is raised with the explicit heading 'Jiashan addressed the assembly, saying' (夾山示眾云). As a raised case, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 目前無法。意在目前。他不是目前法。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compendium of the Five Lamps (五燈會元). A master cites the same clauses in a hall address, introducing them with 'this old monk says' (老僧道). This is a raised formula, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大道只在目前，要且目前難覩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書). The statement says that the Great Way is only right before you, yet what is before you is hard to see (大道只在目前，要且目前難覩).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如來今在何所，令我莫著？文殊云：只在目前。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要). 'Only right before you' (只在目前) appears as an answer in a raised dialogue between an emperor and Manjusri (文殊).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是一色？師曰：目前無闍黎，此間無老僧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書). The exchange uses the emptied-locus line 'before your eyes there is no monk-you; here there is no old teacher' (目前無闍黎，此間無老僧).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘blind, deaf, and mute.’ In the Chan record the full phrase chiefly names the persons in Xuansha’s ‘three kinds of invalids’ public question: if someone who is blind cannot see the raised mallet or whisk, someone deaf cannot hear spoken complete command, and someone mute cannot answer, ‘how do you receive them?’ Yuanwu preserves those three clauses and warns explicitly that taking the matter merely as blind, deaf, and mute misses it; he later asks whether his audience knows the standing of ‘the fellow who is blind, deaf, and mute’ and quotes Xuedou’s verse beginning with the same four graphs. Later records identify it as ‘Xuansha’s three-invalids case,’ ask again ‘how is blind, deaf, and mute?’, and attach new verses. A Yunmen episode applies the disabilities turn by turn: Yunmen asks whether the monk is deaf when he fails to respond, then whether he is mute when he says he does not understand; Xuedou later calls him ‘this blind, deaf, and mute fellow.’ The phrase also occurs literally outside the case, including lists of disabilities and people said to be unable to resolve doubt ‘like the blind, deaf, and mute.’ Zen usage bends the disability list into the stable name and repeated wording of a public interview about receiving people for whom the usual visible, audible, and spoken exchanges are unavailable.
Senses.Note: One referent family: persons described as blind, deaf, and mute. The Xuansha case is the primary Zen-loaded deployment, but the literal list and the case wording do not denote incompatible things. The entry does not supply a figurative diagnosis where the texts merely state disabilities.

Occurrences.Kwic: 患盲者。拈鎚竪拂他又不見。患聾者。語言三昧他又不聞。患啞者。教他說又說不得。且作麼生接。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing three-invalids question enumerates sight, hearing, and speech constraints.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今人若作盲聾瘖啞會。卒摸索不著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu explicitly warns against stopping at a merely literal handling of the phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還識盲聾瘖啞底漢子落處麼。看取雪竇頌云。盲聾瘖啞杳絕機宜天上天下堪笑堪悲
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu asks about the fellow's standing and quotes Xuedou's verse opening.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門云：『汝不是患聾麼？』又云：『會麼？』僧云：『不會。』門云：『汝不是患啞麼？』僧于是有省。雪竇便喝云：『這盲聾瘖啞漢，若不是雲門，驢年去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Yunmen exchange deploys deafness and muteness turn by turn; Xuedou applies the full phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頌玄沙三種病話。盲聾瘖啞，捉敗了也。更問：如何盲聾瘖啞？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record labels the material Xuansha's three-invalids case, verses it, and renews the question.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 22 times in 16 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a master's meetings with people.
Senses.Note: The English follows the graph meaning 'straight' (直) and the texts' own oppositions: straight versus crooked (直／曲), genuine versus false (真實／虛假), and straight conduct versus flattering crookedness (諂曲). The direct definition 'without bends or twists' occurs once, while the site-of-the-Way formula occurs across multiple independent records. No master-specific sense is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 起信論云：直心。直心者，無委曲故。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later Chan record cites a compact definition: straight mind means without bends or twists.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫心行諂曲，口說法直，口說一行三昧，不行直心，非佛弟子。但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著，名一行三昧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Platform Record. Huineng contrasts speaking straight while acting crookedly with carrying out straight mind, then says to have no grasping regarding anything.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An assembly address coordinates straight mind, speech, conduct, and verification in four parallel clauses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所云直心是道場，無虛假故。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record supplies the direct predicate: straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但能直心直行，無許多人我是非、邪妄諂曲
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text describes straight mind and straight conduct through the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, flattery, and crookedness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與人相見惟以直心直行、本色本分
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biographical notice characterizes the master's meetings with people by straight mind, straight conduct, original color, and original share.

Senses.PreferredTarget: directly pointing at the human mind
AlternateTargets: pointing straight at the person's mind
Senses.Explanation: (直) = directly/straight, (指) = point, (人心) = the person's mind. One of the four stock phrases the corpus attaches to Bodhidharma's coming from the West, paired with (見性成佛) ('see nature, become Buddha') in 470 of its 624 allowlist hits (190 files) and preceded by (不立文字) ('not setting up words') in 118 (79 files). Attested deployment: (a) the slogan of what Bodhidharma brought -- (達磨西來不立文字)。(直指人心見性成佛) ('Bodhidharma came from the West not setting up words -- directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha'; Dahui, T47n1997); (達磨西來直指人心見性成佛)。(亦復如是) ('Bodhidharma came from the West directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha; and so it is likewise'; Huitang Zuxin, T51n2077); the Blue Cliff Record (碧巖錄) variant carries (單傳心印) ('the single transmission of the mind-seal') alongside it (謂之教外別傳。單傳心印。直指人心。見性成佛 -- 'this is called a separate transmission outside the teachings, the single transmission of the mind-seal, directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha'; T48n2003); (b) a gloss in a master's own words -- Dahui: (達磨西來不立文字語句)。(唯直指人心)。(若論直指)。(只人人本有) ('Bodhidharma came from the West setting up no words or phrases -- only directly pointing at the human mind; as for direct pointing, just what every person inherently has', T47n1997); (c) a test-question -- (如何是直指人心) ('what is directly pointing at the human mind?'; 4 hits / 4 files), with the recorded answers (舌在口裏) ('the tongue is in the mouth'; the follow-up 如何是見性成佛？師曰：金屑雖貴，落眼成翳 -- 'what is seeing nature and becoming Buddha? The master said: gold dust, though precious, once fallen in the eye becomes a cataract', X82n1571) and (腳跟下分明看取) ('look clearly right under your heels'; answering 如何是直指人心、見性成佛之旨 -- 'what is the purport of directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha?', J34nB311). Collocations: (單傳直指) ('single transmission, direct pointing'; 119 hits / 73 files), (直指單傳) ('direct pointing, single transmission'; 95 / 71), (西來直指) ('the direct pointing of the coming from the West'; 42 / 34), (直指之道) ('the way of direct pointing'; 67 / 34), (若論直指) ('as for direct pointing'; 13 / 13). Beyond recorded lines such as Dahui's (只人人本有) ('just what every person inherently has'), the texts leave the phrase without gloss, and so does this entry.
Senses.Note: 624 hits across 216 files of the 462-file allowlist (XML tags/notes/rdg stripped, whitespace collapsed, punctuation retained -- all counts in this entry use this convention; 見性成佛 ('seeing nature, becoming Buddha') counted as following across at most one punctuation mark). Nearly always in the Bodhidharma four-phrase frame (with 'not setting up words' (不立文字) / 'a separate transmission outside the teachings' (教外別傳) / 'seeing nature, becoming Buddha' (見性成佛)); the paired (見性成佛) is its near-constant companion (470 of 624 hits). Curated occurrences span a master's (語錄) ('recorded sayings'; Dahui), a (古尊宿) ('Ancient Worthies') anthology, a (燈錄) ('lamp record'; the 續傳燈錄, Continued Lamp Record), and the (碧巖錄) (the Blue Cliff Record, T48n2003 -- a 頌古/評唱 collection of verse-comments on old cases and prose expositions, a case-commentary collection, not a lamp record).

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來不立文字。直指人心見性成佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The full Bodhidharma slogan in Dahui's mouth: Bodhidharma came from the West not setting up words -- directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 唯直指人心。若論直指。只人人本有。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's gloss in his own record: (唯直指人心)。(若論直指)。(只人人本有) -- 'only directly pointing at the human mind; as for direct pointing, just what every person inherently has.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來教外別傳一句且道別傳個什麼直指人心見性成佛
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Four-phrase slogan, cross-linking (教外別傳): Bodhidharma came from the West -- a separate transmission outside the teachings, one phrase; tell me, what was transmitted? -- directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature, becoming Buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來直指人心見性成佛。亦復如是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huitang Zuxin (黃龍祖心) in the Continued Lamp Record (續傳燈錄), of what Bodhidharma brought: (達磨西來直指人心見性成佛)。(亦復如是) ('Bodhidharma came from the West directly pointing at the human mind, seeing nature and becoming Buddha; and so it is likewise').

Occurrences.Kwic: 謂之教外別傳。單傳心印。直指人心。見性成佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record pointer: the formula carrying (單傳心印) ('single transmission of the mind-seal') alongside (直指人心).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘mutually deceive.’ The phrase occurs 178 times in 97 allowlisted texts. Its most stable teaching formula is ‘only provide the assenting heart, and we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心，決不相賺), with graphic variants for ‘provide’ (辦 and 辨) and both ‘certainly’ (決) and ‘necessarily’ (必). Masters use it as an assurance to an audience: ‘trust my words; we certainly will not deceive one another’ and ‘I assure you of this matter; in the end it is not false.’ Elsewhere the same literal verb can state that two sides do deceive each other. The reciprocal participants are supplied by context; these are not different things or separate senses.
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary verb of mutual deception into a repeated teaching-seat assurance tied to ‘the assenting heart’ (肯心). The negative formula dominates but does not change the verb’s referent. Family review with ‘conceal from one another’ (相瞞) and ‘deceive’ (誑欺) supports one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古之所謂但辨肯心，決不相賺
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Quotes the established assenting-heart formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但辦肯心必不相賺。珍重。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu closes an address with the concise formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 他日甚有得力，決不相賺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prospective assurance in a separate record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪人當信予言，決不相賺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker directly assures a Chan student that his words will not deceive.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若辦此心，决不相賺。我今為汝保任此事，終不虗也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The mutual-deception assurance is immediately restated as guaranteeing that the matter is not false.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to examine and awaken; in the Chan records, to come to understand. The term occurs 229 times in 98 allowlisted texts, chiefly as a biographical result clause. A monk is told to wash his bowl and suddenly understands; Shigong cannot bring himself to shoot Mazu and understands; a layman is asked whether he understands and suddenly does; and Daowu hears a spirit-medium's song and suddenly understands. An instructional record also says there must be a basis for understanding and warns against stopping after grasping a few fixed phrases. The term records the narrator's or teacher's verdict that understanding occurred; the word itself adds no account of what was understood.
Senses.Note: One verbal event across sudden and unmodified forms. The various occasions—speech, question, action, or heard song—are causes supplied by their narratives, not separate senses of the word.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。洗鉢盂去。其僧忽然省悟。上堂。纔有是非。紛然失心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The wash-your-bowl case uses the term as its narrated result.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石鞏慧藏禪師初為獵人射鹿，因遇馬，祖令自射，無下手處，省悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shigong's biography reports understanding when he cannot shoot Mazu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。還會麼。居士忽然省悟。有頌云。心鏡從來瑩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question to a layman is followed by the narrator's verdict and a verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聞巫者樂神云：識神無。忽然省悟。後參前關南，印其所解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daowu's biography reports sudden understanding on hearing a song, followed by confirmation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須知有省悟之由若真實叅學但恁麼看據現定會些子言句便休也在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instructional record contrasts a basis for understanding with stopping at a few grasped phrases.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). The exact phrase occurs four times in four allowlisted texts; all four are preserved here. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 40 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.
Senses.Note: All four exact witnesses are late records. The broader eyebrow formulas supply family breadth but are not substituted as occurrences for the exact headword. PreferredTarget remains literal; 'penalty for false teaching' is too narrow because the exact witnesses attach it to several different recorded speech/case contexts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趨炎附暖底不顧爛額焦頭、添薪熾炭底那管眉毛墮落？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A rhetorical question asks who, while adding fuel to the blaze, cares whether the eyebrows fall out.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈云：「若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The commentator says that treating Shimen's line as Buddhist teaching-discussion implicates Shimen in eyebrow loss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 看這翠巖眉毛墮落處自救不了，復有三元龍象互相蹴踏，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later review points to where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out in the transmitted exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「丹霞燒木佛，院主為甚麼眉毛墮落？」師云：「脫體風光。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question connects Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha with the monastery director's eyebrow loss; the answer is preserved without interpreting it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "brows intertwined with one another." The phrase occurs 129 times in 80 allowlisted texts. The records use the bodily image for persons brought into exceptionally close conjunction: one master says that for five or six years he has had his brows intertwined with the assembly, yet in fact they have had "no traffic in rice or water" (五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交). Another requires "brows intertwined, sharing life and sharing death" (眉毛廝結，同生同死). It also appears as an answer in a public interview: asked for the phrase for opening the retreat, the master replies, "brows intertwined" (眉毛廝結). Elsewhere a hall address sets saying and silence against each other: "if one speaks, heaven and earth are far apart; if one does not speak, brows are intertwined" (說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結). The Chan use turns a physical impossibility into a compact, repeatable encounter phrase; the accompanying clauses establish proximity or conjunction but do not authorize this entry to decide what speakers intend by it.
Senses.Note: One idiomatic referent covers the sampled uses. Pairings with “no dealings,” “sharing life and death,” speech/silence, and retreat opening are distinct contexts, not distinct objects or word classes. No second sense is created from competing readings of the image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 五六年來雖則與諸人眉毛廝結，其實水米無交
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says his brows have been intertwined with the assembly for years, yet they have had no traffic in rice or water.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須眉毛廝結，同生同死。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is directly paired with “sharing life and sharing death.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「摩竭掩室、毘耶杜口則不問，即今天童結制一句，請師舉唱。」師云：「眉毛廝結。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked to proclaim a phrase for Tiantong's opening of the retreat, the master answers, “brows intertwined.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 說即天地懸殊，不說即眉毛廝結。說與不說，拈放一邊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address contrasts speaking, when heaven and earth are far apart, with not speaking, when brows are intertwined, then sets both aside.

Senses.PreferredTarget: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘look at the talk’: look at the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound most often occurs in ‘look at the saying's head’ (看話頭), and the local wording—not an imported technical label—determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. The records include a monk seeking written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. They also preserve criticism: Mingben reports people calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ and contrasts this with looking left and right at one's own selected saying. Another record demands, ‘if you recognize it and can say it, come out and say it—what does the end of the talk say?’ Thus the Zen deviation is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in recorded exchanges and itself subjected to criticism in the record.
Senses.Note: No separate sense is created for different possible English renderings of “talk” (話) in context; they are readings of the same act and object family. Exact “look at the talk” (看話) also occurs across word boundaries in ordinary prose, so only lexically coherent deployments are curated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說著箇看話頭做工夫。遽引信心銘，謂執之失度，必入邪路。剛謂直指單傳，無如是事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mingben reports and criticizes calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’; the entry does not adopt that category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因看話頭處未通，出紙求指示
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk requests written direction because the saying he is looking at remains unresolved.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初不做工夫、亦不看話頭，一聞恁麼舉便云無下手處
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record explicitly says the hunter had neither done work nor looked at a saying before his reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 識得道得出來道看話端道什麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public challenge asks one who recognizes and can say it to state what the end of the talk says.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘to deceive people.’ The phrase is accusation, warning, and public-interview vocabulary throughout the Chan record. Yunmen asks for ‘a saying that does not deceive people’ (不瞞人底句), then supplies ‘do not say this is the one that deceives people.’ Miyun writes the maxim ‘deceiving people is no good affair; a good affair does not deceive people’ (瞞人不好事，好事不瞞人). Yet the record also refuses a simple division between deceptive speakers and innocent words. The Blue Cliff Record asks whether the patriarchs and buddhas have an intention to deceive, answers by comparing them to rivers and lakes that have no intention to obstruct, and says that when people cannot pass through, the patriarchs and buddhas consequently ‘become deceivers of people.’ Other records pair deceiving people with deceiving oneself and distinguish being able to do one but not the other. Chan thus bends ordinary deception into a recurrent test of sayings, teachers, hearers, and self-deception while retaining the literal verb; the entry does not decide who intends deception where the text expressly denies such intention.
Senses.Note: 259 raw hits in 125 allowlist texts. ‘Deceive people’ (瞞人) and ‘deceive oneself’ (自瞞) take different objects but retain the same verb sense, so no split is warranted. The intention-denying Blue Cliff passage is preserved because it constrains the definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖佛還有瞞人之心也無。牙云。汝道江湖還有礙人之心也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks whether patriarchs and buddhas have an intention to deceive people; the reply compares this with rivers and lakes having an intention to obstruct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖佛雖無瞞人之心。自是時人透不得。祖佛却成瞞人去也。不得道祖佛不瞞人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The commentary denies deceptive intention but says inability to pass through makes the patriarchs and buddhas become deceivers; neither side of the text's contrast may be dropped.

Occurrences.Kwic: 瞞人不好事，好事不瞞人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Miyun states the compact maxim: deceiving people is no good affair; a good affair does not deceive people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝有一對眼，我也有一對眼。汝若瞞，還自瞞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master turns attempted deception back as self-deception: if you deceive, you deceive yourself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若只解瞞人，不能自瞞，此人有手無眼；若只自瞞得過，不能瞞人，此人有眼無手
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wuzhun's record explicitly distinguishes competence at deceiving people from competence at deceiving oneself.

Senses.Explanation: Knowing (知) joined to interpreting or explaining (解): intellectual understanding, or knowing reached through explanation. The corpus overwhelmingly uses the term as a rebuke or warning. Its flagship form is 'a follower of the intellectual-understanding lineage' (知解宗徒, 35 occurrences), a label applied to Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi: even Shenhui and Guifeng were rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒). In an origin case, a student names the matter 'Buddha-nature at the original source' (本源佛性), and the master says that even if this fellow later founds a place, he will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (此子已後設有把茅蓋頭，只成得箇知解宗徒). Another passage puts a whole list of teaching styles under the same verdict (此等見解盡屬知解宗徒). The common gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) occurs 80 times. Its continuation says that when intellectual understanding does not arise, one is like the king's sword, killing or giving life according to the occasion (知解既不生，如王寶劍，殺活臨時). Other records say people are deceived by intellectual understanding and conjecture (多被知解卜度瞞過), or that the matter is not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding (不是知解邊事). The headword occurs 1,044 times in 215 allowlist texts. This entry reports the corpus's repeated pejorative deployment without turning it into a general theory of mind. The Huangbo record extends the term through a food-and-digestion comparison stated by the text: after calling the students' condition 'food not digested' (食不消), it says, 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥). Parallel witnesses preserve the same wording in the Records of the Schools (宗門統要續集) and the Eye of Humans and Devas (人天眼目).
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide pejorative. The origin rebuke and the naming of Shenhui and Zongmi as followers of intellectual understanding (知解宗徒) are raised material, while 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) is a stock proclamation. Compare distinguishing (分別), deliberation (思量), emotional consciousness (情識), and conjecture (卜度).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此子已後設有把茅蓋頭只成得箇知解宗徒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄), section raising an old case (舉古). A student who names it 'Buddha-nature at the original source' (本源佛性) is rebuked as someone who will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (只成得箇知解宗徒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings at Guangfu Chan Cloister on Niushan in Xinning County (住新寧縣牛山廣福禪院語錄). The address names Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi as people rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此等見解盡屬知解宗徒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings at Wukong Chan Temple on Longmen in Hangzhou (住杭州龍門悟空禪寺語錄). A list of teaching styles, including direct pointing at the human mind (直指人心), is placed under the verdict 'followers of intellectual understanding' (知解宗徒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 入此門來，莫存知解。知解既不生，如王寶劍
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), section on imperial guiding principles (受勅奉旨提綱). The gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) is followed by the king's sword that kills or gives life according to the occasion (如王寶劍，殺活臨時).

Occurrences.Kwic: 多被知解卜度瞞過
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Letter replying to the student of letters Mao Xuanshu (復毛文學玄淑). Intellectual understanding and conjecture are named as what deceives people (被知解卜度瞞過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 葢為這箇不是知解邊事也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄). The speaker marks the matter off as 'not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding' (不是知解邊事).

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Essentials of Mind Transmission from Chan Master Huangbo Duanji (黃檗山斷際禪師傳心法要): 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥). The preceding line calls it 'food not digested' (食不消).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a stone woman; the wording also names a woman unable to bear children. The expression occurs 1,114 times in 233 allowlisted texts. Chan verses and answers give this impossible figure actions associated with life and movement: she bears a child, dances when the wooden man sings, sings herself, spins hemp, weaves, puts on flowers, and calls back a dream. “The stone woman bears a child” occurs 42 times in 37 texts, while “stone woman's child” occurs 49 times in 35. Guangqing lists a stone woman bearing a child beside dust rising from a well and waves rising from a mountain, then asks how the inherited sayings should be understood and rejects a menu of proposed readings. Dongshan's verse pairs the wooden man's song with the stone woman's dance and says it is not reached by discriminating consciousness or admitted by deliberation. A later speaker calls being pressed to preach like forcing a stone woman to bear a child or making a rooster lay an egg. The corpus's deviation is the stable impossible actor: it repeatedly gives generation, speech, craft, and motion to what its own parallel constructions treat as unable to perform them.
Senses.Note: The literal and reproductive force belong to the same stock figure. The many actions are predicates of that one figure, not separate senses or interpretive readings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古今相承，皆云塵生井底，浪起山頭。結子空華，生兒石女。且作麼生會？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guangqing places the child-bearing stone woman in an inherited series of reversed or impossible events and asks how it is understood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 木人方歌，石女起舞。非情識到，寧容思慮。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan pairs the wooden man's singing with the stone woman's dancing and explicitly excludes discriminating consciousness and deliberation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：木人把板雲中拍。曰：意旨如何？師曰：石女拈笙水底吹。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interview answer makes the stone woman play a reed organ under water, paired with a wooden man clapping a board in the clouds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰如何是不來不去底人。師曰。石女喚回三界夢。木人坐斷六門機。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Danxia answers a question with the stone woman calling back the dream of the three realms.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今是東禪法姪特請弁山為眾說法，大似逼石女生兒，教雄雞下蛋，不免杜譔一偈，聊塞眾聽：
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later public address explicitly compares being pressed to preach with forcing a stone woman to bear a child and a rooster to lay an egg.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。無角鐵牛眠少室。生兒石女老黃梅。僧云。恁麼則韶陽兒孫祖峯嫡于。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage answer couples the child-bearing stone woman with a hornless iron ox.

Senses.Explanation: To violate a binding precept; with a person-word, one who has done so. The compound appears 245 times in 99 allowlisted texts. Juelang’s instruction makes the ordinary threshold explicit: one must be cautious in every word and movement and ‘not wait until the traces show before calling it breaking the precepts’ (勿待形跡發露，而後為破戒也). In public interviews the term becomes a live question rather than a cancelled rule. One lamp case asks how a pure practitioner does not enter nirvana and a precept-breaking monk does not enter hell; another asks whether hearing ornaments through a wall counts as breaking the precepts and then tests a crowded scene of gold, silver, crimson, and purple. Yongjue likewise asks why a precept-breaking monk does not fall into hell. The Chan record also widens what can receive the label. Baizhang says that every seeking mind is called a ‘precept-breaking monk’ (但有一切求心盡名破戒比丘), while Juelang contrasts two assignments: entering birth and death counts as breaking for a lesser-vehicle person, but abandoning birth and death counts as breaking for a great being (二乘人以生死菩提為二，以涉生死為破戒；大士以生死菩提為不二，以捨生死為破戒). The deviation is therefore attestable in both the public use of a real violation category and the record’s explicit reassignment of what constitutes the breach.
Senses.Note: The entry reports the recorded questions without supplying an answer absent from those passages. The corpus’s interview deployment retains the stated violation category. Exact count: 245 hits in 99 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一言一動，必須戒慎恐懼，無使心行有少過差。勿待形跡發露，而後為破戒也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang says not to wait for outward traces before calling it precept-breaking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問清淨行者不入涅槃。破戒比丘不入地獄如何。師曰。度盡無遺影還他越涅槃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question pairs the pure practitioner and the precept-breaking monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 律中道。隔壁聞釵釧聲即名破戒。見覩金銀合雜朱紫駢闐。是破戒不是破戒。師曰。好箇入路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher cites a code’s boundary and tests it against a crowded visual scene.

Occurrences.Kwic: 經云：破戒比丘不入地獄。既是破戒比丘，因甚不入地獄？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue poses the precept-breaker’s non-fall as a direct question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 秖如今但有一切求心盡名破戒比丘名字羅漢盡名野干
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baizhang applies ‘precept-breaking monk’ to anyone with a seeking mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二乘人以生死菩提為二，以涉生死為破戒；大士以生死菩提為不二，以捨生死為破戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang explicitly assigns opposite breaches: entering birth and death for the lesser-vehicle person, abandoning it for the great being.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, worn-out or torn straw sandals. Straw sandals are the footwear of travel on foot between teachers, and the fixed phrase “wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) records that travel. The compound is also spoken as an answer and a comparison. Huangbo says, “the patriarchs' dark purport is worn-out straw sandals; it would be best to go barefoot and not put them on” (祖師玄旨是破草鞋，寧可赤脚不著最好). Another master answers “what is the Way?” with “worn-out straw sandals—throw them in the lake.” Other records answer “what is buddha?” with “wear out the straw sandals and walk barefoot,” and admonish people who have worn out sandals and abandoned teachers and parents to travel on foot that they must be alert. Zen thus bends discarded travel footwear into a blunt answer and an explicit comparison for revered formulations; the object remains sandals, and the entry adds no symbolic property beyond the texts' own comparisons.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 418 matches in 147 texts. The retained set covers the direct comparison to the patriarchs' dark purport, a direct Way question, a buddha question, the travel-on-foot institutional collocation, and the barefoot consequence. Family revalidation against “straw sandals” (草鞋), “travel on foot” (行脚), and “wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) confirms one object sense. ‘Wear out sandals’ is a verb phrase involving that object, not a second thing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師玄旨是破草鞋。寧可赤脚不著最好。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo explicitly says, ‘The patriarchs' dark purport is worn-out straw sandals. It would be best to go barefoot and not put them on.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是道。師曰。破草鞋。與拋向湖裏著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘What is the Way?’ the master answers, ‘Worn-out straw sandals—throw them in the lake.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 踏破草鞋赤脚走。僧問：須彌納芥子即不問，微塵裏轉大法輪時如何？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-hall line says, ‘Wear out the straw sandals and walk barefoot,’ before the next monk's question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一等是踏破草鞋，拋却師長父母行脚，直須著些子精彩始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master addresses those who ‘wear out straw sandals, abandon teachers and parents, and travel on foot,’ saying they must show some alertness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是佛？師云：踏破草鞋赤脚走。云：如何是佛向上事？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘What is buddha?’ the master answers, ‘Wear out the straw sandals and walk barefoot’; the monk then asks about the matter beyond buddha.

Senses.PreferredTarget: polishing a tile to make a mirror
AlternateTargets: grinding a brick into a mirror
polish a tile and make a mirror
Senses.Explanation: Literally, polishing or grinding (磨) a tile or brick (磚) to make (作) a mirror (鏡): "polishing a tile to make a mirror." This graph form occurs 43 times in 37 allowlisted texts. Graphic variants include "polishing a tile to make a mirror" (磨甎作鏡, 19 hits in 13 texts) and the form with another tile graph (磨塼作鏡, 5 in 5); "polishing a tile into a mirror" (磨磚成鏡) occurs 8 times in 5. In the defining encounter, Mazu Daoyi is sitting Chan to become a buddha. Nan'yue Huairang polishes a tile; asked why, he says he is making a mirror. Mazu says, "how could polishing a tile make a mirror?" Huairang answers, "if polishing a tile cannot make a mirror, how could your sitting Chan make a buddha?" (磨甎既不成鏡，汝坐禪豈得成佛). The exchange continues with the comparison of a cart that will not move: should one strike the cart or the ox? Later records use the compact phrase as the name of this encounter and as an explicit comparison for futile effort: Huanglong pairs "searching the sea and counting sand, vainly spending strength" with "polishing a tile to make a mirror, uselessly applying effort" (入海算沙，空自費力；磨塼作鏡，枉用功夫). Fachang compares private explanations and forced elaboration to it. Songgu compilations preserve named comments that call "sitting Chan to become a buddha" a sickness in the heart and "making a mirror by polishing a tile" a flower before the eyes. Zen therefore bends an impossible craft operation into the roster-name of Huairang's encounter with Mazu and a corpus-attested comparison for wasted construction; its application to sitting Chan is spoken by Huairang inside the case, not supplied by this entry.
Senses.Note: The graph for "tile" alternates among the standard form (磚) and two graphic variants (甎 and 塼) across witnesses. The first graphic variant (甎) appears in important early lamp and case-compilation witnesses. This entry groups those orthographic variants but does not count them toward the exact 43-hit headword total.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：磨甎作什麼？讓曰：磨甎作鏡。師曰：磨甎豈得成鏡？讓曰：磨甎既不成鏡，汝坐禪豈得成佛？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Continued Lamp Record preserves the defining Huairang-Mazu exchange: the impossible mirror is directly compared with sitting Chan to become a buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 入海算沙。空自費力。磨塼作鏡。枉用功夫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong Huinan pairs counting sand in the sea with polishing a tile into a mirror and explicitly predicates vain strength and useless effort.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫只與麼業識茫茫，無明人我，私心作解，妄生穿鑿，如磨磚作鏡相似，多少贅訛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fachang Yiyu compares private explanations and forced elaboration to polishing a tile to make a mirror.

Occurrences.Kwic: 坐禪成佛心中病，作鏡磨甎眼裏花
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The classified collection attributes to Fodeng Xun a verse pairing becoming buddha by sitting Chan with making a mirror by polishing a tile.

Occurrences.Kwic: 磨磚作鏡、打車打牛，小兒子戲；黃檗喫棒、大愚還拳，小兒子戲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending Yikui groups polishing the tile and striking cart or ox together as children's play, showing the compact phrase functioning as the name of the case.

Senses.Explanation: To address or instruct the assembled community publicly. The term occurs 12,002 times in 399 allowlisted texts and is a standard discourse heading beside the formal hall address (上堂) and small convocation (小參): a master “addresses the assembly, saying” (示眾云/曰), sometimes after ascending the seat. The corpus groups the formal hall address (上堂) and address to the assembly (示眾) as public formats and compares a small convocation with an address to the assembly. It can be delivered in writing as a verse after the assembly answers a question. The format also includes final instructions (臨終示眾), as when Luopu begins by asking the assembly about one matter. Chan turns “show to the assembly” into a recurring name for the master’s public verbal address; it is not a private exchange.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-institutional sense. Split from physically displaying an object. The formal hall address (上堂) and small convocation (小參) remain neighboring format entries. Written-verse instruction belongs here because the verse addresses the assembly; it does not create a third sense merely by changing medium.

Occurrences.Kwic: 陞座示眾云。鉤頭有餌。句裏無私。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (圓悟佛果禪師語錄) (Yuanwu Keqin's yulu); the whole record is Yuanwu's teaching. Standard genre form: (陞座示眾云) = ascending the seat, instructing the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂示眾，不立別名者，俱借五參一事統攝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Editorial preface of (列祖提綱錄), describing (上堂) and (示眾) as categories of a master's address subsumed under the five-day convocation. Definitional evidence that (示眾) is a genre-label.

Occurrences.Kwic: 黃檗和尚示眾云：汝等諸人盡是不著便底
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Cited (復舉) in (列祖提綱錄); the address to the assembly is Huangbo's (the well-known 盡是不著便底 / 大唐國裏無禪師 admonition).

Occurrences.Kwic: 夜來撾鼓升堂，喚作小參；今日陞堂撾鼓，謂之示眾。示眾、小參，初無二說；夜來、今日，豈有兩般？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuejiang Zhengyin's Recorded Sayings (月江正印禪師語錄): 'last night, beating the drum and ascending the hall was called a small gathering; today, ascending the hall and beating the drum is called an address to the assembly. Address to the assembly and small gathering originally have no two statements; how could last night and today be two different things?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 洛浦臨終示眾云：「今有一事問你諸人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Luopu’s final address opens by saying that he has one matter to ask the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 尊者從三昧起。示眾曰。我所得法。而非有故。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A patriarch emerges from absorbed stillness and verbally declares to the assembly what teaching he obtained.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因中也設問，眾荅之，不愜師意，故書偈示眾曰：秪因日起明中暗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the assembly’s answers do not accord, the master writes a verse and presents it to the assembly. This anchors written-verse public instruction rather than another spoken heading.

Senses.Explanation: To physically show or raise an object before the assembly. The Zen Buddha holds up a flower while everyone remains silent (拈花示眾). Masters likewise raise a whisk, garment, or mirror and then question the assembly. These are observable public displays, not verbal-address headings. The flower occurrence defines the Zen Buddha through the flower-sermon deployment; the whisk occurrence shows the master’s teaching-seat implement in use without assigning it an unattested meaning.
Senses.Note: Different physical objects instantiate one display action; they are not separate senses. Split from spoken instruction because displaying an object and delivering an address are different acts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊在靈山會上，拈花示眾，眾皆默然
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (聯燈會要), the Vulture-Peak flower-holding story: (拈花示眾) shows the literal display root of the word — the World-Honored One held up a flower and showed it to the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉拂示眾云。大眾見麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master raises the whisk before the assembly and asks whether they see.

Occurrences.Kwic: 藥山提起示眾曰。法身還具四大也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yaoshan raises a donated garment and asks the assembly whether the teaching-body has the four elements.

Occurrences.Kwic: 仰山寂禪師住東平時，溈山令僧送書并鏡與師。師上堂，提起示眾曰：
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yangshan ascends the hall and raises a mirror sent by Guishan before the assembly.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West
AlternateTargets: what the Patriarch came from the West for
the point of Bodhidharma's coming from the West
Senses.Explanation: A fixed liturgical question, almost always in the frame (如何是祖師西來意) — 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?' The Patriarch is Bodhidharma (the First Patriarch); 'coming from the West' is his journey from India to China, so the question literally asks why he came and what he brought. In the records it is one of the most common test-questions a monk puts to a master, and the recorded answers are turning-words rather than explanations — Zhaozhou 'the cypress tree in the front garden' (庭前柏樹子), Xianglin 'you sit long and get tired' (坐久成勞), Longya 'when the stone tortoise talks I'll tell you', Guishan 'what a fine lantern' (大好燈籠), Mazu answers with a kick to the chest. Linji's record engages the question on its own word (意): (問)。(如何是西來意)。(師云)。(若有意)。(自救不了)。(云)。(既無意)。(云何二祖得法)。(師云)。(得者是不得) ('If there were a meaning, he could not save even himself.' — 'If there is no meaning, how did the Second Patriarch obtain the teaching?' — 'The getting is not-getting'); the same record has Zhaozhou put the question while Linji is washing his feet and receive (恰值老僧洗脚) ('you happen to catch this old monk washing his feet'), and Longya — handed the Chan board (禪板) he was told to fetch and struck with it — reply (打即任打)。(要且無祖師意) ('hit me if you like; still there is no Patriarch's meaning'), the whole exchange then repeating at Cuiwei with a cushion. Xiangyan's tree case states the stakes of the question itself: (樹下有人)。(問西來意)。(不對即違他所問)。(若對又喪身失命) ('someone under the tree asks the meaning of the coming from the West; not answering fails his question, answering costs body and life'). The records also pair it with the scriptural teaching: the double-question (祖意教意是同是別) ('are the Patriarch's meaning and the teaching's meaning the same or different?') is itself a stock question, and Zhaozhou's own record answers it (會得祖意)。(便會教意) ('understand the Patriarch's meaning and you understand the teaching's meaning'). Render it literally — 'the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West'.
Senses.Note: Overwhelmingly attested: 1736 raw occurrences across 239 allowlist texts. The five curated occurrences are chosen as classic, mutually independent answers to the stock question. Frame counts (462-text allowlist grep): the fixed question (如何是祖師西來意) 1858 hits in 231 texts; short forms (西來意) 3071 in 314 and (祖師意) 645 in 185; intensified (西來的的意) 112 in 54; (達磨西來) 494 in 181; the answer-tag (庭前柏樹子) 317 in 130; the paired question (祖意教意是同是別) 32 in 19. Refs: Linji material T47n1985 0502a08 (若有意。自救不了), 0504a16 (恰值老僧洗脚), 0504b03–06 (龍牙/翠微); Xiangyan tree case T48n2005 0293c03; Zhaozhou's (會得祖意)。(便會教意) J24nB137 0367b30.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to make a ritual bow or prostration
Senses.Explanation: The graphs join rite or reverence (禮) to bowing or obeisance (拜): to bow or prostrate oneself. The word occurs 9,933 times across 403 allowlisted texts. In encounter dialogue it is a standard bodily response after an exchange, including at awakening: Xuefeng, at Yantou's words, has a great awakening and “thereupon bowed” (便禮拜). It also marks movement through the public event: a monk “bowed and withdrew” (禮拜而退), another “bowed and returned to the assembly” (禮拜歸眾), and one “bowed, rose” (禮拜起來), and took up a sandal. The performers include monks, masters, officials, commanders, and an emperor; the emperor bows and then asks another question. The same act can be challenged—Mazu asks Preacher Liang, “what are you bowing for?” (禮拜作麼)—or immediately met with a blow. Elsewhere a commander bows and takes the master as teacher. The Chan deviation is observable encounter choreography: this ordinary ritual bow is recorded as a public response that may precede a question, return to the assembly, recall, strike, or teacher-student bond. The texts do not make those different outcomes different meanings of the bow, and this entry assigns the gesture no unstated intent.
Senses.Note: One ritual action is performed by many actors and placed at different points in an encounter. Actor, rank, and narrative consequence do not create different referents. Compare “thereupon struck” (便打), “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), the hands-folded greeting (問訊), the parting salute (珍重), and the head-to-the-ground bow (頂禮).

Senses.PreferredTarget: the myriad things return to one
AlternateTargets: the ten thousand things return to one
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the myriad things return to one' (萬法歸一). It most often forms the first clause of the stock question, 'The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一一歸何處). The Zhaozhou case records the answer, 'When I was in Qingzhou I made a cloth shirt weighing seven catties' (我在青州作一領布衫重七斤). The corpus also records other answers under other masters: Wenshu Yingzhen answers, 'The Yellow River has nine bends' (黃河九曲); Luohan Guichen answers, 'There has not been a single person who did not ask' (未有一箇人不問); and later dialogues divide the stock question into 'What is the myriad things returning to one?' (如何是萬法歸一) followed by 'Where does the one finally return?' (畢竟一歸何處). The phrase occurs as the question itself, as the name of the Zhaozhou exchange, in headings for verses on that exchange, and in later masters' renewed questions and answers.
Senses.Note: The exact four-character string occurs 852 times in 219 allowlisted texts. The unpunctuated full question 'the myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一一歸何處) occurs 41 times in 16 texts, while 'where does the one return?' (一歸何處) occurs 755 times in 203 texts. Searches for definition patterns including 'as for the myriad things returning to one' (萬法歸一者), 'the so-called myriad things return to one' (所謂萬法歸一), 'it is called the myriad things return to one' (謂之萬法歸一 and 名為萬法歸一), and 'what is meant by the myriad things returning to one?' (何謂萬法歸一) yielded no direct self-definition. The answers remain attached to their respective speakers; this entry does not turn any one answer into a general gloss for the phrase.

Senses.PreferredTarget: take up the whisk (preside from the teaching seat)
Senses.Explanation: Literally “grasp the whisk.” In the Chan institution this is a delegated presiding office, not merely holding an object. The monastic procedure has the abbot invite the head monks, identifies the “whisk-holder” (秉拂人), and says the head monk borrows the teaching seat and teaching drum. Recorded sayings then show an invited head monk “taking up the whisk and ascending the hall,” with a monk immediately asking a question. Separate “whisk-holding records” (秉拂語錄) and chamber headings preserve the resulting addresses. The corpus also places taking up the whisk beside receipt of the teaching robe and records an assembly inviting a head monk out to do it. Thus the whisk's teaching-seat authority is visible in who is invited, what institutional equipment is borrowed, and the public questioning that follows. The corpus does not connect the whisk here with flies, insects, or the not-killing precept.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 843 hits in 144 texts. Companion forms include “take up the whisk and ascend the hall” (秉拂上堂, 49 hits / 24 texts), “take up the whisk at a small gathering” (秉拂小參, 26 / 17), “request someone to take up the whisk” (請秉拂, 39 / 13), and “take up the whisk for a general address” (秉拂普說, 7 / 5). These formats overlap but are not synonyms: “take up the whisk” (秉拂) marks who presides with the implement; “ascend the hall” (上堂), “small gathering” (小參), and “general address” (普說) name address formats.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the empty eon. The term occurs 838 times in 206 allowlisted texts, most often in 'before the empty eon' or 'before the empty eon was over,' language for before heaven and earth were divided or before the world was established. The records make it public-interview vocabulary: Dongshan is asked about 'oneself before the empty eon,' asks who lives in the empty-eon house with no people, and later collections ask about the affair before the empty eon. Verses call its road broad and idle or say that nobody knows the far-off empty eon. A discourse itself expands the phrase as 'before heaven and earth were divided.' It is a stock Chan time-beyond-cosmic-time formula.
Senses.Note: One referent across compounds and questions: an imagined eon before the formed world. Different answers and poetic predicates are deployments, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是空劫已前自己。師曰。白馬入蘆華。官人問。有人修行否。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan is publicly asked about oneself before the empty eon.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan asks who inhabits the empty-eon house with no people.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later collection preserves the question 'what is the affair before the empty eon?'

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse directly expands 'before the empty eon' as before heaven and earth were divided and contrasts it with the world's establishment.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat verse says the affair before the empty eon is plainly presented and warns against presenting it wrongly.

Senses.Explanation: Literally a nest or mortar; in the Chan record, a fixed mould into which words and conduct settle. The corpus speaks of falling into another's rut (墮他窠臼, "fall into his fixed rut") as oil enters flour and cannot get out, and of both inherited gestures and current fashions as ruts: "killing buddhas and patriarchs" falls within the old people's enclosure, while wielding the staff and shout does not escape the present-day rut (殺佛殺祖，盡落古人圜繢；行棒行喝，不脫今時窠臼). One record pairs new and old while saying "jump out of the rut" (一新一舊，跳出窠臼). The decisive corpus warning is recursive: pupils may mistake a master's refusal to establish a rut and thereby make "no rut" into a rut (以無窠臼為窠臼, "take having no rut as a rut"). Thus the Chan deviation is not merely an ordinary habit: the term names repeatable religious speech, gestures, formats, and even anti-formulas once followers preserve them as a template.
Senses.Note: Count: 969 occurrences in 243 allowlisted texts. One corpus-wide figurative thing; nest and mortar supply the literal image but the curated Chan occurrences all denote a fixed pattern. No separate sense was made for old versus current patterns, which are different instances of the same thing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record compares falling into another's fixed rut to oil entering flour and being unable to emerge.

Senses.Explanation: An adverb meaning 'on the spot' or 'immediately.' Chan texts place it before getting it, becoming a buddha, awakening, and verdicts such as 'a dead fellow on the spot.' A master says, 'I now wait for you to get it on the spot,' without added effort. The recurring Chan bend is the demand for the event or verdict right where the person is, rather than at another place or a deferred time.
Senses.Note: Primary adverbial sense. Exact posture uses are separated below; the previously included 'the buddhas stand listening' witness belongs there, not here.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address says that if the listeners were to awaken on the spot, birth and death and the ten directions would all disappear.

Senses.Explanation: The literal posture of standing at a place. A hall address tells the assembly not to stand there dozing; the flame sermon has the buddhas of the three times stand and listen; another speaker says, 'I now stand here watching you.' These describe bodily posture and location, not immediate occurrence.
Senses.Note: Physical-posture referent, independently anchored across three texts. Larger compounds such as 'stand upright between heaven and earth' remain outside this narrower entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三世諸佛立地聽
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's recorded line has the buddhas of the three times stand and listen while flames turn the teaching wheel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我今立地看你，縱修行百千年，木食草衣，只與吾一般。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A speaker says, 'I now stand here watching you,' before describing the addressee's long cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “plant and steady the heels”; in its primary Chan deployment, “establish firm footing.” The phrase occurs 24 times in 18 allowlisted texts, mainly in later instructions, verses, and public exchanges. One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: one master says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.
Senses.Note: This is distinct from the literal archer’s planted stance below. Different circumstances in which a person is told to remain steady are deployments of one figurative sense, not additional senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 行腳住世先要立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓。
一向立定腳跟，最怕輥入異類，子細檢點來，正是偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢。
師云：「立定腳跟好。」進云：「等閒垂一釣，驚動碧波鱗。」
萬頃波中一片石，立定腳跟赤骨歷，縱橫無礙百千般，都緣應化非真實。

Senses.Explanation: The same four graphs also describe a literal bodily stance. Wuyi Yuanlai compares possessing the eye of inquiry to a skilled archer who “plants his heels firmly, then takes up the bow and sets the arrow, and only then can hit the target” (立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的). Here the phrase names what the archer physically does before shooting, not a second reading of figurative steadiness.
Senses.Note: One independent allowlisted source in the researched concordance clearly anchors this physical referent, so the sense remains provisional. It is placed second because the Zen-loaded figurative sense is primary in this corpus.

Occurrences.Kwic: 譬如善射者，立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的也。

Senses.PreferredTarget: where you stand is all genuine
AlternateTargets: the place you take is entirely real
Senses.Explanation: Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position (立處), all is genuine or real (皆真): "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" (隨處作主，立處皆真，境來回換不得). The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Later records reverse its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" (立處皆真，隨方作主), attach it to "take it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), and explicitly quote Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" (把來便用，立處皆真). Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.
Senses.Note: The variant "where you stand is immediately genuine" (立處即真) occurs 19 times in 15 texts. The wording is shared beyond Linji quotations, so no master-specific SenseKey is needed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爾且隨處作主，立處皆真，境來回換不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own record preserves the central three-part formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直要不受人惑，隨處作主，立處皆真，但有來者皆不得受。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's second formulation foregrounds not receiving another person's delusion.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道無動靜法本隨緣。立處皆真隨方作主。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huiwen reverses the order of the two Linji clauses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若能取捨俱忘，觸目無滯，拈來便用，立處皆真
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later high-seat passage pairs the phrase with taking up and immediately using.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我這裏是活祖師西來意，把來便用，立處皆真。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage explicitly introduces this as Linji's saying and pairs it with immediate use.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to stand in snow. In the Chan record the phrase predominantly names Huike's vigil before Bodhidharma: Shen-guang stands unmoving through a night of heavy snow until it rises above his knees, and Bodhidharma asks, “You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?” (汝久立雪中，當求何事). Retrospective formulas join “standing in the snow” with “cutting off the arm” (立雪斷臂), transmission of the robe and bowl, and Huike's request for the buddhas' essential way. Later masters preserve conflicting appraisals: one says, “standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing,” while another calls “the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind” unworthy. It also becomes a stock public question—“what is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?”—to which the quoted master answers, “a leap month comes once in three years.” The ordinary weather action has thus become the compact name of a lineage encounter and a recurring interview prompt.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 507 matches in 186 texts. This sense covers the full narrative, the fixed standing-snow/cut-arm formula, transmission retrospective, later praise and criticism, and a direct public question. Standing-snow/cut-arm (立雪斷臂), the Second Patriarch standing in snow (二祖立雪), and standing waist-deep in snow (立雪齊腰) all name or appraise the same Huike event. Family revalidation with cutting off the arm (斷臂), facing a wall (面壁), transmitting the robe (傳衣), Huike, and Bodhidharma preserves that event as the Zen-loaded primary sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其年十二月九日夜。天大雨雪。光堅立不動。遲明積雪過膝。祖憫而問曰。汝久立雪中。當求何事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The narrative says Shen-guang stands unmoving through heavy night snow until it rises above his knees; Bodhidharma asks, ‘You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 有神光法師，立雪斷臂，堅求諸佛要道，師為易名慧可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission retrospective joins the two actions: ‘Master Shen-guang stood in the snow and cut off his arm, firmly seeking the buddhas' essential way’; Bodhidharma renamed him Huike.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是西來的的意。師曰。立雪未為勞。斷臂方為的。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked the exact meaning of coming from the West, the master says, ‘Standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨九年面壁，鬼魅之由。二祖立雪求心，飜成不肖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master criticizes both stock acts: ‘Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall—the source of ghosts; the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind—turned into unworthiness.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：二祖立雪齊腰，意旨如何？師曰：三年逢一閏。曰：為甚麼付法傳衣？師曰：村酒足人酤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks, ‘What is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?’ The master answers, ‘A leap month comes once in three years,’ then answers a follow-up about transmitting the teaching and robe.

Senses.Explanation: The same graphs also describe the physical posture of a bird in a snowy scene. A master answers a question about proceeding within the four deportments with “a heron stands in the snow” (鷺鶿立雪). A verse separately compares a heron standing in snow with the bright moon and reed flowers. In these passages the subject is a heron and the phrase denotes its visible posture, not Huike's lineage encounter.
Senses.Note: The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問四威儀中如何履踐。師曰。鷺鶿立雪。曰恁麼則聞鐘持鉢日上闌干。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘How does one proceed within the four deportments?’ the master says, ‘A heron stands in the snow.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 鷺鷥立雪非同色，明月蘆花不似他。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘A heron standing in snow is not of the same color; the bright moon and reed flowers are not alike.’

Senses.Explanation: A verb-object phrase: "raise" or "hold upright" (竪) the whisk (拂), usually the master's fly-whisk (拂子). This seeded graph form occurs 471 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the common orthographic form with the other graph for "raise" (豎拂) occurs 2,438 times. The corpus records the action as a direct answer, as a demonstration followed by lowering the whisk, and as a recurrent action whose import students ask about. Nanta Guangyong answers "who is Manjusri's teacher?" by raising the whisk to show him (如何是文殊師；師竪拂子示之). Zhaozhou raises the whisk when asked whether he will receive "the person who sets the realm in order" (撥亂乾坤底人來，師還接否；師竪拂子). Yunmen raises the older Zifu exchange in which a monk asks, "what is the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk?" (古人拈槌竪拂意旨如何). A later Deshan record explicitly classifies "raise a finger and raise the whisk" as a dead phrase (舉指竪拂，是死句). These records do not give the raised whisk one uniform gloss, and this entry does not add one.
Senses.Note: The two orthographic forms, the older graph for "raise" (竪) and its dominant variant (豎), do not create a second sense. Corpus counts: "raise the whisk" with the seeded spelling (竪拂), 471; "raise the whisk" with the dominant spelling (豎拂), 2,438; "raise the fly-whisk" (竪拂子), 189; "raise up the fly-whisk" (竪起拂子), 492; "pick up the mallet and raise the whisk" (拈槌竪拂), 108; "raise a finger and raise the whisk" (舉指竪拂), 4. The seeded SourceTerm is retained for ID stability, while the dominant written variant is documented here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰如何是文殊師。師竪拂子示之。僧曰。莫遮箇是麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Nanta Guangyong section of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp: a monk asks, "who is Manjusri's teacher?" The master raises the whisk to show him; the monk asks, "is it not this?" Nanta Guangyong has no roster link used here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃竪起拂子云。只這是要知示現受生麼。竪拂子云。只這是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yuanwu Keqin's fourth informal address: he raises the whisk and says, "just this is it"; asks whether they want to know manifestation and receiving birth; then raises the whisk and again says, "just this is it."

Occurrences.Kwic: 師竪拂子。僧曰。恁麼則得遇明君去也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Zhaozhou Congshen's section of the Compendium of Five Lamps. After a monk asks whether he will receive one who sets the realm in order, Zhaozhou raises the whisk; the monk replies, "then I have met a wise ruler."

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問資福。古人拈槌竪拂意旨如何。福云。古人與麼那。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's chamber sayings raise a Zifu case: a monk asks Zifu, "what is the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk?" Zifu replies, "did the ancients do that?" MasterName is null because this is an explicitly raised two-speaker case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 揚眉瞬目，舉指竪拂，是死句。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Deshan Yuanmi section of the Strict Lineage of Five Lamps: "raise the brows and blink the eyes; raise a finger and raise the whisk—these are dead phrases." The exact section master lacks a validated roster link used here.

AlternateTargets: a step forward atop the pole
advance from the top of the pole
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘stepping forward from the pole-top,’ the shortened case label and fixed phrase drawn from ‘atop a hundred-foot pole one must step forward’ (百尺竿頭須進步). The verse says that the person sitting atop the pole, although having gained entry, is not yet real, then gives the step-forward line and ‘the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body.’ Wumen's Barrier titles Case 46 ‘Stepping Forward from the Pole-top’ and frames the question as Shishuang's: ‘atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?’ Other records ask ‘what is the phrase of stepping forward atop a hundred-foot pole?’ and preserve answers such as ‘the southern continent and the northern continent.’ Later verse commentary explicitly names Old Changsha and also joins the pole-top step with Chaling's donkey-fall story. Thus the ordinary impossibility of stepping beyond a pole's tip becomes a named case, a recurrent public question, and a quoted verse-line. The entry reports those textual relations and does not state what the step is intended to accomplish.
Senses.Note: This is the event/action member of the “hundred-foot pole-top” (百尺竿頭) family, not a second reading of the pole-top location. It remains one sense across title, question, and quotation because each names the same step from the same pole-top image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 竿頭進步石霜和尚云。百尺竿頭如何進步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's case title is followed by the pole-top question attributed only as Shishuang; the identity is left unresolved.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百尺竿頭坐底人。雖然得入。未為真。百尺竿頭須進步十方世界現全身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The case preserves the old verse's own gained-entry/not-yet-real contrast and its required step.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百尺竿頭進步時築着磕著自家底老長沙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Later commentary explicitly associates the pole-top step with Old Changsha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是百尺竿頭進步底句師云南贍部洲北欝單越
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The fixed phrase is asked as a public question; the record gives the southern and northern continents as the reply.

Senses.Explanation: Gruel (粥) is the thin cooked-grain meal served in the monastery, ordinarily the morning member of the recurring pair ‘gruel and rice’ (粥飯). The word retains that concrete referent throughout the record: the monastic code directs that opening the bowl and eating gruel or rice, tea or broth, must be done carefully and in order (展鉢喫粥喫飰或茶或湯，皆須細齊整), and a kitchen exchange distinguishes cooking gruel from steaming rice (煮粥耶？蒸飯耶？). Chan bends this everyday meal by repeatedly putting it into public answers and named cases. Asked for ‘talk that surpasses buddhas and patriarchs,’ Changping answers ‘eating gruel and eating rice’ (喫粥喫飯); asked about the student's own self, Guizong answers ‘when the gruel is thin, sit down later’ (粥稀後坐). In Zhaozhou's case, a newly arrived monk asks for instruction; Zhaozhou asks, ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ (喫粥了也未), and after the monk says he has, tells him, ‘go wash your bowl’ (洗鉢盂去). Yunmen preserves the exchange and explicitly asks whether Zhaozhou gave an instruction. Later records repeatedly quote and comment on the same question-and-answer. The meal also supplies the record's language for the ordinary allotment: Baichi says ‘eating gruel and eating rice is your own basic lot’ (喫粥喫飯是汝本分事), while a Zhaozhou saying names the two daily gruel-and-rice meals as his only occasion of ‘mixed use of mind’ (除二時粥飯是雜用心處). In the Ganzhi–Nanquan case, Ganzhi provides gruel and requests the meal recitation; Nanquan dedicates it to ‘the tabby cat and white ox’ (貍奴白牯), after which Ganzhi leaves and Nanquan breaks the cooking pot. Thus the corpus does not turn gruel into a second object or an abstract substance: it keeps the food concrete while deploying eating, serving, and washing up in answers, institutional schedules, and public cases.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist concordance: gruel (粥) has 2,824 hits in 341 files; eat gruel (喫粥) 748/182; gruel and rice (粥飯) 668/223; ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ (喫粥了也未) 101/67; and gruel-and-rice monk (粥飯僧) 59/42. No definition-formula search supplied a definition of the food: ‘what is gruel?’ (如何是粥), ‘so-called gruel’ (所謂粥), ‘termed gruel’ (謂之粥), ‘named gruel’ (名為粥), and ‘called gruel’ (喚作粥) all returned zero. The 18 hits for the grammatical string ‘as for gruel’ or ‘one who handles gruel’ (粥者) occur in contexts such as ‘the one serving gruel’ or inside the named phrase ‘Jiang's thin gruel’; they are not definitions. Sense audit: ordinary breakfast gruel, offered or cooked gruel, and the gruel in Zhaozhou's case are the same food, hence one sense. Related entries should keep separate the eating bowl (鉢盂) from the robe-and-bowl succession token (衣鉢), and should give the scorn epithet ‘gruel-and-rice monk’ (粥飯僧) its own lexical article rather than assigning that human referent to the standalone word ‘gruel’ (粥).

Occurrences.Kwic: 堂中座位衣單掛鉢展鉢喫粥喫飰或茶或湯。皆須󱶂細齊整。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Monastic Regulations for the Chan Garden, in its section on the head seat, treats eating gruel as an ordered communal meal: opening the bowl and eating gruel, rice, tea, or broth must be done carefully and neatly. This anchors the institutional deployment and the concrete food sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問趙州。某甲乍入叢林。乞師指示。州云。喫粥了也未。僧云。喫粥了也。州云。洗鉢盂去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's record quotes the complete Zhaozhou exchange: the newcomer asks for instruction, Zhaozhou asks whether he has eaten his gruel, and then tells him to go wash his bowl. The following lines have Yunmen ask whether an instruction was given.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫粥喫飯是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baichi's record places eating gruel and rice in a series of ordinary activities and calls it ‘your own basic lot.’ The local speaker was not independently resolved, so the master field remains unset.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今早起來。無言可說。下牀著鞋。後架洗面。堂內展鉢喫粥。粥後打睡。睡起喫茶。見客相喚。齋時喫飯。日日相似。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fayan's lamp-record section lists the ordinary daily sequence: rise, put on shoes, wash, open the bowl and eat gruel in the hall, sleep after gruel, drink tea, greet guests, and eat rice at mealtime—‘each day alike.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰汝炊飯耶煮粥耶。對曰。人工淘米著火。行者煮粥炊飯。曰汝作甚麼。對曰。和尚慈悲放他閑去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the kitchen exchange in the Continued Transmission of the Lamp, Touzi asks Daokai whether he steams rice or cooks gruel. Daokai assigns washing rice and lighting the fire to workmen, and cooking gruel and rice to attendants. It independently anchors preparation of the literal meal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧行脚時，除二時粥飯是雜用心處，除外更無別用心處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The collected outlines quote Zhaozhou: while travelling, apart from the two daily gruel-and-rice meals as occasions of mixed use of mind, he had no other such occasion. This anchors the institutional two-meal formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是超佛越祖之談。師曰。喫粥喫飯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Changping's lamp-record section, a monk asks what talk surpasses buddhas and patriarchs; the answer is ‘eating gruel and eating rice.’ This anchors gruel as the content of a public answer without assigning an unstated interpretation to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是學人自己。師曰。牀窄先臥。粥稀後坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked about the student's own self, Guizong Daoquan answers with the paired household maxim: ‘when the bed is narrow, lie down first; when the gruel is thin, sit down later.’ This anchors ordinary gruel inside an attested public answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又於南泉設粥云請和尚念誦南泉云甘贄行者設粥請大眾為貍奴白牯念摩訶般若波羅蜜甘乃禮拜便出去南泉却到厨內打破鍋子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The abridged transmission record preserves the Ganzhi–Nanquan case: Ganzhi provides gruel and asks Nanquan to recite; Nanquan announces a dedication for the tabby cat and white ox; Ganzhi leaves, and Nanquan breaks the pot in the kitchen.

Senses.Explanation: The joined food words are also the institutional name for a monastery's scheduled meals and food support. The monastic code schedules “gruel and rice at the two meal-times; tea and hot water at the third” (二時上粥飯。三時上茶湯). Zhaozhou likewise identifies “the two gruel-and-rice meals” (二時粥飯) as the only occasions that divided his attention while travelling. An abbot calls himself a “gruel-and-rice host” (粥飯主人), receiving travellers with salt, vinegar, enough gruel, and enough rice. In these passages the headword does not merely inventory two foods: it names the recurring communal provision, its times, and the host responsible for it.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 668 hits in 223 texts. Institutional families include the two gruel-and-rice meal-times (二時粥飯), gruel-and-rice circumstances or support (粥飯因緣), and the gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人). These are deployments of one communal meal system, not separate senses. The institution is distinct from the physical gruel and cooked rice in the literal sense below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二時上粥飯。三時上茶湯。大眾諷經
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code gives an institutional schedule: gruel and rice at two times, tea and hot water at three.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧行脚時。除二時粥飯是雜用心處。除外更無別用心處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou says that during his travels only the two scheduled gruel-and-rice meals were mixed employment of mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 推向十字路頭住箇破院，作粥飯主人接待南北，事不獲已，隨分有鹽有醋、粥足飯足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An abbot describes being made to inhabit a ruined monastery as the gruel-and-rice host who receives travellers from north and south and maintains the meal provision.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the first graph names gruel and the second cooked rice or a rice meal. The corpus uses the pair as physical food: a verse says that mountain-field gruel and rice smell fragrant, and a discourse observes that after three days without being fed gruel and rice a person cannot move, but can move after eating some. Another address enumerates eating gruel and eating rice beside relieving oneself, walking, sitting, and sleeping as the listener's own fundamental matter. The rebuke “puffing gruel-and-rice breath” (鼓粥飯氣) is a food-derived fixed compound; it depends on consumed food but does not turn the literal food pair into the institutional schedule above.
Senses.Note: Literal food predicates include eating, being fed, smelling fragrant, and having enough gruel and rice. The gruel-and-rice breath phrase (粥飯氣) and the gruel-and-rice monk (粥飯僧) are longer compounds and remain separate lexical articles or families. Their existence does not collapse physical food into the communal meal system.

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪學道是汝本分事、喫粥喫飯是汝本分事、屙屎撒尿是汝本分事、行坐打眠是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker enumerates eating gruel and cooked rice among ordinary bodily activities called the listener's own fundamental matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 設問答到彌勒下生，勾鎖連環，盛水不漏，也祇是空鼓粥飯氣，於自己了沒交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The rebuke calls flawless linked question-and-answer merely empty puffing of gruel-and-rice breath, preserving a fixed compound derived from consumed food.

Occurrences.Kwic: 繭紙衣裳軟，山田粥飯香，此生隨分過，無可得思量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘Silkworm-paper clothes are soft; mountain-field gruel and rice are fragrant.’ Fragrance is a predicate of the physical food.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不與粥飯喫三日時還動得麼定是動不得也纔方喫得些粥飯方能動得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse asks whether someone unfed gruel and rice for three days can still move, then says that after eating some gruel and rice the person can move. The predicate is bodily nourishment by physical food.

Senses.Explanation: In institutional self-description, “gruel-and-rice monk” names an ordinary resident who remains within the monastery's communal support rather than accepting a public or abbatial post. One master, repeatedly summoned by governors to prestigious monasteries, says, “I am a long-term gruel-and-rice monk; transmitting the buddha-mind lineage is no small matter” (我長行粥飯僧，傳佛心宗非細事也) and refuses eight invitations. Another declines an invitation to lead Nanyuan by saying, “I have long been a gruel-and-rice monk and vow not to emerge into the human world” (我長作粥飯僧，誓不願出人間世矣). A third master answers a question about himself simply, “If you ask me, I am a gruel-and-rice monk” (若問我，我則粥飯僧). These passages use the compound as an institutional identity, not as a literal claim that the monk does nothing except eat.

Long-term or regular forms (長行粥飯僧 and 常行粥飯僧) must be assigned by context: they can name this resident identity or the eating-only classification below.
