Senses.PreferredTarget: a monk who merely eats communal meals
Senses.Explanation: In a separate literal and contrastive classification, the compound denotes a monk characterized as consuming the community's gruel and rice without the activity set against it. An official asks whether Weishan's assembly consists of “monks who eat gruel and rice” or “monks who investigate Chan” (喫粥飯僧 / 參禪僧); Weishan rejects both offered categories. Zhenjing tells the assembly not to become “long-term gruel-and-rice monks” (不可作長行粥飯僧). Xiangyan says that he will cease studying the buddha teaching and become such a monk, sparing his mind the labor. Later records reuse the same eat-versus-study contrast. Here the headword classifies a monk by meal consumption, not by the non-abbatial institutional identity in the primary sense.
Senses.Note: Dismissive external use, self-directed use, and Weishan's refusal are readings within this meal-consuming classification, not further senses. The gruel-and-rice food pair (粥飯), rice-bag fellow (飯袋子), and wine-lees fellow (酒糟漢) are related but lexically distinct. Eating gruel and rice in one's own fundamental matter (本分事) does not by itself apply this classification to a monk.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, purple (紫) fungus (芝). In Chan verse the plant is gathered beside a stream, while the named Purple Fungus Song circulates far more widely. One direct public question asks, 'what is the Purple Fungus Song?' and the master answers by clapping; an independent transmission answers, 'it is not a Wu sound—it must be Han speech.' Mountain poems place its singing among clouds, pines, cranes, and secluded huts: one names a solitary recluse and asks who will sing together, while another places groups of two and three singing on stones beneath pine roots. The corpus separately invokes the Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang in a verse that names their 'one heart of withdrawal' and says Mount Shang remains green. This supports the requested eremitic field, but the exact concordance does not directly join the Four Hoaryheads to the purple fungus, so this entry keeps the two strands distinct. The Zen deviation is the plant-name's circulation as a song spoken, answered, and sung in Chan halls and mountain-retreat verse, not a general account of the plant or the recluses.
Senses.Note: Unsplit string: 136 hits in 72 allowlisted texts, substantially including proper names and places. Purple Fungus Song (紫芝歌) has 20 hits in 18 texts; Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang (商山四皓) 9 in 8; gather purple fungus (採紫芝) 1 in 1. Zizhi-named lineage figures belong on the roster, while Purple-Fungus Hermitage (紫芝菴) and Purple-Fungus Crag (紫芝巖) are place compounds; they are excluded from the lexical sense rather than blurred into it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, bind or establish, and regulation or restriction. In Chan records the term labels the formal beginning of a bounded communal period and also functions as a verb for beginning it. It occurs 2,026 times in 255 allowlisted texts. Records repeatedly mark a discourse or small talk as delivered at this beginning, contrast it with release from the restriction, and identify the date: one record calls the fifteenth day of the tenth month the restriction and the fifteenth day of the first month its release; another describes the interval from the former date to the Lantern Festival. A tea talk parses the two graphs as joining companions of one purpose and holding a wild mind in check. Individual answers remain concrete: asked what the restriction is, one master says, 'Return to your place.'
Senses.Note: The term overlaps with beginning the summer session, but the corpus also attests a winter restriction, so 'summer session' is too narrow as the head gloss. Release from the restriction is the consistent opposite. The corpus has 136 instances of the compact heading 'restriction-period discourse' and 20 of 'restriction-period small talk.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘after being completely cut off, revive again.’ The phrase occurs 222 times in 119 allowlisted texts. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. One master explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary death-and-revival image into a stock saying repeatedly quoted in teaching-seat discourse and biographies. It belongs with ‘let go at the cliff’ (懸崖撒手), ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), and ‘gain life within death’ (死中得活), but remains one figurative referent rather than separate literal and technical objects.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to 'go along walking' or 'walk about.' The term occurs 1,022 times in 273 allowed texts and names an observable bodily action. A late biography makes the direction explicit: at night a recluse goes outside the crag to walk about, the visiting master follows, and 'each walks east and west' (隱者出巖外經行，師亦隨之，第東西各步). A Five Lamps address pairs physical condition and action: 'when well, walk about; when tired, rest' (健即經行困即歇). The same collection records Layman Feng Ji walking about the teaching hall with Foyan when a child recites a line, and records another monk 'walking under the pines one evening' when he hears a mountain spring (一夕，松下經行，聞巖泉聲). In the collected old cases, Sudhana searches in all four directions for seven days and finds Meghashri 'walking slowly on another peak' (在別峰上徐步經行). Daily timing is also explicit: a biography says a monk ate only after serving the assembly, while Bingseng watched him 'walk about after each meal' (每飯罷經行時). The term is frequently coordinated with sitting and lying as one of the body's recorded activities. These places, times, directions, companions, and contrasts support the plain action word.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched; no stable nominal self-definition was found. Distinct deployment shapes retained are walking east-west at night, walking when well versus resting when tired, walking with another person in a hall, walking under pines, slow walking on another peak, and walking after a meal. The entry adds no special category beyond what the people in the records physically do.

Senses.Explanation: Vimalakirti is the pre-Zen householder whom Chan masters repeatedly raise in public interviews and comments. His name occurs 263 times in 116 allowlisted texts. The dominant Zen deployment is the sickroom exchange: Manjusri asks him to state the entry into the gate of not-two, Vimalakirti remains silent, and Manjusri praises the absence of speech and writing. Later masters do not leave that episode uncontested. Xuedou asks, "what did Vimalakirti say?" (維摩道甚麼) and says he has examined him through; another master says both Vimalakirti and Manjusri deserve thirty blows; public questions repeatedly ask the purport of "Vimalakirti's one silence" (維摩一默). A direct answer to that question is "Hanshan visits Shide" (寒山訪拾得), followed by a hiss when the monk labels it the gate of not-two. The Zen Vimalakirti is therefore the seated, silent figure whom masters question, rebuke, praise, and reuse in interviews—not a imported account of his life.
Senses.Note: One person sense covers the evidence. Occurrences inside scripture titles still use the person's name as a title constituent and do not establish a second thing denoted by the bare headword. The shorter form Vimalakirti (維摩) is the dominant variant and belongs to the same figure family.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'main cord and ancestral line' (綱宗): the main cord of a net (綱) joined to the ancestral line or school (宗). In Chan records it names the organizing framework by which a lineage's inherited sayings and distinctions are arranged and identified. The preface to the Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) places 'the key outlines of the five houses' (五宗綱要) beside 'the terms of the lineage framework' (綱宗語句), including the names and decisive details that an abbot is expected to know. Other texts specify 'the Linji lineage framework' (臨濟綱宗), 'the Dongshan lineage framework' (洞上綱宗), and 'the Caodong lineage framework' (曹洞綱宗), showing that the compound can be qualified by a named house. A record quoting Yantou says, 'Only recognize the lineage framework; originally there is no actual thing' (但識綱宗本無實法), and another version gives, 'For the great governing lineage framework, first one must recognize the phrase' (大統綱宗先須識句). The term also occurs with verbs such as establish, uphold, display, grasp, and restore, and with enumerated house vocabulary such as Linji's 'three mysteries and three essentials' (三玄三要).
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 689 times in 188 allowlisted texts. Searches for definition patterns including 'as for the lineage framework' (綱宗者), 'the so-called lineage framework' (所謂綱宗), 'it is called the lineage framework' (謂之綱宗 and 名為綱宗), 'call it the lineage framework' (喚作綱宗), and 'what is the lineage framework?' (何謂綱宗 and 如何是綱宗) did not produce a simple dictionary-style self-definition. The strongest structural evidence is instead the corpus's explicit pairing of 'five-house key outlines' (五宗綱要) with 'lineage-framework terms' (綱宗語句), Yantou's two quoted formulas, and the named-house collocations. This is a corpus-wide category; a Linji or Caodong collocation does not create a master-specific sense.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs describe fine fibers held closely together; the corpus applies the compound to speech, a house style, continuity, and careful handling. A direct definition asks “what is close-woven?” and answers: the brows are knit with empty space, a needle cannot enter, water cannot wet it, and not the slightest gap is permitted (何謂綿密？眉毛與虗空廝結，針劄不入，水洒不濕，不容有毫釐間隙). Dahui critically reports people who attach an answer directly to a student's question and call it close-woven, not falling among affective objects (喚作綿密不落情塵); he also reports one-sentence answers called close-woven and called not running away (謂之綿密，謂之不走). Yongjue is asked for a close-woven house style and answers, “the golden needle does not permit knowing” (如何是綿密門風？金針不許知). A biographical appraisal calls a teacher's phrases close-woven and not falling into beginning or end (語句綿密，不落終始). The reduplicated form “continuously and closely” (綿綿密密) occurs 106 times in 62 files; Yuanwu uses it in parallel with picking up and setting down. The base compound occurs 447 times in 165 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The corpus itself supplies both the textile image and the no-gap explanation. Dahui's two labeling passages are explicitly critical reports; they establish what speakers called close-woven without making their label his approval.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to have no measure or placement available. The phrase occurs 936 times in 220 allowlisted texts and most characteristically records the moment after a question, silence, shout, blow, or other public exchange when a participant has no response. Wenxi remains at a loss after the master answers his question about himself with silence; an emperor is at a loss when National Teacher Nanyang Huizhong sits silent after requesting a seamless-stupa design; and in Linji's record a monk is at a loss after Linji laughs and is then struck. Later records also use it retrospectively: the later Baoshou is at a loss when asked for the original face before his parents were born. The expression names the reported failure to answer; the records do not make the word itself a diagnosis of an inward state.
Senses.Note: No separate Zen-technical object emerged. Ordinary inability to know what to do is bent into a recurrent public-interview report, commonly placed directly before the master's next action. Formula searches produced no corpus definition of the word; the deployment, not an imported psychological gloss, fixes the entry.

Senses.Explanation: An old (老) monk (僧): “old monk.” The form occurs 11,424 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Its characteristic Chan deployment is a monk's humble first-person self-reference, conventionally translated “this old monk” and grammatically serving as “I” or “me.” A master speaks of “this old monk's place,” redirects a public interview by saying “this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly,” recalls receiving a shout, or addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces “an old monk named Puhui.” Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide human-role sense. Render it as “this old monk” when a speaker uses it for himself and “an/the old monk” in third-person narration. Do not restore the former article/deixis split. A separate local sense below is retained only because that passage explicitly uses the source term (老僧) for a different referent.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an old woman's concern is pressing
AlternateTargets: old-woman concern pressed to the utmost

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "an old woman's concern is pressing": old woman or granny (老婆) plus the concern being urgent or pressed hard (心切). The phrase occurs 270 times in 129 allowlisted texts. It is a predicate applied to a speaker's insistent words or actions toward someone else, not the name of an inner state or a sentimental ideal. In the Linji–Huangbo–Dayu case, Dayu says Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that "for you he exhausted himself completely" (為汝得徹困); when Linji returns, he says it was "only because the old-woman concern was pressing" (祇為老婆心切). In another exchange, a layman calls Huitang's concern pressing and Huitang replies, "I only want you to arrive home" (秖要公到家耳). The records thus show the idiom through predicates, agents, and replies rather than through a modern emotional gloss.
Senses.Note: The phrase is neither automatically praise nor a guarantee that the action described is harmless. A commentary reports that people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing "pressing old-woman concern," then rejects their reading: it is "arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to put it in their mouths" (以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口). Elsewhere the location of Yaoshan's pressing concern is itself made the next interview question: "where is the place of his pressing old-woman concern?" (那裏是他老婆心切處). It can also enter verse, as in "pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short" (老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長). Common frames include "only because" (只為老婆心切, 24 occurrences; variant 祇為, 7) and "so very" (得恁麼老婆心切, 18). These uses support a forceful relational appraisal while preserving the possibility of criticism.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'old-woman Chan.' The expression occurs 211 times in 112 allowed texts and functions as a label applied to sayings, explanations, and handling that records compare with an old woman's solicitous speech. The verbal form 'speak old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪) occurs 55 times in 36 texts. Dahui asks whether the National Teacher's three calls to his attendant may be called 'speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water' (說老婆禪，拖泥帶水), and elsewhere says that if he had initially spoken old-woman Chan and explained everything to a student, the student would later have cursed him. A later letter contrasts a master's 'pungent handling' (手段辛辣) with people elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan. The label is also attached to actual old-woman encounters: verses call the Chan of the old woman in the Floating Cup case and the old woman on the road to Mount Wutai 'old-woman Chan.' Other records apply it more broadly. A verse calls a line 'old-woman Chan in the great Tang country' (大唐國裏老婆禪), and a case pointer asks whether someone with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan. The term is therefore an attested appraisal label rather than the name of a separate lineage: records apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to different sayings and encounters.
Senses.Note: The entry retains the literal gendered image because the corpus repeatedly connects the compound with an old woman's speech and with the broader collocation 'old-woman heart' (老婆心), which occurs 706 times in 214 texts; 'old-woman heart is urgent' (老婆心切) occurs 270 times in 129. The exact definition formulas yield two occurrences of 'one who speaks old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪者) and two of 'call it old-woman Chan' (喚作老婆禪), but no stable equation that narrows the label beyond the recorded comparisons and deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'link the lamps.' Outside the book title, records use the phrase for succession from one Chan teacher or generation to another. A history of Drum Mountain says that from the founding of Xingsheng, 'the linked lamps were unbroken for more than seventy generations' (聯燈不絕，七十餘代), and later describes 'those who linked the lamps and continued the flame for more than seventy generations' (聯燈續焰者七十餘代). Memorial words say, 'continue the flame, link the lamp—the Way is not alone' (續燄聯燈道不孤); another memorial says two teachers later 'linked lamps, each in a different region' (聯燈各一方). An ancestral-hall address speaks of 'one portrait, in succession linking the lamp far away' (一㡧次第聯燈遠). The lamp image is defined in the same record: the Chan houses' transmission through successive generations is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and shows things, and because its illumination can be continued without end.
Senses.Note: The corpus contains 104 occurrences of the graphs in 28 allowed texts, but 77 occurrences in 13 texts belong to the proper title 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要). This primary sense records the free verb/noun phrase in temple histories, memorials, and ancestral-hall addresses. Its recurring partner is 'continue the flame' (續燄／續焰).

Senses.Explanation: A proper-title and record-name use, chiefly within 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要). Its own preface says that more than six hundred teachers were selected, their encounters, questions and answers, comments on old cases, and essential statements arranged under each person's chapter, divided into thirty fascicles, and 'named Linked-Lamp Essentials' (命曰聯燈會要). Another preface says the work was designated by that title and carved for circulation. Later histories place the linked-lamp work among the five lamp records: Transmission of the Lamp, Expanded Lamp, Continued Lamp, Linked Lamp, and Universal Lamp. Biographical notices say that Huiweng Wuming compiled the Linked-Lamp Essentials and transmitted it in Chan communities or circulated it in the world.
Senses.Note: This sense is separate because the graphs form a proper title or abbreviated record name rather than a predicate of lineage continuation. The full title 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要) occurs 77 times in 13 allowed texts; the shorter title 'Linked-Lamp Record' (聯燈錄) occurs once.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “the one phrase before sound.” Across 89 occurrences in 55 allowlisted texts, it is chiefly a public-interview question and case-commentary heading, not a term the corpus leaves outside speech. Asked “what is the phrase before sound?” one master answers with the vocalization “un” (吽), and another says, “it is just like not saying” (恰似不道). Huanglian directly answers, “before sound there is no phrase; after the sound, bring your question” (聲前無句，聲後問將來). Later addresses make contrary predicates within the same public record: one says “everyone originally has” the phrase, while the Blue Cliff Record says “the thousand sages do not transmit” it. These are attested answers and claims, not grounds for choosing an ineffable reading. Zen bends the temporal phrase into a recurrent interview prompt whose answers may themselves be spoken sounds; this entry preserves that observable deployment and the corpus’s own disagreement.
Senses.Note: The phrase as question, heading, and quoted line denotes the same interview expression. Different answers—including sound, refusal, possession, and denial—are readings or responses, not different things and therefore not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count for the unsplit string: 2,214 hits in 311 texts. Primary family check: 'visible form/color' (色), 'sound' (聲), 'seeing and hearing' (見聞), 'sound, form, and language' (聲色言語), and 'sound, form, and names' (聲色名字). The ordinary 'sensual attractions' and the idiom 'without changing voice or expression' refer to different things and are split below under depth-gate item 8.

Senses.Explanation: A distinct ordinary referent in biographical and admonitory prose: worldly sensual attractions or entertainments, commonly coordinated with wealth, status, and profit. Zhao Bian's biography says that after forty he 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) and turned his attention to the records of the school. Another record warns against simultaneously pursuing achievement, receiving wealth and honor, 'indulging in sensual attractions' (耽聲色), and attending to worldly affairs. This is not the eye-and-ear field concretely demonstrated by a whisk and struck seat, so it remains a separate sense.
Senses.Note: The phrase 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) occurs in nine allowlist texts, chiefly recensions of the same Zhao Bian biography; 'indulge in sensual attractions' (耽聲色) supplies a structurally independent witness. No distinctively Chan lexical bend was found for this ordinary sense.
