Senses.Explanation: The two outward signs in the fixed phrase 'without changing voice or expression' (不動聲色): voice or tone (聲) and facial look or demeanor (色). A record praises Huanglong's forty years presiding over a community as 'holding the seat of the community without changing voice or expression' (坐鎮道場，不動聲色); a public interview likewise asks whether something can be discerned 'without changing voice or expression.' This idiomatic human demeanor is a different referent from sounds and visible objects in the sensory field.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count for 'without changing voice or expression' (不動聲色): 20 hits in 15 texts. Kept separate because a person's voice and expression and the field of heard and seen objects cannot share one precise English gloss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南禪師住黃龍四十年，坐鎮道場，不動聲色。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical appraisal: forty years presiding at Huanglong without changing voice or expression.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「打鼓弄琵琶，相逢兩作家，秪如不動聲色還辯得麼？」師云：「三千里外少知音。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public interview use of the fixed idiom: can it still be discerned without changing voice or expression?

Senses.Explanation: Foot (腳) plus heel (跟), deployed in Chan verdicts for one's footing or the place under one's heels. The locative “under the heel” or “right where one stands” (腳跟下) appears in the stock verdict “right under his heel, worth thirty blows” (腳跟下好與三十棒), in statements about something shining through past and present right under the assembly's heels, and in the compound “the affair under the heel” (腳跟下事, 60 occurrences). The records also set two stance expressions against each other. “Plant the heels firmly” (立定腳跟, 24) appears in the instruction that one who travels and resides in the world must first plant the heels firmly and not be stirred by the eight winds. “The heels do not touch the ground” (腳跟不點地, 21; variant 脚跟不點地, 40) is used as a verdict about footing rather than a report of anatomy. The combined locative counts are 672 for the headword spelling and 731 for the variant spelling.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense, with the graphic variant “heel” (脚跟). The headword spelling has 1,607 hits in 211 allowlisted texts. The locative and opposed stance expressions retain the heel image but denote footing; literal injured or painful heels belong to the anatomical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 腳跟下好與三十棒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan (破山禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). The stock locative verdict says, 'right under his heel, worth thirty blows' (腳跟下好與三十棒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 即是現前諸公腳跟下有一段輝騰今古
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong (朝宗禪師語錄), recorded sayings at Shier Mountain in Xinan (住新安石耳山語錄). The phrase 'under the heels' (腳跟下) identifies the place right where the assembled people stand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只為闍黎腳跟不點地。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yangzhuo Ming at Miyin Temple on Mount Dawei (大溈密印寺養拙明禪師語錄), recorded encounters (機緣). The verdict 'your heels do not touch the ground' (闍黎腳跟不點地) tells the questioner that he lacks footing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 行腳住世先要立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan (破山禪師語錄), instruction to the Chan monk Yunyi (示允一禪人). The line says to plant the heels firmly (立定腳跟) and not be stirred by the eight winds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因甚在汝脚跟下？師曰：當面蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Tudu Zhice (塗毒智䇿禪師). The variant spelling 'under your heel' (脚跟下) occurs in a dialogue with the answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過).

Senses.Explanation: The anatomical heel as a body part. The records predicate bleeding and injury of it: “the heel bleeds” (腳跟流血) and “the heel was suddenly injured by an axe” (腳跟忽被斧頭傷). These are bodily events, unlike verdicts about where someone stands or whether the heels touch the ground.
Senses.Note: No special Zen deviation is asserted for this ordinary anatomical sense. Two independent records anchor bodily predicates and prevent their absorption into the footing sense. The superficially anatomical phrase “heel pain, give [him] a beating” (腳跟痛與一頓) was excluded because its grammar awards blows rather than securely reporting pain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打開腦蓋，腳跟流血
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase directly predicates bleeding of the heel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 腳跟忽被斧頭傷
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct report that the heel was injured by an axe.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, beneath the heel. Chan interviews repeatedly turn this ordinary location back upon the person questioned. A reply can be appraised with 'right under your heels, thirty blows would be fitting'; a master can ask 'how deep is the water under your heels?', direct a questioner to 'recognize it right under your heels,' or answer a request for direct pointing with 'look clearly right under your heels.' The phrase also marks relative position in a public comparison: if the monk can distinguish the kinds of leakage, Dongshan is under his heels; if not, he is under Dongshan's heels. A stock question asks about 'the matter under your heels' and receives 'putting a head atop your head.' The Chan-specific bend is consistent and observable: the spatial phrase becomes the immediate locus of an interviewer's demand, appraisal, or reversal, often contrasted with what the questioner seeks elsewhere or above. The texts do not supply a further object hidden beneath the feet, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 672 hits in 176 texts. Deployment inventory includes blow-verdict, direct instruction, question, spatial reversal, and the compound 'the matter under your heels' (腳跟下事). Family check with heel (腳跟), underfoot (腳下), on the spot (立地), one's own part (本分), thirty blows (三十棒), and atop the head (頭上) supports one spatial referent used in several interview acts. Literal and loaded uses were not split because the loaded deployment keeps the same deictic location rather than naming a different thing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 死去生來不依本分，過在甚麼處？」師云：「腳跟下好與三十棒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked where the fault lies, the master answers, 'right under your heels, thirty blows would be fitting.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 若明辨得出，洞山只在闍黎腳跟下；若明辨不出，闍黎卻在洞山腳跟下。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A reversible appraisal: distinguish it and Dongshan is under your heels; fail and you are under Dongshan's heels.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「闍黎腳跟下水深多少？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct counter-question: 'how deep is the water under your heels?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是道？」師云：「只須向腳跟下薦取。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked 'what is the Way?', the master says, 'you need only recognize it right under your heels.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是直指人心、見性成佛之旨？」師云：「腳跟下分明看取。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked the meaning of direct pointing, the reply is 'look clearly right under your heels.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 第一義諦即不問，腳跟下事是如何？」師云：「頭上安頭。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The stock 'matter under your heels' is asked publicly; the reply is 'putting a head atop your head.'

Senses.Explanation: The named shout associated by the Chan record with Linji Yixuan. Device lists pair 'Linji's shout' with 'Deshan's staff,' and later sermons compare the shout to rushing thunder. The phrase is not merely a historical label: masters publicly ask what its purport is, demand that a monk produce it, or declare that they have no use for it today. The corpus also polices the inherited emblem. When asked what indication lies beyond Deshan's staff and Linji's shout, one master strikes and says that calling it 'staff-and-shout' sends one to hell like an arrow. Thus Zen bends an ordinary shout into a named lineage implement and object of later interview, imitation, comparison, and criticism; the entry reports only those recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: Wave-plan frequency: 410; related-entry counts report roughly 442 hits in 155 allowlist texts. Family comparison with the shout (喝), the staff or blow (棒), Deshan's staff (德山棒), and staff-and-shout (棒喝) confirms a genuinely Linji-specific named phrase, hence MasterName is set. The physical vocal act and the inherited label refer to the same named shout, not two things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟喝，德山棒，留與禪人作模範
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A device list explicitly pairs Linji's shout with Deshan's staff and calls them models left to Chan people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山棒如雨點。臨濟喝似雷奔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record carries the stock similes: Deshan's staff like raindrops and Linji's shout like rushing thunder.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問德山棒臨濟喝意旨如何師云寶應今日不用
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks the purport of the paired devices; the master says Baoying has no use for them today.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「德山棒、臨濟喝，除此二途，有何指示？」師打云：「喚作棒喝，入地獄如箭。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked for an indication beyond the two devices, the master strikes and warns against naming the action 'staff-and-shout.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally "existing in oneself" or "being at one's own disposal" (自在): "free and at ease," "unconstrained," or adverbially "freely," attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. A record closes an address with "everyone drink tea in the hall, free and at ease" (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Another says, "only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired" (卷舒自在，應用無虧). A later compilation uses the result phrase "obtain great freedom" (獲大自在), while Zhe'an Fan says "unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time" (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui says, "then one enters birth and death and obtains great freedom" (出生入死得大自在). Other records say one can be freely at ease at every time and place, pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. The word thus appears as adjective, adverb, result noun, and reduplicated "free and at ease" (自由自在), without requiring a further religious abstraction.
Senses.Note: Counted constructions: "free and at ease" (自由自在), 185; "free and unobstructed" (自在無礙), 50; "obtain great freedom" (得大自在), 258; "not at ease" (不自在), 134. The compound personal/title name "Contemplating Freely" (觀自在, 278) and personal names such as Yun Zizai are proper-name uses and are not merged into this adjectival sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各自大家堂中喫茶自由自在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Address ending: "everyone drink tea in the hall, free and at ease." The governing speaker is not roster-linked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到這裏始能卷舒自在，應用無虧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen Lingkan's section: "only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 境智融通，色空無礙，獲大自在
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compilation prose: "objects and knowing interpenetrate; form and space are unobstructed; obtain great freedom."

Occurrences.Kwic: 一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an Fan: "unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time."

Occurrences.Kwic: 則出生入死得大自在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's address: "then one enters birth and death and obtains great freedom."

Occurrences.Kwic: 便乃一切時一切處。任運自在。應用無方。諸人還委悉麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's record says: 'at every time and in every place, proceed freely and at ease, responding without fixed direction,' then asks whether the assembly understands.

Occurrences.Kwic: 透得一句生死自在；透得二句來去自由；三句透得，可以為人天師；四句總透得，可以為佛祖師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An enumerated address pairs being free in birth and death after penetrating one phrase with free coming and going after two.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當知欲驗臨終受生自在不自在，但驗尋常行心於塵境自由不自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compilation gives an explicit test: whether one is free at death is checked against whether one's ordinary conduct is free amid encountered objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛秖是去住自由，不同眾生。佛不是虗空受苦，何得不苦？若說不苦，此語違負。等閑莫說，錯說佛神通自在不自在。具慙愧人，不敢說佛是有為是無為，不敢說佛自由不自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The record cautions against casually declaring whether a buddha is free or not free, pairing that restraint with refusing to call a buddha conditioned or unconditioned.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, one's own nature, or the nature belonging to the subject under discussion. The expression occurs 2,091 times in 260 allowlisted texts. The Platform Record says that one's own nature is originally clean, contains the ten thousand things, and is not apart from them; another recension lists it as originally clean, not arising or perishing, complete in itself, unmoving, and able to produce the ten thousand things. These are the record's predicates, not an imported definition. Other Chan records use the term in questions about seeing, clarifying, or being unaware of one's own nature. One discourse says that what is reluctantly named the naturally true buddha of one's own nature is also called the master of one's own house. Direct answers do not settle into a single formula: asked 'What is one's own nature?' one master says, 'I will not say'; asked about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature while tending a fire, another tells the monk to bring a bundle of firewood.
Senses.Note: The possessive force varies with the grammatical subject: a person's own nature, or the nature of a thing. The mirror record supplies 605 of the 2,091 hits, so the entry balances its evidence with the Platform Record, lamp material, and individual discourse records. The named compound 'accomplished own-nature' receives a later text's separate body-and-function classification and is not used to redefine every bare occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道俗一千餘人，同時作禮，願聞法要。大師告眾曰：「善知識！菩提自性，本來清淨，但用此心，直了成佛。善知識！且聽惠能行由，得法事意。惠
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record opens its autobiographical section with the statement that awakening and one's own nature are originally clean.

Occurrences.Kwic: 起六識：眼識、耳識、鼻識、舌識、身識、意識，六門、六塵。自性含萬法，名為含藏識。思量即轉識，生六識，出六門、六塵，是三六十
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An early Platform Record recension says that one's own nature contains the ten thousand things and names the resulting inclusive designation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又非甚高難行之事，只是你日用常行，見成受用底，強而名之，喚作自性天真佛，又喚作自己主人公。近而言之，你一切時一切處，用釋迦老子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address explicitly says that the reluctant name 'naturally true buddha of one's own nature' is also called the master of one's own house.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道一句看？」學人無對。師曰：「你被語音塞卻口。」問：「如何是自性？」師曰：「不說，不說。」曰：「如何不說？」師曰：「恐你
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a direct exchange, the master answers the bare question 'What is one's own nature?' by refusing to say.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後向甚麼處去？師曰，千株松下，百草頭邊。師燒火次，僧問，如何是自性天真佛。師曰，與我搬一束柴來。僧肩柴至，又問。師曰，者奴子好惡
Occurrences.AttributionNote: While tending a fire, a master answers a question about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature by asking for a bundle of firewood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而生其心語，祖於言下大徹，遂啟五祖曰：一切萬法不離自性，何期自性本自清淨？何期自性本不生滅？何期自性本自具足？何期自性本無動搖？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record quotes Huineng's list of four predicates for one's own nature and begins by saying that all things are not apart from it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise something and ask. Chan records use it when a speaker carries a saying, exchange, or disputed comparison into a further interview and asks another master about it. Zhenjue raises before Xuanwu a description of light from the eye illuminating mountains and rivers, then asks where that person is at fault. Dongshan raises before Yunju the statement that there is no Maitreya in heaven or on earth; Yunju replies by asking who then gave him his name. Jiashan and Dingshan take their opposed sayings about buddha in birth-and-death to a master, and Jiashan raises the matter by asking whose view is more intimate; the answer distinguishes one as intimate and one as remote. Another monk raises the staff of Deshan and shout of Linji and asks what side they clarify; the master tells him to try to say, and tests his ensuing shout. The deviation is institutional and textual: raising is not merely lifting an object, but re-presenting prior words or actions to a Chan interlocutor so that the case continues through another public question and response.
Senses.Note: This compound includes both operations: “raise” (舉) re-presents prior material and “ask” (問) directs a question about it. It overlaps with “raise a case” (舉) and “question-and-answer” (問答), while differing from a master's newly bestowed question (垂問).

Occurrences.Kwic: 真覺大師舉問玄晤大師：「眼門放光，照破山河。山河大地，不礙眼光。此人過在什摩處，只欠濤汰。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhenjue raises a statement before Xuanwu and asks where the described person is at fault.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山舉問雲居，居云：天上無彌勒，地下無彌勒，未審誰與安名？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan raises an earlier Maitreya statement before Yunju, whose response is another question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二人上山參禮。夾山便舉問師。未審二人見處那箇較親。師云。一親一疎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After two opposed sayings, Jiashan raises their views and asks which is more intimate; the master gives a paired verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉問德山棒臨濟喝未審明得什麼邊事師云你試道看僧便喝師云瞎
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk raises Deshan's staff and Linji's shout for questioning; the master asks him to try to say and judges his shouted response.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise up and make prominent. The expression occurs 1,627 times in 275 allowlisted texts. Chan records make it a public teaching-seat verb: a master proclaims the sect's purport, presents 'this matter' before the assembly, or is asked in an interview to present a cited event. One opening discourse pairs opening the hall with 'proclaiming the teaching of the school'; another records a whisk transmitted with the charge to present this matter before the human and heavenly assembly. A later discourse says that one sentence had already been presented before the listeners entered the gate.
Senses.Note: No definition formula was found. The deviation is institutional and observable: the ordinary verb becomes a recurrent description of a master's public work from the teaching seat. The corpus does not support separate senses for different subjects raised; all are objects of the same transitive act.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爍破重關，徹法源底，逼得山僧無藏隱處，今日不免對眾舉揚。煩維那宣讀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master says he cannot avoid presenting it publicly before the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 為國開堂，舉揚宗教，山僧不敢囊藏被葢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An opening-hall discourse pairs the ceremony with proclaiming the teaching of the school.

Occurrences.Kwic: 擲鉢峰前事，請師為舉揚。師云：風不來，樹不動。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk publicly asks the master to present an earlier event, and the master answers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人未入門時，一句子已向汝舉揚了也，更待興問酬荅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse says one sentence had already been presented before question and response began.

Occurrences.Kwic: 付與山僧，曰：『向後人天眾前舉揚個事去。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmitted whisk accompanies an explicit charge to present this matter before the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “the tongue” (舌頭), deployed in Chan verdicts as a person's capacity to speak. “The tongue has no bone” (舌頭無骨) answers both “what is the great meaning of the buddha teaching?” and “opening the mouth loses; closing it perishes—how can one speak?” A student says that he no longer doubts “the tongues of the old masters everywhere” (天下老和尚舌頭), and his teacher immediately asks him to state what he understands. In the Linji succession account Huangbo predicts that Linji will “sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven” (坐斷天下人舌頭); the same countable verdict recurs widely without narrating bodily injury. The concrete organ is thus the corpus's recurring word for what is tested, trusted, shortened, or cut off in public speech.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. The headword has 2,473 hits in 325 allowlisted texts; the speech deployment is independently anchored in lamp, lineage, and case-commentary sources. This is a different referent from the anatomical tongue that is bitten or injured, not a second reading imposed on the same passage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 住後僧問。如何是佛法大意。師曰。舌頭無骨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Continued Lamp encounter gives ‘the tongue has no bone’ as the answer to the great meaning of the buddha teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問開口即失閉口即喪。未審如何說。師曰。舌頭無骨。僧曰。不會。師曰。對牛彈琴。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate master answers the open-mouth/closed-mouth dilemma with ‘the tongue has no bone.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 師當下大悟云。某甲不疑天下老和尚舌頭也。山曰。汝會處作麼生。與我說來看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student says he no longer doubts old masters' tongues; the teacher requires him to state his understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子但將去。已後坐斷天下人舌頭去在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo predicts that Linji will later sit across and cut off everyone's tongue.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊被魔王坐斷舌頭，龍淵路見不平，要與雪屈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old-case commentary applies the same speech-verdict collocation to the Buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，僧出擬問，師曰：不動舌頭道將一句來。僧喝，師曰：猶涉唇吻在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public teaching encounter, the master demands a statement without moving the tongue, explicitly testing the monk's capacity to speak.

Senses.Explanation: The anatomical tongue, a bodily organ that can be bitten. The records say “while eating, bite the tongue” (喫飯咬著舌頭) and “just now, eating melon seeds, [I] bit through the tongue” (適纔吃瓜子，咬破舌頭). These bodily predicates identify a separate referent from the tongue used as the capacity for public speech.
Senses.Note: No special Zen deviation is asserted for this ordinary anatomical sense. Independent bodily witnesses prevent the speech sense from absorbing literal anatomy.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫飯咬著舌頭
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct bodily use: biting the tongue while eating.

Occurrences.Kwic: 適纔吃瓜子，咬破舌頭
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second independent bodily use: biting through the tongue while eating melon seeds.

Senses.Explanation: A considerable duration: “a good while.” The headword occurs 11,566 times across 387 allowlisted texts. In dialogue and hall addresses it is often rendered “after a long pause”: a master says nothing and then speaks, shouts, raises the fly-whisk, plants the staff, or steps down. A monk can also be the one who pauses, so the word does not itself encode a master's authoritative silence. The interval may be an entire assembly's unanswered wait: after the master asks whether anyone has a question, no one asks for a good while and he leaves. The pause may also constitute the whole recorded answer, as when a monk asks the master to say it directly and responds after the master's silence. Chan records repeatedly deploy the World-Honored One in this mode when a non-Buddhist asks about neither the spoken nor the unspoken. They also deploy Kāśyapa ascending the seat before King Ajātaśatru, waiting a good while, and descending without preaching. Elsewhere the headword marks ordinary elapsed narrative time before a summons and reply. All of these denote the same interval; the entry records its duration without assigning the silence an unstated meaning.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide temporal sense. Held silence in dialogue is the dominant Chan deployment, not part of the denotation in every occurrence. The curated passages include a monk's pause, an assembly's unanswered wait for questions, pauses followed by a whisk or staff gesture, the World-Honored One and Kāśyapa seat cases, and ordinary elapsed narrative time. Raised cases and generic dialogue frames keep null speaker fields.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊良久。外道讚歎曰：「世尊大慈，開我迷雲，令我得入。」乃作禮而去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised case: the World-Honored One pauses for a long while after a non-Buddhist says he asks about neither the spoken nor the unspoken; the questioner then praises him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 外道問佛云不問有言不問無言世尊良久外道禮拜云善哉世尊大慈大悲開我迷雲令我得入
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Highlights of the Lamp independently preserves the World-Honored One case, with the questioner bowing rather than praising.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是佛師良久云會麼僧云不會師云何不高聲問
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: after being asked what buddha is, the master pauses and then asks, “Do you get it?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問不涉思量處從上宗乘請師直道師良久僧曰恁麼即聽響之流徒勞側耳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Highlights of the Lamp, section on Zongxian Minghui: when asked to say it directly, the master pauses for a long while and the monk responds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 寶在什麼處良久喝一喝下座
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters: a hall address closes with a long pause, one shout, and stepping down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧良久。師曰。會麼僧。曰。不會
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk, rather than the master, pauses for a good while before the master asks whether he understands.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久豎拂子云：「會麼？相知不用多杯酒，一盞清茶也醉人。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After the interval, the master raises the fly-whisk, asks whether the assembly understands, and continues with a line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久卓拄杖云拄杖子𨁝跳出來道和尚棒教誰喫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a good while, the master plants the staff and voices the staff's question about who is to receive the beating.

Occurrences.Kwic: 阿闍世王請師說法，師受請升座，良久乃下。王問師：「何故不為弟子說？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised Kāśyapa case: at King Ajātaśatru's request, Kāśyapa ascends the seat, remains for a good while, and descends without preaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 陽曰得。良久乃召師。師應諾。陽曰。與爾箇入路。師於言下有省
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ordinary elapsed narrative time: after a while Dayang calls the visitor, who answers and has insight at the following words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫有問話者麼。良久無人問。師乃去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a hall address the master asks whether anyone has a question; after a good while with no question, he leaves. The interval belongs to the assembly's public nonresponse.

AlternateTargets: after a long while, he said
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'after a good while, said.' This fixed narrative formula occurs 2,037 times in 79 allowed texts. It marks an interval before quoted speech in dialogues and assembly addresses. In the Five Lamps Complete Collection, Tianyi Yihuai asks, 'Then what is it?' and after a while says, 'Do you understand? Take care!' (且作麼生即是？良久曰：還會麼？珍重). In a Five Lamps Rigorous Continuation address, the speaker ascends the hall, waits, says, 'Assembly, look, look,' and descends (上堂，良久曰：大眾看看。便下座). Another record asks where Maitreya is and, after a while, answers, 'When walking at night do not tread on white; if it is not water, it is stone' (且道彌勒在甚麼處？良久曰：夜行莫踏白，不是水便是石). The Continued Transmission of the Lamp supplies both extended statements and short closings after the formula: 'a drop of spring rain is slick as oil' (春雨一滴滑如油) and 'fine food does not suit a full person,' followed by descent from the seat (美食不中飽人喫。便下座). The punctuation varies by edition, but the sequence remains interval, speech verb, and quotation.
Senses.Note: The close variant 'after a while, said' with the alternate speech graph (良久云) occurs 1,403 times in 169 texts. 'Silently for a long while' (默然良久) occurs 45 times in 32 texts, while three records have 'after a while, descended from the seat' (良久下座) without the speech verb. Those forms confirm the components but are not merged into the headword count. No self-definition formula is applicable to this narrative connector.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂良久曰。夫行脚禪流直須著忖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp, under the heirs of Shoushan Shengnian. The formula opens an assembly statement; the nearest heading does not supply a safe roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久曰。春雨一滴滑如油。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master in the Shoushan-heir section waits before giving the one-line statement about a drop of spring rain. The broader lineage heading is insufficient for a link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久曰。美食不中飽人喫。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp, under the heirs of Zhimen Guangzuo. The formula introduces a final sentence immediately before descent from the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且作麼生即是？良久曰：還會麼？珍重！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Tianyi Yihuai section. His question is followed by the interval formula and a short closing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，良久曰：大眾看看。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Rigorous Continuation, Wuyun Zhifeng section. The master waits, tells the assembly to look, and descends.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道彌勒在甚麼處？良久曰：夜行莫踏白，不是水便是石。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Lamp's Correct Lineage, Xuansha Sengzhao section. A question about Maitreya is followed by the interval and the recorded answer.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs name a mustard seed. The allowlisted corpus has 442 hits in 146 texts. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, 67 hits in 50 texts), as when a teacher speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, 46 hits in 30 texts) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, 59 hits in 44 texts). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched. One ‘What is the mustard seed?’ question is included because its answer, ‘It blocks your eye,’ is an attested direct response, not adopted here as a universal lexical equation. Deployment inventory includes the small-measure construction, both Sumeru constructions, question-and-answer use, and a later expanded list of what is placed inside the seed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 教中所言。須彌納芥子。㴾即不疑。芥子納須彌。莫是妄譚否。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Li Bo contrasts the two directions of the Sumeru-and-mustard-seed statement in his question to Guizong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。如何是芥子。師曰。塞將汝眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Shishi Shandao’s section, the teacher answers ‘What is the mustard seed?’ with ‘It blocks your eye.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 若有一疑如芥子許，是汝真善知識。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daomin’s address uses a mustard seed as the size comparison for a doubt.

Occurrences.Kwic: 將山河大地、艸木叢林、若僧若俗、若聖若凡納入芥子，而芥子不見其窄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A winter-retreat conclusion places an enumerated world inside a mustard seed and says the seed does not become narrow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是芥子納須彌？王云：易。問：如何是須彌納芥子？王云：難。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A paired exchange asks about each direction and records the king’s answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 須彌芥子父。芥子須彌爺。山水坦然平。敲氷來煮茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes Fu Dashi’s reciprocal father-and-grandfather wording for Sumeru and the mustard seed.

Senses.Explanation: To be blankly at a loss. In Chan encounter narratives it is an observable failure to answer or proceed: after being asked "who observes, and what is quiet?" a monk is at a loss; after being seized and ordered "speak! speak!" a monk is at a loss and is pushed away. The record makes the absence of an answer explicit in "the master was at a loss and did not know how to reply" (師茫然不知對). It also applies collectively: after the answer "clear conversation face to face—if not buddha, then who?" the assembly is all at a loss (眾皆茫然). A training biography records a student being required to give one fitting word and withdrawing at a loss (師茫然退). The Zen deviation lies in this recurring public-interview function: the adjective marks the recorded point where a participant or assembly has no response, not a mystical state and not an explanation of why the exchange defeated them.
Senses.Note: Count: 609 occurrences in 178 allowlisted texts. One state word. Individual, collective, and narrative occurrences differ only in subject and trigger, not referent. The entry avoids the planning gloss 'non-comprehension' where the text shows only loss for words or response.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰汝何不自觀自靜。彼僧茫然。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question leaves the monk at a loss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是佛。師曰。清譚對面。非佛而誰。眾皆茫然。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The subject is the whole assembly after a public answer to 'what is buddha?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 三界唯心，萬法唯識。今目前萬象摐然，心識安在？師茫然不知對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The narrative explicitly expands the word as not knowing how to answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師搊住云：道！道！僧茫然，師遂托開。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public demand to speak is followed by being at a loss and being pushed away.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇要你一言下諦當，便是汝見處。師茫然退。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography records the student withdrawing at a loss when required to give one fitting word.

Senses.Explanation: Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” (踏破草鞋) and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” (更買草鞋行脚三十年) make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Huangbo calls “the patriarchs' dark purport” (祖師玄旨) “worn-out straw sandals” (破草鞋) and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.
Senses.Note: The exact term occurs 2,237 times in 301 allowlisted texts. High-value shapes are literal footwear, the travel collocations “wear out sandals” and “buy sandals,” the Deshan departure, the Zhaozhou-on-the-head case, and Huangbo's explicit comparison. No independent self-definition was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山背却法堂。著草鞋便行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record's Deshan case: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his straw sandals, and leaves; the head monk later reports the same action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州外歸。泉舉似州。州乃脫履。安頭上而出。泉云。子若在即救得猫兒。無門曰。且道。趙州頂草鞋意作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Gateless Barrier's Nanquan cat case: Zhaozhou removes a sandal, puts it on his head, and exits; Wumen asks about “Zhaozhou carrying the straw sandal on his head.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師玄旨是破草鞋。寧可赤脚不著最好。僧問。如何是佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo's section explicitly compares “the patriarchs' dark purport” to “worn-out straw sandals” and says going barefoot would be best.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師九年面壁。何不慚惶。若恁麼會得。更買草鞋行脚三十年。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A recorded old adept says that if one understands Bodhidharma's nine years facing the wall in that way, one should “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years.”

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.
Senses.Note: Dream, mourning story, scholarly reference, sword line, and poetic address all name the same person. They are different deployments, not different referents or readings to split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠。
昔日莊周妻死，惠子吊之，周乃鼓盆而歌
莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通。
師於孔老莊周百家之學，無不會通。
寄語莊周休擬議。樹中不是負趍人。
三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平。

Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as a master's warning attached directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, one master answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere a master warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 168 hits in 73 texts. Variants include emphatic take care not to get it wrong (莫錯會好) and just do not get it wrong (且莫錯會). One imperative sense; preceding statements do not create different referents.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是西來意。師曰。是即是。莫錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public interview: the warning is attached to an answer about the west-coming intention.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫錯會好莫見與麼道便向不圓不頓處卜度者裏也須是箇人始得莫將依師語相似語測度語到處呈中將為自己見解莫錯會
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text specifies several wrong receptions: inference, borrowed phrases, and calculated phrases presented as one's own.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還委悉麼？莫道語默動靜無非佛事好，且莫錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Assembly warning against a stated generalization about speech, silence, movement, and stillness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昨日雪，今日消。仔細高著眼，莫錯會好！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hall-address use after an ordinary seasonal statement, without an explanatory gloss.

Senses.Explanation: The binding precepts designated for a bodhisattva. The expression occurs 163 times in 63 allowlisted texts. Chan biographies record rulers receiving them from masters and masters regularly conferring them: the Five Lamps says King Zhongyi summoned Yongming Yanshou to receive the bodhisattva precepts, and later says Yanshou continually conferred them on the seven groups. A public address places novice, monk, and bodhisattva precepts together, then says acting knowingly against them is also possible; the statement is preserved without turning it into a general licence. The corpus also preserves an explicit rule contrast: a cited scripture says an auditor's precepts are strict where bodhisattva precepts are lenient, and closed where bodhisattva precepts are open; the following citation says keeping an auditor's precept can be breaking a bodhisattva precept. Thus Chan deployment includes institutional ordination administered by masters, public handling of breach, and an attested permit/prohibit contrast within rule discourse.
Senses.Note: The entry reports the institutional acts and preserves the text's own strict/lenient and closed/open contrast without extending it beyond the cited wording.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忠懿王命入府受菩薩戒。署慈化定慧禪師。建大伽藍。號慧日永明。請居之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: King Zhongyi summons Yongming Yanshou to receive the bodhisattva precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 常與七眾授菩薩戒。夜施鬼神食。朝放諸生類。不可稱算。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yanshou is recorded as continually conferring the precepts on the seven groups.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聲聞戒急，菩薩戒緩；聲聞戒塞，菩薩戒開。』又經云：『聲聞持戒，是菩薩破戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text quotes an explicit tight/lenient and closed/open contrast between two classes of rules.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一時周禮沙彌戒，比丘戒，菩薩戒。逢場作戲也可，到處稱尊也可，知而故犯也可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address groups three classes of rules and explicitly includes knowingly acting against them.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an attached comment on a case
Senses.Explanation: An attached short comment on a case, one line of dialogue, or a verse; verbal constructions describe attaching that same comment. The headword occurs hundreds of times in the allowlisted corpus. The Blue Cliff Record directly says, “in the assembly this is called an attached comment” (眾中謂之著語), and elsewhere, “this is called an attached comment” (此謂之著語). Xuedou attaches a comment and then gives its words; other records specify the exact point where Xuedou or Dahui comments, such as “at the words ‘do not think falsely’” or “at the point of stepping down.” A living master can also be asked to attach comments to a set of twelve questions. Chan makes the comment and its attachment a formal device of case commentary, not generic speech. The act and resulting words are grammatical views of one commentarial object and remain one sense.
Senses.Note: The former operation/product targets were not distinguishable as different referents from their glosses alone: both name the same attached comment. Keep it distinct from laying down a response (下語), answering in another's place (代語), extended appraisal-commentary (評唱), and a verse on an old case (頌古).

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇著語云。勘破了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuedou performs the commenting operation and supplies the words “Seen through!”

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇著語云。今日共者漢游山。圖箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's Extensive Record (宏智禪師廣錄), in the hall-address record of Master Jue of Mount Tiantong. Xuedou attaches words to a raised case in the main running text, showing the formula 'attached the words, saying' (著語云) followed by a terse phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇顯於莫妄想處著語云：塞却鼻孔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Old Cases Raised in the Lineage (宗門拈古彙集). Xuedou Chongxian attaches words at the 'do not think falsely' point of the case (雪竇顯於莫妄想處著語云).

Occurrences.Kwic: 徑山杲於下座處著語云：葛藤不少。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Collected Old Cases Raised in the Lineage (宗門拈古彙集). Dahui Zonggao, named as Jingshan Gao (徑山杲), attaches words at the point where the speaker steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 五臺山有一尊宿，設十二問，請師著語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Wutai elder sets twelve questions and asks the master to attach comments to them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中謂之著語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The commentary directly says, “in the assembly this is called an attached comment.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 此謂之著語。落在兩邊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second direct naming formula calls the preceding words an attached comment and says that it lands on both sides.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 63 times in 37 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立). The same collection says that people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). There are 37 occurrences of 'not fall into blankness' (不落空) and 21 of the warning 'do not fall into blankness' (莫落空).
Senses.Note: The translation 'blankness' follows the records' direct corrections: 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立), and 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). The entry records the corpus's accusations, warnings, and replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 纔聞善知識說無所得法。便心裏疑惑。怕落空去。妙喜每見如此說者。即問他。只這怕落空者。還空也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui describes the fear and responds by questioning whether the one who fears falling into blankness is itself empty.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古德喚作落空亡外道魂不散死人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui cites an older description: 'an outsider fallen into blank annihilation, a dead person whose ghost has not dispersed.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 有律師法明。謂師曰。禪師家多落空。師曰。却是坐主家多落空。法明大驚曰。何得落空。師曰。經論是紙墨文字。紙墨文字者俱空。設於聲上建立名句等法。無非是空。坐主執滯教體。豈不落空。法明曰。禪師落空否。師曰。不落空。曰何却不落空。師曰。文字等皆從智慧而生。大用現前那得落空。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of the Transmission of the Lamp. The exchange turns the accusation back and says that letters arise from wisdom, so great function appearing before one does not fall into blankness; the two-speaker occurrence remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰本來無莫落空否。師曰。空既是無墮從何立。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct exchange rejects the premise: if blankness is absent, no falling can be established.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人不敢忘心。是恐落空無撈摸處。不知空本無空唯一真界耳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text says people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says that blankness itself is originally not blank.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the 'place where something falls.' The term occurs 2,117 times in 310 allowed texts. Chan records apply it to words, answers, cases, actions, people, and one's life: 'know where it lands' (知落處) occurs 770 times in 205 texts, while 'not know where it lands' (不知落處) occurs 172 times in 89 texts. Yuanwu says that as soon as Danxia raised it, he knew where it landed (才方舉起便知落處), and his Blue Cliff prose twice contrasts knowing and not knowing where Mazu's public case lands. Dahui asks whether the assembly knows where his teacher's words land and says that knowing it identifies the top graduate (還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元). Changqing asks a monk, 'Do you understand where it lands?' (還委落處麼). A lamp record joins origin and destination: 'if you know where it arises, then you know where life lands' (若知起處。便知身命落處). Xiuyelin gives the richest explicit relation found: 'the fundamental matter is precisely where the person's own life-source lands' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). The article therefore keeps the verbal image and reports what the texts assign a landing point; it does not replace that image with an imported abstraction.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas and obvious variants were searched. No formula directly defines the bare headword. The Xiuyelin sentence instead defines the fundamental matter by means of it and is retained as the strongest relational witness. Questions about knowing, not knowing, and asking where something lands form one broad corpus-wide family rather than master-specific senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiuyelin's instruction to Layman Pan directly identifies the fundamental matter as where the person's own life-source lands. No exact roster link was assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此箇公案。若知落處便獨步丹霄。若不知落處。往往枯木巖前差路去在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff prose comments on Mazu's sun-face buddha and moon-face buddha case, explicitly contrasting knowing and not knowing where the case lands.

Occurrences.Kwic: 才方舉起便知落處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yuanwu's sixth volume of assembly addresses, Yuanwu says that Danxia knew where it landed as soon as it was raised.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敢問諸人還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui asks the assembly whether they know where his teacher's words land and states the consequence in his own assembly address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。還委落處麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Changqing Huileng section. Changqing asks a monk whether he understands where it lands; the short dialogue remains unlinked because no roster spelling was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若知起處。便知身命落處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Emperor Taizong section. A teacher links knowing where thunder arises with knowing where life lands; the emperor is the section subject, not the speaker.

Senses.Explanation: Literally kudzu-and-wisteria creepers — vines that twist, cling and choke. In Chan it is the standing metaphor for WORDS that entangle: talk, verbiage, verbal complication, the case (公案) as a thicket of language. Yuanwu equates it outright with speech — (那裏如此葛藤)。(須是斬斷語言) 'why all this vine-tangle here? one must cut off words.' A teacher who explains too much is (打葛藤) 'spinning out vines'; the cases themselves are (葛藤公案) 'vine-tangle cases'; merely wordy Chan is disparaged as (葛藤禪) 'vine-Chan' (one pejorative label in a whole doxographic list of bad 'Chans'). The word carries a negative, self-deprecating cast — even a master opening a talk calls it (與諸人葛藤) 'getting tangled up in vines with you all.' It names the tangle of language, which the texts speak of cutting through (截斷／斬斷葛藤). The deployment range is wide: (截斷葛藤) ('cut off the vines') is spoken as a standalone dismissal in live exchanges — (師以拄杖畫一畫云)。(截斷葛藤) ('the master drew one stroke with his staff and said: cut off the vines'), (喝一喝)。(截斷葛藤) ('gave a shout: cut off the vines'); the tangle is a nest one sits or crashes into, (葛藤窠) — (坐在葛藤窠裡) ('sitting in the vine-nest'), (商量也依前撞入葛藤窠) ('discuss it and you crash into the vine-nest as before'); and the label reaches all the way up to the canon itself — (一大藏教閑葛藤)。(千七百則絆殺人) ('the whole great treasury of the teachings: idle vine-tangle; the seventeen hundred cases trip men to death'), and independently (一大藏教閑葛藤)。(盡大地人跳不出) ('idle vine-tangle the whole earth's people cannot jump clear of').
Senses.Note: Single corpus-wide metaphorical sense. The literal botanical 'kudzu vine' underlies it but in the Zen records the term is almost always the figurative 'verbal entanglement.' Counts (462-text allowlist grep): (葛藤) 2530 hits in 334 of the 462 texts; (打葛藤) 188 in 98; (葛藤窠) 144 in 81 (坐在葛藤窠裡 J10nA158 0004b05; 撞入葛藤窠 C078n1720 0669b19); (截斷葛藤) 80 in 60 (staff-stroke dismissals J25nB171 0519a07, 0535c08; 喝一喝 J26nB177 0038c28); (葛藤露布) 33 in 27; (葛藤禪) 21 in 18; (閑葛藤) 5 in 5 (一大藏教閑葛藤 J34nB299 0126a19 and X71n1420 0640a07).

Occurrences.Kwic: 那裏如此葛藤。須是斬斷語言。格外見諦。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (碧巖錄), Yuanwu's commentary glossing (葛藤) directly as (語言) (words): 'why such vine-tangle here? one must cut off words and see the truth beyond the letter.' The defining equation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 許多葛藤公案。具眼者。試說看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu: 'so many vine-tangle cases — let the clear-eyed one try to explain.' The collocation (葛藤公案) (case-as-verbal-thicket).

Occurrences.Kwic: 道者禪葛藤禪。更有脫略機境不受差排者。喚作向上禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Doxographic passage listing pejorative Chan-types (…棒喝禪拍盲禪道者禪葛藤禪), with (向上禪) above them all. (葛藤禪) = 'vine-Chan' — Chan that is all verbal entanglement. Speaker unnamed in this stretch.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。事不獲已。與諸人葛藤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), head (杭州慶善院普能禪師): 'Taking the hall — unavoidably, I'll spin out vines with you all.' A master's self-deprecating opening; (與諸人葛藤) = deal you some verbiage.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "empty" or "vacant" (虛) "space" (空): "empty space," also the open sky, attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it as a location, comparison, and grammatical object. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 90 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.
Senses.Note: The headword spans ordinary spatial reference, comparisons, verse imagery, questions, and compounds. The curated witnesses foreground recurrent Chan deployment rather than the hundreds of scholastic similes in one prolific compilation. The exact graph pair remains "empty space" even where English idiom favors "sky."

Occurrences.Kwic: 此一瓣香虛空包不住。大地載不起。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's incense statement: "this one petal of incense cannot be contained by empty space or supported by the great earth."

Occurrences.Kwic: 者裏明得，虛空可量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an Fan's formal address: "if understood here, empty space can be measured." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉頭頓忘迷悟如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Memorial narrative: "raising his head, he suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, lucid like empty space and impossible to approach or lodge in." Historical narration remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「待虛空粉碎來向汝道。」云：「粉碎後如何？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In public exchange, the master postpones his answer until empty space shatters, and the monk asks what follows the shattering.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。一棒打破虛空。進云。過在什麼處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master answers a request for the upward road with one blow that breaks empty space; the questioner immediately asks where the fault lies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 虛空無內外，心法亦如是。若了虛空故，是達真如理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmitted verse predicates that empty space has neither inside nor outside and uses it as the stated comparison for mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫向虛空裏釘橛有一屠兒身上常出乳香舍利
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A comment warns against driving a stake into empty space before introducing the butcher account.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你若揀辨，大似虛空中畫疆界；你若不揀辨，又是漆桶裏坐墨煤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address compares discriminating there to drawing territorial boundaries in empty space, then gives the contrary warning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾請偈，師不荅。將二鼓，復索筆書曰：一燈在望，更無言說。大地平沉，虛空迸裂。書畢，泊然而寂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At the assembly's request, a dying master writes a final verse in which the great earth sinks flat and empty space bursts apart, then dies peacefully.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：達磨正宗，衲僧巴鼻。充塞虛空，無處回避。堪笑迷流，白日青天開却眼，只管瞌睡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address says that Bodhidharma's true lineage, the Chan monk's defining feature, fills empty space and leaves nowhere to evade it.

Senses.Explanation: The connective or transmission line running through Chan cases, sayings, and teacher-successor succession. The word occurs 174 times in 86 allowlisted texts. In the dry-tree dragon-song case, Caoshan answers that “the connective line is unbroken” (血脈不斷). Yuanwu applies the same phrase to the structure of an exchange—“the question is at the answer; the answer is at the question” (問在答處，答在問處)—and says that differing speakers do not lose the line sentence by sentence. A succession address says that Shouchang’s line is continued while Boshan’s house style is extended. Chan bends bodily and hereditary continuity into an attested line through speech, cases, houses, and succession.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. Split from hereditary descent and bodily blood circulation because those passages refer to different things. Repeated copies of the unbroken-line formula were excluded after the case, question-answer, direct naming, sentence continuity, and succession deployments were represented.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧又問曹山。如何是枯木裏龍吟。山云。血脈不斷。如何是髑髏裏眼睛。山云乾不盡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Raised Caoshan case: the answer to a dragon singing inside a withered tree is that the bloodline is unbroken; the paired skull-eye answer is that it is not dried out.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人自是血脈不斷。所以道。問在答處。答在問處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's comment says the ancients' bloodline is naturally unbroken and immediately describes the question as present at the answer and the answer at the question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人謂之血脈不斷。血脈不斷，猶目機銖兩也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct naming formula: the ancients called the preceding question-answer and speech-silence precision the bloodline unbroken; the text then compares it to measuring the mechanism by minute weights.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人見徹此事。各各雖不同。道得出來。百發百中。須有出身之路。句句不失血脈。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu says the ancients differed from one another but, when they spoke, each sentence did not lose the bloodline.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此是先大師受用不盡底付與雪關；雪關受用不盡送與石頭長老，接壽昌之血脈、展博山之家風。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Succession statement: what the former master could not exhaust was given to Xueguan, then passed to Elder Shitou, continuing Shouchang's bloodline and spreading Boshan's family style.

RelatedTerms: the bloodline is unbroken (血脈不斷)
the bloodline connects throughout (血脈貫通)
dragon singing inside a withered tree (枯木裏龍吟)

Senses.Explanation: A family line inherited through descent. One allowlisted address speaks of the father-son bloodline as inherited without interruption (父子血脈相承、本無斷絕). This is hereditary descent, not the bodily vessels and not the Chan connective line built from that image.
Senses.Note: Literal family referent. Kept separate from physiology under the different-thing test.

Occurrences.Kwic: 父子血脈相承、本無斷絕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker invokes the uninterrupted bloodline inherited by father and son as a comparison.

Senses.Explanation: The bodily network or circulation of blood. A medical comparison describes an illness caused by an external influence, treatment by a skilled doctor, and the blood circulation restored to mutual generation (血脈相生). The physiological referent is a different thing from family descent or Chan transmission.
Senses.Note: Physiological control sense. No external medical framework is imported; the entry reports only the explicit illness-and-doctor comparison.

Occurrences.Kwic: 偶因外感，發一奇病，幸遇良醫調治，血脈相生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A medical comparison describes external illness, a skilled doctor’s treatment, and blood circulation restored to mutual generation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "go" (行) on one's "feet" (腳): "travel on foot," attested 1,333 times in 192 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it for a monk leaving one place and traveling through the various quarters, visiting monasteries and teachers. In the Ancestral Hall Collection, a monk requests permission: "I wish to travel on foot; I ask the teacher for directions" (某甲欲得行腳，乞和尚處分). Another teacher asks, "Have you come traveling on foot through the various quarters to seek the hard-to-obtain thing?" (汝諸方行腳來覓取難得底物來不). A later record explicitly says, "though traveling a thousand miles on foot, [one does so] to seek a teacher of the lineage" (千里行腳，為尋宗師). Productive forms include "person traveling on foot" (行腳人), "patch-robed monk traveling on foot" (行腳衲僧), and "leave home and travel on foot" (出家行腳).
Senses.Note: The corpus also turns the activity into a test. Asked "What is the affair of traveling on foot?" (如何是行腳事), Poshan answers, "face to face, looking at one another, the mouth is like wood" (面面相看口如木). Another instruction calls someone who has passed through a cited exchange a "true person traveling on foot" (真行腳人). No formula in the corpus makes the term a separate prescribed system.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是行腳事？」師云：「面面相看口如木。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Poshan's upper-hall answer: face to face, looking at one another, the mouth is like wood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 某甲欲得行腳，乞和尚處分。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An Ancestral Hall Collection narrative: the monk wishes to travel on foot and asks his teacher for directions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝諸方行腳來覓取難得底物來不？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher asks a traveler whether he came through the various quarters seeking the hard-to-obtain thing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖則千里行腳，為尋宗師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shanhui states the distance and object together: a thousand miles traveling on foot to seek a lineage teacher.

Occurrences.Kwic: 於此透過方是真行腳人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction says that passing through the preceding exchange is what makes a true person traveling on foot.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs name a robe and an alms bowl. The allowlisted corpus has 513 hits in 115 texts, including records in which the objects are thrown onto a rock, lifted, carried, guarded, inventoried, or burned with a person’s other implements. Monastic regulations also name a ‘robe-and-bowl attendant’ (衣鉢侍者, 9 hits in 3 texts), who receives the seal in one installation procedure. In the Caoqi record, this attendant raises the robe associated with the object that could not be lifted at Dayu Ridge. These passages keep the material objects and their custodial office visible even where the same pair also marks succession.
Senses.Note: This first sense covers the material pair and its administrative extension to personal effects and the attendant responsible for them. It is separated from the succession-token sense because regulations can order the objects burned or placed in custody without describing succession.

Occurrences.Kwic: 盧見師奔至。即擲衣鉢於磐石曰。此衣表信。可力爭邪。任君將去。師遂舉之。如山不動。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Daoming account says Huineng threw the robe and bowl onto a rock, called the robe a token of trust, and Daoming could not lift it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 集眾燒衣鉢道具。遣逐偏門而出者。示耻辱也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The community-regulation section orders a dismissed person’s robe, bowl, and implements burned before expulsion through a side gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打印過，付衣鉢侍者收，知事全班列前上首。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An installation procedure assigns the seal to the robe-and-bowl attendant after it has been impressed.

Senses.Explanation: The pair also names the objects as passed evidence of succession. The corpus records ‘transmit the robe and bowl’ (傳衣鉢, 31 hits in 26 texts), ‘entrust the robe and bowl’ (付衣鉢, 10 hits in 8 texts), and one exact occurrence of ‘robe and bowl transmitted in succession’ (衣鉢相傳). The Dayu Ridge account explicitly calls the robe ‘a token of trust.’ Later addresses say that Huangmei’s robe and bowl were entrusted to Lu, while another asks which robe and bowl Lu actually transmitted. The question is recorded as a question rather than resolved here into an object different from the material robe and bowl.
Senses.Note: Historical succession does not make this a master-specific sense. The selected passages show the physical token, later transmission language, and a later challenge about what was transmitted. The seven required definition formulas were searched; no additional lexical self-definition was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爭似老盧無用處，却傳衣鉢振真風。大眾，且道那個是老盧傳底衣鉢？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wenyi’s address says that Lu transmitted the robe and bowl, then asks the assembly which robe and bowl he transmitted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 黃梅衣鉢，付與盧公。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address in Xingduan’s section says that Huangmei’s robe and bowl were entrusted to Lu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曹溪守衣鉢侍者，因僧到，乃提起衣曰：者是大庾嶺頭提不起底。僧曰：為什麼却在上座手裏？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A collected case has Caoqi’s robe-and-bowl attendant identify the raised robe with the Dayu Ridge account, after which a monk asks why it is in the attendant’s hand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 衣鉢僅為師弟古卓老宿所藏。卓翁又終，其衣鉢相傳於南明之手十有餘年。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage account says the robe and bowl were kept by one elder and then transmitted into Nanming's hands for more than ten years.

Senses.Explanation: Literally a monk (僧) in a patched robe (衲), a “patch-robed monk,” attested 8,708 times in 376 allowlisted texts. The term names the Chan monk as a participant addressed, questioned, or assessed in the records. Asked “what is a patch-robed monk?” (如何是衲僧), one teacher answers, “investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way” (參尋訪道). Another exchange asks for “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧分上事) and answers, “when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit” (要行即行，要坐即坐). The corpus also asks directly about “the patch-robed monk's eye” (衲僧眼) and “the patch-robed monk's place of conduct” (衲僧行履處). It speaks institutionally of what can be used “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), and appraises an assembly as lacking anyone with “the air of a patch-robed monk” (衲僧氣息). The Chan deviation lies in this public standard: the robe-word names the person expected to answer within the encounter record, while the compounds test that person's eye, conduct, handle, own affair, and house. These are attested compound deployments, not claims about an inner state.
Senses.Note: The records use the same human-role noun individually, collectively, and possessively. Yuanwu calls raising one and understanding three “ordinary tea and rice for the household of patch-robed monks” (衲僧家尋常茶飯), and elsewhere calls activity that ferries beings “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧家本分事). Eye, gate, conduct, air, household, own portion, and handle compounds do not denote a second kind of monk. Compare monk (僧), master or preceptor (和尚), this old monk (老僧), the household of patch-robed monks (衲僧家), and patched robe (衲衣).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是衲僧。師曰。參尋訪道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under the heading for Yun'gaishan Zhiyuan: "What is a patch-robed monk?" The teacher says, "investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way." The roster has no safe exact link for the heading name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。如何是衲僧分上事。師曰。要行即行。要坐即坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under the same heading: "What is the patch-robed monk's own affair?" The teacher answers, "when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit."

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉一明三。目機銖兩。是衲僧家尋常茶飯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Instruction introducing a Blue Cliff case: "raise one, understand three; assess the pivot by the slightest weight—this is ordinary tea and rice for the household of patch-robed monks." The structural heading is not a safe speaker attribution.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梯航三有津濟四生。是衲僧家本分事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu says, "serve as ladder and boat across the three modes of existence and ferry the four kinds of birth: this is the patch-robed monk's own affair."

Occurrences.Kwic: 句能剗意意能剗句。意句交馳衲僧巴鼻。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu says, "sentences can strip intent and intent can strip sentences; intent and sentences racing across one another are the patch-robed monk's handle."

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是衲僧眼師云朝看東南暮看西北
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public interview asks, “what is the patch-robed monk's eye?” (如何是衲僧眼). The teacher answers, “in the morning look southeast; in the evening look northwest” (朝看東南暮看西北).

Occurrences.Kwic: 若論衲僧門下，一點也用不得。作麼生是衲僧門下事？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says that, “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), not one bit of the preceding material can be used, then asks, “what is the affair under the patch-robed monk's gate?” (作麼生是衲僧門下事).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是衲僧行履處。師曰。頭上喫棒。口裏喃喃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked “what is the patch-robed monk's place of conduct?” (如何是衲僧行履處), the teacher answers, “taking a staff-blow on the head, muttering in the mouth” (頭上喫棒，口裏喃喃).

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中更無一人有衲僧氣息。諸人還見世尊以手摩胸麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says, “in the assembly there is not even one person with the air of a patch-robed monk” (眾中更無一人有衲僧氣息), then asks whether they saw the World-Honored One rub his chest with his hand.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a 'patched-robed person': 'patched robe' (衲) plus the person-noun (子). The term occurs 2,174 times in 317 allowed texts and names the monks who travel among, gather around, question, and are addressed by Chan teachers. A later small assembly gives the only direct naming formula found: 'all of you wear hats and waist-packs and are called patch-robed monks; the name and the reality ought to match' (箇箇都是頂笠腰包，名為衲子，要當名實相稱). In Nanquan's recorded exchange with Zhaozhou, Nanquan says, 'dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; patch-robed monks are hard to fool' (龍蛇易辨衲子難謾). A biography says that after a monastery was built, 'patch-robed monks hastened there like clouds' (衲子雲趨). Ciming speaks of sitting on a rock and at times discussing the profound with 'patch-robed monks from the five lakes' (與五湖衲子時話玄微); the longer form 'five-lakes patch-robed monks' (五湖衲子) occurs 57 times. Qingchu praises a traveller twice: 'Fine patch-robed monk! Fine patch-robed monk!' (衲子俊哉。衲子俊哉). A biography of Shending Yin describes him as 'extraordinary even among patch-robed monks; none dared enter his gate' (衲子非人類精奇。無敢登其門者). The noun therefore functions as singular praise, plural group-name, travelling population, and the object of tests and appraisals.
Senses.Note: No other required direct-definition formula was found; three late 'what is a patch-robed monk' questions give case-specific replies. The direct naming line, robe morphology, and broad early corpus deployment support the plain target without adding an imported religious category.

Senses.Explanation: Literally (見) 'see' + (性) 'nature': to see one's own nature. It is the operative half of the four-phrase slogan that defines the Chan school — (教外別傳)，(不立文字)，(直指人心)，(見性成佛) ('a separate transmission outside the teachings; not setting up words; pointing straight at the human mind; seeing [one's] nature and becoming Buddha') — and recurs in the near-synonyms (明心見性) ('clarify the mind and see nature') and (識心見性) ('know the mind and see nature'), the latter being what Zhaozhou calls 'the road that does not go wrong.' In the Bodhidharma-cycle case of the heretic-king (異見王), the venerable Boluoti (波羅提) says (見性是佛), 'seeing nature is Buddha.' A monk brings Xuefeng the canonical grading (a śrāvaka sees nature 'as one sees the moon at night,' a bodhisattva 'as one sees the sun by day'), and Xuefeng answers with three blows (打三下). Guizong says even (悟明見性) ('awakening and seeing nature') is (錯用心) ('misusing the mind'). Render it literally as 'see [one's] nature,' following the plain reading of (見性成佛) as 'see nature, become Buddha.' An in-corpus definition survives as a case: asked (如何是見性) (itself a live test-question, 15 hits in 13 allowlist texts), the master answers (性即是見)，(見即是性)，(不可以性更見性)；(聞即是性)，(不可以性更聞性) (nature is precisely seeing, seeing is precisely nature; one cannot see nature by means of nature again — 天聖廣燈錄 X78n1553; parallel 古尊宿語錄 C077n1710), and (五燈會元續略) carries the same definition credited to (大顛): (僧問大顛)：(如何是見性)？(顛曰)：(見即是性) (X80n1566). (傳燈玉英集) states (見性者即非凡夫頓悟上乘超凡越聖) (one who sees nature is no ordinary man — sudden awakening to the higher vehicle, beyond the ordinary and beyond the holy) and (若見性者號之為佛) (if one sees nature he is titled a Buddha) (B14n0082). Other recorded answers to the question do not define at all: asked (如何是見性明心之旨), a master answers (快煎茶來)，(與雷居士喫) (quick — brew tea for layman Lei; J39nB466). The Jingde-era lamp record preserves another direct definition in the exchange of Tiantai Yunju Zhi: 'one has never seen; when the place and form of seeing cannot be obtained, the one able to see and what is seen are both cut off; this is called seeing nature' (未嘗見。求見處體相不可得。能所俱絕。名為見性). Parallel recensions carry the same exchange in the Chan Gate Treasury Record (禪門寶藏錄), the Combined Essentials of the Five Lamps (聯燈會要), and later lamp compilations.
Senses.Note: Very widely attested: (見性) has 2,148 occurrences across 304 allowlist texts. The exact unpunctuated sequence (直指人心見性成佛) appears 63 times in 29 texts, while (直指人心) alone has 624 hits in 216 texts. Collocation counts: (見性成佛) 684 hits/213 texts, (明心見性) 146/84, (識心見性) 39/24, (見性是佛) 37/34. Curated occurrences span the slogan, the (見性是佛) case, Zhaozhou, Xuefeng's three blows to the monk's moon/sun grading, and Guizong's (錯用心) line.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歸宗和尚道：『參學人，切忌錯用心。悟明見性，是錯用心；成佛作祖，是錯用心；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guizong: even (悟明見性) ('awakening and seeing nature') is (錯用心) ('misusing the mind').

Occurrences.Kwic: 未嘗見。求見處體相不可得。能所俱絕。名為見性。

AlternateTargets: see the nature and become a Buddha
Senses.Explanation: (見) 'see' + (性) 'nature' + (成佛) 'become Buddha': the claim that awakening is seeing one's own (Buddha-)nature, and that in that seeing one becomes Buddha. It is the culminating clause of the four-phrase slogan by which the Chan school defines itself — (教外別傳)，(不立文字)，(直指人心)，(見性成佛) ('a separate transmission outside the teachings; not setting up words; pointing straight at the human mind; seeing [one's] nature and becoming Buddha') — and appears as the Southern school's slogan, the teaching Yaoshan reports hearing of ('甞聞南方直指人心。見性成佛。實未明了'). When a master glosses it, the gloss is equational: the venerable of Yunju answers (繼宗)'s question 'what does (見性成佛) mean?' with (性即佛)。(佛即性)。(故曰見性成佛) ('the nature is just Buddha, Buddha is just the nature; therefore it is called seeing-nature-becoming-Buddha'). One hall-discourse makes it the whole of the matter — (祖師西來只道見性成佛)。(其餘所說不及此說) ('the Patriarch came from the West only to say see-nature-become-Buddha; nothing else said measures up'). A second in-corpus self-definition appears in (續燈正統): (天奇本瑞), opening an instruction with (祖師西來)，(不立文字)，(直指人心)，(見性成佛)，(更無別法) ('…there is no other teaching'), states (須知所謂見性成佛者)，(見性不是見他人之性)，(成佛不是成他人之佛)，(決定是汝諸人本有之性) ('know that in what is called seeing-the-nature-becoming-Buddha, the seeing of the nature is not seeing someone else's nature, and the becoming Buddha is not becoming someone else's Buddha: it is decidedly the nature you all inherently have'), adding (人人本具)，(箇箇不無) ('each person inherently equipped with it, not one without it'). (遠菴僼禪師語錄) answers the question form directly: (何謂直指人心)、(見性成佛者)？(不教人千劫學威儀)、(萬劫修相好)，(只要人於善知識一言一句下)，(頓脫無始結使纏縛) ('what is meant by pointing straight at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha? It does not have people study deportment for a thousand kalpas or refine the marks for ten thousand kalpas; it only wants a person, at one word or phrase from a good teacher, to suddenly cast off the beginningless bonds and fetters'). Render it literally as 'see [one's] nature, become Buddha'. It CONTAINS (見性) ('seeing nature', its own entry): (見性成佛) is (見性) with its consequence (成佛) stated — keep the two distinct but cross-referenced.
Senses.Note: Very widely attested (approximately 684 raw occurrences across 213 allowlist texts, independent strict count; an earlier tally of 602/206 did not reproduce); the four-clause (直指人心見性成佛) formula alone is pervasive. Uniform meaning across the corpus — a shared banner/topic, not a master-specific coinage — so one corpus-wide sense is honest. Curated witnesses span three independent texts: (六祖大師法寶壇經) (T48n2008, Huineng), (五燈會元) (X80n1565, the Yunju gloss and the Yaoshan report), and (景德傳燈錄) (T51n2076). Per the nested-term rule (§5b): (見性成佛) CONTAINS the standalone entry (見性); both kept as separate entries and cross-referenced in RelatedTerms, not merged. Slogan-family counts (Zen-scoped): the contiguous (直指人心見性成佛) 63x/29 texts; companions (直指人心) 624x/216, (教外別傳) 640x/211, (不立文字) 435x/188; the contained (見性) 2,148x/304. The (天奇本瑞) self-definition: X84n1583 (續燈正統) ed="X" lb 0571a06; the (遠菴僼) answer: J37nB386 lb 0403c22.

AlternateTargets: what one sees, hears, senses, and knows
Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Chan texts warn against constructing an additional understanding from them or treating some separate entity as standing behind them. The same functions can be described as the cause of birth and death and, without changing the wording, as the root of release. Other passages say that they neither obstruct complete command nor bind a person in themselves. Translate the four actions directly; do not replace them with an imported technical noun such as 'awareness.'
Senses.Note: The corpus has 787 matches in 162 files. Sixty-six matches in forty-six files occur in constructions about leaving or being apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Five passages in five files use the explicit nominal form 'as for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,' and three in three use 'the so-called seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.' The corrective passages show that the compound names the four functions themselves, not a separate faculty.

Senses.PreferredTarget: having sought the mind, I could not find it
AlternateTargets: I searched for the mind and could not find it at all
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘having sought the mind, it was altogether unobtainable.’ The phrase occurs 90 times in 48 allowlisted texts and belongs to the Bodhidharma–Huike exchange. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma says, ‘bring the mind and I will set it at ease’; Huike answers with this phrase; Bodhidharma replies, ‘I have finished setting your mind at ease.’ Later masters quote the line, ask why Huike answered only this rather than offering other responses, contrast it with claims by later students to say the same words, and press its grammar: if it is altogether unobtainable, ‘what is there to regulate?’ The corpus thereby uses Huike's sentence as a repeatedly examined lineage case, not as a general dictionary proposition about mind.
Senses.Note: The deviation is the promotion of one first-person reply into the fixed hinge of the lineage's ‘setting the mind at ease’ case. Huike is a lineage patriarch and remains on the master roster; this entry defines his quoted words, not the person. No second thing appears in shortened quotations.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'look through' or 'look and break through.' The compound occurs 509 times in 154 allowed texts. It is used transitively of a saying, case, person, condition, or distinction; in passive clauses someone or something is 'seen through.' Hongzhi asks, 'What is the eye with which you can see through it?' (作麼生是儞覷得破底眼). A later address sets out a repeated contrast: 'if you cannot see through it, stand steadily on it, or tread it; if you can see through it, stand steadily on it, and tread it' (若覷不破、立不穩、踏不著；若覷得破，立得穩、踏得著). Comments on earlier cases say that someone saw through Lingyun and Mahakasyapa, that Tianning saw through Dahui, or that an interlocutor should see through an action before it occurs. The passive form appears in a warning about being seen through by someone at a later time (他時異日被人覷破). The fuller form 'be able to see through' (覷得破) occurs 40 times in 25 texts, while the emphatic 'with one look, see through' (一覷覷破) occurs 19 times in 17. The texts do not supply a separate technical definition beyond these observable objects, contrasts, questions, and active/passive constructions.
Senses.Note: The two hits for 'one who sees through this' (覷破者) use the final graph as the pronoun 'this,' not as a definition formula. They were therefore not treated as self-definitions. The corpus range is grammatical rather than polysemous: the same verb occurs with people, words, cases, and named distinctions as its object.
