Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'look at mind' or 'inspect mind.' The compound occurs 474 times in 84 allowed texts, but 257 hits are concentrated in the Record of the Source-Mirror. The corpus does not give it one uniform set of predicates. In the Daoxin-Niutou Farong encounter, Farong answers 'inspecting mind' when asked what he is doing; Daoxin asks, 'Who is doing the inspecting, and what thing is mind?' (觀是何人，心是何物), and Farong gives no answer. The Treatise on Breaking Appearances says, 'Only inspecting mind, this one thing, gathers all things' (唯觀心一法，總攝諸法), then asks, 'How does inspecting mind count as understanding?' (云何觀心稱之為了). Its reply distinguishes a clean mind and a soiled mind and later says, 'Inspecting mind in this way may be called understanding' (如是觀心可名為了). The Record of the Source-Mirror quotes a different direct formula: 'Inspect mind as no mind; things do not dwell on things; my mind is itself empty; fault and fortune have no owner—this is called correct inspection' (觀心無心，法不住法，我心自空，罪福無主，即是無心無數，名為正觀). Other Chan witnesses criticize particular deployments. An imperial anthology says that making silence final and 'then devoting oneself to quietly inspecting mind' is 'escaping a pit and falling into a ditch' (便務靜觀心，又所謂逃坑落塹), while its verses say, 'closing the eyes, vainly seek seeing; inspecting mind, mistakenly seek penetration' (閉目妄求見，觀心誤覓通) and 'holding mind and inspecting mind divide guest and host' (持心觀心紛主客). Huineng separately calls 'dwelling on mind and observing quiet' sickness rather than Chan (住心觀靜，是病非禪), and Linji lists dwelling on mind, looking at quiet, looking outward, clarifying inward, and congealing mind and entering settledness as contrivances. These are text-drawn criticisms of named actions; they do not supply a single imported category for the headword.
Senses.Note: The record supports the literal verbal target 'inspect mind,' followed by speaker-specific predicates and objections. The two dominant treatise witnesses are presented as claims made by those texts; their concentration of hits does not erase the independent Chan encounter and criticism witnesses. Title and table-of-contents hits were excluded.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, untie or release, and regulation or restriction. The compound occurs 1,683 times in 241 allowlisted texts and names the formal ending of a bounded communal period. It is the corpus's regular counterpart to beginning the restriction. Records use it as a calendar label and in discourse headings: 153 instances in 43 texts say that a discourse was delivered at release, and nine instances in seven texts mark a small talk. The dates depend on the seasonal period. One record calls the fifteenth day of the first month the winter release after the restriction began on the fifteenth day of the tenth month; another names the fifteenth day of the seventh month as release after an opening on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. Direct answers use the event's own language: 'the monastery gate is wide open,' 'tighten your sandals,' and a release-day discourse says that the brothers go east and west.
Senses.Note: The graph pair can also be used by speakers for an asserted personal release, but those later extensions retain the explicit contrast with binding the restriction. The stable lexicographic center is the dated communal event. The headword occurs in 28 direct binding/release pairings across 22 texts, 23 'release day' strings in 16 texts, and 50 'today release' strings in 36 texts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to understand and grasp. In Chan records the word commonly names understanding made from discriminations, words, or received knowledge rather than a neutral success at understanding. Yuanwu reports that many people make an emotionally conditioned construction of a public case and then explain Huichao's answer as simply meaning that Huichao himself is buddha. A record warns that seeking words and pursuing phrases in order to find such understanding produces proliferating differences and verbal facility. Huangbo's record says that construing the way as seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing leaves one far from it. The observable Chan bend is therefore critical: the ordinary verb 'understand' repeatedly labels the very explanatory grasp that masters reject. The term can still occur neutrally in a question such as 'how should this be understood'; this is the same act under different appraisal, not a different referent or word class.
Senses.Note: Wave-plan frequency: 539. Searches covered emotionally conditioned construction, word-and-phrase seeking, knowledge-based understanding, neutral interrogative use, and the related terms construing the words (話會) and acquired understanding (知解). One verbal referent fits all uses; positive and negative appraisals are readings, not senses. Unlike construing the words (話會), forming an understanding (解會) need not keep a particular saying in view.

Occurrences.Kwic: 尋言逐句，求覓解會，千差萬別，廣設問難
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon links pursuing words and phrases for understanding with multiplying distinctions and questions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若作見聞覺知解會。與道懸殊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huangbo says that construing the way as seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing leaves one far from it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to touch or meet the eye; in context, whatever meets the eye. The term occurs 653 times in 207 allowlisted texts. It forms public questions—'what is the affair that meets the eye?' and 'what is awakening that meets the eye?'—to which Xuefeng answers with a question, 'what is it?', with 'heavens!', by lifting the whisk, or by pointing out a bare pillar. Yunmen's statement 'even if whatever meets the eye is unobstructed' becomes a repeatedly quoted and tested formula. One later master raises a whisk and says that calling it a whisk leaves obstruction in what meets the eye, while not calling it a whisk does too. Linji's record says 'whatever meets the eye is it,' and immediately supplies its own stated obstruction: feelings arise, knowledge separates, and thought changes the object. The ordinary visual phrase is thus heavily loaded as interview and teaching-seat vocabulary.
Senses.Note: Noun-like English and verbal Chinese environments refer to the same visual field, not different things. 'Awakening that meets the eye' is a linked compound, not the definition of every occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是觸目事？師云：是什麼？問：如何是句外事？師云：問，問。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuefeng answers the direct question about the affair meeting the eye with 'what is it?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是觸目菩提？師云：好箇露柱。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuefeng answers the question about awakening meeting the eye with the bare pillar.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master raises the whisk and states that both naming and not naming it leave obstruction in what meets the eye.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。舉。雲門示眾。直得觸目無滯。達得名身句身。一切法空。山河大地是名。名亦不可得。

AlternateTargets: what meets the eye is awakening
Senses.Explanation: The graphs say “meet or strike the eye” and “awakening”: “awakening wherever the eye meets.” The exact question “What is awakening wherever the eye meets?” accounts for 69 of the headword’s 127 occurrences. The answers and follow-up actions vary. When Shishuang Qingzhu asks Daowu, Daowu calls a novice, tells him to add water to the clean-water jar, later asks Shishuang what he had just asked, and leaves as Shishuang begins to repeat it; the narrative then says Shishuang woke up. Another exchange answers, “All things constantly abide”; when asked what that means, the teacher answers with the headword again. Elsewhere the answer is “the buddha hall before you,” a teacher kicks a dog so that it runs off making a sound, or Xuansha says, “Before a dead monk is precisely awakening wherever the eye meets.” Linquan’s later comment on the Daowu case says that it has “no empty gap.” The records preserve these named exchanges and different predicates; this entry gives no single explanation in place of their different answers.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 127 times in 58 allowlisted texts. The direct question occurs 69 times in 31 texts, while Xuansha’s line about the dead monk occurs 8 times in 8. The related saying “what meets the eye is the Way” occurs 7 times in 7 texts. The case witnesses must not be collapsed: Daowu’s novice-and-water-jar exchange, the reciprocal “all things constantly abide” answer, the buddha-hall answer, the kicked-dog action, and Xuansha’s dead-monk statement are distinct recorded deployments.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師後參道吾問。如何是觸目菩提。道吾喚沙彌。沙彌應諾。吾曰。添淨缾水著。吾却問師。汝適來問什麼。師乃舉前問道吾便起去。師從此惺覺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, under Daowu Yuanzhi’s lineage heirs: Shishuang asks Daowu the headword question. Occurrences.Kwic: 有人問：「如何是觸目菩提？」師答曰：「一切法常住。」「如何是一切法常住？」師曰：「觸目菩提。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Patriarchs’ Hall Collection: “What is awakening wherever the eye meets?”—“All things constantly abide.” Asked what that means, the teacher answers, “Awakening wherever the eye meets.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是觸目菩提。師曰。面前佛殿。

Occurrences.Kwic: 有僧問如何是觸目菩提。師踢狗子作聲走。僧無對。師曰。小狗子不消一踢。

Occurrences.Kwic: 以此觀來，觸目菩提無空缺處，更嫌何處不分明？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linquan’s comment on the Daowu and Shishuang case: “Viewed from this, awakening wherever the eye meets has no empty gap; what further place could be faulted as unclear?”

AlternateTargets: greatly awakened upon hearing the words
Senses.Explanation: A narrative formula: “at the words” or “under the words” (言下) plus “greatly awakened” (大悟). It occurs 542 times in 160 allowlisted texts and marks the reported moment immediately following a spoken exchange. The words vary from case to case. Daoxin is reported greatly awakened after Sengcan asks, “Who binds you?” and then, “Why seek release?”; Damei Fachang after Mazu says, “Mind itself is buddha” (即心是佛); Wuxie Lingmo after Shitou says, “From birth to death it is only this; why turn your head and move your brain?” (從生至死祇是者個，回頭轉腦作麼); Yanyang after Zhaozhou says, “If you cannot put it down, carry it away” (放不下，擔取去); and Huanglong Huinan after Ciming asks, “Do you take that as scolding?” (你作罵會那). What follows the formula also varies: the records may mention a bow, a verse, a reply, breaking a staff, residence with a teacher, or later teaching activity. The formula reports the event and its position after speech; it does not itself explain what was awakened to.
Senses.Note: Related narrative formulas show the same productive construction: “awakened at the words” (言下契悟), 41 hits in 28 texts; “suddenly awakened at the words” (言下頓悟), 65 in 40; “at the words, suddenly greatly awakened” (言下豁然大悟), 10 in 9; “thoroughly penetrated at the words” (言下大徹), 34 in 31; and “had an insight at the words” (言下有省), 215 in 89. These are related formulas, not alternate spellings of the four-character headword.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, before words or ahead of speech. The term occurs 338 times in 155 allowlisted texts. Its most visible Chan deployment is the paired formula 'discern before the words' and 'accord after the phrase.' Multiple records immediately refuse both positions: discerning before the words fails one's whole life, while according after the phrase departs from the body of the Way; Yuanwu similarly quotes discernment before words as still confined by a shell. The corpus also uses the phrase nominally for 'the matter before the words' and in a preface says the mind seal may be discerned before words. These are grammatical forms of the same temporal-relational phrase. They show a stock Chan axis for examining an answer's relation to spoken words, not a named realm or separate object.
Senses.Note: One relational sense. Nominal 'the matter before words,' adverbial 'discern before words,' and contrast with 'after the phrase' do not denote different things. The entry reports the corpus's paired verdicts without deciding what lies before speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 言前薦得，孤負平生。句後投機，全乖道體。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat statement gives the recurring before-words/after-phrase pair and rejects both.

Occurrences.Kwic: 設使言前薦得。猶是滯殼迷封。縱饒句下精通。未免觸塗狂見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes discernment before words and says it remains confined by a shell.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp narrative uses the nominal expression 'the matter before the words.'

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record preface says the mind seal may be discerned before words.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the road of language is cut off
AlternateTargets: the course of words is severed
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "the road" or "course" (道) of "language and words" (言語) is "cut off" (斷): "the road of language is cut off," attested 171 times in 71 allowlisted texts. It is most often paired with "the place of mental activity is extinguished" (心行處滅, 128 occurrences); the unpunctuated full pair occurs 12 times and the punctuated pair 17 times. The Trust in Mind verse places it in "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present" (信心不二，不二信心，言語道斷，非去來今). A lamp record gives an explicit correction: closing the eyes and seeing nothing in the dark is not what is called "the road of language is cut off" (不是閉目藏睛、暗覩無所見喚作言語道斷). A later address first quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished," then answers, "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished" (亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅). Hongzhi asks directly, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?" (言語道斷心行處滅，又作麼生). The entry reports the fixed phrase, its paired formula, its correction, and its counter-formulation without turning silence or shut eyes into its definition.
Senses.Note: Dahui quotes a correspondent who says that looking at a saying leaves "the road of language cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished, with no words to say and no principle to advance" (看此話，直得言語道斷心行處滅，無言可說，無理可伸); the following context is Dahui's reply to that report, so the quoted claim is not assigned to him. The exact collocation "close the eyes and hide the pupils" (閉目藏睛) occurs 29 times, but the lamp record explicitly rejects it as the definition here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可以智知，不可以識識，言語道斷，心行處滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address in Continued Essential Sayings of Ancient Worthies quotes: "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished."

Occurrences.Kwic: 亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same address immediately supplies its counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished."

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇如言語道斷心行處滅。又作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Hongzhi Zhengjue's record: "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 看此話。直得言語道斷心行處滅。無言可說。無理可伸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record quotes a correspondent: "looking at this saying, directly the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished; there are no words to say and no principle to advance." MasterName is null because these are the correspondent's words, not Dahui's.

Occurrences.Kwic: 信心不二。不二信心。言語道斷。非去來今。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of Five Lamps quotes the Trust in Mind verse in Sengcan's section: "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present." This is quoted verse, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Appraisal-commentary on old cases or verses, including the activity, resulting text, and collections of that commentary. The term occurs 103 times in 28 allowlisted texts. Title constructions name Yuanwu appraising Xuedou's verses, Wansong appraising Tiantong's verses, and Linquan appraising verses associated with Touzi and Danxia. A preface gives the documentary sequence: “from recorded encounters, verses on old cases were made; from verses on old cases, appraisal-commentary collections were made” (由機緣而頌古作，由頌古而評唱集). A later poem heading speaks of “burning Wansong's appraisal-commentary on public cases” (焚萬松評唱公案), treating the text as a physical work. Chan makes appraisal-commentary a named layer of case literature beside verses on old cases and shorter attached comments. Commenting and the commentary produced are one commentarial event/product family, not different lexical referents.
Senses.Note: The former activity/product targets described the same appraisal-commentary and could not be distinguished as separate referents from the targets alone. Keep the genre distinct from an attached comment (著語), a substitute response (代語), laying down a response (下語), a verse on an old case (頌古), and picking up an old case (拈古).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師住澧州夾山靈泉禪院評唱雪竇顯和尚頌古語要
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record's opening heading: "the master, residing at Jiashan Lingquan Chan Cloister in Lizhou, appraised and commented on the essentials of Master Xuedou Xian's verses on old cases."

Occurrences.Kwic: 萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Repeated title formula of the Book of Serenity: "The Congrong Cloister Record of Old Man Wansong's appraisal and commentary on Master Tiantong Jue's verses on old cases." It names both Wansong and Tiantong, so the title occurrence is left unlinked.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Title of the Empty Hall Collection: "Old Man Linquan's appraisal and commentary on Master Danxia Chun's verses on old cases."

Occurrences.Kwic: 由機緣而頌古作，由頌古而評唱集
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A preface describes the sequence: “from recorded encounters, verses on old cases were made; from verses on old cases, appraisal-commentary collections were made.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 焚萬松評唱公案
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A poem heading in Guxue's record reads “burning Wansong's appraisal-commentary on public cases.” It is retained as an attested critical deployment, not as approval of the action.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a slip of speech (being caught out / defeated in a dialogue by one's own words)
AlternateTargets: a slip of the tongue that loses the exchange
Senses.Explanation: Literally 'speech-fall' (話 speech + 墮 to fall/drop). Its dominant attested form is a verdict spoken in dialogue -- (話墮也) (164 hits / 58 allowlist files), with second-person forms (汝話墮) (16 / 7), (你話墮) (9 / 5), (爾話墮) (2 / 1), the variant (話墮了也) (32 / 22), and the fixed reply (是汝話墮也) (one exchange, following 如何是好手人, carried in 5 witness files). The one so judged presses back with (什麼處是話墮)/(話墮處) (7 hits / 6 files); the recorded answers to that question are Muzhou's (擔枷過狀萬里崖州自領出去) and Yunmen's (七棒對十三). The word is not reserved to the master's side: monks and commentators say it of a master (和尚話墮也, 6 hits / 6 files -- e.g. X69n1343, where a master raises Yunmen's 話墮也 verdict, asks 爾見什麼處是話墮處, and the monk answers 和尚話墮也); masters say it of themselves (山僧話墮, 2 files; 老僧話墮也。明眼者試辨看, J27nB189), of both parties at once (師曰。彼此話墮, T51n2076), of absent masters (恁麼則趙州話墮。僧便出。師曰：恁麼則山僧話墮, X82n1571; 法眼和尚話墮也不知, X79n1559), and of Bodhidharma (老胡九年話墮。可惜當時放過 -- in Dahui's own record T47n1998A, and 9 hits / 9 files counting retellings); in one exchange the master who declares (爾話墮也) adds (我話亦墮汝作麼生) (one case, 5 witness files). The corpus contains no passage defining the term (no 謂之話墮, 話墮者, or 名為話墮 anywhere in the allowlist); when asked where the slip lies, the masters answer as quoted above. The texts leave (話墮) without gloss, and so does this entry.
Senses.Note: 577 hits across 172 files of the 462-file allowlist (XML tags/notes/rdg stripped, whitespace collapsed, punctuation retained -- all counts in this entry use this convention). The reciprocal uses are two separate cases: (我話亦墮) (the curated Baozi occurrence; one exchange carried in 5 witness files T51n2076, X79n1557, X80n1565, X80n1568, X81n1571) and (彼此話墮) (T51n2076 0401c02: 師問僧。汝念什麼經。曰法華經。師曰。彼此話墮). Curated occurrences span (語錄), (廣錄), (燈錄) and (會元).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云你為什麼話墮進云什麼處是話墮處師云擔枷過狀萬里崖州自領出去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Muzhou: (你為什麼話墮) ('why have you slipped?') -- monk: (什麼處是話墮處) ('where is the slip?') -- Muzhou: (擔枷過狀萬里崖州自領出去) ('shoulder the cangue and file your own complaint; take yourself off the ten thousand li to Yazhou').

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。話墮也。進云。什麼處是話墮。師云。七棒對十三。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yunmen's own Extensive Record: the verdict (話墮也), the monk's (什麼處是話墮) ('where is the slip?'), and the recorded answer (七棒對十三) ('seven blows against thirteen').

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。爾話墮也。又曰。我話亦墮汝作麼生。僧無對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baozi Xiaowu (婺州金鱗報恩院寶資曉悟大師; not in the roster). The master declares (爾話墮也), then adds (我話亦墮汝作麼生) ('my speech has fallen too -- what do you make of it?'); the monk had no reply (僧無對).

Occurrences.Kwic: 老胡九年話墮。可惜當時放過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says it of Bodhidharma (老胡, 'the old foreigner') and his nine years facing the wall: 'the old foreigner's nine years -- a speech-fall; a pity it was let pass at the time.' Also in Dahui's own record (老胡九年話墮。可惜當時放過, T47n1998A); 9 hits / 9 files counting retellings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 和尚因甚麼如此。師曰。汝話墮也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verdict form: the monk asks (和尚因甚麼如此) ('why are you like this?'), and Guichen replies (汝話墮也).

AlternateTargets: to make an interpretation of the saying
to understand it as talk about something
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to understand or construe speech. In Chan records it repeatedly names an auditor's reduction of a reply or case to an explanatory category. Yuanwu reports that people construe Dongshan's 'three pounds of hemp' as an answer based on his work weighing hemp; Dahui says blind fellows construe Zhaozhou's instruction as merely 'wash the bowl'; and Fayan says that for twenty years he construed Jiashan's line only as talk about scenery. The records also expose competing constructions: a collection says people construed Vimalakirti's response as silence, a pause, remaining seated, or not answering, but none reached it. A master can therefore warn, after answering 'what is buddha?', 'do not construe it as answer-buddha talk.' Elsewhere the word is itself put under interview pressure: 'without relying on the three-inch tongue, try to construe it.' The Chan-specific bend is observable and critical: construing the words (話會) is not neutral comprehension but the named act of fitting a live saying into talk about a subject. The entry does not decide what an unexplained saying ultimately means.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 745 hits in 224 texts. Definition-formula searches and high-frequency files were reviewed; no distinct referent or word class emerged. Family check: understanding a saying (解會) and intellectual understanding (知解) concern grasping more broadly, while construing the words (話會) specifically keeps the spoken saying or words in view. The answer-buddha, scenery, bowl-washing, competing-construction, and no-tongue deployments are separately anchored.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是佛。師曰。卭州多出九節杖。曰謝師指示。師曰。且莫作答佛話會却。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After answering 'what is buddha?' with 'Qiongzhou produces many nine-jointed staffs,' the master warns: 'do not construe it as answer-buddha talk.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 人多作話會道。洞山是時在庫下。秤麻。有僧問。所以如此答。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu reports the common construction that Dongshan answered 'three pounds of hemp' because he was weighing hemp in the storehouse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而今諸方有一種瞎漢。往往盡作洗鉢盂話會了。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says blind fellows commonly make Zhaozhou's case merely a 'wash-the-bowl' construction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後來法眼云我二十年秪作境話會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fayan says, 'for twenty years I construed it only as talk about scenery.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 者一轉語，叢林話會不少，有道默然，有道良久，有道據坐，有道不對，要且摸索不著
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The collection inventories several constructions of one turning phrase—silence, a pause, remaining seated, or not answering—and says they still do not reach it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 到這裏不假三寸試話會看。不假耳試釆聽看。不假眼試辯白看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Interview challenge: 'here, without relying on the three-inch tongue, try to construe it; without ears, try to listen; without eyes, try to distinguish.'

Senses.PreferredTarget: the word or saying raised for investigation
Senses.Explanation: The first graph means speech or a saying (話); the second can mark a head or end and also serves as a noun-forming suffix (頭). In the passages grouped here, the compound names a word, question, or saying that someone is explicitly told to look at, raise, take up, remember, recite, or investigate. Dahui Zonggao says to 'look at a saying' (看箇話頭) and immediately supplies Zhaozhou's question, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' (狗子還有佛性也無), answered 'no' (無). The corpus likewise supplies Zhaozhou's cypress tree in the courtyard, Yunmen's dry shit-stick, and other named exchanges after directions to look at a saying. Later records define the term directly. Hanyue Fazang says, 'What is called a saying is one matter or one thing before the eyes' (所謂話頭者，即目前一事一法也), and elsewhere says that this one question gathers all spoken and unspoken words of the worldly and world-transcending, therefore it is called the saying (只者一問，便收盡世出世間一切有言無言等語，故謂之話頭). Ruibai Mingxue says that what is spoken of as the saying is one's own native scenery, distinctly and singly bright, not interrupted by a hair's breadth (所言話頭者，即自己本地風光，歷歷孤明，不可絲毫間斷). A later retrospective reports that only in the Song did talk of looking at sayings and exerting effort arise (直至宋朝，始有看話頭、作工夫之說), and says people were told to take up a saying and look at what principle it was. The Discourse on Forging in the Chan Gate criticizes guarding a dead saying without raising doubt (死守話頭，不起疑情). Current allowlist counts show the range: the headword as 'saying' (話頭), 2,575 hits in 297 texts; 'investigate a saying' (參話頭), 187 in 76; 'look at a saying' (看話頭), 118 in 46; 'one saying' (一句話頭), 136 in 30; 'one's originally investigated saying' (本參話頭), 89 in 50; 'raise a saying' (舉話頭), 35 in 24; 'take up a saying' (提話頭), 32 in 24; 'the saying consisting of the word no' (無字話頭), 14 in 12; and 'dead saying' (死話頭), 40 in 33.
Senses.Note: This is a word or saying in the Chinese record, not the name of a separate object, exercise, mantra, or special category. The sense is corpus-wide even though Dahui is a prominent early source: later masters define and deploy it independently, so historical prominence does not justify a master-specific SenseKey. Hanyue also records the comparison, 'In ancestral-teacher Chan it is called the saying; among Confucians it is called investigating things' (在祖師禪謂之話頭，在儒家謂之格物). Tiemei's record asks separately about the head, tail, and waist of a saying (話頭、話尾、話腰). The corpus has only two hits for 'saying-tail' (話尾) and one for 'saying-waist' (話腰), so those forms are recorded as wordplay rather than general definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只就動止處。看箇話頭。便是釋迦老子達磨大師出來也。只是這箇。僧問趙州。狗子還有佛性也無。州云無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui’s own record. He says to “look at a saying” and immediately gives Zhaozhou’s dog question and the answer “no.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 單單提起箇無義味話頭，自最初一日立定脚頭，不得分毫移動，密密與之做向前去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben’s Miscellaneous Records, in his address to the assembly at Shunxin Hermitage. He tells the assembly to take up a saying “without the flavor of meaning” and continue with it from the first day.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂話頭者，即目前一事一法也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hanyue Fazang’s own Extended Record. This is an explicit definition: “What is called a saying is one matter or one thing before the eyes.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 只者一問，便收盡世出世間一切有言無言等語，故謂之話頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hanyue’s second explicit definition: “This one question gathers all spoken and unspoken words of the worldly and world-transcending; therefore it is called the saying.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 在祖師禪謂之話頭，在儒家謂之格物。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hanyue draws the comparison himself: “In ancestral-teacher Chan it is called the saying; among Confucians it is called investigating things.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 所言話頭者，即自己本地風光，歷歷孤明，不可絲毫間斷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ruibai Mingxue’s own record. The sentence explicitly begins “What is spoken of as the saying…” and gives Ruibai’s definition; the entry reports it as his wording rather than a universal gloss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直至宋朝，始有看話頭、作工夫之說。當時只教人提起箇話頭，看是什麼道理？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Weilin Daopei’s Return to the Mountain gives this later historical retrospective: only in the Song did talk of “looking at the saying” and “doing the work” arise; people were told to take up a saying and look at its principle.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而世有教人死守話頭，不起疑情者，此參禪大病也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Discourse on Forging in the Chan Gate supplies a text-drawn negative contrast: teaching people to guard a dead saying without raising doubt is called a major illness in investigating Chan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「如何是話頭？」師云：「腳上生腳。」「如何是話尾？」師云：「如牛無角。」「如何是話腰？」師云：「你且行路。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Recorded Sayings of Master Tiemei Sanbazhang preserves an interview asking separately, “What is saying-head?”, “What is saying-tail?”, and “What is saying-waist?” The three answers are retained as an attested wordplay sequence without assigning them a further gloss.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a saying, remark, or turn in an exchange
Senses.Explanation: In encounter records, the same word denotes words spoken in an exchange: a saying, a remark, or the turn being carried by the speakers. Dongshan Liangjie appraises one as “a fine saying; it only lacks a follow-up line” (好箇話頭，只欠進語). Yunmen Xianqin speaks after a long silence and calls it “a fine saying” (好箇話頭), adding that it must not be recited wrongly elsewhere. Yunmen Wenyan asks for “my saying” to be returned (還我話頭來). In the “three pounds of hemp” exchange, Fuyan Liangya says that Dongshan Shouchu supposed Liangya did not understand “his saying” (他這話頭), referring to Dongshan’s answer. Recurrent forms confirm the deployment: “return my saying” (還我話頭來), 78 hits in 44 texts; “does not even recognize the saying” (話頭也不識), 185 hits in 87 texts; “remember the saying” (記得話頭), 68 hits in 61 texts; and “a fine saying” (好箇話頭), 24 hits in 21 texts. The records do not assign one further gloss to all of these conversational uses.
Senses.Note: This sense covers a unit within recorded speech rather than a specified word, question, or saying that someone is told to investigate. It remains lexically connected to the first sense; the split records the distinct constructions and deployments rather than positing two unrelated words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山，山云：好箇話頭，只欠進語。曹云：進甚麼語？洞云：何不問？為甚麼不道？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan calls the remark “a fine saying” and says it lacks only a follow-up line. The passage then records the requested follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。一口吞盡時如何。師曰。我在你肚裏。曰。和尚為甚麼在學人肚裏。師曰。還我話頭來。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium, in Yunmen Wenyan’s section. In a direct exchange, Yunmen answers the follow-up with “Return my saying to me.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。良久曰。好箇話頭。若到諸方。不得錯舉。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium, in Yunmen Xianqin’s section. After a long silence, Xianqin says, “A fine saying; if you reach other places, do not recite it wrongly,” and steps down. Xianqin lacks a verified project-roster spelling, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧出問。如何是佛。山答曰。麻三斤。參罷。山至寮謂師曰。我今日答這僧話。得麼。曰。恰值某淨髮。山曰。你元來作這去就。拂袖便出。師曰。這老漢將謂我明他這話頭不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium, in Fuyan Liangya’s section. Dongshan Shouchu answers “three pounds of hemp”; Liangya later calls that answer “his saying.” Two speakers are present and Liangya lacks a verified project-roster spelling, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Master Zhigong is the pre-Zen figure whom Chan records quote, identify with a direct answer, and place in exchanges at Emperor Wu's court. His name occurs 494 times in 133 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is buddha?" a master answers, "Master Zhigong" (誌公和尚); when challenged, he says, "Zhigong is not an idle monk" (誌公不是閑和尚). In the Fu Dashi case, Fu mounts the seat, strikes the desk once, and descends; Zhigong asks Emperor Wu whether he understands, then says, "the great man has finished lecturing the scripture" (大士講經竟). Later masters repeatedly quote and criticize that verdict. His sayings are also treated as named textual material: the Twelve-Hour Song, Fourteen Sections, and Great-Vehicle Praises. Zen therefore deploys Zhigong as a named answer to "what is buddha?," court interlocutor and adjudicator of Fu Dashi's action, and quoted author.
Senses.Note: One person sense. Zhigong (誌公), Master Zhigong (誌公和尚), and Baozhi (寶誌公) name the same figure in this corpus. Titles of works attributed to him are named works, not a second sense of the bare personal name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是佛。師曰。誌公和尚。曰。學人問佛。何故答誌公和尚。師曰。誌公不是閑和尚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master answers “what is buddha?” with Zhigong and defends the answer by saying Zhigong is not an idle monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 梁武帝請講金剛經，士纔陞座，以尺揮按一下，便下座，帝愕然。誌公曰：陛下會麼？帝曰：不會。誌公曰：大士講經竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Fu Dashi case records Zhigong questioning Emperor Wu and declaring the lecture finished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 却被誌公云陛下還會麼。帝云。不會。誌公云。大士講經竟也。是一人作頭。一人作尾。誌公恁麼道。還夢見傅大士麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff commentary quotes Zhigong's verdict, calls the pair head and tail, and questions whether Zhigong even dreamed of Fu Dashi.

Occurrences.Kwic: 誌公和尚大乘讚十首誌公和尚十二時頌十二首誌公和尚十四科頌
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record contents section names three groups of works attributed to Zhigong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 誌公和尚云。內外追尋覔總無。境上施為渾大有。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master quotes Zhigong's contrast between finding nothing in inner and outer search and abundant activity on objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 被誌公和尚一喝曰。大士莫作是說。別更道看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhigong shouts at Fu Dashi, rejects his first saying, and asks him to speak again.

Senses.PreferredTarget: mistake the servant for the master
AlternateTargets: take the slave for the gentleman
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “recognize the servant as the master/gentleman.” The corpus records 143 occurrences in 91 allowlisted texts. Masters use the household reversal as an adverse appraisal in public exchanges and comments. It is repeatedly coupled with “point to a deer as a horse” (指鹿為馬). One address applies both verdicts even to the old advice “seek only from yourself, do not look elsewhere” (但向己求，莫從他覓); another identifies “taking the one capable of seeing and hearing as real” (認著一箇能見能聞……執以為真) as precisely mistaking servant for master. Elsewhere a student is allowed to bow but warned, “you must not mistake the servant for the master” (不得認奴作郎), while later case commentary applies the same verdict to Deshan. The ordinary status reversal becomes a portable Chan verdict on a proposed identification; which identification receives it is supplied by each passage.
Senses.Note: The graph “gentleman/master” (郎) is rendered “master” here because the fixed contrast is household rank, not because the graph universally means a household master. The passages do not support separate senses for each object criticized.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但向己求，莫從他覓。古人與麼說話，大似認奴作郎，指鹿為馬。
祇認著一箇能見能聞、處處具足的執以為真，此正認奴作郎，顛倒知見。
禮拜一任禮拜。不得認奴作郎。
龍潭將蝦釣鯉，德山認奴作郎，兩個老漢好與三十痛棒。
若也識得，正是認奴作郎；若也不識，作麼生免得古人恁麼道？

Senses.PreferredTarget: mistake the thief for your son
AlternateTargets: take the thief as your son
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to recognize or take (認) a thief (賊) as (為) one's son (子). The records preserve the quoted formulation 'if what can infer is your mind, then you mistake the thief for your son,' and immediately state that 'in the patch-robed monk's gate this is called mistaking the servant for the master' (衲僧門下謂之認奴作郎). Chan records then use the kinship error in admonition and public interview: pursuing external objects as mind is named with the phrase; a question asks how to judge, in darkness, mistaking thief for son and son for thief and receives 'thirty blows each'; and a master raises his staff and says that calling it the master-in-charge is mistaking thief for son, while denying it is fleeing the father and seeking outside. The Zen deviation is this recurrent use as a public diagnostic accusation, linked by the texts themselves to servant/master and host language. The entry reports those applications without deciding what should count as the 'true son.'
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 132 hits in 88 texts. One metaphorical referent across applications. Related inverse and servant/master phrases are linked, not collapsed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天童略舉云：若能推底是汝心，則認賊為子。衲僧門下謂之認奴作郎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Quoted formulation followed by the text's explicit Chan recasting as mistaking servant for master.

Occurrences.Kwic: 慎勿向外逐境為心。是認賊為子。為有貪瞋癡即立戒定慧。本無煩惱焉有菩提。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Admonitory deployment naming pursuit of external objects as mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「黑夜中，認賊為子、認子為賊，作何判斷？」答：「各打三十棒。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public question pairs the phrase with its inverse; the answer assigns thirty blows to each.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉起拄杖，云：「若喚這箇作主人公，也是認賊為子、喚奴作郎；若喚這箇不是主人公，猶是捨父逃逝、向外馳求。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Teaching-seat deployment with raised staff and host, servant/master, and father imagery.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, talking (說) about food (食). Across Chan records it is a stock bodily comparison: talking about food does not fill a person, relieve hunger, or cure hunger, just as talking about drink does not cure thirst and talking about clothing does not stop cold. Masters attach the comparison to verbal fluency, borrowed understanding, and merely speaking of realization; several passages explicitly set it beside eating and drinking for oneself. One verse couples it with a painted cake: talking food never fills, and a painted cake is no remedy. A later snow-day exchange playfully reverses the inherited ranking and calls the monk talking food by the stove the most intimate of three monks, citing 'one filling forgets a hundred hungers'; this is an attested comic reversal, not the dominant sense. The Zen deviation is the term's stable use as the record's hunger test for words: the comparison remains physiological and the texts themselves state the failure.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 108 exact occurrences in 73 allowlisted files. Variants include 'talking food never fills' (說食終不飽), 'talking food cannot fill people' (說食豈能飽人), 'talking food does not cure hunger' (說食不療飢), and the paired 'talking drink and talking food' (說飲說食). The snow-day three-monks exchange is retained as a documented reversal rather than used to erase the dominant corpus comparison.

Occurrences.Kwic: 住！住！說食豈能飽人？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a retrospective biography, Huitang interrupts a visitor's sharp discussion: 'Stop! Stop! Can talking food fill a person?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 說飲說食豈能救療？直須自飲水、自喫飯，方有實効處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct paired contrast: talking drink and food cannot cure; one must drink water and eat rice oneself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 身上著衣方免寒；若徒弄舌弄脣，口裏說食終不飽。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A small talk pairs clothing on the body with relief from cold and says mere tongue-and-lip activity, talking food in the mouth, never fills.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說食不療飢。說衣不治寒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Extended Record of Zhongfeng states the parallel compactly: talking food does not cure hunger; talking clothing does not cure cold.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說食終不飽，畫餅亦安宜
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse couples talking food, which never fills, with the painted-cake image.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, request an increase or benefit; in Chan records, ask a teacher for further instruction or clarification. The expression occurs 1,659 times in 286 allowlisted texts. It is used as a verb with the person asked, in biographies of travel from one teacher to another, and after an encounter when an attendant follows a master into his quarters to ask about what was said. Speakers also announce, 'I have come especially to request further instruction.' The Blue Cliff Record gives two explicit genre descriptions. It calls the condition of a long-standing student who has seen but not penetrated, or penetrated but not clarified, 'requesting further instruction'; elsewhere it says that the opening part of a particular monk's question is called requesting further instruction, then separately calls it a question presenting understanding and a concealed-edge question. A later list of question types asks, 'What is a request-for-instruction question?' and receives the answer, 'The monastery gate is wide open.'
Senses.Note: The 23 strings ending in 'one who requests further instruction' mostly count or describe inquirers; they are not graph-formula definitions. The term can name the act, the inquirer, or a classified question. One lamp exchange explicitly contrasts obtaining something by reading texts, obtaining it by requesting instruction, and obtaining it by neither.

Occurrences.Kwic: 可謂如龍得水。似虎靠山。久參先德。有見而未透。透而未明。謂之請益。若是見得透請益。却要語句上周旋。無有凝滯。久參請益。與
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff commentary explicitly labels the state of a long-standing student who has seen but not penetrated, or penetrated but not clarified.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非目前事時如何門云。倒一說。這僧不妨是箇作家。解恁麼問。頭邊謂之請益。此是呈解問。亦謂之藏鋒問。若不是雲門。也不奈他何。雲門
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second Blue Cliff passage classifies the opening portion of a monk's question as requesting further instruction and supplies two additional question labels.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the king of elephants. Chan records repeatedly take the elephant king's bearing, stride, and backward look as publicly recognizable forms of a master's conduct. One master looks right and says, 'the bearing of the elephant king—how could it forget the backward look?' Another stock pairing says, 'in the lion's den there is no other beast; where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease.' The backward look itself enters encounter history: when a teacher mounts the seat and says 'the lion frowns; the elephant king looks back,' a monk awakens, enters the room, and presents his understanding. Later verse calls the lion's vigorous motion world-shaking and the elephant king's backward look effortless. The line can also be tested rather than merely praised: when a monk quotes 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease,' the master drives him out with blows. The Chan-specific bend is this deployment of a royal animal's gait and backward glance as teaching-seat bearing and encounter language. The records assign no further gloss to the image, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 809 hits in 242 texts. Family check covered the elephant king's stride (象王行), backward look or turn (象王回顧／回旋), the lion's roar or vigorous motion (師子吼／奮迅), the fragrant elephant (香象), and Samantabhadra's (普賢) white elephant. The primary Chan image and the Buddhist narrative animal share the same royal-elephant referent, so differing deployments were not split into readings. The narrative white-elephant witness remains listed in SourceTexts but was not curated because it adds outside-story identity rather than defining the Chan bend.

Occurrences.Kwic: 顧右邊曰：象王之儀，寧忘回顧。

Occurrences.Kwic: 遠禪師陞堂，顧視大眾云：師子嚬呻，象王回顧。師忽有省，入室陳解。

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云：「象王行處絕狐蹤。」師直打退

Occurrences.Kwic: 師子奮迅𠔃搖蕩乾坤象王回𣒀兮不費餘力
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse pairing: 'the lion's vigorous motion shakes heaven and earth; the elephant king's backward look expends no extra strength.'

Senses.Explanation: The word means a cat. Its most heavily transmitted Zen deployment is the public case in which the eastern and western halls fight over a cat: Nanquan lifts it and says, "if you can speak, I will not cut it; if you cannot speak, I will cut it" (道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻). The assembly does not answer and the record says he cuts it; when Zhaozhou returns, he puts a straw sandal on his head, and Nanquan says he would have saved the cat. Later teachers repeatedly ask about, title, verse, and comment on "Nanquan cuts the cat" (南泉斬貓). The same word also retains its ordinary animal use, including a cat's fixed attention while catching a mouse.
Senses.Note: Later Chan records explicitly debate the killing rather than silently resolving it. One late account says one hall cited a rule that "the bodhisattva precepts do not permit keeping cats, foxes, pigs, and dogs" (菩薩戒中不許長養貓狸豬狗), while the other wanted the cat to control mice; that speaker later calls the killing a sin. Another transmitted verdict answers the question about the case with only "it takes a Nanquan" (須是南泉始得). These are attested later deployments; this entry does not project their precept explanation backward as the early record's stated intent. The simplified spelling of “cat” (猫兒) is a separate searchable entry but not a different meaning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉東西兩堂爭貓兒，泉來堂內，提起貓兒云：「道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou's record gives the dispute and Nanquan's condition for sparing or cutting the cat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉斬貓兒。意旨如何。印曰。須是南泉始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later exchange asks the purport of Nanquan cutting the cat and answers, “It takes a Nanquan.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩薩戒中不許長養貓狸豬狗，放他去了罷；一個是尖酸鬼，說這兩日老鼠多，前日一釜羹被鼠糞污卻，昨日兩個老鼠走入牛角去，留他這個貓兒努起眼睛照管照管也好。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A late retelling makes one hall cite a bodhisattva-precept rule against keeping cats, foxes, pigs, and dogs, while the other wants this cat to watch the mice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 生生的把個貓兒一刀兩段。可憐，可憐！好個玉面小貓兒，七條性命無事無辜斷送在南泉手裏
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same late speaker describes the cat as cut in two and laments its innocent death; the surrounding passage calls this killing a sin.

Occurrences.Kwic: 子見貓兒捕鼠乎？目睛不瞬，四足踞地，諸根順向，首尾一直，擬無不中。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An ordinary-animal comparison describes a cat catching a mouse, eyes unblinking and body aligned.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'host within guest.' In the later systematic account of Linji's four guest-host configurations, this is the configuration named when 'the student has nostrils' (學人有鼻孔, 'the student has nostrils'). Records then raise the label as a public question and preserve different answers, including 'facing him, there is no companion.' This is one member of the fourfold set alongside host-within-host, guest-within-host, and guest-within-guest. The texts explicitly say that Linji's guest-host system differs from Caodong's, so the shared graphs must not blur the two school-specific things.
Senses.Note: Primary sense because the wave groups the term with Linji's four guest-host configurations. Family check with the four guest-host configurations (四賓主) and guest and host (賓主) preserves its explicit nostrils-definition and the stated contrast with Caodong. Split is required under §5 #0f.8: the corpus says the identically written category belongs to two different named systems.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是賓中主。穴云。入市雙瞳瞽。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Eye of Humans and Gods preserves a direct guest-within-host question with the answer 'entering the market, both pupils blind.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰如何是賓中主。師曰。對面無儔侶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public interview asks for host-within-guest; the master answers, 'facing him, there is no companion.'

Senses.Explanation: In Caodong guest-host discourse the same words name a position paired with host-within-guest's converse and with the bent-and-upright vocabulary. The Eye of Humans and Gods explicitly glosses Caodong's host-within-guest as 'function within essence' (用中體) and says this fourfold guest-host system is not the same as Linji's. In the Dongshan encounter, Dongshan asks 'what is host within guest?' and receives 'white clouds cover the green mountain'; another transmitted version assigns 'long years not leaving the house.' Later verse can say 'host within guest is precisely guest within host' and tell the hearer not to recognize a fixed pattern in reversal and accord. These are recorded formulas and answers, not an invitation to supply an interpretation beyond them.
Senses.Note: Separate school-specific referent, not a competing reading of one saying. Variant answers are retained as deployments within the Caodong positional category and are not split further.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山便問：「如何是賓中主？」云：「白雲蓋青山。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dongshan asks the positional question and receives 'white clouds cover the green mountain.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是賓中主。師曰。長年不出戶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmitted encounter gives the answer 'long years not leaving the house.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 賓中主即主中賓，逆順縱橫莫認真
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse pairs the two reciprocal position names and warns against fixing on their reversal and accord.

Occurrences.Kwic: 四賓主。不同臨濟。主中賓。體中用也。賓中主。用中體也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Eye of Humans and Gods explicitly says that this four-guest-host set differs from Linji's and glosses the Caodong host-within-guest position as function within essence.

AlternateTargets: the guest and the host in an encounter
Senses.Explanation: The paired roles of guest and host in a face-to-face meeting. The stock verdict 'guest and host stand out distinctly' (賓主歷然) states that the roles are distinct. Fixed forms carry the same pair across the records: Linji's 'guest-host phrase' (賓主句), 'one shout distinguishes guest and host' (一喝分賓主), and Zhaozhou's 'no-guest-no-host story' (無賓主話). Caodong records deploy the pair positionally in 'guest and host exchange places' (賓主互換), pair it with bent and upright (偏正), and expand it into host-within-guest, guest-within-host, host-within-host, and guest-within-guest. Linji's named 'four guest-and-host' (四賓主) is a taxonomy built from this same pair; the added graph 'four' names that lexical object, which has its own entry. It does not give the base pair a second referent.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Interchange, distinction, negation, positional compounds, and the fourfold taxonomy are deployments or larger compounds of the same guest-host pair. Linji and Caodong organize related labels differently, but the term 'guest and host' (賓主) itself continues to name the pair.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問師：「還有賓主也無？」師云：「賓主歷然。」師云：「大眾要會臨濟賓主句，問取堂中二首座。」便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji says guest and host are perfectly distinct and names his guest-host phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 賓主互換，偏正不拘，至位融和，所謂無礙。

Occurrences.Kwic: 未免賓主相待，彼此回互。直須賓不是賓、賓中有主，主不是主、主中有賓，賓主交參、互換無位

Senses.Explanation: A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner' (赤灑灑地).
Senses.Note: The English follows the term's directly attached predicates. It does not treat the phrase as a named experience, attainment, or procedure. Graph-level 'red' is not forced into the translation because the corpus repeatedly explains the compound through bareness, exposure, lack of covering, and lack of anything to grasp.

Occurrences.Kwic: 淨躶躶脫塵情。赤灑灑無蓋覆。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's recorded sayings. The paired clauses describe being cleanly naked and free of dusty feelings, then bare and without covering.

Occurrences.Kwic: 淨躶躶絕思惟。赤灑灑沒可把。猶未離這邊事在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu directly qualifies the paired description: cleanly naked and cut off from thought, bare and with nothing to grasp, yet still not beyond 'this-side affairs.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 淨裸裸無遺。赤灑灑全露。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu gives two compact parallel expansions: nothing left over, and fully exposed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 出得荊棘林。淨裸裸赤灑灑。依前似平常人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record prose. Having come out of the thorn forest, the person is cleanly naked and bare, and still resembles an ordinary person as before.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是知赤灑灑處恁麼即易，明歷歷處恁麼還難。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Collection of the Five Lamps. A later address contrasts the ease of being bare in this way with the difficulty of being distinctly evident.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒淨躶躶，赤灑灑，沒可把，尚有廉纖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Collection of the Five Lamps. The record explicitly says that even clean nakedness, bareness, and nothing to grasp still leave something fine remaining.

Senses.PreferredTarget: on the lump of red flesh
AlternateTargets: on this mass of bare flesh
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "on" or "upon" (上) the "lump of red flesh" (赤肉團): "on the lump of red flesh," attested 316 times in 144 allowlisted texts. Its most frequent named deployment quotes Linji: "on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, constantly going in and out through the face-gate of each of you; those who have not verified this, look, look" (赤肉團上有一無位真人，常在汝諸人面門出入，未證據者看看). The phrase also heads Nanyuan Huiyong's recorded saying, "on the lump of red flesh, a wall stands a thousand fathoms" (赤肉團上，壁立千仞), followed by a monk repeating the sentence and overturning the Chan seat. Later records quote both formulations, combine the phrase with the "true person of no rank" (無位真人), and use it as the location of other stated predicates. The broader form "lump of red flesh" (赤肉團) occurs 441 times, while "beside the lump of red flesh" (赤肉團邊) occurs 36 times. No exact occurrence using "inside" in place of "on" was found. The entry preserves the literal bodily wording and the two principal recorded sayings without replacing them with an imported abstraction.
Senses.Note: The Linji and Nanyuan sayings are distinct public-record lines and are not cross-attributed. Linji's line is transmitted in his own collected record and many lamp and commentarial witnesses. Nanyuan's line generates a separate exchange: the monk asks whether it is the master's saying, overturns the Chan seat after confirmation, is rebuked, deliberates, and is driven out. The phrase itself receives no separate one-line lexical definition in the searched formula set.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂云赤肉團上有一無位真人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Linji Yixuan's own collected record: "he addressed the assembly, saying: on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank."

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾云：赤肉團上有一無位真人，常在汝諸人面門出入，未證據者看看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's section of the Linked Lamps preserves the fuller statement: "on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, constantly going in and out through the face-gate of each of you; those who have not verified this, look, look."

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂云赤肉團上壁立千仞有僧問赤肉團上壁立千仞豈不是和尚語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Nanyuan Huiyong record embedded in Ancient Worthies: "on the lump of red flesh, a wall stands a thousand fathoms." A monk repeats it and asks, "is this not the master's saying?" Nanyuan has no validated roster link used here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南院顒禪師。上堂：赤肉團上，壁立千仞。僧問：赤肉團上，壁立千仞，豈不是和尚道？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Guidelines of the Patriarchs' independent witness names Nanyuan Huiyong, records "on the lump of red flesh, a wall stands a thousand fathoms," and begins the monk's reply. MasterName remains null because no exact roster primary name was established.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與赤肉團上無位真人現前清淨大眾。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Dahui Zonggao's summer-retreat address: "together with the present assembly and the true person of no rank on the lump of red flesh."

AlternateTargets: a lion crouched on the ground
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘a lion crouching on the ground.’ In Linji Yixuan's fourfold account of a shout, a shout may be like the precious sword of the Diamond King, like a crouching lion, like a probing pole and shadow-grass, or may not function as a shout; Linji then shouts when the monk hesitates. Later records preserve the four as an identification test, asking which of three successive shouts is the sword, the crouching lion, or the probing pole. They also transfer the same roster to another teaching-seat implement: a raised staff may act as the sword, crouching lion, probing pole, or not as a staff. Public questions ask ‘what is a shout like a crouching lion?’ and receive recorded replies including ‘it frightens the wild foxes to death’; another later master answers all four questions simply with a shout. The Zen bend is therefore not an ordinary zoological lion but Linji's named comparison within the four deployments of a shout, later reused to classify shouts and staffs in teaching-seat encounters. The record supplies varied replies but no separate definition of a hidden quality.
Senses.Note: The master-specific sense is warranted because the phrase's recurrent referent is Linji's named member of the four shouts. Later applications to staffs preserve that same roster rather than naming a different animal or a second reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有時一喝如金剛王寶劒。有時一喝如踞地師子。有時一喝如探竿影草。有時一喝不作一喝用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own fourfold enumeration places the crouching lion among four deployments of a shout.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有一喝是金剛王寶劒有一喝是踞地師子有一喝是探竿影草
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record turns the three named comparisons into an identification test among three shouts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拄杖子有時作出水蛟龍。萬里雲煙不斷。有時作踞地師子。百年妖怪潛蹤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later teaching-seat address transfers the crouching-lion deployment to a staff.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是一喝如踞地師子。師曰。驚殺野狐狸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks specifically for a shout like the crouching lion; the answer says it frightens wild foxes to death.

Senses.Explanation: To slip or misstep (蹉) while passing (過): 'to slip past' or 'to miss it.' The record uses it when someone fails to catch what is directly before him. One recurrent line says, 'by the time you raise an eyebrow, it has already slipped past' (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) occurs 158 times in 65 texts. Another passage warns not to miss it face-to-face and says that, if one does, one knows only affairs passing before the eyes (切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過). The near-synonym 'missed it' (錯過) occurs 863 times, including 134 instances of 'missed it face-to-face' (當面錯過). The headword itself occurs 1,340 times in 213 allowlist texts, and the completed form 'let it slip past' (蹉過了) occurs 117 times. In dialogue it can be paired with 'under your heel' (腳跟下), as when a question about why something is under the monk's heel receives the answer 'missed it face-to-face.'
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The dominant collocation is 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過), a recurring answer and verdict; the near-synonym is 'missed it' (錯過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 眨上眉毛，早是蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Tudu Zhice (塗毒智䇿禪師), in a hall address (上堂). The line says that by the time one raises an eyebrow, it has already slipped past (眨上眉毛，早是蹉過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 向上還有事也無？師曰：當面蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Correct Lineage of the Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統), entry for Chan Master Yunbian (雲辯禪師). The stock answer 'missed it face-to-face' (當面蹉過) follows the question whether there is still a further matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 切不得當面蹉過；若蹉過，只知事逐眼前過
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Monk Tianyin (天隱和尚語錄), recorded sayings at Baoen Chan Cloister (報恩禪院語錄). The warning not to miss it face-to-face (切不得當面蹉過) is paired with affairs passing before the eyes (事逐眼前過).

Occurrences.Kwic: 眨上眉毛蹉過。大似開眼尿床。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Yuanwu Foguo (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), in a hall address (上堂). The stock line says that raising the eyebrow misses it (眨上眉毛蹉過), followed by the comparison to wetting the bed with one's eyes open.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因甚在汝脚跟下？師曰：當面蹉過。

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to differ by a little; in the records, to be somewhat closer or a little better by comparison. The phrase occurs 854 times in 224 allowlisted texts. It is a recurrent, often qualified appraisal: Huangbo says that among Mazu's eighty-four teachers only Guizong is somewhat closer; Wuye says a monk who tries to help is somewhat closer; another master replies that the student's not understanding is a little closer. Yuanwu says that being entirely unlike a list of proposed identifications is only then somewhat closer, and immediately asks why. The phrase can also qualify silence, withdrawal, or the condition before a question, while still withholding full approval.
Senses.Note: The Chan deployment turns an ordinary small comparison into a clipped public verdict: 'closer' regularly does not mean accepted or complete. The texts supply the compared speech or action and retain the phrase as a comparative appraisal. All occurrences are comparative appraisals of the same kind, so no sense split is warranted.

Senses.Explanation: A turning word (轉語) is a single pivoting response that turns a stuck situation and settles a case. A master demands one — 'lay down a turning word' (下一轉語 / 著一轉語 / 道一轉語) — or supplies one in another's place (代一轉語). The locus classicus is Baizhang's wild fox: an old man, reborn five hundred times as a fox for once telling a student that a person of great conduct 'does not fall into cause-and-effect' (不落因果), begs Baizhang for a turning word said in his place (代一轉語); Baizhang's turning word — 'do not be blind to cause-and-effect' (不昧因果) — frees him. In the case commentaries masters challenge students to produce one: Wumen repeatedly challenges 'if right here you can lay down a turning word...' (若向者裏下得一轉語), and Xuedou invites 'let each Zen guest lay down a turning word' (請禪客各下一轉語). Baling gave his teacher Yunmen three turning words (三轉語) in place of a lineage-heir letter, and Yunmen said that on his memorial day he would simply cite those three and consider the debt repaid. The stakes of the fox case are stated in-corpus: 'answer a turning word wrongly and you fall into a fox's body' (錯答一轉語者，墮野狐身, the Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings 御選語錄, X68n1319); the case's paired answers survive in near parity — 'does not fall into cause-and-effect' (不落因果) 133 allowlist hits, 'not blind to cause-and-effect' (不昧因果) 126. Besides Baling's three, the record names 'Zhaozhou's three turning words shown to the assembly' (趙州示眾三轉語) (Blue Cliff case 96: 'Raised: Zhaozhou showed the assembly three turning words' 舉。趙州示眾三轉語, T48n2003; also X78n1556, J39nB441) — the three lines 'a golden buddha does not get through a furnace, a wooden buddha does not get through fire, a clay buddha does not get through water' (金佛不度爐。木佛不度火。泥佛不度水。) followed by 'the true buddha sits within' (真佛內裏坐) (X80n1565; 金佛不度爐 122 hits in 78 texts).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide technical sense, shared across houses; no single master owns it. Multi-source across a lamp record (the Wudeng Huiyuan 五燈會元, 'Five Lamps Merged'), a case collection with comments (the Wumenguan 無門關, 'Gateless Checkpoint'), and case commentary (the Blue Cliff Record 碧巖錄), with distinct masters. Zen-allowlist grep counts: 'turning word' (轉語), 1,435 hits in 265 of 462 texts; 'a turning word' (一轉語) 877, 'lay down a turning word' (下一轉語) 185, 'three turning words' (三轉語) 157, 'a turning word in another's place' (代一轉語) 100, 'able to lay down a turning word' (下得一轉語) 88, 'say a turning word' (道一轉語) 16, 'set down a turning word' (著一轉語) 11, 'each lay down a turning word' (各下一轉語) 11, and the compact form 'lay down a turning word' (下轉語), 9.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “turn” (轉) the “body or self” (身): to turn oneself around, attested 2,135 times in 327 allowlisted texts. The action can be direct bodily narration: Magu turns intending to sit and is struck, while another master turns and immediately walks away. Chan records also build a productive family from the same turning action. Yuanwu defines a “place to turn oneself” by “speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done” (無言處言得，行不得處行得，謂之轉身處). Hongzhi says one must know a road to turn; another record directly asks what that road is and answers, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village” (汝行荒草裏，我又入深村). A monk asks “what is a turning phrase?” (如何是轉身句) and receives a recorded answer. Other addresses say that bright-eyed patch-robed monks have “no road to turn” (轉身無路), or pair turning with shifting step. Literal motion and the road, place, and phrase compounds preserve one turning action; the former targets were paraphrases, not different referents.
Senses.Note: Further collocations include “turn and shift step” (轉身移步), “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and “turn, then…” (轉身便). Later records use “turning phrase” (轉身句) as a label in stylized exchanges, while Zhongfeng criticizes stock phrases called by that name. Compare road to turn (轉身一路), turning phrase (轉身句), place to turn (轉身處), and shifting step (移步).

Senses.Explanation: Kashyapa is the figure whom the Chan record places at the first public handover. At the Vulture Peak assembly, the World-Honored One holds up a flower before the silent gathering; Kashyapa alone breaks into a smile, after which the Buddha says that he entrusts the treasury of the true eye of the teaching to Mahakashyapa. Later Chan records do not leave him inside a biography: they repeatedly raise, question, and comment on this scene. Yuelin says that when the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kashyapa smiled, both deserved thirty blows. Kashyapa also appears at the teaching seat: after the assembly gathers, he strikes the sounding block and announces, “the World-Honored One has finished speaking the teaching,” and the Buddha leaves the seat. In the succession encounter with Ananda, Ananda asks what was transmitted besides the gold-thread robe; Kashyapa calls “Ananda,” receives his answer, and says, “knock down the flagpole before the gate.” These public acts—smile and announced entrustment, closing the Buddha's assembly, and the robe-and-flagpole exchange with Ananda—are Kashyapa's defining Chan deployment.
Senses.Note: This sense is Mahakashyapa, identifiable in the cited Chan cases by the flower, the entrusted eye-treasury, Ananda, or the gold-thread robe. The earlier Kashyapa Buddha is a different figure and is recorded separately below by his Zen deployment.

Senses.Explanation: The same name also identifies Kashyapa Buddha, the earlier buddha invoked at the opening of Baizhang's wild-fox case. The old man says that in Kashyapa Buddha's time he lived on that mountain, answered that a person of great cultivation does not fall into cause and effect, and consequently fell into a wild-fox body for five hundred lives. Chan texts deploy this earlier Buddha as the time-marker that makes the old man's former teaching office and karmic consequence intelligible; this is a different figure from Mahakashyapa of the flower, robe, and Ananda cases.
Senses.Note: Three allowlisted records anchor the exact phrase “in the time of the former Kashyapa Buddha” (過去迦葉佛時) in the public wild-fox case. The definition stays with that Zen deployment and does not import an external buddha biography.

Senses.PreferredTarget: turn the light around and shine back
AlternateTargets: turn the light back and illuminate
turn illumination around and shine back
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'turn the light around and shine back': 'turn around' (迴), 'light' (光), 'return' (返), and 'shine or illuminate' (照). This written form occurs 50 times in 35 allowed texts; the common variant 'turn the light around and shine back' (回光返照) occurs 168 times in 88 texts, and the reversed order 'shine back and turn the light' (返照回光) occurs 16 times. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp gives the literal instruction, 'turn the light around and shine back; look: what are body and mind?' (迴光返照看身心是何物). Shitou's Grass Hut Song says, 'turn the light around and shine back, then return' (迴光返照便歸來). Linji tells his listeners that at the words they should 'themselves turn the light around and shine back, seeking nothing else' (便自迴光返照，更不別求). Chengtian Cique says, 'only turn the light around and shine back; carefully search beneath your own heels and look what it is' (但自迴光返照，向自己脚根下子細推尋，看是箇什麼). Gongchen Jueke closes an address with 'each of you, please turn the light around and shine back; do not hesitate further' (各請迴光返照，休更踟躕). Fenyang's verse supplies a result-clause: 'turn the light around and shine back, illuminating present and past' (迴光返照明今古). The corpus thus records an imperative verb phrase, a poetic return, a prohibition on seeking elsewhere, and direct objects or complements such as body and mind, beneath one's heels, and present and past.
Senses.Note: No required direct-definition formula was found. The entry translates the four graphs and the actions explicitly attached to them. It does not rename those instructions as a special exercise or import an external system. The common orthographic variant is recorded in the explanation, while the assigned headword and all curated anchors retain the assigned written form.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "be lost or confused" (迷) and "awaken or understand" (悟): "confusion and awakening," attested 1,115 times in 231 allowlisted texts. The pair is repeatedly coordinated with ordinary and holy, motion and stillness, and true and false. One verse says, "the nature of confusion and awakening is empty; that empty nature has neither end nor beginning" (迷悟性皆空，性空無終始). Zhongxuan asks, "ordinary and holy are originally not two; how could confusion and awakening have different roads?" (凡聖本來不二，迷悟豈有殊途). Zhe'an says, "confusion and awakening are not different; motion and stillness have one source" (迷悟不異，動靜一源).
Senses.Note: The records also correct bare negation of the pair. A quoted line says, "originally there is no person of confusion or awakening; only understand today" (本無迷悟人，祇要今日了); the teacher immediately asks, "if there is no confusion or awakening, what do you understand?" (既無迷悟，了箇甚麼). Zhe'an likewise says that claiming confusion and awakening no longer exist is still halfway, then asks for confusion not to obstruct awakening and awakening not to obstruct confusion. These are explicit textual relations, not separate senses.
