Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an pairs the terms: confusion and awakening are not different; motion and stillness have one source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若謂迷悟不存，塵垢銷落，猶在半途，未為究竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhe'an's corrective: saying confusion and awakening do not remain and dust has fallen away is still halfway.

Senses.PreferredTarget: lose the head and take the shadow for it
AlternateTargets: mistake the shadow while losing the head
lose sight of the head and recognize its shadow
Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “lose or be confused about the head” and “recognize or take the shadow”: “lose the head and take the shadow for it.” Five Lamps Compendium states the image through Yajnadatta: while confused, his head has not been lost; when he awakens, it is not newly gained. A direct question asks, “How is losing the head and taking the shadow for it stopped?” The answers ask whom one would tell, say that seeking from another only goes farther away, and finally ask, “Where is the head?” Another record expands the wording: people have long forgotten the head and taken the shadow, but once the head is recognized, why manage the shadow? It then states that a head necessarily has a shadow and a shadow necessarily has a head. The phrase also appears beside “abandon the root and pursue the tips,” in a chamber test contrasting recognition before a sound with taking on after a phrase, and as the answer “a person who loses the head and takes the shadow” to a question about the guest within the guest. These records supply both the head-and-shadow description and its different uses.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 136 times in 76 allowlisted texts. The reversed form “take the shadow and lose the head” occurs 64 times in 40 texts; “forget the head and take the shadow” occurs once. The exact question about how it stops occurs in 5 independent texts. The expression is used as an appraisal, a named person-type, a test phrase, and a question; this entry stays with the recorded image and its stated corrections.

Occurrences.Kwic: 譬如演若達多認影迷頭。豈不擔頭覓頭。然正迷之時。頭且不失。及乎悟去。亦不為得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, section on Xiangshan Chengzhao: “Like Yajnadatta taking the shadow and losing the head—carrying the head while searching for it. At the very time of confusion, the head is not lost; on awakening, it is not gained.” This is the reversed headword form.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問迷頭認影如何止。師曰。告阿誰曰如何即是。師曰。從人覓即轉遠也。曰不從人覓時如何。師曰。頭在什麼處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, under the lineage heirs of Yunju Daoying: asked how losing the head and taking the shadow is stopped, the teacher says seeking from another goes farther away and asks where the head is.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛云：迷頭認影。祇為眾生一向忘頭認影，熟了錯認顛倒。既識得頭了，管他影作麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings, “Inscription on One Thread”: “The buddha says, losing the head and taking the shadow. People have long forgotten the head and taken the shadow... Once the head is recognized, why manage the shadow?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 有般漢迷頭認影棄本逐末守個昭昭靈靈為悟主人公以舉足動步搖唇皷舌的為常住心體
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Puji Yulin, a hall address: some people are said to lose the head, take the shadow, abandon the root, pursue the tips, keep a bright and numinous object as the awakened master of the house, and treat bodily movement and speech as a constantly abiding mind-body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：句裏無私則不問，如何是賓中賓？師曰：迷頭認影人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps, a small convocation in the section on Luohan Shenming Che: asked “What is the guest within the guest?”, the teacher answers, “A person who loses the head and takes the shadow.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 聲前薦得，落在今時。句後承當，迷頭認影。作麼生是空劫已前自己？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps, a chamber test: “Recognize before the sound—fallen into the present time. Take on after the phrase—lose the head and take the shadow. What is the self before the empty age?”

Senses.Explanation: The paired graphs mean to wander or roam at ease. In a lamp narrative, Tianhuang tells Longtan, “roam at ease according to your nature and range freely following conditions; exhaust the ordinary mind, with no other superior understanding” (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). An Ancestral Hall narrative describes someone “delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying” (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Productive forms include “roam at ease and be unbound” (逍遙自在), “range freely and roam at ease” (放曠逍遙), and “roam at ease according to one's nature” (任性逍遙).
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 974 hits in 245 texts. Yongjue gives a direct corrective definition: “what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely” is being aloof and unattached amid every false scene, “like a bird flying through the sky with not the slightest thing tying it, like a dragon leaving the sea with not the slightest thing obstructing it” (如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). He warns against mistaking the wording for reckless indulgence. A community rule likewise attacks “taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease” (將狂妄作逍遙). A direct question about “a person roaming at ease outside things” receives the answer “red and festering all over, unable to be supported” (遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Roaming through mountains and valleys (逍遙山谷) is verb plus object and remains here, not under the place name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須知所謂逍遙放曠者，乃是於一切妄境，超然不著
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue's direct corrective definition begins: what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely is being aloof and unattached amid every false scene.

Occurrences.Kwic: 任性逍遙隨緣放曠。但盡凡心無別勝解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianhuang's words to Longtan: roam at ease according to your nature, range freely following conditions, exhaust the ordinary mind, and have no other superior understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 樂乎雲水，去住逍遙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Narrative description: delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拄杖子豈不逍遙自在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyin raises his staff and asks, ‘Is the staff not roaming at ease and unbound?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 將狂妄作逍遙者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A community rule criticizes those who take crazed delusion as roaming at ease.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是逍遙物外底人。師曰。遍身紅爛不可扶持。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks about a person roaming at ease outside things; the teacher answers, ‘red and festering all over, unable to be supported.’

Senses.Explanation: The graphs also name a Chan master. Independent lineage notices identify Master Xiaoyao as a successor of Jiashan and locate him at Gao'an. His preserved record has him seated on the Chan seat; in the encounter with Luxi he strikes Luxi across the mouth with the fly-whisk and then addresses the assembly. This personal name is a different referent from roaming at ease.
Senses.Note: Master Xiaoyao is absent from the current canonical master roster, so the sense and occurrences remain unlinked rather than assigning an invented canonical name. He is not Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao: the lineage notice makes Xiaoyao Jiashan's successor, while the mountain headings explicitly name Huaizhong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 逍遙和尚逍遙和尚。一日師在禪床上坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The heading says, ‘Master Xiaoyao.’ The record continues, ‘One day the master was sitting on the Chan seat.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 逍遙和尚○逍遙嗣夾山，在高安。未睹行錄，不決始終。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The lineage notice says, ‘Master Xiaoyao. Xiaoyao succeeded Jiashan and was at Gao'an. His record of conduct has not been seen, so his beginning and end cannot be determined.’

Senses.Explanation: In Chan master headings the graphs also form the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Independent compilations name “Chan Master Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao in Jiangxi” (江西逍遙山懷忠禪師). The mountain is the monastery location attached to Huaizhong, not Master Xiaoyao and not the act of roaming.
Senses.Note: Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao is absent from the current canonical master roster, so the person is translated in prose but not entered as an unverified RelatedMasters value. Roaming through mountains and valleys (逍遙山谷) is ordinary verb-plus-object syntax and is excluded from this place sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 江西逍遙山懷忠禪師江西逍遙山懷忠禪師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The heading says, ‘Chan Master Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao in Jiangxi.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 江西逍遙山懷忠禪師江西逍遙山懷忠禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent compilation gives the same heading: ‘Chan Master Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao in Jiangxi.’

Senses.PreferredTarget: a golden-scaled fish through the net
AlternateTargets: the golden fish that has passed through the net
Senses.Explanation: Literally “a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net,” attested 257 times in 120 allowlisted texts. The phrase is anchored in Sansheng’s public question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden-scaled fish through the net feed on?” (透網金鱗未審以何為食); Xuefeng replies that he will tell him after he comes out of the net. Yuanwu’s prose supplies the corpus’s direct definition: “only with an eye at the crown is one called a golden-scaled fish through the net” (頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗). The image then becomes an appraisal of monks: one teacher hails a monk as “excellent—a patch-robed monk, a golden-scaled fish through the net” (俊哉衲子，透網金鱗), while later interviews ask why such a fish is still held up by water.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the fish-and-net image functioning as a public question and a teacher’s appraisal of a monk, with the Blue Cliff Record's explicit crown-eye formula. The fish, the case question, and later appraisals refer to the same corpus image; they are deployment shapes rather than separate senses. In the family check, “golden-scaled fish” (金鱗) is broader, while “through the net” (透網) supplies the defining escaped-net morphology.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's direct definition: only one with an eye at the crown is called a golden-scaled fish through the net.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三聖問雪峯。透網金鱗未審以何為食
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The core Sansheng–Xuefeng public case begins with the question about the escaped fish's food.

Occurrences.Kwic: 俊哉衲子，透網金鱗。出語標宗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher directly appraises a monk as a golden-scaled fish through the net.

Occurrences.Kwic: 透網金鱗，因甚猶還滯水？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later interview asks why the golden-scaled fish through the net is still impeded by water.

Senses.Explanation: A verb-object phrase: "pass completely through" (透) the "barrier" or "pass" (關), attested 266 times in 112 allowlisted texts. A Huanglong retrospective distinguishes the one who has passed from one who has not: "one who has already passed the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on—how would he know there is a gatekeeper? One who asks the gatekeeper whether he may pass is one who has not passed the barrier" (已過關者掉臂徑去，安知有關吏；從吏問可否，此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all the old and new public cases onto one string and call this "passing the barrier," while "the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed" (盡將古今公案一串穿却謂之透關；脚跟下一座生死牢關，政好不曾透得). The phrase also builds the recurrent noun "an eye that passes the barrier" (透關眼, 97 occurrences), used by Yuanwu and later speakers to ask whether anyone present has such an eye, and the rare "phrase that passes the barrier" (透關句, 1). Chijue Daochong's exchange says, "passing the barrier must be [done with] an eye that passes the barrier; returning a treasure takes one who can distinguish treasures" (透關須是透關眼，得寶還佗別寶人). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.
Senses.Note: The attributive forms "one who has passed the barrier" (已透關者) and "one who has not passed the barrier" (未透關者) occur 12 and 14 times respectively. The broader verbs "get through" (透得) and "pass through" (透過) occur 1,057 and 624 times and are not counted as headword occurrences unless followed by the graph for barrier. Zhongfeng explicitly distinguishes passing through language from passing the tight barrier underfoot; that text-drawn distinction is retained.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已過關者掉臂徑去。安知有關吏。從吏問可否。此未透關者也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Huanglong retrospective in the Continued Transmission of the Lamp: "one who has already passed the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on—how would he know there is a gatekeeper? One who asks the gatekeeper whether he may pass is one who has not passed the barrier." It is historical narration, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 盡將古今公案一串穿却謂之透關。殊不知脚跟下一座生死牢關。政好不曾透得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben's Mountain-Room Night Talks: "they thread all old and new public cases onto one string and call it passing the barrier; they do not know that the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed." No roster link is set because the exact primary name was not revalidated in this batch.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫有具透關眼底。便請出來激揚看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Yuanwu Keqin's third formal address: "is there anyone who has an eye that passes the barrier? Then please come out and raise it for examination."

Occurrences.Kwic: 透關須是透關眼，得寶還佗別寶人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Chijue Daochong's Jiangshan record, a monk says: "passing the barrier must be [done with] an eye that passes the barrier; returning a treasure takes one who can distinguish treasures." It is the monk's turn, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “chasing the clod.” In the corpus it belongs to a recurrent animal comparison: “the lion bites the person; the hound chases the clod.” The phrase appears as an appraisal after exchanges and in admonitions such as “you must be a lion that bites the person; do not imitate the hound chasing the clod.” Related forms call people “mad dogs chasing the clod” and say “chasing the clod and tracking the scent does not yet make a good dog.” The headword occurs 326 times across 148 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: The hound and mad-dog variants share one literal image and one corpus deployment; they are not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An admonition states the corpus's own contrast: be the lion that bites the person, not the hound chasing the clod.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師子咬人韓獹逐塊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Case verse preserves the compact lion/hound antithesis.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「獅子咬人，韓盧逐塊。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master gives the paired phrase as his appraisal of a monk's move in public exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此等輩，皆是狂狗逐塊，何曾夢見有獅子奮迅的牙爪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address expands the image into mad dogs chasing a clod and contrasts them with a lion's teeth and claws.

Occurrences.Kwic: 逐塊尋香，未為好狗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A rebuke pairs chasing the clod with tracking scent and denies that this makes a good dog.

Senses.Explanation: A proximal demonstrative, literally 'this one,' whose referent is supplied by the speaker's immediate words, gesture, or situation. Chan records repeatedly make that ordinary dependency visible in public encounters. A master raises a fist and asks whether the place a visitor came from has 'this'; another raises a whisk and says 'this is form,' then strikes the Chan seat and says 'this is sound.' In the Buddha-and-pig exchange, Buddha points linguistically to a pig being carried past and asks, 'what is this?' (這箇是甚麼); when challenged that an all-knowing buddha should recognize it, he answers, 'it still had to be asked' (也須問過). The phrase also points to an unspoken residue in the repeated exchange 'there is still this' / 'what is this?' (猶有這箇在／這箇是甚麼), and to a charge being handed on when a departing master raises his staff and asks, 'to whom is this entrusted?' (這箇分付阿誰). Prose and address uses show the same grammar: a record says 'set this aside' before its next case, Yuanwu asks whether there is still 'this news,' and a rebuke says the buddha teaching is not 'this reasoning.' The Zen bend is therefore not a special hidden object called 'this': the demonstrative remains grammatically open while gestures, objects, questions, discourse, and succession scenes publicly furnish its referent.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 4,672 hits in 226 texts. Family comparison with 'that one' (那箇), the variant forms of 'this one' (者箇 and 這个), 'what is it?' (是什麼), and 'who?' (阿誰). Different referents do not create different senses: fist, whisk, sound, pig, residual 'this,' and entrusted charge all instantiate the same proximal demonstrative function. No master-specific meaning found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲識大道真體。不離聲色言語。舉起拂子云。這箇是色。擊禪床云。這箇是聲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Gesture supplies two successive referents: the raised whisk is identified as form; the struck Chan seat is identified as sound.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山竪起拳曰。漢上還有這箇麼。師曰。這箇是甚麼盌鳴聲。山曰瞎。師曰。恰是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public encounter, Shoushan raises his fist before asking whether Hanshang has 'this'; the visible gesture supplies the demonstrative's immediate referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日坐次。見二人舁豬過。乃問。這箇是甚麼。曰。佛具一切智。豬子也不識。世尊曰。也須問過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Zen Buddha asks 'what is this?' of a pig being carried past and answers the all-knowledge challenge with 'it still had to be asked.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖乃舉兩手作怖勢。師曰。猶有這箇在。祖曰。這箇是甚麼。師無語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Repeated deictic questioning: 'there is still this' followed by 'what is this?' after a two-handed fearful gesture.

Occurrences.Kwic: 言畢，舉拄杖曰：且道這箇分付阿誰？徐與靈源皆屏息，遂擲杖投床，枕臂而化。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A departure scene: raising the staff, the master asks to whom 'this' is entrusted; two named hearers remain silent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇且置，又有箇婆子遣人送錢到趙州觀音院請轉藏經
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prose transition says 'set this aside' before introducing the next recorded case; the preceding account supplies the demonstrative's referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。無陰陽地上。還有這箇消息也無。日南長至晷運推移。錯。下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu asks whether the place without yin and yang still has 'this news,' with the seasonal address supplying what 'this' points back to.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：亂道作麼？乃曰：佛法不是這箇道理。要會麼？言發非聲，色前不物。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A rebuke says the buddha teaching is not 'this reasoning'; the rejected proposal in the exchange supplies the referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：慧寂有驗處，但見僧來，便豎起拂子問伊：諸方還說這箇不說？又曰：這箇且置，諸方老宿意作麼生？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yangshan describes his examiner's procedure: raise the whisk, ask whether other places speak of 'this,' then set 'this' aside and ask what their elders mean.

AlternateTargets: the entire body is an eye
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the whole body is eyes.' The phrase occurs 168 times in 83 allowlisted texts. Chan records make the whole body an organ of seeing, commonly beside whole-body hearing, speaking, or acting. Yuanwu says, 'the whole body is eyes, yet seeing does not reach it,' and extends the same construction to ears, mouth, and mind. Another discourse pairs 'the whole body is a mouth' with 'the whole body is eyes,' then assigns the former speech and the latter use. In public questioning, 'the Great Compassionate One does not extend a hand; the whole body is eyes' answers the class 'meaning and phrase both arrive.' Later case comments use the phrase as an appraisal of a master and as wording that itself still requires investigation.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is grammatical and recurrent: the records redistribute seeing from two eyes to the entire body, then coordinate that whole-body eye with whole-body ear, mouth, mind, and hand language. This entry reports those attested deployments without deciding what the image signifies. The corpus evidence does not require a second referent or word-class sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 通身是眼見不及。通身是耳聞不徹。通身是口說不著。通身是心鑑不出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu coordinates whole-body seeing, hearing, speaking, and discerning, while saying each fails to reach.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。通身是口說得一半。通身是眼用得一橛。用不到處說有餘。說不到處用無盡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record discourse contrasts the whole-body mouth's speaking with the whole-body eye's use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：如何是意句俱到？師曰：大悲不展手，通身是眼睛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange uses the expanded form 'the whole body is eyeballs' as an answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 縱使明招通身是眼，也未免一狀領過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later case comment applies the phrase directly to Mingzhao.

Occurrences.Kwic: 換骨洗腸重整頓。通身是眼更須參。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says that even being eyes throughout the whole body still requires investigation.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative made from “quickly” and “say.” In Chan public interviews it presses the person addressed to produce an answer at once. The formula is often doubled—“Speak, quickly! Speak, quickly!”—and appears after a question, after alternatives have been barred, or with “bring forth” to demand the reply. The records place bodily consequences directly around it: a master holds a fork at a monk's neck, a monk pulls the master from the seat, or a staff beating follows. Other occurrences put it in a monk's request, “please, Master, answer quickly.” Its distinctive Chan use is timed pressure for an answer in a public interview; the phrase denotes the demand itself.
Senses.Note: Speaker direction changes—master to monk or monk to master—but the imperative denotes the same act, so no sense split is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道得也叉下死。道不得也叉下死。速道。速道。學徒鮮有對者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The demand is doubled while a fork is held at the addressee's neck: whether he can speak or cannot, the case says death follows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悲千手眼那箇是正眼速道速道麻谷拽師下座
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji repeats Magu's question about the true eye, commands “Speak, quickly!” twice, and Magu pulls him from the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 併却咽喉唇吻，速道將來。溈山出眾云：某甲道不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The assembly is told to close throat and lips yet “bring forth [an answer], quickly”; Guishan steps out and says he cannot speak it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不得下語，不得無語。速道！速道！僧曰：請和尚放下竹篦
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the bamboo-comb case, both giving words and remaining wordless are barred before the doubled demand; the monk asks the master to put the comb down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不凡不聖請師速道田云老僧秪与麼師便喝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Here a visitor asks the master to answer quickly concerning “neither ordinary nor holy”; the exchange continues with the master's words and a shout.

Senses.PreferredTarget: meet a buddha, kill the buddha
AlternateTargets: on meeting a buddha, kill the buddha
when you meet a buddha, kill the buddha
encountering a buddha, kill the buddha
Senses.Explanation: The four graphs mean “meet,” “buddha,” “kill,” and “buddha”: “meet a buddha, kill the buddha.” In Linji's recorded address to followers, it is the first member of a longer series: do not be deluded by others; whatever is met inside or outside is to be killed on contact—buddha, patriarch, arhat, father and mother, and kin—only then obtaining release. Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters preserves the same passage without punctuation. A later lamp record explicitly attributes the saying to Linji and then asks why someone called a good teacher would want to kill people and what principle this is; the question is left standing. In the Five Lamps Compendium, Jingyin Kumu Facheng uses the shorter pair “meet a buddha, kill the buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch,” followed by “heaven cannot contain him; hell has no gate to gather him.” These records provide the wording, its surrounding series, later questions about it, and later deployments; this entry does not supply an interpretation they do not state.
Senses.Note: Linji's full series supplies the earliest frame represented here. The headword alone occurs 60 times across 50 allowlisted texts, while the extended pair with “meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch” also circulates. Later records both quote the saying under Linji's name and place its short form inside other masters' addresses. Compare “meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch” and “kill buddhas and patriarchs.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 向裏向外逢著便殺——逢佛殺佛、逢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own record: an address to followers. The excerpt preserves the frame and first member of the complete five-part killing series, which closes with “only then obtaining release.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 便殺逢佛殺佛逢祖殺祖逢羅漢殺羅漢逢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters independently preserves Linji's same address and complete series without punctuation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以臨濟和尚道。逢佛殺佛逢祖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Lamp Record explicitly attributes the three-part quotation to Linji, asks why a good teacher would want to kill people, and asks what principle this is. This is a raised quotation, so the speaker field remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無佛種性。逢佛殺佛。逢祖殺祖。天
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, in the section on Jingyin Kumu Facheng: the short pair is incorporated into an address and followed by statements that heaven cannot contain him and hell has no gate to gather him.

Senses.PreferredTarget: meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch
AlternateTargets: on meeting a patriarch, kill the patriarch
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch" (逢祖殺祖). Linji's surviving record places it inside a five-member roster: "meet buddha, kill buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" (逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷). This is the Chan bend: the honored religious and familial titles become the grammatical objects of the same repeated verb, and later masters preserve, question, and redeploy that severe roster. A successor record explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people after quoting the three religious members, without supplying a prose gloss. Later uses attach the phrase to a sharp sword, place it opposite "carry the infant and encourage the child" (提攜赤子，撫獎嬰兒) in a contrast about grandmotherly kindness, or quote it in a New Year's address before comments on lineage descent. The records use killing language literally in the formula but do not record bodily killings in these deployments; this entry adds no symbolic object behind the named roster.
Senses.Note: The exact shorter string has 57 hits in 47 allowlisted texts. It is almost always paired with 'meet buddha, kill buddha' and often extended with 'meet an arhat, kill the arhat.' Linji's fuller roster is primary; later uses include quotation, interrogation, sword language, verse, and explicit contrast with grandmotherly care.

Occurrences.Kwic: 向裏向外逢著便殺——逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢、逢父母殺父母、逢親眷殺親眷——始得解脫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's record supplies the fullest roster, extending the repeated verb from buddha and patriarch through arhat, parents, and kin.

Occurrences.Kwic: 逢佛殺佛逢祖殺祖逢羅漢殺羅漢。既稱善知識。為什麼却要殺人去。且道是什麼道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Continued Lamp record quotes Linji's three religious objects and explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 逢佛殺佛、逢祖殺祖、逢羅漢殺羅漢。真淨老人自謂臨濟正傳黃龍的子，七出八沒，得大自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A New Year's address quotes the three-part roster immediately before examining a claim to Linji succession through Huanglong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或問：『為何二十五年前無老婆心？』但云：『逢佛殺佛，逢祖殺祖。』『二十五年後為何有老婆心？』但云：『提攜赤子，撫獎嬰兒。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baiyu places the phrase as the answer for lacking grandmotherly kindness, opposite carrying an infant and encouraging a child.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單提一把吹毛利劒。逢佛殺佛逢祖殺祖。直教一物不得當其前。一法莫能隨其後。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's address places the paired formula after taking up a hair-blowing sharp sword and before allowing no thing or formulation ahead of it.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “do you yet understand?” In Chan records it is a recurring public-interview question after a master has spoken, displayed an object, stood up, or made another gesture. The addressee may answer “I do not understand”; a master may then speak again, request an object, or close the address. In hall discourse it also turns from an exposition to the assembly: “Do you get it? If not yet…” A long pause, a verse, a staff gesture, or the closing “take care” is frequently recorded after the question. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore not a private report of comprehension but an observable demand made to an emperor, official, monk, or whole assembly in a recorded encounter.
Senses.Note: One interrogative formula; its different follow-up actions are deployment shapes, not different senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 陛下還會麼。帝曰。不會。聖師曰。大士講經竟
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After Fu Dashi mounts the seat, strikes once with a ruler, and leaves, the imperial teacher asks the emperor, “Does Your Majesty get it?” The emperor says, “I do not.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還會麼。其或未然。更煩知音底人。為我說破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi asks the whole assembly, “Do you get it? If perhaps not yet, I will trouble one who knows the tune to explain it for me.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 還會麼？若也未會，拄杖子重說偈言去也。擊禪牀一下
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address asks “Do you get it?” then says the staff will recite a verse again if not, followed by a strike on the Chan seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師乃起立曰。還會麼。曰不會。師曰。與老僧過淨瓶來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In response to a question, the master stands and asks “Do you get it?”; after “I do not,” he asks for his water bottle.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'that bank/side,' hence 'that side,' 'the other side,' or 'beyond.' The allowlisted record has 786 occurrences in 220 texts. The deictic contrast is explicit: questions set 'the matter on that side' (那畔事) against 'the matter on this side' (者邊事), and one exchange says that as soon as words are involved one falls on 'this side' (遮畔) before asking for news from 'that side' (那畔底消息). The word builds noun phrases for a matter, person, saying, road, or news located on that side. Its most frequent fixed expansion is 'beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔), which occurs in addresses and verses; other recurrent forms include 'the matter beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔事), 'a person beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔人), and 'a saying from beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔一句). A funeral address asks, 'what is the road on that side?' (如何是那畔路). These are the corpus's locative and attributive deployments; the entry does not replace 'that side' with an imported category.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 786 hits in 220 texts. 'Beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔) has 419 hits in 161 texts; 'the matter on that side' (那畔事), 33/25; 'a person on that side' (那畔人), 10/7; 'a saying on that side' (那畔一句), 4/3; 'what is that side...?' (如何是那畔), 5/5; and 'one on that side' (那畔者), 4/4. Searches for 'X means that side,' 'is called that side,' and related equation formulas returned no Chinese Chan definition. Evidence outside the Chinese record was excluded.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問僧：「如何是那畔事？」僧云：「不是山，不是水。」師云：「如何是者邊事？」僧云：「是山是水。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the 'testing encounters' section of the record of Faxi Yin (法璽印禪師), the master asks a monk first for 'the matter on that side' and then for 'the matter on this side.' The monk answers 'not mountains, not waters' and 'mountains are mountains and waters are waters.' Faxi Yin has no exact roster spelling, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一涉言詮，便落遮畔。如何是那畔底消息？」師云：「你在遮畔多少時也？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Shending record of Yunwai Ze (神鼎雲外澤禪師), a monk says, 'once words are involved, one falls on this side; what is the news from that side?' The master asks, 'how long have you been on this side?' The exchange itself supplies the deictic opposition. The named master lacks an exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一等要行那畔路。且道：如何是那畔路？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Cishou Huaishen's extended record, in a funeral address for the Chan teacher Yincheng: 'all alike must travel the road on that side; now say, what is the road on that side?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音那畔一句圓該，全體現前纖塵不立
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Opening address at the Ancient Dongshan Anou Chan Monastery in the record of Yuanjie Ying (元潔瑩禪師): 'a saying from beyond Awesome Sound encompasses the whole; the complete body is present and not a mote is established.' The named master lacks an exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 威音那畔，洗腳上床，和衣倒臥，秖得一橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Zhe'an Fan record (蔗菴範禪師語錄), under addresses at Ancient Zisheng Monastery, the speaker says: 'beyond Awesome Sound: wash the feet, get on the bed, lie down in one's clothes—only one piece.' The named master lacks an exact roster spelling.

Senses.Explanation: A pronoun rendered 'which one?' in questions and 'that one' when used distally. The expression occurs 2,913 times in 283 allowlisted texts, with the expanded interrogative form occurring 421 times. It drives public interviews by demanding selection or identification: which Mañjuśrī Kāśyapa intended to expel, which eye is the true eye, which is stillness and which illumination, and which is Senior Ming's original face. The same pronoun can contrast with 'this one,' as in Yaoshan's bathing-the-Buddha exchange: 'you can bathe this one; can you also bathe that one?' Another exchange contrasts 'this is the Tathāgata's nirvana' with 'that one is the lecturer's nirvana?' These interrogative and distal constructions are different contextual readings of one deictic pronoun, not different things.
Senses.Note: The expanded interrogative form (阿那箇) remains within this corpus-wide sense. Public questions, object demonstrations, person identification, and explicit this/that contrasts establish the deployment range without creating master-specific meanings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊遂問迦葉。汝擬擯那箇文殊。迦葉無對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The World-Honored One asks Kāśyapa which Mañjuśrī he intended to expel; Kāśyapa has no answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大悲千手眼，那箇是正眼？速道！速道！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct public demand to identify which eye is the true eye.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃竪起拂子云：這箇是拂子，且道那箇是寂？那箇是照？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Danxia Zichun raises the whisk, identifies it, then asks which is stillness and which illumination.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不思善、不思惡，那箇是明上座本來面目？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The interrogative appears in the transmitted Huineng-Huiming original-face question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 藥山問。汝祇浴得這箇。還浴得那箇麼。遵云。把將那箇來。藥山便休。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong quotes Yaoshan's this-one/that-one bathing exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇從汝浴。還浴得那箇麼。遵曰。把將那箇來。師乃休。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent lamp-record transmission preserves the distal contrast.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拄杖是緣，那箇是佛種？拄杖是一乘法，那箇是緣？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A staff demonstration reverses the items in two successive identification questions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇是如來涅槃，那箇是法師涅槃？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate exchange places the distal pronoun opposite this one while contrasting the Tathāgata's and the lecturer's nirvana.

Senses.Explanation: In its primary Zen-loaded use, Handan names the imitator in the stock verdict “Handan learns the Tang gait” (邯鄲學唐步), attested 43 times in 31 allowlisted files; the shorter “learn the Handan gait” (邯鄲學步) occurs eight times in seven. Jingqing applies the verdict when a monk walks away after being asked how he understands Zhaozhou’s “drink tea”; Xuedou then asks, “this monk is not a Handan man—why does he learn the Tang gait?” (這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步). Other instructions attach it to uneven footing, warn that turning inside verbal sequences invites ridicule as “Handan learning to walk,” and speak of “losing the patch-robed monk’s nose and forgetting Handan’s former gait” (打失衲僧鼻孔，忘却邯鄲故步). Chan thus turns the place-name into a stock person/type and verdict in case commentary and direct appraisal. The corpus’s explicit walking, gait, and imitation language controls this target.
Senses.Note: This person/type differs from the actual place and the personal title below. Variants with “Tang gait,” “learn to walk,” and “former gait” belong to one imitation family, not separate readings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 清云：邯鄲學唐步。雪竇顯云：這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步？
脚下若參差，邯鄲學唐步。
不可在語脈裡轉嫫母效顰邯鄲學步見笑大方取譏識者
打失衲僧鼻孔，忘却邯鄲故步。

Senses.Explanation: The graphs also name the actual city of Handan. One verse says, “my home is in Handan” (妾家邯鄲住). Chan writing also preserves the city as the setting of the yellow-millet dream: “one pillow at Handan: he passed through fifty years of glory; on waking, the yellow millet was not yet cooked” (邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟). Literal residence and the dream’s setting retain the same geographic referent; the literary allusion does not make a new place.
Senses.Note: This sense covers the place itself, including when a poem invokes the dream located there. It is secondary because the imitation formula dominates the Chan concordance.

Occurrences.Kwic: 妾家邯鄲住，歌聲亦抑揚
邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟

Senses.Explanation: In one biographical passage, “Handan” is part of a personal title rather than the city or imitator: “the Duke of Handan, personal name Shu, was then seven years old” (邯鄲公諱淑，時方七歲). The title identifies the named child in that retrospective.
Senses.Note: This distinct title/person use has one allowlisted source and is therefore provisional. It is not merged into the geographic sense merely because the title contains the place-name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 邯鄲公諱淑，時方七歲。

Senses.Explanation: Śākyamuni, the name by which the Chan corpus identifies the buddha of its founding cases. The Ancestral Hall Collection gives the in-corpus name gloss: “Śākyamuni: translated, it says ‘Able and Benevolent’” (釋迦者，譯言能仁也). The record then bends the name through case and appraisal. It names Śākyamuni as the one who holds up the flower before Kāśyapa’s smile and as the one who mounts the seat before Mañjuśrī strikes the sounding block. It also makes him the subject of public questions: Yunmen answers “What is Śākyamuni’s body?” (如何是釋迦身) with “a dry shit-stick” (乾屎橛). Other recorded appraisals are equally direct: Guoqing Feng calls Śākyamuni “an ox-headed jailer” (牛頭獄卒), and Shaoshan describes him as “the general of a defeated army” (敗軍之將), alongside Kāśyapa as “a man who has lost his life” (喪身失命底人). Nantái Yungong says, “Śākyamuni has already perished; Maitreya has not yet been born” (釋迦已滅，彌勒未生), then raises the whisk and locates the handling of the buddha-teaching in that day’s teaching seat. The deviation is this range: the proper name is not protected as a remote sacred biography; it is a recurrent actor in the flower and seat cases, a subject put into public questions, and a figure whom masters openly compare, re-stage, and appraise.
Senses.Note: The 6,608 exact matches occur in 395 allowlisted files. “Śākyamuni” is the name-form. “The World-Honored One” (世尊) is a title used heavily in the flower, seat, and silence cases; “old man Śākyamuni” (釋迦老子) is a longer familiar form with its own strongly marked Chan deployment. Matches inside the longer form overlap mechanically but do not erase that lexical distinction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 姓釋迦。釋迦者，譯言能仁也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancestral Hall Collection; the passage itself gives the name gloss: “The surname was Śākyamuni. Śākyamuni, translated, means ‘Able and Benevolent.’”

Occurrences.Kwic: 當時釋迦拈花何等直捷？迦葉微笑何等快便？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Master Zhu Yuheng of Purple Bamboo Grove; a later address explicitly pairs “Śākyamuni held up the flower” with “Kāśyapa smiled,” appraising the former as direct and the latter as quick.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是釋迦身。師云。乾屎橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extended Record of Yunmen; in a public question, “What is Śākyamuni’s body?”, Yunmen answers, “A dry shit-stick.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是佛法大意？師云：釋迦是牛頭獄卒，祖師是馬面阿傍。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Collection, Guoqing Feng section; asked the main meaning of the buddha-teaching, Feng says, “Śākyamuni is an ox-headed jailer; the ancestral teacher is a horse-faced attendant.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 我道釋迦是敗軍之將。迦葉是喪身失命底人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Transmission of the Lamp; Shaoshan says, “I say Śākyamuni is the general of a defeated army; Kāśyapa is a man who has lost his life.” This is a direct recorded appraisal, not an annotator’s interpretation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何謂釋迦已滅，彌勒未生？拈起拂子云：正當今日，佛法盡在山僧拂子頭上放行把住，一切臨時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Collection, Nantái Yungong section; he says, “Śākyamuni has already perished; Maitreya has not yet been born,” raises the whisk, and says that today the buddha-teaching’s releasing and holding are entirely at the end of his whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 豈不見釋迦陞座，文殊白椎，馬祖陞堂，百丈捲席
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Eryin Mi's record; Śākyamuni mounting the seat and Mañjuśrī striking the block are placed beside Mazu mounting the hall and Baizhang rolling up the mat. This anchors Śākyamuni as an actor in the teaching-seat case, not as outside biography.

Occurrences.Kwic: 衲僧家高揖釋迦，不拜彌勒，未為分外。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Fayun Faxiu section; for patch-robed monks to salute Śākyamuni from on high and not bow to Maitreya is still not beyond their part. This anchors the masters' direct handling of the named figure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：一塵一佛國，一葉一釋迦。學人如何下足？師曰：大地草漫漫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Caoshan Baoji Xiong section; 'one buddha-land in a mote, one Śākyamuni on a leaf' becomes the premise of a public question about where the student can set foot. The named figure is deployed inside the interview's scale-making image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦之為釋迦，非增也；木石之為木石，非滅也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hefeng's record, teaching-seat address; 'Śākyamuni being Śākyamuni is no increase; wood and stone being wood and stone is no decrease.' The name is set directly beside ordinary things in a recorded contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “old man Śākyamuni.” In the Chan record this familiar name-form removes formal distance: masters quote what “old man Śākyamuni said,” stage his arrival with a staff or whisk, claim to speak where he could not, threaten him with blows, and attach coarse appraisals to his name. Longji Shaoxiu raises his staff and cries, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived!” (釋迦老子來也) as his answer to “What is great function appearing?” (如何是大用現前). Dahui Zonggao likewise raises the whisk and says that the old man has arrived, then asks whether the assembly sees him. In another record, a master says that even if old man Śākyamuni came there, he would receive thirty blows; Dahui comments on a story of Śākyamuni disputing the buddha-teaching with Indra by saying, “This old fellow deserves thirty staff-blows” (這老漢好與三十拄杖). The form also remains a quotation label: Yunmen says, “Old man Śākyamuni has already spoken; Maitreya still does not know” (釋迦老子道了也，彌勒猶自不知). A later master says, “Speak a sentence where old man Śākyamuni could not speak; take a step where the great teacher Bodhidharma could not go” (釋迦老子說不到處，說取一句；達磨大師行不到處，行取一步). The strongest coarse appraisal is textual and explicit: “Śākyamuni is a dry shit-stick” (釋迦老子是乾屎橛), paired with “Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shit-carrying fellows” (文殊普賢是擔屎漢). The deviation lies in the form’s repeated Chan use: a revered name becomes an immediately addressable “old man” whom masters quote, enact, out-say, rebuke, and strike in public discourse.
Senses.Note: The exact longer form occurs 2,409 times in 281 allowlisted files. The suffix “old man” (老子) is translated rather than omitted: it is what distinguishes this headword from bare “Śākyamuni” (釋迦). The examples preserve separate deployment classes—quotation label, enacted arrival, comparison, rebuke, and coarse appraisal—rather than treating every overlap with the shorter name as equivalent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨是老臊胡。釋迦老子是乾屎橛。文殊普賢是擔屎漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps United at the Source; a recorded address says, “Bodhidharma is an old stinking foreigner; old man Śākyamuni is a dry shit-stick; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shit-carrying fellows.” The entry reports the wording without assigning an unspoken intent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大用現前。不存軌則。時有僧問。如何是大用現前。師拈起拄杖。高聲唱曰。釋迦老子來也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps United at the Source, Longji Shaoxiu section; asked “What is great function appearing?”, Longji raises his staff and loudly cries, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived!”

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉起云。釋迦老子來也。還見麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Dahui Pujue; after striking the Chan seat with the whisk and raising it again, Dahui says, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived! Do you see him?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒釋迦老子到這裏也與三十棒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Old Worthies; the master says, “Even if old man Śākyamuni came here, I would give him thirty blows.” The nearby section heading identifies the Fengxue lineage material, but the occurrence is left unattributed because the rough head pointer is not a secure speaker label.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云釋迦老子道了也彌勒猶自不知
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Old Worthies; after an elder asks how to discern at all times, Yunmen says, “Old man Śākyamuni has already spoken; Maitreya still does not know.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦老子說不到處，說取一句；達磨大師行不到處，行取一步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Chan Master Shanhui; in a small address the master says, “Speak a sentence where old man Śākyamuni could not speak; take a step where the great teacher Bodhidharma could not go.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦老子與天帝釋。在中庭裏相爭佛法甚鬧。師云。這老漢好與三十拄杖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Dahui Pujue; after raising Yunmen’s saying that old man Śākyamuni and Indra were noisily disputing the buddha-teaching in the courtyard, Dahui says, “This old fellow deserves thirty staff-blows.”

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a repeated, layered, or weighty barrier. The expression occurs 739 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Counts range from one to ten thousand barriers; one passes, breaks, opens, guards, or remains separated by them. The recurring warning says, ‘do not say no-mind is the Way; no-mind still leaves one further barrier.’ Speakers also ask who has passed it, request presentation of ‘the final barrier,’ and direct a questioner to ‘ask the gatekeeper.’ A late discourse gives its own named description of ‘passing through the further barrier’; this is preserved as that text’s account, not made universal. Zen bends the checkpoint image into a public measure, but the corpus names no fixed numbered stage shared by every use.
Senses.Note: Family check: “one further barrier” (一重關), “two barriers” (兩重關), “four barriers” (四重關), “a thousand and ten thousand barriers” (千重萬重), “the final formidable barrier” (末後重關), “the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ formidable barrier” (佛祖重關), and “pass through the formidable barrier” (透重關) vary scale or sequence, not referent. No split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫謂無心云是道，無心猶隔一重關。示眾，云：泥佛不度水，木佛不度火，金佛不度爐，真佛內裏坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The repeated warning presents no-mind as still separated by one further barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：木馬衝開千騎路，鐵牛透過萬重關。木馬鐵牛，即今在甚麼處？良久曰：驚起暮天沙上雁，海門斜去兩三行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The iron ox passes through ten thousand barriers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「如何過得這重關？」師云：「問取把關吏。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A question asks how to pass it; the answer names the gatekeeper.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「大開爐煹，鋾鑄聖凡，末後重關，請師拈出。」師云：「但得雪消後，自然春到來。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk requests presentation of the final barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 境智融通，色空無礙，獲大自在，常住不動，是則名為透重關，名為大死大活者。透重關後，家舍即在途中，途中不離家舍
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A late text gives an explicit formula for what it calls passing the barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾中莫有透出重關者麼？出來與華藏相見。良久，云：無人知此意，令我憶南泉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public challenge asks whether anyone has passed it.

Senses.Explanation: As part of the stable labels 'Baizhang's wild fox' (百丈野狐), 'the wild-fox story' (野狐話), and 'the wild-fox public case' (野狐公案), the word names the public case attached to Baizhang. Masters raise, debate, and versify this case. Its recorded hinge is the contrast between 'does not fall under cause and effect' (不落因果) and 'is not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果). This is a named lexical object, not the animal body inside its narrative and not a person rebuked as a wild-fox spirit.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. The corpus bends an animal name into a stable case-name, explicitly marking it with 'raise' (舉), 'story' (話), and 'public case' (公案).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師室中常舉百丈野狐話問僧，對者多不契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master repeatedly raises Baizhang's wild-fox story in the chamber to question monks, explicitly deploying it as a named case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉百丈野狐話，乃曰：不是翻濤手，徒誇跨海鯨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a hall address the master raises Baizhang's wild-fox story and comments on it, again treating the phrase as a case-title.

Senses.Explanation: The concrete transformed animal body within the Baizhang account. The old man says that an answer of 'does not fall under cause and effect' led to five hundred births in a wild-fox body; after Baizhang answers 'is not blind to cause and effect,' the old man reports release from that body. Later records debate whether either formula leaves, produces, or releases the wild-fox body. Those debates still refer to the narrative body and do not turn each reading of the exchange into another sense.
Senses.Note: Literal narrative referent. It remains separate from the case as a textual object and from the abusive wild-fox-spirit label.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不落因果。遂五百生墮野狐身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Baizhang account connects the answer 'does not fall under cause and effect' with five hundred births in a wild-fox body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不昧囙果老人於言下大悟告辝師云某甲已免野狐身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After Baizhang says 'is not blind to cause and effect,' the old man reports release from the wild-fox body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不昧因果，也未脫得野狐身。一云：不落因果，又何曾墮野狐來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two monks explicitly debate the two formulas through the continued or denied wild-fox body.

Senses.Explanation: As 'wild-fox spirit' (野狐精), the word forms an abusive epithet for a person or view. Masters shout it at interlocutors, and Dahui warns against making a 'wild-fox-spirit interpretation' (野狐精見解). The referent is the person or understanding being denounced, not the animal body in the Baizhang narrative or the case as a textual object.
Senses.Note: The distinct referent is established by direct address and by the evaluative compound for an interpretation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師叱曰：這野狐精
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master rebukes an interlocutor directly as 'this wild-fox spirit.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可總作野狐精見解
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui rejects treating the matter as a wild-fox-spirit interpretation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "wild fox" (野狐) plus "Chan" (禪): "wild-fox Chan," attested 16 times in 15 allowlisted texts. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that the speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after a monk shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).
Senses.Note: The label is related by wording to the Baizhang wild-fox case (百丈野狐), but the corpus does not restrict it to citations of that case. Its verbs are openly corrective: "tear apart" (裂破), "sweep away" (掃), and "show off tricks" (逞伎倆). A verse placed under the Baizhang case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round" (修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓). The verse's own narrative language is retained as a recorded case allusion and not generalized beyond that witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 句句盡同師子吼，聲聲裂破野狐禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Liao'an's verse says, "each sentence is entirely like a lion's roar; each sound tears apart wild-fox Chan." Liao'an has no exact project-roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方野狐禪以達磨對梁王實無功德一語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ruibai criticizes "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" that takes Bodhidharma's one reply to the Liang emperor, "really, no merit," as a lineage label. Ruibai has no safe exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「野狐禪逞甚伎倆？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After a monk shouts and then gives no answer, the teacher says, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" The record's teacher has no safe exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse under the Baizhang wild-fox case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round." This is a later verse on a raised case, not a safely linkable speaker turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 掃盡諸方野狐禪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A portrait verse says its subject "sweeps away all the wild-fox Chan of the various quarters." The verse heading does not supply a safe roster identity for the described subject.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a gold buddha does not pass through the furnace
AlternateTargets: the gold buddha cannot cross the furnace
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a gold buddha does not pass through the furnace.' The phrase occurs 122 times in 78 allowlisted texts. Zhaozhou's recorded four-part saying sets it beside 'a wooden buddha does not pass through fire,' 'a clay buddha does not pass through water,' and 'the true buddha sits within.' The material nouns name buddha images: gold meets the smelting furnace, wood fire, and clay water. The formula is repeatedly quoted as Zhaozhou's saying, reordered, versified, and commented upon. One later discourse records a counter-form—gold, wood, and clay buddhas do pass their respective trials—and calls that wording an added layer. Another contrasts Zhaozhou's answer 'the one in the hall' with his later three-material-buddha statement and asks whether they are answer and instruction respectively.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the case-formula's treatment of buddha images by their material limits, followed by a 'true buddha' indoors. The recorded formula gives the final member no predicate beyond 'sits within,' and this entry adds none. 'Gold buddha' remains the same referent throughout; affirmative counter-verses are different statements about that image, not a second thing named by this headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：金佛不度爐，木佛不度火，泥佛不度水，真佛內裏坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp compilation records Zhaozhou's four-part statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州上堂金佛不度爐木佛不度火泥佛不度水真佛內裏坐。頌曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case collection identifies Zhaozhou, preserves the full formula, and introduces verses on it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：金佛不度爐，木佛不度火，泥佛不度水，真佛屋裏坐。趙州和尚吐心吐膽，恁麼告報了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later discourse quotes and explicitly attributes the statement to Zhaozhou.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古德道金佛不度爐木佛不度火泥佛不度水真佛內裡坐可謂慈悲之故而有落草之談又有云金佛度爐木佛度火泥佛度水真佛聻土上加泥又一重
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later discourse juxtaposes the established formula with an affirmative counter-form and calls the latter an added layer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 趙州答僧問如何是佛云殿裡的一日示眾卻云金佛不度爐木佛不度火泥佛不度水
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse compares Zhaozhou's public answer about buddha with his later material-buddha instruction.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘the Diamond King's jeweled sword.’ Linji's own record places it first in a fourfold classification: at times one shout is like this sword, at times like a crouching golden-haired lion, at times like a probing pole and shadow grass, and at times it does not function as a shout. Later masters quote all four, ask publicly which kind a particular shout is, and answer questions about the sword-shout with such phrases as ‘body divided in two’ (分身兩段) and ‘buddhas and demons slain together’ (魔佛同誅). The image also moves beyond the shout: one record says a raised staff can function as the Diamond King's jeweled sword, alongside the other Linji classifications. In these records the weapon-name is a classified deployment of a shout and, by later extension, another teaching-seat implement. The cited answers supply the cutting language; the sources quoted here give no separate prose definition of the sword-name.
Senses.Note: 271 raw hits in 111 allowlist texts. The headword is corpus-wide as a quoted and extended Linji classification, not a master-specific sense. Cross-checked the complete four: the Diamond King's jeweled sword (金剛王寶劍), the crouching golden-haired lion (踞地金毛師子; also 踞地師子), probing pole and shadow grass (探竿影草), and a shout not functioning as a shout (一喝不作一喝用).

Occurrences.Kwic: 有時一喝如金剛王寶劍、有時一喝如踞地金毛師子、有時一喝如探竿影草、有時一喝不作一喝用，汝作麼生會？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji gives the complete fourfold classification and asks a monk how he understands it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有時一喝如金剛王寶劍』」，師云：「魔佛同誅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master quotes the first classification and answers, ‘buddhas and demons slain together.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是一喝如金剛王寶劍？」師云：「分身兩段。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks for the sword-like shout; the answer is ‘body divided in two.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 智海拄杖，或作金剛王寶劍，或作踞地獅子，或作探竿影草，或不作拄杖用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record applies Linji's fourfold language to a raised staff, explicitly extending the classification beyond a shout.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'diamond eyes' or 'diamond-hard eyes.' The compound occurs 179 times in 73 allowed texts. The corpus says people 'possess diamond eyes' (具金剛眼睛, 58 occurrences), asks 'what are diamond eyes?' (如何是金剛眼睛, seven), and repeats the measured line 'diamond eyes weigh twelve ounces; in a patch-robed monk's hand the balance-head hangs low' (金剛眼睛十二兩。衲僧手裏秤頭低, 12). One recorded assembly says that the five thousand teaching texts and the myriad labors are 'still not diamond eyes,' then asks what diamond eyes are and, after a pause, answers 'blind' (瞎). Langye tells the assembly, 'each of you possesses diamond eyes' (各具金剛眼睛). A four-part enumeration lists 'the ancestors' handle,' 'possessing diamond eyes,' 'having a lion's claws and teeth,' and 'obtaining a patch-robed monk's killing and bringing to life.' Tiantai Deshao says, 'the worlds in all ten directions are diamond eyes' (十方世界是金剛眼睛). The records therefore use the ocular image in possession statements, a definition-question, a numbered list, a measured verse-line, and a world-wide predication.
Senses.Note: The direct answer 'blind' and the line weighing the eyes at twelve ounces are recorded verbatim and are not reconciled into an unstated theory. The singular English alternate reflects ordinary English number, while the headword itself is morphologically plural 'eyes.' No imported claim about special perception has been added.

Occurrences.Kwic: 猶未是金剛眼睛在。如何是金剛眼睛。良久曰瞎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp, under the heirs of Guyin Cong. The master says the preceding items are still not diamond eyes, asks what diamond eyes are, pauses, and says 'blind.' The nearest index does not expose a safe roster identity, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝等諸人，各具金剛眼睛，到者裏作麼生會？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of Ancient Worthies' Essential Sayings, Langye Jiao's record: 'Each of you possesses diamond eyes; how do you understand here?' Langye's roster identity is not unambiguous in the project roster, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一者祖師巴鼻。二具金剛眼睛。三有師子爪牙。四得衲僧殺活。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp. An assembly address raises a saying attributed to Fushan Yuan and enumerates four items; because this is a quotation inside another master's section, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 金剛眼睛十二兩。衲僧手裏秤頭低。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp, under Baiyun Duan's heirs. The verse-like line weighs diamond eyes at twelve ounces and says the balance-head hangs low in a patch-robed monk's hand. The local master is not safely identified by the rough head, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十方世界是金剛眼睛。無事。珍重。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Tiantai Deshao section: 'the worlds in all ten directions are diamond eyes. Nothing further. Take care.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘golden-haired lion.’ The phrase occurs 202 times in 85 allowlisted texts. The records retain Mañjuśrī riding the golden-haired lion, but also use the animal alone as an answer in public interview, describe its cub roaring immediately on leaving the den, and contrast it with lesser animals: one passage says a supposed golden-haired lion turned out to be a jackal’s kin; another has the golden-haired lion turn into a dog. The lion can also name what a staff-blow becomes: ‘sometimes one blow makes a golden-haired lion.’ These are the corpus’s observable deployments; the entry does not supply a hidden quality shared by them.
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is the image’s migration from Mañjuśrī’s mount into answers, appraisals, contrasts, and teaching-seat verse. The image and the term ‘lion’ (師子) are related; the phrase does not designate a different physical species.

Occurrences.Kwic: 文殊乘金毛師子往來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Preserves the inherited image of Mañjuśrī and his mount.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。金毛師子。問。如何是塵塵三昧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is delivered by itself as an answer in public interview.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有時一棒作金毛師子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A staff blow is said to make the golden-haired lion.

Occurrences.Kwic: 將謂是金毛師子，元來是野犴眷屬
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An explicit lion-versus-jackal appraisal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 金毛師子子，出窟便哮吼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A cub is described as roaring upon leaving the den.

Senses.Explanation: The lineage master Jinniu, whose name is recorded with a recurring mealtime action. At the meal hour he carries a rice bucket before the monks' hall, dances, laughs, claps, and calls, 'Bodhisattva children, come eat.' The Blue Cliff Record and an independent lamp witness both name the master and preserve the action. The person belongs on the master roster; this sense identifies him without turning his name into a biography or collapsing him into the later case shorthand.
Senses.Note: Person referent. The name's later use in Jinniu's meal-call case is a separate allusive referent, while the ordinary golden ox is a lexical collision.

Occurrences.Kwic: 金牛和尚每至齋時。自將飯桶。於僧堂前作舞。呵呵大笑云。菩薩子喫飯來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record names Master Jinniu and records his meal-hour action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 鎮州金牛和尚師凡喫飯時，舁飯桶到堂前作舞云：菩薩子喫飯來。乃撫掌呵呵大笑。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent lamp witness names Zhenzhou Jinniu and records the meal call, dance, clapping, and laughter.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded meal call attached to Master Jinniu, raised later as a case allusion. One address groups 'Jinniu calls them to the meal' with Nanquan cutting the cat, Guizong cutting the snake, and Zhaozhou drinking tea, then supplies its own critical appraisal. Another invites the assembly to eat 'Jinniu's meal' alongside other named case objects. These compressed expressions refer to the inherited meal-call case, not directly to the person and not to a golden ox.
Senses.Note: Case referent. The entry reports the textual grouping and appraisal without deriving a shared precept meaning or assigning a motive to Jinniu's action.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉斬貓、歸宗斬蛇、金牛喚飯、趙州喫茶，盡謂是宗門向上全提底時節，仔細簡點將來，俱未作家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guxue Zhe groups Jinniu's meal call with the cat, snake, and tea cases, then supplies his own appraisal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 來！來！喫金牛飯，飲洞山茶，穿睦州艸履，擎祕魔木杈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address abbreviates the allusion as eating Jinniu's meal, alongside other masters' named case objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰，如何是人境俱不奪。師曰，雲門胡餅金牛飯，空腹而來滿腹歸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public interview uses Jinniu's meal in an answer to the question about neither person nor environment being taken away; this is a distinct deployment from merely listing the inherited case.

Senses.Explanation: A golden ox, distinct from Master Jinniu and the meal-call case attached to his name. One recorded address tells of a blue-green purple-gold ox that changes into a stone horse. The animal predicate secures an ordinary or imaginative compound rather than a personal or case name.
Senses.Note: Jinniu Lake, Jinniu Mountain, institutions, and later people bearing the same name are proper-name collisions and remain excluded from the curated lexical evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昨日三茅真君下降吳山頂上，產下個碧綠紫金牛，金牛變作石馬
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An imaginative sequence speaks of a blue-green purple-gold ox that changes into a stone horse; the referent is an ox, not the master.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a lock made of gold; in some verse contexts the image can be a golden chain or fastening. Chan records overwhelmingly place it in obstruction-and-opening language: it is difficult (金鎖難, “the golden lock is difficult”), must be pierced, opened, smashed, or pulled apart, and repeatedly joins “dark barrier” or “dark road” in the compounds “golden-lock dark barrier” (金鎖玄關) and “golden-lock dark road” (金鎖玄路). The sharpest deviation is what the texts put behind this valuable fastening. Yongjue says, “ordinary feelings and holy views are the golden-lock dark road” (凡情聖見是金鎖玄路); another record says, “an inactive person with nothing going on is still a difficult golden lock” (無為無事人，猶是金鎖難). Later verses speak of a qilin pulling apart a golden lock and teachers call for striking through or smashing the golden-lock barrier. The gold does not make the fastening an attainment: the corpus applies the obstructing image to prized religious formulations and person-types. This is an observable textual comparison, not a claim about a hidden spiritual force.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 349 matches in 155 texts. Retained classes are the explicit ordinary-feelings/holy-views equation, the person-with-nothing-going-on correction, pierce/open/smash collocations, golden-chain verse morphology, and the “dark barrier” (玄關) / “dark road” (玄路) family. Family revalidation against the “golden-lock dark road” (金鎖玄路), “dark barrier” (玄關), “ordinary feelings and holy views” (凡情聖見), and “person with nothing going on” (無事人) narrows the preferred target to the literal fastening while recording ‘chain’ only where “pull apart” (掣斷) warrants it. These are image variants of one fastening, not separate referents under item 8.

Occurrences.Kwic: 凡情聖見，是金鎖玄路，故先聖以法淘汰之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue states, ‘Ordinary feelings and holy views are the golden-lock dark road; therefore earlier sages washed them away with the teaching.’ The entry records his complete statement while using only its explicit equation as lexical evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無為無事人。猶是金鎖難。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The line says, ‘An inactive person with nothing going on is still a difficult golden lock,’ applying the obstruction to an apparently prized person-type.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須打透金鎖元關，一任縱橫妙用。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-hall passage says one ‘must strike through the golden-lock dark barrier,’ after which it speaks of unhindered use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 麒麟掣斷黃金鎖。如何是不設牢關句？」師曰：「古路如弦直。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk says, ‘The qilin pulls apart the golden chain,’ then asks for the phrase that sets up no tight barrier; the teacher answers, ‘The old road is straight as a bowstring.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 若是箇漢，信手拈來，纖毫不犯，直下劃開情塵見網，當陽擊碎金鎖玄關
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record describes directly cutting open a net of feelings and views and ‘in full daylight smashing the golden-lock dark barrier.’

Senses.PreferredTarget: the golden lock on the dark road
AlternateTargets: a golden lock on the dark road
the golden lock of the dark road
Senses.Explanation: A Caodong expression built from golden lock (金鎖) and dark road (玄路). Caoshan's recorded statement identifies ordinary feelings and holy views as this golden lock and says they must interchange (凡情聖見是金鎖玄路，直須回互). A verse transmitted with Dongshan's record places the heading beside the lines 'interchanging, dark within light; with the effort equal, turning awareness is difficult; strength exhausted, forget advance and retreat' (交互明中暗，功齊轉覺難，力窮忘進退). Later records quote Caoshan, ask directly 'What is the golden lock on the dark road?' (如何是金鎖玄路), and apply the expression to an approving mind that has accepted its own view. The translation keeps the physical image of a lock obstructing a road; it does not replace the recorded phrase with a theory.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 25 exact occurrences in 18 texts. Variant witnesses write golden pin (金銷) or use dark pass (玄關), especially in the Caoshan formula. SenseKey is null because the expression circulates as shared Caodong vocabulary and as a stock quotation, although Caoshan supplies its clearest definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 席大興。學者雲萃。洞山之宗。至師為盛。師示眾曰。凡情聖見。是金鎖玄路。直須回互。夫取正命食者。須具三種墮。一者披毛戴角。二者不斷
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Caoshan Benji (撫州曹山本寂禪師語錄). Caoshan states that ordinary feelings and holy views are the golden lock on the dark road and must interchange.
