Senses.PreferredTarget: a silver mountain and iron wall
AlternateTargets: like a silver mountain and iron wall
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a silver mountain and iron wall.' The compound occurs 317 times in 142 allowed texts; 53 occurrences say 'like a silver mountain and iron wall' (如銀山鐵壁), and 21 use the exact longer comparison ending in 'resembling' (銀山鐵壁相似). Foyan asks, 'What is a silver mountain and iron wall?' (如何是銀山鐵壁) and answers, 'originally it is an affair inside one's own house' (元來是自家屋裏事); the same passage says that before he understood, it was like a silver mountain and iron wall, and after understanding, 'originally I am the iron wall' (元來我是鐵壁). Xueyan records cases 'without a route of meaning, like a silver mountain and iron wall' (無義路如銀山鐵壁者), and separately quotes Baiyun Duan: 'an inherited word or half-phrase not yet passed through is like a silver mountain and iron wall; once passed through, originally oneself is the silver mountain and iron wall' (從上留下一言半句未透者，如銀山鐵壁。及乎透了，元來自己便是銀山鐵壁). Zhongfeng applies the comparison when the words 'life and death' stop someone and says that 'impermanence of life and death, silver mountain and iron wall' are all present in Zhaozhou's question. A verse also records 'with one press, the silver mountain and iron wall collapse' (一拶銀山鐵壁摧).
Senses.Note: The corpus uses the compound as an image, a direct question, a self-report, a quotation about inherited sayings, and a verse. It can be something not passed through, something that collapses, or—according to Foyan and the Baiyun quotation—oneself after passing through. Those attested predicates are retained without replacing the image with an abstract interpretation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且如何是銀山鐵壁元來是自家屋裏事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies Record, 'Longmen Foyan's Record, part seven.' Foyan asks, 'What is the silver mountain and iron wall?' and immediately says, 'Originally it is an affair inside one's own house.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 無義路如銀山鐵壁者，又却都會不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueyan Zuqin's own general address. He distinguishes old cases with a route of meaning from those 'without a route of meaning, like a silver mountain and iron wall,' which he says he could not understand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 從上留下一言半句未透者，如銀山鐵壁。及乎透了，元來自己便是銀山鐵壁。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueyan's general address quotes Baiyun Duan: an inherited word or half-phrase not yet passed through is like the silver mountain and iron wall; once passed through, oneself is it. MasterName keys the containing speaker, while the note preserves the quoted source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但是說著箇生死。如撞著銀山鐵壁相似一礙礙住。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's instruction to five elders: when 'life and death' is mentioned, it is 'like colliding with a silver mountain and iron wall' and being stopped. This records the simile's verbal deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 生死無常銀山鐵壁。盡在此問處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng, instruction to Zongyu, comments on Zhaozhou's recorded 'the myriad things return to one' question: 'impermanence of life and death, silver mountain and iron wall—these are all in this question.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 一拶銀山鐵壁摧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Linked-Pearls Collection of Verses on Old Cases records the verse line, 'with one press, the silver mountain and iron wall collapse.' The nearby broad compilation head does not safely identify the verse author, so MasterName is null.

Senses.PreferredTarget: snow heaped in a silver bowl
AlternateTargets: a silver bowl filled with snow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "snow heaped in a silver bowl." In the founding public exchange, a monk asks Baling, "What is the school of Kanadeva?" and Baling answers with this phrase (如何是提婆宗？銀碗裏盛雪). The record preserves it as one of Baling's three turning phrases, alongside answers about the sharpest sword and the eye of the true teaching; Yunmen says that raising those three phrases is enough to repay Baling. Later masters continue to quote, question, and redeploy the exact wording. Tianyin quotes the answer while addressing his assembly, while Dayu sets "mountains are mountains, waters are waters—a silver bowl filled with snow" against "mountains are not mountains, waters are not waters—washing charcoal in ink" (山是山、水是水，銀碗裏盛雪；山不是山、水不是水，墨汁裏洗炭). The distinctive Chan deployment is the phrase's life as Baling's answer and a quotable turning phrase in later public teaching. The texts leave the concrete phrase without a further explicit gloss, and so does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attested 15 times in 14 allowlisted texts. The founding answer, later quotation, paired contrast, and free redeployment all refer to the same spoken image; no different thing or master-specific sense was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問巴陵：「如何是提婆宗？」陵曰：「銀碗裏盛雪。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The founding public exchange: asked about the school of Kanadeva, Baling answers, snow heaped in a silver bowl.

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉：「巴陵鑒禪師，有僧問：『如何是提婆宗？』陵云：『銀碗裏盛雪。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueguan later raises Baling's answer as part of the three-turning-phrase case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 憶昔當時僧問巴陵：『如何是提婆宗？』陵云：『銀碗裏盛雪。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyin quotes Baling's public answer while addressing his assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 辨得即山是山、水是水，銀碗裏盛雪；辨不得山不是山、水不是水，墨汁裏洗炭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dayu redeploys the phrase in a text-drawn contrast with washing charcoal in ink.

Occurrences.Kwic: 銀碗裏盛雪也好，秤錘裏掜汁也好，破沙盆裏煬羹也好
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yezhu lists the phrase alongside other concrete images before setting the whole list aside for his question.

AlternateTargets: a bronze head and iron brow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “bronze-headed and iron-browed.” Chan texts use the compact bodily description as an epithet for unusually formidable people, especially monks imagined as able to withstand severe encounter. One hall address places “bronze-headed and iron-browed” directly under “the patch-robed monk's gate.” Verses nevertheless say that even such a fellow receives a welt from one staff-blow, or stands bloodied under the staff's command. Elsewhere the phrase itself answers “What is buddha?”, followed by the equally concrete “bird's beak and fish's gills.” These occurrences establish the epithet and its Chan setting; they do not establish literal metal anatomy or an occult quality. The headword occurs 208 times across 114 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Adjectival and substantivized uses refer to the same kind of formidable person and do not require separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十地心驚，二乘罔測，衲僧門下，銅頭鐵額
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address places the bronze-headed and iron-browed under the patch-robed monk's gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是佛？師云：銅頭鐵額。僧曰：意旨如何？師云：鳥觜魚腮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In public interview the phrase answers “What is buddha?”, followed by “bird's beak and fish's gills.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 縱使銅頭鐵額漢，也須一棒一條痕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse on Deshan says even a bronze-headed, iron-browed fellow must bear one welt from one blow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 銅頭鐵額漢，盡在此山中
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says the bronze-headed, iron-browed fellows are all within this mountain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一棒施行該百令，銅頭鐵額血淋身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An entering-room verse puts the epithet under one staff-blow and describes the body as bloodied.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to understand wrongly. The expression occurs 680 times in 182 allowlisted texts. It is frequently a public verdict: a master says that someone has already misconstrued an action, an answer, silence, or an earlier master's words. The common warning 'do not misconstrue it' precedes or follows a case presentation. Yuanwu repeatedly rejects specific reported explanations as misconstruals, including treating Mazu's look as a symbolic pairing of sun and moon and taking Fayan's fire-seeking exchange as a self-referential explanation. In the whisk case, Jinfeng raises the whisk and immediately tells the monk who assumes a listening posture that he has already misconstrued it. The word marks an attested adverse judgment in interviews and commentary; the entry does not replace that judgment with a proposed correct interpretation.
Senses.Note: One verbal sense covers warnings, third-person reports, and direct verdicts. What was misconstrued varies; the act of misconstruing does not.

Occurrences.Kwic: 峯云：我有一則因緣舉似你，只是不得錯會。僧云：請和尚舉。峯豎起拂子，僧作聽勢，峯云：早錯會了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jinfeng first warns against misconstruing the case, then directly judges the monk's listening posture a misconstrual.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今眾中多錯會瞠眼云。在這裏。左眼是日面。右眼是月面。有什麼交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu reports and rejects a specific explanation of Mazu's look.

Occurrences.Kwic: 法眼云。好語。恐爾錯會。可更說看則云。丙丁屬火。以火求火。如某甲是佛。更去覓佛。法眼云。監院果然錯會了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fayan tests the superintendent's explanation and twice names misconstrual.

Occurrences.Kwic: 常時默坐，廢七蒲團，以淨名杜口答之，錯會者認為良久。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Commentary says misconstruers take a recorded silence merely as a long pause.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人有箇生緣。那箇是上座生緣。便道某是某州人事。是何言歟。且莫錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse gives an example answer and immediately warns not to misconstrue the question.

Senses.Explanation: The named cast iron-ox landmark of Shaanfu. The full headword occurs 1,583 times in 263 allowlisted texts, and the Shaanfu form is repeatedly used as a public answer and animated stage object. One master answers a question about turning around by saying to water the Shaanfu iron ox (陝府灌鐵牛); another address makes it enter western Shu (陝府鐵牛入西蜀). The impossible actions remain predicated of the same named landmark, so watering, traveling, or swallowing do not create separate senses.
Senses.Note: Primary named-object sense. Split from generic or imagined iron-ox figures and explicit comparisons. Further Shaanfu animations were excluded after watering and travel established the productive deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是學人轉身處？師云：陝府灌鐵牛。問：如何是學人親切處？師云：河西弄師子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fenyang answers a question about the student's turning place with watering the Shaanfu iron ox.

Occurrences.Kwic: 嘉州大像出關來。陝府鐵牛入西蜀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address makes the named Shaanfu iron ox enter western Shu while the Jiading great image comes through the pass.

RelatedTerms: great image of Jiading (嘉州大像)

Senses.Explanation: An imagined iron ox used as a comparison, mechanism, or stock figure. Funiu compares his position at Shitou to a mosquito on an iron ox; another saying adds that there is nowhere to put its mouth. The patriarchal mind-seal is explicitly compared to “the mechanism of an iron ox” (狀似鐵牛之機). Hornless iron oxen also break an iron barrier or answer a question about lineage succession. These uses construct an iron-ox figure rather than naming the Shaanfu landmark.
Senses.Note: Figurative family sense. Mosquito, mechanism, barrier, and lineage-answer deployments are different predicates of the same productive iron-ox figure, not four additional senses. No symbolic meaning is assigned beyond the explicit comparisons and actions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。某甲在石頭處。如蚊子上鐵牛。祖曰。汝既如是。善自護持。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Funiu explicitly compares his former position at Shitou to a mosquito on an iron ox.

Occurrences.Kwic: 聲前非聲。色後非色。蚊子上鐵牛。無汝下觜處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jiashan states the image's concrete obstruction: there is nowhere to put one's mouth.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師心印。狀似鐵牛之機。去即印住。住即印破。祇如不去不住。印即是。不印即是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Deshan's record supplies the widely repeated iron-ox mechanism formula and its moving/staying contrast.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石門巇嶮鐵關牢。舉目重重萬仞高。無角鐵牛衝得破。毘盧海內作波濤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hornless iron ox is made to break through an iron barrier in a public address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。祖祖相傳傳祖印。師今得法嗣何人。師曰。無角鐵牛眠少室。生兒石女老黃梅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The hornless iron ox appears in a lineage question alongside the stone woman who bears a child.

Occurrences.Kwic: 學人有鐵牛之機，請師不搭印。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student claims to possess the iron-ox mechanism and asks the master not to apply the seal. This is a public-interview use of the mechanism, distinct from the repeated comparison formula.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the gate and courtyard — a teaching house's frontage and its approach
Senses.Explanation: Literally the gate and courtyard (門庭) at the front of a house; in the records, the frontage and distinctive approach of a teaching house. It is used for establishing a house in the forms 'set up a gate and courtyard' (立門庭, 79 occurrences), 'each set up a gate and courtyard' (各立門庭, 20), and 'establish a gate and courtyard' (建立門庭, 25). The common compound 'arrangements at the gate and courtyard' (門庭施設) occurs 180 times in 92 texts. The texts themselves set these outer arrangements against the inner hall and the upward road: one passage says that this is still an affair at the edge of Shouchang's gate-and-courtyard arrangements and that the honored upward road is separately distinguished (此猶是壽昌門庭施設邊事，須知向上一路尊貴自別); another says that this is still a small wonder among the gate-and-courtyard arrangements and has no connection at all with a patch-robed monk's own share (此猶是門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉). A house's demanding style is described as 'high and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭高峻, 34 occurrences) or 'solitary and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭孤峻, 44). The headword occurs 1,462 times in 291 allowlist texts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The record itself contrasts the arrangements at the gate and courtyard (門庭施設) with the inner hall (堂奧) and the upward road (向上一路).

Occurrences.Kwic: 分宗列派，各立門庭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), guiding principles for the evening informal convocation (當晚小參提綱). The line says that divisions and branches each establish their own gate and courtyard (分宗列派，各立門庭).

Occurrences.Kwic: 門庭施設，誑謼小兒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Shangfeng Huihe (上封慧和禪師). It calls the arrangements at the gate and courtyard something used to deceive children (門庭施設，誑謼小兒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此猶是壽昌門庭施設邊事，須知向上一路尊貴自別。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Record of Chan Master Juelang Daosheng of Tianjie (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), hall address on the master's birthday (師誕日上堂). The text contrasts affairs at the edge of Shouchang's gate-and-courtyard arrangements (壽昌門庭施設邊事) with the upward road (向上一路).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此猶是門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai (無異元來禪師廣錄), recorded sayings at Baolin Chan Temple on Mount Dayang (住大仰寶林禪寺語錄). It calls the gate-and-courtyard arrangements a small wonder with no connection to a patch-robed monk's own share (門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉).

Occurrences.Kwic: 其奈門庭高峻，波瀾浩大。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu (三宜盂禪師語錄), recorded sayings at old Zhuming Temple (住古朱明寺語錄). The expression 'high and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭高峻) describes a house's demanding frontage.

Senses.PreferredTarget: open your mouth and you are already wrong
AlternateTargets: the moment you open your mouth, it is wrong
Senses.Explanation: Literally, open (開) the mouth (口) and immediately or already (即) be wrong (錯): "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" (開口便錯) occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has a monk ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" (我開口即錯). The monk calls him truly his teacher; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" (今日向弟子手裏死), so the record shows the verdict catching the speaker's own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" (開口即錯，擬心即差). Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" (動念即乖). Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening (開口即錯，閉口即喪，不開不合，十萬八千). The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells a monk, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!" The monk answers, "wrong," and Baishan answers with another stock retort. Chan thus bends an ordinary judgment of erroneous speech into a self-applying verdict, a fixed parallel line, and a demand used while requiring an answer; the records preserve the resulting replies rather than defining silence as the solution.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase is not a ban on all recorded speech: masters utter it, ask for rapid answers after it, pair it with closed-mouth loss, and continue the exchange. Those observable deployments are why the preferred target preserves the self-applying grammar.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有僧問。除上去下請師便道。師曰。我開口即錯。僧曰。真是學人師。師曰。今日向弟子手裏死。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dabe's early exchange makes the line explicitly first-person and records his acknowledgment that the disciple caught him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 開口即錯，擬心即差
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Po'an Zuxian preserves the fixed parallel with aiming the mind and immediately missing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 開口即錯，閉口即喪。不開不合，十萬八千。到這裏如何通信？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wuzhun Shifan supplies the closed-mouth contrast and then asks how communication is possible.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：「開口即錯，動念即乖。去此二途，速道！速道！」曰：「錯。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baishan demands a rapid answer after stating the paired verdict; the monk replies with the word 'wrong.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問僧，開口即錯，閉口即失。去此二途，如何通信？僧曰，兩眼對兩眼。師曰，瞎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanzhi Benyuan tests a monk with opening-mouth error versus closed-mouth loss and rejects the reply 'two eyes facing two eyes' as blind.

Senses.Explanation: (開) 'open' + (悟) 'awaken/realize': to open into awakening — the event of a person coming to realization. In the Chan record it names the moment understanding opens, most often marked as sudden and triggered by a teacher's word or gesture: (豁然開悟) ('all at once opened into awakening'), (心忽開悟) ('the mind suddenly opened into awakening'), (遇百丈開悟) ('met Baizhang and opened into awakening'), (其僧於是開悟) ('the monk thereupon opened into awakening'). Yongming reads the opening as instantaneous — (若開悟時)，(不隔剎那)，(便成佛果) ('when one opens into awakening, not a kṣaṇa apart, one accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood'). The same word is also used transitively/causatively — (令汝等開悟) ('to make you all open into awakening'), (開悟眾生) — with no change of core meaning, only of who does the awakening. Distinguish (大悟) (great awakening, esp. the stock 言下大悟 'greatly awakened at the words') and (頓悟) (sudden awakening), which name the same event under different emphasis; (見性成佛) names its content. The corpus's own collocation pattern draws that line: the words-trigger formula (言下) pairs almost exclusively with (大悟) (言下大悟 450 hits in 148 allowlist texts, against 言下開悟 4 hits), while (開悟) takes the suddenness adverbs — (豁然開悟) 68 hits in 38 texts, (忽然開悟) 18 in 16.
Senses.Note: Very widely attested (566 raw occurrences across 147 allowlist texts). Uniform core meaning; no master bends it, so a single corpus-wide sense is honest. The intransitive 'X opened into awakening' is dominant; a transitive-causative valence ('to open others to awakening', 令汝等開悟 / 開悟眾生, especially in Yongming's 宗鏡錄 and Mazu's address to the assembly) is the same lexical sense and is documented in the occurrences. Curated witnesses span three independent texts: (景德傳燈錄) (T51n2076), (五燈會元) (X80n1565), and (宗鏡錄) (T48n2016). Collocation counts (462-text allowlist grep): (豁然開悟) 68 hits in 38 texts; (忽然開悟) 18 in 16; (言下開悟) 4 in 3 — versus (言下大悟) 450 in 148 and (豁然大悟) 353 in 126; the transitive (開悟眾生) 3 in 2.

Occurrences.Kwic: 行脚遇百丈開悟。却迴本寺。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄) narration of (福州古靈神贊禪師): on pilgrimage he 'met Baizhang and opened into awakening,' then returned to his home temple. Narrator's voice, not the master speaking — MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 殃崛聞之。心忽開悟。遂棄刃。投佛出家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元) (X-canon; FromLb is the ed="X" number, not the co-located ed="R138" reprint): Aṅgulimāla, hearing the Buddha, 'the mind suddenly opened into awakening,' cast down the blade and left home. Independent witness of the intransitive event.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若開悟時。不隔剎那。便成佛果。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (宗鏡錄), Yongming Yanshou: awakening is instantaneous — 'when one opens into awakening, not a kṣaṇa apart, one accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood.' The non-gradual, instantaneous reading.

Occurrences.Kwic: 傳上乘一心之法。令汝等開悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元), (馬祖道一) addressing his assembly (謂眾曰) and describing Bodhidharma: '[Bodhidharma] transmitted the highest-vehicle teaching of the one mind to make you all open into awakening.' Documents the transitive-causative valence ('to open others to awakening'). Speaker is Mazu (expository/two-speaker), MasterName null. FromLb is the ed="X" number.

Occurrences.Kwic: 搖三五下作蟬響聲。其僧於是開悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄): a master mimics a cicada's cry and 'the monk thereupon opened into awakening' — the event triggered by a gesture. Two-speaker narration, MasterName null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally to open and show: to disclose something or give a showing. In Chan public interviews an assembly or monk asks a master to disclose and show, and the master's spoken reply follows. One monk asks for the intention of the patriarch's coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; another assembly asks and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). Biographical prose also says a teacher used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學). A later speaker says, “having received the master's disclosure” (承師開示), treating the reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.
Senses.Note: The term occurs 1,446 times in 267 allowlisted texts. The former verb/result targets were request and receipt grammar for the same showing and are merged. Compare raising and expounding (舉揚), question-and-answer (問答), offering an indication (垂示), addressing the assembly (示眾), and formal instruction words (法語). No mystical content is assigned to the act or its received result.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：祖意西來，願垂開示。師曰：泥牛吞巨浪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question requests disclosure and receives a recorded answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：大眾雲臻，請師開示。師曰：又靜不知雲去處，地寒留得雪多時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An assembled audience requests the master's public showing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今日福山大眾請和尚開示
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A named assembly's request is immediately followed by the master's answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我既得法。當往何國而作佛事。願垂開示。尊者曰。汝雖得法未可遠遊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission narrative uses the same polite request formula and supplies an answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「承師開示，腳底蓮花步步階。」師云：「一法通時萬法通。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker treats the master's disclosure as instruction already received, then continues the exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 學人久依和尚。不蒙開示心要。皇曰。你擎茶來我則舉手。你來問訊我則低頭。那裏不是與你開示心要處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Longtan complains that he has not been shown the essentials of mind; Tianhuang lists his responses to tea and greetings and asks where he was not showing them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 常以啐啄之機。開示後學。善能應機說法。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical prose says Jingqing regularly used the hatching dynamic to show later students and was skilled at responding to the situation in speech.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'opening and blocking': in precept language, permission and prohibition. The compound occurs 78 times in 65 allowlisted texts and regularly joins 'keeping and breaking' as a paired field of rule judgment. An instruction for beginners requires knowing keeping, breaking, permission, and prohibition, and says to follow the Buddha's words rather than common talk. A Vinaya-master description likewise says such a teacher penetrates keeping and breaking and understands permission and prohibition. Chan polemic turns on the same pair: Zhongfeng quotes claims that embracing a wife, abusing Shakyamuni, drunkenness, and striking Maitreya make discussion of permission, prohibition, keeping, and breaking needless, then interrupts, 'Stop, stop.' A following verse instead says investigating Chan must not destroy or transgress and permission and prohibition must not be confused. Yulin gives an institutional application: because uncovered heads show respect in India whereas full dress shows respect in China, the regulations preserve permission and prohibition while accommodating local custom. The term thus marks real rule-bound distinctions that Chan authors criticize others for discarding and also apply to circumstances.
Senses.Note: No single list of permissions and prohibitions is asserted by this entry; the record uses the compound as a category of precept judgment and repeatedly pairs it with keeping/breaking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫初心之人。須遠離惡友親近賢善。受五戒十戒等。善知持犯開遮。但依金口聖言。莫順庸流妄說。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An instruction for beginners places permission/prohibition beside keeping/breaking and the reception of five or ten precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫律師者啟毗尼之法藏傳壽命之遺風洞持犯而達開遮秉威儀
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A description of a Vinaya master lists understanding permission and prohibition as part of the office.

Occurrences.Kwic: 叅禪莫毀犯動輙成過患作止誠可分開遮豈容濫內外絕安排自他俱了辨
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says investigating Chan must not transgress and that permission and prohibition cannot be confused.

Occurrences.Kwic: 抱妻罵釋迦。醉酒打彌勒。俱成一行三昧。說甚麼開遮持犯等。故永嘉亦云。大悟不拘於小節。闢曰。且住且住。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng quotes the claimed abolition of permission/prohibition and keeping/breaking, then explicitly interrupts it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 西竺以露頂跣足表至敬東土以冠履備整顯極恭然禮隨國制所行便為虔敬之儀又云葢律依西制結集時仍列開遮宜隨國風以護譏嫌
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yulin applies permission/prohibition to differing Indian and Chinese signs of respect while retaining the authority of the regulations.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, idle or unnecessary (閑) kudzu-and-wisteria creepers (葛藤). The parent term's Chan use is verbal tangle; this exact compound sharpens it to talk treated as idle or unnecessary. An early record warns people not to gather and talk idle vine-tangle, adding that the old man may catch and examine them. Two later verses call the whole great treasury of teachings 'idle vine-tangle': one immediately adds that the seventeen hundred cases trip people to death. A separate verse says that a massive volume already carries idle vine-tangle and puns that there is no need to send more 'idle furnishings.' The Zen deviation is the extension of the corpus's vine-language from individual words to gathered discussion, large books, the canon, and the case collection. The texts make those appraisals; this entry does not generalize them to every written record.
Senses.Note: Exact-form count: 5 hits in 5 allowlisted texts. The orthographic variant idle vine-tangle (閒葛藤) has 2 hits in 2 texts. One verbal-entanglement sense, cross-checked against vine-tangle (葛藤), spinning out vines (打葛藤), vine-tangle case (葛藤公案), and cutting off the vines (截斷葛藤). The D-canon witness was not curated under the Chinese-Chan-only gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫空不識好惡矻矻地聚頭說閑葛藤。莫教老漢見捉來勘不相當搥折脚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct warning against gathering to talk idle vine-tangle, followed by threat of examination.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一大藏教閑葛藤，千七百則絆殺人。三玄本無安排，五位何來等級？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Appraisal of the canon as idle vine-tangle and the seventeen hundred cases as tripping people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 巨帙已載閑葛藤，何堪又送閑家具。開眼一看笑呵呵，猶有這箇可奈何，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse wordplay: a large volume of idle vine-tangle versus unwanted idle furnishings.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an at-ease person of the Way
AlternateTargets: an unoccupied person of the Way
an idle person of the Way
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" (閑道人). Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" (絕學無為閑道人). Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" (絕學), and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" (大寂滅海), "the ground of actual principle" (實際理地), and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" (大休). The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find (茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人). The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.
Senses.Note: The exact short form has 37 hits in 33 allowlisted texts. Its stable expansion is 'ended-study, doing-nothing-contrived, at-ease person of the Way.' Evidence includes explicit naming formulas, a list of synonyms, prose distinctions among kinds of study, and verse deployment. The ordinary reading 'idle person' alone misses the corpus-defined epithet.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人心利纔聞一言便乃絕學所以喚作絕學無為閑道人今時人只欲得多知多觧廣求文義
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Ancient Venerables preserves Huangbo's naming formula and contrasts the epithet with seeking much knowledge and explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謂之大寂滅海，謂之實際理地，謂之絕學無為閑道人，皆大休之異名也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianru gives three explicit names for great rest, including the full epithet.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此一念萬年、萬年一念，猶太虛空，不與萬象森羅為礙，豈不名絕學無為閑道人也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Guting applies the full epithet after describing one thought for ten thousand years and no obstruction by the array of appearances.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人。棒喝交馳成藥忌，了亡藥忌未天真。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Complete Lamp discourse contrasts a world of buddha-seekers with the rarity of the at-ease person of the Way.

Occurrences.Kwic: 習學既盡。謂之絕學無為閑道人。及至絕學。方始與道相近。直得過此二學。是謂真過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record distinguishes completed accumulated study, ended study, drawing near the Way, and passing beyond both kinds of study.

Senses.Explanation: An interrogative pronoun: 'who?' or, according to syntax, 'whom?' The records put it to several public uses. It asks a monk's identity inside the exchange 'what is buddha?' — 'who are you?' / 'so-and-so' / 'do you recognize so-and-so?' (汝是阿誰／某甲／汝識某甲否). It asks lineage in the stock interview formula 'whose song does the master sing; to whom does the house style succeed?' (師唱誰家曲，宗風嗣阿誰), agency in 'who can go?' (阿誰去得), authorship in 'who spoke this scripture?' (此經是阿誰說), and the beneficiary of activity in 'for whom are you busy every day?' (每日區區為阿誰). The Chan deviation lies in this concentration inside public identity, lineage, authorship, and accountability questions; the word itself remains the ordinary interrogative and does not name a special inward self.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 2,924 hits in 345 texts. Family comparison: 'who?' (誰) and 'which one?' (阿那箇) are interrogatives; 'that one' (那箇) and 'this one' (這箇) are demonstratives; 'who?' (阿誰) does not acquire a separate 'true self' sense merely because identity is sometimes its subject. Agent, author, beneficiary, and lineage predecessor are different answers to the same pronoun, not different referents encoded by the word.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是佛。師曰。汝是阿誰。曰。某甲。師曰。汝識某甲否。曰。分明箇。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public identity questioning follows 'what is buddha?': who are you, and do you recognize the conventional self-name supplied?

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：師唱誰家曲，宗風嗣阿誰？師云：窣堵那叱掌上擎。僧曰：恁麼則北塔嫡子，韶石兒孫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Stock lineage interview asking whose house style the master succeeds to; the follow-up names lineage descent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰。此經是阿誰說。僧抗聲曰。禪師相弄。豈不知是佛說耶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Authorship question: 'who spoke this scripture?' The lecturer answers that Buddha did.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師謂眾曰。我要一人。傳語西堂。阿誰去得。五峯曰。某甲去。師曰。汝作麼生傳語。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Agency question to the assembly: who can carry a message to Xitang? Wufeng volunteers and is questioned further.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雲巖問和尚每日區區為阿誰師曰有一人要巖曰囙甚麼不教伊自作師曰他無家活
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunyan asks for whom the master is busy every day; the exchange supplies 'there is one who needs it.'

Senses.Explanation: Ananda is deployed in the Chan record as the figure who questions the succession after the Buddha. He asks Kashyapa, “besides the gold-thread robe transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted?” Kashyapa calls his name; Ananda answers; Kashyapa says, “knock down the flagpole before the gate.” Later masters raise the exchange as a public case and add their own comments: one says that before the flagpole is down it pierces people's skulls and changes their eyes, then asks where old man Shakyamuni is seen after it falls. The robe question and flagpole response, rather than a general life story, are Ananda's primary Chan deployment. The records also place him in direct exchanges with the Buddha. In one repeatedly raised bowl case, the Buddha tells him to enter the city carrying the bowl; when Ananda asks for the procedure of the seven buddhas, the Buddha calls “Ananda,” Ananda answers, and the Buddha says, “carry the bowl and go.” At another seated assembly Ananda strikes the sounding block and asks the World-Honored One to speak the teaching. The transmission record later says that Ananda finished entrusting the eye-treasury of the teaching. Thus the name repeatedly occupies public questioning, assembly, and succession positions in cases later masters cite.
Senses.Note: Across the cited Chan records, Ananda recurs as the questioner in the robe-and-flagpole succession exchange and as the respondent to a direct name-call. The entry is limited to those recorded exchanges, teaching-seat actions, and transmission notices.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日問迦葉曰。師兄。世尊傳金襴袈裟外。別傳箇甚麼。迦葉召阿難。阿難應諾。迦葉曰。倒却門前剎竿著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The succession case records Ananda's robe question, Kashyapa's name-call, Ananda's answer, and the instruction to knock down the gate-front flagpole.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉阿難問迦葉：世尊傳金襴外，別傳何法？迦葉召阿難，阿難應諾。迦葉曰：倒却門前剎竿著。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master publicly raises the same robe-and-flagpole exchange as a case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 迦葉曰：倒却門前剎竿著。師曰：剎竿未倒，穿却諸人髑髏，換却諸人眼睛。剎竿倒後，向甚麼處見釋迦老子？參！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The later comment distinguishes the flagpole before and after its fall and asks where old man Shakyamuni is then seen.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉世尊一日勅阿難食時將至汝當入城持鉢阿難應諾世尊曰汝既持鉢須依過去七佛議式阿難便問如何是七佛儀式世尊召阿難阿難應諾世尊曰持鉢去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address raises the bowl case: Ananda asks about the procedure, answers when called, and is told to carry the bowl and go.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊一日陞座。默然而坐。阿難白椎曰。請世尊說法。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At the teaching seat, Ananda strikes the sounding block and asks the World-Honored One to speak the teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本來付有法付了言無法各各須自悟悟了無無法阿難付法眼藏竟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp narrative closes its transmission verse by saying that Ananda finished entrusting the eye-treasury of the teaching.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "go along with it." In the named Dasui case, a monk asks whether "this" is destroyed when the world is destroyed by the kalpa fire. Dasui answers, "destroyed." The monk asks, "then it goes along with it?" and Dasui answers, "go along with it." Later collections repeatedly set this answer beside Longji's contrary "not destroyed" and preserve it as the case's answer-line. Elsewhere the same ordinary phrase can mean following a person or thing; the fixed Chan deployment is its repeated use for Dasui's answer.
Senses.Note: 209 occurrences in 87 allowlisted texts. The master's name has two written forms, "Dasui" (大隋) and the homophonous "Dasui" (大隨); the answer varies between "go along with it" (隨他去) and "go along with it, go along with it" (隨他隨他去). These are transmission variants, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧遂問刼火洞然大千俱壞未審此箇性壞不壞師云壞進云恁麼則隨他去也師云隨他隨他去也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The early record gives the complete exchange and repeats the answer: "go along with it, go along with it."

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問大隋。劫火洞然大千俱壞。未審這箇壞不壞隋云。壞僧云。恁麼則隨他去也隋云。隨他去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record presents Dasui's exchange as case 29.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問大隨。劫火洞然大。千俱壞。未審這箇壞不壞隨云。壞僧云。恁麼則隨他去也隨云。隨他去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Book of Serenity transmits the same answer before placing it beside Longji's "not destroyed."

Senses.PreferredTarget: fixed phrase: following the waves, chasing the swells
Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “follow or go along with” (隨), “waves” (波), “chase or pursue” (逐), and “swells” (浪): "following the waves, chasing the swells." As a technical Chan term it names (隨波逐浪句), the third of the three phrases (三句) that (德山緣密) (Deshan Yuanming), an heir of (雲門文偃), states in his (上堂): (我有三句語示汝諸人)：(一句函葢乾坤)，(一句截斷眾流)，(一句隨波逐浪)。(作麼生辯)？ The three are handled as a fixed set (函蓋乾坤 · 截斷眾流 · 隨波逐浪) and recur as a stock test-question across the lamp records — (如何是隨波逐浪句)？ — answered with a turning phrase (隨；闊；春生夏長；船子下揚州). The texts pair (隨波逐浪) with (截斷眾流): on a raised (趙州) case a master says (一人隨波逐浪)，(一人截斷眾流), and an (上堂) handles the two phrases together: (看風使帆)，(正是隨波逐浪)。(截斷眾流)，(未免依前滲漏). The corpus assigns the phrase no gloss beyond this deployment, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The three-phrase formulation is (德山緣密)'s own (上堂); do not attribute it to (雲門文偃) himself — (緣密) is his heir and the corpus states the set in (緣密)'s section (in X81n1568 under the header 雲門偃禪師法嗣). The (上堂) is carried in six allowlist texts — five in (緣密)'s section (X68n1319, X80n1565, X81n1568, X81n1571, X85n1593), while X64n1260 (列祖提綱錄) carries it in the topical (五參提綱) anthology, attributed inline (德山密禪師上堂) (X85n1593 writes 函蓋乾坤, the others 函葢/圅葢). The (如何是隨波逐浪句) test-question is likewise witnessed across ≥2 independent texts. Cross-ref (截斷眾流), (函蓋乾坤). Sense 2 below is the plain idiom, distinct from this named phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 函葢乾坤，一句截斷眾流，一句隨波逐浪。作麼生辯？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈嚴統), mulu head (鼎州德山緣密圓明禪師) (roster: 德山緣密 / Deshan Yuanming). His own (上堂) stating the three phrases: (我有三句語示汝諸人)，(一句函葢乾坤)，(一句截斷眾流)，(一句隨波逐浪). Line opens with (一句) on the prior lb 0113c18; KWIC begins at ed=X 0113c19. Source writes (函葢) (variant of 函蓋).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是隨波逐浪句？師曰：隨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈嚴統), mulu head (明州瑞巖智才禪師) (not on roster). A monk asks the three-phrase test-question (如何是隨波逐浪句) and the section master answers "follow" (隨). Deployment as a stock test-question; the answer is the section master's, off-roster, so MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：一人隨波逐浪，一人截斷眾流。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈會元續略), mulu head (慶元府育王孤雲權禪師) (not on roster). A raised (趙州) case (…者如何？州曰：死) on which the section master gives the verdict (一人隨波逐浪)，(一人截斷眾流) — the corpus pairing (隨波逐浪) ↔ (截斷眾流). Raised case + commenting master off-roster, so MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 看風使帆，正是隨波逐浪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (五燈嚴統), mulu head (東京法雲寺法秀圓通禪師) (roster: 圓通法秀 / Yuantong Faxiu, Yunmen line — the reversed name order 法秀圓通 vs roster 圓通法秀 caused an earlier off-roster miss). His own (上堂) under his governing mulu handles the two named phrases together: (看風使帆)，(正是隨波逐浪)。(截斷眾流)，(未免依前滲漏) — the phrase-pair deployment, not the plain idiom. Attributed to (圓通法秀).

Senses.PreferredTarget: plain idiom: drift with the waves
AlternateTargets: following the waves, chasing the swells
Senses.Explanation: The plain idiom: to go along with the waves and chase the swells. The records speak it of persons: of (一切眾生) — (祇為心塵未脫)，(情量不除)，(見色聞聲)，(隨波逐浪)，(流轉三界) (a 上堂 in 禪宗正脉); as a rebuke — (終日隨波逐浪)、(妄生枝節者哉) (a 小參 in 續燈正統); and autobiographically — (明芳愚懦無知)，(自少隨波逐浪) (五燈全書). This ordinary sense is distinct from the named (隨波逐浪句) of sense 1, though both turn on the same image of moving with the water. The texts attach no gloss beyond the literal image, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attested as the plain idiom across independent lamp records (禪宗正脉 X85n1593, 續燈正統 X84n1583, 五燈全書 X82n1571). The (看風使帆)，(正是隨波逐浪) line (五燈嚴統) pairs the phrase with (截斷眾流) and is therefore treated under sense 1, not here.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'follow circumstances.' The expression occurs 1,829 times in 308 allowlisted texts. Its subject may be a person, conduct, an event, or a thing's functioning. Records pair it with eating and drinking, going on one's way, passing one's days in a boat, responding to people and things, and being free and unconfined. One paired description is 'follow circumstances, free and unconfined; respond to things and act' (隨緣放曠，應物施為). A biography records the saying, 'In all affairs, follow circumstances; this is a way of ease.' A recurrent exchange asks, 'What is following circumstances as the site of the Way?' (如何是隨緣即道場); Baizhang answers, 'Today the summer session begins' (今日結夏). Another text pairs following circumstances with not losing one's nature, describing change in response to circumstances while the subject is not lost.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide verbal sense, supported across biographies, recorded exchanges, and assembly addresses. Common paired shapes include 'follow circumstances and proceed of itself' in both word orders (27 hits each), 'follow circumstances in eating and drinking' (13), 'follow circumstances, free and unconfined' (107), and 'in all affairs follow circumstances' (10). The site-of-the-Way question receives the calendar answer 'Today the summer session begins' (今日結夏).

Senses.Explanation: Literally and throughout the sampled corpus, “wherever” or “in every place.” Its Chan value lies chiefly in the predicates whose scope it sets. Linji's record has the fixed line “act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine” (隨處作主，立處皆真). Yuanwu preserves the paired formula “act as host wherever you are; on meeting conditions, they are the source” (隨處作主，遇緣即宗). A teaching-seat address defines the work of a lineage teacher with “wherever he is, he raises the guiding principle; he answers questions according to the occasion” (隨處提綱，應機問答). Other records use the same distributive word in “named wherever [it appears]” (隨處立名), “arise right here and perish wherever” (當處出生，隨處滅盡), and “clear wherever [you are]” (隨處明了). These predicates are distinct; the location word is not. No departure from its ordinary distributive meaning was found, and none is manufactured.
Senses.Note: Keep this constituent distinct from the full fixed entry “act as host wherever you are” (隨處作主), while linking the two entries.

Senses.PreferredTarget: act as host wherever you are
AlternateTargets: make yourself host in every place
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'wherever the place, act as host.' The expression occurs 136 times in 85 allowed texts. Linji's record gives its best-known continuation twice: 'act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine' (隨處作主，立處皆真). The first occurrence continues, 'circumstances come and cannot turn you around' (境來回換不得); the second says that whatever comes is not to be received. Later records most often pair the phrase with 'on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (遇緣即宗). Yuanwu records variants including 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (隨處作主，遇緣即宗) and 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, immediately act' (隨處作主，遇緣即行). A later collection reverses the order—'the teaching has no fixed form: on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source; the Way does not travel in vain: act as host wherever you are' (法無定相，遇緣即宗；道不虗行，隨處作主)—and another places the phrase beside 'establish the source and set up the purport' (建宗立旨). The records deploy it as a direct imperative, a quoted Linji saying, and a predicate within assembly addresses.
Senses.Note: The graph 'host/master' (主) is translated as 'host' in the preferred target because Linji's surrounding record repeatedly distinguishes guest and host (賓主); 'master' is retained as an alternate graph-literal rendering. The unpunctuated full Linji continuation 'act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine' (隨處作主立處皆真) occurs twice in the Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies. The phrase later circulates across houses with the circumstance/source pairing and is therefore corpus-wide rather than Linji-specific.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “clouds and water”; in Chan community language, the compound names itinerant monks and visitors. It occurs 789 times in 238 allowlisted texts. Hongzhi directly tells an addressee, “Cloud-and-water is you; you are cloud-and-water,” immediately after describing a patch-robed monk taking a staff and circling the world. Records count cloud-and-water monks in the two halls, build hundreds of rooms to receive cloud-and-water itinerants, and name a cloud-and-water hall where visitors can take an assigned place. The expanded noun “cloud-and-water monk” occurs 17 times in 14 texts. These institutional and direct-address uses establish the collective without requiring an origin story for the wording.
Senses.Note: The technical collective can stand without an explicit word for monk, as shown by reception and release-day contexts. No formula equates it with a prescribed activity. The sole exact question asks for the 'meaning of cloud-and-water' and receives a verse-like answer rather than a lexical definition.

Senses.Explanation: The same graphs also retain the literal landscape sense, “clouds and water.” In a boatman song, the speaker says, “Roaming freely between heaven and earth amid clouds and water; looking back, green mountains are everywhere. Because this secondary sense is represented here by one curated text, it remains provisional.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the white ox in the open ground
AlternateTargets: the great white ox on open ground
the white ox out in the open
Senses.Explanation: The white ox standing out on the bare open ground (露地). In the records it appears in the ox-herding image beside “the water buffalo” (水牯牛): after the buffalo has been watched and reined back from the crops for years, 'it now turns into the white ox in the open ground' (如今變作箇露地白牛) — it stands naked in plain sight, needs no more herding, and can be let loose without wandering off (躶躶地放他不肯去). These passages call it “the white ox in the open” (露地白牛), say that it has changed after years of tending, and record that when released it does not go away. One corpus text glosses the image element by element: the (五冠山瑞雲寺和尚) chapter of (祖堂集) (B25n0144) has (所言露地白牛者)，(露地是所證之法故)，(即遮那是也)。(白牛是能證之人故)，(即是文殊是也), continuing (白牛運轉)，(不住此處故)，(即普賢是也) — 'the open ground is what is realized… the white ox is the person who realizes… the ox's moving on, not staying in this place…'. The image is drawn from the Lotus Sutra’s burning-house passage (the great white-ox cart the father gives out on the open ground; 白牛車: 99 hits in 68 allowlist texts), and Chan writers cite that pedigree explicitly ('華嚴論主深歎法華經中露地白牛'). Its classic Chan locus is the Guiyang ox-herding line credited to Changqing Da'an at Guishan's assembly — the very 'watch one water-buffalo... now it becomes the white ox in the open' line that floats between Da'an and Nanquan in the sources (flagged in the 水牯牛 pilot). It is also a stock test-question in its own right — (如何是露地白牛) 'What is the white ox in the open?' occurs 59 times in 30 allowlist texts, drawing answers as varied as Deshan's lowing (吽)！(吽)！ 'Moo! Moo!', the herding-shout (叱叱) (given by both 溈山 and 投子 in C078n1720), (針劄不入) 'a needle can't prick in' (D48n8939), (破盆子) 'a broken basin' and (月下不用色) (both D48n8939). In (傳燈玉英集) (B14n0082, 𣵠州杏山鑒洪禪師 section) Linji himself puts the question — (臨濟問如何是露地白牛師曰吽濟曰啞却杏山口師曰老兄作麼生濟曰遮畜生) 'Linji asked: what is the white ox in the open? The master [Xingshan] said: Moo. Linji said: mute Xingshan's mouth! The master said: elder brother, how then? Linji said: this beast!' — so the record carries the lowing answer under (杏山鑒洪) questioned by Linji (B14n0082) and, separately, under (德山鑑禪師) questioned by a monk (X67n1299); the two attributions should not be merged. Finally it is the subject of Beichan Zhixian's much-quoted year-end talk, 'cooking the white ox in the open to see out the year' (烹露地白牛分歲) — the cooking phrase (烹露地白牛) alone recurs 83 times across 64 allowlist texts. A shortened (露地牛) also circulates (53 hits, 43 texts), notably in the verse line (玉角霜毛露地牛) 'jade horns, frost-white coat — the ox in the open', headed (洞山聰頌云) in X67n1299.
Senses.Note: Cross-reference “water buffalo” (水牯牛; entry t_36aa29eb1287): the texts place “the white ox in the open” (露地白牛) after the years of watching and reining in the buffalo. 341 raw occurrences across 153 allowlist texts. Grep-verified deployment split (Zen allowlist): test-question (如何是露地白牛) 79 hits / 34 texts; year-end cooking phrase (烹露地白牛) 83 / 64; short form (露地牛) 49 / 40 (verse line 玉角霜毛露地牛 4 / 3); Lotus cart (白牛車) 93 / 65 (大白牛車 6 / 6). Whose image? No single owner — Lotus-Sutra-derived, with the Guiyang ox-herding line (Da'an, floating to Nanquan) as its Chan locus classicus; strongly multi-source.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, an exposed or bare (露) pillar (柱): "the exposed pillar." It occurs 2,729 times in 325 allowlisted texts. In Chan halls it is not merely architecture: masters address it, strike it, point questioners to it, and pair it with the lantern. Danxia greets a pillar with joined palms as "World-Honored One"; when a monk says, "Master, that is an exposed pillar," Danxia answers with a verse about crying blood to no use. Shitou answers "what is the meaning of coming from the west?" with "ask the exposed pillar" (問取露柱); when the questioner cannot understand, Shitou says he understands even less. Asked to whom his teaching will be entrusted after his death, one master answers, "exposed pillar, fire stove" and reverses the pair after the follow-up. The pillar is also made an impossible animate figure: "like an exposed pillar bearing a child" (如露柱懷胎), a phrase found 87 times in 67 texts. Another verse says oxhide is stretched over the pillar, the pillar cries out, ordinary ears do not hear it, and the sages laugh. The Zen deviation is therefore concrete and institutional: a fixed hall support becomes a named interlocutor, recipient, speaker, and pregnant figure in encounters, commonly partnered with lantern or stove. These are the corpus's recorded actions; the entry adds no symbolic meaning.
Senses.Note: The common pair "lantern and exposed pillar" (燈籠露柱) occurs 288 times in 147 texts, while the reversed order "exposed pillar and lantern" (露柱燈籠) occurs 210 times in 121. Those pairings support the hall-fixture deployment but remain separate phrases.
