Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff case twenty-seven raises Yunmen's exchange before beginning its commentary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 審和尚以何顯道？師曰：山僧祇似鐵。乃曰：極目青天無片雲，萬象森羅全體露。若也擬議更商量，特地翻成箇露布。久立，歸堂喫茶去。上堂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse joins the reverse-order array of the ten thousand forms to 'the whole body exposed.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 聞舉少林面壁，頓悟。述二偈以呈，龍許之。住後，上堂，舉：體露堂堂，十方無󳬩礙。千聖不能傳，萬靈成頂戴。擬欲共商量，開口百
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp biography preserves a verse beginning 'fully exposed, imposing and evident.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 」舉火。「花似錦，水如藍。無生國，儘安閒。即今葉落歸根，如何是體露金風句？」遂下火曰：「掣斷黃金鎖，推倒須彌山。」蒲菴師太封龕。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: At a cremation fire, the officiant asks what the body-exposed-in-autumn-wind saying is and answers while lowering the flame.

AlternateTargets: stand at the top of the high peak
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "stand atop the high, high peak." The phrase occurs 55 times in 38 allowlisted texts. It is overwhelmingly paired with "walk on the floor of the deepest sea" (深深海底行). In a recorded biography, Zhaojue asks a student, "stand atop the highest peak; walk on the floor of the deepest sea—how do you understand it?" The student awakens at the words and says, "my heels are nailed fast" (釘殺脚跟也); Zhaojue then raises the whisk and asks another question. The paired line also serves as a direct answer in public interview and as an instruction to an assembly: "at this point it is just right to stand atop the highest peak and walk on the floor of the deepest sea" (到恁麼地，正好高高峰頂立，深深海底行). Another address distributes the pair across dates: before the twenty-fifth, the ocean-floor line; after it, the summit line; on the twenty-fifth, all ten directions cut off. Zen turns impossible vertical extremes into a fixed paired demand, question, answer, and biographical exchange; the corpus does not require this entry to decode the image further.
Senses.Note: The summit half is retained as its own headword because it recurs independently, but its dominant corpus relation is the sea-floor half. Question, answer, instruction, and date-pairing all use the same spatial action; they do not warrant multiple senses. The biography names a student's awakening at the question but does not define the phrase as awakening itself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 覺一日問師：高高峰頂立，深深海底行。汝作麼生會？師于言下頓悟曰：釘殺脚跟也。覺拈起拂子曰：這箇又作麼生？師一笑而出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaojue asks how the student understands the paired line; the biography records awakening at the words, an answer about nailed heels, and a follow-up with the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸仁者！到恁麼地，正好高高峰頂立，深深海底行，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An assembly is told that at this point it is just right to stand atop the highest peak and walk on the deepest sea floor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「高高峰頂立，深深海底行。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The complete paired line is delivered as an answer in a public exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二十五日已前，虛空包不住，深深海底行；二十五日已後，大地載不起，高高峰頂立；正當二十五日，十方俱坐斷，縱橫得自由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address assigns the sea-floor half before the twenty-fifth, the summit half after it, and a third line to the day itself.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, flourishing or luxuriant (鬱鬱) yellow flowers (黃花): "flourishing yellow flowers." The phrase occurs 57 times in 41 allowlisted texts. Its distinctively Chan deployment is the frequently quoted proposition, "the green bamboo is entirely the body of the teaching; the flourishing yellow flowers are nothing other than wisdom" (青青翠竹，盡是法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若). The fuller exact yellow-flower formula occurs 18 times in 17 texts, while "green bamboo" (青青翠竹) occurs 116 times in 68. The records preserve disagreement rather than a single unopposed gloss. A question to National Teacher Huizhong says that some call the proposition an erroneous saying while others trust it as inconceivable; his recorded answer accepts it by placing bamboo and flowers within the range of the teaching body and wisdom. The same transmitted passage then has a Huayan lecturer ask Dazhu Huihai why he does not permit the formula; Dazhu distinguishes appearing in response to bamboo and flowers from wisdom or the teaching body being located in those objects. Later, Shending Yikui rebukes people who hear the formula, hold rigidly to it, and never shift at all, calling a fitting phrase "a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand ages" (一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛). In another exchange he asks how wisdom is understood when the yellow flowers are right here, and tells the respondent that he has let the yellow flowers down. Chan thus bends a scene of colored plants into a portable, disputed proposition and a live examination question; this entry reports the acceptance, distinction, and correction recorded by the texts without deciding among them.
Senses.Note: The fixed pair with green bamboo is lexicographically central. Other hits use the flowers literally in autumn poems; those ordinary deployments do not establish an additional Chan sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問忠國師：『青青翠竹，盡是法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若。有人不許，云是邪說；亦有信者，云不思議。不知若為？』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jinming Jin quotes a question to National Teacher Huizhong that explicitly records opposed assessments of the bamboo-and-yellow-flower proposition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪師何故不許青青翠竹盡是法身，鬱鬱黃花無非般若？』珠云：『法身無象，應翠竹以成形；般若無知，對黃花而顯相。非彼黃花翠竹而有般若法身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The quoted Dazhu Huihai exchange distinguishes manifestation in response to flowers and bamboo from locating wisdom or the teaching body in those objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 見說青青翠竹無非法身、鬱鬱黃花無非般若，一據據定，更不移易絲毫。殊不知，一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending Yikui criticizes rigid adherence to the stock line and calls a fitting phrase a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand ages.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問眾：「鬱鬱黃花無非般若花，在此作麼生會般若？」品維那云：「從來不眼花。」師云：「辜負黃花也。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending turns the formula into a question with the flowers present and rejects the officer's reply as letting the flowers down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。青青翠竹。盡是真如。鬱鬱黃花。無非般若。如何是般若。師曰。黃泉無老少。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Jiuxian Yuxian's section, the formula supplies the premise for 'what is wisdom?' and the master answers, 'at the Yellow Springs there is neither old nor young.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'inside a ghost cave.' The phrase occurs 309 times in 122 allowed texts. The corpus repeatedly extends it as 'making a living inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏作活計, 164 occurrences), 'sitting inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏坐, 17), and 'inside a ghost cave beneath the black mountain' (黑山下鬼窟裏, 15). Dahui warns, 'take special care not to reckon inside a ghost cave' (切忌向鬼窟裏卜度), and elsewhere describes remaining motionless inside a ghost cave below the black mountain. Yuanwu writes that activity based on conscious calculation is 'making a living inside a ghost cave' and repeats the wording after 'as soon as you calculate' (纔作計較). Yunmen's record sets up a conditional choice: if the monk cannot answer, he is 'sitting inside a ghost cave.' These are the corpus's own spatial and verbal extensions of the image; the texts do not supply a separate object-definition for the cave.
Senses.Note: No required direct-definition formula was found. The headword is productive with verbs of reckoning, calculating, sitting, entering, emerging, and making a living. The common longer form adds 'below the black mountain.' The article preserves that observable usage without converting the phrase into a category not stated by the records.

Occurrences.Kwic: 切忌向鬼窟裏卜度。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own record, an assembly comment following the raised Luzhu and Nanquan encounter: 'take special care not to reckon inside a ghost cave.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 便向燃燈佛肚裏座。黑山下鬼窟裏不動坐得骨臀生胝
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own record. He describes sitting motionless 'inside a ghost cave below the black mountain' until the buttocks become callused; the concrete wording is preserved as written.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不是心機意識思量鬼窟裏作活計。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record commentary says it is not 'making a living inside a ghost cave' through conscious calculation. The phrase is part of Yuanwu's prose comment, not a speaker turn in the raised case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 纔作計較。便是黑山鬼窟裏作活計。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record commentary: 'as soon as you calculate, it is making a living inside a ghost cave on the black mountain.' This independently attests both the black-mountain variant and the stock verbal extension.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若道不得又在鬼窟裏坐作麼生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies Record, Yunmen's discourse record: 'if you cannot say it, again you sit inside a ghost cave—what then?' The section head explicitly identifies Yunmen's record.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “bird path,” a recurrent Chan expression posed in questions and answers. One record explicitly introduces a three-item set: “From now on, permit him to study three roads, namely the dark road, the bird path, and extending the hands.” Dongshan is asked about his ordinary instruction to travel the bird path and answers, “not meeting a single person”; when asked how to travel it, he says that one’s footing must have no private interest. Yet when asked for the original face, he answers, “not traveling the bird path.” Other records answer with setting foot without touching dust or say that the bird path has never lodged. The entry records this explicit list, the questions, and the differing answers without recasting the phrase as a prescribed procedure or abstract symbol.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 627 matches in 168 files. Twenty-three matches in twenty-one files ask, 'What is the bird path?' Forms translated as 'travel the bird path' occur 136 times in fifty-one files; 'the bird path has never lodged' occurs four times in four files, while 'the bird path is difficult to pass through' occurs eighteen times in sixteen. The direct correction 'not traveling the bird path' is essential to the sense inventory and prevents treating Dongshan's earlier answer as a standalone prescription.

Occurrences.Kwic: 和尚尋常教人行鳥道，未審如何是鳥道？山曰：不逢一人。曰：如何行？山曰：直須足下無私。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Dongshan, 'You ordinarily teach people to travel the bird path; what is the bird path?' Dongshan answers, 'Not meeting a single person.' Asked how to travel it, he answers, 'Your footing must have no private interest.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰：如何是本來面目？山曰：不行鳥道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks Dongshan, 'What is the original face?' Dongshan answers, 'Not traveling the bird path.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 行盡千山路。玄機事若何。師曰。鳥道不曾棲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A question says, 'Having traveled all the roads through a thousand mountains, what about the matter of the dark pivot?' The teacher answers, 'The bird path has never lodged.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 今時向去。許伊三路學。所謂玄路鳥道展手。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Fenyang Wude explicitly introduces the list: “From now on, permit him to study three roads, namely the dark road, the bird path, and extending the hands.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是鳥道接人？師云：下足不沾塵。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks, 'How does the bird path receive people?' The teacher answers, 'Setting foot without touching dust.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the king (王) of geese (鵝). In the Chan corpus this bird is overwhelmingly the goose king that selects milk from water. One instruction gives the image directly: 'there is milk in water; people do not see it; the goose king selects it.' Another says that when water and milk are mixed, the goose king eats the milk. Masters then use the fixed line 'the goose king selects the milk, naturally not of the duck kind' as an appraisal after cases and answers. In a hall exchange a monk asks the purport of that line and the master answers, 'south of the river there is; north of the river there is not,' without explaining the bird further. Another address pairs capacities: it takes a goose king to select milk and a lion to bite. A verse also reverses the stock contrast: under one strike, 'the goose king becomes a duck; the soft-shelled turtle becomes a tortoise.' The Zen deviation is this legendary bird's repeated use—and deliberate reversal—as a teaching-seat appraisal of selection and discrimination; the entry does not add a hidden object beyond the milk, water, goose, and duck named by the records.
Senses.Note: Exact count: 129 hits in 79 allowlisted texts. The goose-king-selects-milk formula (鵝王擇乳) has 69 hits in 48 texts; not-of-the-duck-kind (素非鴨類) has 55 in 36. One legendary-bird sense. Family checked against selecting milk (擇乳), water and milk (水乳), duck kind (鴨類), choosing the teaching (擇法), and possessing the eye (具眼).

Occurrences.Kwic: 水中有乳，人莫之見，在鵝王擇之矣。如爾之見地，阿誰知之？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct description: milk is in water unseen by people, and the goose king selects it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 秖如今有一箇佛魔同體不分，如水乳合鵝王喫乳，如明眼道流魔佛俱打。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Concrete mixed-water-and-milk form: the goose king eats the milk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂云。鵝王擇乳。素非鴨類。問鵝王擇乳。素非鴨類。意旨如何。師云。江南有江北無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Formal hall question asks the formula's purport and preserves the master's answer without a gloss.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須是鵝王，始能擇乳；苟非獅子，爭解咬人？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Text-drawn capacity pair: goose selecting milk and lion biting.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久云。鵝王擇乳。素非鴨類。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The stock formula delivered after a long pause as appraisal in a hall address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 七佛之師下一槌鵝王成鴨鱉成龜滿筵龍象齊傾耳咲殺靈山老古錐
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse inversion of the stock contrast: under one strike the goose king becomes a duck and the soft-shelled turtle a tortoise.

Senses.Explanation: Literally (麻) (hemp) + (三斤) (three catties, a weight): 'three catties of hemp.' It is Dongshan Shouchu's (洞山守初, 910–990) answer to the stock question (如何是佛) 'what is Buddha' — (五燈會元), under the head (襄州洞山守初宗慧禪師): (問)。(如何是佛)。(師曰)。(麻三斤). The question-and-answer form recurs across the record (如何是佛 answered by 麻三斤: 31× in 25 allowlist files; 麻三斤 in all positions: 490× in 174 files), and the Blue Cliff Record's own commentary lists it among the (答佛話), the recorded answers to the Buddha-question: (古人有多少答佛話)。(或云)。(殿裏底)。(或云)。(三十二相)。(或云)。(杖林山下竹筋鞭)。(及至洞山)。(却道麻三斤) (T48n2003). The record pairs it with Yunmen's (乾屎橛) ('dried shit-stick') — B25n0145: (惟雲門乾屎橛)。(洞山麻三斤)。(却較些子) — and the same text groups it with the cases it describes as (略無義路): (如庭前栢樹子麻三斤乾屎橛之類)。(略無義路與人穿鑿) ('the likes of the cypress in the courtyard, three catties of hemp, the dry shit-stick — with hardly any reasoning-path for people to bore into'). It circulates as a fixed case: Wumenguan Case 18 (洞山三斤, verse 突出麻三斤), Blue Cliff Record Case 12, and countless (拈古)/(頌古) verses; masters and monks probe it as an established saying under examination (X80n1565: 洞山麻三斤。意旨如何 — the probe form 麻三斤 + 意旨如何 appears in 11 allowlist files), and the probes draw their own recorded answers: (說破不值錢) (J29nB244, the master posing it to a monk; the same answer master-to-master in J40nB483), (秤頭八兩)，(秤尾半斤) (J33nB280), (八十婆婆不粧梳) (X78n1553), (智門)'s (花簇簇錦簇簇) (raised in T48n2003). The Blue Cliff Record also records the readings circulating in its day — (人多作話會道)。(洞山是時在庫下)。(秤麻) (he was weighing hemp in the storehouse when asked); (有底道)。(洞山問東答西); (有底道)。(爾是佛)。(更去問佛)。(所以洞山遶路答之) — and of the reading (只這麻三斤便是佛) it says (且得沒交涉) ('no connection whatsoever'). The texts record the answer and the probes on it without assigning the phrase a gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attribution trap: in later citations plain (洞山) here = Dongshan Shouchu (守初) (910–990), the Yunmen-line master who gave this answer, NOT the Caodong founder Dongshan Liangjie (良价) (807–869). The texts disambiguate him as (洞山初) / (洞山初和尚) / (襄州洞山守初宗慧禪師). Orthographic variant: (麻三觔) (觔 = 斤) is the same word and appears 107× in 46 allowlist files; it will not substring-match this head term (麻三斤). Collocations (allowlist, grep-verified): (洞山麻三斤) 76× in 54 files; the idiom (貼秤麻)(三斤) 12× in 10 files (e.g. C077n1710: 賤賣擔板漢貼秤麻三斤). All occurrences except the (五燈會元) biographical one are raised/quoted cases (舉…, 因僧問…, or list-of-answers), so their MasterName is null per the governing section head; only the (五燈會元) head (襄州洞山守初宗慧禪師) attributes the answer to Dongshan Shouchu himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是佛。師曰。麻三斤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The origin. Sits in Dongshan Shouchu's own biography in (五燈會元) (governing head 襄州洞山守初宗慧禪師); (師) = Dongshan Shouchu answering.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問洞山。如何是佛。洞山云。麻三斤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Earliest transmission-record witness (景德傳燈錄, ~1004). Raised inside the entry of (雙泉師寬) (Shuangquan Shikuan, 隋州雙泉山師寬明教大師, a 法嗣 of Yunmen), who comments on it (師聞之乃曰…); a quoted case (僧問洞山), so MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 突出麻三斤言親意更親
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen Huikai's capping verse to Wumenguan Case 18 (洞山三斤). A raised case + verse comment; MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 及至洞山。却道麻三斤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin's pointer in Blue Cliff Record Case 12, listing (麻三斤) among the stock answers to 'what is Buddha' (殿裏底 / 三十二相 / 杖林山下竹筋鞭 …). Raised case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 惟雲門乾屎橛。洞山麻三斤。却較些子。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Singles out (惟…却較些子) Yunmen's (乾屎橛) and Dongshan's (麻三斤) together; elsewhere the same text groups them among cases (略無義路與人穿鑿) (hardly any reasoning-path to bore into). General discussion listing cases; MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山麻三斤。意旨如何。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk (under the head 自巖上座) probes the meaning of the established saying — evidence that (麻三斤) had become a fixed case people question.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a black lacquer bucket.' The compound occurs 105 times in 63 allowlisted Chinese Chan texts. The records call for 'breaking the black lacquer bucket' (打破黑漆桶, seven occurrences), speak of being 'inside the black lacquer bucket' (黑漆桶裏, 16), and mention its bottom (黑漆桶底, ten). Rujing twice says, 'break the black lacquer bucket; the ten directions are open and empty' (打破黑漆桶。十方空豁豁). Tui'an Xiu calls people from 'this land and India' 'one gang of black lacquer buckets' (一隊黑漆桶). In another recorded exchange, a monk asks, 'What is the face before one's parents were born?' (如何是父母未生前面目), and Chuiwan Guangzhen answers, 'a black lacquer bucket' (黑漆桶). Wumen Huikai's verse says, 'beside the black lacquer bucket, the hoop breaks; within the peaceful country, a free person' (黑漆桶邊篐子斷，太平國內自由人). A letter records a student's self-comparison: 'with respect to this matter, I am just like a black lacquer bucket' (某甲於此事，如黑漆桶一樣). Zhongfeng gives the bucket an action: 'the black lacquer bucket leaps toward empty space' (黑漆桶望空𨁝跳). These attest an object-name used as an answer, a label for people, a self-comparison, and an image whose hoop, bottom, or whole body may break. The entry retains each text's stated continuation without replacing the bucket with an imported mental-state category.
Senses.Note: No required direct-definition formula was found. The texts themselves supply the bucket's morphology—bottom and hoop—and its verbs—enter, break, overturn, and leap. The entry preserves those concrete relations and the attested applications 'one gang of black lacquer buckets' (一隊黑漆桶) and 'like a black lacquer bucket' (如黑漆桶一樣), without assigning one unstated referent to every occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打破黑漆桶。十方空豁豁。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Rujing's own Ruiyan Monastery record: 'break the black lacquer bucket; the ten directions are open and empty.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 此土與西天，一隊黑漆桶，誑惑世間人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Orthodox Lamp, explicit Jianfu Tui'an Xiu section: 'this land and India, one gang of black lacquer buckets, deceive people in the world.' The master lacks an exact roster link, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是父母未生前面目？師曰：黑漆桶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Orthodox Lamp, Chuiwan Guangzhen section. The master answers the question about the face before one's parents were born with 'black lacquer bucket.' No exact roster link is available.

Occurrences.Kwic: 黑漆桶邊篐子斷，太平國內自由人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continuation of the Orthodox Lamp, explicit Wumen Huikai section. The verse states that the hoop beside the black lacquer bucket breaks and follows it with a free person in a peaceful country.

Occurrences.Kwic: 某甲於此事，如黑漆桶一樣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Lushan Tianran's record, reply to Yuan Cheng. The letter quotes the student's report: 'with respect to this matter, I am just like a black lacquer bucket.' Because the words belong to the correspondent, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 黑漆桶望空𨁝跳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's general address: 'the black lacquer bucket leaps toward empty space.' This gives the noun an independently attested action without explaining it away.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "silent" or "wordless" (默) and "illumination" or "illuminate" (照): "silent illumination," attested 113 times in 61 allowlisted texts. The corpus does not give it one uniformly approved category. Hongzhi says, "one who knows the sound discerns; one of silent illumination is numinous" (知音者鑑，默照者神), and elsewhere writes "at the place of silently illuminating, the sky is clear in autumn" (默默照處天宇澄秋). Dahui uses the same compound critically. He calls certain recent people in the monasteries "those called silent illumination" (謂之默照者), says "although silent illumination is not permitted, everyone must face the wall" (雖然不許默照，須要人人面壁), and lamp witnesses report his phrase "followers of silent illumination sit year after year in a ghost cave" (默照之徒，鬼窟長年打坐). A later Sanfeng record supplies a direct naming formula and rejects what it names: "if while sitting one illuminates something bright and numinous and takes it as oneself, this is called silent-illumination Chan" (若坐中照得昭昭靈靈為自己者，謂之默照禪), followed immediately by the author's adverse classification. Thus the entry preserves Hongzhi's affirmative compound, Dahui's explicit opposition, and the later critical definition as a contested Chinese term.
Senses.Note: Corpus collocations: "silent-illumination Chan" (默照禪), 5; "followers of silent illumination" (默照之徒), 12; "silent illumination is not permitted" (不許默照), 2; "withered Chan and silent illumination" (枯禪默照), 6; "oppose silent illumination" (排默照), 14; "at the place of silently illuminating" (默默照處), 1. These counts show both self-description and sustained criticism in the Chinese record.

Occurrences.Kwic: 知音者鑑。默照者神。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's formal address: "one who knows the sound discerns; one of silent illumination is numinous."

Occurrences.Kwic: 近日叢林無鼻孔輩。謂之默照者。是也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's reply to Professor Yan: "the recent noseless lot in the monasteries—these are those called silent illumination." This is overt criticism.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然不許默照。須要人人面壁。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's formal address: "although silent illumination is not permitted, everyone must face the wall."

Occurrences.Kwic: 致令默照之徒，鬼窟長年打坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's section of the Orthodox Continuation of the Lamps: "causing followers of silent illumination to sit year after year in a ghost cave."

Occurrences.Kwic: 若坐中照得昭昭靈靈為自己者，謂之默照禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct naming formula in the Sanfeng record: "if while sitting one illuminates something bright and numinous and takes it as oneself, this is called silent-illumination Chan." The author immediately rejects the named category; no roster link is set.

Senses.Explanation: (鼻) nose + (孔) hole: "the nostrils." In the corpus the word is deployed overwhelmingly as a person's handle/spot — the place by which one is taken hold of, led, possessed, or lost, and by which one holds one's own ground. Attested collocations (grep counts, allowlist): it is pierced and led like an ox — (穿卻鼻孔) / (穿鼻孔) (29), "pull the nostrils around," (拽轉鼻孔 4), e.g. "already had the nostrils pierced by the whisk" (已被拂子穿卻鼻孔) and "had his nostrils casually pulled around by that layman" (被箇俗漢等閑拽轉鼻孔); it is placed in another's control — "the nostrils are in someone else's hands," (鼻孔在別人手裏 9), (殊不知鼻孔在別人手裏); it is lost — (失卻鼻孔) (11), and asked after as a fault, "why have you lost your nostrils these days?" (你日來因甚失卻鼻孔); it is groped for and found — (摸著鼻孔) (82), (摸著舊時鼻孔)，(依前只在面皮上便見); and it is held up in independence — (鼻孔遼天) (287) / (鼻孔撩天) (208) ("nostrils to the sky"), (人人鼻孔遼天)，(各各壁立千仞). The texts draw the contrast between (鼻孔在別人手裏) (a nose held by another) and (鼻孔遼天)／(撩天) (a nose held to the sky). They also say that a speaker seeks to "breathe through the same nostrils as the old ones" (與古人同一鼻孔出氣), making the same body opening the shared outlet of a voice. The word carries no gloss in the texts beyond the body-part and its use as this handle or outlet, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide idiom (6246 occ / 386 texts). All curated occurrences are stock deployments of the idiom, not a named master's coinage, so MasterName is null. The literal graphs mean the nostrils; the recurring collocations (穿/拽/失卻/摸著/遼天) are the attested pattern — pierced/led like an ox, held by another, lost, groped for, or held to the sky. Not to be confused with the separate compound-heads (鼻孔遼天) / (鼻孔撩天) (their own idioms).

Occurrences.Kwic: 殊不知鼻孔在別人手裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄) (Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record); prose commentary — the nostrils held in another's hands as the image of being controlled. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已被拂子穿卻鼻孔
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (朝宗禪師語錄); the nostrils pierced by the raised whisk (拂子) — the ox-lead image applied to an interlocutor. Span crosses lb 0254b07→0254b08. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 被箇俗漢等閑拽轉鼻孔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大慧普覺禪師語錄) (Dahui's record; passage in the 塔銘 section) — the nostrils pulled around (拽轉) by another. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人鼻孔遼天，各各壁立千仞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (列祖提綱錄); the contrasting pole — nostrils held to the sky (遼天), everyone standing on his own thousand-fathom wall. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 摸著舊時鼻孔，依前只在面皮上便見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雪巖祖欽禪師語錄); groping for and finding one's own old nostrils (摸著舊時鼻孔). Span crosses lb 0633c05→0633c06. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你日來因甚失卻鼻孔？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雨山和尚語錄); a master's test-question treating loss of the nostrils (失卻鼻孔) as a fault, answered "pierced yours, master" (穿卻和尚的). Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰我鼻孔被大師𢬟得痛不徹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Venerables Record; an attendant says, 'My nostrils were pinched by the great master so painfully it has not gone through.' This is the literal physical body-part anchor against which the corpus's handle idioms were re-tested.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧如此批判，要與古人同一鼻孔出氣。且道諸人還甘麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xingkong Zhen's record; 'this mountain monk judges it this way in order to breathe through the same nostrils as the old ones.' The shared-breath idiom extends the same bodily image to speaking in concert.
